column5: Permissibility for the institution to receive an amount (seriousness margin) from the party who pledges to hire its services is based on need and interest.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the seriousness margin is permitted on the basis of need and interest.

column5: The following is required in the Waqf asset:
column6: It should be a Shari'a-wise appraisable asset (māl mutaqawwim), and it should be known or to be known.
column7: The Waqif should own the Waqf asset in full ownership, or it should be appurtenant to an asset owned by the Waqif, e.g., yet-to-be-declared dividends on shares held by him.
column8: It should be real estate or subordinate (tābiʿ) to real estate.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per 2/4/5/1, the asset must be appraisable and known, and owned by the Waqif or appurtenant to his asset; movables, cash etc. are also permitted.

column5: A person whose debts exceed his assets, but who has not been declared insolvent:
column6: Is obliged to apply to the court for a declaration of his own insolvency.
column7: Is free to dispose of his assets as he wishes, since the restrictions apply only after the judicial declaration of insolvency.
column8: Has a moral obligation in Shari'ah to refrain from any action that may harm the creditors.
column9: Is legally barred from all dispositions of his property, even without a court ruling.
column11: Per 3/1, he has a moral obligation to refrain from harming the creditors even if not declared insolvent; only the court can declare insolvency (4/5).

column5: A fitting example of selling a debt for another debt that may be ignored when it comes in the context of a subsidiary contract is:
column6: Selling a Salam commodity before taking possession of it.
column7: Exchanging a debt owed by one party for a debt owed by another party in an independent contract.
column8: Purchasing (on debt) the shares of an indebted company.
column9: Rescheduling a Murabahah debt against an increase in its amount.
column11: Per 5/2/4, buying on debt the shares of an indebted company is the cited example of a debt-for-debt sale overlooked as subsidiary.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: An IFI agreed to sell to a customer one car out of a number of cars in its showroom, without specifying which car is sold and without giving the customer the option of specification. The price and the general type of the cars were agreed. The ruling on this sale is:
column6: It is null and void, because it is a sale of a non-owned commodity.
column7: It is null and void, because of Gharar resulting from lack of knowledge of the sold commodity in particular (non-specification of the commodity).
column8: It is valid, because the type of the cars and the price are known, and Gharar in the specification of the car does not affect the contract.
column9: It is valid, because the Gharar involved is minor Gharar that a contract could hardly avoid, and is not sufficient to generate dispute.
column11: Per 5/2/1/3, sale of a non-specified car from a number of cars in a showroom, without the option of specification, nullifies the contract.

column5: According to the Maliki Fuqaha, application of the principle of Sadd al-Zara`i' should be based on two requirements:
column6: The Zari'ah should have been used at least once by the parties, and their intention should be declared in the contract, with the court's approval of the arrangement before it is implemented.
column7: The Zari'ah should be stipulated in the contract, and the court should declare it prohibited.
column8: There should be a need or lawful interest for using the Zari'ah, and the parties should be Muslims.
column9: Resort to the Zari'ah should be very frequent and excessive in view of normal practice, and there should be a strong accusation that rules out any good intention behind using it.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Malikis require very frequent resort to the Zari'ah and a strong accusation ruling out good intention.

column5: After the conclusion of an Istisna'a contract, the manufacturer and the ultimate purchaser may agree on amending the specifications or introducing additional requirements:
column6: Without any change in the price, since the contract is binding and its terms cannot be altered after its conclusion.
column7: On condition that the price is adjusted accordingly and a reasonable period for executing the new requirements is granted.
column8: Only if the ultimate purchaser imposes them, without the need for the manufacturer's consent, provided he adjusts the price.
column9: Only before the commencement of the work, and not once the manufacturer has started production of the subject-matter.
column11: Per 4/1/1, amendments are allowed by agreement with a price adjustment and a reasonable period; per 4/1/2 the manufacturer's consent is required.

column5: The Nisab for gold regardless of its form is (……….) of pure gold or its equivalent in currency, and for silver it is (……….) of pure silver.
column6: 595 grams .... 85 grams
column7: 85 grams .... 595 grams
column8: 85 grams .... 653 grams
column9: 653 grams .... 595 grams
column11: Per 3/2/2, the Nisab is 85 grams of pure gold and 595 grams of pure silver; 653 kg is the Nisab of agricultural produce (5/4/1).

column5: Transfer of the ownership in the leased property in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek cannot be made by:
column6: A promise to sell for a token consideration, evidenced in a document separate from the Ijarah contract.
column7: A promise to give it as a gift, evidenced in a document separate from the Ijarah contract.
column8: Executing, along with the Ijarah, a sale contract that will become effective on a future date.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/7, a sale contract executed with the Ijarah to take effect on a future date cannot transfer ownership.

column5: Amounts retained from contracts (guarantee amounts held by the clients to ensure that the Institution will honor its commitments):
column6: If the Institution has not been enabled to invest them it should not pay Zakah on them; however, on receipt of the amounts it has to pay Zakah on them for only one year.
column7: The Institution should pay Zakah on them annually, even if it has not been enabled to invest them.
column8: On receipt of the amounts, the Institution has to pay Zakah on them for the whole past period, even if it has not been enabled to invest them.
column9: The Institution should never pay Zakah on them.
column11: Per 5/3/4/4, if the Institution could not invest such retentions, no Zakah is due while held; on receipt it pays Zakah for one year only.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Possession (Qabd) does not cover:
column6: Possession in usurpation (Ghasb) and the like.
column7: The nature of possession with respect to liability for compensation or otherwise.
column8: Possession in set-offs.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 1, the standard excludes acts other than contracts (e.g. Ghasb), the nature of possession regarding liability, and possession in set-offs.

column5: The arbitration decision:
column6: Should not necessarily meet the consent of the two parties of the dispute; it is binding on them spontaneously, unless revoked for being counter to the rules of Shari'ah or public order.
column7: Should necessarily be issued in the presence of the two parties of the dispute, otherwise it is null and void, even if both parties were duly notified of the session and chose not to attend.
column8: Requires official registration or submission to the concerned court in all cases for its validity, even if the parties agreed otherwise and the law of the country does not require it.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 11/12 the decision binds without consent unless revoked; presence of parties is only better (11/10) and registration is not needed for validity (12/3).

column5: Examples of necessary costs for which debt may be incurred against tangible Waqf assets include:
column6: Acquiring an additional building that would generate extra revenue for the Waqf, in order to increase the amounts distributed to the Waqf beneficiaries in future years.
column7: Fulfilling the financial obligations of the Waqf (e.g., fees and utility bills) and paying dues owed to those in charge of the Waqf and its employees.
column8: Advance distribution of revenue to the Waqf beneficiaries before it is collected.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1, examples are maintenance, fees and utility bills, and dues to staff; debt for extra benefit is not an essential purpose.

column5: With respect to the prohibited component of income that must be eliminated:
column6: It is not permissible to utilise it in any way whatsoever, nor is any legal fiction to be created to do so, even if this is through the payment of taxes.
column7: It may be used to pay the taxes due on the shares, since taxes are an unavoidable expense of the investment, provided that the Shari'ah Supervisory Board approves such use.
column8: It may be used to cover the expenses of the elimination process.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/4/6/5, the prohibited component may not be utilised in any way, not even through payment of taxes.

column5: For the purpose of the Standard, ………… is given when a party informs another of its resolute intention (undertaking) to act in the future in the interest of the other, with the other having the option to avail itself of the promise:
column6: A future contract.
column7: A bilateral promise.
column8: A master agreement (general framework).
column9: A unilateral promise.
column11: Per 2/1, this defines a unilateral promise; a bilateral promise is an exchange of two back-to-back promises (2/2).

column5: Loss reinsurance is widely used in the insurances which involve big amounts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/3, loss reinsurance is widely used in insurances involving big amounts.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: It is permissible to take consideration for transfer or waiver of easement rights, by means of sale or otherwise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/3, consideration may be taken for transfer or waiver of easement rights, by sale or otherwise.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring that the market value of the asset substituted for the subject of Salam not exceed the market value of the subject of Salam at the time of delivery is:
column6: That otherwise it would be an extinction of debt in debt (faskh al-dayn fī al-dayn).
column7: That otherwise the substitution would involve excessive gharar.
column8: That otherwise the creditor would profit from what he has not assumed the risk of, and it could result in a loan that brings a benefit to the creditor.
column9: That otherwise it could be a means of selling a ribawī commodity for a ribawī commodity on a deferred basis, since the substitute is delivered after the maturity date without possession in the session.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1/1/3, it prevents profit without risk and a loan yielding a benefit.

column5: Adjusting the rental retrospectively to the prevailing market rate when transfer of ownership in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek becomes impossible without cause attributable to the lessee is, according to the Shari'ah basis, analogous to:
column6: The principle of Ujrat al-Mithl applied to floating rentals where the rental was not specified in the contract.
column7: The gift sent by the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Negus.
column8: The principle that the price must be discounted when a sold crop has suffered damage from natural calamities.
column9: The Maliki ruling allowing the lessee's heirs to terminate an onerous lease on the death of their legator, whatever the cause.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the refund is analogous to discounting the price of a sold crop damaged by natural calamities.

column5: In the covered card, if the cover was provided via financing from the card issuer:
column6: The card issuer may lower the due financing instalment according to the condition of cover usage during the period of instalment.
column7: Settlement of the amounts due and of cash withdrawals will be out of the funds of the card issuer, not the cash cover.
column8: The card issuer is obliged to lower the due financing instalment whenever the cover is not used.
column9: The cardholder may not use the card in cash withdrawal.
column11: Per 6/2/1, usage is settled from the cash cover, and the issuer may (not must) lower the financing instalment by cover usage.

column5: It is permissible in contracts involving indebtedness (such as Murabahah) to stipulate an undertaking by the debtor that, in case of procrastinating in payment:
column6: He will donate an amount to the Institution, which it may add to its own income.
column7: He will pay the Institution an amount or a percentage of the debt as compensation for its opportunity loss.
column8: He will donate an amount or a percentage of the debt to be spent for charitable causes through the Institution.
column9: He will pay an additional profit at the Murabahah profit rate for the period of delay.
column11: Per 2/1/8, the debtor may undertake to donate an amount or percentage, spent on charitable causes through the Institution.

column5: If a new Murabaha is entered into with a delinquent customer to establish a new debt:
column6: The new Murabaha is not permitted in any case.
column7: The new Murabaha is permitted only if the first debt is settled on the same day.
column8: The Institution may add compensation for the delay in settling the first debt to the profit rate of the new Murabaha, provided that the compensation does not exceed the actual loss and is disclosed in the contract.
column9: The Institution may not compensate itself, directly or indirectly, for the delinquency in settling the first debt, and the profit rate should not exceed that for such a customer were he not delinquent.
column11: Per 4/1/3/4 (d), no direct or indirect compensation for delinquency; the profit rate is capped at the non-delinquent rate.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: An IFI appointed an agent to purchase a quantity of a commodity on its behalf and specified that the price should not exceed USD 100,000. The market price of the quantity was USD 103,000, yet the agent purchased it for USD 110,000. The IFI decided to maintain the contract. The correct ruling is:
column6: The agent is not liable for any compensation, because the IFI chose to maintain the contract.
column7: The agent should compensate the IFI with USD 7,000, being the difference between the purchase price and the market price.
column8: The agent should compensate the IFI with USD 10,000, being the difference between the purchase price and the price set by the IFI.
column9: The agent should compensate the IFI with USD 3,000, being the difference between the market price and the price set by the IFI.
column11: Per 6/3/2, buying above both market and set price obliges the agent to pay the difference between purchase price and market price.

column5: Where a master agreement is drawn up covering a number of Ijarah transactions between the Institution and the customer, each Ijarah transaction may be concluded by:
column6: A separate lease contract for each transaction, in a specific written document signed by the two parties.
column7: An exchange of notices of offer and acceptance between the two parties by referring to the terms and conditions contained in the master agreement.
column8: The master agreement itself, which constitutes a lease of all future assets covered by it without any further offer and acceptance.
column9: (a) or (b).
column11: Per 2/2, under a master agreement each lease is either a separate signed contract or an exchange of offer and acceptance referring to its terms.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of a revocable documentary credit is that:
column6: It is a form of agency contract, and it cannot be classified as a guarantee because it conflicts with the requirements of guarantee, in which an option is not permissible.
column7: It is a guarantee contract coupled with an option for the guarantor to withdraw from the guarantee at any time before the documents are presented to the bank by the beneficiary.
column8: It is a Qard (loan) contract granted by the bank to the beneficiary against the documents presented.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, revocable credit is agency; it is not a guarantee, which allows no option.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Examples of excessive Gharar that sets the contract null and void include:
column6: Selling of fruits before production.
column7: Signing a lease contract for an unspecified period.
column8: Sale of a Salam commodity that is not usually available on the date of delivery.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/2/1, all three are cited as examples of excessive Gharar that sets the contract null and void.

column5: A businessman signed a document stating that his commercial building shall become a Waqf for a university upon his death. The building represents half of his estate. A year later, he informed the university that he wishes to revoke this Waqf. The correct ruling is:
column6: The Waqf is binding from the instance of its creation, so he cannot resile from it, and it takes effect over the whole building upon his death.
column7: The Waqf is deemed a bequest that takes effect only upon his death, it shall not exceed one-third of his estate, and he is permitted to resile from it.
column8: The Waqf is void, because the initial presumption is that Waqf must come into effect immediately and it cannot be made contingent.
column9: The Waqf is deemed a bequest over the whole building, as Waqf is not subject to the one-third limit, but he cannot resile from it.
column11: Per 2/4/1/4, Waqf contingent on death is a bequest: effective on death, capped at one-third of the estate, and revocable.

column5: ………… entails pre-specification of the time, place, and method of announcing the readings of the index so that the process does not involve Jahalah (ignorance or uncertainty):
column6: Neutrality.
column7: Accuracy.
column8: Transparency.
column9: Objectivity.
column11: Per 3/2, transparency is pre-specifying the time, place and method of announcing index readings to avoid Jahalah.

column5: The basis for the right of a debtor to request a declaration of his own insolvency is the Shafi'i opinion and the fact that it is in his interest to stabilize his financial situation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/3/2, it is the Shafi'i opinion and the debtor's interest in stabilizing his finances.

column5: It is not permitted to trade in financial securities based on securitization of monetary debts unless:
column6: They are traded at their face value, which equals the amount of the debts securitized.
column7: Tangible assets represent at least one third of the underlying assets, whatever the ratio of debts.
column8: Their trading is against a commodity, usufruct or service whose subject delivery is ascertained.
column9: The debtors consent to their trading, in addition to the consent of the originator.
column11: Per 9/5/2, such securities may be traded only against a commodity, usufruct or service with ascertained subject delivery (5/2).

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: A lost car can be the object of a mortgage (Rahn) contract, since Rahn can permissibly involve a degree of Gharar that is not allowed in sale. In this case:
column6: The mortgage is valid only if the mortgagor guarantees that the car will be found.
column7: The mortgage contract is null and void until the car is found.
column8: The mortgagee may sell the mortgagor's right to the lost car for settlement of the debt when the debt falls due.
column9: The car cannot be sold for settlement of the debt unless it is found.
column11: Per 6/1, a lost car may be mortgaged, but it cannot be sold to settle the debt unless the car is found.

column5: Regarding the manufacturer's liability for defects and maintenance of the subject-matter:
column6: The parties may agree on a period during which the manufacturer will be liable for any defects or the maintenance of the subject-matter.
column7: The manufacturer may stipulate in the contract that he is not liable for defects, if the ultimate purchaser agrees.
column8: The determination of liability for defects and maintenance may not be left to customary practice.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 3/1/7, the parties may set a liability period or leave it to custom; per 2/2/3, a defect exclusion clause is not permitted.

column5: Attestation in financial transactions is recommended by Shari'ah. As for giving testimony, it is:
column6: Merely permissible.
column7: Commendable, and in case of necessity it is obligatory.
column8: Disliked where the transaction is documented in writing.
column9: Obligatory in all cases.
column11: Per 2/4/2, giving testimony is commendable and obligatory in case of necessity; perjury is a major sin.

column5: In Mugharasah certificates (Mugharasah Sukuk), the certificate holders become entitled to:
column6: A share in the land and the plantation.
column7: A share in the crop only, according to the terms of the agreement.
column8: The rental of the land planted with trees.
column9: The cost of maintaining the plantation plus a fixed return.
column11: Per 3/9 and 5/1/5/11, Mugharasah certificate holders are entitled to a share in both the land and the trees (plantation).

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, when the ratio of the equity shares of the partners changes:
column6: The ratio of profit sharing must automatically change to match the new equity shares, and the ratio of loss sharing may remain unchanged at the original ratio fixed at the inception of the partnership.
column7: The ratio of profit sharing may never be amended after the conclusion of the contract, even by agreement of all the partners.
column8: The partners may either maintain the ratio of profit already determined or agree on amending it, provided that losses remain allocated according to the ratio of equity ownership.
column9: The ratio of loss sharing may be kept at the original ratio agreed at the inception, whatever the change in equity shares.
column11: Per 5/5, the profit ratio may be kept or amended, but losses must follow the current equity ratio.

column5: After the declaration of insolvency is revoked, an asset is discovered that came into the ownership of the insolvent debtor before the declaration of insolvency as a gift. This asset:
column6: Remains the property of the debtor, since the declaration of insolvency has been revoked.
column7: Is sequestered to be distributed among the creditors whose debts were outstanding before the declaration of insolvency.
column8: Is sequestered only if the debtor is declared insolvent a second time.
column9: Is distributed among all the debtor's creditors, including those whose debts arose after the revocation.
column11: Per 10/2, such an asset is sequestered for the creditors whose debts were outstanding before the declaration of insolvency.

column5: It is permissible to mortgage a debt, whether such debt is owed by the mortgagee or by anyone else.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/11, debt may be mortgaged whether owed by the mortgagee or anyone else, subject to item 5.

column5: It is permissible to issue Tamattu' shares provided that their holders are entitled to profit lesser than that given to the owners of shares based on capital.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/7, it is not permissible to issue Tamattu' shares at all; the lesser profit is a feature of them, not a condition for permissibility.

column5: For spontaneous renewal of the hiring contract:
column6: The consent of the employer alone is sufficient at the end of each period.
column7: Spontaneous renewal is impermissible; renewal must be declared by both parties before expiry of the original contract.
column8: A condition is to be stated in the contract indicating that it shall spontaneously become renewed on the commencement of a new period, if none of the two parties notifies the other about his disinterest in renewal.
column9: No condition is required in the contract; the contract is spontaneously renewed by default on the commencement of a new period whenever neither of the two parties objects to renewal.
column11: Per 8/2/6, spontaneous renewal requires a condition in the contract, operating unless either party notifies the other of disinterest.

column5: The undertaking of the confirming bank, and similar undertakings of banks that participate in the issuance or confirmation of the credit, is characterized in Shari'ah as:
column6: A back-up guarantee, which is permissible.
column7: An agency with remuneration.
column8: A Hawalah of the right of the beneficiary.
column9: A loan to the issuing bank.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the confirming bank's undertaking is an act of back-up guarantee, permissible in Shari'ah.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: If the buyer of an item becomes insolvent and the seller finds that specific item in the insolvency assets:
column6: The seller stands equally with the other creditors in all cases.
column7: The seller has a priority proprietary right to it, if the applicable regulations of the jurisdiction allow it.
column8: The seller has a priority proprietary right to it in all cases, regardless of the applicable regulations.
column9: The sale contract is automatically rescinded.
column11: Per 12/2(c), the seller has a priority proprietary right to his item found among the insolvent buyer's assets if regulations allow it.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The permissibility of the option to revoke due to breach of description is the opinion of the majority of Fuqaha, while other Fuqaha categorized this option under:
column6: The option of deception (Khiyar al-Tadlis).
column7: The option of price gouging (Khiyar al-Ghabn).
column8: The option to revoke due to defect.
column9: The option to revoke owing to deal fragmentation.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for item 4, some Fuqaha classed breach of description under Khiyar al-Tadlis.

column5: In Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, the promise to transfer ownership may be included as an integral part of the Ijarah contract, provided it is signed by both parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/1, it must be in a separate document independent of the Ijarah contract, not an integral part of it.

column5: An IFI appointed its customer (the purchase orderer) as its agent to buy equipment. In one document signed on the day of purchase, the customer confirmed that he had bought the equipment as the IFI's agent and that he thereby bought it from the IFI by Murabahah at cost plus 8%. This arrangement is:
column6: Permissible, provided the IFI paid the price directly to the supplier.
column7: Impermissible, because the liability of the Institution and that of the customer as agent must be separated by an interval in time: the customer's notice of performance and offer to purchase, then the Institution's acceptance.
column8: Permissible, because the customer disclosed his agency in the document.
column9: Impermissible, because the customer may never act as the Institution's agent for acquiring the item, whatever the need, whether or not the price is paid directly to the supplier, and even if the Institution obtains the supplier's sale documents.
column11: Per 3/1/3 and 3/1/5, the agent may not sell to himself; an interval between agency performance and the Murabahah must separate the liabilities.

column5: Within the contract of Qard, it is not permissible to stipulate:
column6: A contract of Bay' (exchange, sale).
column7: The repayment of the Qard at a place other than that where the loan was made.
column8: A period for the repayment of the Qard.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 7, stipulating a sale, Ijarah or other commutative contract in Qard is not permissible; another place (4/2) and a period (6) are allowed.

column5: The prohibition of a binding bilateral promise in an exchange of currencies, supported by the majority of Shari'ah jurists, is based on:
column6: The promise being made in a currency different from the currency of settlement.
column7: Promises in financial transactions never being binding in Shari'ah.
column8: The exchange rate being unknown at the time of the promise, which involves Gharar, and the countervalues not being specified in the promise, so that the exchange amounts to a sale of what is not yet owned.
column9: Binding bilateral promises from two parties being equivalent to a contract, and the promise not being immediately followed by taking possession of the countervalues.
column11: Per the basis, a binding bilateral promise equals a contract and is not followed by immediate possession of the countervalues.

column5: When the term of an investment agency expires, the agent:
column6: May enter into new investments provided they are of the same kind as the existing ones.
column7: May continue entering into new investments until the funds are returned to the principal.
column8: Must immediately liquidate all ongoing investments and return the proceeds to the principal.
column9: Is required not to enter into new investment activities.
column11: Per 4/3, on expiry the agent is required not to enter into new investment activities; ongoing investments are not to be liquidated.

column5: Distribution of the insurance surplus or part thereof among the policyholders may be made in the following forms, provided that the selected form is explicitly mentioned in the regulations:
column6: In proportion to their respective contributions, regardless of whether the policyholder has received indemnity during the financial period or not.
column7: Among the policyholders who have not received indemnity during the financial period.
column8: Among policyholders after deducting the amounts of indemnity they receive during the same financial period.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 12/2/1 to 12/2/3, all three are permitted forms of surplus distribution, if the chosen form is stated in the regulations.

column5: Trespassing of dealers' online data is impermissible, and it is strictly prohibited to sell such data or transmit it to others without the permission of its owners.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/1/3, trespassing dealers' online data is impermissible, as is selling or transmitting it without the owners' permission.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the ruling that Gharar does not affect donation contracts is:
column6: Donation contracts are corollary contracts signed for documentation, and are not meant in themselves, so the Gharar in them is forgiven as in Rahn, which is also a donation-based contract.
column7: Donation contracts are non-binding, and the donor may revoke them at any time.
column8: Gharar in exchange-based contracts would lead to unlawful acquisition of the wealth of others, whereas no dispute arises in donation contracts, since the recipient incurs no loss.
column9: Donation contracts are always justified by a Shari'ah-recognizable need, whether public or private, which enjoys the same status of necessity, so Gharar is forgiven in them as in all contracts of need.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (first condition), Gharar in exchange contracts leads to unlawful taking of wealth; a donation recipient incurs no loss, so no dispute.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: If the Institution obliges the charge cardholder to deposit a sum of money as a guarantee that is not available for his use, it must be made clear that the Institution will invest it for the cardholder's benefit on the basis of Mudarabah, sharing any profit according to a specified percentage.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/2, a blocked guarantee deposit must be invested on a Mudarabah basis for the cardholder with an agreed profit share.

column5: The pre-operating expenses of the joint stock company that manages Islamic insurance are borne by the insurance account.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/3, the company bears its pre-operating expenses and the expenses of its own business and investments.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: A discriminating minor may become an agent:
column6: Provided that all the contractual commitments are the sole responsibility of the principal.
column7: Provided that his guardian approves each act that he performs as an agent.
column8: Under no circumstances, because the agent should have full legal capacity.
column9: Only in non-paid agency, and for matters that result in absolute benefit to the principal.
column11: Per 3/2/1, a discriminating minor may be an agent provided all contractual commitments are the sole responsibility of the principal.

column5: Institutions may provide banking services against fees payable:
column6: In lump sum only, because a percentage fee leads to Gharar, which is not tolerated in banking services.
column7: In lump sum or as a percentage share of the value of the service in question.
column8: Only in an amount equal to the actual cost of the service.
column9: As a percentage share of the value of the service only.
column11: Per clause 2, banking service fees may be a lump sum or a percentage of the value of the service.

column5: In a partnership in commendum, the sleeping partners are entitled to take part in the management of the company, provided their names are mentioned at the registration of the company.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/3/1/3-4, sleeping partners may not interfere in or manage the company; their names are not even mentioned at registration.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: It is permissible for the cardholder to withdraw an amount of cash beyond his available funds with the agreement of the Institution issuing the card, provided no interest is charged.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/5/1 and the basis, withdrawing more than available funds with the issuer's agreement and without interest is a permissible loan.

column5: According to the Shafi'i scholars, keeping the mortgaged asset in the hands of a notary is impermissible, because the right belongs to the mortgagee alone.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the Shafi'is permit a notary "because the right belongs to the two parties, so they can agree on that".

column5: It is prohibited to enter into forward currency contracts. This rule applies:
column6: Only where such contracts are effected through the exchange of deferred transfers of debt.
column7: Unless the purpose is hedging to avoid a loss of profit on a particular transaction effected in a currency whose value is expected to decline, in which case dealing in the forward currency market is permitted.
column8: Whether such contracts are effected through the exchange of deferred transfers of debt or through the execution of a deferred contract in which the concurrent possession of both countervalues by both parties does not take place.
column9: Only where such contracts are executed as a deferred contract in which the concurrent possession of both countervalues by both parties does not take place, and not where they are effected through the exchange of deferred transfers of debt.
column11: Per 2/2 the prohibition covers both forms; per 2/3 it applies even if the purpose is hedging.

column5: It is permissible to scribe or witness borrowing on the basis of interest, provided the scribe or witness is not a party to the loan.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/3, it is not permitted to scribe or witness acts prohibited by Shari'ah, such as borrowing on interest.

column5: The Waqf beneficiaries of a residential building are the Waqif's grandchildren (specific persons). The overseer intends to allocate part of the Waqf revenue to add a new floor to the building itself to increase its revenue. The Waqif did not stipulate anything in this regard. This is permitted:
column6: Under no circumstances, because the Waqf revenue belongs exclusively to the Waqf beneficiaries, who are specific persons entitled to the entire revenue.
column7: With the consent of the grandchildren only, without the need for permission from the relevant authority, since the revenue belongs to them.
column8: After obtaining permission from the relevant authority, with the consent of the grandchildren and the prevalence of a preferred interest that materializes for the Waqf and the beneficiaries.
column9: At the sole discretion of the overseer, since he is responsible for developing the Waqf, provided that the cost does not exceed one third of the annual revenue and the grandchildren are informed.
column11: Per 9/6, redeploying revenue in the Waqf asset needs authority permission and a preferred interest, plus consent of specific beneficiaries.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: It is permissible to specify a time limit for agency, because agency is a contract that could have a specific duration, like Ijarah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, a time limit is allowed because agency, like Ijarah, can have a specific duration.

column5: If the seller fails to deliver al-Muslam Fihi on the due date owing to insolvency:
column6: The buyer may claim the market value of al-Muslam Fihi in excess of the capital of Salam.
column7: The Salam contract becomes void.
column8: He should be granted an extension of time for delivery.
column9: He must pay a penalty for each day of delay in delivery.
column11: Per 5/6, an insolvent seller should be granted an extension of time; a penalty clause for delay is not permitted (5/7).

column5: If the worker (irrigator) stops working before the crop materializes, he is entitled to a wage at the market rate for similar work for the period he worked.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/4, a worker who stops working before the crop materializes is not entitled to any share.

column5: If the quality of the delivered goods in Salam is inferior to that required by the contractual specifications:
column6: The buyer is entitled to reject the goods.
column7: The buyer may accept the goods in that condition, and his action is considered as ethical acceptance.
column8: The two parties may agree to a settlement on terms for acceptance of the goods, even at a discounted price.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3, for inferior goods the buyer may reject, accept them as ethical acceptance, or settle on acceptance at a discounted price.

column5: If the contract concluded prior to the opening of the documentary credit is nullified by a court decision, the bank remains obliged to execute the credit upon presentation of conforming documents.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/4, if a court nullifies the underlying contract, execution of the credit is subject to a new agreement.

column5: Scholars differ on whether a Hawalah contract becomes binding once all its conditions are met.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the basis, once all its conditions are met, Hawalah becomes binding without any difference of opinion among scholars.

column5: The contract of a joint-liability partnership is not binding; hence, a partner is entitled to withdraw from it on the following conditions, excluding:
column6: That the unilateral withdrawal from the partnership would not cause damage to other partners.
column7: That the partners did not set a duration for the company; if they agreed on a duration, it must be observed.
column8: That the partner brings in a substitute for himself, even without the agreement of the other partners.
column9: That the partner notifies the other partners of his intention to withdraw.
column11: Per 4/2/2/2 the first three are conditions; per 4/2/2/3 a substitute may not be brought in without the others' agreement.

column5: If another creditor appears before the distribution of the insolvent debtor's assets:
column6: He has no share in the distribution, because he did not join the application for the declaration of insolvency.
column7: He takes his share only after the creditors who applied for the declaration of insolvency have been paid in full.
column8: He is entitled to a pro-rata share of the distribution.
column9: He should obtain his share from each of the existing creditors, either by mutual consent or through litigation.
column11: Per 4/4, a creditor appearing before distribution takes a pro-rata share; recourse to each existing creditor applies after distribution (8/3/6).

column5: The owner can revoke the Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) contract:
column6: When the worker is unable to work, or stops working and cannot be compelled to continue.
column7: At any time after the commencement of work, without cause, provided that he pays the worker's wage.
column8: Only by mutual consent (Iqalah).
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 13/2, the owner may revoke on the worker's inability to work or unenforceable stoppage; Iqalah is a separate route (13/1).

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Regarding the sale of a commodity that the buyer has not viewed (Bay' al-Ayn al-Gha'ibah):
column6: A commodity can be sold on the basis of mere description, whether made by the seller or someone else, provided it includes all those characteristics which could affect the price.
column7: It is permissible to sell an asset that the buyer has seen sometime before the time of signing the contract, provided that it has undergone no change since that time.
column8: A sale can be concluded on the basis of a model that indicates the characteristics of the sold commodity.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/8/1, 5/8/2 and 5/8/3, sale by full description, by prior viewing (no change since), and by a model are all permissible.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Misuse of Shari'ah exemptions, where making use of an exemption embodies a related act that the Fuqaha unanimously consider as prohibited, or leads to issuing different Fatwas for two identical incidences, is known in Fiqh as:
column6: Sadd al-Zara`i' (blocking the means).
column7: Talfiq (fabrication).
column8: Maslahah Mursalah (public interest).
column9: Istihsan (Shari'ah approbation).
column11: Per 8/4, such misuse of Shari'ah exemptions is known in Fiqh as Talfiq (fabrication).

column5: In principle, Zakah is to be paid as soon as it is due, yet it can be delayed:
column6: For not more than one year, due to shortage of funds, or if its distribution is made according to a certain time schedule, or for any other obvious interest.
column7: For not more than two years, due to shortage of funds or for any other obvious interest, with the approval of the Shari'ah Board.
column8: In no case, since delay of Zakah is impermissible.
column9: For any period, as long as the Zakah amount is retained in a special Zakah fund or account.
column11: Per 10/2, Zakah may be delayed for not more than one year for shortage of funds, a distribution schedule, or another obvious interest.

column5: The contemporary forms of misconduct and negligence by the investment manager include:
column6: Not taking securities even when it is necessary.
column7: Not conducting a feasibility study despite its necessity by way of stipulation or custom (Ꜥurf).
column8: Not storing the commodities in a place appropriate for their storage.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3, all three are listed contemporary forms, together with non-disclosure of what custom or law requires to be disclosed.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: A farm that has not yet reached the stage of giving yield can be the object of a mortgage contract, but it cannot be sold for settlement of the debt until it has reached the stage of giving yield.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/1, such a farm may be mortgaged but cannot be sold to settle the debt until it reaches the stage of giving yield.

column5: If the customer obtains from the supplier a statement of prices with no reference to any named customer (general offer), this statement is considered:
column6: A binding offer of sale to the customer that obliges the Institution to buy the item from that supplier.
column7: An offer of sale addressed to the Institution, effective up to the end of a specified period.
column8: An invitation to negotiate, and not an offer of sale.
column9: A concluded sale contract between the supplier and the customer, upon which the Institution may no longer carry out Murabahah.
column11: Per 2/1/4, a general offer not addressed to a named customer is only an invitation to negotiate, not an offer of sale.

column5: It is permissible to undertake transactions in the three types of commercial paper on the condition that this does not amount to a contravention of the Shari'ah, like Riba or delay that is legally prohibited.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1, dealing in bills, notes and cheques is allowed absent Riba or prohibited delay.

column5: In Istisna'a certificates (Istisna'a Sukuk):
column6: The issuer is the Mudarib, the subscribers are the owners of capital, and the funds realised from subscription are the Mudarabah capital.
column7: The issuer is the manufacturer (supplier/seller), the subscribers are the buyers of the intended product, and the funds realised from subscription are the cost of the product.
column8: The issuer is the buyer of the intended product, the subscribers are the manufacturers, and the funds realised from subscription are the Istisna'a price.
column9: The certificate holders own the product but are not entitled to the sale price of the product sold on the basis of a Parallel Istisna'a.
column11: Per 5/1/5/4, the issuer is the manufacturer, subscribers are buyers of the product, funds are its cost; holders get the Parallel Istisna'a sale price, if any.

column5: The concession of overlooking Gharar in subsidiary and implicit contracts is based on the Hadith:
column6: Prohibiting two sales in one deal.
column7: Concerning the purchase of a palm tree that has not yet been pollinated, whose fruits belong to the seller unless the buyer stipulates that he should be entitled to them.
column8: Narrated by Ibn Umar about selling camels at Al-Baqi' in dinars and receiving the value in dirhams.
column9: Concerning the purchase of a slave who has money, whose money goes to the seller unless the buyer stipulates that he should get it.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (5/2/1), the unpollinated palm tree Hadith shows Gharar is overlooked where the fruits are implicit.

column5: During the period of the Qard, it is not permissible for the borrower to offer tangible property or extend a benefit to the lender when this is done for the sake of Qard, unless:
column6: Giving of such benefits is a practice continuing among the parties from a time prior to the contract of Qard.
column7: The lender consents to receive it.
column8: The benefit is of small value.
column9: The benefit is given in kind and not in cash, provided that it is of the same kind as the subject-matter of the Qard.
column11: Per 5/1, such benefits during the Qard period are prohibited unless the practice existed between the parties before the Qard.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The conditions applicable to the option to revoke due to defect include:
column6: Appearance of a material defect, i.e., one that renders the item defective according to custom, makes it unfit for purpose or diminishes its value.
column7: The defective item being incapable of repair except by incurring cost.
column8: The hidden defect not being caused by the buyer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/1, 2/2/2 and 2/2/5, all three are conditions of the option to revoke due to defect.

column5: Zakah on the produce of a rented agricultural land:
column6: Should be shared equally between the landlord and the tenant.
column7: Should be paid by the tenant; in case of Muzara'ah, Zakah shall be paid by the landowner only.
column8: Should be paid by the landlord, as the owner of the land.
column9: Should be paid by the tenant; in case of Muzara'ah or Musaqat, Zakah shall be paid by the two parties proportionately.
column11: Per 5/4/9, the tenant pays Zakah on produce of rented land; in Muzara'ah or Musaqat the two parties pay proportionately.

column5: It is not permitted to pledge (……….) even when availing a debt against the Waqf, whereas it is permitted to pledge (……….) whenever it is permitted to incur debt against them.
column6: Cash Waqf .... Waqf of real estate.
column7: Investment Waqfs .... tangible Waqf assets.
column8: Tangible Waqf assets .... investment Waqfs.
column9: Waqf of usufructs .... Waqf of moral rights.
column11: Per 6/1 tangible Waqf assets may not be pledged; per 6/2 investment Waqfs may be pledged when debt against them is permitted.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The funds which the institution fails to transfer to their owners because of change of address:
column6: Shall be kept in a suspended account for the specified period before being added to the charity account, and paid out to the owners from it if their addresses become known later.
column7: Shall be added to the profits of the holders of investment accounts after the specified period, and shall not be paid to their owners even if their addresses come to be known later on.
column8: Shall be added to the income of the institution after the specified period.
column9: Shall be added to the charity account immediately, and may not be paid back to their owners even if their addresses become known and they claim the funds within the specified period.
column11: Per 2/2/7, such funds are suspended for the set period, then go to charity, and are repaid from charity if the owners are later traced.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a fixed remuneration in the Sharikah contract for a partner who assists in the management is that:
column6: The partner becomes an employee of the company and is no longer a partner, so he cannot share in the profit or the loss of the venture, whatever the amount of capital he has contributed.
column7: The remuneration constitutes a form of Riba al-Fadl, because it is an unequal exchange of a sum of money for a share of money.
column8: This may lead to guaranteeing the capital of this partner, or to his not being exposed to the risk of loss in proportion to his contribution to the capital.
column9: Management of the partnership is a donation by the partner, for which no consideration of any kind may be taken from the other partners.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a fixed fee may guarantee his capital or shield him from his proportionate share of loss.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: According to one viewpoint stated in the Shari'ah basis, the commitment to offer the agent a certain share of the profit in addition to his principal remuneration can be considered as:
column6: A conditional gift, or Ju'alah.
column7: A guarantee of return given by the principal to the agent.
column8: A Mudarabah share that makes the agent a partner in the profit.
column9: A deferred part of the principal remuneration, which must be known at the time of the contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the pledged profit share is a pledge of donation: a conditional gift or Ju'alah (another view: a subsidiary addition).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the borrower bearing the expenses of delivery and recovery in a contract of Qard is that:
column6: The lender has undertaken a good act, and costs are not to be imposed on one who does a good act.
column7: The borrower is the seller of the loan amount and must deliver it.
column8: The lender is a trustee who is not liable for any costs whatsoever.
column9: Expenses of delivery are always borne by the recipient of property in all contracts.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/2, the lender does a good act and costs are not imposed on one who does good.

column5: A customer borrowed equipment from his brother, with his permission to mortgage it, and mortgaged it to an IFI by registration (formal mortgage) while it remained in the customer's possession. The equipment then perished in the customer's hands without transgression or negligence on his part. The correct ruling is:
column6: The IFI has to compensate the brother, being the mortgagee.
column7: The customer owes his brother nothing, because the perish was not due to transgression or negligence.
column8: The debt owed by the customer to the IFI is extinguished.
column9: The customer has to compensate his brother, being the owner of the borrowed asset.
column11: Per 3/2/6, a borrowed mortgage asset perishing in the mortgagor's hands must be compensated to its owner, unlike a rented asset.

column5: If the Institution has, even after the drawing up of the Murabahah contract, received from the supplier a discount for the same item sold on a Murabahah basis:
column6: The discount must be spent on charitable causes under the supervision of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column7: The customer benefits from the discount only if it was received before the Murabahah contract was concluded.
column8: The discount belongs exclusively to the Institution, since it was received after the contract was concluded.
column9: The customer should benefit from the discount by a reduction of the total Murabahah selling price in proportion to the discount.
column11: Per 4/5, a supplier's discount, even post-contract, reduces the total Murabahah price in proportion, since Murabahah is a mark-up sale.

column5: A restricted Mudarabah contract is a contract in which the capital provider restricts the actions of the Mudarib to a particular location or to a particular type of investment as he considers appropriate:
column6: Provided the Mudarib is compensated by a fixed fee for the restriction.
column7: But not in a manner that would unduly constrain the Mudarib in his operations.
column8: In any manner he wishes, even if this prevents the Mudarib from achieving profit.
column9: Provided the restriction is approved by the regulatory authority.
column11: Per 5/2, the capital provider may restrict location or type of investment, but not so as to unduly constrain the Mudarib.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, Istisna'a is a mere promise and not a binding contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. The Shari'ah basis states that Istisna'a is a binding contract and not a mere promise.

column5: An IFI owns a network of ATMs and charges holders of cards issued by other banks USD 3 per cash withdrawal from its ATMs. The IFI also issues a card based on Qard Hasan. With regard to the fee for cash withdrawal by its own cardholders from its ATMs:
column6: The IFI may charge its cardholders more than USD 3, since they also benefit from the loan, provided that the excess is disclosed to them in advance.
column7: The IFI must observe the actual direct cost requirement, and may not charge its cardholders a fee above the USD 3 charged to cardholders of other banks.
column8: The IFI is not permitted to charge its cardholders any fee for cash withdrawal from its ATMs, even to recover the actual cost of operating them or the fees paid to the network.
column9: The IFI may charge its cardholders any agreed fee, since it is the owner of the ATM and the cardholders accepted the fee in the card agreement, even if it exceeds the actual cost.
column11: Per 5/1/2/4, an ATM owner that is also the issuer observes the actual cost rule and may not charge more than it charges other banks' cardholders.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: A customer wishes to exchange, at spot, his 18K gold jewelry for 21K gold jewelry owned by an Institution's jewelry outlet. The substances added to the gold are only for standardizing its karatage. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The exchange is permissible at any weights, since it is made at spot.
column7: The exchange is permissible provided that the weight of pure gold in each of the two counter-values is equal.
column8: The exchange is permissible if the customer pays the difference in karatage in cash.
column9: The exchange is permissible provided that the total weight of the two pieces of jewelry is equal.
column11: Per 3/3/1/2, karatage substances are not intended per se, so the exchange must be spot with equal weights of pure gold on each side.

column5: Waqf made by a person during his terminal illness is deemed to be a bequest.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/3/4, Waqf during terminal illness is deemed to be a bequest.

column5: The price for an Istisna'a contract:
column6: May be the usufruct of an asset other than the subject-matter, but never the usufruct of the subject-matter itself, even where a government offers it to the builder for a particular duration in lieu of the price.
column7: Must be in cash only, and paid in full at the conclusion of the contract.
column8: Must be known at the conclusion of the contract, and may be cash, tangible goods, or the usufruct of an asset for a particular duration, whether of another asset or of the subject-matter itself.
column9: May be determined after completion of the work on the basis of the actual cost incurred, plus an agreed percentage of profit to the manufacturer.
column11: Per 3/2/1, the price must be known at conclusion and may be cash, goods or usufruct, including the subject-matter's own usufruct (BOT).

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: The term Fatwa refers to:
column6: A Shari'ah opinion presented to a person who seeks it with regard to an incidence that has occurred or is expected to occur; it does not refer to answering queries pertaining to hypothetical incidences.
column7: A Shari'ah opinion presented to a person who seeks it with regard to any incidence, whether actual, expected or hypothetical, since the Fatwa covers all queries raised by the inquirer, whether or not they are related to a real incident.
column8: A binding ruling issued by a court on a dispute between two parties.
column9: A Shari'ah opinion issued by the Mufti on his own initiative regarding hypothetical incidences, without any request from a person who seeks it.
column11: Per 2/1, Fatwa is an opinion given on request on an actual or expected incidence, not on hypothetical ones.

column5: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) is:
column6: A non-binding contract which either party may terminate at any time, even after the commencement of the work and before its expiry.
column7: A binding contract from the moment of its conclusion, irrespective of whether the work has commenced.
column8: A contract binding on the owner of the trees only, while the worker may withdraw at any time.
column9: A permissible contract that becomes binding on commencement of the work or if mutually agreed between the two parties not to terminate the contract before its expiry.
column11: Per item 3, Musaqat is permissible and becomes binding on commencement of work or by agreement not to terminate before expiry.

column5: If partners have contributed their partnership capital in different currencies:
column6: They must be translated into the currency of the Sharikah at current exchange rates to determine each partner's share and liabilities.
column7: Each partner's contribution is kept in its own currency and his profit is distributed in that currency, whatever the fluctuation in exchange rates.
column8: The currencies are translated at an exchange rate agreed upon by the partners on the date of liquidation, whatever the market rate at that date.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 3/1/2/2, different currencies must be translated into the Sharikah currency at current exchange rates to fix each partner's share.

column5: The customer's wish to acquire an item through the Institution in a Murabahah to the purchase orderer:
column6: Does not constitute a promise or commitment except when it has been expressed in due form.
column7: May be included, together with a promise to buy the item from the Institution, in a single set of documentation to be signed by the customer.
column8: May be expressed in a document prepared by the customer, or in a standard application form prepared by the Institution and signed by the customer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1/3, the wish binds only when expressed in due form, and may be combined with the promise in one document prepared by either party.

column5: If one of the parties to a Mudarabah contract stipulates that he should receive a lump sum of money:
column6: The condition is void, but the Mudarabah contract remains valid.
column7: The Mudarabah contract shall be void.
column8: The stipulation is permissible if the lump sum is less than the expected profit.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 8/5, a stipulated lump sum voids the Mudarabah contract itself, except the agreement on profit above a ceiling.

column5: The meaning of the Hadith "Mortgage should not be foreclosed from its owner who should get its benefit and bear its expenses" is that:
column6: The mortgagee may not sell the mortgaged asset in case of default, even with the permission of the court.
column7: The mortgaged asset may not be kept by a notary.
column8: The mortgagor's failure to redeem the asset does not make the mortgagee entitled to it.
column9: The mortgagor may not benefit from the mortgaged asset during the mortgage, and its benefits belong to the mortgagee.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith means default does not entitle the mortgagee to the asset, unlike the pre-Islamic practice of seizure.

column5: Rab Al Maal delegated the investment agent to sell an asset at a specified price of 100. The agent sold it at 95 without the principal's permission. The ruling is:
column6: The agent is liable for the difference of 5 between the price sold by him and the price specified to him.
column7: The agent is not liable, since his possession is fiduciary and there was no loss of capital.
column8: The agent is liable for the difference only if the market price at the time of sale was 100 or more.
column9: The sale is void, and the agent is liable for the full specified price of 100.
column11: Per 7/2, an agent who sells below the specified price without permission is liable for the difference.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The basis for the impermissibility of selling the abstract rights mentioned in item 10 (such as put or call options and the right of Shuf'ah) is:
column6: The fact that they are personal rights arising from the liability of another person, which cannot be transferred.
column7: The lack of monetary value in Shari'ah, and the presence of Gharar (uncertainty) and Jahalah (ambiguity).
column8: The fact that they cannot be inherited.
column9: The fact that they constitute Riba al-Nasi'ah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, these abstract rights lack monetary value in Shari'ah and involve Gharar and Jahalah.

column5: The basis for nullifying a Mudarabah contract that is silent on the ratio of profit, where there is no customary practice, is that the Mudarib has breached the requirements of trust.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, profit is the subject matter of Mudarabah, and lack of knowledge of the subject matter nullifies contracts.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Effectiveness of the agency contract can be linked to fulfillment of a certain condition or to a future date because:
column6: Agency is a non-binding contract that either party may revoke at any time.
column7: Non-paid agency is a form of donation, in which suspension is tolerated.
column8: Agency is delegation of power rather than an act of ownership transfer that could be required immediately.
column9: Paid agency falls under the rulings on Ijarah, which may be added to a future date.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, agency may be conditional or future because it delegates power and does not transfer ownership.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, a cheque drawn by the client upon a bank with which he does not have a balance is characterized as:
column6: Hawalah upon one with no liability (absolute Hawalah), according to those who do not require that the transferee be indebted to the transferor.
column7: An agency for borrowing.
column8: A guarantee (Kafalah) given by the bank to the beneficiary.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is Hawalah (on one with no liability) or, per a second view, agency for borrowing; both are valid.

column5: Projects financed through syndication:
column6: Should be channeled towards investment activities that are permissible in Shari'ah.
column7: Should not be totally or partially directed towards projects that encounter Shari'ah restriction or constitute Riba.
column8: May be partially directed towards impermissible projects, if the impermissible part is minor in relation to the whole financing.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per clause 3, syndication must go to permissible activities and not, wholly or partly, to restricted projects or Riba.

column5: When the arbitrator issues a verdict on an issue that should not be resolved through arbitration, his verdict is valid if both parties of the dispute consent to it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/3, a verdict on an issue that should not be resolved through arbitration is null and void.

column5: If the proceeds of sale of the sequestered assets are not sufficient to pay off his debts, the insolvent debtor is required to earn or take out a loan to settle the balance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/3, the debtor is not required to earn or take out a loan if the sale proceeds are insufficient.

column5: An investment agency is restricted to activities that yield a minimum profit margin of 8%. The agent did not find such an investment and, without seeking the principal's consent, invested in transactions yielding 5%, while the average profit prevalent in the market was 6%. The agent:
column6: Is liable to compensate the principal for 1%, the difference between the profit earned and the average profit prevalent in the market.
column7: Is not liable for anything, since the principal's capital was not lost.
column8: Is liable to compensate the principal for 3%, the difference between the profit earned and the stipulated minimum margin.
column9: Is liable to compensate the principal for 2%, the difference between the stipulated margin and the market average.
column11: Per 10/2, he compensates the gap between profit earned and the market average, not the stipulated minimum margin.

column5: The obligatory Zakah on 45 camels (freely grazing most of the year) is:
column6: Hiqqah camel (at the fourth year of age).
column7: Bint Makhad camel (at the second year of age).
column8: Bint Labun camel (at the third year of age).
column9: 4 goats.
column11: Per the table in 11/1, 36 to 45 camels require one Bint Labun (at the third year of age).

column5: Unless it has stipulated a sale on an 'as is' basis (Bay' al-Bara'ah), the Institution shall be responsible for:
column6: New (recent) defects that arise after the conclusion of the contract and taking delivery by the customer.
column7: Pre-existing hidden defects which appear after the conclusion of the contract.
column8: Neither pre-existing nor new defects, once the contract of Murabahah is concluded.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/10, the Institution answers for pre-existing hidden defects, not new defects arising after conclusion and delivery to the customer.

column5: In case of operating Ijarah, if the customer breaches his promise to lease and the Institution (promisee) does not sell the asset to a third party:
column6: The promisor shall be charged the rentals for the period he promised to lease the asset.
column7: The promisor shall be charged the difference between the cost of acquisition and the market value of the asset.
column8: The promisee shall not be entitled to receive any compensation.
column9: The Institution may retain the whole sum paid by the customer to ensure his seriousness.
column11: Per 2/3, in operating Ijarah damage is cost minus resale price to a third party; if the asset is not sold, no compensation is due.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for applying a shortfall in Waqf revenue to all the exclusive and specific Waqf beneficiaries in proportion to their shares is the analogy upon:
column6: The reduction (ʿawl) of inheritance portions, and the creditors of a bankrupt.
column7: The distribution of losses among partners in a Musharakah in proportion to their capital contributions.
column8: The distribution of Zakah among its eight categories.
column9: The bearing of loss by the capital provider in Mudarabah.
column11: Per the Basis of 9/10/3, analogy with ʿawl in inheritance and with the creditors of a bankrupt.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a Murabahah deal when the customer has accepted the deal directly from the supplier, even if the customer has not yet paid the price, is that:
column6: The sale is not concluded until the price is paid, so the Institution would be buying an item whose ownership is still uncertain, and the customer would remain liable to the supplier for the unpaid price until the Institution has paid it.
column7: A sale contract has taken place between the customer and the supplier and the commodity has entered into the customer's ownership; payment of the price is a consequence of the contract, not a condition for it.
column8: It falls under the heading of sale of debt, which is prohibited by Shari'ah.
column9: It amounts to a bilateral binding promise, which is a contract prior to the acquisition of the item to be sold.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the commodity has entered the customer's ownership; payment is a consequence of the contract, not a condition of it.

column5: An Ijarah contract terminates (expires):
column6: With the death of either party to the contract, whether the lessor or the lessee, since the contract is personal to the contracting parties.
column7: With the total destruction of the leased asset in the case of leasing a specific asset.
column8: Upon the sale of the leased asset by the lessor to a third party, whether or not the purchaser knew of the Ijarah contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/2/4 and 7/1/3, total destruction of a specific asset ends the Ijarah; death (7/2/3) and sale to a third party (7/1/2) do not.

column5: The customer's promise to purchase, and the related contractual framework, are not integral to a Murabahah transaction; if the Institution has other opportunities to sell the item, it may not need such a promise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/3/2, the promise only assures completion of the deal and is not integral to Murabahah.

column5: B accepted a Hawalah from A, his debtor, on C without stipulating that C be solvent. Before paying the debt, C was declared bankrupt by a court in his lifetime. In this case B:
column6: Is entitled to have a right of recourse against A.
column7: Has no right of recourse against A, since he did not stipulate the solvency of C.
column8: May claim from A only if C dies.
column9: May only share pro rata in C's assets with C's other creditors.
column11: Per 7/2 (III), the payer being declared bankrupt in his lifetime gives the transferee recourse against the transferor.

column5: In a joint ownership partnership (Sharikat al-Mulk), a partner who sells his share to the other partner may promise to buy it back:
column6: At the market value.
column7: At a price mutually agreed at the time of performance.
column8: At a specified price.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/4/3, in an ownership partnership the buyback promise may be at market value, an agreed price at the time, or a specified price.

column5: Upon issuance of the card, the relationship between the card issuer and the cardholder is characterized as a relationship of:
column6: Novation (Hawalah) of the card acceptor to the card issuer, so that the issuer pays the merchant on the cardholder's behalf.
column7: Guarantee (Kafalah) by the card issuer of the cardholder's obligations.
column8: Provision of services to the cardholder, represented in issuing the card and its continuation to be valid for use.
column9: Loan (Qard) from the card issuer to the cardholder.
column11: Per 2/2/1/1, upon issuance the relationship is provision of services: issuing the card and keeping it valid for use.

column5: The commodity sold in Monetization shall be well identified so as to become distinct from the other assets of the seller. This may be done by:
column6: Separating the commodity from the other assets of the seller.
column7: Recording the numbers of its identifying documents, such as storing certificates.
column8: Relying on the seller's general undertaking that he holds sufficient quantities of the commodity in his stock.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2, identification is by separating the commodity from the seller's other assets or recording the numbers of its documents such as storing certificates.

column5: In a contractual set-off, if the two debts are not equal in amount, the party that is owed the larger debt is deemed to have relinquished the remaining balance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2/3, set-off occurs for an equivalent amount and the party owed the larger debt may request payment of the balance.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of Parallel Salam is that:
column6: Taking possession of part of a thing is like taking possession of the whole, so delivery under the first Salam is treated as delivery under the second.
column7: It represents two Salam deals that are separable despite the similar descriptions of the subject matter, and does not lead to two sales in one.
column8: The buyer may benefit by acquiring the commodity at a price below the market price, which justifies linking the two contracts to each other.
column9: Iqalah is encouraged in all sales.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Parallel Salam is two separable Salam deals despite similar descriptions, not two sales in one.

column5: ………… is a credit instrument via lending within a specific limit for a period specified at the start, and it is also a settlement instrument, but its arrangement does not provide facilities of revolving credit to the cardholder:
column6: Credit Card (revolving credit card).
column7: Prepaid Card.
column8: Debit Card.
column9: Charge Card.
column11: Per 3/3/1 and 3/3/3, the charge card is a credit (lending) and settlement instrument without revolving credit facilities.

column5: If the Mudarabah contract is actually concluded on the basis of a memorandum of understanding:
column6: The contents of the memorandum become an integral part of any future contract, unless the parties originally agreed to exempt themselves from some of the obligations in it.
column7: The memorandum has no legal effect, as only the Mudarabah contract governs the relationship, even if the parties intended to incorporate the memorandum.
column8: The memorandum prevails over the terms of the Mudarabah contract in case of conflict, even if the parties agreed to modify it at the conclusion of the contract, or the memorandum is not signed by them.
column9: The memorandum becomes binding only if it is registered officially with the competent authority.
column11: Per 3/3, the MoU becomes an integral part of the contract unless the parties originally exempted themselves from some obligations.

column5: Regarding prizes given on points (loyalty programs), it is permissible:
column6: For a member who lacks some of the points required at the time of purchase to purchase new points for cash and to use them, because the use of these points is deemed to be payment of a part of the price.
column7: For the Institution to adopt the terms and conditions of such a program without resorting to its Shari'ah Supervisory Board, if the program is free of subscription fees.
column8: To enter a program against a subscription fee even if it does not enable the member to have any services or benefits that are valuable in Shari'ah.
column9: For a member to purchase new points for cash, but not to use them towards the price, since this would be a sale of points.
column11: Per 3/6/3, a member may buy missing points for cash and use them as part payment of the price; a fee needs valuable benefits; SSB review is required.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the Musaqat worker acting in a fiduciary capacity (rather than a position of liability) is that:
column6: He is a co-owner of the trees for the term of the contract by virtue of his common share in the produce.
column7: He is a hired worker entitled to a fixed wage for his work.
column8: He is an agent on behalf of the owner in the preservation and care of trees and fruits.
column9: He has been granted unfettered access to the trees by the owner so that he may perform his duties as per the contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 6/3, the worker is the owner's agent in preserving and caring for the trees and fruits.

column5: Commercial websites are considered as private properties of their owners; however, their trespassing does not necessitate compensation unless it results in the theft of money.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/1/1, websites are their owners' private property and trespassing them could necessitate compensation; no such restriction is made.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Rights of Shuf'ah are extinguished upon the death of the Shafi' (preemptor), and are not inherited by his heirs.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/2/3, rights of Shuf'ah are not extinguished by the preemptor's death but are inherited by his heirs.

column5: It is permissible to distribute the realised Mudarabah profit among the parties on account, in which case the distribution will be revised when actual or constructive valuation takes place.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/8, on-account distribution is allowed, subject to revision on actual or constructive valuation.

column5: Industrial accessories (spare parts) used in production equipment are not part of zakatable assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/6/4 (and 4/1), spare parts used in production equipment are not zakatable.

column5: A bilateral promise between the customer and the Institution in Murabahah to the purchase orderer is permissible only if:
