column6: The Institution has acquired actual or constructive possession of the item before the promise is signed.
column7: The customer pays Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit) at the time of signing the promise.
column8: The promise is documented in a single set of documentation together with the customer's wish to acquire the item.
column9: There is an option to cancel the promise which may be exercised either by both promisors or by either one of them.
column11: Per 2/3/3, a bilateral promise is allowed only with an option to cancel exercisable by both promisors or either of them.

column5: The death of the mortgagor terminates the mortgage contract, whereas the death of the mortgagee has no effect on it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/5, the death of either the mortgagor or the mortgagee has no effect on the mortgage; their inheritors substitute them.

column5: Among the bases for prohibiting the Ijarah of tangible Waqf assets for less than the fair rent, in the absence of a preferred interest, is the maxim:
column6: Hardship begets facility.
column7: The overseer's disposition of Waqf is contingent upon the interest thereto.
column8: Certainty is not removed by doubt.
column9: Repulsion of harm has precedence over acquisition of interest.
column11: Per the Basis of 8/5, the maxim: the overseer's disposition of Waqf is contingent upon its interest; plus repelling favouritism.

column5: Upon the death of a party to an Ijarah contract:
column6: The contract does not terminate, but the heirs of the lessee may terminate it if they prove that it has become too onerous for their resources and in excess of their needs.
column7: The heirs of either party may terminate the contract if they prove that it has become too onerous for them, and the same right belongs to the lessor's heirs in respect of the leased asset.
column8: The contract terminates automatically.
column9: The heirs of the lessor may terminate the contract, since ownership of the asset passes to them, and the lessee must then vacate the asset or conclude a new contract with them.
column11: Per 7/2/3, death does not end the Ijarah; only the lessee's heirs may terminate if they prove it is too onerous and beyond their needs.

column5: Waqf by a person interdicted for prodigal grounds (safah):
column6: Is valid, but it shall not exceed one-third of his assets.
column7: Is contingent upon the authorization of his creditors.
column8: Is not concluded.
column9: Is valid and enforceable, since Waqf is a donation.
column11: Per 2/4/3/3, Waqf by a prodigal interdicted person is not concluded; Waqf by one interdicted for debt depends on creditors' authorization.

column5: The issuance of a cheque against a current account is a form of Hawalah if the beneficiary is a creditor of the issuer, in which case the issuer, the bank and the beneficiary are respectively:
column6: The payer, the transferor and the transferee.
column7: The transferor, the payer and the transferee.
column8: The transferee, the payer and the transferor.
column9: The transferor, the transferee and the payer.
column11: Per 12/1, the issuer is the transferor, the bank the payer and the beneficiary the transferee.

column5: All rulings applicable to debtors in default are applicable to guarantors in default, except the stipulation that all outstanding instalments become due.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2(b), all rulings applicable to defaulting debtors apply equally to defaulting guarantors, without exception.

column5: The amount of money deposited by the customer as Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit) can be held:
column6: Only in a current account held at the discretion of the Institution, since a security deposit may not be invested, and the customer is entitled to no profit on it under any arrangement.
column7: As 'Arboun (Earnest Money) which becomes the property of the Institution upon payment.
column8: As an investment trust on the basis of Mudarabah between the customer and the Institution if the customer permits investment, or in a current account at the customer's discretion.
column9: As an investment on the basis of Musharakah, with any profit belonging exclusively to the Institution, whether or not the customer permits it to invest the deposit.
column11: Per 2/5/3, Hamish Jiddiyyah is held as a Mudarabah investment trust if the customer permits investment, or in a current account at his discretion.

column5: Which of the following is permissible in Waqf?
column6: Declaring the Waqf as effective starting from a future date, as when the donor declares his property to become Waqf starting from next year.
column7: Temporary Waqf, when the donor desires to get back his property after a specific period.
column8: Waqf for an impermissible purpose, provided that it is not for a charitable purpose.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/3 and 3/1/4, future-dated and temporary Waqf are permissible; per 3/3/1, Waqf may never be for an impermissible purpose.

column5: If the Waqf of Sukuk and units of investment funds is on a perpetuity basis:
column6: Upon cancellation of the Sukuk or units, the Waqf ends, since the Waqf asset has ceased to exist.
column7: Periodic distributions are disbursed in the avenues of Waqf disposal, and upon cancellation, the proceeds are also disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries as revenue, since cancellation is a redemption of the capital that the beneficiaries are entitled to enjoy, whatever the Waqif stipulated.
column8: Periodic distributions are disbursed in the avenues of Waqf disposal, and upon cancellation, the proceeds are reinvested in other Sukuk, units of other funds or any revenue-generating asset, as stipulated by the Waqif and required by the Waqf's interest.
column9: Periodic distributions are added to the Waqf asset, and upon cancellation, the proceeds return to the Waqif.
column11: Per 2/4/15/1(a), distributions go to the avenues of disposal and cancellation proceeds are reinvested in revenue-generating assets.

column5: For legitimizing the execution of the arbitration verdict, it is permissible to approach courts that do not observe the rules of Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 13/2, approaching such courts to legitimize execution of the verdict is permissible.

column5: A customer leased a car from an IFI, and the car is in the customer's possession. During the lease period, the IFI agreed to sell the car to the same customer. With respect to the possession required under the sale:
column6: The customer's prior possession as lessee stands in place of the subsequent possession under the sale, irrespective of whether the prior possession was one of liability or trust.
column7: The prior possession is not sufficient, because the nature of possession under the lease differs from the nature of possession under the sale, so the car must be re-delivered to the IFI before the sale.
column8: Possession under the sale is realised only when the customer pays the full price.
column9: The car must be returned to the IFI and then re-delivered to the customer for possession under the sale to be realised.
column11: Per 3/6, prior possession of a tangible thing stands in place of subsequent lawful possession, whatever the nature of either possession.

column5: Issuing documentary credit to a client against another documentary credit (back-to-back credit and transferable credit) is permissible, because:
column6: The second documentary credit is a guarantee for which a fee may be charged by the bank, as in any other contract of guarantee.
column7: A documentary credit creates a debt owed by the bank to the client, and such debt can be mortgaged to obtain a new debt.
column8: A documentary credit is a tangible asset that can be possessed.
column9: The issuing bank owns the goods covered by the first documentary credit and may therefore pledge them against the second one.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a documentary credit creates a debt owed by the bank to the client, and debts may be mortgaged.

column5: Using an index like LIBOR, or a certain share/commodity price index, as a basis for determining the profit of a Murabahah pledge is:
column6: Permissible, provided that the contract is to be concluded on a specific profit that does not vary with further changes in the index.
column7: Permissible, and the profit may vary with further changes in the index during the financing period, provided that the variation is stated in the contract.
column8: Permissible only for the Murabahah of commodities traded in organized markets.
column9: Not permissible, because LIBOR is an interest rate.
column11: Per 5/3, an index may be used to set Murabahah profit if the contract is concluded on a fixed profit unaffected by later index moves.

column5: Compensation for trespassing of commercial websites:
column6: Must be claimed within a specific time limit from the date of trespassing, after which it lapses in all cases.
column7: Becomes due automatically once the trespassing is verified, even if it is not claimed.
column8: Becomes due only when it is claimed, whereas claiming it does not have a specific time limit after the incident of trespassing is known.
column9: Becomes due only if the trespasser has stolen money, and not for trespassing of data.
column11: Per 8/1/6, compensation is due only when claimed, and claiming it has no specific time limit after the trespassing is known.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for preventing the overseer from leasing the Waqf asset to himself or his child is:
column6: A lease to a relative is null and void in all contracts.
column7: The overseer may not be a party to any contract concerning the Waqf, since the same person cannot be both offeror and acceptor in any contract.
column8: The fear, as human nature, of favouritism for himself or his child and of not choosing what is more favourable for the Waqf.
column9: The rent received from a relative is considered a gift to the Waqf.
column11: Per the Basis of 3/8/3, there is a natural fear of favouritism towards himself or his child instead of choosing what is best for the Waqf.

column5: An undertaking by a third party to indemnify against a loss of capital resulting from the investment manager's wilful misconduct or negligence is:
column6: Impermissible, because it results in making the investment manager liable for the loss.
column7: Permissible without consideration, but the guarantor has no right of recourse to the investment manager.
column8: Permissible for a fee, as it is a form of Takaful for the benefit of the investors.
column9: Permissible without receiving consideration for it, and the guarantor has the right of recourse to the investment manager.
column11: Per 4/2/5, such a gratuitous undertaking is permissible, with a right of recourse against the misconducting or negligent manager.

column5: It is not permissible to initiate several Salam contracts with different parties through negotiations; a master agreement must first be drawn up.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/1/1, several Salam contracts may be initiated through negotiations; a master agreement is merely permissible.

column5: It is permissible for the Islamic reinsurance company to provide reinsurance services to traditional insurance companies using the traditional reinsurance contract, provided that the reinsurance does not involve a Shari'ah prohibited object.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/3, the contract used must be the Islamic reinsurance contract, with no linkage and no prohibited object.

column5: An unrestricted investment agency:
column6: Is impermissible, because an investment agency must be restricted to a particular kind of investment or a specific place.
column7: Is still restricted by customary practice and by the requirement that the agent acts in the principal's best interests.
column8: Allows the agent to invest in any manner he sees fit, without regard to customary practice.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/3, an unrestricted agency is permissible but remains restricted by custom and the principal's best interests.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: A converting bank that concludes a sale-and-leaseback deal by selling some of its assets for liquidity and leasing them back by means of an Ijarah contract must ensure that:
column6: The asset is sold at a price lower than its market value to reflect the lease rental.
column7: The lease is stipulated as a condition in the contract of sale.
column8: The contract of sale is independent from the contract of lease, i.e. the two contracts remain separate from each other.
column9: The lessee undertakes to repurchase the asset at the original sale price at the end of the lease.
column11: Per 6/2/4, sale and leaseback must observe the Ijarah standards, keeping the sale and lease contracts separate.

column5: Upon marketing and promoting the card, the card issuing Institution:
column6: Should comply with the requirements of transparency and disclosure, especially concerning the amounts of fees and the profit percentage, and avoid misguiding and tempting to excessive consumption.
column7: May tempt customers towards consumption, provided the amounts of the fees are disclosed.
column8: Is not required to stipulate on the cardholder not to transact the card in what is prohibited, as this is the cardholder's own responsibility under the card agreement and the applicable law and regulations.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/9/1 transparency is required and tempting to excess consumption avoided; per 5/9/2 the issuer must bar prohibited use.

column5: An IFI acts as investment agent for a group of investors. The investment agency contract stipulates that the IFI guarantees the investors' capital together with a return of 6% per annum. This stipulation is:
column6: Permissible, because the IFI as agent is a trustee who may guarantee the investment.
column7: Permissible as to the capital, but impermissible as to the return.
column8: Impermissible, because combining agency and guarantee in the same party turns the transaction into an interest-based loan, as though the agent had borrowed and repaid with an additional sum.
column9: Impermissible only because the return is fixed; a guarantee of the capital alone in the agency contract would be permissible, since the agent would then be a guarantor in respect of the funds he holds as a trustee.
column11: Per 2/2/1-2/2/2, an agent may not be required to guarantee capital or profit; doing so turns it into an interest-based loan.

column5: On securitization under the rules for an entity in which commingling is materialized, the ratio of tangible assets and the like must exceed (……….) of the value of the entity's assets, and in all instances must not fall at any time below (……….).
column11: Per 8/2/2–8/2/3, tangible assets must exceed 50% and must never fall below 33% of the value of the assets.

column5: It is permissible in Shari'ah to combine more than one contract in one set:
column6: Only if the combined contracts are concluded for separate values.
column7: Without making one contract a condition in the other, and provided that each is permissible on its own, unless a Shari'ah restriction entails its prohibition on an exceptional basis.
column8: Absolutely, provided that the combined set as a whole achieves a lawful interest for the two parties, even if one contract is imposed as a condition in the other or an individual contract encounters a Shari'ah restriction.
column9: Only if the combined contracts are of the same nature, such as two sales.
column11: Per clause 3, combination is allowed without conditioning one contract on the other if each is permissible, barring an exceptional restriction.

column5: The buyer may take delivery of the sale item during the 'Arboun option period, and such delivery does not on its own indicate confirmation of the contract unless the buyer's conduct indicates that he has accepted the sale item.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per item 7, delivery during the option period is not by itself confirmation unless the buyer's conduct indicates acceptance.

column5: It is permissible to take 'Arboun from a buyer or lessee when a sale or lease contract is concluded, on condition that:
column6: The seller or lessor deducts from it only the actual damage sustained, this being obligatory.
column7: The 'Arboun is taken before the conclusion of the contract, as security for a binding promise.
column8: The 'Arboun is refunded in full if the buyer terminates the contract within the option period, and is retained by the seller or lessor only if the contract is not performed after the option period has expired, in which case he deducts nothing.
column9: If the contract is not terminated within the option period, the amount is considered part of the consideration, and if the buyer or lessee fails to perform within this period, the seller or lessor may retain it.
column11: Per 6/8/3, 'Arboun counts toward the price or may be retained on non-performance; refunding the balance after damage is only preferable.

column5: An IFI leased a vessel to a shipping company. The Ijarah contract stipulates that the lessee shall bear the major maintenance needed to keep the vessel seaworthy and shall bear the cost of insuring it. The correct ruling on these two stipulations is:
column6: Both are permissible, since they are agreed in the contract.
column7: Only the stipulation on insurance is impermissible; major maintenance may be imposed on the lessee, as he has possession of the vessel throughout the lease, and the lessor bears only the cost of insuring the asset.
column8: Only the stipulation on major maintenance is impermissible; insurance may be charged to the lessee, who bears the cost of insuring the asset as its user.
column9: Both are impermissible, since major maintenance and insurance are the lessor's responsibility, although he may delegate both tasks to the lessee at the lessor's cost.
column11: Per 5/1/7 and 5/1/8, the lessor bears major maintenance and insurance; he may delegate these tasks to the lessee at the lessor's cost.

column5: Regarding renewal and extension of credit facilities:
column6: Renewal and extension of facilities should be done by entering into new contracts, rather than by extending the duration of the ongoing ones.
column7: The institution may obtain returns against extending the date of repayment of debts, provided they are agreed upon at the time of rescheduling.
column8: Commission for renewal or extension of credit facilities is treated like commission for credit study, and is therefore permissible.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3/2/4/2, renewal is by new contracts; per 5/3/1/3 and 5/3/2/4/1, renewal commission and returns for extension are not allowed.

column5: Among the Shari'ah bases for the validity of a Waqf whose beneficiary is a body that will be discontinued is that perpetuity is not a condition in Waqf.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 2/4/4/3, perpetuity is not a condition in Waqf.

column5: In the case of self-dedicated Waqf (al-Waqf 'Ala al-Nafs):
column6: The donor retains the ownership of the donated property, and may sell it at any time during his lifetime.
column7: The donor retains the income/usufruct of the donated property for himself as long as he is alive, and indicates the charitable purpose which shall be entitled to the income/usufruct after his death.
column8: The income/usufruct is reserved for the donor's family members during his lifetime, and goes to the charitable purpose indicated by him after his death.
column9: The property is donated to family as well as charitable purposes, and the income/usufruct is shared accordingly between the family and the charitable purpose.
column11: Per 2/3/4, the donor keeps the income/usufruct for himself while alive and names the charitable purpose entitled to it after his death.

column5: The expenses of deposit and withdrawal in a contract of deposit (Wadi'ah) shall be borne by the depositee (the custodian), since he holds the deposit as a trust.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/3, the expenses of deposit and withdrawal are borne by the depositor (the owner of the deposit).

column5: An IFI signed a 12-month Ijarah contract for a machine at a monthly rental of 1,000, specifying delivery on 1 January. The IFI actually delivered the machine on 1 March. Nothing was agreed regarding extension of the lease. The IFI demanded rental from 1 January. The correct ruling is:
column6: The contract is automatically terminated due to the late delivery.
column7: Rental is due from 1 January, since the rental is made obligatory by the contract.
column8: Rental is due from 1 January, but the lessee may claim compensation for the delay.
column9: No rental is due for January and February, and the rental is reduced accordingly.
column11: Per 4/1/3, no rental is due between the agreed and actual delivery dates unless the parties agree to extend the lease by an equal period.

column5: A owes B 10 dinars, and C owes A 20 dinars. A concludes a restricted Hawalah transferring B to collect his debt from C. B is entitled to collect from C:
column6: Nothing, since the two debts are not equal in amount.
column7: Any amount up to 20 dinars agreed between the transferor and the transferee.
column8: 20 dinars, the whole amount owed by C to A.
column9: 10 dinars only, the equivalent amount of his debt.
column11: Per 6/6 and its basis, the Hawalah is valid though amounts differ, but B may take only the equivalent of his debt.

column5: With regard to a personal guarantee:
column6: The guarantor may take remuneration for providing the guarantee per se, provided it is a fixed amount and not a percentage.
column7: The guarantor is entitled to claim any expenses actually incurred during the period of the personal guarantee.
column8: The debtor may pay a commission to the guarantor for obtaining the guarantee.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/5, no remuneration or commission for a guarantee per se is allowed; only actual expenses may be claimed.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Primary proprietary rights, such as rights arising from full and complete ownership, are independent rights that do not rely on the existence of any other right.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/1, primary proprietary rights, e.g. full ownership, are independent and do not rely on any other right.

column5: Transactions that entail instant delivery of the transacted objects are considered as incidental credit facilities.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/3, transactions entailing instant delivery of the transacted objects are not considered part of credit facilities at all.

column5: An IFI issued Musaqat Sukuk in which the certificate holders act as workers who undertake to provide irrigation works for trees owned by a landowner. The subscription has closed, the certificates have been allotted and the activity has commenced. One of the certificate holders wishes to sell his certificates. The ruling is:
column6: Trading is permissible irrespective of whether the certificate holders are owners of the land or workers.
column7: Trading is permissible only if the buyer is another holder of the same Sukuk.
column8: Trading is permissible, since subscription has closed, the certificates have been allotted and the activity has commenced.
column9: Trading in these certificates is not permissible before the maturity of the fruits and plants.
column11: Per 5/2/17, where Musaqat holders act as workers, trading is not permissible before the maturity of the fruits and plants.

column5: The guarantee (performance deed) that the Institution may obtain from the customer regarding the good performance by the supplier of his contractual obligations:
column6: Is required in all Murabahah transactions, whether or not the customer has suggested a particular source of supply, and it lapses if the Murabahah contract is not executed or the item is destroyed.
column7: Is given by the customer in his personal capacity, not as purchase orderer or as agent of the Institution, so it remains valid even if the Murabahah contract is not executed.
column8: Covers the hazards that may affect the item, such as damage and destruction during a period of shipment or storage, and is given by the customer as purchase orderer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/5/1, the customer guarantees in his personal capacity and it survives non-execution; it applies only if he suggested the supplier; 2/5/2 bars hazard cover.

column5: When the employee accepts a period of delay for a pay that has to be settled in advance:
column6: Such acceptance is considered a respite which the employee has willingly granted to the employer, and can by no means be considered a right of the latter.
column7: The contract is converted into a deferred-payment contract that binds the employee for the rest of the hiring period, and the pay of later periods is also deferred.
column8: The employee becomes entitled to an increment in the pay for the delay.
column9: The employer becomes entitled to that delay as a contractual right, which the employee cannot withdraw.
column11: Per 6/2, the employee's acceptance of delay is a voluntary respite to the employer, not a right of the employer.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: For the revocation of the contract by the owner of a cooling-off option to be valid, it is not required that the other party know of the revocation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/7/2, the other party must know of the revocation for it to be valid.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for applying all the general rules for partnerships, especially the rules for 'Inan partnership, to diminishing partnerships is:
column6: That diminishing partnership is a form of ownership partnership, in which the partners share the assets but not the management of the business, and the client is therefore not obliged to purchase the units.
column7: That the client is in the position of a Mudarib, who manages the assets of the Institution for a share of the profit.
column8: To safeguard this form of partnership from becoming a mere interest-based financing transaction in which a client pays another party for his finance in addition to a share in income.
column9: That the Institution acts as an agent of the client in purchasing the asset and holds the asset on his behalf until the units are bought.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, applying 'Inan rules prevents diminishing Musharakah from becoming an interest-based financing.

column5: It is permissible to stipulate that the investment agent, in addition to his fee:
column6: Is entitled to all or part of any amount over and above the expected profit as a performance incentive.
column7: Is entitled to a guaranteed minimum return on the funds invested.
column8: Is entitled to all the profit of the investment, while the principal receives the capital.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/4, the agent may be given all or part of any profit above the expected profit as a performance incentive.

column5: Selling a commercial paper that has not become due for an amount that is more than its value involves:
column6: No Riba, since the buyer pays more than the value.
column7: Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl.
column8: Riba al-Fadl only.
column9: Riba al-Nasi'ah only.
column11: Per 6/2, selling it for more than its value is Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl; for a similar amount, Riba al-Nasi'ah.

column5: A holder of a utilization concession:
column6: Is entitled to undertake all the activities required for utilization, such as establishing refineries and treatment laboratories and acquiring transportation devices and facilities, and becomes the sole owner of such rights throughout the concession period.
column7: Is entitled only to extract the minerals; activities such as refining and transportation require separate concessions, and the licensee may not establish refineries or treatment laboratories or acquire transportation facilities without the approval of the State in each case.
column8: Shares these rights with other licensees in the same area.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/5, the holder may undertake all activities required for utilization and is the sole owner of such rights during the concession.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When remuneration for agency is not specified, the agency is considered non-paid and the agent is not entitled to any remuneration.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2/4, an unspecified fee may be measured by the prevailing market rate for similar effort.

column5: The lease expires upon the expiry of its term, but it may remain operative for a good cause, such as the late harvesting period for land leased for crop cultivation. In this case, the lease continues:
column6: With the rental based on the prevailing market value.
column7: Without any rental, since the delay is for a good cause.
column8: With a rental to be determined by the lessor alone.
column9: With the rental specified in the original contract.
column11: Per 7/2/6, a lease extended for good cause (e.g. late harvest) continues at the prevailing market rental.

column5: If the Istisna'a contract is concluded with a condition that the production shall be carried out by the Institution using its own resources:
column6: The Institution may still assign the production to another manufacturer by way of Parallel Istisna'a, since such a condition does not bind it.
column7: The Institution may deliver items produced by other parties that existed before the contract was concluded.
column8: The Institution has to abide by this condition and may not assign the production to another entity.
column9: The condition is void, since the Institution is not itself a manufacturer and cannot bind itself to produce.
column11: Per 3/1/4, if own-resource production is stipulated, the Institution must comply and may not assign production to another entity.

column5: Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Murabahah and Diminishing Musharakah are cited as examples of combined contracts that take the form of:
column6: Contracts that reveal contradiction with regard to their underlying rulings and ultimate goals, which are permitted only when each of them is concluded for a separate counter value and at different times.
column7: A single lump sum counter value for all the combined contracts.
column8: An exhaustive contractual statement comprising a number of successive parts and stages, which finally lead to realization of the desire of the two parties to conclude the deal.
column9: Muwata`ah to form up Riba tricks.
column11: Per 2/2/4, these transactions are combined contracts in the form of an exhaustive statement of successive parts and stages.

column5: A private employee, who works for and under the supervision of a single employer:
column6: Is absolutely responsible for damage to what he works on, like the shared employee.
column7: Should be informed about the work, its type and specifications only, without the hiring period.
column8: Has no right to work, at the same time, for anyone else, except on permission of his employer.
column9: May work for others at the same time, as long as his work for the employer is not affected.
column11: Per 4/3, a private employee may not work for anyone else at the same time without his employer's permission; a shared employee has no such restriction.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: It is permissible to have two or more options to reconsider in one contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2, two or more options to reconsider may be combined in one contract, as this does not contradict their prerequisites.

column5: ………… is anyone who undertakes the investment of funds of another person with the latter's permission:
column6: The third-party obligor.
column7: The investment manager.
column8: Rab Al Maal.
column9: The service agent.
column11: Per 2/1, the investment manager is anyone who invests another person's funds with his permission.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: Purchasing gold, silver or currencies with a debit card satisfies the condition of taking possession, because an accounting entry is considered to be constructive possession.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis (item 7) and IIFA Resolution 53, an accounting entry is constructive possession, satisfying the possession condition.

column5: The basis for regarding a Mudarabah contract initially as non-binding is that the Mudarib uses the capital provider's funds with his consent in a relationship in which he is just an agent, and an agency contract is not binding.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the Mudarib is just an agent, and agency is non-binding.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: When a well-established benchmark/index mutually agreed upon between the parties is used in determining the profit during the undertaking stage (Wa'd) or when concluding the transaction:
column6: The total price, the dates and amounts of the installments, if any, must be stipulated and must not vary with the movement of the benchmark/index.
column7: The installments may be adjusted periodically according to the movement of the benchmark/index, provided the total price is stipulated.
column8: The benchmark may be used only in the undertaking stage, and not when concluding the transaction.
column9: The total price may be left open and determined at maturity according to the benchmark/index agreed upon.
column11: Per 6/2, a benchmark may be used at Wa'd or contract stage, but the total price and installments are fixed and do not vary with it.

column5: Default in payment is established when:
column6: A court declares the debtor to be in default.
column7: The debtor fails to pay on the due date, even without any demand for payment, provided he has not proved that he is insolvent and no grace period was agreed.
column8: Following a normal demand for payment, a debtor who has not proved that he is insolvent fails to settle the debt on its due date.
column9: The debtor fails to pay two instalments after being notified.
column11: Per 2/6, default is established when, after a normal demand, a debtor not proven insolvent fails to pay on the due date.

column5: An IFI sold a car to a customer by Murabahah on deferred payment, stipulated that the customer mortgage the car to it after taking possession, and that the customer appoint the IFI as an agent to sell the car and repay the debt out of its value in case of default, without resorting to judiciary. Later, the customer wished to revoke this agency. The ruling is:
column6: The customer does not have the right to retreat from such agency once agreed upon.
column7: The stipulation is void, because the seller may not stipulate that the buyer mortgage the sold item to him.
column8: The customer may revoke the agency at any time, because agency is a non-binding contract.
column9: The customer may revoke the agency, provided that he pays part of the debt.
column11: Per 3/1/4 and 3/2/7, such stipulations are valid and the mortgagor may not retreat from the agency to sell once agreed upon.

column5: The insurance policy expires:
column6: On complete damage of the insured property in property insurance, and the participant's entitlement to indemnity is thereby nullified.
column7: On death of the insured person in persons' insurance, and the beneficiary's entitlement to the insurance benefits is thereby nullified, since the contribution paid for the period is forfeited in favour of the other participants of the fund and no part of the investment balance is payable to the heirs.
column8: At the end of the period agreed upon; in property insurance, it may be stipulated that the contract is automatically renewable unless the participant informs the company, within a specific period before expiry, of his desire not to renew.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 13/1, the policy ends at the agreed term and may auto-renew; per 13/3-13/4 damage or death do not nullify entitlements.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Paid agency is permissible in Shari'ah:
column6: Provided that the agent guarantees to the principal the asset in question.
column7: Whether remuneration is explicitly stipulated in the contract or ascertained in accordance with customary practices, as when the agent does not provide such service except for remuneration.
column8: Only if remuneration is a lump sum, and not a share of a specific amount of income.
column9: Only if remuneration is explicitly stipulated in the contract at the time of its conclusion, and is a definite lump sum fixed before the agent commences his work, since an unspecified remuneration entails Gharar and invalidates the agency.
column11: Per 4/2/1, paid agency is permissible whether the fee is stipulated or established by custom (agent who serves only for a fee).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Where the percentage of pure gold in an alloy mixed with substances other than silver is 50% or less:
column6: It is not deemed a sale of gold in any case, and spot exchange is not required even if it is sold for currencies.
column7: It is deemed a sale of gold only if it is sold for gold, in which case equality in the weight of the two alloys is required.
column8: It is not deemed a sale of gold, unless it is sold for gold, silver or currencies, in which case spot exchange of the counter-values is required.
column9: It is deemed a sale of gold, and equality in weight is required whatever the counter-value.
column11: Per 3/3/1/1 (second type), it is not a sale of gold, but spot exchange is required if it is sold for gold, silver or currencies.

column5: In an unrestricted Mudarabah, the wide range of trade or business freedom given to the Mudarib:
column6: Must be exercised only in accordance with the interests of the parties and the objectives of the Mudarabah contract, which is making profit, so his actions must follow business customs relating to Mudarabah.
column7: Is absolute, so the Mudarib may also make gifts and charitable donations out of the Mudarabah funds, and may delegate the management of the funds to others without the consent of the capital provider, since the Mudarib acts as an owner of the capital.
column8: Is limited to the location of the capital provider and to the type of business he conducts.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 5/1, unrestricted freedom must serve the parties' interests and the profit objective, per business customs; gifts are barred (9/6).

column5: If the Waqf was created with an option to rescind that is held by a third party:
column6: Its creation is contingent upon the authorization of the holder of the option; if authorization is granted, the Waqf takes effect from the date of the authorization.
column7: The Waqf is null and void from the start in all cases, because the Waqf asset is tied up with a third-party right.
column8: The Waqf is valid and enforceable, and the option of the third party lapses by the creation of the Waqf.
column9: Its creation is contingent upon the authorization of the holder of the option; if authorization is granted, the Waqf takes effect from its creation, otherwise it is null and void from the start.
column11: Per 2/4/5/2, such Waqf depends on the option holder's authorization; if granted it takes effect from creation, else it is void ab initio.

column5: A capital provider gave a Mudarib 800,000 on the basis that the Mudarib receives 40% of the Mudarabah profit. The Mudarib commingled 200,000 of his own funds with the Mudarabah funds, and the total profit realised was 100,000. The total profit due to the Mudarib is:
column11: Per 8/9: 20,000 for his own 20% of funds, plus 40% of the remaining 80,000 (32,000) = 52,000.

column5: It is valid to create a Waqf over an asset which a third party may claim under pre-emption (shufʿa) rights, and if the asset is granted to that party, the Waqif must deploy the received consideration in a similar type of Waqf.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/5/3, such Waqf is valid; if the asset goes to the pre-emptor, the consideration is deployed in a similar Waqf.

column5: If the transferor dies or a transferor Institution is liquidated after a Hawalah transaction:
column6: The transferee must recover his debt from the transferor's estate.
column7: The Hawalah is not annulled; the transferee is the sole owner of the debt payable by the payer, which cannot be included in the transferor's assets distributed among creditors pro rata.
column8: The Hawalah remains valid, but the transferred debt is included in the transferor's assets distributed among creditors.
column9: The Hawalah is annulled, and the transferee shares pro rata with the other creditors of the transferor in the estate or liquidation proceeds, recovering only a proportion of his debt after the liquidation costs are deducted.
column11: Per 10/1, the Hawalah survives; the transferred debt belongs solely to the transferee and is outside the transferor's estate.

column5: An online contract in which the offer is addressed to the public in general, with uniform details, and in which the offering party alone stipulates the terms and conditions, is considered as an "adhesion contract" ('Uqud al-Iz'an) when:
column6: The price in the contract comprises excessive injustice for the adhering party, even if the commodity is available from many suppliers and the adhering party can easily dispense with it.
column7: The other party is an individual and the offering party is an institution, whatever the commodity or its availability from other providers.
column8: It relates to a commodity or usufruct that nobody can do without, and the offering party has actual and legal monopoly or faces only a meager degree of competition in supplying it.
column9: It is concluded online, whatever the commodity or usufruct involved, because the adhering party cannot negotiate its terms.
column11: Per 8/3/1, such a contract is an adhesion contract when it concerns an indispensable commodity or usufruct supplied under monopoly or meager competition.

column5: The right of the State to regulate survey or exploration of minerals, water and the like by offering exclusive rights of utilization stems from:
column6: The State's ownership of all lands in its territory.
column7: The view of the Hanbalis permitting Mudarabah on income-generating assets, which allows the State to entrust such assets to private parties against a share of the output and to fix the profit share at its discretion.
column8: The rule that the Kharaj imposed on land is one fifth.
column9: Such an act leads to realization of public interest and prevention of disputes, a reasoning of the Fuqaha who argue that development of wasteland requires State permission.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the State's regulation serves public interest and prevents disputes, as with State permission for wasteland development.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: Cooling-off options to revoke may be stipulated in credit facility agreements to be triggered by:
column6: Events of default relating to solvency.
column7: Potential insolvency, before it occurs.
column8: Breach of a restrictive covenant in the contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 11/1, the triggers may be events of default relating to solvency, potential insolvency before it occurs, or breach of a restrictive covenant.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When more than one agent are appointed in the same contract:
column6: Each of them has the right to discharge his responsibilities independently, unless the principal requires joint action from them.
column7: None of them should become the sole decision-maker unless with the authorization of the principal.
column8: The appointment of the later agent revokes the agency of the earlier one.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/5, agents appointed in the same contract may not act alone without the principal's authorization; (a) applies to separate contracts.

column5: It is not permissible for the Institution, as far as possible, to present bills of exchange that it undertakes to pay to clients whose debts to the Institution are represented by these bills, so as to get them discounted by other banks.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/7/5, the Institution should not, as far as possible, enable discounting of such bills by other banks.

column5: In subscription arrangement services, the Institution:
column6: May arrange, and receive fees for, engaging a third party to underwrite the subscription.
column7: May underwrite the subscription itself, without charging any fees for the mere act of underwriting.
column8: May charge the actual expenses it incurs in providing other services like conducting studies or marketing the shares.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/3/2, all three are true: fees for arranging a third-party underwriter, no fee for its own underwriting, actual costs for other services.

column5: The underwriter of a share subscription is entitled to receive consideration for:
column6: The guarantee of the subscription per se, provided the shares are underwritten at the offer value.
column7: The risk it assumes in purchasing the unsubscribed shares at the offer value after the expiry of the offer period.
column8: A service other than the guarantee, such as conducting a feasibility study or marketing the shares.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/7/2, consideration is allowed only for services other than the guarantee, such as feasibility studies or marketing.

column5: Finance can be extended to clients through other financing operations which include, among others, Qard Hasan, customer overdraft balances, letters of guarantee and letters of credit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/7, other financing operations include Qard Hasan, customer overdraft balances, letters of guarantee and letters of credit.

column5: Stipulating that a debtor pay compensation in case of default, or having a legal claim for compensation against him, is not permitted whether such arrangements are made at the beginning of the contract or on its maturity, because:
column6: This would constitute Riba, and any such stipulation or arrangement is null and void.
column7: The amount of compensation is unknown at the time of contracting, which involves Gharar.
column8: The debtor may be insolvent at maturity.
column9: It amounts to a sale of debt to a party other than the debtor.
column11: Per the basis, compensation for late payment is Riba and the stipulation is null and void (IIFA Resolution 51).

column5: The permissibility of remunerating the licensee in a construction concession by allowing him to benefit from the project before handing it over to the licensor relates to the fact that:
column6: The rent in Ijarah must always be in money.
column7: In Istisna'a, temporary benefiting from the product may constitute the price of its production, since the price can be either money or usufruct, including that of the product itself.
column8: The licensee is the owner of the land on which the project is built, and the usufruct of the project therefore belongs to him by right of ownership and not as a price for the construction, so that he may retain the project permanently.
column9: The project is treated as a Waqf during the concession period.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 6/3/1, in Istisna'a the price may be usufruct, including temporary use of the product itself.

column5: An IFI financed a customer and took his land as a mortgage. The mortgage contract included a clause that, on default, the land becomes the property of the IFI in settlement of the debt. This clause is:
column6: Permissible, provided that the value of the land at the time of contract equals the amount of the debt, so that neither party suffers any loss from the transfer.
column7: Permissible, provided that a court approves the transfer of ownership, in which case the land is deemed sold to the IFI for the amount of the debt at the date of default, whatever its market value.
column8: Impermissible, since the mortgagee may not stipulate that he owns the asset on default; he may only purchase it from the mortgagor at market value and take his entitled portion.
column9: Permissible, because the two parties agreed upon it and Muslims are bound by their conditions, and the mortgagee thereby avoids the cost of selling the land on default.
column11: Per 3/4/2, the mortgagee may not stipulate ownership on default; he may buy the asset at market value and take what he is owed.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the transferability of the option to revoke for breach of description to heirs is that it falls in the category of physical asset ('Ayn) ownership.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/5, it transfers to heirs because it falls under ownership of a physical asset ('Ayn).

column5: The obligatory Zakah on 130 goats (freely grazing most of the year) is:
column6: 2 goats.
column7: 1 goat.
column8: 3 goats.
column9: Nothing, until the number reaches 200.
column11: Per the table in 11/3, 121 to 200 goats require 2 goats.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: If the party deceived by price gouging accepts the contract:
column6: He is entitled to compensation equal to the excess over the market price.
column7: He may accept the contract and claim a refund of the excess from the seller, who may not refuse it if the excess is proved by experts.
column8: He is not entitled to compensation, but the parties may agree upon an indemnification amount instead of revocation.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/4/1-4/4/2, accepting means no compensation claim, though the parties may agree on indemnification instead of revocation.

column5: It is permissible to stipulate in an investment agreement that the investment manager is unconditionally liable for any loss of capital, provided that the capital provider accepts a smaller share of the profit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/6, the manager may not be made liable for loss other than for wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In internal conversion, if the bank's liabilities are in the form of payment of interest:
column6: The bank may pay the interest and recover it from the shareholders.
column7: The bank should employ all lawful means to avoid paying such interest, a rule that does not apply to the principal of the debts or loans; it should not pay interest except in dire need.
column8: The bank must pay the interest, since it is a contractual obligation concluded before conversion.
column9: The bank should avoid paying both the interest and the principal amounts of the loans, since both are tainted by the prohibited contract, and should seek to be released from them by all lawful means.
column11: Per 9/1/1, the bank avoids paying interest by lawful means (not the principal), paying it only out of dire need.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If services such as safekeeping, allocating, minting and physical delivery of gold involve exchange of gold for gold, the fee charged shall be based on the actual expenses.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/7, fees for such services are permissible, but where gold is exchanged for gold they must be based on actual expenses.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When somebody acted on behalf of another and later on came to know that he is an agent of the latter, the preceding act falls under the agency contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/2, the agent must know of his status; the preceding act does not fall under the agency contract.

column5: Regarding insurance of the item at the stage of the Institution's acquisition of ownership of the asset:
column6: Agency in carrying out the procedures of obtaining insurance cover is permitted, but the Institution must bear the cost.
column7: The Institution may not include the expenses of insurance in the Murabahah cost price, even if the insurance is on the basis of Takaful.
column8: The insurance lies with the customer as purchase orderer before the item is sold to him.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2/7, insurance agency is allowed but the Institution bears the cost; per 3/2/6, it owns and insures the item and may add the cost to the price.

column5: The mortgagor can mortgage to the mortgagee an asset which the mortgagee keeps as a trust, such as deposited or lent assets and investment accounts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/5, the mortgagor may mortgage an asset held by the mortgagee on trust, e.g. deposited or lent assets and investment accounts.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: When loss is incurred in one Mudarabah operation of the investment accounts:
column6: It can be covered from the profits of other operations, and any excess from capital, since what matters is the final result of liquidation at the end of the financial period.
column7: It has to be borne by the Mudarib, because it managed the operation.
column8: It has to be borne only by the holders of the accounts whose funds were invested in that operation, at the time of the loss, and may not be offset against the profits of other operations.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 3/2/1, a loss on one operation is covered from other operations' profits, then from capital; the end-of-period result is decisive.

column5: The debtor may, entirely at his own discretion without any condition or customary practice, pay an additional amount when settling the debt, and this is part of good settlement.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis (b), a discretionary extra payment without condition or custom is good settlement, as the Prophet did.

column5: ………… are certificates of equal value representing undivided shares in ownership of tangible assets, usufruct and services or (in the ownership of) the assets of particular projects or special investment activity:
column6: Shares of joint stock companies.
column7: Certificates of investment funds and portfolios.
column8: Bonds.
column9: Investment Sukuk.
column11: Per 2, this is the definition of Investment Sukuk, so designated to distinguish them from shares and bonds.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: The card that is issued to a customer with available funds in his account, and confers on him the right to withdraw cash or to pay for goods or services up to the limit of the available funds, the debit to his account being immediate and without providing him with any credit, is:
column6: The charge card.
column7: The debit card.
column8: The credit card.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/1/1-2/1/2, the debit card is limited to the available balance, with immediate debit and no credit.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: ………… refer to those incidents which occur suddenly and cause significant influence on commitments that are properly stipulated:
column6: Defects of will.
column7: Termination due to excuses.
column8: Termination of commitments on mutual consent.
column9: Contingent incidents.
column11: Per 2, contingent incidents occur suddenly and significantly affect properly stipulated commitments; defects of will exist from the time of signing.

column5: The subject-matter of elimination is the prohibited income specific to the share, whether or not the profits have been distributed and whether or not the corporation has declared a profit or suffered a loss.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/4/6/2, elimination applies regardless of distribution of profits or the corporation's profit or loss.

column5: An offer for the sale of currency made for a stated period, which is transmitted by one of the prescribed means of communication:
column6: Is not binding on the offeror, who may withdraw it at any time before acceptance, unless the offeree has already begun to take possession of the countervalues.
column7: Remains binding on the offeror during that period, and the contract is completed upon acceptance by the offeree, possession being taken afterwards within the customary settlement period.
column8: Is binding on both the offeror and the offeree from the time it is received.
column9: Remains binding on the offeror during that period; the contract is not completed until the offeree accepts and both parties take possession (actual or constructive) of the countervalues.
column11: Per 2/8/2, the offer binds the offeror for the period; the contract completes only on acceptance plus possession by both parties.

column5: If the seller offers delivered goods of a quality superior to that required by the contractual specifications:
column6: The buyer must accept them even if the inferior description specified in the contract is vital, provided the seller does not seek a higher price.
column7: The buyer must accept them and pay the seller the difference in value, unless the inferior description specified in the contract is itself deemed vital.
column8: The buyer may refuse them in all cases, since they differ from the specifications, and the seller must then deliver goods of the contractual quality.
column9: The buyer must accept them, provided the seller does not seek a higher price, unless the (inferior) description in the contract is itself deemed vital.
column11: Per 5/2, the buyer must accept better quality at no extra price, unless the contractual (inferior) description is itself vital.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, swap contracts for the dividends of shares include Riba in both its forms if:
column6: The shares are of a corporation whose activity is impermissible.
column7: The contracts involve two different currencies.
column8: The dividends are paid annually.
column9: The contracts involve the same currency.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/14, same-currency swaps involve both forms of Riba; different currencies involve Riba al-Nasi'ah alone.

column5: Under the Standard on 'Arboun (Earnest Money), it is not permissible:
column6: To negotiate/trade options arising from payments of 'Arboun (Earnest Money).
column7: For the buyer to stipulate in the contract a refund of the earnest money in specific situations, such as his failure to obtain licenses from the relevant authorities.
column8: For the buyer to take delivery of the sale item during the option period.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 9/4, options arising from 'Arboun may not be traded; a refund stipulation (item 10) and delivery during the option period (item 7) are permissible.

column5: Debts owed by the Institution which have arisen from obtaining non-zakatable fixed assets:
column6: Should be deducted from the Zakah base if they fall due within one year.
column7: Should not be deducted from the Zakah base.
column8: Should be deducted from the Zakah base after adding back the value of the fixed assets.
column9: Should be deducted from the Zakah base in full.
column11: Per 6/2/2, debts from acquiring non-zakatable fixed assets are not deducted; per 6/2/1, debts from acquiring zakatable trade assets are deducted.

column5: When a debt is mortgaged, the mortgagee becomes more entitled to it than anyone else.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/12, once a debt is mortgaged the mortgagee becomes more entitled to it than anyone else.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: ………… is the sale in which the seller throws a stone and the buyer has to accept the item on which the stone falls:
column6: Bay' al-Munabadhah.
column7: Bay' al-Juzaf.
column8: Bay' al-Hasah.
column9: Bay' al-Thunya.
column11: Per 5/1/2, Bay' al-Hasah is sale by stone throwing; in Bay' al-Munabadhah the seller throws one of the commodities to the buyer.

column5: Among the forms that are not permitted is the customer of an Institution entering into currency trading for an amount exceeding what he owns, using credit facilities granted by the Institution which handles the currency trading.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/12/1, trading beyond one's own funds using the dealing Institution's credit facilities is not permitted.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the payer must consent in the unrestricted Hawalah because:
column6: He might not want a third party to pay the debt on his behalf, and may therefore be asked to give security to the payer or to refuse the payment.
column7: People differ in various aspects when it comes to payment of debts.
column8: The effect of the Hawalah is to make the payer liable for payment, and there is no liability without an acceptance of it.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis (c), the payer becomes liable and no liability exists without acceptance; (a) and (b) are the reasons for the other parties.

column5: The issuance of shares is permissible:
column6: If the objectives for which the corporation was established are permissible according to the Shari'ah.
column7: Absolutely, irrespective of the objectives of the corporation, since shares are merely a form of partnership.
column8: Only if the full value of the shares is paid at the time of subscription.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/1, issuance is permissible if the corporation's objectives are permissible; payment in instalments is also allowed (2/5).

column5: A customer may use the institution as an agent for concluding contracts such as sale, purchase, and lease contracts, against a fee payable to the institution.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2, the institution may act as contracting agent for sale, purchase and lease contracts against a fee.

column5: A customer signed a contract with a dealer to buy a fleet of trucks and paid part of the price. He then asked an IFI to pay the rest by taking over (assignment of) his contract with the dealer, after which the IFI would sell the trucks to him by Murabahah on deferred payment. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because the customer has not yet paid the full price, so the sale is not yet concluded and the supplier retains ownership of the trucks until payment, and the customer is not entitled to them before then.
column7: Impermissible, because a contract executed between the customer and the supplier may not be assigned to the Institution, and any prior contractual relationship must be genuinely excluded.
column8: Permissible, provided the IFI takes actual possession of the trucks before selling them to the customer.
column9: Permissible, provided the dealer is not wholly or majority-owned by the customer.
column11: Per 2/2/2, any prior contract between customer and supplier must be genuinely excluded, and assigning it to the Institution is barred.

column5: An IFI concluded an Istisna'a with a customer to build a hospital for 10 million, estimating its cost at 8.5 million. It then concluded a Parallel Istisna'a with a contractor and later obtained a discount from him, so that its actual cost became 7.6 million. The customer requested a corresponding discount. The correct ruling is:
column6: The customer is entitled to a reduction of the price in proportion to the discount, as in Murabahah, since the cost became known after the contract.
column7: The saving of 0.9 million must be shared equally between the IFI and the customer, since both parties benefited from the Parallel Istisna'a.
column8: The IFI is not obliged to give a discount, and the customer is not entitled to the amount the IFI has gained over the estimated cost.
column9: The customer is entitled to a discount of 0.9 million, i.e. the full saving over the estimated cost, because the contract price was based on that estimate.
column11: Per 3/2/6, the IFI need not pass on savings or a discount from the parallel contractor, since the two contracts are independent.

column5: The commitments of the employer include:
column6: Provision of facilities/requirements to the employee in all cases, even if the work does not require them and they are not stipulated in the contract.
column7: Payment of the pay as agreed; in the absence of agreement, after rendering the complete service, or on expiry of the hiring period in case of private employment.
column8: Allowing the private employee to be absent during the hiring period whenever he wishes.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/2/1, the employer pays as agreed (else after full service or at period end); facilities only if the work requires or the contract stipulates.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: With regard to termination of commitment due to excuses, when the emergence of an incidental excuse in Ijarah leads to abnormal harm:
column6: The harmed party has the right to terminate the contract.
column7: The party who encounters the incident may terminate the contract even if acceptability of his excuse is doubtful.
column8: If acceptability of the excuse is doubtful, the contract remains binding and the issue may not be referred to law.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 5/4, the harmed party may terminate; the other party only if his excuse is obvious, and a doubtful excuse goes to mutual agreement or law.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: Stipulation of cooling-off options applies only to binding contracts, because non-binding contracts are by their nature revocable by one or both parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, cooling-off options apply only to binding contracts, since non-binding ones are revocable by nature.

column5: In a contract of loan (Qard):
column6: The expenses for delivery and recovery, and the expenses pertaining to ascertainment through one of the customary units of measure, shall be borne by the borrower.
column7: The expenses for drawing up documents, promissory notes and title deeds required for the loan shall be borne by the lender, since he benefits from the documentation.
column8: The expenses of recovery only are borne by the borrower, while the expenses of delivery are borne by the lender.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/1 and 4/2/2, the borrower bears expenses of delivery, recovery and ascertainment as well as documentation of the loan.

column5: The institution may conduct feasibility studies or other studies relating to the issuance of shares:
column6: Only free of charge.
column7: Only if it also underwrites the issue.
column8: Only against a fee equal to the actual cost of the studies.
column9: Against a fee or free of charge.
column11: Per 2/4/1, the institution may conduct such studies against a fee or free of charge.

column5: The rules of Sharikat al-'Inan apply to the stock company except:
column6: On the requirement that losses be borne in proportion to the shares in capital, and not in any other ratio.
column7: On the limited liability of the shareholders and on the fact that the company cannot be unilaterally terminated by one party or a minority of shareholders.
column8: On the manner of distributing profits between the shareholders, according to the percentages agreed in the articles of association and approved by the general assembly.
column9: On the prohibition of guaranteeing the capital of the shareholders by the company or by any other partner.
column11: Per 4/1/1/1, 'Inan rules apply except for shareholders' limited liability and that one party or a minority cannot terminate it.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the rule that the subject-matter of Qard be a fungible item is that:
column6: Only such an item can be returned by the borrower, and fungible items are compensated through similar substitutes in usurpation and destruction.
column7: Fungible items are always money.
column8: The lender must be able to sell the item to a third party.
column9: Non-fungible items cannot be possessed by the borrower, and the lender therefore has no right to claim them back except by their value in cash at the date of the contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, only a fungible item can be returned by a similar one, as in compensation for usurpation and destruction.

column5: It is impermissible for the Institution to obtain commission for offering credit facilities (i.e., against allocating and specifying the limit of the facility), because:
column6: Such commission is charged only when the deal is finalized, whereas the facility is usually granted free of charge.
column7: The client has not benefited from the credit study, which is performed for the benefit of the Institution alone.
column8: The mere willingness to enter into a lending and borrowing transaction does not justify remuneration.
column9: Such commission must be included in the cost of preparing the contracts, which is borne by the client.
column11: Per 5/3/1/2, offering commission is impermissible because the mere indication of willingness to lend does not justify remuneration.

column5: Al-Muslam Fihi may be secured by a mortgage or a guarantee or any other permissible means of securing payment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 3/3.

column5: A company obtained a piece of land on lease from the State, against an undertaking to construct a toll bridge on it and to hand the bridge over to the State after 25 years. The Shari'ah adaptation of this contract is:
column6: Ijarah, in which the rent is the project itself, which will be handed over to the State at the end of the contractual period.
column7: Mudarabah, in which the capital is the land and the profit is shared between the State and the company in proportion to the tolls collected.
column8: Ju'alah, in which the State is the Ja'il.
column9: Istisna'a, in which the price is the right to utilize the project.
column11: Per 6/2/2, where land is leased from the State against handing over the project later, it is Ijarah and the rent is the project itself.

column5: ………… is the Waqf whose revenue and benefit are for the progeny or relatives of the Waqif or other specific persons, and it includes Self Waqf (Waqf on oneself):
column6: Private or Dynasty Waqf.
column7: Investment Waqf.
column8: Charitable Waqf.
column9: Joint Waqf.
column11: Per 2/2/1/2, Private or Dynasty Waqf is for the progeny, relatives or other specific persons, including Self Waqf.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: In the context of the Standard on Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions, profit means:
column6: The amount distributed to investment accountholders after the deduction of reserves.
column7: The methods used to determine the amount of profit in the institution's financing and investment operations.
column8: The amount generated in excess of the original capital or cost in financing and investment operations.
column9: The excess of the institution's total revenues over its total expenses for the financial period.
column11: Per item 2, profit is the excess over original capital or cost.

column5: The issuer of the certificates is permitted to offer some tangible or personal guarantees:
column6: To guarantee the nominal value of the certificates in all cases.
column7: With respect to its wrongful acts or negligence.
column8: To guarantee a fixed percentage of profit, provided that the guarantee is free of charge.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/8/7, the issuer may offer tangible or personal guarantees only for its wrongful acts or negligence, not for capital or a fixed profit.

column5: According to the Standard, Musharakah and Mudarabah, when used by the Institution as cash facilities:
column6: Are classified as incidental facilities, because they result in an incidental commitment owed by the Institution.
column7: Result in a debt owed by the client from the time the Institution presents the funds.
column8: Are not considered credit facilities, because the Institution presents funds in cash rather than in the form of an asset or usufruct.
column9: Do not result in a debt owed by the client except in case of transgression or negligence.
column11: Per 2/2/1, Musharakah and Mudarabah are cash facilities that do not result in a debt owed by the client except in case of transgression or negligence.

column5: According to traditional Fuqaha, the evidential value of attestation is stronger than that of written documentation, although in modern times paramount importance is given to written documentary evidence.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, traditional Fuqaha ranked attestation higher, while modern laws give paramount importance to written evidence.

column5: According to Shari'ah, online adhesion contracts:
column6: Are never binding on the adhering party, even if the price is fair and the terms entail no injustice, because the contract is concluded without negotiation and its terms are set unilaterally.
column7: Should be subject to state control so as to protect dealers by endorsing what is equitable and eliminating what is inequitable in these contracts, before launching them.
column8: Are impermissible, because the adhering party has no right to change their terms and conditions and cannot negotiate the price.
column9: Should be left to the offering party, provided that the adhering party may withdraw at any time, without any intervention of the state.
column11: Per 8/3/2, online adhesion contracts should be subject to state control, endorsing what is equitable and eliminating what is not, before launch.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for stipulating the ascertainment (setting aside) of movable property through customary units of measure for the realisation of possession is:
column6: The words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "He who buys food (wheat) is not to sell it until he has measured it."
column7: The tradition of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit: "Gold for gold, silver for silver ... from hand to hand."
column8: The verse: "No ground (of complaint) can there be against those who do good."
column9: The principle: "Gains are based on the bearing of costs."
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the hadith requiring measurement of food before resale shows possession here is by measure; other units follow by analogy.

column5: Intermingling the incomes of various Waqfs:
column6: Is not permitted, even if the disposal avenue of the Waqfs is the same, since each Waqf has a separate legal personality and its revenues may not be commingled in any manner.
column7: Is permitted absolutely whenever the overseer of the Waqfs is the same person, since the overseer is responsible for all of them and may therefore dispose of their revenues as one.
column8: Is permitted if their disposal avenue is the same and the purpose is to distribute the revenues to the same avenue, while each Waqf remains independent in its financial status, overseer's remuneration, and so on.
column9: Is permitted, and the intermingled Waqfs become one Waqf with one remuneration for the overseer, provided that the relevant authority approves the merger and the Waqif's conditions are respected, whatever the avenues.
column11: Per 9/9, incomes may be intermingled where the avenue is the same, yet each Waqf stays independent in finances, overseer remuneration, etc.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for prohibiting a partner in a contractual partnership (Sharikat al-Aqd) from undertaking to buy his partner's share at a predetermined price is:
column6: That it results in a deferred currency exchange, since the price of the share is payable in a currency different from the capital.
column7: That the partner is a third party with respect to his partner's share, and neither partner disposes of the other's share without his permission.
column8: That such an undertaking is tantamount to a contingent sale, since the price is determined before the performance date.
column9: That it contradicts the intended effect of profit and loss sharing, whereas market value reflects the partnership's profit or loss at execution.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/4/2, a fixed price defeats profit and loss sharing; market value reflects actual profit or loss.

column5: In the case of the Institution receiving a mortgage from the customer, the Institution is entitled to stipulate that the customer make an assignment to enable it to sell the mortgaged asset to recover the amount due without recourse to the judiciary.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the rule in 5/5.

column5: The reason why insurance expenses must be borne by the lessor is that the owner of the asset is responsible for insuring it, and the lessor is the owner.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 5/1/8.

column5: An IFI sold Sukuk to a bank at a spot price, and the bank gave a separate unilateral promise to resell them to the IFI at a spot price of 100 on a specified date. On that date the bank repudiated its promise, and the IFI had to purchase the same Sukuk in the market at 108. The IFI is entitled to claim:
column6: Nothing, since a unilateral promise does not give rise to any compensation.
column7: 8, the difference between the purchase price on the date the promise was to be performed and the promised price.
column8: 8, in addition to the profit the IFI expected to earn on the Sukuk had the bank honoured its promise to resell them on that date.
column9: 108, being the full price the IFI paid in the market.
column11: Per 5/1/7, for a promise to sell, actual damage is the purchase price on the performance date less the promised price; lost profit is excluded.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: In a spot contract, any delay in the delivery of an existing and ascertained commodity, or in the acceptance of the spot price, renders the contract invalid, even if the delay was not stipulated.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/4, an unstipulated delay in delivery of an existing, ascertained commodity or in accepting the spot price does not affect validity.

column5: The rate of Zakah applicable to the agricultural produce of partially irrigated lands is:
column11: Per 3/3 and 5/4/1: 10% for non-irrigated, 5% for irrigated, and three quarters of the tenth (7.5%) for partially irrigated lands.

column5: As a result of concluding an Istisna'a contract in the capacity of a producer or supplier, the Institution:
column6: Must assume liability for ownership risk and maintenance and insurance expenses prior to delivering the subject-matter to the ultimate purchaser.
