column7: May transfer to the manufacturer, in the Parallel Istisna'a, the risk arising from its obligations towards the customer.
column8: May stipulate in the Parallel Istisna'a, as purchaser, a penalty clause similar to, or different from, that stipulated by the customer in the first contract.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 7/3–7/4, the Institution bears ownership risk and costs before delivery and may set its own terms, but may not shift its risk to the manufacturer.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of the pledgee stipulating the right to utilize the pledged gold for its own benefit is:
column6: To avoid Gharar arising from the change in the market price of gold, since the pledgee could not know the value of the benefit he is utilizing.
column7: To prevent combining a loan and a sale in a single arrangement, as the stipulation renders the pledged asset a loan for which the pledgee is liable.
column8: That gold is a Ribawi item that cannot be used as a pledge, since a pledge of a Ribawi item requires spot exchange of the pledged gold and the debt.
column9: That the pledgee holds the gold in a fiduciary capacity, and a fiduciary may not benefit from the asset held, even with the pledgor's permission.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 7/1/4, such a stipulation turns the pledge into a loan, combining loan and sale in one arrangement.

column5: It is permitted to provide the cardholder, for free, with benefits permissible as per Shari'ah, such as:
column6: Air-miles, talk times, and free night stays at hotels.
column7: Receiving cash back as a percentage of the price of merchandise or services.
column8: Giving priority to the cardholder to get services.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/6/2, all of these are permissible free benefits (subject to 4/1/2 and 4/1/3).

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: In paid agency:
column6: Expenses such as those of transportation, storage, taxation, maintenance and insurance should not be stated in the contract as payable by the agent now or in the future.
column7: The agency is binding.
column8: It is permissible to leave remuneration undetermined and allow the agent to take an unspecified share from the entitlements of the principal.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per 5/1/1 such expenses may not be put on the paid agent, and per 4/3/2 paid agency is binding; (c) is barred by 4/2/3.

column5: The contractual relationships in Islamic insurance include:
column6: The Musharakah (partnership) among the participants.
column7: The relationship between the company and the policyholders' fund, which is a Wakalah relationship in regard to management, and a Mudarabah or investment agency relationship in regard to investment of the fund's assets.
column8: The relationship between the policyholders and the fund, which takes the form of donation commitment at the stage of making contributions, and indemnification commitment at the stage of providing compensation for injury.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1 to 4/3, these are the three contractual relationships in Islamic insurance.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Tawarruq deals concluded by the converting bank to acquire liquidity require that the commodity bought on a deferred payment basis be sold to a third party, other than the previous seller, for immediate payment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2/5, the commodity bought on deferred terms is sold for cash to a third party other than the original seller.

column5: In case of default by the employer in the settlement of any installment of the pay:
column6: It is permissible to stipulate that all other installments shall become due and eligible for premature settlement, though the employee does not own the prepaid installments finally until he completes the work of the whole hiring period.
column7: It is permissible to stipulate an increment in the pay agreed upon, as compensation to the employee.
column8: The contract may include a pledge by the employer to donate a percentage of the pay for charitable purposes, under the supervision of the Shari'ah Board of the institution.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 5/2/7, acceleration of installments may be stipulated; per 5/2/8, an increment is barred but a pledge to donate to charity is allowed.

column5: The issuance of the prospectus of Sukuk represents, in principle:
column6: The issuer's invitation to subscription, so that subscription represents an offer, and acceptance is the issuer's approval of the subscription.
column7: A binding promise by the issuer to allot the Sukuk to every subscriber.
column8: An acceptance, while the subscription represents the offer.
column9: An offer in all cases, while the subscription represents the acceptance, so that the contract is concluded as soon as the subscription is made and no allotment is required.
column11: Per 5/1/7, the prospectus is an invitation; subscription is the offer and the issuer's approval is acceptance, unless the prospectus expressly states it is an offer.

column5: The most important common characteristics among all well-known indices in the capital and commodity markets are:
column6: Transparency, liquidity and comprehensiveness.
column7: Objectivity, neutrality and stability.
column8: Accuracy, objectivity and transparency.
column9: Accuracy, liquidity and profitability.
column11: Per 3/2, the most important common characteristics of indices are accuracy, objectivity and transparency.

column5: A prize offered on financing, currency exchange services and fund transfers and awarded based on a draw is:
column6: Permissible, provided that no additional amount is charged on financing or services fees in return for the prize.
column7: Impermissible, because it is a benefit linked to a debt.
column8: Permissible only if the prize is awarded to every customer without a draw.
column9: Permissible, provided that the value of the prize does not exceed the fees charged for the service.
column11: Per 3/5/3, a draw-based prize on financing, exchange and transfers is permissible if nothing is added to financing or fees for the prize.

column5: One of the conditions for exempting participation or trading in shares of corporations whose primary activity is permissible but which borrow on interest is that the collective amount raised as loan on interest, whether long-term or short-term, does not exceed:
column6: 5% of the total income of the corporation.
column7: 50% of the market capitalization of the corporation.
column8: 30% of the market capitalization of the corporation.
column9: One-third of the total assets of the corporation.
column11: Per 3/4/2, interest-bearing borrowing must not exceed 30% of market capitalization, though borrowing on interest is itself prohibited.

column5: When investment agency is used for financing working capital as a substitute for an overdraft:
column6: The amount provided to the client is regarded as the institution's undivided share in the client's working capital, and losses occurring after the agency, if any, are borne by both parties on a pro-rata basis.
column7: The amount provided is the institution's share in the working capital, but losses occurring after the agency are borne by the client alone, since he is the agent.
column8: The amount provided is a loan to the client, repayable on demand together with a fixed return agreed upon in advance.
column9: The client may not use the withdrawn amount to settle his liabilities or pay his employees' salaries.
column11: Per 12/2, the amount is the institution's undivided share in working capital, and later losses are borne pro-rata.

column5: The condition that the holder of a utilization concession should sustain the activity in question originates from:
column6: The view of the Hanbalis permitting Mudarabah on income-generating assets like animals, which requires the manager to keep the capital productive throughout the contract period.
column7: The Shari'ah ruling on a person who retains a piece of wasteland for a period without developing it, as narrated from Umar Ibn Al-Khattab.
column8: A resolution of the Al Baraka Seminar on Istisna'a.
column9: The rule that the Kharaj imposed on land is one fifth.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/6, it derives from the ruling on retained but undeveloped wasteland narrated from Umar Ibn Al-Khattab.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for considering the Mudarib a trustee with respect to the Mudarabah funds is that:
column6: The Mudarib has provided guarantees that are adequate and enforceable, which the capital provider may enforce at any time, and holds the funds as a trustee for that reason.
column7: The Mudarib owns the Mudarabah funds once they are put at his disposal, and holds them as a trustee of his own property.
column8: The Mudarib uses another person's money with his consent and both share the benefits; a trustee is not liable for losses, which are borne by the Mudarabah funds.
column9: The Mudarabah contract is binding once the work has commenced, and the Mudarib therefore holds the funds for the whole term.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, he uses another's money with consent for shared benefit, so losses fall on the Mudarabah funds.

column5: The ruling that the period of hiring should be specified stems from the fact that:
column6: Hiring of persons is judged by analogy to Salam, in which the date of delivery must be known to the two parties, and the price is paid at the session.
column7: Non-specification could result in prohibited Gharar and Jahalah which lead to dispute, and hiring of persons is in essence a sale of service/work.
column8: Hiring of persons is a non-binding contract that ends at the will of either party, and the period must be known so that the party can fix the notice of termination.
column9: A private employee cannot work for anyone else during the hiring period.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, unspecified periods cause Gharar and Jahalah leading to dispute; hiring of persons is in essence a sale of service/work.

column5: Maintenance or repair of the Waqf asset:
column6: Is borne by the Waqf beneficiaries in proportion to their shares.
column7: Is given priority over other expenditures, and maintenance and reconstruction of damaged Waqf assets need no express stipulation from the Waqif.
column8: Is given priority over other expenditures only if the Waqif has expressly stipulated it, otherwise it is subject to the discretion of the overseer.
column9: Comes after the disbursement of the shares of the Waqf beneficiaries.
column11: Per 4/1, maintenance and repair have priority over other expenditures and do not depend on the Waqif's express stipulation.

column5: It is not permissible to use as capital in a Mudarabah contract:
column6: Cash that is partially put at the disposal of the Mudarib.
column7: Tangible assets whose value is determined by experts.
column8: Tangible assets whose value is agreed upon by the contracting parties.
column9: A debt owed by the Mudarib or by another party to the capital provider.
column11: Per 7/3, a debt owed by the Mudarib or another party may not be Mudarabah capital; valued assets and partial delivery are allowed.

column5: Subsidiary and implicit contracts may be relieved from some prerequisites that underline the validity of contracts (such as offer and acceptance):
column6: When such relief is dictated by need or desire to achieve a permissible interest.
column7: Only when the relief is stipulated as a condition in the main contract.
column8: Only when the subsidiary contract is concluded for a separate value.
column9: In all cases, without any restriction.
column11: Per 5/2/5, such relief is allowed when dictated by need or the desire to achieve a permissible interest.

column5: Whenever a Mudarabah operation incurs losses:
column6: The losses are borne by the Mudarib up to the amount of his share of profits in previous periods, which he must refund to the capital provider.
column7: The losses are immediately deducted from the capital and may not be set against future profits of the Mudarabah operations.
column8: Such losses are to be compensated by the profits of future operations, and the losses brought forward are set against future profits.
column9: The losses are shared equally between the capital provider and the Mudarib, whatever their shares of profit.
column11: Per 8/7, losses are compensated by future profits; distribution depends on the final result at liquidation.

column5: An IFI issues a card under which purchases are established as an interest-free loan owed to it. On the settlement date, if the cardholder lacks liquidity, the IFI executes Murabaha-based Tawarruq as agent of the cardholder to settle the loan, leaving him with Murabaha instalments that exceed the loan amount. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: It is permitted, since the Tawarruq is executed through agency (wakālah) on behalf of the cardholder, who bears the risk of the commodity and the cost of its sale, so no qalb al-dayn arises.
column7: It is permitted, provided the Murabaha profit does not exceed the prevailing market rate.
column8: It is not permitted to design the card in this way, as it is a rollover of the loan liability (qalb al-dayn) via Tawarruq resulting in a debt more than the base loan.
column9: It is permitted, since the cardholder has the option to settle the amount out of his own liquidity, and he is not obliged to resort to Tawarruq if he has funds available.
column11: Per 6/3/2, rolling over the card loan via Tawarruq into a larger debt (qalb al-dayn) is not permitted.

column5: An IFI granted a customer a Qard Hasan of USD 20,000, on condition that the customer leases from the IFI one of its warehouses for one year at the market rental. This arrangement is:
column6: Impermissible, because it is not permissible to stipulate a contract of Ijarah or other commutative contract within the contract of Qard.
column7: Impermissible only if the rental exceeds the market rate.
column8: Permissible, because the rental is at the market rate and no excess is stipulated.
column9: Permissible, provided that the Ijarah contract is signed after the Qard amount is delivered and the rental does not include any excess over the market rate.
column11: Per 7, stipulating an Ijarah or any commutative contract within a Qard is not permissible, regardless of the rental.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: Permissible profit is that which results from:
column6: Any transaction based on mutual consent, even if the contract is invalid.
column7: A permissible transaction such as sale, lease or partnership, complying with Shari'ah rules on contracts.
column8: An interest-based contract, if the interest is incorporated into the price and disclosed to the customer.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/1-3/2, permissible profit comes from permissible, Shari'ah-compliant transactions; interest and invalid contracts yield impermissible profit.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of back-to-back loans extended on an equal footing is:
column6: That the loans constitute a loan against a loan (lend me and I lend you) with a condition for the lender's benefit.
column7: That the benefit extracted from the loan does not belong solely to the lender but to both parties, by analogy to Suftajah.
column8: That interest is calculated equally on both loans, so it cancels out.
column9: That the points are convertible into cash, ensuring fairness.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/6/3/2, the benefit accrues to both parties, as in Suftajah, unlike a conditional "lend me and I lend you".

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Acceptance of the Fatwa of a Shari'ah scholar whose knowledge is confined to only one branch of Fiqh, such as financial transactions in institutions, is based on:
column6: The principle of necessity, since scholars competent in all areas are scarce.
column7: The principle of Sadd al-Zara`i'.
column8: The viewpoint that Ijtihad (reasoning) and Fatwa may be made partially.
column9: The view that an opinion supported by a large group of scholars is more reliable.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it rests on the view that Ijtihad and Fatwa may be made partially.

column5: In a company limited by shares, the losses are borne:
column6: Equally between the managing partners and the sleeping partners, whatever their respective shares in the capital of the company or their liability.
column7: By the sleeping partners only, since they are the capital providers, while the managing partners bear no part of the loss.
column8: By the managing and sleeping shareholding partners according to their shares in the capital, and any excess losses by the managing partners.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/4/2/4, losses follow shares in capital, with any excess losses borne by the managing partners.

column5: When a client intends to purchase imported goods from the Institution through Murabahah financing of the documentary credit:
column6: The client should be the party who opens the credit in his own name and the Institution guarantees it for a fee.
column7: The Institution should lend the price of the goods to the client against a commission.
column8: The client should purchase the goods from the supplier and then sell them to the Institution.
column9: The Institution should be the party who purchases from the supplier, and then sells to the client through Murabahah.
column11: Per 3/5/2, the Institution must buy from the supplier and then sell to the client by Murabahah per the Murabahah standard.

column5: It is not permissible in Murabahah:
column6: To postpone the registration of the asset in the customer's name as a guarantee of the full payment of the selling price.
column7: For the Institution to receive authority from the customer to sell the asset in case the customer delays payment of the selling price.
column8: To stipulate that the ownership of the item will not be transferred to the customer until the full payment of the selling price.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/4, transfer of ownership may not be deferred to full payment; postponing registration and an authority to sell are allowed.

column5: Intangible rights prepared for trade, such as copyright, patent rights, trademarks and computer software, should be subject to Zakah on articles of trade.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/7, intangible rights prepared for trade are subject to Zakah on articles of trade (operational intangibles are not, 4/1).

column5: With respect to the termination of a Sharikah by one of the partners:
column6: A partner may withdraw only with the consent of all the other partners, and his withdrawal necessarily terminates the partnership for the remaining partners, unless the Sharikah contract is for an unlimited period or is renewed.
column7: Each partner is entitled to withdraw after giving his partners due notice, in which case he is entitled to his share, and his withdrawal does not necessitate the termination of the partnership of the remaining partners.
column8: The withdrawal of one partner automatically terminates the partnership of all the partners, and the obligations that took place before termination lapse.
column9: A partner may withdraw only at the expiry date of the Sharikah, even if the partners entered into no binding promise for its continuity.
column11: Per 3/1/6/1, any partner may withdraw after due notice and take his share; the others' partnership continues.

column5: There is no Shari'ah prohibition for either a private or a shared employee to receive 'Arboun (Earnest Money) at the time of signing the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/11, both private and shared employees may receive 'Arboun at the time of signing the contract.

column5: Fees on cards that are not restricted to the actual cost, and can be as per the agreement, include:
column6: Fees charged by the card issuer in cards that do not involve lending, such as fees on cash withdrawal, card issuance, renewal, replacement, limit increase or exchange rate.
column7: Fees of issuance and renewal charged by the card issuer in the credit card, which are linked to the loan.
column8: The cost of currency exchange charged by the card issuer in a lending-based card used in a currency other than the currency of the card.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/2/3, fees in non-lending cards are by agreement; loan-linked fees and exchange cost in lending cards are capped at actual cost (5/1/1).

column5: Regarding 'Arboun (Earnest Money):
column6: It is deducted from the zakatable assets of the buyer, while the seller pays Zakah on it as part of his zakatable assets, since he will get the amount whether the contract is concluded or not.
column7: Both the buyer and the seller pay Zakah on it.
column8: Neither the buyer nor the seller pays Zakah on it until the contract is concluded.
column9: It is deducted from the zakatable assets of the seller, while the buyer pays Zakah on it as part of his zakatable assets until the contract is concluded.
column11: Per 5/1/5/4, 'Arboun is deducted from the buyer's zakatable assets, and the seller pays Zakah on it as he gets it whether or not the contract is concluded.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, re-leasing an asset that is already leased out to an existing lessee is not suitable as an investment instrument, because:
column6: It constitutes an impermissible sale of the rent receivable pursuant to providing new lessees with an asset already leased out.
column7: It is a form of 'Inah, by varying the rent or the duration of the lease for the new lessees, which leads to a deferred sale of the rent.
column8: The lessee's ownership of the usufruct is limited by the lessor's conditions.
column9: It involves two sales in one sale.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, re-leasing an already leased asset amounts to an impermissible sale of rent receivable.

column5: At the time when the Institution appoints someone as its agent for the acquisition of the item, the two parties may agree that the agent acquire the item without disclosing the existence of the agency agreement. In this case:
column6: The agent becomes the owner of the item and must sell it to the Institution under a separate sale contract.
column7: The agent will act as principal in dealing with other parties and purchase directly in his name but on behalf of the Institution as principal; it is preferable that the agent's role be disclosed.
column8: The arrangement is impermissible, because the agency must always be disclosed to the supplier.
column9: The agent purchases in his own name and on his own behalf, and it is preferable that the agency not be disclosed to the supplier, in which case the Institution acquires title only when the agent delivers the item to it.
column11: Per 3/1/7, an undisclosed agent buys in his name on the Institution's behalf as principal, though disclosure of the agency is preferable.

column5: A private employee is responsible for damage:
column6: Only if the contract stipulates that he guarantees what he works on, even if there was no transgression.
column7: In no case, since he works under the supervision of the employer.
column8: Absolutely, as he has to guarantee what he is paid to work on, whether or not he was negligent.
column9: Only if it is due to his own transgression, negligence, or breach of a stipulated condition.
column11: Per 4/5, a private employee is not responsible for damage unless due to his transgression, negligence or breach of a stipulated condition.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: With respect to the right of occupancy:
column6: If the incumbent tenant agrees to hand over occupancy to a new tenant after the end of the lease period, he may take a payment for it, because he held the occupancy.
column7: In long-term lease contracts, the tenant may sub-lease or assign the property to another tenant in return for payment without the agreement of the owner, if the law of the jurisdiction permits it.
column8: In long-term lease contracts, the Shari'ah does not permit the tenant to sub-lease or assign the property to another tenant in return for payment except with the agreement of the owner.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/3, paid sub-leasing or assignment in long leases needs the owner's agreement, and no payment may be taken after the lease ends.

column5: The maintenance reserve retained from the Waqf income:
column6: Shall be retained every year even if the Waqif has not stipulated it, may be invested in a safe and easily liquidated form, and the beneficiaries have no right on it unless part of it proves to be in excess of actual needs.
column7: May be retained only if the Waqif has stipulated such a condition, otherwise the whole income is distributed to the beneficiaries every year, and any maintenance is financed from borrowing or from the superintendent's own funds.
column8: Belongs to the beneficiaries, who may claim it at any time, since it is part of the income of the Waqf that was due to them.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/1/2, the reserve is retained yearly without a condition, may be safely invested with returns added, and beneficiaries have no right to it except any excess.

column5: If the creditor discharges the guarantor from liability, the debtor is also discharged automatically from the debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/3/2, discharging the guarantor leaves the debtor in debt; only discharging the debtor discharges the guarantor.

column5: Upon usage of the card, the relationship between the card issuer and the cardholder is that:
column6: The cardholder novates the card acceptor to the card issuer, which pays out of the balance of the cardholder held with it.
column7: The card issuer pays the card acceptor out of its own funds, so that the paid amount shall be a debt to be claimed from the cardholder.
column8: It would be a guarantee if the card was used to block an amount or to deduct an amount to secure what shall be outstanding on the cardholder.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/1/2, on usage there is novation paid from the balance or from the issuer's funds as a debt, and guarantee when an amount is blocked.

column5: In risk sharing reinsurance:
column6: The reinsurance company accepts all the risks which fall within the scope of the agreement.
column7: The insurance company seeks reinsurance for a percentage of the insurance policies it issues (50% or 25%), whether such coverage is within or in excess of its own insurance capacity.
column8: The insurance company keeps all the insurance policies whose risks it can easily tolerate, and seeks reinsurance only for those it cannot tolerate.
column9: The reinsurance company bears the losses beyond the specific limit agreed upon.
column11: Per 5/1, risk sharing reinsurance covers a percentage (e.g. 50% or 25%) of the policies issued, whether within or beyond the insurer's capacity.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for treating the purchase of an asset and its lease to the seller under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek as not being 'Inah is:
column6: That the rent is paid in return for the usufruct and is renewable over the term of the Ijarah, so the subject matter of the Ijarah differs from that of the first sale.
column7: That the validity of the transaction depends on the lapse of a period between the first sale and re-ownership, during which the asset's characteristics or value would change.
column8: That ensuing ownership will usually be either through gift (Hibah) or purchase at a price lower than the initial price.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/2, all three reasons are given for why sale-and-Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek to the seller is not 'Inah.

column5: The fee that the Institution gains from a remittance in the same currency that constitutes a transfer of debt is an additional amount gained over the amount transferred and is therefore Riba.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 12/6, the fee is consideration for delivering the money, not an additional amount over the sum transferred.

column5: Developing indices is permissible in Shari'ah because:
column6: They are financial papers that represent real assets in the markets, so that their holders are co-owners of the assets of the corporations included in the index and entitled to a proportionate share in their profits.
column7: They constitute a method of forecasting and a means of observing the state of circumstances (inferences), and resorting to inferences is a well-recognized practice in judicature and financial transactions.
column8: They are a form of Murabahah pricing that the Fuqaha unanimously approve.
column9: The International Islamic Fiqh Academy approved trading in them.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, indices are a forecasting method and means of inference, a practice recognized in judicature and dealings.

column5: In a Mudarabah contract, it is permissible to agree that:
column6: The profit from a particular transaction goes to the Mudarib and the profit from another transaction goes to the capital provider, as agreed in advance by the parties in the contract.
column7: The profit of one financial period is taken by the Mudarib and the profit of the following period by the capital provider, as agreed at the outset.
column8: If the profit is over a particular ceiling one of the parties takes the additional profit, and if it is below or equal to the ceiling it is distributed as agreed.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 8/5, the ceiling arrangement is permissible; per 8/6, assigning profits by transaction or period is not.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The return of a defective sold item is prevented where:
column6: The buyer has erected a building on the land sold.
column7: The buyer has received dividends on the shares sold.
column8: The buyer has received rent from the leased asset sold.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/6/3, a building prevents return; separate yields such as dividends and rent do not.

column5: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of tangible assets:
column6: May not be traded prior to a contract for sub-leasing the assets, but may be traded freely after the assets are sub-leased, since the certificate then represents the usufruct of an existing asset.
column7: May be traded prior to a contract for sub-leasing the assets; once the assets are sub-leased, the certificate represents rent receivables subject to the rules for disposal of debts.
column8: May be traded freely, at any price, both before and after sub-leasing the assets.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/2/6, trading is allowed before sub-leasing; after sub-leasing the certificate represents rent receivables (a debt), subject to rules of debt disposal.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar does not affect donation contracts, such as gift and will contracts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1, Gharar affects exchange-based contracts such as sale, lease and partnership, but not donation contracts such as gift and will.

column5: With regard to the guarantee relating to documentary credits, letters of guarantee and bank suretyship:
column6: The institution may not obtain any return for agency in documentary credits, because the agency is inseparable from the guarantee given to the beneficiary.
column7: The institution may obtain returns on the guarantee as a percentage of the guaranteed amount, since the guarantee exposes it to the risk of default by the client.
column8: The institution may obtain no return on the guarantee except actual expenses, but it may obtain returns for agency in documentary credits.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/3/2/3, no return on the guarantee except actual expenses, but returns may be obtained for agency in documentary credits.

column5: The ruling that the responsibility of providing the evidence lies with the participant is based on the general rule that evidence should be established by the claimant.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the participant bears the burden of evidence as the claimant.

column5: The basis for determining the mode of possession in things is:
column6: Physical transportation of the thing in all cases.
column7: The stipulation of the seller.
column8: Custom ('Urf).
column9: The law of the country in which the thing is located.
column11: Per 3/1, custom ('Urf) determines the mode of possession, which is why it differs with the nature of things and people's practices.

column5: It is not permitted for a seller to deliver al-Muslam Fihi in the form of a commodity different from the one agreed upon if it belongs to the same genus (e.g. wheat instead of corn). Delivery in the form of a different type of commodity may take place:
column6: Whenever the buyer agrees, even if stipulated in the contract and before the delivery date.
column7: At the option of the seller, provided its value equals that of al-Muslam Fihi.
column8: Under no circumstances.
column9: Only on the basis of the conditions for the replacement of al-Muslam Fihi by other goods.
column11: Per 5/4, a different commodity may be delivered only under the replacement conditions of 4/2.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Permissible applications of cooling-off options include:
column6: The institution, whether as seller or buyer, stipulates an option to reconsider whether or not it is worth selling or buying an item.
column7: The institution stipulates an option to reconsider when purchasing items from suppliers to offer them to its clients without a binding promise from them, returning the items to the seller if the clients do not wish to purchase.
column8: The institution stipulates an option to reconsider in order to avoid price fluctuations during the option period.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/8/1-2/8/2, (a) and (b) are permissible; using the option to avoid price fluctuations is not permissible (2/8/5).

column5: The Monetization beneficiary (Mutawarriq) may be:
column6: The Institution only, when it purchases the commodity from the customer or another Institution and sells it to a third party, provided that it faces the danger of a liquidity shortage.
column7: Any party who purchases a commodity for a deferred price and sells it back to the same seller for a lower spot price to obtain liquidity.
column8: The customer only, who purchases the commodity from the Institution and sells it to a third party; the Institution itself may not be a Monetization beneficiary, since Monetization is not a mode of financing.
column9: A customer who purchases the commodity from the Institution and sells it to a third party to obtain liquidity, or the Institution itself when it purchases the commodity from the customer or another Institution and sells it to a third party to obtain liquidity.
column11: Per 3/1, the Mutawarriq may be the customer or the Institution itself, each selling to a third party; selling back to the same seller is 'Inah.

column5: It is permitted to invest the revenue of the Waqf, where it does not affect its distribution to the Waqf beneficiaries:
column6: If the Waqif stipulates investing part of the revenue, or if the investment is made during the waiting period for the beneficiaries.
column7: At the discretion of the overseer, even if the distribution to the beneficiaries is deferred, provided that the investment is in low-risk modes.
column8: Only in the case of investment Waqfs.
column9: Only if all the Waqf beneficiaries consent in writing.
column11: Per 8/1, revenue may be invested if the Waqif stipulates it or during the beneficiaries' waiting period, without affecting distribution.

column5: An IFI issued Murabahah Sukuk and used the proceeds to purchase a quantity of steel, which it then sold on a deferred-payment Murabahah to a customer and delivered to him. One of the Sukuk holders now wishes to sell his Sukuk in the secondary market at a price higher than its nominal value. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because the certificate holders own the Murabahah commodity and are entitled to its sale price, and the Sukuk may therefore be sold at a price higher than the nominal value.
column7: Permissible, because trading in Murabahah certificates is allowed after purchasing the Murabahah commodity.
column8: Impermissible, because after delivery of the commodity to the buyer the certificates represent a monetary debt, tradable only within the limits of debt trading.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/2/15 and the Shari'ah basis, after delivery to the buyer Murabahah certificates represent a monetary debt; trading is allowed only per debt-trading rules.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: A creditor is entitled to stipulate the right to accelerate all installments and the right to revoke the contract, or one of them:
column6: After notifying the debtor, in the event that the debtor fails to pay two or more instalments, even if this is owing to his insolvency.
column7: After notifying the debtor, in the event that the debtor fails to pay two or more instalments despite being solvent.
column8: In the event that the debtor fails to pay a single instalment, whether he is solvent or insolvent.
column9: Without notifying the debtor, in the event that the debtor fails to pay two or more instalments owing to insolvency.
column11: Per 11/3, the right applies after notifying the debtor, where he fails to pay two or more instalments despite being solvent.

column5: Unlike the shared employee who has to guarantee what he is paid to work on, the investment agent who is permitted to utilize the money:
column6: Guarantees a minimum return on the invested money.
column7: Does not guarantee, except in case of transgression or negligence.
column8: Guarantees the capital whenever he receives a fee for the agency.
column9: Guarantees the capital absolutely, being paid for his work.
column11: Per 4/6, the shared employee's liability rule does not apply to an investment agent, who does not guarantee except in transgression or negligence.

column5: Using credit facilities refers to commencement of the client to utilize the facility by:
column6: Submitting a request for a letter of guarantee or a letter of credit.
column7: Receiving from the Institution the letter of granting the facility.
column8: Receiving from the Institution a letter for renewal or extension of the period of the already approved facility.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 2/5, use begins when the client requests an L/G or L/C, or pledges to buy a commodity or hire an asset; approval or renewal letters do not count.

column5: A shareholder in a stock company is entitled to dissolve the company in respect of his shares, provided he gives due notice to the other shareholders.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/2/1, no one may dissolve the company in respect of his shares; he may only sell or relinquish them.

column5: The mortgagee has the right to appoint an agent to possess the mortgage on his behalf, and the agent thus appointed should have the same rights of disposition which the principal has.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/3, the mortgagee may appoint an agent to possess the mortgage, with the same rights of disposition as the principal.

column5: Istibdal can take place when the Waqf becomes ruined, even if Istibdal has been prevented by the Waqif.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/2, Istibdal may take place by the Waqif's condition, or when the Waqf becomes ruined even if the Waqif prevented it.

column5: Where the Institution did not invest the funds paid to it in its general pool, the investor is still deemed a partner by virtue of the contract, because pooling (commingling of funds) is not a prerequisite for the validity of partnership.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 7/3, the investor is a partner by contract; commingling is not a prerequisite for partnership.

column5: Full ownership, as a condition for Zakah obligation, materializes when:
column6: The owner has held the asset for a full solar year.
column7: Nobody else has a right in the asset, the owner can dispose of it the way he likes, and the owner is the sole owner of the income generated from it.
column8: The asset is registered in the owner's name, even if others have a right in it.
column9: The asset is not allocated for any specific purpose, including implementation of investment projects, and the owner can dispose of it the way he likes.
column11: Per 3/2/1, full ownership needs no other's right, free disposal and sole ownership of income; allocation to investment projects does not affect it.

column5: All partners in a Sharikah contract maintain the assets of the Sharikah on a trust basis. Therefore:
column6: A partner may guarantee the capital of another partner if this is stipulated in the contract and the guarantee is given without consideration or is secured by a mortgage over the managing partner's assets.
column7: Each partner is liable for losses in proportion to his share of profit, which may differ from his share in the capital.
column8: The managing partner is liable for any loss of capital, since he controls the assets, unless the other partners agree to bear it.
column9: No one is liable except in cases of misconduct, negligence or breach of contract, and it is not permitted to stipulate that a partner guarantees the capital of another.
column11: Per 3/1/4/1, partners are trustees, liable only for misconduct, negligence or breach; guaranteeing another partner's capital is barred.

column5: The Waqif may stipulate, with regard to his Waqf:
column6: That he or his heirs will benefit from the Waqf during his lifetime or for a defined period, or that his debts be settled from it.
column7: That the Waqf asset may be sold and its price distributed to his heirs whenever they need it, without the conditions of substitution.
column8: That the overseers may not be dismissed under any circumstances.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/6/2 the Waqif may stipulate benefit for himself or heirs or settling his debts; per 2/6/4 non-dismissal of overseers is a void condition.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Agreement between the two Mudarabah parties, at the time of distribution, on changing the profit ratios agreed upon or donating part of the profit is impermissible, because it leads to Jahalah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, only postponing ratios causes Jahalah; changing ratios or donating profit at distribution is the parties' right.

column5: Red clause or advance payment credit is a credit whereby:
column6: The credit issued is guaranteed by another credit.
column7: The bank is allowed to pay a certain percentage of the credit before submission of the documents, against an undertaking by the beneficiary to repay it if the goods are not shipped or the credit is not used during its validity.
column8: The beneficiary can repeatedly submit new documents for new operations within the limits of the credit amount, which is automatically restored after each utilisation, without any need for an amendment of the credit by the applicant or the issuing bank.
column9: Payment is conditional upon the failure of the beneficiary (the contractor) to perform, in which case the bank pays the applicant the amount of the guarantee given.
column11: Per 2/3/3, red clause credit allows advance payment of a percentage before documents, against the beneficiary's undertaking to repay.

column5: The basis for not permitting the use of the card at the card acceptor to obtain cash in the currency of the card less than the amount entered on the payment terminal is:
column6: The existence of riba of excess (riba al-fadl).
column7: The sale of debt to a non-debtor.
column8: Gharar (excessive uncertainty) in the amount of the cash.
column9: The combination of a sale and a loan.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/8/2, there is riba of excess between what the acceptor pays out and what it receives from the issuer.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Absence of explicit directives in the Qur'an and Sunnah on a given issue, or non-existence of the issue in the prevailing Fiqh literature, justifies refraining from seeking Fatwa on that issue.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/3, this does not justify refraining; Fatwa may be derived through Shari'ah-sanctioned methods of deduction.

column5: It is not permissible to undertake trading in the shares of a corporation if the entire assets of the corporation are composed of debts, unless:
column6: The debts are secured by mortgage.
column7: The activity of the corporation is permissible.
column8: The rules for dealing in debts are observed.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/18, shares of a corporation whose assets are entirely debts may be traded only by observing the rules for dealing in debts.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: A warehousing company kept a merchant's goods as a bailee against a monthly fee. The merchant failed to pay the fees due and demanded the return of his goods. The correct ruling is:
column6: The bailee may retain the goods and sell them immediately to recover his fee.
column7: The bailee must return the goods and claim his fee through the courts, as he has no right of retention.
column8: The bailee has the right to retain the bailed property until he receives his fee.
column9: The bailee may retain the goods only if the right of retention was expressly stipulated in the contract.
column11: Per 12/2(b)(V), a bailee has a right of lien to retain the bailed property until he receives his fee.

column5: With regard to the effect of a personal guarantee, the creditor is entitled to claim the amount of his debt:
column6: From the guarantor only after the debtor has been declared bankrupt by a court, and only if the guarantor stipulated at the conclusion of the contract of guarantee that the creditor shall first claim payment from the principal debtor.
column7: From the debtor first in all cases, and then from the guarantor, even where the guarantor has not stipulated any order of liability at the conclusion of the contract of guarantee.
column8: From the guarantor first, since he has assumed the liability for the debt.
column9: From either the debtor or the guarantor, having the choice of claiming from either, unless the guarantor stipulated at the conclusion of the guarantee that the creditor shall first claim payment from the principal debtor.
column11: Per 3/3/1, the creditor may claim from either, but the guarantor may stipulate that the debtor be claimed from first.

column5: In the debit card, the Institution charges, on each transaction of cash withdrawal carried through its ATMs using cards issued by other institutions:
column6: A fee only if the card was issued by a conventional bank.
column7: No fee, since the withdrawal is from the balance of the cardholder.
column8: A fee as a lump sum or a percentage of the withdrawn amount.
column9: A fee as a lump sum only, since a percentage is not permitted.
column11: Per 3/1/6, the Institution charges a lump sum or a percentage of the amount withdrawn through its ATMs with other institutions' cards.

column5: While Muslim scholars have agreed on the permissibility of punishing a solvent debtor who defaults, an insolvent debtor should be granted a grace period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis on default, scholars agree a solvent defaulter may be punished, while an insolvent debtor is given a grace period.

column5: It is permissible to acquire compensation for work, like the preparation of feasibility studies or the marketing of shares, irrespective of the work being undertaken by the underwriter or someone else, if such compensation is not in lieu of a guarantee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4, compensation for actual work is allowed if it is not in lieu of the underwriting guarantee.

column5: ………… entitles the beneficiary to request the executing bank to make the credit available, partially or totally, to another beneficiary or beneficiaries.
column6: Revolving or renewable credit.
column7: Transferable documentary credit.
column8: Red clause credit.
column9: Back-to-back credit.
column11: Per 2/3/3, a transferable credit lets the beneficiary have the credit made available to other beneficiaries.

column5: All the conditions stipulated by each Waqif must be read or interpreted in light of the prevailing customs in his time and place.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/6/1, each Waqif's conditions are interpreted in light of the prevailing customs in his time and place.

column5: Hanafi jurists have stipulated that if a lock is placed on the immovable property, it is sufficient for the delivery of possession to deliver the key along with relinquishment, so as to enable the possessor to open it without difficulty.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis for 3/2 cites this Hanafi view on delivering the key along with relinquishment.

column5: If the commitment of the licensee in a construction concession contract includes construction works as well as provision of materials, which is the predominant case, the contract is that of:
column6: Istisna'a.
column7: Ju'alah.
column8: Ijarah.
column9: Mudarabah.
column11: Per 6/2/1, construction with provision of materials is Istisna'a; its value is the licensee's right to utilize the project for a period.

column5: If the parties to a Mudarabah did not stipulate the ratio of profit distribution, and the customary practice is that profit is distributed equally, the contract is void and the Mudarib receives a common market price for his services.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/4, customary practice is applied, so profit is shared equally; nullity arises only where there is no custom.

column5: If the online contract is concluded on the basis of describing the sold object, or on the basis that the buyer has previously seen it, or on presentation of a model resembling it, whereas at the time of delivery the sold object is found to be different, the buyer should have the choice of:
column6: Concluding the contract.
column7: Terminating the contract.
column8: Negotiating with the seller appropriate means of settlement.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/4, the buyer may conclude the contract, terminate it, or negotiate with the seller appropriate means of settlement.

column5: Waqf is permissible in movable assets, whether such movable assets are part of a real estate or independent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/4/3, Waqf is permissible in movable assets, whether part of a real estate or independent.

column5: ………… means appointing another person to invest and grow one's wealth, with or without a fee:
column6: General agency (Al-Wakalah Al-Ammah).
column7: Uncommissioned agency (Fodooli) for the growth of wealth.
column8: Mudarabah.
column9: Investment Agency (Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar).
column11: Per 2/1, Investment Agency is appointing another person to invest and grow one's wealth, with or without a fee.

column5: If the crop does not materialize during the stipulated term of the Irrigation Partnership:
column6: The worker is entitled to his share of the expected crop at the end of the term.
column7: The contract is automatically extended until the crop materializes, with a wage at the market rate for the worker for the extension.
column8: The owner must pay the worker a wage at the market rate for similar work for the stipulated term, and the contract terminates.
column9: The worker has the option either to stop working or to continue his work without a wage until the crop materializes and thereafter take his share.
column11: Per 10/2, the worker may stop, or continue without a wage until the crop materializes and then take his share.

column5: Regarding the sale of the debt to the debtor in the future:
column6: A bilaterally binding promise is permitted, but an agreement at origination is not.
column7: An agreement at origination to sell the debt to the debtor in the future, and a bilaterally binding promise, are not permitted; a unilaterally binding promise is permitted if the rules of sale of debt to the debtor are met in the promised sale.
column8: Both unilateral and bilateral promises to sell the debt to the debtor are prohibited, since the debtor cannot be bound by any promise relating to his debt.
column9: An agreement at the origination of the debt to sell it to the debtor in the future is permitted, since the debtor is the possessor of the debt, provided that the price is fixed at the market value on the date of sale and the sale is executed by a separate contract.
column11: Per 4/2, an agreement at origination or a bilaterally binding promise is barred; a unilaterally binding promise meeting 4/1 is allowed.

column5: Among the differences between Islamic insurance and commercial insurance stated in the Shari'ah basis:
column6: In Islamic insurance, the company is an original party that signs the contract in its own name.
column7: In Islamic insurance, it is the insurance account rather than the company that owns the contributions.
column8: In Islamic insurance, the returns on investment of the premium assets belong to the company.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the insurance account owns the contributions; the company is an agent and returns go to the policyholders.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Charity is a way of disposing of impermissible earnings because, by transferring ownership of these earnings, their characterisation of prohibition changes and they become permissible for the beneficiary.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, transfer of ownership changes the prohibited character; what is prohibited for one may be permissible for another.

column5: Fees on cards that are not permitted to be more than the actual direct cost include:
column6: Fees charged by the card issuer from the cardholder that are linked to the loan in the credit card, such as issuance, renewal and replacement fees.
column7: Fees charged by the acquirer from the card acceptor, such as the merchant discount rate charged as a percentage of the goods and services paid for by the card.
column8: Subscription fees and service charges paid by the card issuer to the card network.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/1, loan-linked fees charged to the cardholder are capped at actual direct cost; acquirer and network fees are by agreement (5/1/2).

column5: The lessor may not delegate to the lessee the task of carrying out the major maintenance of the leased asset, even at the lessor's cost.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/1/7, the lessor may not stipulate it on the lessee, but may delegate it to the lessee at the lessor's cost.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The loss of a certain financial period of the investment accounts:
column6: Should be covered from the profits of the next financial period.
column7: Should be recovered from the profits distributed to the holders in the previous period.
column8: Should not be covered from the profits of another period, except in the case of covering losses from reserves.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/2/1, a period's loss is not covered from another period's profits, except where losses are covered from reserves.

column5: If the seller retains the legal registration of the sold asset in a buyback arrangement:
column6: No document is required, since legal registration is only for documentation purposes and does not affect ownership, yield or risk of loss.
column7: The buyback is impermissible, since the sale is not real and ownership does not transfer to the buyer while the seller retains the registration, whatever the document executed, and the buyer cannot claim the yield.
column8: It is required to execute a document confirming the buyer's ownership, provided that the retention does not affect his ownership, yield or risk of loss; the seller's possession is deemed a trust.
column9: The seller's possession of the asset is deemed a liability possession, and he bears its risk of loss and is entitled to its yield, provided that a counter deed confirming the buyer's ownership is executed.
column11: Per 4/2, a counter deed or similar must confirm the buyer's ownership, yield and risk; the seller holds the asset as a trust.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If gold is not the primary asset of a commercial entity whose activities do not involve trading in gold, silver and currencies, and the entity or a part thereof is sold along with that gold:
column6: The sale is not subject to the rulings for currency exchange (al-Sarf); however, it is not permissible to deliberately establish a portfolio specifically for trading in gold unless it complies with those rulings.
column7: The sale is permissible, and it is likewise permissible to establish a portfolio specifically for trading in gold on the same basis, provided that the gold does not exceed half of the portfolio's assets and is paid for at spot.
column8: The sale is subject to the rulings for currency exchange (al-Sarf), and the gold must be paid for at spot.
column9: The sale is permissible only if the gold represents less than one third of the entity's assets, and the price of the gold is then paid at spot.
column11: Per 3/1/2, al-Sarf does not govern such a sale, but setting up a portfolio specifically to trade gold must comply with al-Sarf.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting a Murabaha at the request of an indebted non-insolvent customer, resulting in a new debt higher than the first, is:
column6: That the benefit belongs to both parties, by analogy to Suftajah, because the customer obtains liquidity and the Institution a profit, and the first debt is settled from the proceeds.
column7: The principle of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya), by which the new debt follows the first debt as an accessory.
column8: The analogy of ḥawāla (novation).
column9: That the rules make it a new, independent Murabaha; there may be no proceeds at all, and any settlement is at the customer's disposition over which the Institution has no authority.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1/3/4, the rules make it independent financing, and any settlement is at the customer's own disposition.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The right of Tahjir expires if the land is not utilised for:
column6: Ten years, or as provided by applicable regulations.
column7: Three years, or as provided by applicable regulations.
column8: Five years, or as provided by applicable regulations.
column9: One year, or as provided by applicable regulations.
column11: Per 9/4, the right of Tahjir expires if the land is not utilised for three years, or as applicable regulations provide.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the entitlement of the buyer in Murabahah to benefit from a discount acquired by the Institution from the supplier is that:
column6: The original principle in respect of stipulations is validity and permissibility.
column7: Any amount received by the Institution after the contract is a prohibited increase over the debt.
column8: Murabahah is a mark-up sale, so if the purchasing price decreases, the cost price is the amount remaining after the discount.
column9: The discount for early payment is a form of settlement endorsed by Shari'ah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Murabahah is a mark-up sale, so the cost price is what remains after the discount.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: A company sold to an IFI, without any option, a quantity of goods that the company was going to import from abroad, at a time when it was not sure whether a license for importing the goods would be obtained. This sale is:
column6: Null and void, because of Gharar pertaining to failure in delivery.
column7: Valid, because the Gharar involved is medium Gharar, which does not affect the contract.
column8: Valid, because the goods have been fully described.
column9: Null and void, because of Gharar in the form of the contract.
column11: Per 5/4, selling, without option, goods to be imported when the import license is uncertain is Gharar in delivery, which nullifies the contract.

column5: It is not permitted to sell a debt that is a usufruct or a service described in liability (mawṣūfa fī dhimma), whether it is sold for cash, a commodity, a usufruct or a service.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/4, a usufruct or service debt mawṣūfa fī dhimma may not be sold for any consideration.

column5: Upon Waqf of shares, the company's Memorandum of Association and the legal framework upon which the company was established are deemed as conditions of the Waqif, unless they violate the principles and rulings of Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/14/4, the company's constitutive documents are deemed the Waqif's conditions unless they violate Shari'ah.

column5: In syndicated financing, receiving commitment commission is:
column6: Not permissible.
column7: Permissible for the lead manager only.
column8: Permissible, provided that it is agreed upon in the syndication documents.
column9: Permissible, provided that it does not exceed the actual cost.
column11: Per 7/2, it is not permissible to receive commitment commission.

column5: There should be a Shari'ah Supervisory Board for an Islamic index, to ensure observation of the Shari'ah precepts in its components and applications, and to conduct periodical review and reporting relating thereto.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/2, an Islamic index should have its own Shari'ah Supervisory Board for oversight, periodic review and reporting.

column5: The relationship between the acquirer and the card acceptor is:
column6: A guarantee by the acquirer of the payments due from the cardholders, against a commission that is a percentage of the prices of the goods, and a loan to the card acceptor of the amounts due.
column7: A Musharakah in the fees and commissions of the card.
column8: A novation of the card issuer to the acquirer.
column9: Provision of services, which include providing payment terminals (POS devices) to the card acceptor, organizing its dealing with the card network, and an agency for recovery.
column11: Per 2/2/2, the acquirer provides services to the merchant: POS devices, organizing dealing with the network, and agency for recovery.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, contracting through online voice communication differs from contracting through a telephone call, and is therefore treated as contracting between two absent parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. The Shari'ah basis states there is no difference between contracting by telephone and by online voice; both are between present parties.

column5: It is a requirement of Murabahah that the transaction between the customer and the original supplier must genuinely, not fictitiously, exclude any prior contractual relationship between them regarding the supply of the item.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/2, any prior contractual relationship between the purchase orderer and the supplier must be genuinely excluded.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The Standard on Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred does not cover:
column6: Non-financial rights.
column7: Khiyarat (options to terminate a contract), such as Khiyar al-Shart and Khiyar al-Naqd.
column8: Rights relating to Waqf (endowments).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 1, non-financial rights, Khiyarat (e.g. Khiyar al-Shart, Khiyar al-Naqd) and Waqf rights are excluded, being covered elsewhere.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: With regard to the charge card, the Institution issuing the card:
column6: Does not charge the cardholder any percentage commission on purchases, but receives a percentage commission from the party accepting the card on purchases made by using the card.
column7: Is obliged to pay the party accepting the card for purchases made by the cardholder within a specified transaction credit limit, and this obligation is direct and independent of the relationship between the party accepting the card and the cardholder.
column8: Has a personal and direct right against the cardholder to be reimbursed for any payments made on his behalf, which is absolute and independent of the relationship between the cardholder and the party accepting the card.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/5, 2/2/6 and 2/2/7, all three statements are characteristics of the charge card.

column5: It is permissible to stipulate in a Ju'alah that the job is done within a specified period, so that the worker will not be entitled to compensation after this period, except:
column6: When the worker is an institution acting through a parallel Ju'alah with another worker.
column7: When the period has ended and the result is close to realisation, in which case it is automatically extended.
column8: When the worker has spent more than half of the period on the work and has delivered a part of the result.
column9: When the offeror has paid part of the compensation in advance, in which case the period is extended accordingly.
column11: Per 5/3/1/2, if the period ends with the result close to realisation, the period is automatically extended.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Fatwa issuers:
column6: Should always pursue Shari'ah exemptions to make matters easier for Institutions.
column7: May direct Institutions to tricks for escaping Shari'ah restrictions when there is a pressing need of the Institution or its clients, provided that the tricks are approved by the management in writing.
column8: Shall not issue Fatwa hastily, declaring prohibition of an act for the mere sense of condemnation toward new habits and traditions, unless they contradict the rules and principles of Shari'ah.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/6, hasty prohibition out of mere dislike of new habits is barred; 8/4 and 8/5 bar the other two.

column5: Among the conditions relating to the work in a Ju'alah contract:
column6: The extent of the work must be precisely determined.
column7: The work must involve some type of effort.
column8: The work may be one that is obligatory for the worker.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3/1/4-6, the work must involve effort and must not be obligatory on the worker; uncertainty about it is tolerated.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: In case of deals that involve the agent's spouse:
column6: The deal is absolutely impermissible.
column7: The agent should obtain the consent of the principal.
column8: The deal is permissible unless it encompasses injustice or favoritism, without any need for the consent of the principal.
column9: The deal is permissible provided that it is concluded at the market price.
column11: Per 6/1/1, deals involving the agent's spouse require the principal's consent.

column5: Determining the value of a management concession as a specific share of the project's income is free of any uncertainty (Jahalah), since the income of the project can be measured precisely.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, a share of income could embody Jahalah as to realizing the agreed amount during the contract period.

column5: When the agency in currency exchange is for the purpose of taking possession only, the juristic rule relates to:
column6: The leaving of the place of execution of the contract by both principals before possession is taken, and not to the agent's doing so.
column7: The leaving of the place of execution of the contract by the agent before possession is taken.
column8: The expiry of the settlement period customary in currency markets.
column9: The leaving of the place of execution of the contract by either the principal or the agent, whichever occurs first.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis on agency, what counts is the principals leaving before possession, not the agent's doing so.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: Contingent incidents are different from defects of will, because:
column6: Contingent incidents exist since the time of signing the contract, although their impact occurs later on.
column7: Defects of will always lead to termination of the contract, whereas contingent incidents only necessitate amendments in it.
column8: Defects of will exist since the time of signing the contract, although their impact occurs later on.
column9: Defects of will occur suddenly after signing the contract and cause significant influence on the commitment.
column11: Per 2, defects of will exist from the signing of the contract though their impact appears later; contingent incidents occur suddenly afterwards.

column5: If a Mudarabah contract is concluded on an unrestricted basis, the Mudarib is permitted, in general, to do what entrepreneurs do in his field of activity, including:
column6: Selling and buying on a deferred payment basis.
column7: Appointing another person to carry out some work if necessary, such as buying a commodity or marketing it for him.
column8: Safeguarding the Mudarabah funds or depositing them in the custody of a trustworthy person whenever appropriate.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 9/1/2, 9/1/4 and 9/1/5, all three acts are within the general powers of the Mudarib in an unrestricted Mudarabah.

column5: Zakah on receipt papers (bills and promissory notes) relating to a commodity sold on debt shall be paid on:
column6: The principal of the debt (amount of the paper), including the increment added to the price, whether the debt represented by the paper is due or not.
column7: The increment added to the price only.
column8: The amount of the paper including the increment, but only when it becomes due.
column9: The principal of the debt (amount of the paper), excluding the increment added to the price, whether due or not, since the increment is deferred income.
column11: Per 5/3/4/3, Zakah is on the amount of the paper incl. the price increment, due or not, since no difficulty is expected in collection.

column5: In addition to the general conditions for the permissibility of competitions, reward-based competitions are permissible subject to the following condition:
column6: The competition is clearly defined so as to remove any ambiguity (Jahalah) as to its timing, location, type, particulars, tools and mode of operation.
column7: The reward is offered by more than one of the competitors, so that the risk is shared among them, and the winner is paid out of the competitors' entry stakes.
column8: The reward is in cash and not in kind.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/3/2, the competition must be well-defined; a reward offered by more than one competitor is not permissible, and no cash-only rule exists.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of the investment manager undertaking to purchase the assets from Sukuk holders at a specific price, and guaranteeing losses arising from exchange rate fluctuations, is:
column6: That this may be tantamount to a guarantee stipulated in the contract, entirely in the former case and partially in the latter.
column7: That this involves the sale of a debt to a non-debtor.
column8: That this constitutes a sale of 'Inah between the investment manager and the Sukuk holders, because the price is fixed at the time of the contract in both cases.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, both undertakings may amount to a stipulated guarantee, wholly in the former and partly in the latter.

column5: If a debt in a ribawī commodity is sold to the debtor for a ribawī commodity of the same kind, such as a debt in sea salt sold against rock salt:
column6: Only possession of the consideration in the contract session is required, even if the quantities differ, since the two are different types.
column7: Only equality of the volume is required, and possession may be deferred.
column8: The sale is not permitted, since a debt may not be substituted with its own kind, even if equal in volume and possessed in the session.
column9: Equality (tamāthul) of the volume of the debt and its consideration, and possession of the consideration in the session, are both required.
column11: Per 4/1/1/1 (b), a same-kind ribawī consideration requires equality of volume and possession in the contract session.

column5: Investment agency contracts, whether remunerated or unremunerated, are:
column6: Binding only if they are remunerated, while unremunerated agency remains non-binding.
column7: Binding on institutions, because they are invariably fixed-term contracts in which both parties agree not to terminate within the period.
column8: Binding on the agent only, while the principal may terminate them at any time without cause.
column9: Non-binding, since agency is in principle a non-binding contract which either party may terminate at will, even where a fixed term was agreed upon.
column11: Per 4/1, remunerated or not, they bind institutions as fixed-term contracts in which both parties agree not to terminate.

column5: During the distribution of the insolvent debtor's assets, priority should first be given to:
column6: Creditors of undue debts that were accelerated by the declaration of insolvency.
column7: Paying the fees of the administrators and their assistants who manage the process of sale and distribution.
column8: Creditors of due debts, each receiving an amount pro-rata to his share of the total debt.
column9: Secured creditors, as per the rules of granting security, followed by the fees of the administrators.
column11: Per 8/3/1, administrators' fees come first; secured creditors are next in order (8/3/2).

column5: The basis for prohibiting the issuance of revolving credit cards by the Institutions in the manner described in the standard is that:
column6: It involves gharar, because the amounts of usage are unknown at the time of issuance, and the profit on the revolving balance cannot be determined in advance.
column7: The fees of the card exceed the actual direct cost.
column8: It is based on a contract which allows the cardholder to obtain a revolving loan over time against riba-based increment.
column9: It combines Hawalah and Kafalah in one contract.
column11: Per the Basis of 4/4, the card rests on a contract for a revolving loan against riba-based increment, prohibited by text and consensus.

column5: The share of each partner in the capital of a Sharikah should be determined, whether it is contributed in the form of one lump sum or by more than one payment over time.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/2/3, each partner's share must be determined whether paid at once or in several payments over time.

column5: Possession of the mortgaged asset that is legal, through registration and documentation, is known as:
column6: Borrowed mortgage, because the asset remains in the hands of its owner.
column7: Security or formal mortgage, which is not binding until actual possession by putting a hand on the property takes place.
column8: Security or formal mortgage, and it is subject to the same rulings as seizure mortgage.
column9: Seizure mortgage, and it is subject to the same rulings as security mortgage.
column11: Per 3/1/2, legal possession through registration is security (formal) mortgage; it and seizure mortgage are subject to the same rulings.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: The commission charged by the card issuing Institution to the party accepting the card, based on the prices of purchases or services, is permissible because it can be considered as:
column6: A share in the profit realised by the party accepting the card on the sale.
column7: Partly a brokerage and marketing fee as well as a service charge for the collection of the debt.
column8: A fee for guaranteeing the creditworthiness of the cardholder.
column9: Compensation for the credit period granted to the cardholder.
column11: Per the basis (item 5), the merchant commission is partly brokerage and marketing and partly a service charge for collecting the debt.

column5: Under Islamic reinsurance, the reinsurance fund:
column6: Has a distinct legal personality and independent financial liability, and is formed by contributions out of insurance funds paid by the insureds on the basis of donation.
column7: Is owned by the reinsurance company, and is formed up through premiums paid in exchange for the compensation.
column8: Is formed up through contributions paid by the insurance companies out of their shareholders' funds on the basis of loan, and is owned by those companies in proportion to their contributions.
column9: Has no independent personality, and forms part of the equity of the reinsurance company.
column11: Per 2/1, the reinsurance fund has distinct legal personality and independent liability, built from donation-based contributions of the insurance funds.

column5: The prospectus of Sukuk must:
column6: Include all contractual conditions and adequate statements about the participants in the issue, such as the issue agent, issue manager, originator, investment trustee, the party covering the loss and payment agent, along with the conditions of their appointment and dismissal.
column7: Include the identification of the contract on the basis of which the certificates are to be issued, such as sale of tangible leased assets, Ijarah, Murabahah, Istisna'a, Salam, Mudarabah or Musharakah.
column8: Explicitly mention the obligation to abide by the rules and principles of the Shari'ah, and that there is a Shari'ah Supervisory Board that approves the procedures of the issue and monitors the implementation of the project throughout its duration.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/8/1, 5/1/8/2 and 5/1/8/4, the prospectus must include all three of these matters.

column5: It is permitted for the acquirer to agree with the card network to settle the amounts owed to it in a currency other than the currency of the price of goods or services, provided the exchange rate is known.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/5/3, this is permitted provided the exchange rate is known, observing the referenced rule of SS 59.

column5: The elements of Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) include:
