column6: Offer and acceptance exchanged explicitly or implicitly by means of a recognised form of indication.
column7: Legal competence of each of the two parties.
column8: The relevant trees should be identified, arable (productive), and in need of irrigation and plant husbandry.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1-4/3, all three are elements of Irrigation Partnership.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, impermissibility of commercial reinsurance is based on the fact that:
column6: Commercial reinsurance companies do not invest the premiums.
column7: Commercial reinsurance is based on donation and cooperation.
column8: Commercial reinsurance depends on the idea of commercial insurance and involves Shari'ah-prohibited Gharar.
column9: The commercial reinsurance company acts as an agent of the reinsurance account, which is prohibited for a fee.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, commercial reinsurance derives from commercial insurance and involves Gharar, prohibited by the Hadith on Bay' al-Gharar.

column5: The acceptance of Hawalah by the transferee is:
column6: Recommended in all cases, whatever the financial status of the payer.
column7: Obligatory in all cases, whatever the financial status of the payer.
column8: Mubah if the payer is known to be solvent, and impermissible if the payer's financial status or creditworthiness is unknown, since Hawalah then benefits neither party.
column9: Recommended if the potential payer is known to be solvent and honours payments, and Mubah (permissible) if his financial status and creditworthiness are unknown.
column11: Per 3/2, acceptance is recommended where the payer is solvent and reliable, and merely Mubah where his status is unknown.

column5: The profit of a Sharikah may be finally distributed on the basis of the proceeds of selling all the existing assets, known as (……….), or on the basis of the valuation of the assets of the Sharikah at fair value, known as (……….).
column6: Actual valuation .... constructive valuation.
column7: Constructive valuation .... distribution on account.
column8: Actual valuation .... expected profit.
column9: Constructive valuation .... actual valuation.
column11: Per 3/1/5/9, selling all assets is actual valuation; valuing them at fair value is constructive valuation.

column5: In a Musharakah with the client to finance documentary credit for imported goods, it is permissible for the Institution, after receipt of the goods, to sell its share to a third party or to its partner through a spot or deferred payment Murabahah, provided that:
column6: The sale to the partner is not based on prior binding promises nor stipulated in the Musharakah contract.
column7: The sale to the partner is stipulated in the Musharakah contract to protect the Institution against loss.
column8: The partner pays a commission for the opening of the credit and for the sale of the share.
column9: The sale to the partner is at the face value of the Institution's share, regardless of the market value at the time of the sale.
column11: Per 3/6/1, sale to the partner must not rest on prior binding bilateral promises or be stipulated in the Musharakah contract.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: It is permissible to make the execution of a unilateral promise to purchase gold contingent upon the performance of a specific index.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/2, execution of a unilateral promise to purchase gold may be made contingent on a specific index's performance.

column5: The arbitration decision is to be issued under the signature of all members of the arbitration panel, except those who raise objections against it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 11/8, all members sign, including objectors, who may state their objections; or most members sign, with reasons for non-signing given.

column5: When a private employee fails to report to work on the date specified in the hiring contract:
column6: He is entitled to no pay for the period between the specified and actual dates of work commencement, and the employer has the right to terminate the contract, unless the two parties agree on a compensatory period at the end of the contract.
column7: He is entitled to the full pay for the whole period, provided that he compensates the absence period at the end of the contract, and the employer has no right to terminate the contract, even if the absence has no excuse and causes harm to the employer.
column8: The employer may deduct from his pay double the pay of the absence period, but has no right to terminate the contract.
column9: The contract becomes null and void automatically.
column11: Per 4/9, he gets no pay for the absence period and the employer may terminate, unless they agree on a compensatory period at the end.

column5: Islamic insurance companies should not keep any cash reserves for ongoing risks that belong to traditional reinsurance companies and on which interest has to be paid.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2, Islamic insurers may not keep interest-bearing cash reserves for ongoing risks belonging to traditional reinsurers.

column5: In one sense, arbitration seems like (……….) on behalf of the two parties, although it also seems to involve (……….) in another sense.
column6: Suretyship .... public custodianship
column7: Agency .... private custodianship
column8: Reconciliation (Sulh) .... agency
column9: Hiring .... agency
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, arbitration resembles agency on behalf of the two parties, and in another sense involves private custodianship.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: In either-or options:
column6: The items must be fungible and of equal price, so that the buyer's choice does not affect the price.
column7: The items need not be fungible or of equal price, but if their prices differ, the price of each must be specified.
column8: The items must be of equal price, but need not be fungible, and the option period must be specified and not exceed three days.
column9: The option period may not exceed three days, by analogy with the cooling-off option.
column11: Per 4/1/2-4/1/3, items need not be fungible or equal in price (each price is specified); there is no min or max period.

column5: Where the Institution and the customer are partners in a Musharakah, it is permissible:
column6: To agree to form a Musharakah in a specified deal together with a promise from one of them to buy the other's share by means of Murabahah on deferred payment terms.
column7: To agree to form a Musharakah in a project together with a promise from one of them to buy the other's share by means of Murabahah, provided it is on spot payment terms.
column8: For one partner to promise to purchase the other's share at market price or at a price to be agreed upon at the time of sale, provided a new contract is drawn up; this sale may be on spot or deferred payment terms.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/2/5, a promise to buy the partner's share by Murabahah (spot or deferred) is barred; a promise at market or agreed price with a new contract is allowed.

column5: The registration of hypothecation of mobile movables like cars, trains, steamers and airplanes, through registration that is valid under the law:
column6: Is deemed constructive possession only if the pledgee also takes physical possession of the property.
column7: Stands in place of actual possession with respect to its rules and legal effects.
column8: Is deemed constructive possession for immovables only, and not for movables.
column9: Is not deemed possession, since the hypothecated property remains with the pledgor.
column11: Per 3/4, legally valid registration of hypothecation of mobile movables is constructive possession and stands in place of actual possession.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: Types of deal fragmentation in which the option to revoke is granted include:
column6: When it transpires that part of the sold items is the property of a third party.
column7: When part of the sold items is destroyed before delivery (actual or constructive).
column8: When part of the sold items in a Salam contract is not available on the delivery date.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/2-3/3/4, all three are types of deal fragmentation giving the buyer the option to revoke.

column5: A lessee may invite others to share with him in the usufruct he owns, so that they become co-owners in the usufruct of the leased property. This:
column6: Can only be done after the lessee has sub-leased the property.
column7: Can be done either before or after the lessee enters into a sub-lease of the property, the co-owners then sharing the sub-lease rental equally irrespective of their shares in the usufruct.
column8: Can only be done before entering into a sub-lease; if sub-leased afterwards, each co-owner is entitled to a share in the sub-lease rental pro rata to his share in the usufruct.
column9: Is impermissible, because the lessee does not own the usufruct.
column11: Per 4/2/4, co-lessees must be brought in before any sub-lease; once sub-leased, the lessee no longer owns the usufruct to share.

column5: The basis for the permissibility of dealing in cheques for bank transfers, when the transfer is in the same currency in which payment is to be made, is that it is a form of Da' wa Ta'ajjal.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, it belongs to the category of Suftajah, permissible according to one of two juristic opinions.

column5: Waqf by a person whose debts exceed the value of his assets is enforceable without the authorization of his creditors, as long as he has not been subjected to a ruling of bankruptcy or interdiction.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/3/3, such Waqf is contingent upon the creditors' authorization even without a ruling of bankruptcy or interdiction.

column5: Iqalah is permissible in Salam because the Prophet (peace be upon him) encouraged Iqalah in general and Salam is a form of sale; moreover, the possibility of regret is greater in Salam than in the sale of tangible goods.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 4/3.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: It is permissible to take consideration for the following, excluding:
column6: Transfer or waiver of easement rights, by means of sale or otherwise.
column7: Sale of rights to use.
column8: Transfer of put or call option rights.
column9: Sale of rights arising from first use.
column11: Per 10/1, no consideration may be taken for transfer of put or call options; per 10/3-4, easements and rights to use or of first use may be sold.

column5: It is permissible to issue new shares for increasing the capital of a corporation if such shares are issued at:
column6: The book value stated in the last balance sheet only.
column7: A price determined freely by the founders, irrespective of the value of the old shares, provided that the general assembly approves the price by majority vote.
column8: The nominal value of the old shares only.
column9: A price equivalent to the value of the old shares, worked out through expert valuation of the corporation's assets or on the basis of the market value.
column11: Per 2/3, new shares are issued at the value of the old shares, by expert valuation or market value, at a premium or discount to issue price.

column5: The basis for the buyer bearing the expenses of constructive possession represented by official registration of the sale of immovable property is the customary practice, which secures the interest of the buyer and is supported by the rule that gain is linked to the bearing of expenses.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis cites customary practice and the rule that gain is linked to bearing expenses.

column5: The arbitrator has the right to appoint an alternate arbitrator to replace him, without the permission of the party that appointed him, when:
column6: He is a volunteer who is not entitled to remuneration, since arbitration is not binding for him and he can terminate himself.
column7: Arbitration is assigned to an Institution or an arbitration committee whose members are appointed with due consideration for its declared conditions of selection.
column8: The period specified for arbitration is about to expire.
column9: The alternate arbitrator meets the same Shari'ah conditions required for the selection of judges, including non-partiality.
column11: Per 8/6, he may not appoint an alternate without permission as he was accepted in person, except where arbitration is assigned to an Institution or committee.

column5: The allocation of profits in a Sharikah contract must be made in a manner that gives each partner:
column6: A sum of money.
column7: A percentage of the capital.
column8: A sum of money plus a percentage of the remaining profit.
column9: An undivided percentage of profit.
column11: Per 3/1/5/1, each partner must get an undivided percentage of profit, not a sum of money or a percentage of capital.

column5: When a debt in a ribawī commodity is sold to the debtor himself, it is permitted:
column6: To substitute a debt in gold with silver, provided that possession of the silver is taken in the contract session, even if there is a difference in quantity.
column7: To substitute a debt in dates with another type of dates in a larger quantity, provided that possession is taken in the contract session.
column8: To substitute a debt in Egyptian Pounds with Pounds Sterling, with the Sterling amount payable within one week.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/1/1, a different ribawī kind needs possession in the session; the same kind needs equality as well; deferred currency substitution is barred.

column5: Permissibility of declaring Waqf as effective starting from a future date can be viewed in terms of analogy between Waqf and:
column6: 'Ariyah (a lent thing).
column7: Ijarah (lease).
column8: Hibah (gift).
column9: Wasiyyah (will).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a future-dated Waqf is justified by analogy with Wasiyyah (will).

column5: An IFI signed a contract with a client to provide him with a well-described and specified training program to start in six months' time, although the IFI had not yet contracted with the trainers. The ruling on this contract is:
column6: Permissible, since hiring can be for a well-described future service, with due consideration to the IFI's ability to own the service and deliver it on time, by itself or through others.
column7: Permissible, only if the client pays the full pay in advance, since hiring for a future service is judged by analogy to Salam, and the pay must be received at the session.
column8: Impermissible, because the IFI must perform the service through its own staff.
column9: Impermissible, because the IFI may not sign a hiring contract with the client before it possesses the service and becomes able to deliver it, even if it can contract with the trainers later.
column11: Per 5/1/6, a well-described future service may be contracted before owning it if the IFI can deliver on time; the 5/1/5 bar applies to specific services.

column5: If the worker (irrigator) commissions or subcontracts a third party to carry out his work without the permission of the owner:
column6: The worker forfeits his share of the crop.
column7: The owner of the trees has the option to ratify the third party contract or reject it.
column8: The subcontract is valid and binding on the owner, since the worker remains liable for the work.
column9: The Irrigation Partnership contract is automatically void, and the worker is entitled to a wage.
column11: Per 6/1/2, the owner of the trees has the option to ratify or reject the third-party contract.

column5: To secure lawful interests, it is permissible for specialised official agencies to organize trading in some shares so that it cannot be undertaken except through specialised brokers or those licensed to undertake the activity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/8, official agencies may restrict trading in some shares to specialised or licensed brokers.

column5: Animals other than camels, cows and goats are not subject to Zakah payment, unless they are owned for trade.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/6/4, other animals are not zakatable unless owned for trade; if used for production they are not included.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: If the board's Fatwa is proved to be wrong on reviewing, or on examination by a higher body:
column6: The board has to retreat from it and inform the Institution, which has to correct all the actions based on the wrong Fatwa and refrain from adopting it any more.
column7: The Fatwa remains valid for past actions, and the Institution need not rectify them.
column8: The board may retreat from it only with the approval of the General Assembly of the Institution, since the Fatwa is binding on the board once it has been communicated.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 11/1, the board must retreat and inform the Institution, which must correct all actions based on the wrong Fatwa.

column5: Parallel purchase and sale of currencies is:
column6: Permissible if the two contracts of currency exchange are not made conditional on each other, even though delivery and receipt of the two currencies are deferred, since each contract is then independent of the other.
column7: Permissible for the purpose of hedging against currency devaluation risk.
column8: Not permissible, as it incorporates invalidating factors such as the absence of delivery and receipt of the two currencies bought and sold, so that the contract amounts to a deferred sale of currency.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/9/2, parallel purchase and sale of currencies is not permissible because it involves deferred sale, conditional exchange or a binding bilateral promise.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for prohibiting the manager from undertaking to buy the investment assets at their face value or at a value initially agreed upon is that:
column6: The manager would be receiving a fee in exchange for a guarantee.
column7: It entails excessive ambiguity because the market value of the assets at maturity is unknown.
column8: This condition results in the manager undertaking to bear the partial or complete loss of the assets' value.
column9: It is a form of conventional option contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/3, such an undertaking makes the manager bear partial or complete loss of value, a forbidden condition.

column5: The institution may act as an agent of its customers in performing services that relate to real estate properties and movable assets, but only against a fee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/2, the institution may perform such agency services for a fee or free of charge.

column5: An IFI invited bids for constructing its new head office and required a final cash security of USD 10,000 from the successful bidder. After the award, the successful bidder withdrew, and the IFI's actual financial damage in the tendering process amounted to USD 3,000. The IFI may:
column6: Confiscate only USD 3,000, as compensation for the financial damage actually sustained.
column7: Confiscate the whole USD 10,000, since the bidder breached his commitment and the IFI sustained damage in the tendering process.
column8: Not deduct anything, since the security is held on trust.
column9: Confiscate the whole USD 10,000 as 'Arboun.
column11: Per 6/8/1, tender security is a trust and may be confiscated only for the equivalent of actual financial damage.

column5: In buyback, the subsequent purchase:
column6: May be concluded by a bilateral promise binding upon both parties, which takes the place of the contract, provided that it is documented in a separate deed.
column7: Must be concluded in writing, and a contract by action (conduct) is not sufficient, even where custom treats conduct as acceptance.
column8: May occur automatically upon the lapse of the agreed duration, if this was stipulated in the first contract and the price was fixed in it.
column9: Must occur via an independent contract that transfers ownership, whether verbal or by action, not automatically upon the lapse of the duration.
column11: Per 3/2–3/4, the second purchase needs its own contract (verbal or by action); it cannot be automatic, stipulated in the first, or bilaterally promised.

column5: If the customer, in case of Ijarah associated with a promise to transfer ownership, breaches his promise to lease, the promisor shall be charged:
column6: The total rentals that he promised to pay for the full term of the lease.
column7: The difference between the cost of the asset intended to be leased and the total lease rentals for the asset leased on Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek to a third party.
column8: The whole amount deposited by him to ensure his seriousness, regardless of the actual damage.
column9: The difference between the cost of acquisition and the total selling price if the asset is sold to a third party by the Institution, which is the charge applicable in operating Ijarah.
column11: Per 2/3, for a promise of Ijarah with transfer of ownership, damage = asset cost minus total rentals from re-leasing it by IMB to a third party.

column5: In unrestricted Hawalah:
column6: The payer may have recourse to the transferor even if the transfer for payment was not made on the transferor's order, provided the transferor was not a creditor of the payer and the transferee consented.
column7: The transferor is not a creditor to the payer, who pays the debt from his own funds and afterwards has recourse to the transferor, provided the transfer for payment was made on the transferor's order.
column8: The payer pays the debt from his own funds and has no recourse to the transferor.
column9: The payer settles the transferred debt from an asset belonging to the transferor that is in his possession, and has no recourse to the transferor.
column11: Per 5/1/2, the payer pays from his own funds and has recourse to the transferor if the transfer was on the transferor's order.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, profit sharing ratios must be commensurate to shareholding ratios, because profit is deserved only for contribution of funds.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, ratios may or may not match shareholdings, since profit is deserved for funds, work or guarantee (Hanbali view).

column5: If a partner in a common share Waqf wants a division of the Waqf that is indivisible, the party which refrained will be compelled to sell, and the price of the Waqf share will be deployed in a similar Waqf.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/1/4, for indivisible assets the refraining party is compelled to sell, and the Waqf share's price is put in a similar Waqf.

column5: If the ownership of the mortgaged asset is transferred (through sale, gift or will) on permission of the mortgagee:
column6: The mortgage contract remains valid in all cases, and the new owner is bound by it.
column7: The transfer is void, because the mortgaged asset may not be disposed of.
column8: The validity of the mortgage contract expires, unless the new owner accepts to keep the mortgage contract.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/1/6, transfer of ownership with the mortgagee's permission ends the mortgage, unless the new owner accepts to keep it.

column5: Taking into account the rule on sleeping partners, it is permissible to agree in a Sharikah contract that:
column6: If the profit realised is above a certain ceiling, the profit in excess of the ceiling belongs to a particular partner.
column7: A particular partner receives a lump sum out of the profit each year, whatever the amount of profit realised or the capital contributed.
column8: A particular partner receives as profit a specific percentage of his capital, whether or not any profit is realised.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 3/1/5/8, profit above a ceiling may go to a particular partner; lump sums or a percentage of capital are void (3/1/5/7).

column5: In a set-off on demand, the two debts should be:
column6: Similar in kind and type, but not necessarily in quality and date of maturity.
column7: Equal in kind, type, description and maturity.
column8: Similar in quality and date of maturity, but not necessarily in kind.
column9: Not necessarily similar in kind, type, description or maturity.
column11: Per 2/1/4(c), set-off on demand needs similarity in kind and type only; (b) is compulsory set-off and (c) contractual set-off.

column5: The statutory reserve of the joint stock company:
column6: Is deducted from the profits of both the shareholders and the policyholders in proportion to their funds, and is distributed to the shareholders upon liquidation of the company after the policyholders have been reimbursed.
column7: Is deducted from the insurance surplus, and belongs to the shareholders.
column8: Is deducted from its share capital and becomes part of shareholders' equity, and no deduction shall be made from the policyholders' fund or profits for the benefit of the shareholders.
column9: Is deducted from the policyholders' fund, since the company manages it.
column11: Per 10/4, the statutory reserve comes from share capital and is shareholders' equity; nothing is deducted from the fund for them.

column5: The subject matter of Ijarah may be a share in an undivided asset held in common with the lessee:
column6: Whether the lessee is a partner with the lessor or not, the lessee benefiting from the leased share as the lessor used to, e.g. by Muhaya'ah by time or by a particular part of the property.
column7: It is impermissible, because the usufruct of an undivided share cannot be delivered to the lessee, nor can he benefit from a share held in common with other co-owners, whether or not they are his partners.
column8: Only after the asset has been physically divided between the co-owners.
column9: Only if the lessee is a partner with the lessor in the asset.
column11: Per 5/1/2, an undivided share may be leased whether or not the lessee is a partner, with use by Muhaya'ah or other agreed means.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In case of any change in the conditions or profit sharing ratios of investment accounts:
column6: The changes require the explicit written consent of every accountholder in all cases, which the institution must obtain by registered correspondence before the changes take effect from the next period.
column7: The changes become effective immediately upon their publication on the institution's website, and the silence of the accountholders for the first thirty days is deemed implicit acceptance, even where they were never notified individually or have objected in the meantime.
column8: The institution may change them unilaterally without any notification, because it is the Mudarib, provided that the changes take effect only from the beginning of the next financial period.
column9: In principle, the institution should write to the holders; however, it may notify them by advertisement or on its website, so that implicit acceptance is obtained if no protest is received within a specific period, effective from the next period.
column11: Per 2/2/8, notice or web publication with no protest within a set period gives implicit acceptance; changes apply from the next period.

column5: According to the view that gives the seller the right to reclamation, if an inseparable increase occurred in the asset, such as an increase in the weight of livestock, and the seller chose reclamation:
column6: The right to reclamation lapses, because the characteristics of the asset have changed.
column7: He takes the asset, but must pay the insolvent the value of the inseparable increase that occurred in it.
column8: He takes the asset together with any separate increase arising from it.
column9: He takes the asset as it is, and he will only have that; a separate increase, however, would belong to the insolvent.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, with an inseparable increase he takes only the asset; a separate increase belongs to the insolvent.

column5: Loans or debts owed by the seller to the Institution as a result of previous transactions may be recognised as the capital of Salam, provided they have fallen due.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/4, a debt may not be the capital of Salam, as this renders it a sale of debt.

column5: An investment manager divided the capital into two parts: the first was used in Murabahah contracts with parties having strong credit ratings, so that the principal and the Murabahah profit protect the initial capital; the second was used in 'Arboun contracts to purchase assets. If the value of the assets declines:
column6: The 'Arboun contracts may be traded to third parties in order to recover their value, while the capital remains protected by the Murabahah contracts.
column7: The purchase contracts are not completed and the loss is limited to the amount of the 'Arboun, while the capital is protected by the Murabahah contracts.
column8: The purchase contracts are not completed, and the investment manager is liable to the investors for the amount of the 'Arboun.
column9: The purchase contracts must be completed and the resulting loss is borne by the investment manager.
column11: Per 4/2/7(d), the purchases are not completed and the loss is limited to the 'Arboun; trading 'Arboun contracts is impermissible.

column5: If money is paid together with an agreement to execute a contract in the future (an agreement to sell), it is considered 'Arboun (Earnest Money) and may be forfeited by the seller if the buyer does not conclude the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2, an agreement to sell is a promise and not a contract, so money paid with it is not 'Arboun.

column5: When the card issuer of a charge card demands depositing a cash amount as a guarantee:
column6: It is not permitted, as a charge card may not be secured by a cash guarantee.
column7: It should not stipulate that the cardholder deposit it in the current account; rather, the cardholder is given the option to deposit it in the current or investment account.
column8: It should stipulate that the amount be deposited in the current account, so that it remains available for recovery by the card issuer at any time, and the issuer may use it for its own benefit during the period.
column9: It should stipulate that the amount be deposited in an investment account only.
column11: Per 4/3/2, the issuer may not require the guarantee in a current account; the cardholder chooses a current or investment account.

column5: It is permissible to stipulate in the insurance policy special cases that lead to deprivation from indemnity, provided that justice, preservation of rights, and avoidance of abusive conditions are well observed.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/2, such deprivation cases may be stipulated if justice, preservation of rights and avoidance of abusive terms are observed.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: In a commutative contract where 'Arboun is permissible, gold may be used as 'Arboun provided that:
column6: The 'Arboun is equal in weight to the gold content of the subject matter.
column7: The subject matter of the contract is not gold, silver or currencies.
column8: The subject matter of the contract is gold, so that the 'Arboun is of the same kind.
column9: The 'Arboun is returned to the buyer if the sale is terminated.
column11: Per 7/3, gold may be 'Arboun if the subject matter is not gold, silver or currencies; the seller owns it whether the sale completes or not.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of obtaining earnest money ('Arboun) to secure performance is:
column6: The opinion of Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar of the Maliki school on the commitment to donate.
column7: The Hadith of Ibn Umar about selling camels in Al-Baqi' for dinars and taking dirhams.
column8: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh, to whom the Prophet (peace be upon him) granted a three-day option, which the majority of jurists extended to earnest money.
column9: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab in the presence of some companions of the Prophet (peace be upon him), permitted by Imam Ahmad.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, 'Arboun rests on the practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab before the companions, permitted by Imam Ahmad.

column5: The Waqf Deed shall include:
column6: The acceptance of the Waqf beneficiaries, signed by each of them.
column7: The approval of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Institution that manages the Waqf.
column8: The determination of the overseer, his duties and his remuneration, and the date when the Waqf comes into effect.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/5/2, the deed includes the overseer, his duties and remuneration and the effective date; beneficiaries' acceptance is not required (2/4/1/1).

column5: An IFI hired an employee full-time for a monthly salary. During the first month the employee put himself at the disposal of the IFI, but the IFI did not assign him any task, and it then refused to pay his salary for that month. The correct ruling is:
column6: Only half the salary is due, as the employee was available at the disposal of the IFI but did not actually perform any work during the month.
column7: Only the normal pay for similar services (Ajr al-Mithl) is due, since no specific task was assigned to him.
column8: The salary is due, since the pay is payable on making the service available, when the employee puts himself at the disposal of the employer, even if no task has been assigned.
column9: No salary is due, since the employee has not delivered any work and the pay is made in exchange of the benefit.
column11: Per 5/2/3, the pay is payable on delivery or on making the service available; per the basis the employer has no excuse for not benefiting.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: A commercial license is a right given by the relevant authority to certain businesses to engage in specified activities. The license holder may dispose of it:
column6: Without consideration only.
column7: For consideration only, and never as a gift.
column8: In no case, since it is confined to his personal use.
column9: For or without consideration, unless specifically prohibited by law.
column11: Per 3/3/3/3, a commercial license may be disposed of for or without consideration unless the law specifically prohibits it.

column5: The hired service shall be permissible, because what is prohibited by Shari'ah cannot be an object of a Shari'ah-recognizable contract, and impermissible hiring entails support to wrongdoing.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/1/1, a prohibited service cannot be the object of a valid contract and would support sin and transgression.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The following are examples of medium Gharar, except:
column6: Sale of commodities that cannot be known unless broken.
column7: Fixed-term Mudarabah.
column8: Leasing of fruit trees.
column9: Selling of fruits before production.
column11: Per 4/2/1, selling fruits before production is excessive Gharar; the others are listed as medium Gharar in 4/2/3.

column5: Where the rental is payable in instalments and the lessor has stipulated that the lessee shall immediately pay the remaining instalments if he delays, without a valid reason and after a specified period of due notice, payment of one instalment or more:
column6: The lessor may also stipulate an increase in the rental due because of the delay.
column7: The asset shall be made available for the lessee to use for the remaining period, and the accelerated rental is settled at the end of the Ijarah period or upon earlier termination.
column8: The accelerated rental becomes final and is not subject to any settlement.
column9: The lessor may repossess the asset and retain all the accelerated rentals, since the lessee has breached the contract by delaying payment of the rental after due notice, and the lessee has no claim to any settlement at the end of the period.
column11: Per 6/2, acceleration requires the asset to remain available to the lessee, and accelerated rent is settled at expiry or termination.

column5: In a credit transaction, stipulating a right for the Institution to freeze the customer's current account:
column6: Is permitted if the frozen amount is limited to the amount of the debt, as with investment accounts.
column7: Is not permitted, unless the customer has freely, willingly and absolutely agreed to it.
column8: Is permitted in all cases, as with investment accounts.
column9: Is not permitted in any case, even with the customer's consent.
column11: Per 6/5/2, freezing a current account may not be stipulated, unless the customer freely and absolutely agrees.

column5: Diversifying investment assets by dividing the capital between Murabahah and Musharakah contracts is permissible even though it falls under the prohibition of combining contracts in one contract, because it achieves the interest of the investors.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/2/7, diversification does not fall under that prohibition, as each contract is conducted independently.

column5: The buyer of the debt may stipulate upon the seller that the debt be covered by Islamic insurance (Takaful) before its sale.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/3, the buyer may require a Shari'ah-compliant third-party guarantee, such as Takaful on the debt before sale.

column5: A public complaint about the default in payment of a solvent debtor, and warning other companies about his character, is:
column6: Not a prohibited slander; on the contrary, it is an obligation, as it falls under the category of advice which it is a duty to give.
column7: A prohibited slander, which is permitted only in case of necessity, and then only after a court has established the default.
column8: Permissible only if the debtor consented to it in the contract, since a public complaint requires the consent of the person complained of.
column9: Permissible only if the debtor is not subjected to any other penalty.
column11: Per the basis on non-material penalties, warning others is not slander but a duty of advice.

column5: The elimination of prohibited income specific to the share is obligatory on:
column6: The owner of the share only if the profits have been distributed to him, and only in the proportion of the profits actually received by him in cash during the financial period.
column7: The intermediary, agent or manager, out of part of their commission or wages.
column8: The owner of the share, whether investor or trader, at the end of the financial period; it is not obligatory on one who sells the shares before that date.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/4/6/1-3, the shareholder at period-end must eliminate, whether or not profits are distributed; intermediaries need not.

column5: A discount coupon that gives its holder a specific discount along with the right to enter into a prize draw is:
column6: Permissible absolutely, as it is a free or complementary coupon.
column7: Subject to the same ruling as that for prize draws.
column8: Impermissible, because it combines a discount with a draw.
column9: Subject to the same ruling as that for discount cards issued against a fee.
column11: Per 3/6/2/3 (third type), a coupon with a discount plus a draw right follows the ruling on prize draws in 3/3.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: A customer gave an IFI 50 grams of gold as Hamish Jiddiyyah when promising to buy equipment by Murabahah. Two months later the Murabahah contract was concluded, and the parties agreed that the gold be made part of the price. The gold shall be evaluated at:
column6: The market price of gold at the date of the promise to purchase.
column7: The market price of gold at the time it was deposited as Hamish Jiddiyyah.
column8: The prevailing market price of gold at the time of payment.
column9: Any price agreed by the parties at the time the gold was deposited.
column11: Per 7/2/2, gold given as Hamish Jiddiyyah and made part of the price is evaluated at the prevailing market price at the time of payment.

column5: It is permissible for a partner in a Sharikah contract to stipulate that another partner:
column6: Provides a personal guarantee or a mortgage to cover misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.
column7: Guarantees him a minimum return on his capital, payable even if the Sharikah makes no profit.
column8: Guarantees his capital against any loss resulting from the business, if the guarantee is stated in the contract.
column9: Undertakes to buy his share at its face value at maturity, whatever the value of the assets then.
column11: Per 3/1/4/2, a guarantee or mortgage may be required only to cover misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column5: The basis for non-inclusion of all types of deposits of safekeeping in the insolvency assets is that they are not the property of the insolvent; interdiction only occurs regarding his property, not the property of others entrusted to him.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 9/3, safekeeping deposits are not the insolvent's property, so interdiction does not reach them.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: One of the conditions for the validity of a cooling-off option is that:
column6: The option period must not exceed three days, in accordance with the Hadith of Habban Bin Munqidh.
column7: The option must be stipulated before the conclusion of the contract and cannot be included subsequently.
column8: The option must be granted to both parties to the contract.
column9: The option must have a stipulated time limit; it is not valid if the time limit is unspecified or indeterminate.
column11: Per 2/2/2, a stipulated time limit is required; there is no minimum or maximum, save what custom deems unacceptable.

column5: Statutory and voluntary reserves:
column6: Statutory reserves are deductible from zakatable assets, being required by law and owed to the regulatory authority, whereas voluntary reserves are not deductible since they are set aside at the will of the shareholders.
column7: Both types are not deductible from zakatable assets, because in Shari'ah they are not debt obligations owed by the company, although they appear under liabilities.
column8: Both types are deductible from zakatable assets, since they appear under liabilities and are required by accounting standards.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/2/1, both statutory and voluntary reserves are not deductible; they are owned by the company and zakatable under the net assets method.

column5: It is permissible for the issuer of shares to add a certain percentage to the actual value of the shares on the subscription date in order to recover issuing expenses, provided that such percentage is appropriately estimated to reflect the actual expenses incurred.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1/2/2, an addition to cover issuing expenses is allowed if it reflects the actual expenses.

column5: Works under implementation (constructions) relating to agriculture are part of zakatable assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/4/4, works under implementation relating to agriculture are not part of zakatable assets.

column5: The reason why the lessor may not stipulate that the lessee will undertake the major maintenance of the leased asset is that:
column6: The lessee holds the asset in a fiduciary capacity and is not liable for its damage, even where the damage results from his misconduct, and the cost of major maintenance would be a liability on him.
column7: The owner of the asset is responsible for insuring it.
column8: This condition defeats the purpose of an Ijarah contract, as the lessor's duty is to ensure that the usufruct is intact so that he may be entitled to the rentals.
column9: Major maintenance is a debt that may not be increased.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, shifting major maintenance defeats the contract's purpose; the lessor must keep the usufruct intact to earn rent.

column5: When a person is hired for doing a specific service/work, the employer:
column6: May hire out the service/work to a sub-employer without permission, provided that it is at the same pay agreed upon with the employee.
column7: Has the right to hire out the service/work to a sub-employer absolutely, since he owns the service and becomes able to transfer it to someone else.
column8: Has no right to hire out the service/work of such person to a sub-employer, unless the contract permits sub-hiring, or this has been agreed upon by the two parties.
column9: May never hire out the service/work to a sub-employer, even if the contract permits it.
column11: Per 5/1/3, sub-hiring a specific service/work requires a contractual permission or agreement of the two parties.

column5: In a Salam contract, it is permitted to substitute the subject of Salam (other than cash) after the maturity date by another asset, without stipulating such substitution in the contract, provided that:
column6: The market value of the substitute asset is not less than the Salam capital, and it is fit to be the subject of Salam for the Salam capital.
column7: The substitution was stipulated in the original Salam contract, and the substitute asset is of a different kind from the subject of Salam.
column8: The substitute asset is of the same kind as the subject of Salam, and its market value does not exceed the Salam capital paid at the contract date or the delivery date.
column9: The substitute asset is fit to be the subject of Salam for the Salam capital, and its market value does not exceed that of the subject of Salam at delivery.
column11: Per 4/1/1/3, the substitute (same or different kind) must be fit as a Salam subject for the capital and not worth more than the subject at delivery.

column5: Permissible methods of protecting capital include:
column6: Taking security and guarantees in Murabahah, Salam or Istisna'a contracts to ensure that debts are paid.
column7: Obligating the investment manager to purchase the investment assets at their nominal price.
column8: Stipulating that the investment manager is liable for loss of capital, if the investors so require.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/2/8, taking security in deferred-payment contracts is permissible; B and C are prohibited by 5/3 and 5/1.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: When gold ingots are sold for currencies, constructive possession of the ingot is realized by:
column6: Allocation of the ingot and enabling the buyer to dispose of it.
column7: Holding a certificate representing ownership of a specified ingot distinguishable by serial numbers or other distinct marks, issued on the trade date (T+0) by officially or customarily recognized agencies and enabling the buyer to take physical possession at his request.
column8: Holding a certificate representing an undivided entitlement to unallocated gold, issued within two business days (T+2).
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/4, constructive possession is by allocation and enabling disposal, or by a T+0 certificate of a specified, allocated ingot.

column5: When the company claims indemnity from the party who causes the injury:
column6: It represents the participants in all the tasks relating to the case, such as filing of lawsuits and realization of the consequent rights, and deposits the proceeds in the insurance account.
column7: It deposits the proceeds in its own account as compensation for its efforts.
column8: It may not claim, because the right belongs exclusively to the injured participant.
column9: It pays the proceeds to the injured participant in addition to the indemnity he received from the fund, since the right of recovery belongs to him alone and the company only assists him in filing the claim.
column11: Per 10/6, the company represents participants in pursuing the wrongdoer and deposits the proceeds in the insurance account.

column5: An undertaking by a third party to guarantee the capital for a fee:
column6: Is impermissible, as it is a form of conventional insurance.
column7: Is permissible if the fee does not exceed the actual cost incurred by the guarantor.
column8: Is permissible if the third party is administratively independent of the investment manager.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 5/4, a third-party guarantee of capital for a fee is a form of conventional insurance and is impermissible.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing the negotiation of documents payable on sight, including bills of exchange, for an amount less than their nominal value is that:
column6: It involves taking a commission for a guarantee.
column7: The documents do not represent the goods.
column8: This adopts the form of the sale of debt, which is prohibited.
column9: It amounts to Bay' al-'Inah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, negotiating such documents below nominal value takes the form of a prohibited sale of debt.

column5: Declaring a property as Waqf:
column6: Does not affect the owner's right of ownership until the Waqf is accepted by the beneficiaries.
column7: Transfers the ownership of the property to the Waqf superintendent.
column8: Transfers the ownership of the property to the beneficiaries of the Waqf.
column9: Would spontaneously deprive its donating owner of the right of ownership, since Waqf is a binding commitment.
column11: Per 2/2, Waqf is a binding commitment, so declaring a property Waqf spontaneously deprives the donor of ownership; beneficiaries do not own it.

column5: The exploration licensee, after discovering the minerals, water or any object in question, becomes eligible for the exclusive right of obtaining the utilization concession in the area specified in the license, unless the license stipulates otherwise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/3, discovery gives the exploration licensee the exclusive right to the utilization concession unless the license provides otherwise.

column5: Where the Ijarah is combined, through a separate document, with a gift contingent upon payment of the remaining rent instalments, ownership passes to the lessee once the condition is fulfilled, without the need for any other procedure or document to be signed.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/4, the contingent gift takes effect automatically once all instalments are paid.

column5: The basis for prohibiting, in a lending-based card, burdening the cardholder with the fees deducted by the acquirer from the card acceptor is:
column6: These fees are against services that do not include lending.
column7: Part of these fees is directed to the lender, who is the card issuer, so it would be a loan carrying benefit.
column8: It would be a sale of debt to a third party.
column9: The card acceptor is the only party liable for such fees under the rules of agency, since the acquirer acts as its agent for recovery.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/1/2/1, part of the fees goes to the issuer (the lender), making it a loan carrying benefit.

column5: The two parties may terminate the Ijarah contract before it begins to run.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 7/2/5.

column5: Utilization concession contracts for minerals, water resources and the like are classified by the Shari'ah as a form of Ju'alah because:
column6: Utilization cannot take place without exploration, which entails an unknown amount of effort, while the remuneration of the concession holder is usually a well-defined lump sum or percentage of output.
column7: The State is not the owner of the minerals.
column8: The remuneration of the licensee is always unknown at the time of the contract, since it depends on the quantity of minerals actually extracted, and the effort of utilization is known in advance to both parties.
column9: The licensee bears no risk in the project.
column11: Per 5/3, the effort (exploration) is unknown while the remuneration is well-defined, which is the nature of Ju'alah.

column5: An IFI agreed to provide a client with maintenance services for a monthly fee. The client failed to pay the fees of the past three months and asked to reschedule them over the next year. The IFI agreed, provided that the overdue amount is increased by 5%. This arrangement is:
column6: Impermissible only because the increase exceeds the normal pay for similar services.
column7: Impermissible, because the unpaid pay of past periods is a debt owed by the employer, and stipulating an increase against rescheduling it is Riba.
column8: Permissible, provided that the increase does not exceed the IFI's actual cost of funds for the period of rescheduling.
column9: Permissible, because the pay can be amended on the consent of the two parties, whether it relates to past or future periods.
column11: Per 5/2/5 and its basis, past unpaid pay is a debt; increasing it against extending repayment is Riba. Only future periods' pay may be amended.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting the separation of debts and tangible assets in a legal entity that materializes commingling, and disposing of it without abiding by the rulings of the sale of debt, is:
column6: That formation of the entity meets the requirements of assemblage (tarkīb), which the Mālikīs require in permitting the sale of jewellery ornamented with gold or silver.
column7: The analogy of ḥawāla (novation), since the entity assumes the debts of its partners from the debtors.
column8: The concept of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya) based on turnover of business, by which the debts are ancillary to the activity of the entity, whatever the ratio of the debts to the assets.
column9: That the division is a form of ṣulḥ among the partners, by which each partner settles his claim with a share of the assets.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 8/2, a legal entity meets the Mālikī requirement of assemblage (tarkīb).

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Assessment of whether Gharar is excessive could differ according to place and time, and has to be determined in the light of normal practice ('Urf).
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/1, the assessment of excessive Gharar may differ by place and time and is determined in light of 'Urf.

column5: For Sukuk of usufruct of a described asset, or of services from a party to be specified in the future, it is permissible to set up a parallel Ijarah on tangible assets by employing the same description for the usufruct that was provided to the holders of the Sukuk, provided the two lease contracts remain independent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/11, in the cases of 5/2/8 and 5/2/10, a parallel Ijarah with the same usufruct description is allowed if the two leases remain independent.

column5: Shari'ah permits institutions to provide online access services to users:
column6: On the basis of a Ju'alah contract only, in which the fee is due upon the completion of each transaction.
column7: Free of charge only, because the service is a mere facility offered to clients.
column8: On the basis of subscription contracts or any other similar arrangement, and against a specific fee.
column9: On the basis of an agency contract against a percentage of the value of the transactions concluded by the users.
column11: Per 3/1, online access services may be provided on the basis of subscription contracts or similar arrangements, against a specific fee.

column5: An IFI sold a quantity of wheat through Salam and received the Salam capital, but the wheat had not yet been delivered on the date when Zakah became due. In calculating its Zakah base:
column6: The market value of the wheat at the Zakah date is deducted from zakatable assets, and the Salam capital is excluded from them, since the wheat is owed to the buyer.
column7: The Salam capital received is part of its cash assets, and its amount is deducted from zakatable assets since the undelivered goods constitute a debt.
column8: The Salam capital received is not part of its zakatable assets until the wheat is delivered.
column9: The Salam capital is part of its zakatable assets, and nothing is deducted for the undelivered wheat.
column11: Per 5/3/4/10 the capital received is part of the seller's cash assets; per 6/3/3 the undelivered goods are a debt, so the Salam capital is deducted.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to organize or sponsor competitions in compliance with the following parameters, excluding:
column6: The expenses for the competition, including the reward, should be covered by the Institution out of its own funds (shareholders' funds).
column7: Due consideration must be paid to public interest and appropriate priorities, without indulging in extravagance.
column8: The expenses for the competition may be covered from the funds of the investment accounts, provided that the reward itself is paid from the shareholders' funds.
column9: The competition must be approved by the Institution's Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column11: Per 2/3/3/1, all competition expenses, including the reward, come from shareholders' funds and not from investment account funds.

column5: ………… is the transfer of debt from the transferor (Muheel) to the payer (Muhal Alaihi), whereby a debtor is replaced by another debtor:
column6: Transfer of right (Hawalat al-Haqq).
column7: Hawalah of debt (transfer of debt).
column8: Contractual set-off.
column9: Personal guarantee (Kafalah).
column11: Per 2, Hawalah of debt replaces a debtor with another debtor; transfer of right replaces a creditor with another.

column5: It was determined through constructive liquidation that a Mudarabah investment had accrued profit, which was added to the capital. The investment then suffered a loss due to the Mudarib's negligence. The Mudarib:
column6: Is not liable for the loss of that profit, since a loss of profit is never compensated.
column7: Is liable for the original capital only, while the loss of the accrued profit is borne by the capital provider.
column8: Is liable for the loss of that profit only if it had already been distributed.
column9: Is liable to indemnify for the loss of that profit, as it has become a part of the capital.
column11: Per 3/7, profit accrued and added to capital after liquidation becomes capital, so the negligent Mudarib must indemnify it.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting the sale of a gold–silver alloy for pure gold or pure silver, on condition of spot exchange and that the pure counter-value exceeds its kind in the alloy in weight, is:
column6: That, in terms of ruling (Hukm), majority is tantamount to the whole, so that the alloy is treated as pure gold only when gold predominates.
column7: That a thing which is not permissible in itself may be permissible as an accessory, so that the other substance in the alloy is disregarded altogether.
column8: That the pure counter-value is equal in weight to its kind in the alloy and the excess is in lieu of the other substance, per the Hanafi School.
column9: That there is a different Illah (ratio legis) in each of the counter-values, so that equality in weight is not required and the alloy is treated as a separate commodity.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/3/1/1, the matching weight offsets its kind and the excess counters the other metal, per the Hanafi School.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution, acting either as manufacturer or as ultimate purchaser, to give or demand 'Arboun as a guarantee, which:
column6: Is held as an investment on the basis of Mudarabah until delivery, and the profit is shared between the manufacturer and the ultimate purchaser in equal shares until the date of delivery.
column7: Must be refunded in full if the contract is rescinded, unless the contract expressly provides for forfeiture of a part of it.
column8: Will be part of the price if the contract is fulfilled, or forfeited if the contract is rescinded; it is preferable to limit the forfeited amount to the actual damage.
column9: May be demanded only by the Institution acting as manufacturer, and not by the Institution acting as ultimate purchaser, who may only give it.
column11: Per 3/3/1, 'Arboun becomes part of the price or is forfeited on rescission, preferably only to the extent of actual damage.

column5: When the Institution accepts agency for payment of Zakah on behalf of all or some of its equity holders or the holders of investment accounts:
column6: The agency is valid only if the Institution is itself committed by law to pay Zakah.
column7: Funds should be available, or submitted by the principals of such agency, for payment of Zakah on their behalf.
column8: The Institution must pay the Zakah from its own funds, being their agent, and may not recover it from the principals.
column9: The Institution becomes liable for that Zakah as if it were its own Zakah, even if the principals do not provide the funds.
column11: Per 2/2/2, when the Institution acts as Zakah agent, funds should be available or submitted by the principals for paying Zakah on their behalf.

column5: A penalty clause in an Istisna'a contract for delay in delivery is impermissible, because any increase over the amount agreed in the contract is Riba.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/3 and the basis, penalty clauses are permissible in Istisna'a; the Riba objection applies to delay in settling debts.

column5: Cash amounts of earnest money forwarded on conclusion of written or verbal exchange-based (Mu'awadah) contracts are owned by the Institution, and Zakah has to be paid on them even if the goods in question have not been delivered.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/3/9, such earnest money is owned by the Institution and is not deducted from zakatable assets, even before delivery.

column5: The holder of commercial paper may have recourse to the endorsers and the guarantor only after obtaining a court judgment against the drawer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/2, recourse to signatories severally or jointly arises after the drawer's (or issuer's) refusal to pay.

column5: There is no restriction on the institution if it distinguishes between owners of current accounts with respect to what relates to deposits and withdrawals, like exclusive booths for receiving the owners of some accounts, or distinguishing between the types of cheques.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/1/3, distinguishing between current account holders in matters of deposits and withdrawals is not restricted.

column5: The following animals are not part of zakatable assets:
column6: Working animals, such as animals used in land plowing, irrigation and carrying.
column7: Horses, mules and donkeys used for work or adornment, and not owned for trade.
column8: Chickens acquired for production.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/6/3, 5/6/6 and 5/6/7, working animals, non-trade horses/mules/donkeys, and production chickens (treated as Mustaghallat) are not zakatable.

column5: In principle, the capital of Sharikah should be contributed in the form of monetary assets. Contributing tangible assets (commodities) as the capital of Sharikah is:
column6: Permissible, with the agreement of all partners, after the monetary values of the assets are determined and expressed in currency so as to know the share of each partner.
column7: Permissible at the discretion of the managing partner, with the assets recorded at their historical cost, without the need for the agreement of the other partners.
column8: Absolutely impermissible, because the capital of Sharikah must be in cash and any other asset leads to uncertainty about each partner's share in the capital and in the profit of the venture.
column9: Permissible, provided the assets are valued only upon liquidation of the Sharikah, so that each partner's share is determined at that time.
column11: Per 3/1/2/1, tangible assets may be contributed with all partners' agreement after their monetary value is determined in currency.

column5: If the same asset is mortgaged to more than one mortgagee, and all mortgages are of the same rank:
column6: The consent of the last mortgagee alone has to be sought, and the mortgage right is shared among them equally, whatever their respective debts.
column7: This is impermissible, since the same asset cannot be mortgaged to more than one mortgagee, even with the consent of the parties.
column8: The consent of all the parties has to be sought, and the mortgage right in the asset is shared among them in proportion to their debts.
column9: The first mortgagee has priority to have his debt repaid in full before the others.
column11: Per 3/2/3, with mortgages of the same rank, all parties must consent and the right is shared in proportion to their respective debts.

column5: It is not permissible for the Institution to undertake transactions in documentary credit, for itself or on behalf of another, in the following cases, excluding:
column6: When the credit pertains to goods that are prohibited by the Shari'ah.
column7: When the credit includes interest, charged or paid, whether explicitly or impliedly, as in the case of discounting bills of exchange.
column8: When the credit is irrevocable and confirmed by another bank.
column9: When the credit is based on a contract that is void or irregular according to the Shari'ah due to vitiating conditions.
column11: Per 3/1/3, prohibited goods, void/irregular contracts and interest bar the transaction; irrevocable confirmed credits are allowed.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The terms of an IFI's investment accounts provide that profit is shared 70% for the accountholders and 30% for the IFI as Mudarib, and that if the annual rate of profit exceeds 8%, the excess is taken by the IFI as an incentive. The realized rate of profit for the year was 6%. In this case:
column6: The accountholders receive the whole profit, since the IFI's incentive is linked to exceeding 8%.
column7: The IFI is not entitled to any profit, because the limit of 8% has not been reached.
column8: The incentive clause is void and renders the Mudarabah contract null and void.
column9: The whole realized profit is shared 70% and 30% as agreed upon between the two parties.
column11: Per 4/4, the excess-over-index clause is valid; if profit is at or below the limit it is shared as agreed between the two parties.

column5: An Index is:
column6: A figure computed statistically on a selected package of financial papers or commodities dealt in organized or non-organized financial markets, or both, in which each paper/commodity is given a specific weight according to its market value, and the total value is divided by a constant figure.
column7: The average of the prices of all financial papers dealt in an organized market on a given day.
column8: A financial paper representing a common share in a selected package of financial papers or commodities.
column9: A contract under which money is paid or received on the mere occurrence of certain readings in the financial markets, the amount being determined by multiplying the difference between the readings at the contract date and at maturity by a fixed value per point, and settled in cash without any delivery of the underlying papers.
column11: Per 2/1, an index is a computed figure from a weighted package of papers or commodities, its total divided by a constant figure.

column5: It is permitted to sell a negotiable instrument to the debtor or to a third party, subject to the provisions of the sale of debt to the debtor and to a third party.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/1/1, a negotiable instrument may be sold to the debtor or a third party subject to items 4 and 5.

column5: The basis for depriving the Waqf superintendent of the right of leasing the Waqf to himself or his son (without resorting to legal authorities) is:
column6: The fact that a person cannot be both the lessor and the lessee in the same contract, even on behalf of others.
column7: The fact that such leasing will reduce the chances for investment of the Waqf property, as in the prohibition of lending it.
column8: The fear from favoritism which is part of human nature, so that prohibiting such leasing minimizes the chance of neglecting the interest of the Waqf.
column9: The desire to safeguard the rights of the Waqif's heirs.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the prohibition stems from fear of favoritism, which is part of human nature. Reduced investment chances is the basis for barring lending.

column5: Delivery of the subject-matter of Istisna'a may take place before the due date if it meets the agreed specifications, and the ultimate purchaser is then obliged to accept it unless he has a good reason for rejecting it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the rule in 6/2.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, when the allocations deducted from the solidarity reinsurance fund remain unpaid until the time of liquidation:
column6: They are given to the participants, as in commercial reinsurance companies.
column7: They are spent on charitable purposes and are not given to the participants.
column8: They are transferred to the shareholders of the reinsurance company.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (difference j), unpaid allocations at liquidation go to charity, unlike commercial reinsurers where they go to participants.

column5: Istibdal (exchange) of Waqf assets should be subject to the following conditions:
column6: The Waqf must have reached the stage of generating no income, while there is no money for its development.
column7: There should be no excessive injustice in the sale price.
column8: Istibdal should be permitted by the judiciary.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 9/3, all three are conditions of Istibdal, along with meeting the interest of the Waqf and, for real estate, exchange for real estate.

column5: Investment Sukuk are characterized by the following, excluding:
column6: They represent a common share in the ownership of the assets made available for investment, whether non-monetary assets, usufructs, services or a mixture of these plus intangible rights, debts and monetary assets.
column7: They represent a debt owed to the issuer by the certificate holder.
column8: They are certificates of equal value issued in the name of the owner or bearer in order to establish the claim of the certificate owner over the financial rights and obligations represented by the certificate.
column9: Their owners share the return as stated in the subscription prospectus and bear the losses in proportion to the certificates held by them.
column11: Per 4/2, Investment Sukuk do not represent a debt owed to the issuer by the certificate holder; the other statements are characteristics in 4/1, 4/2, 4/5.

column5: Waqf is permissible in money. In this case:
column6: The income generated from utilization of the money is spent while retaining the principal amount; utilization may include Shari'ah-based lending as well as permissible and safe investments like Mudarabah.
column7: The principal amount is to be spent on the beneficiaries in instalments over the period of the Waqf, since money cannot be retained without being consumed and cannot be invested for the beneficiaries.
column8: The money may be utilized only through investment, since lending generates no income for the beneficiaries.
column9: The money may be utilized only through Shari'ah-based lending, since investment exposes the principal amount to the risk of loss, which is not allowed in Waqf, and the Waqf superintendent guarantees the principal.
column11: Per 3/4/3/2, the principal is retained and the income spent; utilization may be Shari'ah-based lending or safe investments like Mudarabah.

column5: Stipulating on the holder of a charge card to pay interest amounts if he delays in settling what is owed by him is permitted, since the charge card is a credit instrument.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/3/1, the charge card must not lead to lending on interest, including stipulating interest for late settlement.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: A cooling-off option to revoke must be stipulated in the contract using the word "revocation" or a specific word bearing its meaning.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per item 3, the option may be stipulated in any form that indicates it; no specific word with the meaning of revocation is required.

column5: It is permissible for a third party to undertake voluntarily that he will compensate the investment losses of the party to whom the undertaking is given, provided:
column6: The undertaking is stated in the Mudarabah contract as a condition for its enforcement, provided the third party is other than the Mudarib, the investment agent or one of the partners.
column7: The third party receives a fee proportionate to the risk he assumes.
column8: The undertaking is given by the Mudarib after the conclusion of the Mudarabah contract.
column9: The third party is other than the Mudarib, investment agent or a partner, and the guarantee is not linked in any manner to the Mudarabah financing or investment agency contract.
column11: Per 6/6, the volunteer must be other than the Mudarib, agent or partner, and the guarantee must be unlinked to the contract.

column5: A private employee may, at the same time, work for anyone else without the permission of his employer, provided that he observes the hiring period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/3, a private employee has no right to work for anyone else at the same time except with his employer's permission.

column5: Mostly, the customer does not bear any fees or cost for using the debit card, except for:
column6: Cash withdrawal at ATMs of an institution other than the card issuer, or paying the prices of goods and services in a currency other than that of the card balance.
column7: Any cash withdrawal, including withdrawal at the ATMs of the card issuer, as well as inquiring about the balance or printing a statement at the ATMs of any institution.
column8: Paying the prices of goods and services in the currency of the card balance.
column9: Inquiring about the balance at the ATMs of the card issuer.
column11: Per 3/1/4, the debit cardholder mostly pays only for withdrawals at other institutions' ATMs or payments in another currency.

column5: The Standard on Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications covers:
column6: Mortgages requested by the Institution with the aim of documenting the debts and commitments owed to it by other individuals and Institutions.
column7: Mortgages presented by the Institution to other parties in order to document the debts and commitments it owes to them.
column8: Mortgages which the Institution, in its capacity as a notary or agent, keeps for the benefit of other parties.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 1, the scope covers mortgages taken by, given by, and kept as notary or agent by the Institution.

column5: Collusion with a third party to resell a commodity to its original seller at a cash price lower than the deferred price is permissible, because the engagement of the third party changes the essence of the transaction.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/4 and its basis, it is a stratagem for 'Inah; the third party does not change the essence of the transaction.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of dealing in a bill of exchange is that it is in the meaning of:
column6: Hawalah.
column7: Qard (loan).
column8: Suftajah (demand note).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a bill of exchange is in the meaning of Hawalah or Qard, or of Suftajah.

column5: An Islamic insurance company operates in a country where no Islamic reinsurance coverage is available for a class of large risks, and there is a dire public need for such coverage. It wishes to reinsure these risks with a traditional reinsurance company. The correct position is:
column6: It may do so as a transitional arrangement from public need amounting to necessity, with Shari'ah Supervisory Board approval, limited to the minimum size and to periods commensurate to the actual need.
column7: It may do so without any restriction, since Islamic reinsurance is not available.
column8: It may do so, provided that it accepts the redistributions of insurance surplus from the traditional reinsurer and donates them to charity, and that the reinsurance is limited to one year in all cases.
column9: It may not do so in any case, because traditional reinsurance involves prohibited Gharar and a public need cannot justify what the Shari'ah prohibits, however dire.
column11: Per 3/2 and 6, such reinsurance is allowed as a transitional necessity, with SSB approval, minimum size and periods matching actual need.

column5: The right of set-off stipulated by the Institution to recover amounts owed by a defaulting debtor from his accounts with the Institution:
column6: Requires the consent of the debtor at the time of the set-off, even if the right was stipulated in the contract establishing the indebtedness and the debtor has been notified of the default.
column7: Must be documented in a separate agreement concluded after the default.
column8: Does not require the consent of the debtor, but should preferably be documented in the contract establishing the indebtedness, in order to shorten procedures in case of dispute.
column9: Is valid only after a court order establishing the default, even if it was stipulated in the contract, in order to shorten procedures in case of dispute.
column11: Per the basis (d), set-off needs no debtor consent but is preferably documented in the debt contract; it rests on amicable recovery.

column5: The cover of a documentary credit may be any of the following, excluding:
column6: A back-to-back letter of credit.
column7: A letter of guarantee issued by a bank participating in the issuance or confirmation of the credit.
column8: Interest-based receivables.
column9: A transferable letter of credit.
column11: Per 3/4/1 the first three are acceptable cover; per 3/4/2, interest-based receivables may not be accepted.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: In case of partial damage of the object of commitment before actual or legal delivery to the committing party, if the damage is caused by a heavenly factor (Sabab Samawi) which the committed party can by no means avoid:
column6: The committing party should have the right of option.
column7: The commitment becomes absolutely null and void and neither party has any option.
