column8: The committing party remains bound by the entire commitment, and the committed party bears the loss of the damaged part only.
column9: The committed party should have the right of option.
column11: Per 5/2, in partial damage by an unavoidable heavenly factor before delivery, the committing party has the right of option.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The basis for not obliging the bank to dispose of impermissible intangible assets from the previous financial period, i.e. before the year of conversion, is that:
column6: The new owners are not responsible for rights acquired before their ownership.
column7: The responsibility of the shareholders for such rights ends at the end of the previous financial period, and they may recover from the bank any amounts disposed of.
column8: The management of the bank cannot change rights originating in the previous financial period, its responsibility and authority ending at the end of that period.
column9: Such assets are of doubtful permissibility.
column11: Per the basis, management's authority ends with the period; shareholders, however, remain personally responsible for distributions.

column5: A party sells his piece of land to the other party and simultaneously rents his car to the same party for one month, both against one thousand dinars. This is an example of combined contracts:
column6: In which one contract is stipulated as a condition in the other.
column7: Concluded for separate values.
column8: Taking the form of an exhaustive contractual statement comprising a number of successive parts and stages.
column9: Having a single lump sum counter value.
column11: Per 2/2/1, a land sale and car lease together against one thousand dinars is a combination with a single lump sum counter value.

column5: In specific hiring, when the service/work becomes completely useless:
column6: The contract becomes null and void.
column7: The employer only has the right to terminate the contract.
column8: The contract remains valid, and the employee has to deliver a similar service.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/2/1, complete uselessness voids specific hiring; partial uselessness gives the employer a right to terminate; future-delivery hiring stays valid.

column5: The Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) contract terminates upon:
column6: The owner's sale of the trees to a third party, even if the buyer does not accept the contract.
column7: Death of the trees that are the subject matter, or their inability to bear fruit.
column8: A decline in the market price of the crop below the expected level.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 12/4, death of the trees or their inability to bear fruit terminates the contract; (a) and (c) are not listed causes.

column5: Protecting the capital by use of conventional hedging contracts such as futures, options and swaps is permissible if they are used solely to hedge exchange rate risks.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/5, protecting capital by conventional hedging contracts such as futures, options and swaps is not permissible.

column5: Agreement beforehand in syndicated financing on exit at nominal value, or on guaranteeing a certain amount of profit, is:
column6: Permissible, because it is a proper condition that does not contradict the aim of the contract, and the parties are free to agree on any condition in a partnership, provided that the exit price is stated in the syndication agreement.
column7: Prohibited, because such condition entails exact Riba or a suspicion of it, and involves a guarantee against the loss of the other party's share in the capital or of a predetermined rate of profit.
column8: Permissible in a closed syndicated financing operation only.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 10/2 and its basis, pre-agreed exit at nominal value or guaranteed profit entails Riba or its suspicion and is prohibited.

column5: Certificates of equal value issued by the owner of the usufruct of an existing asset (lessee), either on his own or through a financial intermediary, with the aim of subleasing the usufruct and receiving the rental from the revenue of the subscription, are:
column6: Certificates of ownership of services of a specified party.
column7: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets.
column8: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of described future assets.
column9: Certificates of ownership in leased assets.
column11: Per 3/2/1/2, certificates issued by the lessee to sublease the usufruct of an existing asset are a type of certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets.

column5: Opportunity cost is not compensated in the events of wilful misconduct or negligence because it is non-existent wealth which has not been realised yet; however, realised profit after actual or constructive liquidation is treated like capital.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/7, unrealised gain is not compensated, but profit realised on liquidation is treated as capital.

column5: ………… is the form in which the insurance company keeps all the insurance policies whose risks it can easily tolerate, and seeks reinsurance for those which involve risks that it cannot tolerate:
column6: Loss reinsurance (beyond a specific limit).
column7: Risk sharing reinsurance.
column8: Excess risk reinsurance (beyond risk tolerance).
column9: Comprehensive reinsurance (reinsurance agreement).
column11: Per 5/2, excess risk reinsurance reinsures only the policies whose risks the insurer cannot tolerate.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, the difference between investment agency, on the one hand, and Mudarabah and Musharakah, on the other, is that:
column6: Investment agency aims to acquire ownership for the principal, while Mudarabah and Musharakah aim to increase wealth.
column7: Investment agency is always unremunerated, while the Mudarib receives a share of the profit.
column8: Investment agency is a form of Ijarah (hiring), while Mudarabah and Musharakah are forms of partnership.
column9: Investment agency is a form of partnership, while Mudarabah and Musharakah are forms of Ijarah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, all aim to grow wealth, but investment agency is a form of Ijarah while Mudarabah and Musharakah are partnerships.

column5: Regarding insurance of the leased asset:
column6: The lessor may take out permissible insurance on it whenever possible, and the insurance expenses must be borne by the lessor.
column7: The lessor may take the insurance expenses into account implicitly when the lease rental is to be fixed.
column8: After the contract is signed, the lessor may charge the lessee any increase in insurance cost over the cost anticipated when fixing the rent.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1/8, insurance is the lessor's cost and may be priced into the rent, but no cost beyond that anticipated may be charged after signing.

column5: A Murabahah concluded with a prior promise to buy, submitted by a person interested in acquiring goods through the Institution, is called an ordinary Murabahah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, that is 'banking Murabahah' (Murabahah to the purchase orderer); ordinary Murabahah has no prior promise.

column5: An IFI bought 1,000 tons of cotton by Salam from a producer for delivery on 1 June, and sold 1,000 tons of cotton of the same description by Parallel Salam to a textile company for delivery on 15 June. The Parallel Salam contract states that the IFI's obligation to deliver is conditional upon the producer's delivery to the IFI. This arrangement is:
column6: Permissible, because the IFI is merely passing on the producer's risk and the two contracts are for the same quantity.
column7: Impermissible, because Parallel Salam is permitted only where the Institution is the seller in the first contract, not the buyer, and the second contract must then be concluded before the first.
column8: Permissible, because the descriptions of the cotton in the two contracts are similar and the second delivery date follows the first.
column9: Impermissible as drafted, because the obligations under the two Salam contracts may not be linked so that one depends on the outcome of the other.
column11: Per 6/3, the two Salam contracts must stand alone in all respects; making delivery in one conditional on the other is barred.

column5: In a partnership in commendum, it is not permissible to stipulate that a sleeping partner has a right to an amount of profit according to a particular percentage of the capital or a lump sum.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/3/2/2, a sleeping partner may not be given profit as a percentage of capital or a lump sum.

column5: The amendment of rentals in an Ijarah contract by agreement of both parties:
column6: Is permissible for future periods for which the lessee has not yet received any benefit; unpaid rentals of previous periods become a debt that cannot be increased.
column7: Is permissible for both past unpaid periods and future periods, by mutual consent.
column8: Is permissible for past unpaid periods only, if the lessee agrees to a longer deferral, since future periods may not be amended once the contract is signed, and the lessor receives an additional amount for the longer deferral.
column9: Is absolutely impermissible, because it amounts to rescheduling of debt.
column11: Per 5/2/5, future rentals may be amended by agreement; unpaid past rentals are a debt and may not be increased.

column5: The buyer of a debt has the rescission option for misrepresentation (khayār al-taghrīr) if:
column6: The debt seller was aware of the debtor's insolvency or procrastination, and the buyer was not informed of it.
column7: The debtor becomes insolvent after the sale, even if the debt seller was unaware of it at the time of the sale.
column8: The debt is not recovered at maturity.
column9: The debtor did not consent to the sale.
column11: Per 5/7, the buyer has khayār al-taghrīr where the seller knew of the debtor's insolvency or procrastination and did not disclose it.

column5: A person declared his house as Waqf for his children and grandchildren, and stipulated that the Waqf superintendent he designated may never be dismissed for any reason. The ruling is:
column6: The Waqf is invalid, because it contains an invalid condition.
column7: The condition is invalid and should be rejected, while the Waqf remains valid.
column8: Both the Waqf and the condition are valid, since the conditions of the Waqif are as enforceable as Shari'ah conditions.
column9: The Waqf is invalid, because a family Waqf is not a charitable Waqf.
column11: Per 4/1/3, forbidding dismissal of the superintendent for any reason is an invalid condition; it is rejected and the Waqf remains valid.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Institutions have to seek Fatwa:
column6: On incidences that actually occur or are expected to occur.
column7: For every operation that they intend to pursue.
column8: From their own boards, according to the rules and regulations.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/4 and 3/5, Institutions must seek Fatwa on actual or expected incidences and every intended operation, from their own boards.

column5: The traditional terminology for liquidity is Tandid. Tandid by estimation means:
column6: Estimating the withdrawals expected from current accounts in order to determine the liquidity required.
column7: Evaluating commodities in order to arrive at the expected monetary value that can be realized from them.
column8: Converting securities into cash in the money market.
column9: Converting commodities into cash by actually selling them, in order to realise their monetary value.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Tandid by estimation is valuing commodities; actual Tandid is converting them into cash by sale.

column5: Mortgaging investment accounts and units, despite the forgivable degree of gharar due to the changing nature of their underlying assets, is supported by the Maliki scholars' argument that:
column6: Investment accounts are cash amounts, and cash cannot involve gharar, whatever the nature of the underlying assets.
column7: Investment accounts and units involve no gharar at all, because their value is known at the time of mortgaging and does not change thereafter.
column8: Since the mortgagee may lend without documentation, he can logically accept documentation with some gharar; something is better than nothing.
column9: Gharar is forgivable in mortgage only if the mortgagee is an Islamic financial institution and the mortgagor is a natural person.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Maliki view accepts documentation with some gharar since lending without any documentation is allowed.

column5: In Islamic reinsurance, the company owns the contributions against its commitment to pay the reinsurance amount.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis (c), in Islamic reinsurance the contributions are owned by the reinsurance account, not by the company.

column5: Concluding online contracts through audio or audiovisual communication is classified under the category of contracts concluded in the presence of the two parties, because:
column6: The parties confirm their acceptance by electronic signature.
column7: Both parties are deemed to be in the same place by virtue of the website, which constitutes the contracting session itself, so that the unity of place (Itihad al-Majlis) is fulfilled.
column8: Both parties are in fact present at the same time, although not in the same place, so simultaneous presence in terms of time is fulfilled when exchanging offer and acceptance.
column9: The conversation is recorded and can be used as evidence of the contract, which makes the parties present in the legal sense even if they are in different places and times.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the parties are present at the same time though not in the same place, so the required coincidence of presence is met.

column5: It is permissible to appoint an agent to sell currencies without authorising him to take possession of the amount sold, provided:
column6: The agent takes possession within the customary settlement period, even after the principal parties are dispersed.
column7: The principal or another agent takes possession at the closing of the transaction, before the principal parties are dispersed.
column8: The agent guarantees to the principal the delivery of the countervalue.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/7/2, the principal or another agent must take possession at the closing of the transaction, before the principals disperse.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: In the Shari'ah substitute for options based on 'Arboun (earnest money), it is permitted to trade the right established with respect to the earnest money.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/3/1, it is not permitted to trade the right established with respect to the earnest money.

column5: The Mudarib becomes liable for the amount of the Mudarabah capital:
column6: Whenever the Mudarabah operation results in a net loss at liquidation, whatever the cause of the loss and the conduct of the Mudarib, as he is a guarantor of the capital.
column7: In case of breach of the requirements of trust, such as misconduct in respect of the Mudarabah fund, negligence or breach of the terms of the contract.
column8: If he fails to realise the expected profit stated in the memorandum of understanding, even though he has acted with due care and diligence.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 4/4, the Mudarib is a trustee, liable for the capital only for misconduct, negligence or breach of the contract's terms.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Loan (Qard) covers loans and the accompanying benefits or costs only where the institution is the lender.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 1, the standard covers loans and their benefits or costs irrespective of the institution being a lender or a borrower.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the prohibition of an additional payment over the principal debt in consideration for extension of time is that such action is a pre-Islamic form of Riba.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis describes it as a pre-Islamic form of Riba.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The basis for allowing the bank to keep income of doubtful permissibility earned on the basis of the interpretation of a person qualified to perform Ijtihad, or the juristic position of an authoritative school, is that:
column6: The Shari'ah validates actions that occur on the basis of an interpretation believed to be valid until it is proved incorrect.
column7: Disposal of such income would lead to the collapse of the bank.
column8: The management of the bank cannot change rights originating in previous financial periods.
column9: A thing which is prohibited for one person is not necessarily prohibited for another person, so that the bank may keep income of any doubtful nature.
column11: Per the basis, acts based on an interpretation believed valid are validated until proven wrong, as with insurgents' property.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of issuing Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares is that:
column6: The shares are issued at a discount to their nominal value, which amounts to selling shares below the value of the company's assets.
column7: The holders of these shares are not known to the other shareholders, and the company cannot therefore verify their Shari'ah status or their share in the capital.
column8: The funds the certificate holders receive constitute profit on their shares; the claim that the participations are redeemed in consideration for the distributed profit is invalid, so the holders remain owners entitled to proceeds on liquidation.
column9: The shares carry no voting rights, and every shareholder must have a right of vote, so a share without it is invalid as an instrument of partnership in the company and cannot be traded in the market at all, whatever the rights attached to the other shares.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the amounts received are profit, not redemption, so holders remain owners entitled to liquidation proceeds.

column5: If the cardholder requests cancellation of the card once it was made available to him against fees for services other than the issuance, and such services remained available for use:
column6: The card issuer must return the full fees of such services, since the cancellation was before the expiry of the card, and the cardholder is not responsible for the cost already incurred by the issuer.
column7: The card issuer may stipulate, upon approving the cancellation, to retain the fees of such services on a proportionate basis for the period from making them available till the cancellation.
column8: The card issuer may retain the full fees of such services for the entire validity period of the card in all cases, since the fees were paid for a defined term and the issuer has already incurred the cost of the services.
column9: The card issuer may retain the fees of such services only if the cardholder actually used the services.
column11: Per 5/2/2, the issuer may retain service fees pro rata for the period they were available, whether or not they were used.

column5: The fee which traditional institutions charge to the client even if he has not used the facility, also known as the "loan fee", the "indebted-current facility fee" or the "financing fee", is:
column6: The credit study commission, which the institution may charge regardless of whether the facility is used.
column7: The commitment fee, which the institution should not charge.
column8: The commitment fee, which the institution may charge provided it does not exceed actual cost.
column9: 'Arboun, which the institution may charge and own if the client does not use the facility.
column11: Per 5/3/2/1, the commitment fee of interest-based facilities, charged even if the facility is unused, should not be charged.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: An institution sold an item subject to a cooling-off option owned by the seller only. The item was destroyed in the buyer's possession without any negligence or violation on his part. The buyer:
column6: Is liable to pay its price.
column7: Is liable to pay its cost.
column8: Has no liability.
column9: Is liable to pay half of its price.
column11: Per 2/5/3, destruction in the buyer's possession without negligence or violation entails no liability on him.

column5: The Waqif may single out some of his children as Waqf beneficiaries or increase their shares:
column6: Under no circumstances, because it involves preference among the children.
column7: If there is a valid reason, e.g., poor persons, divorcees, or people with special needs.
column8: Absolutely, without the need for any reason, because the Waqf is a donation.
column9: Only with the consent of the remaining children.
column11: Per 2/4/4/5, singling out some children or increasing their shares is permitted for a valid reason, e.g., poverty, divorce, special needs.

column5: It is permitted to sell a monetary debt to a third party for a usufruct or a service whose subject delivery cannot be ascertained at the time of sale, provided that the price is at market value.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2, a monetary debt may not be sold for a usufruct or service with unascertained subject delivery.

column5: If the owner prevents the worker (irrigator) from working after the crop has materialized, the worker is entitled to his stipulated share of the crop.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/5, if this occurs after the crop materializes, the worker is entitled to his stipulated share.

column5: Amounts paid as primary cash security for participating in a bid, and as final cash security when the contract is awarded to the successful bidder:
column6: Are a loan to the offeror, which he must repay with a share of profit.
column7: Are 'Arboun, which the offeror may retain if the bidder withdraws.
column8: Become the property of the offeror, who may confiscate them in full in case of breach, whether or not any financial damage has been sustained in the tendering process, since they are in the nature of earnest money.
column9: Are held on trust by the offeror and are not viewed as 'Arboun; they may be confiscated only in compensation for an equivalent amount of financial damage actually sustained in the tendering process.
column11: Per 6/8/1, tender securities are trusts, not 'Arboun, and may be confiscated only for actual financial damage.

column5: It is not permissible to trade in certificates of ownership of usufructs of a described asset:
column6: After the asset from which the usufruct is to be made available is ascertained.
column7: Before the asset from which the usufruct is to be made available is ascertained, except by observing the rules for disposal of receivables.
column8: Before the asset is sub-leased to a second lessee, even if the asset has been ascertained, unless the certificates are traded at their nominal value.
column9: At any time until the maturity of the Sukuk.
column11: Per 5/2/8, trading before the asset is ascertained is allowed only under the rules for disposal of receivables; once ascertained, trading may take place.

column5: In investment deposits used for liquidity management, it is permitted for the institution, as investment manager:
column6: To volunteer for reparation of the loss upon its occurrence, without prior condition.
column7: To undertake to purchase the underlying assets of the investments at their face value.
column8: To undertake to guarantee a specified return.
column9: To agree that all profits up to a certain limit belong to one party and any excess to the other.
column11: Per 5/6/3/3 (a)–(d), only voluntary reparation of loss after it occurs is permitted; the other undertakings and clauses are barred.

column5: According to the Standard, when the mortgagee pays the expenses of reparation and preservation of the mortgaged asset that should be borne by the mortgagor:
column6: Whether he pays with or without the permission of the mortgagor, he has the right of recourse on the mortgagor for compensation, or he may obtain compensation by benefiting from the mortgaged asset for an equivalent period.
column7: He has no right of recourse in any case, because he holds the asset for his own interest.
column8: He may only obtain compensation by benefiting from the mortgaged asset free of charge for an unlimited period, and has no right of recourse on the mortgagor in any case.
column9: He has the right of recourse only if he paid with the permission of the mortgagor and the mortgagor was unable to pay; otherwise he is considered a donor, and he may not obtain any compensation by benefiting from the mortgaged asset.
column11: Per 3/2/10, with or without the mortgagor's permission, the mortgagee may recover the expenses or take an equivalent period of benefit.

column5: The priority of the rights of liquidators is based on the fact that these rights are considerations determined by the judiciary on the basis of public interest.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis on priority rights, liquidators' rights are considerations determined by the judiciary on public interest.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Realization of profit in investment accounts does not take place before:
column6: Protecting the capital.
column7: Actual or constructive liquidation of the Mudarabah assets.
column8: Paying advance amounts to the holders of the accounts.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1, profit is realized only after the capital is protected and the Mudarabah assets are actually or constructively liquidated.

column5: Where the institution acts as an intermediary in trading shares, with respect to the elimination of the prohibited component of income, the institution:
column6: Is responsible for eliminating it on behalf of all its clients without charge, and bears the cost of elimination from its own funds, since it earns commission on every trade made by them.
column7: Has no responsibility whatsoever in this respect.
column8: Is bound to inform the person dealing in the shares of the mechanism of elimination so that he can undertake it himself, and may offer these services with or without charge.
column9: Must deduct it from the client's account without his consent.
column11: Per 3/4/6/6, in intermediation the institution must inform the dealer of the mechanism and may offer the service with or without a charge.

column5: A bilateral promise to purchase and sell currencies is:
column6: Permissible even if binding, provided the exchange rate applied is the spot rate on the day of execution.
column7: Forbidden, and likewise a promise from one party only is forbidden if it is binding.
column8: Permissible even if binding, provided it is for the purpose of hedging against currency devaluation risk.
column9: Forbidden if the promise is binding, even for the purpose of hedging against currency devaluation risk.
column11: Per 2/9/1, a binding bilateral promise is forbidden even for hedging, whereas a unilateral promise is permissible even if binding.

column5: The basis for considering the registration of hypothecation of mobile movable property (cars, steamers, airplanes and trains) in the official register as constructive possession is:
column6: The governing custom, which considers official registration as the delivery of constructive possession to the beneficiary.
column7: The consensus of the four schools that registration is actual possession, and that the registered owner is liable for loss of the vehicle.
column8: The tradition of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit on exchange from hand to hand.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the governing custom treats official registration as constructive possession substituting actual possession.

column5: It is not permissible for amendments and changes to an Istisna'a contract to be agreed on the basis that:
column6: An additional sum will be paid in consideration for an extension of the period of payment.
column7: The price is adjusted for additional specification requirements, as per expert opinion or an identified price index.
column8: A rebate is given for pre-payment, provided it was not stipulated at the conclusion of the contract.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/3, an extra sum for extending payment is Riba; price adjustment for new specs (4/1/1) and unstipulated prepayment rebates are allowed.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: If the owner of a cooling-off option does not revoke the contract during the stipulated period, the option lapses and the contract becomes binding.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/1 and 2/7/1, if not revoked within the period, the option lapses and the contract becomes binding.

column5: The expenses of delivering the price in a sale, if any, are:
column6: Shared equally between the buyer and the seller.
column7: The responsibility of the buyer in all cases; any stipulation to the contrary is void.
column8: The responsibility of the buyer, unless there is a stipulation or customary practice to the contrary.
column9: The responsibility of the seller, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary.
column11: Per 4/1/1, the buyer bears the expenses of delivering the price unless a stipulation or customary practice provides otherwise.

column5: A declaration of insolvency requires:
column6: An application made by creditors demanding that a debtor whose due debts exceed his assets be declared insolvent.
column7: An application made by the debtor himself, except when the competent judicial authority considers his application to be fraudulent.
column8: An application made by the creditors of undue debts, even if the debtor's due debts do not exceed his assets.
column9: (a) or (b).
column11: Per 4/3, either a creditors' application (due debts exceeding assets) or the debtor's own non-fraudulent application suffices.

column5: If the Waqif stipulates the non-dismissal of the overseers under any circumstances, the Waqf itself becomes void.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/6/4, such a condition is void, but the Waqf remains valid.

column5: Al-Mawardi cited the saying of Yusuf's brothers to their father about racing each other, to which their father did not object, as evidence of the permissibility of competitions in Jacob's religious code, which was not later superseded by abrogation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, Al-Mawardi deduced permissibility of racing from Jacob's non-objection, a rule not abrogated.

column5: If the subject of investment is a tangible asset, the time taken into consideration for determining the extent of the investment manager's liability is the date of the investment contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/4, it is the date on which the loss, shortage or destruction occurred due to the misconduct.

column5: Regarding the currency of the syndicated financing operation:
column6: Participating parties may pay their contributions in other currencies at an exchange rate agreed upon at the time of signing the syndication agreement, and the rate remains fixed throughout the operation, irrespective of the market rate on the dates of payment and of distribution of profits.
column7: A specific currency should be fixed for the operation; however, the participants may pay their contributions in other currencies provided that they are revaluated in terms of the syndication currency at the prevailing exchange rate on the day of payment.
column8: Each participant's contribution remains in its own currency, and profits are distributed in the currency of each contribution.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 9/1, a single currency is fixed; contributions in other currencies are revalued at the prevailing rate on the payment day.

column5: In the constructive valuation of the assets of a Sharikah for the final distribution of profit, the receivables must be valued:
column6: At fair value, after deducting a discount of the amount of the debt as consideration for earlier payment, as in the discounting of commercial paper by banks.
column7: At their face value, without any deduction for doubtful debts, since the receivables are certain to be collected in full.
column8: At the cash value that is expected to be realised, i.e. after deduction of an allowance for doubtful debts, without regard to the time value of money.
column9: At their present value, discounted at the prevailing market interest rate, in order to reflect the time value of money.
column11: Per 3/1/5/9, receivables are valued at expected cash value net of doubtful debts; time value or discounting is not allowed.

column5: The permissibility of Hawalah requires the consent of all parties, namely the transferor, the transferee and the payer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/1, the consent of the transferor, the transferee and the payer is required.

column5: In calculation of the Nisab of agricultural produce and fruits:
column6: Different types of the same kind can be added together, but produce in different geographical locations has its own separate Nisab, since each location has its own harvest season.
column7: Different kinds of produce or fruits can be added together to complete the Nisab, provided that they are owned by the same Institution and harvested in the same year.
column8: Different types of the same kind of produce can be added together, whereas different kinds cannot, and it makes no difference if the produce is in different locations.
column9: Neither different types nor different kinds of produce can be added together.
column11: Per 5/4/2, types of the same kind are combined, different kinds each have a separate Nisab, and different locations of the same owner do not matter.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: Privileges which the Institution may grant to the cardholder include:
column6: Conventional life insurance.
column7: A priority right to services or discounts on hotel, airline or restaurant reservations and the like.
column8: Entrance to prohibited places, provided this is offered free of charge and is not conditional on any payment by the cardholder.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/6/2, non-prohibited privileges like priority and discounts are allowed; per 4/6/1 conventional insurance and prohibited places are not.

column5: The monitoring of the affairs of a defaulting debtor is intended to make recovery out of assets that he may have concealed from the creditor, and such pursuit does not constitute interference in the affairs of others.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis (a), monitoring is a pursuit established by jurists to reach concealed assets and is not interference.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: If the option period of an either-or option expires without the buyer choosing which item he wishes to confirm, he is legally obligated to do so unless the seller chooses to revoke the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/3, the buyer is legally obligated to choose, unless the seller chooses to revoke the contract.

column5: If the Institution failed to disclose to the customer, when concluding the Murabahah contract, certain expenses relating to the item:
column6: It is entitled to include them, provided that they do not exceed a reasonable percentage of the cost price.
column7: It is entitled to include all expenses relating to the item, since disclosure is required only for the profit mark-up and not for the costs incurred, provided they were paid to a third party.
column8: It is absolutely not entitled to include any of them in the cost.
column9: It is not entitled to include them, unless they are customarily considered normal expenses, such as transportation, storage, fees for letters of credit and insurance premiums.
column11: Per 4/3, undisclosed expenses cannot be included unless customarily normal, e.g. transport, storage, letter of credit fees and insurance premiums.

column5: When the company invests the policyholders' funds through Mudarabah:
column6: All the investment expenses are borne by the insurance account.
column7: The deal is subject to the Shari'ah rulings on remunerated agency.
column8: It should bear the expenses that are normally borne by the Mudarib.
column9: The investment expenses are shared between the company and the insurance account equally.
column11: Per 10/7, investing as Mudarib, the company bears the expenses normally borne by the Mudarib.

column5: Extending the date of payment of the Murabahah debt in exchange for an additional payment in case of rescheduling is impermissible only where the debtor is insolvent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/7, it is impermissible irrespective of whether the debtor is solvent or insolvent.

column5: The amount of money deposited by the customer as security for his commitment to lease:
column6: May be held on trust in the custody of the Institution, in which case the Institution may invest it for its own account.
column7: May be held on an investment trust basis, in which case the customer permits the Institution to invest it on the basis of Mudarabah between them.
column8: Must be refunded upon execution of the lease, and may not be treated as an advance payment of the rental.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4, a deposit held on trust may not be invested; it may be invested on Mudarabah if permitted, and may be treated as advance rental.

column5: Company X sold equipment to an IFI for a spot price of 1,000. As is customary between the parties, three months later a company 60%-owned by X bought the same equipment from the IFI for 1,100 payable after one year. The equipment's characteristics and value had not changed. This transaction is:
column6: Impermissible, as it constitutes 'Inah, since the buyer in the second contract is majority-owned by the first seller and the buyback is customary.
column7: Permissible, because the buyer in the second contract is a separate legal entity from the first seller, even though 60% of it is owned by the seller.
column8: Permissible, provided that the deferred price is paid before maturity.
column9: Permissible, because three months elapsed between the two contracts.
column11: Per 3/5 and 3/5/2/3, a customary buyback at a higher deferred price is 'Inah even via another buyer if it is majority-owned by the first seller.

column5: Regarding wages, salaries and income from free occupations:
column6: Zakah is not obligatory on them at the time of receiving such income, whereas it is obligatory on that portion of such income which remains unexpended for a whole year.
column7: Zakah is never obligatory on them, as they are not trade articles.
column8: Zakah is obligatory on them at the time of receipt, at the rate of 10%, by analogy to agricultural produce.
column9: Zakah is obligatory on them at the time of receipt, at the rate of 2.5%, whether or not any portion of such income remains unexpended for a whole year.
column11: Per 3/1/3, no Zakah is due on such income on receipt; it is due on the portion that remains unexpended for a whole year.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The basis for the impermissibility of swaps is that no actual exchange of counter-values takes place thereby, and such swaps usually constitute interest payment, 'Inah, and deferment of one of the counter-values.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis stated for 5/3/2.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: It is permissible for Institutions to issue charge cards on the following conditions:
column6: The cardholder is not obliged to pay interest in the case of delay in paying the amount due.
column7: The Institution stipulates that the cardholder may not use the card for purposes prohibited by the Shari'ah and that the Institution has the right to withdraw the card in case such a condition is violated.
column8: The Institution does not charge the cardholder any membership, renewal or replacement fees.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/2/1 and 3/2/3, (a) and (b) are conditions; per 4/3 membership, renewal and replacement fees are permissible.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Regarding the accounts of the converting bank with other banks:
column6: The bank opens accounts with local or international Islamic banks and revamps its accounts with conventional banks, limiting dealings with conventional banks to the extent of need.
column7: The bank must close all its accounts with conventional banks immediately upon the decision to convert, and deal only with Islamic banks, including for remittances and documentary credits.
column8: The bank may continue its dealings with conventional banks as before, provided it disposes of the interest earned and opens no accounts with Islamic banks until conversion is completed.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 3/6 and 4/2, dealings with conventional banks are revamped on a Riba-free basis and limited to the extent of need.

column5: The State may not offer exploration or utilization concessions directly; it must first grant survey and exploration licenses in the prescribed procedural order.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/5, the State may offer exploration or utilization concessions directly, without resorting to those procedures.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: For the purpose of set-off with the central bank, the converting bank may maintain current accounts that accrue no interest or, if that is impossible, dispose of the interest earned.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1, non-interest current accounts, or disposal of interest if unavoidable, are alternatives for set-off.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the seller being liable for the sale item before delivery and for the buyer being liable for it after delivery is:
column6: The narration that Nafi' Ibn Abdul-Harith purchased a building in Mecca from Safwan Ibn Umayyah.
column7: The saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman".
column8: The maxim: "Ownership (title) shall be established upon the conclusion of the contract, while liability is contingent upon delivery (Qabd)".
column9: The statement of Shurayh: "He who voluntarily makes it incumbent upon himself to do something, then he shall have to honor the condition".
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for item 6, title is established on contract while liability depends on delivery (Qabd).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: In Musharakah, Mudharabah and Investment Wakalah, it is permissible for the parties:
column6: To distribute the profit in gold, provided it is at the market value of gold at the time of profit distribution.
column7: To redeem their capital in gold upon liquidation, provided it is at the market value of gold at the time of redemption.
column8: To redeem their capital in gold upon liquidation at the value of the gold determined at the contract date.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2–4/3, profit and capital may be paid in gold at its market value at the time of distribution or redemption.

column5: It is not permissible for the Institution to authorize another party to take delivery of the item from the supplier on its behalf; the Institution itself must receive the item.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/5, direct receipt is the original principle, but the Institution may authorize another party to take delivery for it.

column5: Taking consideration for a personal guarantee is not permissible, because:
column6: The guarantee is a trust (fiduciary) contract.
column7: The amount guaranteed may be unknown at the time of the guarantee, which involves Gharar, and a valid guarantee may not be given for a future debt or for a debt of unknown amount.
column8: The guarantor does not bear any real risk.
column9: A guarantee is a charitable act to be offered without consideration, indicating readiness to give away the amount of a loan, so consideration for it is Riba.
column11: Per the basis, guarantee is a charitable act implying readiness to lend; consideration for lending is Riba.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of receiving compensation for the guarantee aspect of documentary credit is that:
column6: The guarantee is provided to a non-Muslim beneficiary, who is not entitled to receive services compliant with the Shari'ah rules.
column7: Guarantees in documentary credit are qualified by the conformity of documents, so the Institution is not exposed to any risk of loss.
column8: A guarantee is preparatory to extending a loan and may not be compensated; the four Fiqh schools are unanimous on this.
column9: The guarantee in documentary credit is limited in time by the validity of the credit, so any compensation would be linked to the duration of the credit.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, guarantee is preparatory to lending and may not be compensated, as the four schools agree.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: The permissibility of offering additional information with the Fatwa, beyond what has been requested, is shown by:
column6: The practice of the Sahabah of not feeling shy to say: I do not know, whenever they were asked about a matter they had not studied.
column7: The Hadith: Make things easier not harder.
column8: The statement of the Prophet (peace be upon him), when asked about seawater for Wudu': Seawater is pure and sea carcasses are permissible.
column9: The incident when Caliph Umar issued two different Fatwas on the inheritance of brothers, the second one applying to the case that arose after the first.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (9/5), the seawater Hadith shows extra information may be added to the answer.

column5: The basis for permitting the card issuer to receive incentive amounts from the card network is that these amounts are against promotion of a permissible act, for which it is permitted to take prizes.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 5/3/3, incentives are for promoting a permissible act, for which prizes may be taken.

column5: ………… is the appropriation (allocation for a particular purpose) of an asset and donating its benefit:
column6: Waqf.
column7: Wasiyyah (bequest).
column8: 'Ariyah (commodate loan).
column9: Hibah (gift).
column11: Per 2/1, Waqf is defined as the appropriation of an asset and donating its benefit.

column5: The conditions of the permissibility of compulsory set-off include:
column6: Both debts should be equal in kind, type, description and maturity.
column7: Neither of the two debts should be encumbered by an obligation to a third party, such as the right of a mortgagee to one of the debts.
column8: The two parties should mutually consent to the set-off.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/1/2, (a) and (b) are conditions of compulsory set-off; mutual consent (c) is a condition of contractual set-off (2/2/2).

column5: It is not permitted to sell to a third party:
column6: A monetary debt for a usufruct whose subject delivery can be ascertained at the time of sale.
column7: A debt without obtaining the debtor's consent, where no such condition was agreed.
column8: A commodity debt before taking its possession, whether it is sold against cash, commodity, usufruct or service.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3, a commodity debt may not be sold before possession; sale for an ascertained usufruct (5/2) and without consent (5/6) are allowed.

column5: According to the prevailing viewpoint of the Hanbali School, a mortgage contract signed before the debt contract is valid, whereas Al-Shafi'i considers it invalid.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, it is the reverse: the prevailing Hanbali view holds it invalid, while Al-Shafi'i considers it valid.

column5: When the contract relied upon for a documentary credit stipulates that its interpretation is subject to INCOTERMS or the United Nations Convention on the International Sale of Goods or any other reference:
column6: Such interpretation is binding absolutely, since it reflects international custom.
column7: Such interpretation is circumscribed with the condition that it must not violate the rules of the Shari'ah.
column8: The stipulation renders the documentary credit impermissible.
column9: The stipulation is void, and the contract is interpreted only according to Fiqh books.
column11: Per 3/2/3, reference to INCOTERMS or the UN Convention is acceptable provided its interpretation does not violate Shari'ah.

column5: Giving free Shari'ah compliant benefits to the holder of a lending-based card is not permitted, because the benefits are given by the lender and would amount to a loan carrying benefit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/6/2 and its basis, such benefits are a gift, unaffected by the card being lending-based.

column5: The institution may pay wages and salaries on behalf of its customers, and may execute standing collection and payment orders.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/5/2 and 2/5/3, paying wages and salaries for customers and executing standing orders are permitted services.

column5: In principle, each partner is entitled to act in the interest of the partnership in the following transactions, excluding:
column6: Giving grants or loans, other than short-term minor loans, without the consent of all partners.
column7: Requesting credit facilities in the interest of the partnership, as is customary in the course of trading.
column8: Processing transfers of rights and debts on behalf of the partnership.
column9: Renting the assets of the partnership, as is customary in the interest of trading.
column11: Per 3/1/3/1, a partner may not give grants or loans without all partners' consent, save short-term minor loans; the others are within his authority.

column5: When the mortgagor is bankrupt:
column6: The mortgagee has priority over other creditors for getting his debt repaid from the sale value of the mortgaged asset; if that value is less than his debt, he stands equally with the other creditors with regard to the excess.
column7: The mortgagee stands equally with all other creditors, even with regard to the sale value of the mortgaged asset, because the bankruptcy cancels all the securities.
column8: The mortgagee has priority over other creditors for his whole debt, including the excess over the value of the mortgaged asset, which he may recover from the other assets of the mortgagor before any other creditor, and he may sell the asset without the permission of the judiciary.
column9: The mortgagee becomes the owner of the mortgaged asset in settlement of his debt, whatever its value, and has no further claim against the mortgagor.
column11: Per 3/5/3 (3/4/3), the mortgagee has priority over the mortgaged asset's value; for any excess debt he ranks with the other creditors.

column5: A company announced a draw for a car among customers who buy a certain product during a specified month. The product's price was not increased, the draw offers equal chances to all customers and no entry fee is charged; however, it is reasonably known that customers will not buy this product except for the purpose of winning the car. The ruling on organizing this draw is:
column6: It is permissible, provided that the prize is paid from the company's own funds.
column7: It is not permissible, because it is reasonably known that customers will buy the product only to win the prize.
column8: It is permissible, since the price of the product has not been increased.
column9: It is permissible, since the draw offers equal chances of winning to all customers and no entry fee is charged, whatever their motive for buying.
column11: Per 3/3/3/2, if customers are reasonably known to buy only to win the prize, organizing the draw is not permissible.

column5: In the card based on Qard Hasan with fees, the amount owed by the cardholder due to card usage is settled:
column6: In monthly instalments with a profit margin for the deferment, provided that the margin does not exceed the prevailing market rate or a ceiling set by the regulator.
column7: In monthly equal instalments on specified dates, without an increase in the principal amount of the loan against settlement in instalments.
column8: Through Tawarruq via Murabaha executed by the card issuer on behalf of the cardholder, when he lacks liquidity at the date of settlement of the loan.
column9: In one lump sum at the end of the validity period of the card.
column11: Per 6/1/1, it is settled in equal monthly instalments with no increase in the loan principal for the instalments.

column5: The Standard on Islamic Insurance covers the social insurance schemes arranged by the state.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the scope (clause 1), the Standard does not cover social insurance schemes arranged by the state.

column5: If the service/work that has become useless pertains to hiring on the basis of future delivery of a well-defined service, the contract becomes null and void.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/2/1, such a contract remains valid and the employee has to deliver a similar service.

column5: The view that Gharar has no impact on donation contracts, which supports the permissibility of cooperative insurance, is well known among the Fuqaha of the:
column6: Zahiri School.
column7: Shafi'i School.
column8: Maliki School.
column9: Hanafi School.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is well known among the Maliki Fuqaha that Gharar has no impact on donation contracts.

column5: Obtaining liquidity through overdrafts is permissible provided that the facility is commission-based rather than interest-bearing.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1, obtaining liquidity through overdrafts or interest-bearing or commission-based facilities is prohibited.

column5: It is permissible to execute an Ijarah contract for a house or a chattel in the following cases, except:
column6: Leasing a car for transport.
column7: Leasing premises to be used as headquarters by an institution dealing in interest.
column8: Leasing a computer to store data, where the lessor has no reason to presume an impermissible purpose.
column9: Leasing a house to a non-Muslim for residential purposes, if the use to be made of it is permissible.
column11: Per 5/1/1 and 5/1/3, the benefit must be permissible; leasing premises for an interest-based institution's headquarters is barred.

column5: In Murabahah, the mere mention of the total selling price, without specifying the Institution's profit mark-up:
column6: Is sufficient, provided the customer accepts the total selling price.
column7: Is sufficient if the profit rate was stated by reference to a known indicator in the promise stage, even if it is tied to LIBOR at the time of the contract.
column8: Is not sufficient, as the mark-up must be known; it may be a lump sum or a percentage of the cost price, or of the cost price plus expenses.
column9: Is sufficient where the price is payable in instalments.
column11: Per 4/7, the profit mark-up must be known; stating only the total price is insufficient. It may be a lump sum or a percentage of cost.

column5: Fulfilling a benevolent promise (such as a promise to make a gift or lend an item):
column6: Is neither religiously nor legally obligatory, since it is a gratuitous act, even if it is conditional upon the promisee performing an action.
column7: Is legally binding only if the promisee has already received part of the promised gift or loan.
column8: Is legally binding in all cases, since it is a religious obligation to fulfil it.
column9: Is a religious obligation but not legally binding, unless the promise is conditional upon the promisee performing an action that causes him to incur a liability.
column11: Per 3/6, a benevolent promise binds legally only when conditional on the promisee doing something that makes him incur a liability.

column5: ………… means to make a financial asset or so tied to a debt so that the asset or its value is used for repayment of the debt in case of default:
column6: Hawalah (transfer of debt).
column7: Guarantee (Kafalah).
column8: Mortgage (Rahn).
column9: Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit).
column11: Per 2, mortgage ties a financial asset to a debt so that the asset or its value repays the debt in case of default.

column5: In Tawarruq with the pledge of securities used for liquidity management:
column6: The pledgee may stipulate that it may dispose of the pledged securities by selling them.
column7: The pledged securities remain the property of the pledger, with their yield for him and loss upon him.
column8: The commodity may be sold back to the seller from whom it was purchased, provided the price is spot.
column9: The yield of the pledged securities belongs to the pledgee during the term of the debt.
column11: Per 5/6/3/4(d), pledged securities stay the pledger's, with their yield and loss; the pledgee may not stipulate a right to sell them.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of 'Arboun (Earnest Money) in Sarf and Salam contracts is that:
column6: 'Arboun is embedded with a cooling-off option (Khiyar al-Shart), which according to the majority of Fuqaha is impermissible in Sarf, where possession of both countervalues (Qabd) at the contracting session is required.
column7: In Salam, the price (capital of Salam) must be paid in full before the two parties leave the contracting session.
column8: 'Arboun involves the sale of a debt for a debt, which is prohibited in both contracts.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, 'Arboun carries a cooling-off option barred in Sarf, and Salam requires full payment of the capital at the session.

column5: The arbitration condition is:
column6: Any permissible limitation imposed by the two parties on the arbitration, such as a time limit for the verdict or a restriction of its subject matter.
column7: The commitment of the two parties of the arbitration contract or agreement to resolve their disputes through arbitration, so that there remains no need for agreement at the time of dispute.
column8: The commitment of the two parties to resolve their disputes through arbitration, which must nevertheless be renewed by a new agreement of both parties at the time of dispute, otherwise the arbitration condition lapses.
column9: The acceptance of the arbitrator to perform the task, which is called the arbitration contract.
column11: Per 9/3, the arbitration condition is the parties' commitment to arbitrate; once stipulated, no further agreement is needed at the time of dispute.

column5: It is not permissible to include a personal guarantee together with a mortgage of security in the same contract, since one security is sufficient for the debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/1/2, there is no Shari'ah objection to including several guarantees, such as a personal guarantee and a mortgage, in one contract.

column5: A set-off may take place between a financial Institution accepting a cheque and the drawer of the cheque through the clearing-house, either compulsorily or contractually depending on whether the conditions of compulsory or contractual set-off are met.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2, set-off through the clearing-house may be compulsory or contractual according to the conditions met.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The customer should not be allowed to avoid paying the consideration owed to the converting bank for non-permissible assets or services supplied before conversion, because otherwise:
column6: The customer would end up being entitled to two counter-values of the same transaction: the good or service and the price payable for it.
column7: The bank would suffer a loss that affects its solvency during conversion, and the shareholders would be unable to dispose of other impermissible earnings.
column8: The bank would be unable to pay the Zakah for the previous periods.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/1/4, letting the customer avoid payment would give him both counter-values: the good or service and its price.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to stipulate in the contract of Murabahah a condition that it is free from responsibility for:
column6: Destruction of the asset caused before the possession of the customer.
column7: Diminution of the quantity sold.
column8: All or some of the defects of the asset (Bay' al-Bara'ah).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/9, the Institution may disclaim all or some defects, but not destruction before the customer's possession or diminution of quantity.

column5: In the case of competition of avenues of Waqf disposal (izdiḥām fī al-maṣraf), the revenue shall be disbursed:
column6: To all avenues, including maintenance, in proportion to their shares without any priority, even where the revenue is insufficient for the preservation of the Waqf asset.
column7: First to the Waqf beneficiaries, then for the preservation of the Waqf asset, and then to the administrative employees, as the beneficiaries' rights are the purpose of the Waqf.
column8: First to the administrative employees, then for the preservation of the Waqf asset, and then to the Waqf beneficiaries, as the remuneration of employees is a debt that precedes all else, including the Waqf asset.
column9: First for the preservation of the Waqf asset, then for the Waqf's obligations towards its administrative employees and parties dealing with it, and then as per the sequence stipulated by the Waqif.
column11: Per 9/10/1: preservation of the Waqf asset first, then obligations to employees and dealing parties, then the Waqif's sequence.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for allowing the funds of current accounts to be presented as a contribution to the capital in a Sharikah, although they are juristically classified as loans, is that:
column6: They are presumed to be possessed by the account holders because they are available on demand, the Institution being obliged to pay the owner irrespective of its financial situation.
column7: The Institution guarantees their repayment, which makes them a guaranteed capital, and guaranteed capital is permissible in Sharikah.
column8: They are dependent on other assets according to the principle of Taba'iyyah, since the accounts are linked to the Institution's own assets and therefore share their legal treatment as investments.
column9: They are not loans but trusts (Wadi'ah) held by the Institution, which may therefore not use them in its own operations and must keep them separate from its own funds.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, current account funds are presumed possessed by the holders since they are payable on demand.

column5: It is permissible to mortgage:
column6: Islamic Sukuk and shares of Islamic financial Institutions.
column7: Shares of the companies whose original activities are permissible.
column8: Preference shares and enjoyment shares.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/1 and 4/3, Islamic Sukuk, IFI shares and shares of companies with permissible activities may be mortgaged; preference and enjoyment shares may not.

column5: A rebate for pre-payment of the Istisna'a price is permissible provided it is not stipulated at the conclusion of the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 4/1/3.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the right of Shirb is the right of humans and animals to drink and to use water for purposes like ablution, whereas the right of Shafah is specifically for watering crops and trees.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, it is the reverse: Shirb is for watering crops and trees; Shafah is for drinking by humans and animals, ablution, etc.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In deducting the allocations and reserves relating to the investment so as to arrive at distributable profit:
column6: Allocations for bad debts and reserve for rate of returns have to be deducted from gross profit, whereas reserve for investment risks has to be deducted after deduction of the Mudarib's share.
column7: All allocations and reserves have to be deducted after deduction of the Mudarib's share.
column8: Reserve for investment risks has to be deducted from gross profit, whereas reserve for rate of returns has to be deducted after deduction of the Mudarib's share.
column9: All allocations and reserves have to be deducted from gross profit, before deduction of the Mudarib's share.
column11: Per 3/1/2/3, bad-debt allocations and rate-of-return reserve come out of gross profit; investment risk reserve after the Mudarib's share.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the validity of Waqf made by a non-Muslim includes:
column6: The analogy upon Zakah, which is valid when paid by a non-Muslim, since both are acts of worship that Islam accepts from all.
column7: The analogy upon all transactions, contracts and donations, and the Ḥadīth of Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām (RA), in which the Prophet (PBUH) called his pre-Islamic charity a virtue.
column8: The consensus that Waqf by a non-Muslim is valid only when its beneficiaries are non-Muslims, as the Waqf of a non-Muslim for Muslims is void by agreement of the jurists.
column9: Waqf is purely an act of worship, which is accepted from everyone regardless of belief or intention, so it is valid from a non-Muslim as a pure donation to Allah.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/3/5, analogy with all transactions and donations, and the Ḥadīth of Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām; Waqf is not merely an act of worship.

column5: If, after the ultimate purchaser has been enabled to take control over the completed subject-matter, loss or damage occurs to it without any proof of negligence or misconduct on the part of the manufacturer:
column6: The manufacturer is liable unless the subject-matter was insured.
column7: The ultimate purchaser is liable.
column8: The manufacturer remains liable until physical delivery takes place.
column9: The loss is shared equally between the manufacturer and the ultimate purchaser.
column11: Per 6/3, enabling control is constructive delivery: the manufacturer's liability ends and the purchaser's begins.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of repurchase at a deferred price exceeding the spot price is:
column6: That it constitutes a sale of debt to a non-debtor, which is impermissible by the consensus of the jurists.
column7: That it involves Gharar arising from the unknown future price, which makes the contract uncertain at the time of its conclusion and thus invalid by the narration of Ibn Omar.
column8: That it is tantamount to 'Inah and two sales in one (Bai'tan fi Bai'ah), both impermissible per the narrations of Ibn Omar and Abu Hurairah.
column9: That it results in a deferred currency exchange.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/5, such repurchase amounts to 'Inah and two sales in one, prohibited by the cited Hadiths.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: If a guarantee is not stipulated in the agency contract and the agent voluntarily provides a guarantee to his principals independently of the agency contract, he will remain liable as guarantor even if he is discharged from acting as agent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2 (SS 5, 2/2/2), such an agent is a guarantor in a separate capacity and remains liable after discharge as agent.

column5: Regarding 'Arboun (Earnest Money) in Ijarah:
column6: It may be taken at the execution of the lease, with the lessee having the right to terminate the contract during a specified period, and is treated as an advance payment of the rental.
column7: If the Ijarah contract is not executed for a reason attributable to the lessee, the lessor must refund the 'Arboun in full, even if he has suffered actual damage as a result of the lessee's breach.
column8: It may be taken only at the promise stage, before execution of the lease contract, and is not treated as an advance payment of the rental, being forfeited if the lease is executed.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/4, 'Arboun is taken at execution and treated as advance rent; the lessor may retain it if the lessee is at fault, preferably only actual damage.

column5: ………… is a judge's declaration that a debtor is insolvent, preventing him from disposing of his assets:
column6: Financial difficulty (as defined by Islamic jurisprudence).
column7: Insolvency (Iflas).
column8: Sequestration of the assets by the creditors.
column9: Declaration of insolvency (Taflees).
column11: Per item 2, Taflees is the judge's declaration; Iflas is the state where a person's due debt exceeds his assets.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The basis for making a distinction between the principal of a loan and the interest in the treatment of pre-conversion liabilities is:
column6: The principle of Da' wa Ta'ajjal.
column7: That the principal and the interest are both void, but the principal is paid out of necessity, which is the view of the Hanafi jurists.
column8: That the loan contract per se is valid, and it is the interest associated with it that is forbidden, the view of the Hanafi jurists.
column9: The principle that a thing prohibited for one person may be permissible for another.
column11: Per the basis, following the Hanafis, the loan contract is valid and only the interest condition is void.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of using a certain benchmark or price index to determine rentals of subsequent periods after the first period is that:
column6: The rentals will subsequently be known, as in the principle of Ujrat al-Mithl, so no dispute arises, and it benefits all parties since fluctuation may favour either.
column7: The rentals of future periods are a debt that may be rescheduled.
column8: Ijarah is a contract that involves time and may be contingent on future events, so the rentals of all periods may be left entirely to the benchmark without any ceiling or minimum.
column9: Contractual stipulations are primarily valid and enforceable.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, benchmark rents become known, resemble Ujrat al-Mithl, avoid dispute and may favour either party.

column5: An irrevocable documentary credit can be amended or cancelled by the issuing bank without consulting the beneficiary, provided the applicant consents.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/3/1, irrevocable credit cannot be amended or cancelled without the consent of the parties.

column5: The collection of the amount of commercial papers by the institution on behalf of its client is considered:
column6: An agency, and the institution is entitled to the commission agreed upon or, failing agreement, to what is prevalent in practice.
column7: A purchase of the commercial paper by the institution, which then becomes its owner and bears the loss if the drawee fails to pay it.
column8: A Hawalah of the right from the client to the institution, which then becomes the creditor of the drawee and may claim the amount in its own right.
column9: A loan by the institution to its client, to be repaid when the amount is collected from the drawee, with a fee for the period of the loan.
column11: Per 5, collection is an agency; the commission is as agreed, or else per prevalent practice among institutions.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The Shari'ah substitutes for options include:
column6: Concluding a contract for ascertained assets with payment of part of the price as 'Arboun (earnest money), with the buyer's right to revoke within a specified period in lieu of the seller's entitlement to the earnest money.
column7: Concluding a contract for commodities themselves with the stipulation of an option establishing the right of revocation for one or both parties during a known period.
column8: The issuance of a binding promise by the owner of assets to sell them, or by one desiring to buy them, without specifying a counter-value for the promise.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/2/3/1-5/2/3/3, 'Arboun, a stipulated option of revocation and an uncompensated binding promise are all substitutes (none tradable).

column5: It is permissible to split the value of the share into instalments at the time of subscription, so that one instalment is paid and the remaining instalments are deferred, on the condition that:
column6: The instalments apply to all the shares.
column7: The liability of the corporation remains restricted to the value of the shares subscribed to.
column8: The subscriber is considered a participant to the extent of the full value of the share from the date of subscription.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/5, instalments must apply to all shares and liability stays limited to subscribed value; the subscriber participates only to the extent paid.

column5: Where the Institution acquires the asset to be leased under a sale contract, its ownership is not established unless the title is registered in its name.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1, ownership is possible under a sale even if title is not registered in the Institution's name; it may obtain a counter-deed.

column5: The holder of a commercial paper purchased goods to be delivered later, on the date of maturity of the paper, and after the debt was established as a liability, he transferred the claim of his creditor to his debtor through this paper. This transaction amounts to:
column6: Sale of a debt for a debt.
column7: Salam.
column8: Hawalah.
column9: Discounting of commercial paper.
column11: Per 6/4, transferring the creditor's claim to one's debtor through the paper, after the debt is established, is a Hawalah.

column5: The crop did not materialize during the stipulated term of an Irrigation Partnership. The worker stopped working, with a valid excuse, after working for 8 months, and the crop eventually materialized after a total of 12 months. The worker is entitled to:
column6: Two-thirds of his stipulated share of the crop.
column7: Nothing, since he stopped working before the crop materialized.
column8: His full stipulated share of the crop.
column9: A wage at the market rate for similar work for 8 months.
column11: Per 10/2, with a valid excuse he gets the portion of his share matching time worked over total time (8/12).

column5: ………… means an agreement between two or more parties to combine their assets, labour or liabilities for the purpose of making profits.
column6: Diminishing Musharakah.
column7: Sharikat al-'Aqd (contractual partnership).
column8: Mudarabah.
column9: Sharikat al-Milk (ownership partnership).
column11: Per 2/1, this is the definition of Sharikat al-'Aqd (contractual partnership).

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Fatwa should be sought again:
column6: Only if a higher Shari'ah body overturns the previous Fatwa, or if the General Assembly of the Institution decides by majority vote that the Fatwa is no longer suitable.
column7: If there are new developments, such as change or improvement of conception, new circumstances, or non-existence of some of the underlying reasons of the previous Fatwa.
column8: Whenever the management does not agree with the previous Fatwa.
column9: At the beginning of every financial year, whether or not there are any new developments, so that the Fatwa remains in force for the coming year only.
column11: Per 6/2, Fatwa is sought again on new developments: changed conception, new circumstances or loss of the underlying reasons.

column5: The mortgagee has the right, at the time of signing the contract, to request from the mortgagor to arrange Islamic insurance for the mortgaged asset whenever it is possible.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8, the mortgagee may request at signing that the mortgagor arrange Islamic insurance for the mortgaged asset whenever possible.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Where Gharar in the subject matter of the contract relates to its kind, nature, type or characteristics, the resulting Jahalah cannot be resolved by offering the buyer the option of viewing.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, such Gharar is excessive, involves great Jahalah that may lead to dispute, and cannot be cured by an option of viewing.

column5: It is not permissible that the subject-matter of an Istisna'a contract be:
column6: Items that have perfect substitutes in the market.
column7: Buildings to be constructed on designated land owned by the ultimate purchaser.
column8: An existing and identified capital asset, such as a particular designated car or factory.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/1/3, Istisna'a covers items identified by specification, not by designation; real estate (3/1/8) and fungible items (3/1/2) are allowed.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: When an accountholder exits from the Mudarabah with all his funds or part of them:
column6: The institution may impose on him a penalty as a percentage of the amount withdrawn, to be added to the income of the institution, provided that the penalty is disclosed in the conditions of opening the account and does not exceed the profit earned.
column7: The institution must pay him the full profit he would have earned had he not exited.
column8: Exit is impermissible before the end of the Mudarabah period.
column9: It is permissible for the institution to specify the amount relating to the exit so that it earns no profit, or less profit than without exit; this is exit on the basis of supply and demand, not deprivation of profit.
column11: Per 4/9, exit is allowed and the exit amount may be priced to earn no or less profit, as supply and demand, not deprivation of profit.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The basis for extinguishing Riba-based loans as soon as possible, even if the buyer of the bank has to suggest to the creditors early payment of these loans for a discount, is:
column6: The principle of necessity, which permits the prohibited whenever the bank would otherwise suffer loss, whether or not the loan is interest-based.
column7: The Hanafi view that the loan contract is valid while the condition to pay interest is void, so that only the principal need be repaid, and any early settlement must be at the full amount.
