column8: The principle of Da' wa Ta'ajjal (discount for early payment), endorsed by the International Islamic Fiqh Academy provided it was not agreed upon earlier.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis, it rests on Da' wa Ta'ajjal (IIFA Resolution 64), provided the discount was not agreed earlier.

column5: For the purposes of the Standard, ………… is the sale of a tangible asset or a usufruct followed by the seller's acquisition of it from the buyer or another to whom ownership has passed by any means of ownership acquisition:
column6: Wafa Sale.
column7: Buyback.
column8: Dissolution (Iqala).
column9: 'Inah.
column11: Per item 2, this is the definition of buyback.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Remuneration for agency may be:
column6: An unspecified share that the agent takes from the entitlements of the principal.
column7: Any gain in excess of a specific amount of output of the operation, or a share of the output.
column8: An amount determined by the agent at his own discretion after completion of the work.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/5, the fee may be any gain above a specific output or a share of output; an unspecified share is barred by 4/2/3.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Postponement of the price until known seasons, such as the season of harvesting:
column6: Involves Gharar that can be forgiven, and the two parties should observe the event of harvesting rather than the normal date of the season.
column7: Nullifies the contract, because the duration of the contract is unknown.
column8: Involves Gharar that can be forgiven, and the two parties should observe the normal date of the season rather than the event of harvesting.
column9: Is permissible only in Salam contracts.
column11: Per 5/3/2, Gharar is forgiven in deferring the price to known seasons; the parties observe the normal date of the season, not the harvest itself.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of Salam where the subject matter is a specific and identified thing, such as the products of a specific farm, includes:
column6: The Hadith in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) allowed buying for delivery after a period, but "not for the products of the kin of so and so", and the risk that the specific farm may have no products at delivery, which leads to Gharar.
column7: That the capital of Salam must be paid in full at the place where the contract is concluded, which is not possible when the subject matter is an identified thing, so the contract must instead be concluded as an ordinary spot sale of a present asset.
column8: That such a contract leads to two sales in one.
column9: That trading in such Salam is a form of sale of debt, because the seller owes the products of the farm as a liability and the buyer cannot sell them before taking possession of them at delivery.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith barred Salam on a named farm's produce; such produce may not exist at delivery, causing Gharar.

column5: Current accounts are determined to be loans (Qurud) rather than Wadi'ah (deposit) in the terminology of Fiqh because:
column6: The bank must return the very same notes that were deposited.
column7: The bank is liable for the amounts only in case of its transgression or negligence, and may not employ them without the permission of the account holder, who remains the owner and bears the loss if they perish without negligence.
column8: The account holder shares in the profits of the bank.
column9: The bank comes to own the amounts, may employ them and seek growth in them, and must return a similar amount on demand, guaranteeing it even upon loss, whether or not it was negligent.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 10/1/1, ownership, use and guaranteed return of a similar amount mark Qard; Wadi'ah is a trust.

column5: A Waqf land was leased to a tenant at the rent of similar property. The tenant later developed the land and constructed a new building on it at his own cost, and consequently the normal rent for the land rose. The Waqf superintendent asked the tenant for a rent increment. The ruling is:
column6: The lease contract is automatically terminated, and the building becomes Waqf.
column7: The tenant is not bound to accept the rent increment, since the development and construction were done at his own cost.
column8: The tenant is obliged to accept the rent increment, but may deduct the construction cost from it.
column9: The tenant is obliged to accept the rent increment, since Waqf may not be leased at less than the rent of similar property.
column11: Per 6/2, the tenant must accept an increment if development was at the Waqf's cost, but not if it was done at the tenant's own cost.

column5: The original principle is that the Institution itself purchases the item directly from the supplier. However:
column6: It is permissible for the Institution to authorize an agent, other than the purchase orderer, to execute the purchase; the customer should be appointed as agent only in case of dire need.
column7: It is preferable that the customer be appointed as the Institution's agent, since he knows the specifications of the item he requires, and no interval in time is needed between the agency and the Murabahah sale.
column8: The Institution may not appoint any agent to purchase the item, since possession must be taken by the Institution itself.
column9: The agent may sell the item to himself once he has bought it on behalf of the Institution.
column11: Per 3/1/3, an agent other than the purchase orderer may buy; the customer only in dire need, and the agent may not sell the item to himself.

column5: Combination of contracts may take any of the following forms, excluding:
column6: Combining more than one contract without imposing any of them as a condition in the other, and without prior agreement (Muwata`ah) to do so.
column7: Combining more than one contract subject to prior agreement (Muwata`ah), but without imposing any of them as a condition in the others.
column8: Agreement to conclude the deal through any of different contractual forms as will be finally decided in the future.
column9: Concluding more than one contract between the same two parties at different times, each of them independently of the other.
column11: Per 2/1, combination entails the simultaneous conclusion of more than one contract; the other three are among its listed forms.

column5: ………… of an asset is deemed to have taken place by the seller enabling the other party to take its delivery and dispose of it, even if there is no physical taking of possession:
column6: Partial possession.
column7: Physical possession.
column8: Constructive possession.
column9: Possession by agency.
column11: Per 2/6/5, enabling the other party to take delivery and dispose of the asset is constructive possession; physical possession is hand-to-hand delivery (2/6/4).

column5: The Waqf has a legal personality and financial liability which make it capable of giving and accepting commitment. Accordingly:
column6: Debts incurred by the superintendent for the Waqf fall on the superintendent personally.
column7: The legal personality of the Waqf merges with that of the Waqif.
column8: The legal personality of the Waqf is quite separate from the personality of its manager.
column9: The superintendent may relieve a beneficiary who is indebted to the Waqf from his debt.
column11: Per 3/4/2 the Waqf's personality is separate from its manager's; per the basis, its debts fall on the Waqf, and the superintendent cannot waive debts owed to it.

column5: Underwriting the issue of shares (an undertaking to subscribe at the nominal value to all that remains unsubscribed) is permissible:
column6: Against a commission calculated as a percentage of the unsubscribed shares.
column7: When it is done without compensation in lieu of underwriting.
column8: Only if the underwriter is one of the founders of the corporation.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/4, underwriting is permissible only without compensation in lieu of the underwriting itself.

column5: It is advisable to stipulate in a stipulated option to revoke (khiyar al-Shart) between the Institution and the supplier that the mere offer by the Institution of the item for sale to a third party invalidates the option.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/3/5, it is advisable to stipulate that the mere offer of the item to a third party does NOT invalidate the option.

column5: The capital in a Salam contract must be paid immediately at the place where the contract is concluded. However, as an exception:
column6: Payment may be delayed for two or three days at most, even if stipulated, provided the delay is not equal to or greater than the delivery period for al-Muslam Fihi.
column7: Payment may be delayed until the delivery date of al-Muslam Fihi, if the seller agrees, provided the seller is not insolvent and the delay is recorded in writing.
column8: Payment may be delayed for up to one month, if this is stipulated in the contract and is shorter than the delivery period.
column9: Payment may be delayed for two or three days, provided this delay was not stipulated in the contract, since a stipulated delay renders the Salam contract invalid and the capital must then be refunded.
column11: Per 3/1/3, a delay of two or three days at most is tolerated, even if stipulated, if shorter than the delivery period.

column5: Ijarah contracts executed in respect of the same asset for different periods for several lessees, provided that two contracts are not executed in respect of the same asset for the same period, are called:
column6: Ijarah Mawsufah fi al-Dhimmah.
column7: Successive leases.
column8: Muhaya'ah (time-sharing).
column9: Sub-leases.
column11: Per 4/2/1, these are 'successive leases': each is a future Ijarah following the previous one, not concurrent with it.

column5: A customer owes an IFI USD 100,000 that is due today under a Murabahah. The IFI owes the same customer USD 100,000 for the price of goods it bought from him, due in six months. The IFI requests set-off of the two debts and forgoes the advantage that its debt is already due, but the customer refuses. The ruling is:
column6: The set-off takes place, as a set-off on demand by the creditor for the superior debt who relinquished his privilege, whether or not the other party consents.
column7: The set-off cannot take place, because set-off requires the mutual consent of the two parties, and the customer has refused.
column8: The set-off takes place only if the IFI grants the customer a discount for early settlement, since he is the creditor for the inferior debt and entitled to compensation.
column9: The set-off cannot take place, because the two debts differ in maturity.
column11: Per 2/1/3-2/1/4, the creditor of the superior (due) debt may demand set-off by forgoing his privilege, without the other's consent.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Among the means that may be used for reaching the appropriate Shari'ah ruling on a given issue are:
column6: Building detailed knowledge about the issue through questioning the one who seeks the Fatwa, consulting other boards, resorting to experts and specialized parties, and taking into consideration the prevailing norms and tradition.
column7: Tracing the Shari'ah ruling on the issue in the different schools of Fiqh.
column8: Making use of collective Fatwas, such as the resolutions of the Islamic Fiqh Academy, other Shari'ah Advisory Boards, seminars and conferences.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/5/1 to 7/5/3, all three are means of reaching the appropriate Shari'ah ruling.

column5: A person who took possession of assets via prohibited means:
column6: May not create a Waqf of them under any circumstances, since a Waqf asset must be lawfully owned, and he must dispose of them in other ways such as returning them to his own heirs.
column7: May create a Waqf of them for general charitable causes and stipulate for himself a share of its revenue, provided that his share is less than one third of the revenue, as a reward for his repentance.
column8: May create a Waqf of them for himself and then for his progeny, since the Waqf discharges his liability towards the owner of the assets and is a good deed that he is rewarded for in the Hereafter.
column9: Is required to forfeit them by disbursing them to charitable causes, and he may create a Waqf of them for general charitable causes, but may not benefit from this Waqf in any manner.
column11: Per 2/4/9, he must forfeit them to charity; he may make them Waqf for general charitable causes but may not benefit from it in any manner.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of granting prizes in competitions is:
column6: The Hadith: "There shall be no prizes awarded on racing competitions unless for races on camelback, horseback (or the like) or for throwing a spear", since Sabq, the word used in it, involves the prizes.
column7: The narration of Anas about the Prophet's she-camel al-Adhbaa' being surpassed in a race by a Bedouin.
column8: The narration of Ayishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she raced with the Prophet (peace be upon him) on her feet.
column9: The Qur'anic verse relating what Yusuf's brothers said to their father about racing each other, since it establishes the permissibility of competitions and of stipulating a prize for the winner in them, even in non-racing contests.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith on prizes (Sabq) in racing is the evidence for prizes; the other texts support competitions in general.

column5: The debtor's consent is required for the sale of debt to a third party, unless the debtor and the creditor have agreed otherwise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/6, consent is not required unless the debtor and creditor have agreed otherwise.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting transactions in shares even though the final registration formalities have not been completed is:
column6: The consent of the broker to the transaction.
column7: That shares are fungible items like currencies.
column8: That registration of shares has no effect in the Shari'ah, since the share is a document and ownership passes by the contract of sale alone.
column9: The transfer of the liability for loss (Daman) to the buyer, attained through constructive possession.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/7, Daman passes to the buyer through constructive possession, allowing him to deal in the shares.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: Practical examples of contingencies whose impact is confined to necessitating amendments in the contract, rather than leading to its complete termination, include the following, excluding:
column6: Prevention of importation of the goods to be delivered in fulfillment of a Murabahah or Ijarah contract.
column7: Impossibility of delivery, as when the commitment to supply the requirements of a conference could not be fulfilled before holding the conference.
column8: Levy of custom duties or taxes after signing the contract.
column9: Change in the prices of the commodities used in implementation of a contract in a way that subjects the contractor to serious harm.
column11: Per 4 and 5/1, impossibility or uselessness of delivery is an external reason for termination, not a contingency leading to amendment.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Renting a car at a rent per mile, so that the payable amount of rent is determined after reaching the target destination, is:
column6: Permissible only if the total distance to be travelled and the total rent are fixed in the contract at the time of contracting.
column7: Null and void, because the total amount of rent is unknown at the time of contracting, and Gharar in the rent nullifies the lease contract.
column8: Permissible, and the contract does not become null and void, as it is similar to selling at unit price a quantity whose exact total is not known.
column9: Null and void, because the rent is left to be determined by the lessee's use.
column11: Per 5/2/2, sale or lease at a unit price (per kilogram, per mile) with the total unknown involves forgivable Gharar; the contract is valid.

column5: An IFI is the sole provider in its country of an online payment service that nobody can do without. It offers the service to the public through a standard online contract with uniform terms that users cannot change. One of the terms imposes an unjust condition on the user. The correct ruling is:
column6: The user is bound by all the terms of the contract, because he accepted it by clicking on the acceptance icon, which is a valid expression of free consent.
column7: The user may only claim compensation for the injustice, while the contract and the condition remain binding, since adhesion contracts are enforceable as written.
column8: The contract is void automatically, without any need to resort to law.
column9: The user has the right to resort to law for nullification of the contract or amending its conditions, so as to be relieved of the consequent injustice.
column11: Per 8/3/4, where an online adhesion contract has an unfair price or unjust condition, the adhering party may go to law to nullify or amend it.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: An IFI leased a property to a customer under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, at a rent exceeding the normal rent of similar property in view of the promised transfer of ownership at the end of the lease. Before the end of the lease, ownership could not be transferred to the customer for a reason which the customer could not stop. According to the Standard on contingent incidents:
column6: The amount of rent in excess of the normal rent of similar property is dropped, in application of the rulings of Jawa`ih (calamities).
column7: The customer is entitled to compensation for the full value of the leased property.
column8: The customer bears the full contractual rent, because the Ijarah contract was validly concluded.
column9: The entire rent paid by the customer must be refunded to him, since ownership was not transferred, even for the period in which he benefited from the property.
column11: Per 5/5, in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek the rent in excess of the normal rent of similar property is dropped when ownership cannot be transferred.

column5: It is permissible to use indices:
column6: To link a contract that should not be suspended, like selling, to a specific index, so that the price keeps varying with later changes in the index until the date of delivery.
column7: To connect the amount of a cash debt, at the time of lending, to the price index.
column8: As a benchmark for comparison of funds and investment bonds, or for correlating the bonus of the Mudarib to the results of the Mudarabah.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/2, indices may serve as a benchmark or to link a manager's or Mudarib's bonus; 6/4 and 6/5 prohibit the other two uses.

column5: Livestock that reaches the Nisab becomes subject to the Zakah rate on livestock:
column6: Whether the animals are fed through free grazing or otherwise, and whether they are owned for milk, for progeny or for work.
column7: Only if the animals are fed through free grazing most of the year, whether owned for milk or progeny.
column8: Only if the animals are owned for progeny, and not for milk, whether or not fed by free grazing.
column9: Only if the animals belonging to the same owner are found in the same place and fed through free grazing.
column11: Per 5/6, the livestock rate applies only to animals freely grazing most of the year, for milk or progeny; location of the same owner's animals is irrelevant (5/6/1).

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: If the buyer has not taken delivery and became aware of the defect before taking delivery:
column6: He must first take delivery and then revoke the contract by mutual consent or court order.
column7: He loses his option, since he knew of the defect before taking delivery of the item.
column8: He is entitled only to compensation for the defect (Arsh), and may not revoke before delivery, even if the seller agrees.
column9: He can revoke the contract unilaterally by notice to the seller, and is entitled to a refund of the whole price.
column11: Per 2/5, before delivery he may revoke unilaterally by notice and recover the whole price.

column5: Since a joint-liability company has a juristic personality and an independent financial liability, its partners are not personally responsible for its obligations even if the existing assets cannot meet its liabilities.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2/1/2, all partners are personally responsible if the company's assets cannot meet its liabilities.

column5: An IFI whose general assembly has resolved to commit it to pay Zakah incurred a net loss during the financial year, although its zakatable assets still exceed its liabilities. The correct ruling is:
column6: Zakah is due only on the Institution's liquid assets, excluding articles of trade.
column7: Zakah is due, since the Institution need not be making profits, and incurring losses does not prevent Zakah from becoming due unless its liabilities absorb all its assets.
column8: No Zakah is due for that year, since the Institution has made no profit and Zakah is calculated on the basis of the income statement.
column9: Zakah is postponed until the Institution returns to profitability, and is then paid for the whole past period.
column11: Per 2/3/2, losses do not prevent Zakah from becoming due; the Institution is exempt only when its liabilities absorb all its assets.

column5: The receipt of a voucher by a merchant, signed by the credit card holder (buyer), is constructive possession of the amount of currency entered as payable on the coupon, provided that:
column6: The voucher is denominated in the same currency as the card holder's account.
column7: The card holder has a sufficient balance in the currency of the voucher with the card issuing Institution.
column8: The merchant presents the voucher to the card issuing Institution within the agreed grace period.
column9: The card issuing Institution pays the amount without deferment to the merchant accepting the card.
column11: Per 2/6/5(c), the signed voucher is constructive possession provided the card issuer pays the merchant without deferment.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: ………… can be cited as a fitting example of a contract involving Gharar that is justified by a Shari'ah-recognizable need:
column6: Commercial insurance, in the absence of Takaful (solidarity insurance).
column7: Commercial insurance, even when Takaful (solidarity insurance) is available.
column8: Bay' al-Hasah (sale by stone throwing).
column9: Sale of a Salam commodity that is not usually available on the date of delivery.
column11: Per 4/4, commercial insurance in the absence of Takaful is the example; need must be inevitable, i.e. no permissible alternative.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: ………… is the agency where the validity of the contract is made subject to fulfillment of a certain condition, for instance when a debtor agrees to put his own assets under the management of his creditor in case of default:
column6: Immediate agency.
column7: Future agency.
column8: Conditional agency.
column9: Free agency.
column11: Per 2/2/3/2, conditional agency is where validity depends on a condition, e.g. a debtor's assets managed by his creditor on default.

column5: A client of an IFI requested it to open an irrevocable documentary credit to import a shipment of wine for his hotel, offering full cash cover and a commission for the IFI's services. The correct ruling is:
column6: The IFI may not issue the credit itself, but it may act as an intermediary bank for another bank that issues it, against a commission.
column7: The IFI may not undertake this credit in any capacity, because it pertains to goods prohibited by the Shari'ah, even if the credit is fully covered.
column8: The IFI may open the credit if the client is a non-Muslim, since the prohibition does not apply to him.
column9: The IFI may open the credit, since it is fully covered and does not involve any loan or interest, and the commission is for services only, not for the goods.
column11: Per 3/1/3, the IFI may not deal in a credit for prohibited goods, for itself, for others or by way of collaboration.

column5: Regarding the family Waqf (al-Waqf al-Ahli):
column6: The Waqf superintendent should pay Zakah on the Waqf assets every year from the Waqf income.
column7: The Waqif should pay Zakah on the Waqf assets as long as he is alive.
column8: Zakah is not obligatory on it at all, like the charitable Waqf, since it has no specific owner.
column9: The beneficiaries should pay Zakah, at the end of the year, from that portion of the Waqf income which remains unexpended.
column11: Per 3/1/6, charitable Waqf is exempt, while in family Waqf the beneficiaries pay Zakah on the unexpended Waqf income at year end.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring that the trees be identified and arable (productive) in usual circumstances is:
column6: The rules of justice, so that the owner does not exclusively benefit from the produce.
column7: That work is one of the requisite elements (Arkan) of the contract.
column8: Avoidance of Gharar, as trees that are not arable do not fit the purpose of Musaqat.
column9: The Hadith: "The Pen has been lifted from writing the deeds of three…".
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/3, identification and productivity of the trees are required to avoid Gharar.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Ju'alah covers:
column6: Activities for which the extent of the work required cannot be precisely determined, for it continues throughout the determined period.
column7: The contract of Ijarah for employment/service or leasing.
column8: Stipulations of maintenance in relation to other contracts, such as the requirement of maintenance in an Istisna'a contract.
column9: Maintenance contracts.
column11: Per the Scope, Ju'alah covers work of indeterminable extent; Ijarah, maintenance contracts and maintenance stipulations are excluded.

column5: When the Institution acts as an agent of the founding shareholders of a Shari'ah-accepted and technically licensed joint stock company in performing the various steps of the public issue, it:
column6: May receive fees for such services; however, the fees should not comprise any remuneration for extending credit, if it is part of the service.
column7: May not receive any fees, because subscription arrangement is a gratuitous service and the Institution benefits indirectly from the funds of the subscribers.
column8: May receive fees for such services, including remuneration for any credit it extends as part of the service, provided that the fees are agreed upon in advance as a percentage of the credit extended.
column9: May receive fees only if they are equal to the actual cost it incurs.
column11: Per 2/3/1, the Institution may take fees as agent in the issue, but they may not include any remuneration for extending credit.

column5: Indirect expenses incurred in rendering services for loans, like the salaries of the employees and the rentals of space, may be included in the actual expenses charged to borrowers, provided they are distributed proportionately among all the loans.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/2, indirect expenses such as salaries, rentals and general expenses are not included in actual expenses.

column5: If the price of the goods was in another currency, and the card acceptor made it possible to pay the price in the currency of the card:
column6: It is not permitted for the cardholder to pay in the currency of the card if the card is lending-based, as it combines a loan and an exchange, whatever the entity that carries out the exchange or the rate applied.
column7: The cardholder may choose to pay in the currency of the card, the exchange being carried out through an independent entity providing the service, and this exchange is not bound by the actual cost.
column8: It is not permitted, because the exchange is deferred until settlement by the card network.
column9: The cardholder may choose to pay in the currency of the card, but the exchange rate must not exceed the actual cost.
column11: Per 5/5/2, paying in the card currency is permitted via an independent exchange entity, and this exchange need not abide by actual cost.

column5: It is permissible to connect the fulfillment of a binding pledge on the part of a buyer or a seller to the rate of increase or decrease of a specific index in comparison to the price of the commodity at a particular date, so that any further increase may be added to the price of the commodity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/7, a binding pledge of a buyer or seller may be connected to an index's change against the price at a given date.

column5: It is permissible for a lending institution to charge for services rendered in loans:
column6: An amount equivalent to the actual expenses plus a reasonable profit margin.
column7: A percentage of the loan amount, as determined by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column8: Any amount agreed upon with the borrower, since it is in lieu of a service.
column9: An amount equivalent to the actual amount directly spent on such services.
column11: Per 9/1, the charge must equal the actual amount directly spent on the services; any excess is prohibited.

column5: The debtor's consent for the sale of debt to a third party:
column6: Is required only if the debt is secured by a pledge or a guarantee.
column7: Is not required, unless the debtor and the creditor have agreed otherwise.
column8: Is required only if the debtor is procrastinating.
column9: Is required in all cases.
column11: Per 5/6, the debtor's consent is not required unless the debtor and creditor have agreed otherwise.

column5: If the process of Monetization is to involve a binding promise, the promise shall be binding on both parties so that the Institution is protected.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1, if the process involves a binding promise, it shall be from only one party.

column5: According to the majority of Fuqaha, the basis for the seller's right to terminate a sale on deferred payment terms in case of the buyer's failure to pay is that:
column6: The sold asset remains the property of the seller until full payment of the price.
column7: The debtor may relinquish the deferment and pay before the due date.
column8: The seller has consented to deferred payment only if it will not lead to a loss of what is due to him.
column9: The creditor's right is confined to litigation, unless he has stipulated the right to terminate.
column11: Per the basis, the majority hold the seller accepted deferment only if no loss results.

column5: For concluding restricted Hawalah, it is a condition that:
column6: The transferred debt or portion be equal to the debt owed to the transferee in kind, type, quality and amount; but a lesser debt owed to the transferee may be settled from a larger amount, the transferee being entitled only to its equivalent.
column7: The debt owed to the transferee be equal in amount to the debt owed by the payer to the transferor, and equal in kind, type and quality; otherwise the Hawalah is void, even if the transferee consents and the transferor transfers only a lesser amount of his debt.
column8: The two debts may differ in kind and quality if the transferee consents.
column9: The transferee be entitled to the whole amount owed by the payer to the transferor, even if it exceeds his own debt.
column11: Per 6/6, equality is required in the amount the transferee receives; a larger debt may be the source, to avoid Riba.

column5: With regard to the Ijarah of Waqf assets:
column6: The initial presumption is that its term should not be long as per custom unless there is an evident interest, and in long-term Ijarah it is preferable that the rent be variable, linked with a known benchmark, and at least the fair rate.
column7: Ijarah is not a mode of investment for Waqfs, since it transfers the usufruct to a non-beneficiary, and the Waqf asset would then be under the control of the lessee for the whole term.
column8: The rent in a long-term Ijarah must be fixed for the whole period to avoid uncertainty (gharar), and it may not be linked to any benchmark, even if the fixed rent falls below the fair rate.
column9: Long-term Ijarah of Waqf assets is impermissible under all circumstances, since the Waqf asset may not remain with a lessee for a period exceeding one year, the usufruct becomes the property of the lessee, and the Waqf beneficiaries are thereby deprived of the rent.
column11: Per 8/4, Waqf Ijarah should not be long absent evident interest; in long leases a variable, benchmarked rent of at least fair rate is preferable.

column5: An IFI's Murabahah contract provides that if the customer delays payment, he shall pay the IFI compensation equal to the profit the IFI would have earned on the overdue amount during the period of delay, to be credited to the IFI's income. The ruling on this clause is:
column6: It is impermissible only if the amount of compensation is pre-determined in the contract.
column7: It is permissible, provided the debtor is solvent and the default is established following a normal demand for payment.
column8: It is impermissible, because stipulating financial compensation for delay in settling a debt, including compensation for loss of income, constitutes Riba.
column9: It is permissible, because the compensation represents the actual opportunity loss and is not pre-determined.
column11: Per 2/1/2 and its basis, compensation for delay, even for opportunity loss and not pre-determined, is Riba and void.

column5: If, in hiring for a well-described future service, the employee delivers a service that does not conform to what has been agreed upon:
column6: The employer must accept it, against a reduction in the pay commensurate with the defect.
column7: The employer's only remedy is to terminate the contract.
column8: The contract becomes null and void, and the employer recovers any pay he has made.
column9: The employer has the right to reject it and insist on having a service that conforms to the specifications.
column11: Per 5/1/6, the employer may reject a non-conforming service and insist on one that conforms to the specifications.

column5: If debts and tangible assets are separated in an investment portfolio that is not registered with the relevant authorities, the portfolio may be sold under the rules for a legally recognized entity in which commingling is materialized, provided tangible assets exceed 50%.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/3, an unregistered portfolio is not such an entity, so the sale of debt provisions of item 5 apply.

column5: In diminishing Musharakah applied to concession contracts, the Institution contributes a share in the required capital, and undertakes to sell its share in the project gradually to:
column6: The users of the public utility.
column7: The contractor that builds the project.
column8: Other Institutions in the financing syndicate.
column9: The State.
column11: Per 7/4/2 and 8/3/2, in diminishing Musharakah the Institution's share is sold gradually to the State.

column5: The Institution is not obliged to give a discount to the ultimate purchaser when it secures a discount from the parallel manufacturer, because the Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a contracts are independent in terms of obligations and effects.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the rule in 3/2/6 and its Shari'ah basis.

column5: It is permissible for the licensor to fix or adjust the price of the services to be delivered by the licensee under a management concession:
column6: Only at the time of concluding the contract, and not during its term, since any later change entails Gharar in the price of the service and in the share of the licensee.
column7: Only with the consent of the beneficiaries of the services.
column8: In a way that leads to establishing justice and preservation of the interests of both the licensee and the beneficiaries.
column9: In a way that maximizes the revenue of the State.
column11: Per 10/4, the licensor may fix or adjust prices so as to establish justice and preserve the interests of the licensee and beneficiaries.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting the sale of an established and outstanding debt to the debtor includes:
column6: The principle of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya), by which the debt is sold consequentially along with the tangible assets of the entity that owns it.
column7: The analogy of ḥawāla (novation), since the creditor may demand his right himself or through a party acting on his behalf.
column8: The Hadith of Ibn ꜥUmar on selling camels in al-Baqīꜥ for dinars and taking dirhams, and vice versa, at the rate of the day.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1, the Ibn ꜥUmar Hadith is cited; appurtenance supports 8/1 and ḥawāla supports the no-consent rule (5/6).

column5: When a contract is concluded for the sale of an amount of currency and possession is taken of only part of a countervalue at the closing of the transaction:
column6: The whole transaction is valid, provided the remaining part is delivered within the period customary in currency markets, even after the parties have dispersed from the place of the contract.
column7: The transaction is valid only in respect of the part, possession of which is complete, whereas the remaining part of the transaction remains invalid.
column8: The whole transaction is invalid, including the part of which possession was taken.
column9: The whole transaction is valid, and the remaining part becomes a debt owed by the party who failed to deliver it.
column11: Per 2/6/2, partial possession validates only the part possessed; the remaining part of the transaction remains invalid.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for preventing the pledge of tangible Waqf assets is that:
column6: Pledge is contrary to the provision of Waqf in terms of appropriation, as pledge secures a debt by an asset whose sale is permitted to discharge the debt, whereas the sale of the Waqf asset is not permitted.
column7: Waqf has no legal personality, and therefore it cannot be a pledgor, since a pledgor must have the capacity to own and to dispose of the pledged asset by sale, and the overseer holds the Waqf asset only as a trustee.
column8: The Waqf asset has no value that can secure a debt.
column9: Pledging involves Riba, since the pledgee benefits from the pledge.
column11: Per the Basis of 6/1, a pledge allows sale of the asset to settle the debt, while sale of a Waqf asset is not permitted.

column5: It is permissible to trade in Salam certificates after closing of subscription, allotment of the certificates and commencement of activity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/14, it is not permissible to trade in Salam certificates.

column5: A company engaged a consultancy firm on the basis of Ju'alah to obtain a regulatory licence within six months for a compensation of 100,000. The period ended without the result being close to realisation, but the firm had done part of the work, which will benefit the company. The firm is entitled to:
column6: The full compensation of 100,000.
column7: Reasonable wages (Ujrat al-Mithl).
column8: Nothing, because the result was not realised.
column9: A share of the 100,000 proportionate to the time spent.
column11: Per 5/3/1/3, when the period ends and the worker has done part of the work benefiting the offeror, he gets Ujrat al-Mithl.

column5: Stipulating an absolute guarantee to be provided by the investment manager is impermissible because:
column6: This condition strips partnership and agency contracts of their essence and turns them into a guaranteed loan.
column7: It deprives the investment manager of his share of the profit, which is contrary to justice.
column8: It entails excessive ambiguity, as the extent of the loss is unknown at the inception of the contract and cannot be estimated.
column9: It is a form of conventional hedging, such as futures and options, which are prohibited.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/6, it turns trust-based contracts into a guaranteed loan.

column5: Regarding 'Arboun (Earnest Money) received by the employee at the time of signing the hiring contract:
column6: If the hiring contract is implemented, the amount of earnest money becomes a prepaid part of the employee's pay.
column7: If the contract is not executed, the earnest money goes to the employee, though he is preferably supposed to take from it only the portion which compensates the actual harm caused to him.
column8: Only a private employee, and not a shared employee, may receive earnest money.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/11, both private and shared employees may receive 'Arboun; it is prepaid pay if the contract is implemented, otherwise it goes to the employee.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: A buyer purchased a plot of land and erected a building on it. He then discovered a hidden material defect in the land, of which he was unaware at the time of contract. The buyer:
column6: May not return the land but is entitled to compensation (Arsh) for the inferiority caused by the defect.
column7: May return the land together with the building and recover the whole price, as the building is a part of the land.
column8: May return the land and claim the value of the building from the seller.
column9: Has no remedy, since he has altered the land by erecting the building.
column11: Per 2/6/3-2/6/4, an attached addition not grown from the item (a building) prevents return; the buyer is entitled to Arsh.

column5: The tasks of the Waqf superintendent include:
column6: Mortgaging the Waqf assets for a debt to be obtained for the Waqf or for the beneficiaries, whether or not the legal authorities permit it and whether or not the Waqf can bear the debt.
column7: Changing the operational form of the Waqf assets, such as converting a residential building into a commercial one, to maximize the benefit of the Waqf, with permission of the concerned authorities.
column8: Lending the Waqf assets to others without charge, provided that the borrower is one of the beneficiaries of the Waqf and provides a guarantee for returning them in the same condition at the end of the period of the loan, however long it is.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/2/5, changing the operational form is a task of the superintendent; mortgaging and lending Waqf assets are prohibited (5/3/4, 5/3/5).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of substituting al-Muslam Fihi with a commodity whose price is higher than the market value of al-Muslam Fihi at the date of delivery is:
column6: That this is a form of sale of debts.
column7: To deter the buyer from making a compound profit on one deal.
column8: To avoid two sales in one.
column9: That al-Muslam Fihi is a debt and no excess over the principal may be stipulated.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the cap on the substitute's value deters the buyer from making a compound profit on one deal.

column5: Among the Shari'ah compliant modes of developing Waqf lands:
column6: Diminishing Musharaka in which the Waqf land itself is the subject of the Musharaka with the financier.
column7: Selling part of the Waqf land to the financier to fund the construction of buildings on the remaining part, without observing the conditions of substitution.
column8: Applying Istisna on the Waqf land, which could be through Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/6/1 Istisna (e.g., BOT) is a mode; per 8/6/2 the land is not the subject of the Musharaka; substitution conditions always apply (10/1/5).

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, each partner should contribute part of the capital. The contribution may be in the form of:
column6: Cash.
column7: Tangible assets that can be translated into a monetary value, for example, a land for building or equipment required for the operation of the partnership.
column8: Debts owed to the partner by the other partner.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/4, contributions may be cash or valued tangible assets such as land or equipment; receivables alone are barred (3/1/2/4).

column5: The lessee may lease the asset back to its owner in the first lease period:
column6: For one hundred and ten dinars payable on a deferred basis, where the first rental is one hundred dinars payable on a spot basis.
column7: For the same amount, where the first rental is deferred for one month and the second rental for two months.
column8: For a rental that is lower, the same or higher than what he is paying, if the two rentals are paid on a spot basis.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/4, leasing back is allowed if both rentals are spot; varying rent or deferral periods leads to 'Inah.

column5: With respect to travellers' cheques, the institution issuing them:
column6: May take a commission in lieu of intermediation at issuance or at the time of payment, provided this does not include Riba.
column7: May charge interest on the amount until the cheques are encashed, as compensation for the funds held by it.
column8: May take a commission only at the time of payment, not at issuance, and only in proportion to the amount encashed by the holders.
column9: May not take any commission, since the amount paid for the cheques is a loan, and any benefit from it would be Riba, even if it is a fee for services.
column11: Per 3/3(e), a commission for intermediation is allowed at issuance or at payment, provided it does not include Riba.

column5: The basis for the prohibition of stipulating a right to freeze a customer's current account in a credit transaction is that such a right:
column6: Is a form of set-off without the consent of the debtor.
column7: Is a pledge of an asset held on trust, which may not be pledged, since a trustee is not liable for it.
column8: Amounts to a deferred sale with a condition to provide a loan, which Shari'ah prohibits.
column9: Deprives the customer of the profit on his account.
column11: Per the basis, it combines a deferred sale with a loan (the current account), i.e. a sale conditional on a loan.

column5: If the investment agency expires before the receivables are collected and the agency is not mutually renewed, the investment agent:
column6: Is required to collect the receivables and take necessary actions against the debtors delaying their payments.
column7: Is not entitled to any fee for such collection unless agreed otherwise.
column8: Is required to pay the receivables to the principal from his own funds, or to seek financing like Tawarruq for this purpose.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 12/4, the agent must collect without a fee unless agreed, and is not required to pay from his own funds or via Tawarruq.

column5: In the case of the customer's breach of his binding promise, the Institution:
column6: Is limited to deducting the actual damage, namely the difference between the cost of the item borne by the Institution and the price at which it is sold to a third party.
column7: May deduct the actual damage, including the loss of its mark-up in the Murabahah transaction (its opportunity loss).
column8: May retain the Hamish Jiddiyyah as such, as compensation for the breach.
column9: May deduct the difference between the Murabahah price stated in the promise and the price at which the item is sold to a third party, which is the actual damage including the mark-up it expected to earn.
column11: Per 2/5/4, only actual damage (cost minus resale price) may be deducted; the lost mark-up (opportunity loss) is excluded.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing penalty clauses in Salam is that:
column6: The seller must be granted an extension if he is insolvent, so a penalty for delay would oppress him.
column7: This would deter the buyer from making a compound profit on one deal, which the Shari'ah forbids in all sale contracts.
column8: Al-Muslam Fihi is a debt, and it is not permitted to stipulate payment in excess of the principal of debts.
column9: Salam is a low cost form of sale, and a penalty would raise the price above the market price.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, al-Muslam Fihi is a debt, and no payment in excess of the principal of a debt may be stipulated.

column5: Muwata`ah for combining contracts that contradict or oppose each other is:
column6: Prohibited, because it leads to performing an act that has been strictly banned by Shari'ah.
column7: Prohibited only if the contracts have a single lump sum counter value.
column8: Permissible, as long as the Muwata`ah is not stipulated in the contract.
column9: Permissible, if each of the contracts is permissible on its own.
column11: Per 6/3/4, such Muwata`ah is prohibited because it leads to an act strictly banned by Shari'ah.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The justification for adopting the fiqh viewpoint that suspends the act of the uncommissioned agent, rather than revoking the deal, is:
column6: That the owner is deemed to have consented implicitly by his silence.
column7: That the uncommissioned agent is considered an agent by virtue of customary practices, so that his act is binding on the owner from the outset without any need for the owner's ratification.
column8: That the Gharar involved in such contracts is minor and does not lead to dispute.
column9: That an act of a Muslim should, as far as possible, be preserved from cancellation, in addition to the fact that the act may prove to be useful to the owner.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, suspension preserves a Muslim's act from cancellation as far as possible, and the act may benefit the owner.

column5: It is permissible to use debts (receivables) alone as a contribution to the Sharikah capital, provided they are valued at the cash value expected to be realised.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/2/4, debts alone may not be a capital contribution; they may form part of it only when inseparable from other assets.

column5: In comprehensive reinsurance (reinsurance agreement):
column6: The reinsurance company is committed to accept all risks falling within the scope of the agreement signed with the insurance company.
column7: The reinsurance company studies each individual risk presented to it and decides whether to accept it or not, without any prior commitment under the agreement.
column8: The insurance company reinsures only the policies whose risks it cannot tolerate.
column9: The reinsurance company bears only the losses beyond a specific limit agreed upon.
column11: Per 4/2, in comprehensive reinsurance the reinsurer commits to accept all risks falling within the scope of the agreement.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of a commitment fee in Murabahah is that:
column6: It is not allowed to receive a commission for giving out a loan facility itself, so it is not allowed for mere readiness to finance.
column7: Such a fee is in exchange for the right to contract, which is a mere intention and wish that is not a subject of exchange.
column8: It is a form of guarantee for financial damage that has not yet occurred.
column9: Both parties benefit equally from the commitment, so neither may charge the other.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a commitment fee is paid for the right to contract, a mere wish that cannot be the subject of exchange.

column5: If the ultimate purchaser refuses to accept the subject-matter without a good reason after he is enabled to take possession:
column6: The manufacturer holds the subject-matter as a guarantor and bears the expenses of safe keeping, being liable for any loss or damage whatever its cause, even if he was not negligent, until the ultimate purchaser takes delivery.
column7: The contract is rescinded, and the manufacturer must refund any part of the price received, retaining only the 'Arboun if one was paid.
column8: The manufacturer may sell the subject-matter for his own account and keep the price, and has no recourse to the ultimate purchaser for any shortfall.
column9: The subject-matter stays with the manufacturer on a trust basis; he is liable for loss or damage only if due to his negligence or misconduct, and the purchaser bears the expenses of safe keeping.
column11: Per 6/4, the manufacturer holds on trust, is liable only for negligence or misconduct, and the purchaser bears safe-keeping costs.

column5: With regard to the form of a Hawalah contract:
column6: Hawalah is a binding contract and therefore is not subject to unilateral termination.
column7: It can be concluded by offer and acceptance in a manner that clearly indicates the intention to conclude a Hawalah, and it is not necessary that the word transfer be used.
column8: The transfer of debt must take effect immediately, but it is permissible to defer payment of the transferred debt until a future specified date.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1, 4/2 and 4/3, all three statements are correct.

column5: An IFI sent a client by e-mail an offer to sell him a commodity on Murabahah, containing all the rights and commitments of the contract and stating that the offer is valid for five days. On the third day, before the client had accepted, the IFI wished to withdraw the offer because the market price had risen. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The IFI may withdraw, because the e-mail is only an invitation for contracting and not an offer.
column7: The IFI has no right to withdraw from its offer during that period, and the time allowed for acceptance covers the whole five days.
column8: The IFI may withdraw, provided that it compensates the client for any actual harm.
column9: The IFI may withdraw, because in written communication the contract signing session is discontinued when the offering party retreats from his offer before acceptance.
column11: Per 4/2/2, when the offeror specifies a validity period, acceptance may be made throughout it and the offeror may not withdraw during it.

column5: In the case of investment Waqfs, incurring debt:
column6: Is permitted only if stipulated by the Waqif in the Waqf deed, and only up to one third of the revenue of the Waqf per year.
column7: Is permitted only to cover the essential costs needed to preserve the Waqf asset, and only through Shari'ah compliant borrowing at a fair profit rate, provided that the Waqf asset is not pledged.
column8: Is permitted for developing the Waqfs under the prevailing commercial practices, provided the interest of the Waqf and the adequacy of its revenues to settle the obligations are considered.
column9: Is not permitted under any circumstances.
column11: Per 5/2, investment Waqfs may incur debt for development under commercial practice, considering their interest and revenue adequacy.

column5: In certificates of ownership of leased assets:
column6: The issuer is the lessee of the asset, the subscribers are its lessors and the funds mobilised through subscription are advance rentals.
column7: The certificate holders own the asset through divided (separately allotted) ownership, each of them bearing the profits and losses of his own portion only, and the issuer acts as their agent in leasing it.
column8: The issuer is the seller of a leased asset or an asset to be leased on promise, the subscribers are its buyers, and the funds mobilised through the subscription are its purchase price.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1/5/1, the issuer sells the (to be) leased asset to the subscribers for the subscription funds; holders own it jointly in undivided ownership.

column5: Regarding amendment of the pay in hiring of persons:
column6: It is impermissible to amend the pay of any period after signing the contract, even on the consent of the two parties, since the contract is binding and the pay is part of its essential terms.
column7: It is permissible, with the consent of the two parties, to amend the pay of future periods, whereas unpaid pay of past periods becomes a debt on the employer, and stipulating an increase against rescheduling it is impermissible.
column8: The employer may unilaterally amend the pay of future periods.
column9: It is permissible, on the consent of the two parties, to amend the pay of both past and future periods, including increasing unpaid amounts of past periods against rescheduling, provided that the increase is agreed upon in advance and stated in the contract.
column11: Per 5/2/5, future pay may be amended by mutual consent; past unpaid pay is a debt, so increasing it for rescheduling is impermissible.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Distribution of profits in Mudarabah-based investment accounts should be:
column6: In terms of ratios, and not by specifying a lump sum or a percentage of the capital for any party, or any method that could avoid sharing of profit.
column7: In terms of a lump sum amount for the Mudarib and the remainder for the holders of the accounts.
column8: In terms of a percentage of the capital for the holders of the accounts and the remainder for the Mudarib, provided that the percentage is announced at the time of opening the accounts.
column9: In terms of a fixed amount for each party, plus a ratio of any additional profit.
column11: Per 4/1, profit must be shared by ratios, never by a lump sum or percentage of capital or any method avoiding profit sharing.

column5: The following promises are prohibited by the Shari'ah:
column6: A promise in a loan contract that procures benefit for the lender over and above the repayment of the debt, even if granted in a document separate from the loan contract.
column7: A promise by the buyer in a sale contract that results in a repurchase contract ('Inah), even if the promise is given subsequent to the sale contract.
column8: Selling an item on credit and promising to buy it back on spot for a lower price, through a colluding third party acting as an intermediary in the repurchase.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2 and 3/3, all three promises are prohibited, including 'Inah arranged through a colluding intermediary.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Since rights to intangible assets are recognised as financial rights:
column6: It is permissible to dispose of or transfer them for consideration, provided that such transactions are free of Gharar (ambiguity), deception and fraud.
column7: It is not permissible to transfer them, as they are confined to the personal use of their owners.
column8: It is permissible to transfer them only without consideration.
column9: It is permissible to transfer them for consideration, even if the transaction involves Gharar, because they are intangible.
column11: Per 3/3/3/2, rights to intangible assets may be disposed of or transferred for consideration if free of Gharar, deception and fraud.

column5: Liquidity support made available to institutions by supervisory or regulatory bodies (such as central banks):
column6: Must be provided only through Shari'ah-compliant modes, such as Mudarabah and investment agency.
column7: May be provided through interest-bearing loans, provided that the interest is given to charity.
column8: May be provided through interest-bearing facilities, since it is provided by a regulatory body.
column9: May be provided through commission-based overdraft facilities, provided that no interest is charged.
column11: Per 4/1, central bank liquidity support must be provided only through Shari'ah-compliant modes such as Mudarabah and investment agency.

column5: A mortgage cannot be signed for the following, being a non-debt deal:
column6: A spot sale commodity still in the hands of the seller.
column7: A Salam commodity, whose delivery is deferred to a specific future date.
column8: An Istisna'a commodity, which is to be manufactured and delivered at a later date.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 3/3/1, a spot sale commodity still with the seller is a non-debt deal; Salam and Istisna'a commodities are debts that can be secured.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Options to revoke due to non-payment:
column6: Arise by operation of law when the other party fails to pay on the due date, without the need for stipulation.
column7: Are options stipulated by sellers or buyers to revoke contracts if the other party fails to pay the price or rent on the due date, and are valid only if expressly stipulated.
column8: Are valid even if they are only implied by the circumstances of the contract, such as an instalment schedule or a custom of the market, and need not be stipulated in the contract.
column9: May be stipulated by the seller only, to enable him to revoke if the buyer fails to pay the price.
column11: Per 3/1, either seller or buyer may stipulate it for non-payment of price or rent, and it is valid only if expressly stipulated.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: When delivery becomes impossible or of no use, the commitment shall become null and void if:
column6: Failure to honor the commitment is absolutely inevitable.
column7: Failure to honor the commitment originates from objective rather than personal reasons.
column8: Failure to honor the commitment is caused by an external party.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1, all three conditions are listed: the failure is absolutely inevitable, has objective (not personal) reasons and is caused by an external party.

column5: The relationship between the card network and the other parties of the card is a relationship of provision of services, such as settlement of payments and intermediation in carrying out operations.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/3, the card network provides services to the other parties, such as settlement of payments and intermediation.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In unrestricted investment accounts, the losses:
column6: Are borne by the institution, being the guarantor of the funds received from investors.
column7: Are borne by the holders of the accounts in all cases, including losses arising from the institution's own negligence or breach of the contract, since the capital belongs to them alone.
column8: Are borne by the account holders in proportion to their shares in the capital, except losses arising from transgression, negligence or breach of contract, which the institution bears.
column9: Are shared between the holders of the accounts and the institution according to the agreed profit-sharing ratios, except losses arising from force majeure, which the institution alone bears.
column11: Per 2/1/1, account holders bear losses pro rata to their capital shares; the institution bears losses from its transgression, negligence or breach.

column5: Waqf is considered to be the ongoing charity (Sadaqah Jariyah) referred to in the Hadith, because:
column6: The Waqf is managed by a superintendent under judicial supervision.
column7: The beneficiary does not own the Waqf asset, and accordingly, cannot dispose of it.
column8: The Waqf income must be spent on charitable purposes only.
column9: The Waqif retains the ownership of the Waqf asset during his lifetime.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Waqf is the ongoing charity in the Hadith because the beneficiary does not own the Waqf asset and cannot dispose of it.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of the Institution entering into a Parallel Istisna'a to sell, as manufacturer or supplier, items whose specification conforms to the wishes of another party is that:
column6: Taking possession of part of a thing is like taking possession of the whole thing, so that the Institution is treated as having possessed the items it resells before they are delivered to it.
column7: There are two separate deals of Istisna'a with no link between them, so it is not two sales in one deal, and the separation makes it a type of non-Riba-based financing.
column8: The manufacturer has spent money to manufacture according to specification, and would incur losses if the ultimate purchaser could refuse the goods.
column9: Istisna'a is analogous to Ijarah, in which wages may vary with time, and the price of the second contract may therefore vary with the delivery date.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Parallel Istisna'a is two separate unlinked deals, not two sales in one, which makes it non-Riba financing.

column5: Once the selling price under Murabahah has become a debt payable by instalments, it is not permitted subsequently to demand any extra payment:
column6: In consideration of extra time given for payment.
column7: For delay in payment that is for a reason.
column8: For delay in payment that is for no reason.
column9: In all the above-mentioned cases.
column11: Per 4/8, no extra payment may be demanded for extra time or for delay, whether for a reason or for no reason.

column5: According to the strength of the undertaking, the documentary credit which can be amended or cancelled without consulting the beneficiary is:
column6: Irrevocable credit.
column7: Confirmed credit.
column8: Revocable credit.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/3/1, revocable credit may be amended or cancelled without consulting the beneficiary; irrevocable credit needs the parties' consent.

column5: A customer bought gold jewellery from a shop and paid the price using his charge card issued by an IFI, which grants him a period of 30 days to settle the amount to the card issuer. The ruling on this purchase is:
column6: Permitted, because payment by the card materializes possession through holding the amount in favour of the card acceptor at the time of usage, which is unaffected by the grace period granted to the cardholder.
column7: Permitted only if the jewellery was bought using a debit card or a prepaid card, but not a credit card.
column8: Not permitted, because the cardholder's settlement to the card issuer is deferred, while the price of gold must be paid on the spot, and the grace period makes the exchange a deferred one, which is not valid for gold under any arrangement.
column9: Not permitted, unless the card acceptor receives the cash settlement from the acquirer on the same day.
column11: Per 5/4 and its basis, paying for gold by card is permitted: possession occurs at usage, regardless of settlement delays or grace periods.

column5: Prohibition of Muwata`ah to use Riba excuses (tricks which are permissible in principle) should be judged in the light of two conditions:
column6: The trick should be frequently used in the market, and the parties should be financial institutions.
column7: The intention to use the permissible act as a means of concluding a prohibited deal should be obvious and beyond all doubts, and there should be no obvious need or lawful interest that justifies resorting to such a trick.
column8: There should be an obvious need that justifies the trick, and the intention of the parties should be doubtful.
column9: The intention to use the permissible act as a means of concluding a prohibited deal may be presumed from the nature of the transaction, and there should be no written agreement between the parties.
column11: Per 6/3/2/1, the illicit intention must be obvious beyond doubt, and no obvious need or lawful interest may justify the trick.

column5: Waqf overseership is subject to:
column6: Firstly the instructions of the Waqf beneficiaries, and then the conditions of the Waqif.
column7: Only the laws and regulations of the relevant authorities, irrespective of the Waqif's conditions.
column8: Firstly the relevant Shari'ah rulings, and then the conditions stipulated by the Waqif, provided they conflict neither with Shari'ah rulings nor with the interest of the Waqf.
column9: Firstly the conditions stipulated by the Waqif, which must be complied with absolutely, and then the Shari'ah rulings, to the extent that they do not conflict with those conditions.
column11: Per 3/3/1, overseership is subject first to Shari'ah rulings, then to the Waqif's conditions not conflicting with Shari'ah or the Waqf's interest.

column5: According to the Standard, arbitration can be sought through:
column6: Agreement of the two parties at the time of dispute.
column7: Fulfillment of a previous agreement between the two parties to seek arbitration instead of resorting to law.
column8: Legal imposition of arbitration on the two parties.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1, arbitration may be agreed at the time of dispute, sought under a prior agreement, or legally imposed on the two parties.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: An IFI opened Mudarabah-based investment accounts without specifying, at the time of contracting, the profit sharing ratios between itself and the accountholders, and no normal practice of profit sharing exists for such accounts. At the end of the period a profit was realized. The correct ruling is:
column6: The two parties may specify the profit ratios at the time of distribution of the profit, provided that both agree to them in writing and the contract remains valid.
column7: The profit is shared between the IFI and the accountholders equally.
column8: The Mudarabah is null and void; the IFI is entitled to the wage of similar work, and the whole profit goes to the accountholders as Arbab al-Mal.
column9: The whole profit goes to the accountholders, and the IFI is not entitled to anything, not even the wage of similar work or the expenses it incurred.
column11: Per 4/2, absent agreed ratios and normal practice, the Mudarabah is void: the Mudarib gets a similar-work wage and Rab al-Mal the whole profit.

column5: It is permissible to conduct a draw in order to give a prize without stipulating the purchase of any goods or services.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/3/1, a prize draw without any stipulated purchase is permissible.

column5: The discharge of two debts, when one party owes the other an amount in dinar and the other owes the first an amount in dirham, by agreeing on the rate of exchange between them in order to extinguish the debts wholly or partially, is known as:
column6: Hawalah (transfer of debt).
column7: Parallel purchase and sale of currencies.
column8: Sale of debt for debt.
column9: Al-Muqassah (set-off).
column11: Per 2/10/1, this discharge of two debts in different currencies at an agreed rate is known as al-Muqassah (set-off).

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Fatwa should basically be founded on:
column6: The personal viewpoint of the Mufti, even if it does not cater for the sources of Shari'ah, provided that it serves the interests of the Institution and is approved by the majority of the members of the Board and the General Assembly.
column7: What has been explicitly stated in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, along with what is supported by Ijma' or proved by Qiyas; after these sources, Istihsan and Maslahah Mursalah may be considered as the basis for Fatwa.
column8: Maslahah Mursalah first, then the Qur'an and the Sunnah, Ijma' and Qiyas.
column9: The prevailing customary banking practices, which take precedence over Qiyas, and over Ijma' where the practices of the market are well established and widely accepted.
column11: Per 7/1, Fatwa rests on Qur'an, Sunnah, Ijma' and Qiyas; then the Mufti may consider Istihsan and Maslahah Mursalah.

column5: A competition held for a compensation (reward):
column6: Does not make payment of the reward binding, since the reward is a gift that may be withdrawn before it is received.
column7: Is permissible only if the reward is paid by a third party who is not one of the competitors.
column8: Is permissible only if the reward is paid by all of the competing participants.
column9: Makes payment of the reward binding upon the party committed to paying it.
column11: Per 2/2, a reward-based competition makes payment of the reward binding upon the party committed to paying it.

column5: The evidentiary burden to establish the occurrence of the loss and the absence of misconduct or negligence transfers to the investment manager:
column6: Whenever Rab Al Maal claims that misconduct or negligence has occurred, because the initial presumption is that the investment manager, as a fiduciary, must prove his innocence.
column7: Whenever the investment manager receives a fee for his management.
column8: In case there are pieces of circumstantial evidence (qarā'in) that contradict the investment manager's claim of the loss or of the absence of misconduct and negligence.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per item 6, the claimant bears the burden initially; it shifts by absolute stipulation, regulatory mandate or contrary circumstantial evidence (6/3).

column5: If the sale value of the mortgaged asset happens to be less than the due debt:
column6: The difference is subject to the Shari'ah rulings on normal debt, and the mortgagee has the right of recourse on the mortgagor for its settlement.
column7: The remaining debt is extinguished, since the mortgagee accepted the mortgaged asset as documentation of the debt and took the risk of its insufficiency.
column8: The mortgagee bears the difference, because he chose the mortgaged asset and accepted its value as the limit of his right.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/4/1, any shortfall becomes an ordinary debt and the mortgagee has recourse on the mortgagor for it.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: Levy of custom duties or taxes after signing the contract is an example of contingencies which constitute external reasons for termination of the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1, levy of custom duties or taxes after signing is a contingency leading to amendment of the contract, not its termination.

column5: A promise to transfer ownership in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek by one of the permitted methods:
column6: Is not binding on the lessor, since a promise is not a contract.
column7: Is a binding promise by the lessor, while the other party must have the option not to proceed, to avoid a bilateral promise resembling a concluded contract.
column8: Is binding on the lessee only, as he is the party who has requested the asset, while the lessor retains an option not to proceed with the transfer.
column9: Must be binding on both the lessor and the lessee, to ensure transfer of title and to protect the lessor against any change of mind by the lessee, since a bilateral promise is itself a valid sale.
column11: Per 8/2, the lessor's promise is binding on him alone; the lessee keeps the option not to proceed, since a bilateral promise resembles a contract.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of the manufacturer including a defect exclusion clause in an Istisna'a contract is that:
column6: The manufacturer has spent money to manufacture according to specification, and would incur losses if the ultimate purchaser could refuse the goods.
column7: Such a condition defeats the purpose of the contract, which is the exchange of usufruct for rentals, and makes the manufacturer a lessor of his labour for a fixed period.
column8: A valid Istisna'a is a sale of goods specified for future delivery, and exclusion of liability for defects is valid only in the sale of particular identified goods.
column9: Any exclusion clause renders the transaction a sale of debt for debt.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, defect exclusion is valid only in the sale of identified goods; Istisna'a sells specified future goods.

column5: When the Institution accepts mortgage in the form of investment units in Islamic investment funds, the Institution as a mortgagee:
column6: May suspend the right of the client to get back or draw from the units only in proportion to the amount of the debt, and may not suspend it absolutely.
column7: May take the income of the units for itself in return for the facility granted, as the units are held as a security.
column8: Can suspend the right of the client to get back or draw from the account, absolutely or in proportion to the amount of the debt, whichever is suitable.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/1, the mortgagee may suspend the client's drawing right absolutely or in proportion to the debt, whichever is more suitable.

column5: With regard to the legal personality of Waqf:
column6: Waqf has no independent legal personality; hence any debt incurred for the Waqf is owed personally by the overseer, who then has recourse only to the Waqf beneficiaries for what he has paid, and not to the Waqf asset.
column7: Waqf is an autonomous juridical person with an independent financial liability that allows it to obligate or take obligation, separate and independent from the overseer and the Waqf beneficiaries.
column8: Waqf is a juridical person whose financial liability is shared jointly with the Waqf beneficiaries and the overseer, so that creditors may claim against them personally and not against the Waqf asset.
column9: Waqf is a juridical person, but it can only acquire rights and cannot be liable for obligations, which are borne by the Waqif or his heirs.
column11: Per 2/4/2, Waqf is an autonomous juridical person with independent financial liability, separate from the overseer and beneficiaries.

column5: Under the Standard on Liability of the Investment Manager, the forms of investment management are:
column6: Mudaraba and Investment Agency for a fee only; a partner authorized to invest the funds of the partnership is not an investment manager, since he acts for himself and not for others.
column7: Investment Agency for a fee only, since an agent without a fee is a mere volunteer.
column8: Mudaraba only, since it is the only profit-sharing form of investment.
column9: Mudaraba, Investment Agency (Wakala bi Al Istithmar) whether for or without a fee, and authorizing (tafwīḍ) one of the partners to invest the funds of the partnership.
column11: Per 2/2, the forms are Mudaraba, Wakala bi Al Istithmar (with or without fee) and authorizing a partner to invest partnership funds.

column5: International commodity trading in the financial markets and currency trading, in accordance with Shari'ah, are among the modes of deploying liquidity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/8 and 5/9, both are listed as Shari'ah-compliant modes of deploying liquidity.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Constructive holding indicates the act of releasing the commodity and facilitating the process of its holding.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/6, constructive holding is releasing the commodity and facilitating its holding.

column5: The Shari'ah ruling that the Islamic insurance contract is an act of donation that both parties are bound to honor is measured by analogy to:
column6: Nihd, or donation pledge.
