column7: Mudarabah, in which the participants are Rabb al-Mal and the company is the Mudarib.
column8: Qard Hasan, repayable by the fund from the surplus.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the binding donation in Islamic insurance is measured by analogy to Nihd (donation pledge).

column5: Executing a financial transfer of money (remittance) in a currency different from that presented by the applicant for the transfer is:
column6: Permissible; it consists of a currency exchange effected through actual or constructive possession by delivering an amount of currency evidenced by a bank draft, followed by the transfer; a fee may be charged.
column7: Permissible, provided the Institution does not charge any fee for the transfer, since the transaction includes a currency exchange, and provided the exchange is effected through actual possession of the currency.
column8: Permissible, provided the transfer of the amount takes place before the currency exchange.
column9: Impermissible, because the beneficiary does not take actual possession of the transferred currency at the session of the exchange, so that the transaction amounts to a deferred sale of currency.
column11: Per 2/11, the exchange (evidenced by a bank draft) precedes the transfer, and the Institution may charge a fee for the transfer.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Under Khiyar al-Taghrir, the expenses relating to the return of the item to the place of sale are borne by the buyer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/3, the seller is liable for expenses relating to the return of the item to the place of sale.

column5: Irrespective of the method of contracting, an online contract is considered to be valid since:
column6: The time when the offering party comes to know of the acceptance of the other party.
column7: The time when the confirmation of acceptance is received by the accepting party from the website.
column8: The time when possession of the subject matter of the contract takes place.
column9: The time when the other party accepts the offer, whether the offering party has come to know that or not.
column11: Per 6, an online contract is valid from the time the other party accepts the offer, whether or not the offering party knows of it.

column5: An IFI leased a building to a company for five years. After two years, the IFI sold the building to an investor without informing the company and without telling the investor about the Ijarah. On learning of the lease, the investor objected. The correct ruling is:
column6: The sale is void, because the lessee's consent is necessary for the sale of the leased asset, and the lessor must first obtain it before transferring title to a third party.
column7: The sale is valid without the lessee's consent, but the investor, not having known of the Ijarah contract, may terminate the sale contract.
column8: The investor may terminate the Ijarah contract and take possession of the building.
column9: The Ijarah contract is terminated by the sale, and the company must vacate the building.
column11: Per 7/1/2, the lessee's consent is not needed for a sale to a third party; a purchaser unaware of the Ijarah may terminate the sale.

column5: It is permitted to create Waqf over investment accounts only on a perpetual basis, and the rulings of cash Waqf do not apply to them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/13/2, Waqf over investment accounts may be perpetual or timed, and the rulings of cash Waqf apply to them.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Agency is the act of one party delegating the other to act on its behalf in what can be a subject matter of delegation. Basically, agency is:
column6: A non-binding contract for both the parties thereto; however, it may sometimes become a binding contract.
column7: A binding contract for the principal, but a non-binding contract for the agent.
column8: A binding contract for both the parties once offer and acceptance have been exchanged.
column9: A binding contract for the agent, but a non-binding contract for the principal.
column11: Per 2/1/2, agency is basically non-binding for both parties, though it may become binding in the cases listed in 4/3.

column5: Dealing in documentary credit takes place:
column6: On the basis of inspection of the goods by the issuing bank at the port of arrival.
column7: On the basis of the documents alone, and it is executed without reference to the goods.
column8: On the basis of both the documents and a certificate of acceptance of the goods by the buyer.
column9: On the basis of the sale contract, which the bank must examine for conformity with the goods.
column11: Per 2/4/1, documentary credit deals in documents alone, executed without reference to the goods.

column5: Among the forms of activity that may be agreed upon on the basis of the Ju'alah contract are:
column6: An activity that is intended, through the agreement, to produce a result, such as the extraction of minerals.
column7: Information in which the offeror has an interest, such as presenting a report or study that realises a result, but in which the extent of the work cannot be determined.
column8: An activity that is intended, through the agreement, to return lost property to its seeker.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3/1/1, all three forms of activity may be the subject of Ju'alah.

column5: To attract deposits, an IFI announced that it would give a prize valued at SR 50,000 for every investment of SR 1 million placed in its investment accounts, to be paid out of the shareholders' funds. This prize is:
column6: Permissible, because it is paid out of the shareholders' funds and not out of the funds of the investment accounts.
column7: Permissible, because offering prizes to holders of investment accounts is permissible absolutely.
column8: Impermissible, because it is not permissible to offer prizes to holders of investment accounts in any case.
column9: Impermissible, because it leads to a guarantee of a part of the invested capital.
column11: Per 3/5/2/2, such a prize leads to guaranteeing part of the capital, which is impermissible even if paid from shareholders' funds.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: An IFI appointed a broker as its agent to buy commodities. The agency documents stated only an inclusive purchase price containing the broker's compensation, without any detail about the compensation. This practice is prohibited. A permissible substitute is:
column6: Mentioning the compensation and deducting it from the inclusive price, or adding it to the purchase price, or fixing the sale price and specifying that the excess is the agent's compensation.
column7: Leaving the compensation unspecified but capping it at a maximum percentage of the purchase price, with the exact amount to be determined by the agent after the sale and deducted from the proceeds.
column8: Paying the compensation to the agent as a share of the profit of the principal.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/9, merging the brokerage into the price is prohibited; the substitutes are deducting, adding, or specifying the excess as compensation.

column5: In an Irrigation Partnership due to terminate when the crop is ready for harvest, the owner prevented the worker from continuing his work before the crop materialized and, despite being requested, refused to enable him. The worker is entitled to:
column6: Nothing, as the crop had not materialized.
column7: His stipulated share of the crop plus a wage at the market rate.
column8: A wage at the market rate for similar work.
column9: His stipulated share of the crop.
column11: Per 8/5, if the owner does not enable the worker before the crop materializes, the worker gets a market-rate wage.

column5: Regarding Takaful (Islamic insurance) for the investment to protect the capital:
column6: It may cover only the risk of destruction, not the risks of wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.
column7: It may be obtained only by the investment manager, at his own cost.
column8: Takaful coverage may be obtained either by the investors themselves or through the investment manager on their behalf.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/1, Takaful may cover misconduct, negligence, breach, procrastination, death or bankruptcy, obtained by investors or the manager for them.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the requirement that insolvency should be demanded by the owners of due debts is:
column6: There is no warranted demand for undue debt; even if such a demand is made of the debtor, he does not have to pay it because the deferred period has a share in the price.
column7: Undue debts owed by the debtor do not become due upon insolvency, and therefore cannot be considered in determining whether his debts exceed his assets.
column8: Insolvency needs consideration and Ijtihad, and therefore a judicial decision.
column9: Creditors of undue debts are not entitled to share in the sequestered assets with the creditors of due debts, even after the declaration of insolvency.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, there is no warranted demand for undue debt, since the deferred period has a share in the price.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: An IFI issuing charge cards charges the cardholder an annual membership fee and a fee for replacing a lost card, charges merchants accepting the card a commission of 2% of the purchase price, and charges the cardholder a cash withdrawal fee equal to 1% of the amount withdrawn. Which of these charges is impermissible?
column6: The fee for replacing a lost card.
column7: The cash withdrawal fee equal to 1% of the amount withdrawn.
column8: The annual membership fee.
column9: The 2% commission charged to merchants accepting the card.
column11: Per 4/5/2 the cash withdrawal fee must be flat, not varying with the amount; 4/2 and 4/3 permit the other charges.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: It is permissible for the institution to grant its client a rebate for early payment:
column6: Provided that this rebate is stipulated in the contract, so that the client knows it in advance.
column7: Provided that this rebate was not stipulated in the contract, taking into consideration regulatory directives.
column8: Only if the client is in financial hardship.
column9: Only if the rebate does not exceed the profit for the remaining period.
column11: Per item 11, an early-payment rebate is permissible if not stipulated in the contract, considering regulatory directives.

column5: The capital provider may stipulate that the Mudarib must mix his personal funds with the Mudarabah funds.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/3, the capital provider may not stipulate that the Mudarib mix his personal funds or enter into partnership with others.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring permission from the relevant authorities for substituting tangible Waqf assets includes:
column6: Protection of the Waqf and more support in meeting the interest of the Waqf.
column7: Establishing the public guardianship of the state over the Waqfs.
column8: The ownership by the state of all Waqf assets.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per the Basis of 10/1/5/5, protecting the Waqf and establishing the state's public guardianship; Waqfs are independent of the treasury (3/4/1).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for continuing to apply the trading ruling of Sukuk where, due to a contingency after issuance, tangible assets fall to a percentage not less than 33% is:
column6: The concept of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya) based on turnover, since the debts of the entity are ancillary to the tangible assets which are its main activity.
column7: That contracts are, by default, valid and permitted, and a contingency after issuance cannot alter the ruling applied at the time of issuance.
column8: That supervening matters cannot be repelled, that what can be overlooked in continuance cannot be overlooked at inception, and that less than a third is little.
column9: That the larger portion is given the ruling of the whole, so that the Sukuk remain tradable as long as the tangible assets are the larger portion, which is the case at 33% or more.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 8/2/3, supervening matters are tolerated in continuance, and under a third is deemed little.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In support of the scoring method of profit distribution, the Shari'ah basis states that it is a well established principle in Fiqh literature that:
column6: Much more exemption can be allowed in partnership-based dealings (Musharakat) than in exchange-based dealings (Mu'awadah), and division (Qismah) by approximating shares rests on mutual consent.
column7: No exemption whatsoever can be allowed in partnership-based dealings.
column8: Much more exemptions can be allowed in exchange-based dealings (Mu'awadah) than in partnership-based dealings (Musharakat), and division (Qismah) must rest on exact measurement of shares, even where the partners consent.
column9: Division (Qismah) must always be exact, and cannot be based on approximation of shares.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, partnerships tolerate more exemptions than exchange contracts, and division by approximation rests on mutual consent.

column5: With regard to the contracts executed by the investment agent:
column6: The results of the contract belong to the agent, while the rights and obligations, like pursuit of payment or delivery, belong to the principal, including litigation and recovery of the price.
column7: Both the results and the rights and obligations of the contract belong to the agent.
column8: Both the results of the contract and its rights and obligations, including pursuit of payment and litigation, belong to the principal.
column9: The results (like transfer of ownership) belong to the principal, while the rights and obligations (like pursuit of payment or delivery, including litigation) belong to the agent.
column11: Per item 8, results such as ownership go to the principal; rights and obligations such as pursuit of payment and litigation go to the agent.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Investment Sukuk, units of investment funds and units of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are subject to the rulings for gold if:
column6: Their returns are linked to the price of gold.
column7: More than one third of their assets are gold.
column8: The majority of their assets are gold.
column9: Their entire assets are gold.
column11: Per 10/3, such Sukuk and fund units are subject to the rulings for gold where their entire assets are gold.

column5: If the lessor signs an Ijarah contract for a particular asset for a specified period of time:
column6: He may re-lease the asset to new lessees for the remaining period as an investment instrument.
column7: He cannot sign another Ijarah contract with another lessee for the duration of the existing Ijarah period or for any remaining period thereof.
column8: He may sign another Ijarah contract with another lessee for the same period, provided the rental is different.
column9: He may sign another Ijarah contract with another lessee for the remaining period, provided the first lessee's rental is reduced.
column11: Per 4/2/2, the usufruct already belongs to the first lessee, so no second lease may be signed for the same or remaining period.

column5: An investor holds conventional interest-bearing bonds. He wishes to create a Waqf over them for general charitable causes and consults the Shari'ah adviser of the IFI. The adviser explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The Waqf is valid if the interest income does not exceed 5% of the total yield of the bonds.
column7: The Waqf is valid if those bonds are substituted with assets of permissible yield.
column8: The Waqf is invalid in all cases, because the Waqf asset must be of permissible yield at the time of creation.
column9: The Waqf is valid, and the bonds may be retained provided the interest is disbursed to charitable causes.
column11: Per 2/4/10, Waqf over assets of prohibited yield (e.g., bonds) for general charity is valid if they are substituted with assets of permissible yield.

column5: The contracting parties may set various dates on which the delivery of al-Muslam Fihi may take place, in instalments:
column6: Provided the capital of Salam was paid at the time the contract was originally concluded.
column7: Provided the capital of Salam is paid in corresponding instalments on each delivery date.
column8: This is not permissible, as al-Muslam Fihi must be delivered on a single date.
column9: Provided all the delivery dates fall within one year of the contract.
column11: Per 3/2/9, delivery in instalments on various dates is allowed if the full capital was paid when the contract was concluded.

column5: The leading Institution may receive commission for performing preparatory tasks such as feasibility studies, organization, mobilization of participatory funds and preparation of contracts. This commission:
column6: Should not exceed the actual cost incurred by the Institution for carrying out such tasks, and the balance, if any, should be refunded to the participants, whether or not it is the lead manager.
column7: Is permissible only if the Institution performing such tasks is also the lead manager.
column8: May be equal to, less or more than the actual cost the Institution incurs, and the Institution performing such tasks may or may not be a lead manager.
column9: Must be equal to the actual cost, and must be a definite sum and not a percentage.
column11: Per 7/1, the preparatory-task commission may equal, be below or exceed actual cost, whether or not the Institution is lead manager.

column5: In the event of the promisor's repudiation (nukūl) of a promise to purchase, the promisee is entitled to:
column6: Compensation for the actual damage, estimated by the difference between the cost and the price at which the asset is sold to a third party on the date of performance.
column7: The difference between the promised price and the market price on the date of the promise, as an estimate of the lost profit.
column8: Compensation for the actual damage in addition to the profit lost from the promised price, provided that the loss is proved before the court and the promisor was notified in advance.
column9: Retain the entire promised price as a penalty for the repudiation.
column11: Per 5/1/7, only actual damage is claimable, excluding lost profit; for a promise to purchase it is cost minus the third-party sale price.

column5: If a personal guarantee is made contingent upon a future event, for example by fixing a future date at which liability will commence:
column6: The guarantor may not withdraw the guarantee once it has been concluded.
column7: The guarantee is void, because a guarantee may not be contingent.
column8: The guarantor may validly withdraw the guarantee, by notifying the creditor, before the prospective obligation to be guaranteed arises.
column9: The guarantor may withdraw the guarantee at any time, even after the obligation has arisen, by notifying the creditor.
column11: Per 3/1/4, a contingent guarantee is valid and may be withdrawn by notice before the guaranteed obligation arises.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: It is permissible to purchase gold through a Salam contract, provided that the capital of Salam is paid in currency at the contracting session.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/2, gold may be bought by Salam only if the capital of Salam is not gold, silver or currencies.

column5: Examples of bilateral promises that may be legally binding include:
column6: Bilateral promises in international trade conducted by means of documentary credits.
column7: Bilateral promises in supply agreements.
column8: A bilateral promise to enter into a sale and a loan.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2/1-4/2/2, documentary credits and supply agreements qualify; a bilateral promise of sale and loan is prohibited (4/1).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting the sale of an entity with ongoing activities without observing the rulings of the sale of debt is:
column6: That the larger portion is given the ruling of the whole.
column7: The maxim that what can be overlooked during the continuance cannot be overlooked at the inception.
column8: The concept of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya) and the permissibility of selling consequentially what cannot be sold independently.
column9: The requirements of assemblage (tarkīb) required by the Mālikīs in the sale of ornamented jewellery.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 8/1, the rule rests on appurtenance; assemblage (tarkīb) is the basis of 8/2.

column5: In trading in currencies, the contract shall not contain:
column6: Any conditional option or deferment clause regarding the delivery of one or both countervalues.
column7: Any clause under which the exchange rate between the two currencies is agreed by the two parties.
column8: Any clause under which the contract is concluded between two parties at different remote places using modern means of communication.
column9: Any clause appointing an agent to execute the sale of the currency and to take possession of and deliver the countervalue.
column11: Per 2/1/3, no conditional option or deferment of either countervalue is allowed; agency (2/7) and remote contracting (2/8) are permitted.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The end of the financial period exonerates the shareholders from responsibility for dividends from non-permissible earnings that were distributed to them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the basis, shareholders remain personally obliged to dispose of such dividends after management's responsibility ends.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Monitoring the provisions of the agency contract is the responsibility of the (……….), whereas monitoring the activities stipulated in the contract, except donations, is the responsibility of the (……….).
column6: Agent .... agent
column7: Agent .... principal
column8: Principal .... principal
column9: Principal .... agent
column11: Per 6/2, the principal monitors the contract's provisions; the agent monitors its activities, except donations, which go to the principal.

column5: There should be coordination between the mother company and its subsidiaries with regard to payment of Zakah so as to avoid double payment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/3, the mother company and subsidiaries coordinate Zakah payment to avoid double payment.

column5: An Ijarah contract concluded on a specific (identified) asset does not expire with the total destruction of the asset; instead, the lessor must provide a substitute asset with similar specifications.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/1/3 and 7/2/4, it expires on total destruction of an identified asset; substitution applies to a described Ijarah (7/1/6).

column5: A third party's guarantee to refund the price to the buyer if it appears that the sold commodity belongs to a person other than the seller is known as:
column6: Hamish Jiddiyyah.
column7: A non-recourse guarantee given voluntarily by a third party without the debtor's request or consent.
column8: Daman al-Dark (dealers/business misrepresentation guarantee).
column9: A subscription guarantee given by an underwriter for the shares remaining after the offer period.
column11: Per 3/2, this is Daman al-Dark, an example of a market (business) guarantee of a future obligation.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: A conventional bank whose financial year starts on 1 January was converted by its existing shareholders, the conversion taking effect from 1 July. Interest income of USD 2 million was earned in March of that year, and USD 5 million of interest earned in the previous year had already been distributed as dividends. Which of the following is correct?
column6: The bank need not dispose of the USD 2 million, since it was earned before the conversion took effect on 1 July, but must dispose of the USD 5 million distributed to the shareholders.
column7: The bank must dispose of the USD 2 million; the USD 5 million should be disposed of personally by the shareholders who received it, on ethical grounds, the bank not being bound.
column8: Neither amount needs to be disposed of, since both were earned before the conversion.
column9: The bank must dispose of both the USD 2 million and the USD 5 million.
column11: Per 8/1/2, disposal covers the whole financial period of conversion; prior distributions are the recipients' personal ethical duty.

column5: An IFI that faces no liquidity shortage decided to raise funds for expanding its financing portfolio by purchasing commodities from another Institution on deferred payment basis and selling them to third parties for spot prices, instead of mobilizing funds through Mudarabah, investment agency or Sukuk. The ruling on this is:
column6: Impermissible, because the Institution can never be a Monetization beneficiary; only customers may be.
column7: Permissible, because the Institution may be the Monetization beneficiary when it purchases the commodity from another Institution on deferred payment and sells it to a third party to obtain liquidity.
column8: Impermissible, because Monetization is not a mode of investment or financing, and the Institution shall resort to it only when it faces the danger of a liquidity shortage that could interrupt the flow of its operations and cause losses for its clients.
column9: Permissible, provided that the Institution sells the commodity through brokers and not through its own bodies.
column11: Per 5/1, Institutions shall not use Monetization to mobilize liquidity while neglecting Mudarabah, Sukuk etc.; it is only for a damaging liquidity shortage.

column5: It is permitted to sell with a promise from the seller alone to buy back, or a promise from the buyer alone to resell, subject to rules including:
column6: Both contracts (the first sale and the subsequent one) must be for a spot price.
column7: The promise may be included as a clause in the first sale contract, provided that it is unilateral.
column8: Ownership is transferred automatically upon the promise document once the promised date arrives.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/1–5/1/3, both sales must be spot; the promise must be in a separate deed and ownership passes only by a contract on fulfilment.

column5: The rules governing Ijarah must apply to Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, and none of them should be breached under the pretext that:
column6: The leased asset was bought by the lessor on the basis of a promise by the lessee that he would acquire it.
column7: The lessee pays rentals in excess of those payable for a similar property, similar in amount to the instalments of an instalment sale.
column8: Local laws and conventional banking practices consider the transaction as an instalment sale with a deferred transfer of ownership.
column9: In all the above-mentioned cases.
column11: Per 8/6, Ijarah rules apply to IMB despite the lessee's promise, rentals resembling sale instalments, or local laws treating it as a sale.

column5: If the Mudarib has commingled his own funds with the Mudarabah funds:
column6: He becomes a partner in respect of his own funds and a Mudarib in respect of the capital provider's funds; profit is divided proportionately to the two funds, he takes the profit of his own funds, and the rest is distributed according to the Mudarabah contract.
column7: All the profit is distributed according to the profit-sharing ratio of the Mudarabah contract, since the commingled funds are indistinguishable from one another.
column8: His funds become part of the Mudarabah capital, and he is entitled to his agreed share of the profit only, and he is liable to the capital provider for any loss of the combined funds, even if it occurred without misconduct or negligence on his part, since the funds are inseparable.
column9: The Mudarabah contract becomes void, since commingling is prohibited in all cases.
column11: Per 8/9, the Mudarib is a partner for his own funds and Mudarib for the other's; profit is first split in proportion to the funds.

column5: All forms of endorsement of commercial papers are binding with respect to their legal effects, provided that the endorsements fulfil the legal conditions and regulations determined for them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4, all forms of endorsement are binding if they meet their legal conditions and regulations.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Rights of Shuf'ah (preemption):
column6: May be claimed at any time within one year of the sale, regardless of when the preemptor became aware of it.
column7: Must be claimed immediately upon becoming aware of the sale in accordance with custom or law, failing which they lapse.
column8: May be waived by the preemptor in favour of the buyer for consideration.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 7/2/4, Shuf'ah must be claimed immediately on learning of the sale or it lapses; per 10/2, no consideration may be taken to waive it.

column5: An IFI granted a customer a Qard Hasan. The IFI incurred costs for drawing up the loan documents and promissory notes required for the loan, and for delivering the loan amount to the customer. These costs:
column6: Shall be borne by the IFI, because it is not permissible for the lender to recover any costs from the borrower.
column7: Shall be borne by the borrower.
column8: Shall be borne by the borrower for the documentation only, while delivery costs are borne by the lender.
column9: Shall be shared equally, since the loan benefits both parties.
column11: Per 4/2/1 and 4/2/2, delivery and documentation expenses of a Qard are borne by the borrower.

column5: Taking on the procedures required for the offering of concession rights against specific fees or any compensation stipulated in the contract is:
column6: Impermissible, since concession rights relate to public property, which may not be the subject of any compensation.
column7: Permissible, unless the deal constitutes an element of Riba, Gharar or any other Shari'ah-banned practice.
column8: Permissible only if the fees do not exceed the actual cost of the procedures.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/2, there is no Shari'ah objection to fees or stipulated compensation unless the deal involves Riba, Gharar or other banned practices.

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, it is permissible for either of the partners to lease the share of the other partner for a specified amount and for whatever duration, in which case each partner remains responsible for the periodical maintenance of his share.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/9, either partner may lease the other's share; each remains responsible for periodical maintenance of his share.

column5: The transferee is entitled to have a right of recourse against the transferor in the following situations:
column6: Death of the payer in bankruptcy.
column7: The payer denies concluding the Hawalah contract and has taken a judicial oath to this effect, and there is no evidence to prove otherwise.
column8: The payer, while solvent, delays payment beyond the agreed date.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/2, (a) and (b) are among the cases of recourse; mere delay by a solvent payer is not.

column5: The prospectus of Sukuk must not include any statement to the effect that:
column6: The issuer of the certificate accepts liability to compensate the owner of the certificate up to the nominal value of the certificate in situations other than torts and negligence, or guarantees a fixed percentage of profit.
column7: An independent third party will provide a guarantee free of charge.
column8: The investment of the realised funds and the assets into which the funds are converted will be undertaken through Shari'ah-compliant modes of investment, under the supervision of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the issuer.
column9: Each owner of a certificate participates in the profit and bears a loss in proportion to the financial value represented by his certificates.
column11: Per 5/1/8/7, the issuer may not guarantee nominal value (except for torts/negligence) or a fixed profit; a free third-party guarantee is allowed.

column5: Although arbitration could take place verbally according to Shari'ah, in order to be legally accepted it needs to be written and signed by the arbitrators and the parties of the dispute.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, verbal arbitration is valid, but legal acceptance requires writing and signature by arbitrators and parties.

column5: The investment agent may start investment activity before receiving the funds from the principal, with the principal's permission, by:
column6: Incurring a debt on behalf of the principal by purchasing on credit.
column7: Advancing a loan to the principal by purchasing something on his behalf.
column8: Charging the principal a return on the amounts advanced, in addition to its fee.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/3 and 6/4, both methods are allowed; any loan advanced is interest-free and may bring no benefit to the agent.

column5: The receipt by the Institution of certificates of storage issued by warehouses following appropriate and reliable formalities is considered as constructive possession.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/4, like a bill of lading, reliable warehouse storage certificates amount to constructive possession.

column5: Two Islamic banks agreed to swap their portfolios of Murabaha receivables owed by their respective customers, the two portfolios being of equal value. This transaction is:
column6: Permitted, since the two portfolios are of equal value, and neither bank gains any excess over the other or a deferred benefit.
column7: Permitted, provided that the swap is executed at spot and the portfolios are of equal value and equal tenor.
column8: Not permitted, since it is a sale of a debt to a third party for another debt owed to that party by another.
column9: Permitted, as it is a form of ḥawāla, since each bank assigns its customers to the other bank.
column11: Per 9/7, selling a debt to a third party for another debt owed to it by another party, such as swapping receivables portfolios, is barred.

column5: Articles of trade:
column6: Include anything offered for sale, such as real estate and moveable assets, whether sold in its current state or after manufacturing.
column7: Must be obtained through buying in order to be subject to Zakah, so goods obtained by inheritance, gift or manufacture are excluded from the Zakah base.
column8: Should be valued at cost or market price, whichever is less, at the end of the Zakah year.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/2/1, articles of trade need not be bought; mere intention to sell suffices. Per 5/2/2, they are not valued at the lower of cost or market.

column5: The arbitration period starts at the time when the arbitration document has been signed by all the parties seeking arbitration, and ends at the time when the arbitration verdict has been signed by all these parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/6, the period runs from the signing of the arbitration document by all parties to the signing of the verdict by all of them.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: A company agreed to buy from an IFI 1,000 tonnes of wheat of described specifications, to be delivered after six months, with the price payable on delivery. The contract was concluded using the word "Salam". This contract is:
column6: Permitted, because it was concluded with the word Salam and not with the word sale, and the form of the contract overrides its substance.
column7: Permitted, because it is a forward contract used for hedging.
column8: Not permitted, because it amounts to a Salam contract in which the capital of Salam (Ras al-Mal) is not paid promptly.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/2/2/1, a described commodity with deferred price is not permitted, whether called sale or Salam, as Salam capital is not paid promptly.

column5: Family Waqf (Waqf Ahli or Dhurri) is permissible on the basis of:
column6: The analogy between Waqf and Wasiyyah (will), on which a future-dated Waqf is also based.
column7: The Hanafi viewpoint that the Waqf purpose need not be charitable from the very beginning.
column8: The Hadith about Umar's Waqf, and because family Waqf is, in fact, a charitable Waqf since it will finally become so.
column9: The analogy between Waqf and 'Ariyah (a lent thing).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, family Waqf rests on the Hadith of Umar's Waqf and on its being charitable in the end. The Hanafis require a charitable purpose.

column5: The contract forming a stock company:
column6: Is not binding, so any shareholder may withdraw his share of the capital after giving due notice, and the company continues with the remaining shareholders.
column7: Is binding, so a shareholder may neither sell his shares nor relinquish title to them during the life of the company, unless all the other shareholders consent in writing, and the company may be dissolved only by a unanimous decision of the founders.
column8: Is binding on the founders only, while other shareholders may dissolve the company in respect of their shares after the first financial year.
column9: Is binding during the duration designated by the articles of association, so no one may dissolve the company in respect of his shares, but a shareholder may sell his shares or relinquish title to them in favour of another person.
column11: Per 4/1/2/1, it binds for the designated duration unless the majority agree to dissolve; a shareholder may sell his shares.

column5: If the creditor discharges the debtor from the debt:
column6: The guarantor is also discharged automatically from his liability.
column7: The guarantor's liability is converted into a non-recourse guarantee.
column8: The guarantor remains liable for the debt.
column9: The guarantor remains liable unless the creditor discharges him expressly.
column11: Per 3/3/2, discharging the debtor automatically discharges the guarantor (but discharging the guarantor does not discharge the debtor).

column5: The employer should stick to utilizing the work/service of the hired person as per the permissible conditions that have been agreed upon.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1/4, the employer must use the hired service/work according to the agreed permissible conditions.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for considering prior possession of a thing as a substitute for subsequent possession on grounds acknowledged by the Shari'ah is that:
column6: Possession is a formality that has no effect on the contract.
column7: The purpose behind the realisation of possession is to establish control over, and the ability to undertake transactions in, the thing possessed; if this state is found, possession is found.
column8: Prior possession is always one of liability (Daman), which is stronger than trust, so it stands in place of any subsequent possession regardless of the control the possessor has over the thing.
column9: The subsequent possessor is always the owner of the thing.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/6, possession aims at control and ability to deal; where that exists, possession exists.

column5: Ju'alah contract may be used for securing financing facilities, provided that:
column6: The worker guarantees the repayment of the financing, and the compensation is paid only if the financing is repaid.
column7: The subject matter is valid, such as creation of debt through deferred Murabahah, Ijarah with deferred rental, interest-free loans, letters of guarantee or documentary credit, and it is not employed for raising interest-bearing loans.
column8: The compensation is a percentage of the interest saved by the offeror, who is the party obtaining the financing.
column9: The financing obtained is from an Islamic institution only, irrespective of its type, the worker is also an Islamic institution, and the compensation of the worker is fixed as a percentage of the amount of financing obtained from it over the whole period.
column11: Per 8/3/2, the subject matter must be valid and not used to raise interest-bearing loans via stipulation, custom or inter-bank dealings.

column5: It is permissible to trade in Mugharasah certificates after closing of subscription, allotment of certificates and commencement of activity, but only where the certificate holders are the owners of the land.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/18, Mugharasah certificates may be traded after these stages irrespective of the holders being owners of the land or workers.

column5: A separate, independent Salam contract that the seller concludes with a third party to acquire goods of a similar specification to those in the first Salam contract, so that the first Salam obligation is discharged by delivering these goods, is called:
column6: Parallel Salam.
column7: Salam Sukuk.
column8: Replacement of al-Muslam Fihi.
column9: Istisna'a.
column11: Per 6/1, this is Parallel Salam; the seller in the first Salam becomes the buyer in the second.

column5: Valid arbitration has to fulfill the following requirements, except:
column6: Acceptance of the arbitrator to do the arbitration task.
column7: Attestation of the acceptance of arbitration in the arbitration document.
column8: Agreement between the two parties on arbitration, and their mutual consent on accepting the verdicts of the arbitrator.
column9: Existence of dispute between two parties or more, around a permissible right.
column11: Per 6/2 the three requirements are dispute over a permissible right, agreement and consent, and the arbitrator's acceptance; attestation is only preferable (9/8).

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to benefit from any price offers or quotations that the customer has obtained from other dealers or suppliers, to assist it in evaluating expenses and computing its prospective profit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 2/1/2.

column5: With regard to the investment manager assuming the risk of the investment:
column6: It is neither permitted to stipulate an absolute liability (ḍamān muṭlaq) on him nor permitted for him to volunteer to assume the risk at the time of making the investment contract.
column7: It is not permitted for him to undertake, either explicitly or implicitly, assumption of the risk after making the investment contract.
column8: Following the occurrence of a total or a partial loss, it is permitted for him to volunteer to assume the liability upon his own free will.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2–3/4, absolute liability and volunteering at or after contracting are barred, but he may volunteer after a loss occurs.

column5: When the customer is authorized to purchase the item as the Institution's agent, the procedures to be adopted include all of the following, excluding:
column6: The customer, as agent, may conclude the Murabahah with himself immediately upon purchasing the item, without any further notice.
column7: The Institution itself must pay the supplier, and not pay the price of the item into the account of the customer as agent, whenever possible.
column8: The two liabilities of risk are separated by an interval in time between the performance of the agency contract and the execution of the Murabahah contract.
column9: The Institution should obtain from the supplier the documents that confirm that a sale has taken place.
column11: Per 3/1/4–3/1/5, the Institution pays the supplier, gets sale documents and separates liabilities by a time interval; the agent may not sell to himself.

column5: It is not permissible to sell commercial paper that has not become due for an amount similar to its value, because this involves Riba al-Fadl.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/2, selling it for an amount similar to its value involves Riba al-Nasi'ah, not Riba al-Fadl.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring that a contract be concluded at the time of repurchase, rather than ownership passing on the mere lapse of the duration, is:
column6: That the legal registration is meant only for documentation purposes, while ownership transfers by offer and acceptance.
column7: That repurchase at a deferred price exceeding the spot price is tantamount to 'Inah, which is impermissible as narrated from Ibn Omar, and the second contract would then be concluded automatically.
column8: That contracts and financial dealings are, in principle, assumed to be permissible, in line with Allah's saying: "Allah has permitted sale".
column9: That ownership does not transfer except by a formulation (verbal or by action) on which the contract terms depend, and automatic transfer would be a contingent sale.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/2, ownership passes only by a formulation, and an automatic transfer would be a contingent sale.

column5: ………… is a partnership between two or more parties whereby each partner contributes a specific amount of money in a manner that gives each one a right to deal in the assets of the partnership, on condition that the profit is distributed according to the partnership agreement and that the losses are borne in accordance with the contribution of each partner to the capital.
column6: Sharikat al-Mufawadah.
column7: Partnership in commendum.
column8: Sharikat al-'Inan.
column9: Sharikat al-Wujuh.
column11: Per 3/1, this is the definition of Sharikat al-'Inan.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing the leasing of an asset that is not owned by the lessor is:
column6: That the absence of ownership creates an uncertainty in the term of the lease that might lead to dispute.
column7: That leasing such an asset makes the lessor an accomplice in doing evil.
column8: The well-known Hadith which prohibits two sales in one sale.
column9: The Hadith that prohibits one from selling what he does not own, as Ijarah proper is a sale of usufruct.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Ijarah is a sale of usufruct, so the Hadith forbidding sale of what one does not own applies.

column5: When Muwata`ah is stipulated as part of the contract:
column6: It is a mere moral undertaking that is not enforceable.
column7: It renders the contract void, because a contract may not be based on a prior agreement, whatever the purpose of that agreement and even if it is not stipulated as a condition, since it amounts to two contracts in one.
column8: It becomes a condition precedent to the conclusion of the contract, and the contract is subject to the relevant Shari'ah rulings with regard to permissibility, enforceability and validity.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/2/2, stipulated Muwata`ah becomes a condition precedent, and the contract is subject to rulings on permissibility and validity.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for stating that an Istisna'a contract is binding is:
column6: The view of Imam Abu Yusuf, as stated in the Mejelle, that the manufacturer has spent money to manufacture according to specification and would incur losses if the ultimate purchaser could refuse the goods.
column7: The analogy of Istisna'a to an Ijarah contract in which wages vary with the time taken by the worker, so that the price may be fixed only after completion of the work.
column8: The view of the Maliki scholars that taking possession of part of a thing is like taking possession of the whole thing, so that part-delivery binds the ultimate purchaser to the entire contract and the price becomes due.
column9: The resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on discounting for early payment, which permits the ultimate purchaser to withdraw before the work commences.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, bindingness rests on Abu Yusuf's view (Mejelle): the manufacturer spends money and would lose if the buyer could refuse.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If the converting bank has rights to prohibited non-monetary assets, or is entitled to receive consideration for supplying non-permissible assets or services:
column6: It may receive the assets with the intent to destroy them, and receive the consideration with the intent to donate it to charity; the customer may not avoid paying.
column7: It should waive the consideration, but receive the non-monetary assets in order to destroy them, since the consideration is the price of a prohibited service.
column8: It may receive the consideration and keep it, since the contract was concluded before conversion, provided the bank uses it only for its permissible operations and gives none of it to charity.
column9: It should waive these rights, since collecting them is a dealing in the prohibited, and the customer may then keep the asset or service without paying for it.
column11: Per 8/1/4, assets are received to be destroyed and consideration received to be donated; the customer may not escape payment.

column5: The basis for the termination of the Musaqat contract upon the perishing of the trees or their inability to bear fruit is the Hadith "There should be neither harm nor malice", because the worker would be excessively harmed if obligated to work gratis.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 12/4, termination avoids excessive harm to a worker otherwise working without compensation.

column5: It is permissible to issue new shares in order to increase the capital of a stock company:
column6: Provided the new shares are issued at the fair value of the old shares in accordance with the opinion of valuation experts, i.e. at a premium or discount to nominal value, or at market value.
column7: Only at the nominal value of the old shares, since a share may not be issued at any other price, whether higher or lower, and the new shareholders would otherwise be advantaged.
column8: Only at a premium to the nominal value, in order to protect existing shareholders from dilution of their rights in the reserves and the accumulated profit of the company, and never at a discount.
column9: At any price determined by the board of directors, without regard to the opinion of valuation experts or the market value.
column11: Per 4/1/2/3, new shares are issued at the fair value of old shares per experts: at premium, discount or market value.

column5: The basis for not requiring acceptance from a non-specific Waqf beneficiary is that:
column6: The overseer accepts on behalf of all the Waqf beneficiaries.
column7: Waqf is a binding contract, and binding contracts do not require acceptance.
column8: Acceptance is required only in Charitable Waqf.
column9: Acceptance cannot be envisaged from a non-specific party.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/1/1, acceptance cannot be envisaged from a non-specific party.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The purchase of gold by way of documentary credit is:
column6: Not permissible in any case.
column7: Permissible absolutely, since the bank's undertaking constitutes constructive possession of the gold by the importer, even if the price is paid after presentation of the documents.
column8: Not permissible unless the Shari'ah requirements for trading in gold are complied with, including payment of the price without deferment.
column9: Permissible, provided that the documents are received within two business days of the contract and the price is paid when they are presented.
column11: Per 5/1/2, gold may be bought by documentary credit only in compliance with item 3, including payment of the price without deferment.

column5: An Institution is entitled to guarantee financial commitments without a right of recourse to the debtor (to be a non-recourse guarantor):
column6: If the amount and duration of the guarantee are specified.
column7: If it is already authorised by its shareholders and investors to make donations or perform acts of benevolence.
column8: If it receives a fee for the guarantee.
column9: If the debtor requests or consents to the guarantee and the guarantor retains a right of recourse to the debtor for the amount paid.
column11: Per 3/1/3, an Institution may be a non-recourse guarantor only if authorised by shareholders and investors to donate.

column5: The contract of loan (Qard) is concluded through offer and acceptance:
column6: Only by the words Qard and Salaf, and not by conduct, since the contract cannot be concluded by any other expression.
column7: By the use of the words Qard and Salaf or any other word or act that conveys the meaning of Qard.
column8: Only by the use of the word Qard.
column9: Only in writing, documented by promissory notes.
column11: Per 3/1, Qard is concluded by the words Qard and Salaf or any other word or act conveying the meaning of Qard.

column5: If a loss occurs caused by the Mudarib's wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract, the capital provider:
column6: May not hold the Mudarib liable, since he acts in a fiduciary capacity.
column7: May hold the Mudarib liable for both the loss of capital and the profit that would otherwise have been achieved.
column8: May hold the Mudarib liable for the loss of capital, but not the loss of profit.
column9: May hold the Mudarib liable for the loss of profit only.
column11: Per 3/7, the Mudarib is liable for loss of capital but not for loss of (unrealised) profit.

column5: The compensation in a Ju'alah contract may be:
column6: A portion of the object of work, for instance, a percentage of a debt agreed upon for collection.
column7: The right to utilise, for a determined period, a project whose implementation is agreed upon.
column8: An unknown amount to be determined by the offeror at his discretion after completion of the work.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/3/2/2, (a) and (b) are valid; per 5/3/2/1, the compensation must be known, otherwise reasonable compensation is due.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: With regard to payment for waiver of revocation rights:
column6: It is permissible to stipulate payment for waiver of revocation rights in a sale contract.
column7: In contracts running for specified terms, such as Ijarah, Istisna'a, Hawalat al-Dayn, Muzara'ah, Mugharasah and Wakalah, a party may waive the remaining period for a consideration agreed at the time of waiver.
column8: It is not permissible in any contract to receive a consideration for waiving rights to the remaining period of the contract, since that would be the sale of an unowned right and amount to Riba, whether the waiver is made by the lessor, the lessee or the agent.
column9: Waiver of revocation rights in return for a consideration is permissible in sale contracts only, and not in leases or agency.
column11: Per 10/1, payment for waiver may not be stipulated in sale, but in term contracts a party may waive the remaining period for a consideration agreed on waiver.

column5: The pledges contained in contemporary combined contract sets, such as Murabahah on Order of Purchase, Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek or Diminishing Musharakah:
column6: Are not binding, since they are mere promises.
column7: Are binding to their respective parties.
column8: Are binding on the customer only, since he initiates the transaction.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 7/3, pledges contained in such combined contract sets are binding to their respective parties.

column5: A third party may provide a guarantee to make up a loss of capital of some or all partners in a Sharikah. Among the conditions of this guarantee:
column6: The guarantee may be provided for consideration, provided it is not linked to the Sharikah contract.
column7: The third party guarantor may own up to two-thirds of the capital in the entity to be guaranteed.
column8: The legal capacity and financial liability of the third party as a guarantor are independent from the Sharikah contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/4/3, the guarantor must be independent; the guarantee is without consideration and he may not own more than half.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Fatwa in Institutions is confined to:
column6: Rulings on worshipping only, such as Zakah, prayer and fasting, because financial transactions are decided by the management of the Institution.
column7: Financial rulings only, excluding any matter relating to Zakah.
column8: Operational financial rulings and related issues, such as some rulings on worshipping, as well as permissibility and prohibition in some concerns such as Zakah.
column9: All areas of Fiqh, including personal status and penalties, because the Board acts as the general religious authority of the Institution, its shareholders and its employees.
column11: Per clause 4, Fatwa in Institutions covers operational financial rulings and related issues such as some worship matters and Zakah.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: ………… give one or both of the parties or a third party the right either to continue with the contract or to revoke it within a stipulated period of time:
column6: Cooling-off options.
column7: Either-or options.
column8: Options to revoke due to non-payment.
column9: Options to revoke due to defect.
column11: Per 2/1, cooling-off options give one or both parties or a third party the right to continue or revoke within a stipulated period.

column5: In specific hiring, when the service/work becomes partially useless, the employer has the right to terminate the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/2/1, partial uselessness gives the employer the right to terminate; complete uselessness makes the contract null and void.

column5: An IFI concluded a 10-year Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek in which the rental for the first year is fixed at 50,000, and the rental for each subsequent year is determined by a clearly defined benchmark plus 2%, with no maximum or minimum limit. Under the standard:
column6: The arrangement is impermissible, because the rental must be fixed for the entire term of the Ijarah.
column7: The arrangement is fully compliant as it stands, since the benchmark formula is clear.
column8: Fixing the first-year rental in a lump sum is correct, but the benchmark should be subject to a ceiling on both maximum and minimum levels.
column9: The arrangement is impermissible, because the first-year rental should also be determined by the benchmark.
column11: Per 5/2/3, a floating rental needs a lump-sum first period and a clear benchmark that is subject to maximum and minimum ceilings.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the prohibition of derivatives is that:
column6: They are binding promises that are converted to sale contracts pertaining to the future without an offer and acceptance.
column7: They are concluded through intermediaries who coordinate supply and demand.
column8: They are concluded in organized markets under the supervision of specialised organizations, which guarantee performance and thereby remove Gharar.
column9: They always involve trading in currencies.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, derivatives are binding promises turned into future sale contracts without an offer and acceptance.

column5: Mentioning the Shari'ah or basis of the arbitration decision (reasoning):
column6: Is a condition for valid arbitration in all cases.
column7: Is preferable, yet it does not constitute a condition for valid arbitration, unless the law so requires.
column8: Is impermissible, since the arbitration decision should include the text of the verdict only.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 11/6, reasoning is preferable but not a condition for validity unless the law requires it.

column5: Multiplying or dividing the values of the index at different periods by a constant figure affects the accuracy of its implications.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/3/2, values may be multiplied or divided by a constant figure without affecting the accuracy of their implications.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Gold taken as Hamish Jiddiyyah from a purchase orderer in Murabahah to secure a binding promise:
column6: Is held on a liability basis by the Institution, which may use it until the Murabahah is concluded.
column7: Is held as a trust; in case of default, the actual loss (the difference between the cost and the selling price to a third party) is deducted with the gold evaluated at the market price at the time of its deposit, and the Institution keeps any balance.
column8: Is 'Arboun, and is forfeited in full if the customer fails to conclude the Murabahah.
column9: Is held as a trust and is not 'Arboun; in case of default, only the actual loss (the difference between the cost and the selling price to a third party) is deducted, the gold being valued at the market price at deduction.
column11: Per 7/2/1, it is a trust, not 'Arboun; on default only actual loss is deducted, valuing the gold at market price at the time of deduction.

column5: If the price in an online adhesion contract is fair, and its terms and conditions do not entail any injustice for the adhering party, the contract is permissible but is not binding on the adhering party.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/3/3, such an adhesion contract is permissible and binding on both its parties.

column5: The surplus may be distributed among the policyholders through any method chosen by the managing company, even if that method is not mentioned in the regulations.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 12/2, the selected form must be explicitly mentioned in the regulations; other methods need SSB approval (12/2/4).

column5: An IFI and two customers entered into a Sharikah. One of the customers, who has the required expertise, was appointed as manager of the Sharikah for a fixed monthly salary under a contract that is independent of the Sharikah contract, so that he may be dismissed at any time without amending or terminating the Sharikah contract. This arrangement is:
column6: Permissible, provided the salary is deducted from his share of profit at the end of the year.
column7: Impermissible, because a fixed remuneration for a partner who manages the Sharikah is prohibited in all cases.
column8: Permissible, because the partner in this case becomes an employee of the company and is not acting in the capacity of a partner.
column9: Impermissible, unless the other partners also receive a similar salary.
column11: Per 3/1/3/5 and its basis, a partner appointed by an independent contract may earn a specific remuneration as an employee.

column5: An unrestricted Waqf, wherein the Waqif does not specify the beneficiary of the Waqf, is:
column6: Valid, and it shall be made available for charitable causes as deemed fit by the overseer or the court.
column7: Valid, but it is deemed a Private Waqf for the Waqif himself until he specifies the beneficiary.
column8: Valid, and its revenue shall be disbursed to the poor among the relatives of the Waqif.
column9: Invalid, because specifying the avenues of Waqf disposal is a condition for the validity of Waqf.
column11: Per 2/4/1/6, an unrestricted Waqf is valid and is used for charitable causes as deemed fit by the overseer or the court.

column5: With regard to benefiting from the mortgaged asset:
column6: The mortgagor can benefit from the mortgaged asset on permission of the mortgagee.
column7: On permission of the mortgagor, the mortgagee can utilize the mortgaged asset against the normal pay for similar assets.
column8: The mortgagor can benefit from the mortgaged asset without the permission of the mortgagee, since he is its owner.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/2/9, the mortgagor benefits with the mortgagee's permission; the mortgagee may use it only with permission and against normal pay.

column5: Combining Salam with Ju'alah for the same contract value is a permissible combination, since each of the two contracts is permissible on its own.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/4, Salam with Ju'alah for the same contract value is cited as a combination of contradictory contracts.

column5: Monetization may be used as a means for helping clients to dispose of their previous interest-based debts, after ensuring that they have developed genuine intention not to deal in usurious transactions any more.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis expressly allows this use, conditional on the client's genuine intention to abandon usurious dealings.

column5: In a service partnership, there is no Shari'ah implication regarding any disproportion in the services the partners or their representatives may have rendered.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/3/2, disproportion in services rendered has no Shari'ah implication; partners may divide services among themselves.

column5: Cash security charged for obtaining services such as telephone and electricity services, or security paid on renting shops and equipment:
column6: Zakah is paid by the owner of the amount on refund, for all the past years during which the amount was retained.
column7: Zakah should be paid by the owner of the amount on refund, and for one year, unless he has been enabled to invest the amount before refund.
column8: No Zakah is ever due on such amounts.
column9: Zakah is paid annually by the service provider that holds the amount, as part of its cash assets.
column11: Per 5/1/5/3, the owner pays Zakah on refund for one year, unless he was able to invest it before refund (then 5/1/5/2 applies).

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In principle, the transactions of a converting bank that were concluded before the decision to convert:
column6: May be continued until their maturity, since they were concluded before the decision to convert.
column7: Must be ceased or disposed of immediately, and delaying the clearing out of non-permissible transactions is not permissible unless it becomes a necessity or a pressing need.
column8: May be cleared out gradually over a period determined by the board of directors at its discretion.
column9: Must be ceased immediately, even if this leads to the failure or breakdown of the bank's operations, since the provisions of the standard admit no accommodation of the situation.
column11: Per 2/1, they must be ceased immediately; delay only for necessity or pressing need, to avoid the bank's failure.

column5: Applications of Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) in financial institutions include:
column6: The institution entering into Musaqat contracts with the owners of trees and then hiring workers (irrigators) to carry out the work.
column7: The institution owning trees and entering into Musaqat contracts with other parties to carry out the work.
column8: The institution guaranteeing the worker a minimum quantity of the crop.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 15/1-15/2, the institution may act as worker (hiring irrigators) or as owner of the trees.

column5: Regarding cancellation (Iqalah) of a Salam contract when both parties agree:
column6: Partial cancellation is not permissible; the cancellation must cover the entire al-Muslam Fihi.
column7: The entire Salam contract may be cancelled in return for repayment of more than the capital of Salam, as compensation to the buyer.
column8: The entire Salam contract may be cancelled in return for repayment in full of the amount of the capital of Salam.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/3, full Iqalah is against return of the full capital; partial Iqalah against a corresponding part of the capital is also allowed.

column5: The share certificate, or what stands in its place, may be issued in the name of the owner or to his order, but it is not permitted that it be issued for the bearer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/8, the share certificate may be in the name of the owner, to his order, or for the bearer.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: Options to revoke due to defect exist in:
column6: Gratuitous contracts only, such as gifts without consideration, unconditional endowments and loans, since they involve no counter-value.
column7: Sales only, excluding money exchange and the division of wealth.
column8: Commutative financial contracts, such as sale, money exchange, division of wealth, settlement of debt in kind and Hibat al-Thawab.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/3, the option exists in commutative contracts, including gift conditional upon consideration (Hibat al-Thawab).

column5: The Standard on Competitions and Prizes covers:
column6: The Shari'ah rulings relating to promotional gifts and their application or sponsorship by the Institutions.
column7: Job-related competitions and reverse auctions.
column8: Incentives offered to improve the performance of the Institutions' clients, employees and directors.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per item 1, promotional gifts are covered; job-related competitions, reverse auctions and performance incentives are excluded.

column5: When forgery or an error is committed with regard to the personality or characteristics of one of the two parties to an online contract:
column6: The Institution owning the website bears the responsibility in all cases, even if it is not aware of the forgery or error.
column7: The contract is void from inception, and neither party has any option, even if the error does not relate to a material characteristic of the party.
column8: The contract remains binding, and the other party is only entitled to compensation, however serious the forgery or error is.
column9: The other party has the right to terminate the contract, and the general rules of evidence apply for verifying the forgery or error.
column11: Per 8/2/3-4, the other party may terminate the contract; forgery or error is verified by the general rules of evidence.

column5: A stock company is characterized as a form of:
column6: Personal partnership.
column7: Financing partnership.
column8: Ownership partnership.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/1/1/1, the stock company is a form of financing partnership (joint-liability and limited-by-shares are personal).

column5: The worker (irrigator) becomes entitled to his share of the crop on an indivisible basis only after the crop is harvested and divided.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/2, the worker is entitled to his indivisible share as soon as the crop materializes.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: In a pledge (Rahn) of gold, it is not permissible for the pledgee to stipulate:
column6: Any entitlement to dispose of the pledged gold by way of sale, by using it as a pledge in another transaction or by leasing it, even if he undertakes to return it.
column7: The right to demand sale of the pledged gold if the debtor defaults at maturity, at the prevailing market value, and to return the remaining proceeds to the debtor.
column8: That he will bear the expenses of maintaining and safekeeping the pledged gold.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/1/4, a right to dispose of the pledged gold may not be stipulated; sale on default (7/1/3) and bearing expenses (7/1/6) are allowed.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: The option to revoke on grounds of verbal deception (Khiyar al-Taghrir) lapses if:
column6: The item is destroyed or consumed by the buyer before the deception is discovered, or an impediment prevents its return, or the buyer fails to return it despite being able.
column7: The seller offers to reduce the price to the market price, thereby removing the effect of the deception.
column8: The holder of the option dies, unless his heirs claim it within the period customarily acceptable for revocation.
column9: The buyer does not exercise it within three days of the conclusion of the contract, whether or not he has discovered the deception, in accordance with the cooling-off rule.
column11: Per 2/4/1, it lapses on destruction or consumption before discovery, an impediment to return, or failure to return when able.

column5: A cardholder bought a laptop from a foreign online store using his card issued by an IFI, then returned it due to a defect. The IFI incurred fees and exchange rate differences on the refund. It was established that the store knew about the defect and concealed it. The correct ruling is:
column6: The fees and differences are borne equally by the cardholder and the store.
column7: The IFI may demand the fees and differences from the cardholder, and the cardholder has no right to revert to the store, since the return was due to a defect.
column8: The IFI may demand from the cardholder the fees and exchange rate differences as per their agreement, and the cardholder may revert to the store for them.
column9: The IFI must bear the fees and differences itself, since the return was due to a defect in the goods.
column11: Per 5/7, the issuer may claim these costs from the cardholder, who may revert to the acceptor only if it knew of and concealed the defect.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing the Mudarib to make a loan, gift or charitable donation from the Mudarabah fund is that:
column6: The Mudarib is a guarantor of the Mudarabah funds, and a guarantor may not dispose of them gratuitously, even with the capital provider's consent.
column7: Such actions constitute Riba, because the Mudarib obtains a benefit in return for the funds.
column8: Such actions are prohibited in all contracts of agency, even where the principal has authorised them expressly.
column9: These actions bring no benefit to the Mudarabah operation and involve a potential loss to the capital provider.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, such acts bring no benefit to the Mudarabah and involve potential loss to the capital provider.

column5: ………… is the bank of the merchant:
column6: The acquirer.
column7: The card issuer.
column8: The card acceptor.
column9: The card network.
column11: Per 2/1/4, the acquirer is the bank of the merchant; the card acceptor is the merchant itself.

column5: It is permitted to stipulate a performance incentive clause for the institution as manager of an investment deposit, whereby both parties share in the profits and any excess profit beyond a specified limit accrues to the manager.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/6/3/3 (d), such an incentive clause is permitted, unlike a clause that ends profit-sharing.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: While studying a Fatwa request, the Board felt that the Institution may use the requested Fatwa for committing an impermissible action. In this case, the Board:
column6: Must issue the Fatwa as requested, since issuing Fatwa to the Institution is its duty.
column7: Must report the Institution to the regulatory authority before issuing any Fatwa.
column8: Must transfer the request to a higher Shari'ah board.
column9: May either refrain from issuing the Fatwa, or make it subject to certain restrictions.
column11: Per 7/6, if the Board fears misuse for an impermissible act, it may refrain from the Fatwa or subject it to restrictions.

column5: Al-Shatibi gave examples of acts that become prohibited when combined, though they are individually permissible. These examples include the following, excluding:
column6: Combining sale and lending, as in the Hadith prohibiting a loan and a sale together in one contract.
column7: Selling a house to a party and renting a car to the same party for separate values.
column8: Marrying a woman and her aunt.
column9: Marrying two sisters at the same time, although marrying either one of them alone is permissible.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Al-Shatibi cited sale with lending, two sisters, and a woman with her aunt; sale plus lease is a permissible form.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: A customer bought a car from an IFI under a cooling-off option, paid the price, used the car during the option period and then returned it just before the option period expired to receive his money back, as had been planned from the outset. This arrangement is:
column6: Not permissible, because cooling-off options do not apply to sale contracts.
column7: Not permissible, because it is a ruse to synthesise the effect of a benefit enjoyed by the lender in exchange for giving a loan.
column8: Permissible, provided that the customer pays rent at the market rate for the period of use.
column9: Permissible, because the owner of a cooling-off option may test and use the sold item during the option period.
column11: Per 2/8/4, using a cooling-off option this way is a ruse yielding a benefit for a loan, and is not permissible.

column5: Leasing with selling (i.e. hire-purchase in its traditional form) is:
column6: A permissible combination, as each of the two contracts is permissible on its own.
column7: An example of contradictory contracts which may not be combined.
column8: Permissible, as one of the Shari'ah concessions granted to subsidiary contracts.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/4, leasing with selling (traditional hire-purchase) is cited as a combination of contradictory contracts.

column5: If it is proved that the participant had committed fraud or deceit, or submitted false information about the risks to be insured:
column6: His indemnity becomes proportionate to the accurate information he presented.
column7: The contract is void, and his contributions are returned to him.
column8: He is subject to partial or full deprivation from indemnity.
column9: He is entitled to full indemnity, since his contribution is a donation.
column11: Per 8/1, fraud, deceit or false information leads to partial or full deprivation from indemnity.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Payment of interest by the converted bank is allowed on the basis of necessity where the bank cannot refrain from it because of lack of legal protection and the possibility of being subjected to punishment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, necessity (lack of legal protection, risk of punishment) permits paying interest when unavoidable.

column5: Buyback must not result in deferred currency exchange (ṣarf), such as where the contracting parties collude for one to sell an asset in gold and later buy it back on credit in silver.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/6, buyback must not lead to deferred ṣarf, as in selling for gold or currency and buying back on credit in silver or another currency.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring a time limit for cooling-off options is that:
