column6: The Hadith of Habban Bin Munqidh limits every cooling-off option to three days.
column7: It contravenes the Qabd stipulated in Sarf and Salam contracts.
column8: An untimed option results in Jahalah (obscurity) which may lead to dispute, as the majority of Fuqaha hold.
column9: Detaching the option from the contract contradicts the prerequisites of the contract, as the contract must be binding.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 2/2/2, an untimed option causes Jahalah that may lead to dispute (majority view).

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The conditions of an IFI's investment accounts state that 10% of the deposited amounts are retained for liquidity purposes. Without obtaining the consent of the accountholders, the IFI invested these funds in short-term, easy-to-liquidate investments to cater for withdrawal requests, and earned a return. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The investment is impermissible, because the funds were allocated for liquidity purposes and the accountholders did not consent.
column7: The investment is permissible, and the return belongs to the IFI alone, because the funds are retained for liquidity and the accountholders have no right in them.
column8: The investment is permissible without the accountholders' consent; the return is added to the investment base, shared by the accountholders as Arbab al-Mal and the IFI as Mudarib.
column9: The investment is permissible, and the return belongs to the accountholders alone, because the IFI did not have their consent and therefore acted merely as their agent without any entitlement to a share.
column11: Per 4/10/2, the bank may invest liquidity funds without consent; returns join the investment base and are shared as Mudarabah profit.

column5: Acceptance for paying the value of commercial paper on the part of the drawee is considered:
column6: A sale of the debt by the drawee to the holder, for a price equal to the amount of the paper.
column7: An agency of the drawee to collect the value from the drawer, who remains liable to the holder throughout, whatever the drawee's acceptance.
column8: A mere non-binding promise to pay, which the drawee may withdraw before the date of maturity without liability to the holder, as he is not a party to the debt represented by the paper.
column9: An undertaking and obligation to pay the debt represented by the commercial paper to the holder on the date of maturity, which must be fulfilled according to the Shari'ah.
column11: Per 8/1, the drawee's acceptance is an undertaking and obligation to pay the holder at maturity, to be fulfilled.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Shareholders of a bank that adopted a gradual or partial conversion are not required to accelerate the conversion, provided they follow this standard as a guideline.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2, shareholders are required to accelerate conversion to free themselves from the sin of impermissible activities.

column5: In the absence of an agreement between the client and the institution on the commission for collecting the amount of commercial papers, the practice prevalent among institutions is to be acted upon.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5, the agreed commission applies; absent agreement, the practice prevalent among institutions applies.

column5: An IFI entered into a Mudarabah with a customer as Mudarib to invest in assets denominated in foreign currencies. The contract contains a clause under which the Mudarib undertakes to indemnify the IFI against any loss resulting from exchange rate fluctuations. This clause is:
column6: Permissible, provided the guarantee is limited to currency risk and does not extend to the capital.
column7: Impermissible, because it is not permissible for one of the partners in Musharakah or Mudarabah to be a guarantor for the other partner to protect him from the risks of dealing in currencies.
column8: Impermissible only if the Mudarib receives a separate fee for the guarantee.
column9: Permissible, because the Mudarib is responsible for the investment decisions he takes and for any loss resulting from currency fluctuations, provided the guarantee is stated in the contract and agreed by the other partner.
column11: Per 2/9/3 (confirmed by the Ninth Al Baraka Seminar), a partner may not guarantee the other partner against currency risks.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for exempting trading in the shares of corporations whose primary activity is permissible but which deposit and borrow on the basis of interest is:
column6: That interest that does not exceed 30% is not considered Riba.
column7: The rule of removal of hardship, acknowledging general need and widespread practice, the principles of surplus, shortage and predominance, dealing with one the major part of whose wealth is permissible, and the separation of bargains according to some Jurists.
column8: That necessity permits all prohibited things, and the general need of the Muslim community for investing in listed corporations makes every income derived from such corporations lawful, whatever its source and however large its proportion, as the Shari'ah Supervisory Board may determine.
column9: That the shareholder is not responsible for the corporation's decisions in any case.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/4, the exemption rests on removal of hardship, general need, predominance and related principles.

column5: It is permissible for the partners to appoint a manager other than one of the partners:
column6: And pay him a fixed remuneration that will be included in the expenses of the Sharikah.
column7: And set aside for him a portion of the investment profit plus a fixed remuneration as a form of incentive.
column8: For a percentage share in the profit from the outset, in which case he is classified as a Mudarib and is only entitled to a share in the profit, if any.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/3/3, all three are permissible; if hired from the outset for a profit share, the manager is a Mudarib.

column5: The Mudarib may hire, against the account of the Mudarabah funds, another party at the prevailing rate to execute work that is not by custom the responsibility of the Mudarib.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/4, work outside the Mudarib's customary duties may be hired out at the prevailing rate at the Mudarabah's cost.

column5: Trading in Istisna'a certificates is subject to the rules of disposal of debts:
column6: If the realised funds are immediately paid as a price in a parallel Istisna'a contract.
column7: If the manufactured item is submitted to the ultimate purchaser.
column8: If the funds have been converted, within the period of the Istisna'a, into assets owned by certificate holders.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/2/13, conversion into assets allows trading; payment of funds as a parallel Istisna'a price or delivery to the purchaser makes debt rules apply.

column5: In syndicated financing arranged on the basis of paid agency, the agent:
column6: Becomes entitled to remuneration whether or not profit materializes, and may be given a bonus as a lump sum or a share of profits above a certain limit.
column7: Becomes entitled to a share of the profit as a Mudarib, and bears no part of the loss.
column8: Becomes entitled to remuneration only if profit is actually materialized, and the remuneration may not exceed the profit realised, failing which he must refund the excess to the participants.
column9: May not be given any bonus in addition to the agreed remuneration.
column11: Per 6/3, the paid agent's fee is due whether or not profit materializes, and a lump-sum or above-limit profit bonus is allowed.

column5: Regarding investment in the shares of subsidiaries, when the subsidiary does not pay its Zakah directly:
column6: No Zakah is due on the subsidiary unless the mother company owns all of its shares.
column7: The Zakah of the subsidiary is calculated independently, then the mother company pays its share in proportion to its shareholding, and the remaining part is paid by the other parties (minority rights).
column8: The mother company pays the whole Zakah of the subsidiary, including the share attributable to the minority rights, which it recovers from them at the end of the year.
column9: The mother company pays Zakah on the market value of its shares in the subsidiary, as articles of trade, and the subsidiary itself pays no Zakah on its assets, even if it holds zakatable cash or other zakatable assets.
column11: Per 4/2/5, the subsidiary's Zakah is calculated independently; the mother pays its proportional share, and minority holders pay the rest.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: ………… refers to the termination of a valid and binding contract by virtue of a stipulation in the contract giving one of the parties the option to revoke the contract:
column6: Iqalah (mutual rescission).
column7: Nullification owing to the absence of a condition required by the Shari'ah.
column8: Revocation by exercise of a cooling-off option.
column9: Expiry of the contract at the end of its contractual term.
column11: Per item 2, this is the definition of revocation by exercise of a cooling-off option; expiry and nullification are outside the Standard's scope.

column5: The ruling that the company, which assumes the role of the agent in Islamic reinsurance, should not guarantee is based on:
column6: The Fiqh axiom that Gharar does not affect donation-based contracts.
column7: The general rules of evidence, which state that evidence is to be provided by the alleger and that the denier is to take an oath, so the agent bears the burden.
column8: The unanimous agreement of Fiqh scholars that an agent does not guarantee except in case of transgression, negligence or breach of contract.
column9: The fact that the company owns the contributions and therefore bears their risk.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, scholars agree unanimously that an agent does not guarantee except for transgression, negligence or breach.

column5: The shares of a corporation whose objective and usual activity is dealing in gold, silver or currencies (Sirafah) are listed on the stock exchange. Trading in its shares:
column6: Must be undertaken in the light of the rules of Sarf.
column7: Is permissible at market value with deferred settlement.
column8: Is permissible without regard to the rules of Sarf, if its tangible assets are not less than 30% of its total assets.
column9: Is absolutely impermissible.
column11: Per 3/19, where the corporation's objective and usual activity is Sirafah, trading in its shares must follow the rules of Sarf.

column5: Zakah is obligatory on:
column6: Gold, silver, currencies, trade articles, livestock (camels, cows and goats), agricultural produce, minerals and Rikaz (treasures).
column7: Public wealth (public sector) and the insurance funds of public institutions, since such wealth is owned by the State and its institutions on behalf of the people.
column8: The charitable Waqf (al-Waqf al-Khayri), since its income is generated from assets in which the beneficiaries are the owners.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/2, (a) lists the zakatable funds. Per 3/1/5 and 3/1/6, public wealth, public insurance funds and charitable Waqf are exempt.

column5: Adding a determined percentage to the value of the share at the time of subscription to cover the expenses of issuance is:
column6: Permissible only if the shares are issued at a discount.
column7: Permissible as long as this percentage is fixed and determined to be a reasonable amount.
column8: Permissible at any percentage determined by the board of directors.
column9: Impermissible, because it is an excess over the nominal value of the share.
column11: Per 2/2, a fixed, reasonable percentage may be added to the share value at subscription to cover issuance expenses.

column5: The bases for the permissibility of stipulating repayment of Qard in a land (place) other than that where the Qard was granted include:
column6: Reports from the Companions indicating its permissibility, a view upheld by the Malikis and the Hanbalis and preferred by Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Al-Qayyim.
column7: That it is in the interest of both the lender and the borrower without causing injury to either, along with the existence of a need.
column8: That the basic rule in transactions (Mu'amalat) is permissibility, and such a stipulation is not expressly prohibited by the texts.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/2, all three grounds are cited: Companions' reports, mutual non-injurious benefit, and original permissibility.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Regarding appointing a sub-agent:
column6: The agent has no right to appoint a sub-agent except with the permission of the principal; once a sub-agent is appointed, his termination does not spontaneously follow that of the first agent, but the principal can terminate him.
column7: The agent may appoint a sub-agent without the permission of the principal, and the sub-agent is terminated spontaneously upon the termination of the first agent.
column8: The agent may appoint a sub-agent in general agency without the permission of the principal, and only the agent can terminate him.
column9: The agent has no right to appoint a sub-agent except with the permission of the principal, and the sub-agent is terminated spontaneously upon the termination of the first agent, even if the principal wishes to retain him, and the principal cannot terminate him.
column11: Per 6/4, a sub-agent needs the principal's permission; he is not automatically terminated with the first agent, but the principal can end him.

column5: With regard to allocating an annual amount out of the Waqf revenues for maintenance and repair:
column6: It is permitted only if the Waqif stipulates it in the Waqf deed; the amount is invested in easily liquidated modes, its revenues are distributed to the Waqf beneficiaries, and the surplus is added to the Waqf asset.
column7: It is permitted, and the surplus is added to the Waqf asset, with the investment revenues of the amount being disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries each year.
column8: It is permitted even if the Waqif does not stipulate it; the amount is invested in easily liquidated modes, its revenues are added to it, and the surplus is returned to the Waqf beneficiaries.
column9: It is permitted, but the allocated amount may not be invested, and the surplus is returned to the Waqf beneficiaries at the end of the year.
column11: Per 4/2, the allocation is permitted without stipulation, invested in liquid modes, with the surplus returned to the beneficiaries.

column5: In an Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) contract, the owner may require the worker (irrigator), in addition to the husbandry of the crop and trees, to guard the owner's adjacent warehouse.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2, work is restricted to husbandry of the crop and trees; the owner may not demand any additional work.

column5: A Salam contract between an IFI (buyer) and a supplier contains a clause obliging the supplier to pay the IFI 1% of the Salam capital for each week of delay in delivering al-Muslam Fihi. This clause is:
column6: Permitted, provided the total penalty does not exceed the IFI's actual damage and is paid to the IFI itself.
column7: Not permitted, because a penalty clause in respect of delay in delivery of al-Muslam Fihi may not be stipulated.
column8: Permitted only if the supplier is solvent and the delay is not caused by force majeure.
column9: Permitted, since the supplier agreed to it in the contract and the penalty is a fixed percentage of the capital for each week of delay.
column11: Per 5/7, no penalty clause for late delivery may be stipulated, since al-Muslam Fihi is a debt and no excess may be charged.

column5: In Zakah on agricultural produce, the following is deducted from zakatable assets:
column6: Production requirements such as fertilizers and insecticides, in all cases.
column7: Expenses relating to irrigation, land development, irrigation channels and soil works.
column8: Cost of delivery to recipients.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/4/8, delivery cost is deducted. Irrigation and land costs are not (5/4/7); fertilizers are deducted only if obtained through debt (5/4/5).

column5: The expenses of the Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat), including any Takaful insurance:
column6: Are borne by the worker and the owner in proportion to their shares, unless they agree otherwise.
column7: Are borne by the worker alone, as part of his customary work.
column8: Are borne by the owner of the trees alone, since he benefits from the trees.
column9: Are borne equally by the worker and the owner, irrespective of their shares.
column11: Per 8/2, expenses including Takaful are borne in proportion to their shares, unless agreed otherwise.

column5: The Mudarib is entitled to a share of profit as soon as it is clear that the operations of the Mudarabah have led to the realisation of a profit. This entitlement:
column6: Is not absolute, as it is subject to retention of interim profits for the protection of the capital, and becomes absolute only after distribution through actual or constructive valuation.
column7: Is absolute from the moment the profit is realised, and cannot be affected by subsequent losses, even if the capital is thereby impaired and the Mudarib has received his share of the profit in cash.
column8: Is absolute only if the capital provider has expressly approved the interim accounts, in which case later losses may not be set against it.
column9: Arises only on liquidation, so that no profit may be distributed on account before then, even if the capital provider agrees to it.
column11: Per 8/8, the entitlement is not absolute until distribution by actual or constructive valuation, as interim profits protect capital.

column5: If the Waqf beneficiary body, whether one or more, is discontinued, the avenue of Waqf disposal will be:
column6: Bodies of similar nature, even if the Waqif has arranged a sequence of the beneficiary bodies, and general charitable causes are never resorted to even if no similar body exists.
column7: General charitable causes in all cases, regardless of any sequence arranged by the Waqif or the existence of bodies of similar nature.
column8: The heirs of the Waqif, and if there are none, general charitable causes, since the Waqf ends with the discontinuance of the beneficiary.
column9: The body which comes next, if the Waqif has arranged the sequence of the bodies; otherwise, bodies of similar nature; and if there are none, general charitable causes.
column11: Per 10/2: the next body in the Waqif's sequence; otherwise similar bodies; failing those, general charitable causes.

column5: The basis for recourse to reasonable compensation upon the vitiation of the named compensation in Ju'alah is analogy with Mudarabah, where the Mudarib receives remuneration for similar services.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the analogy is with Ijarah, where reasonable wages apply when the named wages are vitiated.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Trading a promise (Wa'd) to sell gold through sale or purchase is impermissible, because a promise cannot be used as the subject matter of a commutative contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/4 and its Shari'ah basis, promises cannot be traded since they cannot be the subject of a commutative contract.

column5: Zakah on Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit), which the client pays to confirm his binding pledge:
column6: Shall be shared equally between the client and the Institution.
column7: Shall be paid by the Institution which receives it.
column8: Shall be paid by the client.
column9: Is not due, since the amount is retained by the Institution.
column11: Per 5/1/5/1, Zakah on Hamish Jiddiyyah shall be paid by the client.

column5: According to the Fatwa of Aayan Company cited in the Shari'ah basis, the contracts for preparing the credit study should be completely separate from the financing contracts, and the client may use the study in his deals with Aayan Company or with any other party.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The cited Fatwa requires separate study contracts; the study becomes the client's property once he pays, usable with Aayan or any other party.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of concluding options contracts for shares is that:
column6: Options involve only the sale of a debt for a debt.
column7: The share at the time of exercise represents something different from what it represented at the time of the contract.
column8: Options always involve Riba in both its forms, since the premium is paid in advance and the exercise price is settled later, while the option holder also receives a benefit from the loan of the premium.
column9: The right of option is not among the rights that can be sold, as it is related not to wealth but to an abstract thing; dealing in options is also based on Gharar and gambling.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/13, the option right is not a saleable right related to wealth, and options involve Gharar and gambling.

column5: Among the duties of the overseer:
column6: To lease the Waqf assets to himself at the fair rent, to ensure the continuity of the Waqf revenue, provided that the Waqf beneficiaries are informed and the relevant authority is notified of the lease.
column7: To combine the accounts of the Waqf with his own accounts, to reduce the administrative expenses, provided that he keeps a record of the Waqf's share in each transaction.
column8: To secure Shari'ah compliant insurance for the Waqf asset if its nature requires so, and to establish a special purpose vehicle to protect the Waqf from risks of investing its funds.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/6/3 insurance and an SPV are duties; Waqf accounts must be separate (3/6/7); leasing to himself is barred favouritism (3/8/3).

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If a conventional bank is acquired with the intention to convert it to an Islamic bank:
column6: The new owners must dispose of the interest earned before the acquisition and recover it from the previous owners.
column7: The new and previous owners share the disposal of interest in proportion to their periods of ownership.
column8: The new owners must dispose of all interest earned since the establishment of the bank.
column9: The new owners are not obliged to dispose of interest and impermissible earnings that have been earned before such acquisition.
column11: Per 8/1/1, new owners acquiring a bank to convert it need not dispose of earnings made before the acquisition.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the obligation of specifying the wages of the agent, and not merging them with the price, is:
column6: The Hadith: "He who hires a hired worker must make known to him his wages", a rule of Ijarah applicable to agency for wages.
column7: The verse: "... Where Allah has permitted trading ..."
column8: A resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on derivatives.
column9: The saying: "Muslims shall abide by their conditions, except for a condition that legalises the prohibited or prohibits the lawful."
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/2/9, the Hadith on making wages known to a hired worker applies to agency for wages.

column5: Elimination of prohibited income is obligatory on the intermediary, agent or manager out of part of their commission or wages.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4/6/3, it is not obligatory on them, because the commission or wages are their right in lieu of their work.

column5: In syndicated financing arranged on the basis of non-paid agency, the lead manager undertakes to manage the operations for no reward, and the financing Institutions share the profit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/4, in non-paid agency the lead manager manages for no reward and the financing Institutions share the profit.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: In the debit card, the customer will not normally pay any charges for using the card, except when:
column6: The payments made exceed the credit balance available on his account.
column7: It is used to withdraw cash or to purchase another currency through an Institution other than the issuing Institution.
column8: It is used to withdraw cash from the Institution that has issued the card, in which case a fee is payable on every withdrawal.
column9: It is used to pay for goods or services purchased from parties accepting the card, in which case the cardholder pays a commission calculated on the price.
column11: Per 2/1/3, charges arise normally only for cash withdrawal or currency purchase through an Institution other than the issuer.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: A current account in which gold of specific weight and karatage is deposited (gold denominated account) is subject to the rulings for investment accounts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/8, a gold denominated current account is subject to the rulings for current accounts.

column5: It is permitted to substitute Waqf assets, observing the conditions of substitution:
column6: If the Waqf beneficiaries request it, even if the Waqif did not stipulate it and there is no evident benefit for the Waqf.
column7: If the utilities of the Waqf assets are suspended or it is impossible to enjoy the usufruct, by substituting them with a better asset of the same kind.
column8: If a buyer offers the market price of the Waqf asset, even if there is no evident benefit for the Waqf.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/1/2/2, suspended utilities allow substitution with a better asset of the same kind; substitution must serve the Waqf's interest (10/1/5/1).

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, the permissible Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek differs from hire-purchase as commonly practised by conventional banks in that:
column6: In hire-purchase, the lessor bears the risk of the asset, whereas in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek the lessee bears it throughout the term and alone is responsible for major maintenance and insurance of the asset, which is the only distinguishing feature.
column7: In hire-purchase, sale and lease provisions apply together and ownership passes on the last instalment without a separate contract, whereas in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek the provisions of Ijarah apply until the end of the term, after which title is obtained as the Standard explains.
column8: In Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, ownership passes automatically on payment of the last instalment without a separate contract, since the lease and the sale are concluded together in one contract, whereas in hire-purchase a separate document is required and the lessor's promise to sell is not binding.
column9: There is no difference between them other than in name.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, hire-purchase applies sale and lease rules together; IMB applies Ijarah rules until term-end, then title passes.

column5: It is not permissible for al-Muslam Fihi to be an amount of currency, gold or silver:
column6: Unless the quantity of al-Muslam Fihi equals the capital of Salam.
column7: In any case, whatever the form of the capital of Salam.
column8: If the capital of the Salam contract was paid in the form of currency, gold or silver.
column9: If the capital of the Salam contract was paid in the form of fungible goods.
column11: Per 3/2/4, currency, gold or silver may not be al-Muslam Fihi when the Salam capital was paid in currency, gold or silver.

column5: An Islamic bank and a bank in another country agreed to resolve a dispute between them through arbitration, and the arbitrator was obliged to apply the law of that country, one of whose provisions entitles the creditor to interest on delayed payment. The correct position according to the Standard is:
column6: The arbitrator should apply the rulings of Shari'ah; even though he is obliged to apply a certain law, he should still not violate the rulings of Shari'ah.
column7: Arbitration is impermissible, since the dispute is with a party outside the host country of the Institution.
column8: The arbitrator must apply the chosen law in full, since the parties have the right to impose any limitation on the arbitration.
column9: The arbitrator may award the interest, provided that the verdict is executed through courts that do not observe Shari'ah.
column11: Per 9/4, the arbitrator applies Shari'ah and, even if bound to a certain law, may not violate it; limitations must be permissible (9/5).

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Appointing another person as an agent for the purchase of a commodity at a spot price, and the sale of the commodity by the agent to a third person for a deferred price on behalf of the principal, with the agent's compensation determined as an amount or a percentage of the purchase price, is:
column6: 'Inah (buy-back) sale.
column7: Murabahah to the purchase orderer.
column8: Investment Agency operations.
column9: Mudarabah operations.
column11: Per 4/1/1, these are the operations of the Investment Agency; profit-sharing management would be Mudarabah (4/1/2).

column5: A Mudarabah contract may not be concluded in the absence of two contracting parties with absolute legal capacity, or of their agents who enjoy legal capacity similar to that of the contracting parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2, both parties (or their agents) must have full legal capacity to appoint agents and accept agency.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Either-or options entitle:
column6: The buyer to choose to purchase one or more of several items specified in the contract during a stipulated period.
column7: The seller to choose which of several items he will deliver to the buyer, at any time before the price is paid, in return for a higher price.
column8: Either party to revoke the contract within a stipulated period of time.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/1, either-or options let the buyer choose one or more of several specified items within a stipulated period.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: It is permissible for Institutions to issue debit cards, as long as:
column6: The cardholder does not exceed the balance available on his account and no interest charge arises out of the transaction.
column7: The Institution does not charge any commission to the party accepting payment by means of the card.
column8: The Institution does not charge any fee for issuing the card.
column9: The cardholder deposits a guarantee amount that is invested for his benefit on the basis of Mudarabah.
column11: Per 3/1, debit cards are permissible if the balance is not exceeded and no interest arises; issuance fees are allowed (2/1/4).

column5: The policyholders fund is entitled to:
column6: The contributions only, whereas the returns on investing them belong to the managing company.
column7: The contributions and the agency fee.
column8: The contributions and the returns thereon, whereas the insurance surplus is shared between the fund and the managing company.
column9: The contributions and the returns thereon, the provisions and reserves relating to insurance business, and the insurance surplus.
column11: Per 3/2, the fund owns contributions and returns, insurance provisions and reserves, and the surplus.

column5: An asset owned by the Waqf through substitution or sale of some of the Waqf assets shall have the rulings of Waqf revenue.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/5/1, a substituting asset takes the rulings of the substituted assets; revenue rulings apply to what results from revenue (9/5/2).

column5: With regard to the relationship between the transferee and the payer:
column6: The payer may refuse payment to the transferee if the transferee owes him a debt, or if the payer disputes the debt owed to the transferor, since the payer is not a party to the original debt and may be asked for payment only after the transferor defaults.
column7: The transferee may claim payment only from the transferor.
column8: The payer takes the place of the transferor in respect of all rights, legal protections and obligations, and the transferee in restricted Hawalah takes the place of the transferor in respect of them against the payer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 9/1 and 9/2, the payer must pay and has no right to refuse; each party steps into the transferor's position.

column5: The right of claw-back of an item sold to the debtor prior to the declaration of insolvency is established for:
column6: The seller who sold an item to the debtor after the declaration of insolvency.
column7: The seller who has not received any part of the selling price.
column8: Any creditor whose debt was incurred before the declaration of insolvency.
column9: The seller who has received less than half of the selling price.
column11: Per item 6, the right of claw-back is established for the seller who has not received any part of the selling price.

column5: When a monetary debt is discharged in another currency, the discharge must be at the exchange rate prevailing on the day of settlement if:
column6: The parties stipulated the conversion at the origination of the debt.
column7: The debt arose from a Murabaha contract, whether or not the debtor delayed, since a sale debt is always settled at the day rate.
column8: The debt was the result of a loan contract, or the debtor delayed settling the debt when it matured.
column9: The debtor is insolvent or has been declared bankrupt by a court.
column11: Per 4/1/1/2 (c), the settlement-day rate is required where the debt arose from a loan or the debtor delayed after maturity.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: With regard to the ratios for distribution of profits in investment accounts, the institution can:
column6: Specify different ratios for distribution of profits between itself and different categories of holders of investment accounts.
column7: Specify a unified ratio for distribution of profits between itself and all holders of investment accounts.
column8: Make the ratios for distribution of profits among the holders of the investment accounts unified, or varying on the basis of certain weights.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/3, the institution may use different or unified ratios with account categories, and unified or weighted ratios among holders.

column5: To enable an investment manager to offer capital protection to investors, its parent group set up a new company specifically for the purpose of giving Rab Al Maal a commitment to make up any loss in the capital. The new company holds no shares in the investment manager, and the commitment is voluntary and without recourse to the investment manager. This commitment is:
column6: Permissible, since the undertaking is voluntary, without recourse to the investment manager, and given directly to Rab Al Maal for reparation of loss in the capital.
column7: Not permitted, since setting up a company or a legal entity specifically for this purpose is an artifice (ḥīla) to the independence requirement.
column8: Permissible, since the new company holds no shares in the investment manager and therefore satisfies the independence condition in all cases, whatever the purpose of its setting up.
column9: Permissible, provided that it is approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column11: Per 4/1/1, setting up a company or legal entity specifically to give such a commitment is a prohibited artifice (ḥīla).

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: The basis for the permissibility of using different profit rates in Mudarabah transactions is that such a provision does not disrupt the sharing of profits by all parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 7/1, different rates are allowed because all parties still share in the profit.

column5: If a Murabahah sale takes place and it is later discovered that the supplier was owned by way of majority by the customer, the transaction remains valid, but the Institution must give its profit to charity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2/3, such a transaction is void, as it is tantamount to 'Inah.

column5: Each of the following is permissible in a Sharikah, excluding:
column6: Not distributing the profits of the company, based on the articles of association or a decision of the partners.
column7: Stipulating that the share of profit of one partner be a specific percentage of his capital.
column8: Setting aside periodically a certain ratio of profit as a profit equalisation reserve or an investment risk reserve.
column9: Agreeing on setting aside a proportion of profit for non-partners as a charitable donation.
column11: Per 3/1/5/13-14 the first three are permissible; a percentage of capital as profit is prohibited (3/1/5/1, 3/1/5/7).

column5: Participation of non-Muslims in Islamic insurance is:
column6: Permissible, provided that their contributions do not exceed half of the total contributions.
column7: Permissible; non-Muslims may participate with Muslims in the various types of Islamic insurance.
column8: Permissible in property insurance only.
column9: Not permissible, because Islamic insurance is based on donation among Muslims.
column11: Per 7/1, non-Muslims may participate with Muslims in the various types of Islamic insurance.

column5: It is permissible to issue preference shares that give their holders a priority at the date of distribution of profit, provided that such shares carry no voting rights.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/2/14, shares with financial priority in profit or liquidation are not permitted; only procedural privileges are.

column5: Where the Institution purchases the item from the supplier on a "sale or return" basis, the option between the Institution and the supplier:
column6: Expires by the mere presentation of the item to the customer.
column7: Expires by the mere offer by the Institution of the item for sale to a third party, even if no sale takes place within the specified period.
column8: Does not expire by the mere presentation of the item to the customer, but expires by the actual sale to the customer.
column9: Expires once the customer has signed the promise to purchase.
column11: Per 2/3/5, the option survives presentation of the item to the customer and expires only by the actual sale to him.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Loan (Qard) does not cover:
column6: Overdrafts between the institution and its correspondents.
column7: Current accounts.
column8: Charges on credit cards for cash withdrawals from ATMs.
column9: The price in a credit sale and investment accounts.
column11: Per 1, the price in a credit sale and investment accounts are not Qard and have their own standards; the other items are covered in 10.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Under the scoring method, the holders of the accounts are considered to have implicitly exchanged mutual relief from commitment (Mubara`ah) for any aspects that practically cannot be catered for.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1, accountholders are deemed to have implicitly exchanged Mubara`ah for aspects the scoring method cannot practically capture.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: A gold importer deposited an amount of money with the exporter, on the condition that once a specific shipment was ready, a sale contract would be concluded and the price deducted from the deposit on the contract date. The exporter had used the deposited amount in its business. The gold must be sold:
column6: It may not be sold, since the deposit has become a loan.
column7: At the market price prevailing on the date of the contract.
column8: At any price mutually agreed by the parties on the date of the contract.
column9: At the market price prevailing on the date of the deposit.
column11: Per 10/5, if the exporter has used the deposit, the gold must be sold at the market price prevailing on the contract date.

column5: In the case of a Murabahah sale, if the asset sold is still available in the condition in which it was sold, and the buyer has defaulted in the settlement of the price and has later become bankrupt:
column6: The seller may repossess the asset and also claim compensation for the period of delay, provided the compensation is not pre-determined.
column7: The seller shares in the proceeds of the asset pro rata with the other creditors of the buyer.
column8: The seller may repossess the asset only after obtaining a bankruptcy order and after the buyer's other creditors have been settled.
column9: The seller (the Institution) is entitled to repossess the asset instead of initiating procedures to obtain a bankruptcy order.
column11: Per 2/1/7 and the Hadith of Abu Hurayrah, the seller may repossess the asset rather than seek a bankruptcy order.

column5: An Islamic insurance company covering large industrial plants agreed with an Islamic reinsurance company that, for each accident, the insurance company bears the first 20 thousand dollars of compensation, while the reinsurance company bears the rest. This form of reinsurance is:
column6: Loss reinsurance.
column7: Risk sharing reinsurance.
column8: Selective reinsurance.
column9: Excess risk reinsurance (beyond risk tolerance).
column11: Per 5/3, in loss reinsurance the reinsurer bears losses beyond an agreed limit, e.g. after the insurer's first 20 thousand dollars.

column5: It is not permitted to purchase a commodity on credit and then offer it in an auction for cash sale if the first seller is among the bidders.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/3, this is permitted even if the first seller is among the bidders.

column5: According to the Hanafi scholars, if a valid condition such as the mortgage condition stipulated in a sale contract is not honored, the concerned party has the right of option.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hanafis list failure to honor a valid condition like mortgage as a case giving the right of option.

column5: When a due pay is delayed by the employer in spite of notification:
column6: The hiring contract becomes null and void.
column7: The employee must continue working and may only resort to the judiciary for collecting the pay.
column8: The employee has the right to stop work or prevent the employer from utilizing the service that has already been done.
column9: The employee may claim an increment on the delayed pay as compensation.
column11: Per 7/2/1(a), the employee may stop work or prevent the employer from using the service already done when due pay is delayed despite notification.

column5: Waqf may be concluded with an undertaking (promise) by the Waqif to create Waqf, as the form of Waqf creation need not be conclusive.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/1/2, the form must be conclusive (jāzima); Waqf cannot be concluded with an undertaking to create Waqf.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar is excessive when:
column6: It becomes a dominating and distinctive aspect of the contract, and is capable of leading to dispute.
column7: It is the degree of Gharar that a contract could hardly avoid, and is not sufficient to generate dispute.
column8: It relates to the form of the contract only, rather than to its subject matter.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/1, excessive Gharar dominates and distinguishes the contract and can lead to dispute; option (b) describes minor Gharar (4/2/2).

column5: ………… is a contract whereby an institution assigns its trade receivables, invoiced in whole or in specific types, frequently to a party that takes the place of the creditor-institution and stands obliged to pay their amounts immediately or upon maturity, whether or not recovered, in return for a pre-agreed monetary amount:
column6: Ḥawāla (novation).
column7: Discounting of commercial papers.
column8: Securitization of receivables.
column9: Factoring.
column11: Per 9/6/1, this is the definition of factoring.

column5: It is permissible to sell shares in a company subject to the rules and regulations of the company that do not conflict with Shari'ah, such as pre-emptive rights of the existing shareholders to purchase the shares.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1/2/10, sale of shares may be subject to company rules such as pre-emptive rights of existing shareholders.

column5: The basis of the ruling that the reinsurance company may assume the responsibility of managing the reinsurance account against a fee or free of charge is:
column6: The Mudarabah contract, which entails prior specification of profit sharing ratios and does not allow a fixed fee for the manager.
column7: The nature of the Wakalah contract, which Fiqh scholars unanimously declare permissible with or without remuneration.
column8: The practice of Munahadah reported by Al-Bukhari.
column9: The Ju'alah contract, in which remuneration is due only on completion of the work.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, managing the account with or without a fee rests on Wakalah, unanimously allowed with or without remuneration.

column5: With respect to current accounts, it is not permitted for the institution to:
column6: Demand wages for services rendered to the holders of the current accounts, such as the issue of drafts or collection of cheques, even where the wages are limited to the actual cost of the service.
column7: Provide chequebooks and ATM cards to the owners of current accounts without compensation.
column8: Exempt the owners of current accounts, in lieu of such accounts, from credit card charges, deposit box charges, transfer charges and charges for letters of guarantee and credit.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/2, such exemptions are prohibited perquisites; charging wages (10/1/2) and free chequebooks/ATM cards (10/1/3) are allowed.

column5: Local goods are more suitable for Monetization due to the easiness of ensuring their existence, and the chance available to the client to actually hold them if he so desires.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/3 and its Shari'ah basis, local commodities are more preferable for these two reasons.

column5: Among the forms of constructive possession approved by both Shari'ah and business customary practices is crediting a sum of money to the account of the customer:
column6: When the Institution deposits to the credit of a customer's account a sum of money directly or through a bank transfer.
column7: When the customer enters into a spot contract of currency exchange between himself and the Institution, in the case of the purchase of a currency against another currency already deposited in the account of the customer.
column8: When the Institution debits, by the order of the customer, a sum of money to the latter's account and credits it to another account in a different currency, in the same Institution or another Institution, for the benefit of the customer or any other payee.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/6/5(a), all three situations are forms of constructive possession by crediting the customer's account.

column5: A person who finds a specific item of his property in the insolvency assets:
column6: Has a preferred claim over it; such property may include safety deposits, portfolios, investment funds and Mudarabah or agency capital.
column7: Shares it pro-rata with the other creditors according to his share of the total debt, since the property forms part of the insolvency assets.
column8: Has a claim over it only if he has not received any part of its price.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/3/4, the owner who finds his specific property has a preferred claim over it, e.g., deposits, funds, Mudarabah capital.

column5: In an Ijarah of an existing leased property, the lessor bears:
column6: The consequences of any damage to the leased property, even if caused by the misconduct or negligence of the lessee.
column7: The consequences of any damage to the leased property not caused by the misconduct or negligence of the lessee, the related insurance expenses, and the cost of major maintenance needed to keep the property in the necessary condition.
column8: Only the expense of major maintenance, while the risk of damage is borne by the lessee who holds the property.
column9: The consequences of damage not caused by the lessee's misconduct or negligence, while the insurance expenses and major maintenance are borne by the lessee, who holds the property on a trust basis and must keep it in the condition necessary to provide the contractual benefits.
column11: Per 2/3, the lessor bears non-negligent damage, related insurance and major maintenance.

column5: Letters for renewal or extension of the period of already approved facilities carry the same conditions as letters of granting facilities.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4, letters for renewal or extension of approved facilities carry the same conditions as letters granting facilities.

column5: Having taken Hamish Jiddiyyah, the Institution need not demand compensation for damage from the customer who breaches his binding promise, as this may be charged against the Hamish Jiddiyyah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/5/3, the damage may be charged against the Hamish Jiddiyyah.

column5: It is impermissible to mortgage the following financial papers, excluding:
column6: Interest-based bonds issued by governments or companies.
column7: Shares of traditional insurance companies, whose activity is based on commercial insurance.
column8: Usufruct-based Sukuk which represent common shares in usufructs of specific assets.
column9: Certificates of traditional investment deposits issued by conventional banks.
column11: Per 4/2-3, usufruct-based Sukuk may be mortgaged, whereas interest-based bonds, traditional deposit certificates and conventional insurer shares may not.

column5: Hawalah is:
column6: A legitimate and independent contract made out of courtesy, not a contract of sale, permitted to facilitate payments and recovery.
column7: A contract of sale of debt for debt, permitted by way of exception.
column8: A form of agency contract for the collection of debts.
column9: A form of guarantee in which the transferor remains jointly liable with the payer, so that the transferee may claim from either of them.
column11: Per 3/1, Hawalah is an independent courtesy contract, not a sale, permitted to facilitate payment and recovery.

column5: If the customer wishes to pay the Murabahah debt in a currency different from the Murabahah currency:
column6: It is permissible, provided this currency exchange is stipulated in the contract of Murabahah.
column7: It is not permissible, because the debt must be paid in the currency of the Murabahah.
column8: It is permissible with the agreement of the Institution at the time of payment, on condition that the debt, or the amount agreed to be paid in the other currency, is paid in full and no part of the exchange amount remains due.
column9: It is permissible, and part of the exchanged amount may remain as a debt to be paid with the next instalment, provided the exchange is made at the spot rate prevailing on the day of payment and the customer undertakes in writing to settle it.
column11: Per 5/10, payment in another currency is allowed if agreed at payment time and settled in full; it may not be stipulated in the contract.

column5: A customer offered to enter into a Sharikah with an IFI, presenting as his entire share of the capital the receivables owed to him by the IFI itself and by other parties. The ruling on this contribution is:
column6: It is permitted only for the receivables owed by the IFI itself, since they are presumed to be in possession, but not for those owed by other parties, which are not in possession and may never be collected.
column7: It is permitted, provided the receivables are recorded at their face value and the partner guarantees their collection from the debtors.
column8: It is not permitted, because debts (receivables) alone may not be used as capital contribution; they are not assets in possession and may lead to Riba when the partner is the debtor.
column9: It is permitted, because receivables are assets that can be valued at fair value like commodities, after deducting an allowance for doubtful debts.
column11: Per 3/1/2/4 and its basis, receivables alone cannot be a capital contribution: they are not in possession and may lead to Riba.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Pursuing Shari'ah exemptions is prohibited because it leads to relaxation of the rules of Shari'ah, and some Fuqaha hold that it amounts to Fisq (rebellion against Allah's obedience).
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, pursuing exemptions relaxes the rules of Shari'ah, and some Fuqaha deem it Fisq.

column5: The concessions to be granted to implicit and subsidiary contracts should be judged:
column6: In the light of the rulings applicable to independent contracts only.
column7: In the light of traditions, practice and professional experience, and subjected to clearance by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Institution.
column8: By the parties to the contract through mutual consent, without any need for clearance, provided that the concession is limited to the subsidiary contract and does not affect the main contract.
column9: By the management of the Institution, according to its own interest.
column11: Per 5/1, concessions are judged by tradition, practice and experience, and cleared by the Institution's Shari'ah Supervisory Board.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: It is impermissible to sell a commodity on the basis of mere description; the buyer must view the commodity before the contract is concluded.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/8/1, a commodity can be sold on mere description, by the seller or another, covering all characteristics that could affect the price.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The effect of specification of a time limit for agency is:
column6: To make the agency binding on both parties throughout that period.
column7: To invalidate all operations whose effects will succeed the period of the contract.
column8: Confined to restraining the agent from commencing new operations subsequently.
column9: To prevent the principal from terminating the agent before the end of that period.
column11: Per 4/4/2, a time limit only restrains the agent from commencing new operations after it; per 4/4/3 earlier operations may run beyond it.

column5: It is permissible for the Institutions to provide banking services that do not involve interest-based lending and borrowing, because such services serve a permissible interest of the clients.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, such services are permissible because they serve a permissible interest of the clients.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: A plot of land is jointly owned by A (40%), B (20%) and C (40%). C sold his share to an outside buyer for a price payable after one year. Both A and B promptly claimed their right of Shuf'ah. The correct ruling is:
column6: A and B take C's share equally, on the same deferred payment terms, and bear the buyer's liabilities such as the usual conveyancing costs, since both are co-owners with equal claim.
column7: A and B take C's share in proportion to their shares (two-thirds to A and one-third to B), on the same deferred payment terms, and bear the buyer's liabilities such as usual conveyancing costs.
column8: A and B take C's share in proportion to their shares, but must pay the price in cash immediately, since the deferment was granted to the outside buyer personally and does not bind the preemptors.
column9: A alone takes C's share, being the larger co-owner.
column11: Per 7/2/1-2, each preemptor takes in proportion to his share, on the buyer's terms (e.g. deferred payment), assuming the buyer's liabilities.

column5: On repayment of the debt, the mortgagee may keep the mortgaged asset as a collateral for a new debt for which the asset is not mortgaged:
column6: In no case whatsoever.
column7: Only if the new debt arises from the same type of contract as the original debt.
column8: Only when the two parties agree to keep the mortgaged asset as a collateral for any debt between them within a specific period.
column9: Absolutely, because the mortgagee has the right to keep the whole mortgaged asset for any part of the debt.
column11: Per 3/1/7, after repayment the asset cannot secure a new debt, unless the parties agree it secures any debt between them within a specific period.

column5: It is permissible for the partners to agree on the adoption of any method of allocation of profit, either permanent or variable, provided that:
column6: The variable method is linked to a published benchmark rate, such as the prevailing market rate of return.
column7: The method is approved by the regulatory authority and by the Shari'ah supervisory board of the Institution.
column8: The percentages of profit are the same in all periods of the Sharikah and are stated in the contract.
column9: The method does not lead to the likelihood of a partner being precluded from sharing in profit.
column11: Per 3/1/5/5, any permanent or variable method is allowed if it does not risk precluding a partner from the profit.

column5: Which of the following conditions stipulated by the Waqif is invalid?
column6: Absolute forbiddance of Istibdal (exchange) of the Waqf.
column7: A condition that his debts should be settled from the Waqf income after his death.
column8: A condition that the Waqf income has to be spent first on any member of his family who becomes poor, and then on charity purposes.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/3, absolute forbiddance of Istibdal is an invalid condition; (b) and (c) are cited as valid conditions in 4/1/2.

column5: If the documents presented by the beneficiary do not conform to the instructions, the bank reserves the right to accept, reject or seek amendment of the documents.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/4, for non-conforming documents the bank may accept, reject or seek amendment.

column5: Debt, as defined in the Standard on Sale of Debt, is:
column6: An asset that is established and owed, irrespective of its cause; it may be money, commodities or usufructs, and includes debts arising out of a loan, a commutative contract, or misconduct or negligence.
column7: An amount of money owed under a loan contract only.
column8: An obligation arising out of a loan or a commutative contract, excluding liabilities arising out of misconduct or negligence, and it may be in the form of money, commodities or usufructs, whatever its cause.
column9: Money or commodities owed under commutative contracts, excluding usufructs and debts arising from a loan or from misconduct.
column11: Per item 2, debt is any established, owed asset (money, commodities or usufructs) arising from a loan, a commutative contract or misconduct/negligence.

column5: The right of the lessee's heirs to terminate the Ijarah if they prove that it has become too onerous for their resources is an exceptional ruling taken from the Hanbali school.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, this exceptional ruling is taken from the Maliki school, to avoid damage to the heirs.

column5: In Monetization, the commodity shall be received by the buyer:
column6: Actually only, since constructive receipt is not sufficient in Monetization.
column7: Actually or constructively, and there remains no further condition or procedure for receiving it.
column8: Constructively only, through the Institution acting as the client's agent in selling it to the third party.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/4, the commodity shall be actually or constructively received by the buyer, with no further condition or procedure remaining for receiving it.

column5: It is not permissible to protect the capital by Shari'ah non-compliant means, such as:
column6: Stipulating that the investment manager is liable for loss of capital.
column7: An undertaking by a third party to indemnify for loss of capital in cases other than wilful misconduct or negligence of the investment manager, with a right of recourse to the investment manager.
column8: A commitment by, or obligating, the investment manager to purchase the investment assets at their nominal price or at a price that was initially agreed upon.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1-5/3, all three are Shari'ah non-compliant means of protecting capital.

column5: A transaction in which a person who is not a debtor transfers another person to collect an amount from a third party is:
column6: An agency contract for collection of the debt, not a transfer of debt.
column7: An unrestricted Hawalah, in which the payer pays from his own funds and has recourse to the transferor afterwards.
column8: A transfer of right.
column9: A restricted Hawalah.
column11: Per 6/2, Hawalah requires the transferor to be the transferee's debtor; otherwise it is agency for collection.

column5: The Islamic insurance company shall adhere to the rules of Shari'ah in all its activities and investments, especially in refraining from provision of insurance coverage for Shari'ah-banned items, activities or purposes.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/8, the company must adhere to Shari'ah and refrain from covering Shari'ah-banned items, activities or purposes.

column5: The service/work of the employee which constitutes a subject matter of the hiring contract should be:
column6: Well known and permissible, even if it is not accomplishable at present.
column7: Determined in terms of a specific period only, and not in terms of a specific work.
column8: Specific and existing at the time of contracting, since a future service cannot be the subject of hiring.
column9: Well known, accomplishable and permissible in Shari'ah.
column11: Per 5/1/1 it must be well known, accomplishable and permissible; it may be a future service (5/1/6) and set by work, period or both (5/1/2).

column5: Zero-coupon bonds, in which the excess over the loan amount is a part of the value of the bond:
column6: Are permissible, since no periodic interest is paid.
column7: Are prohibited, like other bonds that stipulate the return of the loan amount with an excess.
column8: Are permissible if they are issued by a government, since governmental bonds are issued for public interest and not for profit.
column9: Are permissible if they are traded at their nominal value.
column11: Per 4, bonds stipulating any excess, whether a percentage or a part of the value (zero-coupon), are prohibited, whoever the issuer.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: An IFI calculates the profit on its Murabahah financing on the basis of an annualised percentage of the amount of financing outstanding according to an amortised payment schedule. This method is:
column6: Permissible only if the profit is calculated on the total financing provided for the entire period.
column7: Impermissible, because calculating profit on the outstanding amount resembles interest-based lending and makes the price uncertain.
column8: Permissible, provided that the total sale price varies with the amount of financing outstanding.
column9: Permissible, provided it is done with full disclosure and the total sale price is stated as a fixed amount.
column11: Per item 10, period-based customary methods are permissible with transparency, full disclosure and a fixed total sale price.

column5: In reinsuring with traditional reinsurance companies, Islamic insurance companies should observe the following controls:
column6: They should reinsure first with Islamic reinsurance companies, to the largest possible extent.
column7: The periods of the reinsurance agreements with traditional reinsurance companies should be commensurate to the actual need.
column8: They should seek the approval of their Shari'ah Supervisory Boards before signing agreements with traditional reinsurance companies.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/1, 6/3 and 6/4, all three are controls on reinsuring with traditional reinsurance companies.

column5: Regarding leasing of the Waqf by the Waqf superintendent to his father (one of his Usul) or to his spouse:
column6: He should not lease the Waqf to them for less than the normal rent of similar property, and minor injustice (Ghabn) is not forgivable in this case, although it is forgivable in leasing to nonrelatives.
column7: He may lease the Waqf to them for less than the normal rent if the beneficiaries agree.
column8: He should not lease the Waqf to them for less than the normal rent of similar property, but minor injustice (Ghabn) is forgivable in this case as in leasing to nonrelatives.
column9: He may not lease the Waqf to them at all, even at more than the normal rent, except through the judiciary.
column11: Per 5/3/2, leasing to direct relatives or spouse below normal rent is barred with no forgiveness of minor Ghabn; the judiciary rule applies to himself and dependant sons.

column5: If the worker revokes the Ju'alah contract after commencing the work:
column6: He is entitled to reasonable wages for the work done.
column7: He has no claim against the offeror, unless they had agreed to the contrary.
column8: He is entitled to a part of the compensation proportionate to the work done.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 6/3-6/4, a worker who revokes after commencing has no claim on the offeror unless agreed otherwise.

column5: It is permissible to invest Waqf income in the following cases:
column6: As per a condition stipulated by the Waqif.
column7: During the waiting period (prior to identification of beneficiaries).
column8: Excess income, after payment to beneficiaries.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/1, Waqf income may be invested in all three cases, through permissible methods and in low risk investments.

column5: Where the beneficiary of a bill of exchange is a creditor to the drawer, and there is no debt obligation between the drawer and the paying bank, the issuance of the bill of exchange becomes:
column6: An agency contract to collect the amount of the bill on behalf of the drawer.
column7: A transfer of right.
column8: An unrestricted Hawalah.
column9: A restricted Hawalah.
column11: Per 12/4/1-12/4/2, it is Hawalah as the beneficiary is a creditor, and unrestricted as the bank owes the drawer nothing.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The stipulation of mutual relief from commitments (Mubara`ah) in case of exit, which should be included in the contracts of the Mudarabah-based investment accounts, should indicate that:
column6: The exiting party relieves the depositors from commitment towards his rights in any undistributed or non-apparent profit, and in the remaining part of the reserves for investment risks and rate of return, and of allocations for debts.
column7: The holders of the accounts relieve the exiting party from commitment towards any losses that have not yet become apparent.
column8: On liquidation of the investment base, the remaining parts of the above-mentioned reserves and allocations shall be devoted to charitable purposes.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/4, the Mubara`ah clause covers all three: the exiting party's waiver, the holders' waiver of hidden losses, and residual reserves to charity.

column5: It is permissible to stipulate a condition which leads to a reasonable increment in the pay agreed upon in case of default by the employer, as compensation to the employee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/8, any condition increasing the agreed pay on the employer's default is impermissible; only a pledge to donate to charity is allowed.

column5: If a transaction is an assignment of debt (ḥawāla), it is not considered a sale of debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1, an assignment of debt is not considered a sale of debt (see Standard No. 7 on Hawala).

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: A buyer had an either-or option to purchase one of three items priced at 300, 600 and 900. He took delivery of all three, and all of them were destroyed in his possession. The buyer is liable to pay:
column6: 600, being one third of the price of each item.
column7: 1,800, being the price of all three items.
column8: 900, being the highest price.
column9: 300, being the lowest price.
column11: Per 4/2/1, if all are destroyed and prices differ, he pays the average price for the number purchased: a third of each (100+200+300).

column5: Under Mudarabah as a method of financing used by institutions:
column6: The institution enters as Rab al-Mal, subscribing the funds, while the Mudarib subscribes the work and performs the managerial duties; the entire loss is borne by Rab al-Mal, unless it is due to transgression or negligence of the Mudarib.
column7: The two parties agree on a specific method for profit sharing, and loss is shared between Rab al-Mal and the Mudarib according to the agreed profit-sharing ratio, since each of them is a partner in the Mudarabah capital.
column8: The entire loss has to be borne by the Mudarib, unless it is due to a reason beyond his control.
column9: The institution enters the deal as the Mudarib, while the client subscribes the funds, and the entire loss has to be borne by the Mudarib, whether or not it is due to his transgression or negligence, since the funds are with him and in his possession.
column11: Per 3/2/2, the institution is Rab al-Mal and bears the entire loss, unless it results from the Mudarib's transgression or negligence.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: If the duration of a contract is not stipulated:
column6: The contract is valid, and the duration is determined later according to custom.
column7: The contract is valid, because Gharar in the duration is minor Gharar.
column8: The contract becomes null and void; but if Gharar is removed by knowledge of the contract's duration, or abandonment of the duration, at the time of contracting, the contract becomes valid.
column9: The contract becomes null and void, and it cannot become valid even if the duration becomes known, or the duration is abandoned, at the time of contracting.
column11: Per 5/3/1, an unstipulated duration voids the contract, unless Gharar is removed at contracting by knowing the duration or abandoning it.

column5: Giving prior notice to the debtor before giving effect to the condition accelerating the instalments is merely of the nature of a reminder, so as to provide him with reasonable time for payment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis on maturity of instalments, prior notice is merely a reminder giving the debtor reasonable time to pay.

column5: When the online contract is concluded through audio or audiovisual communication, the contract signing session (Majlis al-'Aqd) is:
column6: The whole period specified by the offering party for the validity of his offer, whether or not the conversation continues, and whether or not the parties shift to another subject, since the offeror may fix any period.
column7: The time of communication between the two parties if the conversation relates to the contract; it is considered to have stopped if the conversation is over or disconnected, or the two parties shift to another subject, unless the disconnection is brief.
column8: The period that continues until the offering party comes to know of the acceptance.
column9: The period from the moment of communicating the offer to the concerned party up to issuance of acceptance, even if the conversation is disconnected for a long time or the two parties shift to another subject unrelated to the contract, since the offer remains valid until it is accepted.
column11: Per 4/1/1, the session is the time of communication about the contract; it stops when the talk ends, is cut (unless briefly) or changes subject.

column5: A participant unintentionally misstated some of the information he submitted about the insured property. When the risk occurred, the company discovered this misrepresentation. The participant's indemnity:
column6: Is denied in full.
column7: Becomes proportionate to the accurate information he presented.
column8: Is paid in full, since the misrepresentation was unintentional.
column9: Is subject to partial or full deprivation, at the discretion of the company.
column11: Per 8/1, in unintentional misrepresentation the indemnity becomes proportionate to the accurate information presented.

column5: The provision for redemption of pre-operating expenses is deductible from zakatable assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/3/1, the provision for redemption of pre-operating expenses is not deductible from zakatable assets.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The conditions imposed on the subject matter of agency, without which conclusion and validity of the contract cannot be attained, are:
column6: Asset ownership by the principal, delivery of the asset to the agent, specification of the agency period, and permissibility of the asset.
column7: Existence of the asset, asset ownership by the principal, possibility of disposing of the asset through agency, and the absence of any Shari'ah restriction that prevents the deal.
column8: Existence of the asset, possession of the asset by the agent, specification of the remuneration, and the absence of any Shari'ah restriction that prevents the deal.
column9: Existence of the asset, legal capacity of the agent, specification of the remuneration, and the absence of Gharar.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the four conditions are existence, ownership by the principal, disposability through agency and no Shari'ah bar.

column5: When one party to a utilization concession contract breaches a contractual condition or commitment:
column6: Only the State has the right to revoke the contract.
column7: The contract continues, but the breaching party pays a penalty to charity, equal to the damages suffered by the other party, and neither party has the right to revoke the contract.
column8: The other party has the right to revoke the contract, and the breaching party has to compensate the other party for any consequent actual damages.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/8, each party may revoke on the other's breach, and the breaching party compensates actual damages.

column5: A personal guarantee that is offered voluntarily by a third party without the debtor's request or consent is:
column6: A non-recourse guarantee (voluntary guarantee).
column7: A market (business) guarantee.
column8: Daman al-Dark.
column9: A guarantee with a right of recourse to the debtor.
column11: Per 3/1/2, a guarantee offered without the debtor's request or consent is the non-recourse (voluntary) guarantee.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Either-or options:
column6: May be sold or transferred to third parties.
column7: Cannot be combined with another option to reconsider in the same contract, as the two options conflict.
column8: Transfer to the heirs of the owner of the option upon his death, who then enjoy all his rights.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/3, they pass to heirs; options to reconsider may not be sold or transferred (5/1) but may be combined (5/2).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of a facility commission is that it is not allowed to receive a commission for giving out a loan facility itself, so it is logical to disallow a commission for mere readiness to finance the customer on a deferred payment basis.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis given for 2/4/2.

column5: An Institution may appoint one of its customers to act as its agent in acquiring an asset that the customer desires, with a view to leasing it to him. Regarding this agency:
column6: It is permissible only in case of dire need.
column7: It is permissible, but it is always preferred that the agent be someone other than the customer (prospective lessee) where possible.
column8: It is preferred that the customer be the agent, since he knows the description of the asset and the price at which it is to be acquired.
column9: It is absolutely impermissible, because it leads to a fictitious transaction.
column11: Per 3/7, the customer may be the purchasing agent, but an agent other than the prospective lessee is always preferred.

column5: The managing partners in a company limited by shares, who are liable for the obligations of the company from their personal assets on the basis of joint liability, are in the position of:
column6: Third-party guarantors of the capital of the sleeping partners.
column7: A person who works as a Mudarib and simultaneously participates in a partnership.
column8: Hired employees of the company.
column9: Capital providers in a Mudarabah contract.
column11: Per 4/4/2/1, managing partners are like a Mudarib who also participates in the partnership; sleeping partners are like capital providers.

column5: The eligibility criteria of the overseer, whether he is an individual or a member of a board of overseership, are:
column6: Discretion (rushd), competence (kifāyah), and holding a professional qualification in investment.
column7: Sanity (ʿaql), competence (kifāyah), and being a relative of the Waqif.
column8: Moral probity (ʿadālah), sanity (ʿaql), discretion (rushd), and competence (kifāyah).
column9: Moral probity (ʿadālah), sanity (ʿaql), and being one of the Waqf beneficiaries.
column11: Per 3/5, the criteria are moral probity, sanity, discretion and competence.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: With regard to the rights of neighbourhood among the owners of the different floors of a building:
column6: Each owner is prohibited to act in a manner that will definitely or most likely cause harm to others.
column7: The owners have the right to enjoy use of common facilities and services.
column8: If a lower storey collapses without any fault of its owner, he is nevertheless liable to reconstruct it in all cases.
column9: (a) and (b).
