column11: Per 6/1 and 6/2/3, harmful acts are prohibited and common facilities are shared; per 6/2/2, a faultless collapse is settled by the courts.

column5: The majority of Fuqaha hold that written documentation of transactions involving future obligations is obligatory, so that one who does not put them in writing commits a sin.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the basis, the majority hold writing is recommended; Ibn Hazm alone held it obligatory.

column5: Hamish Jiddiyyah is considered as 'Arboun (Earnest Money), and therefore the Institution may retain it in full if the customer breaches his binding promise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/5/3–2/5/4, Hamish Jiddiyyah is not 'Arboun; on breach only the actual damage may be deducted from it.

column5: It is not permissible for the Mudarib to:
column6: Make a loan, a gift or a charitable donation out of the Mudarabah funds.
column7: Sell and buy on a deferred payment basis.
column8: Deposit the Mudarabah funds in the custody of a trustworthy person.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 9/6, loans, gifts and donations from Mudarabah funds are prohibited; deferred sales and safe custody are allowed (9/1).

column5: Taking possession of an item of real property by the Institution:
column6: Takes place by the mere vacation of the property, even if the acquirer is not able to have disposal of it.
column7: Takes place only by actual physical delivery of the property to the Institution, as constructive possession is not recognized for real property, whatever the nature of the property or custom.
column8: May take place by the property being vacated and placed at the acquirer's disposal; if the acquirer is unable to dispose of it, the vacation does not convey possession.
column9: Takes place only by registration of the property in the name of the acquirer.
column11: Per 3/2/3, real property is possessed by vacation and placement at the acquirer's disposal; vacation without ability to dispose is not possession.

column5: The basis of giving preference to maintenance over the avenues of Waqf disposal is that the intention of Waqf is the permanence and continuity of its revenue, which cannot continue without maintenance of its assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 4/1, Waqf aims at permanent, continuous revenue, impossible without maintaining its assets.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: With regard to promises in gold, it is permissible:
column6: To trade in promises to sell gold, provided that the promise is unilateral.
column7: To issue a unilaterally binding promise to sell gold.
column8: To issue bilaterally binding promises for the sale of gold.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/1 and 8/4, a unilateral binding promise is permissible, but bilaterally binding promises and trading in promises are not.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting a Waqf limited by time includes:
column6: Some of the Shari'ah texts referring to Waqf are general in nature, and hence apply to perpetual as well as temporary Waqf.
column7: Waqf is a form of donation, and its scope is broadened and carrying it out is encouraged.
column8: It is the view of the Mālikī school and a reported narration of Abū Yūsuf among the Ḥanafīs, and the International Islamic Fiqh Academy issued a resolution along these lines.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/1/5, all three are cited: general texts, Waqf as encouraged donation, and the Mālikī view/Abū Yūsuf and IIFA 181.

column5: The cardholder may take advantage of the benefits offered by the card network provided they are acceptable as per Shari'ah, and the card-issuing Institution should inform the cardholder about these benefits in accordance with what is resolved by its Shari'ah Board.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/6/4, network benefits acceptable per Shari'ah may be used, and the Institution informs the cardholder per its Shari'ah Board.

column5: If it is expressly stated in the prospectus of Sukuk that it is an offer, the prospectus will be considered as an offer and the subscription becomes an acceptance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1/7, an express statement in the prospectus that it is an offer makes the prospectus the offer and the subscription the acceptance.

column5: Taking possession of one of the countervalues by one party without taking possession of the other is not enough to make a currency dealing transaction permissible.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/6/2, possession of one countervalue without the other is insufficient; partial possession is likewise insufficient.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not dismissing the investment manager automatically due to misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions, unless stipulated in the contract, is:
column6: That the investment manager remains liable for the loss and for any breach, so there is no need for dismissal, since Rab Al Maal remains entitled to compensation for the capital and the realized profit.
column7: That dismissal of a fiduciary requires a court order, by analogy with the guardian of an orphan's property whose guardianship ends only by judgment of the court.
column8: That continuity of the contract is an unimpeded public interest (Maslahah Mursalah).
column9: That the contract constitutes an authorization to act on a fiduciary basis which continues though the fiduciary responsibility is breached, by analogy with the pledgee whose pledge remains valid.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the fiduciary authorization continues despite misconduct, by analogy with the pledgee.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If an alloy of gold and silver is sold for another alloy of gold and silver, or for currencies, only the spot exchange of the counter-values is required.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/3/1/1 (first form), alloy for alloy or for currencies requires spot exchange only.

column5: The view of the majority of jurists that the transferee has a right of recourse to the transferor if he accepted the transfer on the basis that the payer is solvent is based on:
column6: The Hadith "Muslims are bound by the conditions they made", this stipulation serving the purpose of the contract.
column7: The report from Uthman Ibn Affan about a payer who died in a state of bankruptcy.
column8: The analogy between Hawalah and transfer of right, which the Hanafis permit because its essence is similar to suretyship permitted by all four schools.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis, the majority rely on the Hadith on conditions; the Uthman report is the Hanafi basis for recourse on death in bankruptcy.

column5: For the sake of serving the policyholders' interest, deducting part of their funds or profits to be used as reserves or allocations pertaining to the insurance fund is:
column6: Permissible, but such deductions should by no means belong to the shareholders of the Joint Stock Company.
column7: Permissible, and such deductions belong to the shareholders upon liquidation of the company.
column8: Not permissible, since the surplus must be fully distributed among the policyholders.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 10/5, such deductions are allowed but never belong to shareholders; the balance goes to charity on liquidation.

column5: An employee was hired to complete a specific work within a period of three months. By the end of the period he had completed only part of the work; the accomplished part is useful and can be benefited from, but the employer is unwilling to extend the period. The employee is entitled to:
column6: The whole pay agreed upon in the contract.
column7: No pay at all, since he has not completed the work within the period.
column8: The amount normally paid for similar work (Ajr al-Mithl).
column9: Twice the pay of the part completed, as compensation for the employer's refusal to extend.
column11: Per 5/1/2, if the completed part is useful and the employer will not extend the period, the employee gets Ajr al-Mithl; if useless, he gets no pay.

column5: The currencies of different countries are considered as being of different kinds because:
column6: Some of them are paper money while others are coins.
column7: They are measured against gold and silver at different rates, so that each currency has its own intrinsic value as a commodity.
column8: They are 'constructive money', and these currencies differ in kind according to the authority that considers them as money.
column9: They differ in their exchange value in the international markets, and their value is determined by the gold reserves held by the issuing country.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (IIFA Resolution 21), currencies are constructive money and differ in kind according to the issuing authority.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations does not cover Mudarabah, because this form of partnership has a separate standard.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Scope, Mudarabah is excluded since it has a separate standard.

column5: It is permissible to trade in currencies, provided that:
column6: Both parties take possession of the countervalues before dispersing, such possession being either actual or constructive.
column7: The dealing in currencies does not aim at establishing a monopoly position, nor entail any evil consequences to the interest of individuals or societies.
column8: The countervalues of the same currency may differ in amount where one of them is in paper money and the other is in coin of the same country.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/1/1 and 2/1/4, (a) and (b) are conditions; per 2/1/2 same-currency countervalues must be equal even if one is paper money and the other coin.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: The Standard on the Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments does not cover:
column6: The contingent incidents encountered in honoring the commitments that stem from application of Islamic modes of financing and investment by Institutions.
column7: Defects of will or the conducts that result from mutual consent of the two parties.
column8: The effects of contingent incidents on commitments.
column9: Contingencies leading to amendment of the contract, such as levy of custom duties or taxes after signing the contract.
column11: Per 1, the Standard does not cover defects of will or the conducts that result from mutual consent of the two parties.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The Shari'ah basis for invalidity of a contract whose duration is unknown is that it could generate dispute.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, unknown duration could generate dispute; the prohibition of Bay' Habal al-Habalah is cited.

column5: It is permissible to offer prizes on holding or using ATM cards and/or credit cards, subject to the following conditions:
column6: The cardholders do not incur any charges in return for their participation in the draw, either through direct payment or by debiting their respective accounts.
column7: The fees charged on the cards during the draw period do not exceed ordinary fees.
column8: The prizes are not confined exclusively to cards linked to current accounts, where the cardholder has no right to link the card to his investment account.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/5/4/1–3/5/4/3, all three are conditions for prizes on ATM and credit cards.

column5: In Islamic insurance, the insurance fund enjoys the status of a legal entity and has independent financial liability.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per clause 2, the insurance fund has the status of a legal entity with independent financial liability.

column5: When an institution invites investors to participate in financing its working capital on a Mudarabah or Musharakah basis:
column6: The investors contribute their capital, while the institution contributes its current assets, after valuation, as its share of the capital.
column7: The institution's fixed assets do not form part of the Musharakah; they are either lent or leased to the venture, and rental payments are accounted as expenses of the Mudarabah or Musharakah.
column8: The institution contributes its fixed assets at their book value as its share of the capital.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2/4, the institution contributes valued current assets; fixed assets are lent or leased to the venture, with rent as an expense.

column5: Securing debt obligations through insurance against doubtful or bad debts:
column6: Is permissible through an Islamic insurance coverage, but not through conventional insurance.
column7: Is permissible through conventional insurance where Islamic insurance is not available, since necessity renders the prohibited permissible.
column8: Is not permissible in any form, since insurance involves Gharar.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/4, only Islamic insurance may secure debts; conventional insurance of debts is not permissible.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Possession of a gold certificate in line with the Standard is deemed as good as taking physical possession of the gold in terms of legal effect, transfer of risk and benefits, and ability to dispose of it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/4, such a certificate equals physical possession in legal effect, risk, benefits and disposal.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility in Istisna'a of payment on deferred terms or on an instalment basis is that:
column6: The subject-matter of Istisna'a is a monetary debt, and a deferred price for a debt is therefore a permissible form of settlement between the parties to the contract.
column7: Labour (transformation and added value) is an important part of the items sold, which makes the transaction similar to leasing, where rentals may be deferred or paid in instalments without being a sale of debt for debt.
column8: Delay in payment of the price is a form of Iqalah, which the parties may agree on after the contract is concluded, and is therefore permissible whatever the stage of the work.
column9: Istisna'a is a sale of identified goods already owned by the seller, so that the price may be deferred as in any cash-and-carry sale of existing goods under a binding contract, which is why no sale of debt for debt arises.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, labour makes Istisna'a akin to leasing, where deferred or instalment rent is not a sale of debt for debt.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In principle, equality in investment opportunities should be ensured between shareholders' funds and the funds of the holders of investment accounts in participatory Mudarabah. In case a different policy is to be adopted:
column6: The institution should disclose that before disposition, having regard to regulatory restrictions and the conditions of opening the accounts.
column7: The institution should disclose that after liquidation, in the profit and loss account, subject to the regulatory restrictions on disclosing such policies.
column8: The institution must obtain the explicit written consent of each accountholder before any such disposition is made.
column9: This is absolutely impermissible.
column11: Per 2/1/3, any departure from equal investment opportunities must be disclosed before disposition, subject to regulations and account conditions.

column5: Official mortgage grants the mortgagee a right over the mortgaged property which gives him, upon the death of the owner or his insolvency, a right prior to all the creditors for the satisfaction of his claim from this property.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis for 3/4 states that official mortgage gives the mortgagee priority over all creditors on death or insolvency.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The institution has the right to dispose of the amounts of current accounts and invest them for its own benefit and under its own responsibility, preferably after indicating this in the application for opening the account.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/1, the institution may use current account funds for its own benefit and risk, preferably stating this in the opening application.

column5: When the pay in the hiring contract is variable:
column6: The pay of each period is to be determined by the employer at the beginning of that period.
column7: The pay of the first period should be known, and an accurate indicator may be used afterwards, without the need for any upper or lower limit, since the indicator removes the Gharar.
column8: The amount of pay for the first period should be known; afterwards an accurate indicator known to and agreed upon by both parties may be used, with an upper and a lower limit.
column9: An accurate indicator known to both parties may be used for all periods, including the first, provided that it has an upper and a lower limit, even if the pay of the first period is not known.
column11: Per 5/2/4, the first period's pay must be known; later periods may follow an agreed accurate indicator that has upper and lower limits.

column5: The relationship between the card issuer and the cardholder at the time of using the card is a (……….) novation if the card issuer pays from the money of the cardholder held in its custody, and a (……….) novation if the card issuer pays from its own funds.
column6: Restricted .... restricted.
column7: Absolute (unrestricted) .... restricted.
column8: Restricted .... absolute (unrestricted).
column9: Absolute (unrestricted) .... absolute (unrestricted).
column11: Per the Basis of 2/2/1/2, paying from the cardholder's funds is restricted novation; paying from the issuer's own funds is absolute novation.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Commercial Papers covers:
column6: The bill of exchange, the promissory note and the cheque, the commercial papers to which the Geneva Uniform Convention confined itself.
column7: Any instrument that may possess the attributes of commercial paper, whatever its form or the law under which it is issued, including instruments not known to the Geneva Convention.
column8: Sukuk and shares traded in financial markets, which are treated as commercial papers for the purposes of this Standard and are governed by the same rules of endorsement.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per the Scope, only bills of exchange, promissory notes and cheques are covered, not other instruments with similar attributes.

column5: With regard to Sukuk based on Salam, Istisna' and Murabaha:
column6: Salam Sukuk may be traded for a cash price at their market value, since the Salam commodity is a tangible asset owned by the Sukuk holders.
column7: It is permitted to exchange Salam Sukuk or Istisna' Sukuk with the debtor, following the rule of sale of debt to the debtor.
column8: Murabaha Sukuk may be traded for cash at their face value.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 9/3, Salam and Murabaha Sukuk may not be traded for cash; Salam or Istisna' Sukuk may be exchanged with the debtor under 4/1.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, the fee for the credit study:
column6: May be charged only if the study results in approval of the financing, since the study is a part of the financing process.
column7: Should not necessarily equal the actual cost of its preparation, since it is a service that can be performed independently within the contract.
column8: Must be determined as a percentage of the amount of the requested financing, because the study is related to the financing amount.
column9: Must be equal to the actual cost of its preparation, otherwise it becomes an implicit fee for the financing, and may not be changed by the agreement of the parties.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the fee need not equal actual cost; it is a fee for the effort exerted as an independent service, irrespective of results.

column5: The permissibility for the parties of the syndication to make their contributions in currencies other than that of the syndication, with revaluation according to the prevailing exchange rates, is derived from the Hadith narrated by Ibn Umar about selling camels at Al-Baqi'.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, this is derived from Ibn Umar's Hadith: no harm if the same day's rate is applied before parting.

column5: Haqq al-Qarar (right to stay), in which the tenant pays a lump sum (Kardar) for development of the Waqf and a rent below that of similar property, is permissible whenever the Waqf superintendent sees an interest in it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/3/2, it is permissible only when dictated by necessity and no tenant will pay the normal rent plus a lump sum for development.

column5: It is not permissible to stipulate in trust (fiduciary) contracts, e.g. agency contracts or contracts of deposits, that a personal guarantee or mortgage of security be produced:
column6: Unless the trustee receives remuneration for his services.
column7: Unless the guarantee is limited to a specified percentage of the asset held on trust.
column8: Unless such a stipulation is intended to cover misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.
column9: In any case, even if the stipulation is intended to cover misconduct or negligence, since a trustee may never be required to give a guarantee.
column11: Per 2/2/1, such stipulation contradicts trust contracts unless confined to misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.

column5: The mortgagee may enjoy free of charge benefit from the mortgaged asset if the mortgagor permits him to do so.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/9, the mortgagee may never benefit free of charge, with or without permission; with permission he may use it at normal pay.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When agency is paid, it falls under the Shari'ah rulings on Ijarah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/2, paid agency falls under the Shari'ah rulings on Ijarah.

column5: It is impermissible to conclude a verbal arbitration contract; the arbitration contract must be concluded in writing.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/7, a verbal arbitration contract is permissible, though Institutions should document the arbitration verdict in writing.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Approval by the owner of a contract concluded by an uncommissioned agent (Fodooli):
column6: Is subject to the discretion of the owner, and should precede revocation of the contract by either of the two parties; otherwise, a new contract has to be initiated.
column7: Is retroactively effective, based on the date of the act of the uncommissioned agent.
column8: Makes the contract effective and subject to all rulings on agency.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/2 and 8/4, approval is at the owner's discretion, must precede revocation, and takes effect retroactively under agency rules.

column5: In selective reinsurance, the reinsurance company becomes committed to all the risks presented to it by the insurance company.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1, in selective reinsurance the reinsurer studies each risk and becomes committed only to what it accepts.

column5: An IFI issued negotiable Musharakah Sukuk. To make them attractive to investors, the IFI wished to undertake in the prospectus of issue to purchase, after the completion of the process of issue, any certificate that may be offered to it. The IFI may undertake to purchase the certificates:
column6: At a price fixed in advance in the prospectus.
column7: At their nominal value.
column8: At their nominal value plus the expected profit.
column9: At market value.
column11: Per 5/2/2, the issuer may undertake in the prospectus to buy negotiable Sukuk at market value, but not at their nominal value.

column5: If the beneficiary of a cheque is a creditor to the issuer, issuing the cheque against the issuer's account without a balance is:
column6: A restricted transfer of debt, whether or not the bank accepts the overdraft.
column7: An unrestricted transfer of debt if the bank accepts the overdraft; if the bank rejects it, it is not a transfer of debt and the beneficiary may have recourse to the issuer.
column8: An agency contract for collection of the amount of the cheque.
column9: An unrestricted transfer of debt, even if the bank rejects the overdraft, since the beneficiary is a creditor to the issuer and the bank is bound to honour the cheque to the extent of the overdraft.
column11: Per 12/2, an accepted overdraft makes it an unrestricted Hawalah; if rejected, no Hawalah and the payee reverts to the issuer.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The Standard on Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts does not cover:
column6: The allocations and reserves to be deducted from the profits.
column7: How profits are to be distributed between the institution as a Mudarib and the holders of investment accounts as Arbab al-Mal.
column8: Accounts managed on the basis of investment agency, because such accounts require a separate standard.
column9: Determination of the expenses to be charged to investment accounts.
column11: Per 1, accounts managed on the basis of investment agency are excluded, as they require a separate standard.

column5: Trading in interest-bearing bonds is:
column6: Permissible if the bonds are governmental.
column7: Prohibited, both sale and purchase, and so is their pledging and endorsement.
column8: Prohibited in sale, but permissible in pledging, provided that the pledgee does not receive the interest accruing on them.
column9: Permissible at their nominal value.
column11: Per 5, sale, purchase, pledging and endorsement of bonds are all prohibited.

column5: By virtue of public guardianship, the judiciary has the authority of overseeing the supervision and management of the Waqf, and of subjecting the Waqf superintendent to disciplinary action.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/5/1, the judiciary oversees Waqf management by public guardianship and may discipline the superintendent.

column5: Reinsurance by Islamic insurance companies with traditional reinsurance companies is:
column6: Impermissible, except when such reinsurance is sought as a transitional arrangement stemming from public need which amounts to necessity.
column7: Permissible whenever the traditional reinsurance company offers lower premiums than Islamic reinsurance companies.
column8: Absolutely impermissible, without any exception.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/2, reinsurance with traditional reinsurers is impermissible except as a transitional arrangement due to public need amounting to necessity.

column5: The basis for permitting the stipulation of a reward for raising loans on the basis of credit status is that it is a counter-value for a service rendered, as the Jurists uphold that a reward may be acquired for recommendations and lending of status.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 8, the reward is a counter-value for a service (recommendation and lending of status).

column5: The basis for considering the delivery of documents pertaining to commodities and goods (like bills of lading and warehouse receipts) as constructive possession of what they represent is:
column6: Customary practice, seeking support from the Maliki view that the mode of possession in movable property not subjected to estimation is recourse to custom ('Urf).
column7: The principle that gains are based on the bearing of costs.
column8: The tradition of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit on exchange from hand to hand.
column9: The Hanafi view that possession of immovables is by delivery of the key along with relinquishment, which is extended by analogy to documents of title to movable goods not yet ascertained.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/5, document possession rests on customary practice, supported by the Maliki view referring possession to custom.

column5: In the method of dividing the capital between Murabahah and 'Arboun contracts, it is compulsory to reserve the assets sold under the 'Arboun contract from the time of contract conclusion until the settlement date, and trading in 'Arboun contracts is impermissible.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/7(d), the 'Arboun rules must be observed, including reserving the assets until settlement and not trading the contracts.

column5: The institution may provide free services to the owners of its current accounts:
column6: Absolutely, without any restriction, since the services are a gift from the institution to its customers.
column7: Provided that the services are not set as a precondition, or a traditionally observed prerequisite, for opening the account.
column8: Provided that the balance of the account exceeds a certain amount, in which case the services may be set as a condition for opening the account.
column9: Under no circumstances, since current accounts are loans to the institution.
column11: Per 2/6/2, free services to current account owners are allowed if not a precondition or customary prerequisite for opening the account.

column5: A framework agreement to regulate the process of hiring between the institution and the client:
column6: Is impermissible, since it binds the two parties before the service exists and creates Gharar in the future pay.
column7: Is permissible only if the pay for all future operations is fixed in it and the hiring period is stated for every operation.
column8: Is permissible, and it constitutes in itself the hiring contract for all future operations, so no separate contracts are needed, and each party may enforce it against the other.
column9: Is permissible; it may comprise the general conditions governing the relationship, whereas a separate hiring contract should be signed by both parties for each operation.
column11: Per 3/1, a framework agreement with general conditions is permissible, but each operation needs a separate signed contract or exchange of offer and acceptance.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the current account is considered as a loan because:
column6: The bank is solvent and able to repay it.
column7: The bank does not pay any profit on it.
column8: The bank has to guarantee its repayment on demand.
column9: The holder of the account does not authorize the bank to invest it.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (IIFA Res. 86 (9/3)), the current account is a loan because the bank guarantees repayment on demand, whatever its solvency.

column5: Currency swaps that are concluded on the basis of Riba are not permissible, because:
column6: In this process, interest-based securities are set-off against interest-based securities.
column7: The two currencies are not exchanged hand to hand at the session of the contract.
column8: They involve a bilateral exchange of promises of future set-off.
column9: Set-off is not permissible between debts denominated in different currencies.
column11: Per 5, Riba-based swaps set off interest-based securities against interest-based securities.

column5: If one party to a legally binding bilateral promise (such as in a documentary credit) defaults in fulfilling it:
column6: The promised contract is deemed concluded automatically on the promised date, without any further offer and acceptance.
column7: The other party can obtain a court order requiring the defaulting party to conclude the contract.
column8: The defaulting party is liable for the other party's opportunity cost.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/3, a court injunction may be obtained; the contract is not automatic and indemnity excludes opportunity cost.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: An IFI leased equipment to a customer, and the contract gave the lessee an option to revoke if the equipment broke down. The equipment broke down; the lessee chose not to revoke and repaired it. Two months later, it broke down again. The lessee's option:
column6: Was permanently waived when he chose not to revoke after the first breakdown.
column7: Remains, and he may still revoke, because the harm attributable to the cause triggering the option is recurring.
column8: Remains only if the IFI consents to its exercise.
column9: Remains, provided that he pays the IFI a consideration for the remaining period of the lease, as the lease must be fully paid.
column11: Per item 9, an option is not waived where the harm attributable to its cause is recurring or continuous, as in repeated breakdown of a leased asset.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: In the joint ownership of gold, where each partner owns an undivided share of a specified percentage in the pool of gold:
column6: The owner of an undivided share may not sell it before its segregation, unless the other partners consent.
column7: In case of loss or damage, the losses are borne by the custodian of the pool alone, whatever the cause of the loss and whether or not he committed misconduct.
column8: The owner of an undivided share may request the segregation of his share, if possible, without prejudice to the other partners.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/5/2–3/5/3, a co-owner may request segregation and may sell without it; losses are borne by the co-owners pro rata.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Mudarabah covers Sukuk of Mudarabah (Mudarabah Certificates) issued by the Institution.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Scope, Sukuk of Mudarabah are not covered, as they have a separate standard.

column5: In compulsory set-off, if the two debts are not equal in amount, a set-off takes place of an equivalent amount on both sides, and the party that is owed the larger debt remains a creditor for the remaining balance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/1/2(b), set-off covers the equivalent amount and the party owed the larger debt remains creditor for the balance.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: If the defective item is damaged or destroyed in the possession of the buyer:
column6: The buyer is entitled only to compensation for the defect and may not return the item, unless the seller accepts the damaged item.
column7: The buyer may return the item and recover the whole price, since the defect existed before the item was damaged, whatever the cause of damage.
column8: The buyer loses both the right to return the item and the right to compensation for the defect.
column9: The seller is obliged to accept the return of the damaged item.
column11: Per 2/6/2, the buyer gets compensation only, and may return the item only if the seller accepts the damaged item.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: It is impermissible in Mudarabah to specify the return for any of the two parties in terms of a lump sum amount or a certain percentage of the capital, because:
column6: Such specification eliminates profit sharing, a fundamental aspect of the Mudarabah contract.
column7: The capital of the Mudarabah is not guaranteed by the Mudarib.
column8: Such specification leads to Jahalah (ignorance) about the profit, since the amount of capital is unknown.
column9: Such specification constitutes Riba al-Fadl.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a lump sum or capital percentage eliminates profit sharing, the essence of Mudarabah, e.g. when profit equals that amount.

column5: The basis of the permissibility of combining currency exchange and transfer of money is:
column6: The need of people for transfers, which justifies deferring possession of one of the countervalues.
column7: That the amount paid for the transfer is a loan (Qard), and the exchange takes place upon receipt by the beneficiary, so that possession by the Institution is not required and the beneficiary may dispose of it before.
column8: The achievement of constructive possession by virtue of a bank draft for the amount given in one currency in return for the amount paid in another currency for the purpose of its transfer.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis (IIFA Resolution 48), constructive possession is achieved through the bank draft; the exchange precedes the transfer.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, only exploration and concession, and not survey, enable the licensee to have an exclusive status because:
column6: Survey is always conducted by the State itself and may not be assigned to others, whereas exploration may be assigned to private licensees against a share of the output.
column7: Exploration is a form of Istisna'a.
column8: Survey licenses are granted free of charge.
column9: Survey is based on mere expectation, while exploration is like Tahjir (retention) in wasteland development, which usually precedes utilization.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, survey is mere expectation while exploration resembles Tahjir, which precedes development and ownership.

column5: It is permissible to agree that the percentages of profit shares in the first period are one set of percentages and in the second period another set, depending on the disparity of the two periods or the magnitude of the realised profit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/5/5, variable allocation is allowed if it does not risk precluding a partner from profit.

column5: Two parties agreed beforehand that one of them would sell a commodity to the other for 110 on deferred payment, and then immediately buy it back for 100 in cash. They then signed two separate contracts, neither of which referred to the other. The ruling on this arrangement is:
column6: Permissible, as it is Muwata`ah for obtaining a Shari'ah exit.
column7: Permissible, since each contract is permissible on its own and neither is stipulated as a condition in the other.
column8: Prohibited, as it is Muwata`ah to form up a Riba trick (Bay' al-'Inah), and the contract so designed is invalid.
column9: Permissible, provided that the seller donates the difference of 10 to charity.
column11: Per 6/3/1 and 4/2, a prior agreement to practice Bay' al-'Inah is a prohibited Riba trick and the contract is invalid.

column5: When the online contract is concluded through written communication, by e-mail, or through access to site:
column6: It becomes subject to the rulings applicable to contracts signed in the absence of the two parties, because such deal is similar to message contracting.
column7: When the offering party specifies a certain period for validity of his offer, he has no right to withdraw from his offer during that period.
column8: When the offering party specifies a certain period for validity of his offer, the time allowed for acceptance should cover the whole period.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/2 and 4/2/2, written online contracts follow message contracting, and a term-offer stays open, unwithdrawable, for its whole period.

column5: A client who has no balance in his account drew a cheque on an IFI in favour of a supplier, and the IFI honoured it (the so-called overdraft). From the Shari'ah perspective, this transaction is:
column6: Absolutely impermissible, because the client has no balance.
column7: A loan (Qard), which is permissible if it is void of Riba.
column8: A sale of debt to a person other than the debtor.
column9: Permissible, even if the IFI charges profits for the period of the overdraft.
column11: Per 3/3(b), a cheque drawn without a balance (overdraft) is a Qard, permissible only if void of Riba.

column5: Registration of a mortgage of immovable property is deemed constructive possession on the basis of custom; however, this does not apply where the property has in it the household assets of the tenant.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/4, registration is constructive possession even if the property contains the tenant's household assets.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of revoking contracts on the grounds of price gouging with a trusting buyer is:
column6: The principle that disposal of the sale item is equivalent to explicit consent.
column7: The Hadith: "No harm and no reciprocal harm".
column8: The Quranic Verse {"Allah has permitted sale"}.
column9: The Hadith: "Overcharging a trusting buyer (Mustarsil) is forbidden".
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is the Hadith forbidding overcharging a Mustarsil; a variant calls it Riba.

column5: In the case of tangible Waqf assets, it is permitted to incur debt against the Waqf:
column6: For any purpose that may serve an interest or result in an additional benefit for the Waqf, without restriction, even if the revenues are insufficient to settle it.
column7: Provided that the Waqf asset is pledged as security for the debt.
column8: Through Shari'ah compliant borrowing, deferred payment purchase or financing at a fair profit rate, to cover necessary costs to preserve the Waqf asset in the absence of sufficient revenues.
column9: Without considering the ability of the Waqf revenues to bear the burden of financing, since the debt is for preserving the Waqf, and the creditor may recover from the Waqf asset itself if needed.
column11: Per 5/1, debt is allowed at a fair rate to preserve the asset when revenues are insufficient; tangible Waqf assets cannot be pledged (6/1).

column5: When an online contract is concluded through audio or audiovisual communication between the two parties:
column6: It is not valid, because the two parties are not in the same place.
column7: It becomes subject to the same Shari'ah rulings on contracts signed in the presence of the two parties, such as simultaneous presence (Itihad al-Majlis) and succession of offer and acceptance.
column8: It becomes subject to the rulings applicable to contracts signed in the absence of the two parties, because it is similar to message contracting, in which the offer remains open until the reply arrives, whatever the period.
column9: It becomes subject to the rulings of adhesion contracts, because its terms are set by the offering party and the other party cannot change them.
column11: Per 4/1, audio or audiovisual online contracts follow the rulings of contracts concluded in the presence of the two parties.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Corporate bylaws may give existing shareholders priority over third parties to subscribe for shares upon a decision to increase the company's share capital. This right of priority:
column6: May not be assigned to a third party in any case.
column7: May be assigned only for a consideration equal to its market value, subject to the approval of the general assembly of shareholders.
column8: May be sold to a third party for consideration.
column9: May be assigned to a third party without consideration, subject to law and the rules of company supervisory bodies.
column11: Per 13/2, the shareholders' priority right may be assigned to a third party without consideration, subject to law and supervisory rules.

column5: Hawalah is Mubah for the transferee where the payer's creditworthiness is unknown, because the Prophet's order to accept a transfer does not make the solvency of the payer a condition for the permissibility of Hawalah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, the Hadith's order does not condition permissibility on the payer's solvency.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring that discharge of a debt in another currency before its due time not be stipulated, noticeable by anticipation or a customary practice is:
column6: That it would otherwise become a deferred currency exchange (ṣarf).
column7: That it would otherwise be a form of ribā al-jāhiliyah.
column8: That it would otherwise be an extinction of debt in debt.
column9: That it would otherwise involve excessive gharar.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1/1/2 (b), such pre-arranged early conversion would amount to a deferred ṣarf.

column5: A participant whose insured car was damaged notified the company three months after the accident, although the policy stipulated a notification period of 15 days. The policy does not provide for denial of indemnity in case of late notification. In this case:
column6: The company must pay full indemnity, and has no claim against the participant.
column7: The insurance contract becomes void, and his contributions are returned.
column8: The company has the right to claim indemnity from him for the actual loss incurred by the insurance account due to such breach of commitment.
column9: The participant loses his entitlement to indemnity absolutely, since the notification period is a condition of the validity of the claim and not merely a contractual commitment.
column11: Per 8/3, if notification is not made in time the company may claim from him the actual loss caused to the insurance account.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Suretyship remains permissible with Gharar even if it is paid for, because it is a corollary contract based on delegation of the right of disposal.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, if suretyship is paid for, it becomes an exchange-based contract and is thus affected by Gharar.

column5: Prize bonds are permissible, since the prize is not stipulated for every bondholder.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4, prize bonds are also prohibited.

column5: ………… is the credit in which indebtedness arises at the beginning of the transaction, such as loans and discounting of commercial papers:
column6: Direct cash credit.
column7: Incidental credit.
column8: Bank acceptances.
column9: Incidental facilities.
column11: Per 2/1, indebtedness arising at the beginning of the transaction is direct cash credit, e.g. loans and discounting of commercial papers.

column5: When adopting the Fiqh viewpoint that considers minerals to be the property of the State, concession contracts may be applied only to State-owned lands, and not to privately-owned lands.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/4/1, under this viewpoint concession contracts may be applied to all types of lands, whether State- or privately-owned.

column5: The two parties of the issue contract of investment Sukuk are:
column6: The originator and the issue agent.
column7: The issuer and the subscribers.
column8: The issue manager and the investment trustee.
column9: The issuer and the underwriter.
column11: Per 5/1/4, the two parties of the issue contract are the issuer and the subscribers.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for limiting the Institution's rights, in case of the customer's breach of promise, to the difference between the cost of the item and its selling price to a third party is that:
column6: The customer has caused the Institution to enter into a deal that it would not have concluded in the absence of the promise, and must therefore compensate it for the lost mark-up.
column7: The lawful right in a guarantee is limited to the amount that compensates for the damage, and claiming the lost mark-up is irrational since no Murabahah took place.
column8: Hamish Jiddiyyah is a form of 'Arboun, which may be retained only in part.
column9: Murabahah is a trust-based contract that depends on transparency as to the cost price.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a guarantee covers only the damage suffered, and there is no mark-up where no Murabahah took place.

column5: Indices that precede price movements may be classified, with regard to central and area fluctuations, into:
column6: Centered oscillating indices, which measure price changes during a specific period in the past, and indicate probable future events.
column7: Ranged oscillating indices (band), which fluctuate between two areas, like overbuying or overselling.
column8: Sectoral indices, which measure the market situation of a certain sector or industry, such as the transport sector.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2, they divide into centered and ranged oscillating indices; sectoral indices belong to the general/specific classification (4/1).

column5: Acceptability of the electronic signature is based on the need to avoid the harm of online forgery of dealers' identities, and on the fact that Shari'ah encourages the use of technological means to preserve wealth, which is one of the five main aims (Maqasid) of Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, e-signature avoids harm from identity forgery and serves preservation of wealth, one of the five Maqasid.

column5: In a temporary Waqf of Sukuk and units of investment funds, the basis for determining the Waqf asset and profit shall be:
column6: The market value of the Sukuk and units at the date of creation of the Waqf, adjusted annually for the change in their purchasing power, whatever the terms of the offering document.
column7: The type of the Sukuk and funds, and the terms and conditions of the offering document or prospectus, to the extent they do not conflict with the Waqif's stipulation.
column8: The discretion of the overseer, even if it conflicts with the Waqif's stipulation.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4/15/1(b), the basis is the type of Sukuk/funds and the offering document terms, to the extent they do not conflict with the Waqif's stipulation.

column5: The managing company in Islamic insurance is entitled to the following, excluding:
column6: A share of the insurance surplus.
column7: The agency fee.
column8: Its own capital and the returns on its capital.
column9: Its specific share of the profits earned by investing the insurance assets through Mudarabah or investment agency.
column11: Per 3/1 the company is entitled to its capital, returns, agency fee and investment profit share; per 5/5 it gets no share of surplus.

column5: In principle, an arbitrator shall be a Muslim. However:
column6: A non-Muslim arbitrator could be appointed when acute need so requires, in order to arrive at a Shari'ah-accepted verdict.
column7: A non-Muslim arbitrator may be appointed only in disputes in which one of the parties is a non-Muslim.
column8: A non-Muslim arbitrator may be appointed whenever the two parties agree, and he may then apply any law chosen by them.
column9: A non-Muslim may be appointed only as chairman of the arbitration panel, but not as a sole arbitrator.
column11: Per 8/2, a non-Muslim arbitrator may be appointed when acute need requires, to arrive at a Shari'ah-accepted verdict (observing 11/1).

column5: In an Istisna'a contract, unless there is a customary practice or stipulation to the contrary, the expenses for delivering the subject matter of Istisna'a are borne by the orderer (Mustasni'), while the expenses for the delivery of the price are borne by the manufacturer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/4, the manufacturer bears the expenses of delivering the subject matter and the orderer bears those of delivering the price.

column5: In case the cardholder cancels the card after its issuance:
column6: The card issuer must return the issuance fees in full, since the card has been cancelled.
column7: The card issuer must return the issuance fees on a proportionate basis for the remaining validity period of the card.
column8: The card issuer may retain the issuance fees only if the card was activated or used.
column9: The card issuer is permitted not to return any part of the amount of the issuance fees.
column11: Per 5/2/1, the issuer need not return any part of the issuance fees, as they are for a job completed upon issuance.

column5: It is necessary to observe the rules for dealing in shares of corporations that deal partly in interest throughout the period of participation or trading; if the rules cannot be applied, it is obligatory to give up such investment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/4/8, the rules apply throughout the holding period, and the investment must be given up if they cannot be applied.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the binding nature of Waqf and the non-permissibility of resiling from it includes:
column6: The statement of the Prophet (PBUH) to ʿUmar (RA): If you wish, you can keep it as a Waqf, whereupon ʿUmar gave the land in charity on the condition that it would neither be sold, nor gifted, nor inherited.
column7: The prohibition of taking back charity, as the Prophet (PBUH) said: he who takes back his alms is like the one who swallows his vomit.
column8: The analogy upon the bequest, which becomes binding from the instance of its making.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/3, the ʿUmar Ḥadīth and the prohibition of taking back alms; a bequest is revocable (2/4/1/4).

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the ruling that no profit is to be sought in Mudarabah before preservation of the capital is:
column6: The Hadith: "When someone liberates a slave he owns with other parties, he should pay partners from his money, and if he has no money, the slave has to be equitably valued for him".
column7: The statement of Ali Ibn Abu Talib: "Profit is to be distributed as per the agreement of the two parties, whereas loss should be borne according to the ratios of contribution to the capital".
column8: The Hadith: "A prayer performer is just like a merchant who obtains profit only after preserving his capital…".
column9: The resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy that demand deposits are loans in the strict Shari'ah sense.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith likening the prayer performer to a merchant who profits only after preserving capital is the basis.

column5: In syndicated financing arranged on the basis of Musharakah, the Institutions participate jointly in providing the funds and bear any losses proportionately, whereas profits are shared as agreed upon.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2, losses are borne proportionately while profits are shared as agreed.

column5: The Mudarib is entitled to waive a right associated with the Mudarabah operation without the consent of the capital provider, if he deems this to be in the interest of the Mudarabah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/6, the Mudarib may not waive a right of the Mudarabah unless the capital provider has consented.

column5: Stipulating a reward for raising loans for another is:
column6: Absolutely impermissible, because it is a benefit arising from Qard.
column7: Absolutely permissible, without any restriction.
column8: Permissible as long as it is not a fictional device (Hilah) for dealing in Riba.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8, a reward for raising loans for another is permissible as long as it is not a Hilah for dealing in Riba.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Agency (Wakalah) is permissible with Gharar, if there are indications or traditions that can be used for specifying its subject matter. This holds true:
column6: Whether the agency is with or without remuneration, since the remuneration is not affected by Gharar in the subject matter.
column7: When the agency is free of charge; otherwise it is treated like Ijarah (hiring) and affected by Gharar.
column8: Only in specific agency, as general agency contracts are impermissible because they involve Gharar in the subject matter.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 6/3, this applies to agency free of charge; paid agency is treated like Ijarah and affected by Gharar. General agency is permissible.

column5: When leasing a Waqf at less than the rent of similar property is inevitable, it should be considered in view of the actual necessity, and hence excessive injustice (Ghabn Fahish) can be accepted.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2, when a lower rent is inevitable, it is considered in view of actual necessity, and excessive injustice can be accepted.

column5: There are two methods for calculation of the Zakah base: the method of net assets and the method of net investment assets. Regarding these two methods:
column6: They have the same basis of assessment; the Standard is based on the net investment assets method.
column7: The Institution must apply both methods and pay the higher of the two amounts of Zakah.
column8: They have different bases of assessment, yet if such difference is well recognized the final outcome will be the same; the Standard is based on the net assets method.
column9: They have different bases of assessment and necessarily lead to different outcomes; the Standard is based on the net investment assets method.
column11: Per 2/1, the two methods differ in basis but give the same outcome if the difference is recognized; the Standard adopts the net assets method.

column5: If the Institution signs a partnership contract with the client to purchase goods prior to the opening of credit and before the client concludes a sale contract with the supplier:
column6: The credit must be opened in the name of the Institution only.
column7: The credit must be opened in the name of the client only.
column8: It is permissible to open the credit in the name of either partner.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/6/1, where partnership precedes the credit and the client's purchase, the credit may be opened in either partner's name.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: An IFI appointed its customer as an agent to purchase a machine on behalf of the IFI. After the customer purchased the machine for the IFI, he wished to buy it from the IFI himself. This is:
column6: Permissible by way of offer and acceptance, provided that the guarantees stemming from the agency contract and the sale contract are kept separate; after conclusion of the sale contract, the machine becomes under the customer's guarantee.
column7: Permissible, but the machine remains under the guarantee of the IFI even after the conclusion of the sale contract.
column8: Not permissible, because the agent should not act for both parties to the contract.
column9: Permissible, and the machine is deemed sold to the customer automatically once he purchases it as agent, without any need for a new offer and acceptance, the price being the cost he incurred in purchasing it for the IFI, and the guarantee passing to him at that moment.
column11: Per 6/1/4, an agent may buy what he bought for the principal by offer and acceptance, keeping guarantees separate; then he bears the risk.

column5: At the time of settlement of the instalments of a credit transaction (such as a Murabahah), the Institution and the customer may agree that payment shall be made in another currency:
column6: Applying the exchange rate prevailing on the date the Murabahah contract was concluded.
column7: Applying the average exchange rate over the period of the credit transaction.
column8: Applying an exchange rate fixed at the time of concluding the Murabahah contract for all the instalments.
column9: Applying the spot exchange rate on the day of payment.
column11: Per 2/5, payment in another currency may be agreed at settlement only at the spot exchange rate on the day of payment.

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, it is permissible to stipulate that the Institution has a right to receive a lump sum out of the profits, since its equity share diminishes over time.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/6, it is not permitted to stipulate that one partner receives a lump sum out of the profits.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for treating commercial paper as a price for ascertained goods is that:
column6: It is a form of Suftajah, which is valid according to the preponderant opinion of the jurists, as it involves a transfer of funds from one place to another, and a transfer of funds is permitted even when the paper is not yet due.
column7: It is a form of Da' wa Ta'ajjal between the holder and the first beneficiary, in which a part of the debt is waived for early payment.
column8: It amounts to the sale of a debt to a person other than the debtor for ascertained goods, which the Maliki school permits if it takes place after possession, so that it does not become a delay of both counter-values.
column9: It is a form of Hawalah, which is agreed upon by consensus, the holder being transferred to the debtor of the drawer.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is a sale of debt to a non-debtor for ascertained goods, allowed by the Malikis with possession.

column5: Jahalah, which affects financial contracts, may be ignored with regard to the object of a subsidiary contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/2, Jahalah may be ignored with regard to the object of a subsidiary contract.

column5: An IFI managed a fund as an investment agent and claimed that the fund had incurred a loss during a year in which comparable funds investing in the same sector were profitable. The contract is silent on the evidentiary burden, and no regulation addresses it. The evidentiary burden:
column6: Transfers to the IFI only if the regulatory authority makes this mandatory.
column7: Is borne by Rab Al Maal, since the initial presumption is that the claimant bears the burden in all cases, even where circumstantial evidence contradicts the fiduciary's claim.
column8: Transfers to the IFI to establish the loss and the absence of misconduct or negligence, because circumstantial evidence contradicts its claim.
column9: Is borne by neither party, since the loss of a fiduciary is presumed.
column11: Per 6/3, a claimed loss while peer investments are profitable is circumstantial evidence that shifts the burden to the investment manager.

column5: The private employee should be informed about (……….), while the shared employee should be informed about (……….).
column6: The pay only .... the hiring period only
column7: The work, its type, and specifications .... the hiring period and the type of work in general
column8: The work, its type, and specifications .... the pay only
column9: The hiring period and the type of work he is supposed to do in general .... the work, its type, and specifications
column11: Per 4/4, the private employee is told the hiring period and the type of work in general; the shared employee the work, its type and specifications.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of issuing interest-bearing bonds is that:
column6: They involve Gharar in the amount of interest, since the rate of interest varies with the market until maturity.
column7: They represent, in their customary nature, a loan, and each loan that yields a benefit is Riba.
column8: They are a sale of a debt for a debt.
column9: They are bearer instruments.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4, bonds are loans by nature, and a loan yielding a benefit is Riba.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: Purchasing gold, silver or currency with cards is permissible:
column6: With a debit card or a charge card, in cases where the issuing Institution is able to settle the amount due to the party accepting the card without any delay.
column7: With a debit card only, because the charge card involves a credit period.
column8: With any type of card, including an interest-bearing credit card, provided the purchase is completed at the point of sale.
column9: Provided the gold, silver or currency is delivered to the cardholder within the free credit period.
column11: Per 4/4, gold, silver or currency may be bought by debit or charge card where the issuer settles with the merchant without delay.

column5: In the case of goods prepared for export through documentary credits to the benefit of the Institution, the amounts retained for the credit:
column6: Are deductible from zakatable assets as liabilities of the Institution towards the importer.
column7: Are neither subject to Zakah nor deductible from zakatable assets, since they have not yet been possessed.
column8: Are subject to Zakah as receivables of the Institution, since the credit is opened to its benefit.
column9: Are both subject to Zakah and deductible from zakatable assets.
column11: Per 5/2/6/8, such amounts are neither zakatable nor deductible, as not yet possessed; goods still held are zakatable as finished goods or in process.

column5: The Islamic reinsurance contract is considered as a binding donation contract, because:
column6: It is analogous to Munahadah (contribution of travelers to a pool of food victuals) or to pledge of donation.
column7: It is an agency contract which is binding on the agent.
column8: A gift is binding only when it is possessed.
column9: It is an exchange-based contract in which the premium is exchanged for the compensation.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the contract is a binding donation, analogous to Munahadah or to a pledge of donation.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Among contracts in which both counter-values are delayed, the following contract is valid even when the price is delayed:
column6: Sale of an ascertained commodity with a stipulated delay in its delivery.
column7: Istisna'a.
column8: Futures contract.
column9: Salam.
column11: Per 3/2/3, an Istisna'a contract is valid even when the price is delayed; the others are not permitted (3/2/2, 3/3).

column5: Al-Khatib Al-Shirbini explained that recourse is to be had to custom ('Urf) in determining possession because:
column6: The Lawgiver has defined possession precisely as physical transportation of the thing, and custom may be consulted only in matters on which the Lawgiver has been silent, such as units of measure.
column7: The language defines possession as taking a thing by hand.
column8: Possession is a matter of intention and not of action.
column9: The Lawgiver has used the term possession in an unqualified sense and deemed it the basis of rules without elaborating it, and there is no definition for it in the language.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, possession was used unqualified by the Lawgiver with no linguistic definition, so custom governs.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Forward contracts (both counter-values delayed) differ from futures transactions insofar as:
column6: They always end in cash settlement.
column7: They are concluded on the trading floor of the exchange.
column8: The price is the sole element that varies, and it is ascertained in the trading hall, while the other elements of the contract are standardised by the exchange.
column9: They are not organized in an exchange, and they are instruments of hedging that do not submit to financial supervision.
column11: Per 3/2/1, forward contracts are not organized in an exchange and are hedging instruments not subject to financial supervision.

column5: As the determination of possession in contracts is based on custom, if the custom of the people changes, the consideration of a mode as possession ceases, except for those things that have been specified by the Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, rules built on custom change with custom, except what the Shari'ah has specified.

column5: The bank is obliged to execute the credit when the documents presented conform to instructions, except:
column6: Upon proof of fraud or forgery of the documents.
column7: If the buyer objects to the quality of the goods after their arrival.
column8: If the market price of the goods has declined since the opening of the credit.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 3/1/4 and 2/4/3, only proof of fraud or forgery (or court nullification of the sale) relieves the bank; goods issues do not.

column5: The prohibition of concluding option contracts based on indices rests only on the prohibition of dealing in options themselves, and not on the reasons for prohibiting trading in indices.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, it rests on the same reasons as trading in indices, in addition to the prohibition of options.

column5: The fees charged by the acquirer from the card acceptor are not restricted to the actual cost, and part of them may go to the card issuer and card network, provided the cardholder shall not bear such fees in cards based on lending.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1/2/1, acquirer fees are by agreement and may be shared, but the cardholder may not bear them in lending-based cards.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Where there is a cooling-off option:
column6: The parties need not pay or deliver unless agreed otherwise, and voluntary payment or delivery does not end the option unless it indicates an intention to transfer ownership.
column7: The parties must make payment and delivery immediately upon the conclusion of the contract, while the option remains in force.
column8: The buyer must pay the price, while the seller may withhold delivery until the option period expires without the option lapsing, and the seller may use the item and keep its returns meanwhile.
column9: Voluntary payment or delivery by either party causes the option to lapse, since it indicates confirmation of the contract.
column11: Per 2/4/3, payment and delivery are not required; voluntary performance does not end the option unless it shows intent to transfer ownership.

column5: If the Institution freezes a customer's investment account to secure a debt, the customer remains entitled to share profits on the whole balance of the account after deducting the Institution's share as Mudarib.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/5/1, the customer still shares profits on the whole balance after the Mudarib's share is deducted.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: A conventional bank decided to convert. It holds in its warehouse a stock of liquor it had foreclosed from a defaulting borrower, and a customer still owes it the price of a quantity of liquor previously sold to him from this stock. The bank should:
column6: Sell the liquor and keep the proceeds, since it was acquired before the decision to convert.
column7: Destroy the liquor in its possession, and receive the price owed by the customer and donate it to charity.
column8: Destroy the liquor and waive the price owed by the customer.
column9: Sell the remaining liquor and donate the proceeds to charity, and waive the price owed by the customer.
column11: Per 8/1/5 and 8/1/4, impermissible commodities are destroyed; the unpaid price is collected and donated, not waived.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the cooling-off option is the Hadith narrated by Habban Bin Munqidh, in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) said:
column6: "If you are concluding a deal say: 'There shall be no Khalabah', then you shall have a 3-day option."
column7: "Overcharging a trusting buyer is forbidden", and in another narration: "is Riba."
column8: "No yield without risk taking", and in another narration: "No gain without risk taking", concerning a serf returned to his seller for a defect.
column9: "Muslims are bound by their conditions."
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for item 2, it is the Hadith of Habban Bin Munqidh on saying "no Khalabah" with a 3-day option.

column5: An Islamic bank underwrote, itself, the subscription of a new share issue of a Shari'ah-accepted company, and also marketed the shares. It charged the company an underwriting fee of 1% of the issue, in addition to the actual marketing expenses it incurred. The ruling is:
column6: Charging the underwriting fee is not permissible, but charging the actual marketing expenses is permissible.
column7: The underwriting fee is permissible, but the marketing expenses may not be charged, since marketing is part of underwriting.
column8: Both the underwriting fee and the marketing expenses are permissible.
column9: Neither the underwriting fee nor the marketing expenses may be charged.
column11: Per 2/3/2, no fee may be charged for the mere act of underwriting, but actual expenses of studies or marketing may be charged.

column5: Newly devised sets of combined contracts in contemporary applications:
column6: Are exempt from the Shari'ah rulings pertaining to combination of contracts, since they are agreed upon beforehand and approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Institution and by the central bank.
column7: May not make use of the Shari'ah concessions for combination of contracts.
column8: Should observe the general rules of Shari'ah with regard to structure, rulings, requirements and conditions, and may make use of the Shari'ah concessions for combination of contracts.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 7/4 and 7/5, such sets must observe Shari'ah general rules and combination rulings, and may use the concessions.

column5: The Waqf decision of a person whose legal competence is restricted:
column6: Because of irrationality is valid if the Waqf is made for a charitable purpose.
column7: Because of indebtedness depends for its validity on confirmation by his creditors.
column8: Because of indebtedness remains valid even if his creditors refrain from confirming it.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/2/3, an indebted person's Waqf depends on creditors' confirmation; an irrational person's Waqf is invalid unless made for himself while alive.

column5: An IFI has a liability (account payable) denominated in euro and fears the future devaluation of its own currency against the euro. Its treasury proposes the following alternatives. The permissible one is:
column6: Entering into a binding bilateral promise with another bank to buy and sell euro in one year.
column7: Executing back to back loans in euro and in local currency with another bank, each loan being made a contractual condition of the other.
column8: Entering into a forward contract to buy euro in one year at a rate fixed today.
column9: Selling goods on credit or by Murabahah in euro, the currency of the exposure.
column11: Per 2/4/2, for an account payable exposure, selling on credit or by Murabahah in that currency is permitted; the others breach 2/2, 2/9/1 and 2/4/1.

column5: In a repurchase agreement, if the contracting party desires liquidity:
column6: It acts as the seller, and the agreement is termed a repurchase agreement.
column7: It acts as the buyer, and the agreement is termed a repurchase agreement.
column8: It acts as the buyer, and the agreement is termed a reverse repurchase agreement.
column9: It acts as the seller, and the agreement is termed a reverse repurchase agreement.
column11: Per 5/6/1, the party seeking liquidity is the seller (repo); the party investing liquidity is the buyer (reverse repo).

column5: Arbitration is impermissible in:
column6: Disputes between an Institution and its employees.
column7: Disputes between Institutions located outside the host country of the Institution.
column8: What constitutes a right of Allah, Glory be to Him, such as Hudud (Shari'ah penalties).
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/2/1, arbitration is impermissible in rights of Allah such as Hudud; disputes with employees and outside the host country are in scope (item 1).

column5: Acts that are prohibited for the sake of blocking the way to excuses become permissible in case of need or desire to achieve a lawful interest.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, such acts become permissible in case of need or to achieve a lawful interest.

column5: An IFI holds Murabaha receivables of 1,000,000 owed by its customers. It agreed with a steel company to transfer these receivables to the company as the Salam capital for steel to be delivered to the IFI after one year. This transaction is:
column6: Permitted, provided that the receivables are secured by a pledge.
column7: Permitted, provided that the customers consent to the transfer.
column8: Permitted, since the debt is sold for a commodity and not for money, and the steel is delivered to the IFI after one year.
column9: Not permitted, since it is a sale of a monetary debt to a third party against a commodity with deferred delivery.
column11: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may not be sold for a deferred commodity, e.g., by making a debt owed by a third party the Salam capital.

column5: A creditor of a joint-liability company:
column6: Must first claim fulfilment of his rights from the company before having recourse to the partners, who are liable only for any shortfall.
column7: May claim from each partner only in proportion to that partner's share in the capital, since liability is divided among the partners according to their shares.
column8: Is entitled to demand fulfilment of all or part of his rights from any of the partners in any way he deems fit, without first claiming from the company.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2/2/1, the creditor may claim all or part from any partner as he deems fit, without first claiming from the company.

column5: The permissibility of stipulating that a debtor in default is obliged to donate a sum of money to be spent by the Institution on charitable causes is based on:
column6: The Hadith: "Default in payment on the part of a solvent debtor is unjust."
column7: The decision of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on penalty clauses in Istisna'a contracts.
column8: The principle that the debtor is liable for the expenses of which he is the cause.
column9: The commitment to make a donation, which is well established in the Maliki school of law.
column11: Per the basis, it is an instance of the commitment to donate, established in the Maliki school (Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar).

column5: A customer's Murabahah debt fell due, and he asked the IFI to extend the date of repayment by six months. The IFI agreed. In this case, the IFI:
column6: May charge an additional return proportional to the extension period, provided it is agreed upon at the time of rescheduling.
column7: Should charge only the actual expenses of the rescheduling transaction.
column8: May not charge anything at all, not even the actual expenses of the rescheduling transaction.
column9: May charge a lump-sum return not linked to the extension period, since it is not interest.
column11: Per 5/3/2/4/1, no return may be taken for extending the repayment date in any credit facility; only actual rescheduling expenses are charged.

column5: When the Institution is the beneficiary of Monetization, it shall use its own bodies for selling the Monetization commodity, though using brokers for this purpose is permissible.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2, Institutions avoid proxy in selling the commodity, even with a third party, and use their own bodies; brokers are permissible.

column5: The cost of preparing the contracts to be signed between the Institution and the client:
