column6: May be fixed as a percentage of the approved facility limit, provided that the percentage is agreed upon in the contract and paid by the client at the date of signing, whatever the actual work load of preparing the contracts.
column7: Should be borne entirely by the client in all cases, being the beneficiary of the facility, irrespective of the actual work load or the terms of the contract.
column8: Should be borne entirely by the Institution in all cases, and nothing of it may be charged to the client, even if the contract indicates otherwise.
column9: Should be shared between the two parties, unless the contract indicates otherwise, and be fair and commensurate with the actual work load so as not to comprise an implicit fee for commitment or for offering the facility.
column11: Per 5/3/1/4/1, the cost is shared unless the contract says otherwise, and must be fair so as not to hide a commitment or offering fee.

column5: It is permissible to charge a commission for providing a credit facility in documentary credit, since the facility is merely a readiness to lend and not the loan itself.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the facility is preparatory to a loan; since commission on a loan is prohibited, so is it on the facility.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, the wisdom of making Salam permissible includes all of the following, excluding:
column6: It facilitates financing for people in need of it, such as farmers, market gardeners and merchants who need working capital.
column7: It meets immediate needs for liquidity, giving the seller flexibility in using the sale proceeds before the commodity is delivered.
column8: The buyer may benefit by acquiring the commodity at a price below the market price.
column9: Its permissibility is confined to agricultural businesses.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Salam is commonly agricultural, but its permissibility is not confined to that; it extends to industry and trade.

column5: Where the amendment of a documentary credit involves a rescheduling of the duration of the credit facility, the Institution is permitted to charge:
column6: Only the actual expenses incurred, as a definite sum and not a percentage.
column7: A percentage of the credit amount for the amendment service, but not for the extended period.
column8: No fees or expenses at all.
column9: An additional fee reflecting the extended duration, as a percentage of the credit amount.
column11: Per 3/3/1, for an amendment rescheduling the credit's duration, only actual expenses as a definite sum may be charged.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: After its conversion, a bank continued to charge its corporate customers an annual commission of 1% on the unused portion of approved credit lines, as consideration for making the facility available. The Shari'ah Supervisory Board should rule that:
column6: It is not permissible to take a commission for providing a mere facility; the commission may be linked to expenses incurred for executing the credit facility.
column7: It is permissible, provided the commission is a fixed amount and not a percentage.
column8: It is permissible, provided the commission is donated to charity.
column9: It is permissible, since no interest is charged on the amounts actually drawn, and the commission is consideration for making the facility available, the bank bearing the risk of the undrawn amount.
column11: Per 5, no commission may be taken for a mere facility; only charges linked to execution expenses are allowed.

column5: Hawalah is a contract of sale of a debt and is therefore subject to the conditions of sale contracts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1, Hawalah is an independent contract made out of courtesy and is not a contract of sale.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When the agent, for no reasonable excuse, refrains from carrying on agency that he has been paid for, and the work he has done was beneficial:
column6: He becomes entitled to the remuneration commensurate with the part of work done, and is not liable for any loss resulting from his refusal, since agency is basically a non-binding contract that either party may terminate at any time without compensation.
column7: He becomes entitled to the remuneration commensurate with the part of work done, within the limits of the contract value for that part, and is bound to indemnify the principal for any actual loss resulting from his refusal to continue.
column8: He is not entitled to any remuneration, and he is bound to indemnify the principal for any actual loss resulting from his refusal to continue the work.
column9: He becomes entitled to the full remuneration agreed upon, because the work done was beneficial.
column11: Per 4/2/7, he gets a proportionate fee within the contract value for that part and indemnifies the principal for actual loss.

column5: It is permitted to create Waqf over a common share of an asset, whether divisible or indivisible, and if the common share is leased, the Waqf is entitled to receive its share of the rent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/11, Waqf of a common share is permitted, and the Waqf receives its share of the rent if it is leased.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: An IFI stipulated in a lease contract that it may add a supplementary rental at the beginning of each lease period to cover maintenance, insurance and taxes levied on owners. At the start of a new period, the lessee refused to accept the supplementary rental. The lessee had previously given a promise to purchase the leased asset. The IFI may:
column6: Exercise its rights under the promise and add the supplementary rent for that lease period to the purchase price.
column7: Revoke the contract, or exercise its rights under the promise and demand performance from the lessee, provided that the supplementary rent for that lease period is not added to the purchase price.
column8: Revoke the contract only, and it thereby loses its rights under the promise to purchase.
column9: Neither revoke the contract nor exercise its rights under the promise, because the amount of the supplementary rental was not known at the time of contract.
column11: Per 11/2, the lessor may revoke, or enforce the purchase promise provided that the supplementary rent for that period is not added to the price.

column5: With respect to preference shares:
column6: It is permissible to issue preference shares that have priority in the distribution of profits, provided the general assembly approves and the priority does not extend to the return of capital at liquidation, and provided that the preference is stated in the articles of association.
column7: It is not permitted to grant certain shares any feature, including voting rights, beyond the rights attached to ordinary shares.
column8: It is not permissible to issue preference shares with special financial features granting priority at liquidation or profit distribution, but procedural or administrative features, like voting rights, may be granted to certain shares.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/6, financial priority is barred, while procedural/administrative features such as voting rights may be granted.

column5: The possession of documents, like bills of lading and warehouse receipts, is deemed constructive possession of what the documents represent provided that:
column6: They are endorsed by a bank, and the commodities have been physically transported to the possessor's warehouse, since mere possession of the documents never represents possession of the commodities.
column7: The commodities are of a kind that is not estimated by weight or measure.
column8: They are issued in the name of the possessor or acknowledge his interest therein, the ascertainment of the commodities is attained through them, and the possessor can undertake transactions in them.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/5, documents in the possessor's name or acknowledging his interest, through which goods are ascertained and can be dealt in, give constructive possession.

column5: Documentation in writing is:
column6: Recommended by Shari'ah, and its form and evidential value are specified by the Shari'ah texts.
column7: Obligatory according to the majority of Fuqaha, relying on the literal meaning of the Quranic verse on transactions involving future obligations, whether it is in the form of ordinary or official documents.
column8: Recommended by Shari'ah only in the form of official documents.
column9: Recommended by Shari'ah, whether in the form of ordinary (private) or official documents, customary practice being applicable in drawing them up and determining their evidential value.
column11: Per 2/4/1 and the basis, writing is recommended and custom governs its form and evidential value; Ibn Hazm alone held it obligatory.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: The board, on its own initiative or on request of the institution, has the right to review a previous Fatwa even if such revision would lead to issuing a new Fatwa that contravenes the former one.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 11/2, the board may review a prior Fatwa; the Institution then follows the new one and rectifies the old one's effects.

column5: The issue contract has all the legal effects of the contract upon which the issued certificates are based. This occurs:
column6: Upon publication of the prospectus.
column7: Upon maturity of the Sukuk.
column8: After closing of the subscription and the allotment of the certificates.
column9: Upon payment of the subscription amount by the first subscriber.
column11: Per 5/1/3, the issue contract takes all legal effects of the underlying contract after closing of subscription and allotment of the certificates.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of agency from the Sunnah is:
column6: The consensus of Fuqaha demonstrated by the author of Al-Bahr Al-Zakhkhar and others.
column7: The fiqh principle that what matters in contracts are intentions and meanings rather than wording and constructions.
column8: The verse: {So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the town, and let him find out which is the good lawful food}.
column9: The Hadith narrated by Urwah Al-Bariqi that the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave him one dinar to purchase a sacrificial sheep for the Prophet.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Sunnah evidence is the Hadith of Urwah Al-Bariqi; the verse is the Qur'anic evidence and the other is Ijma'.

column5: A Hawalah contract cannot be concluded on a deferred basis or subject to the happening of a particular event, because:
column6: It has the character of a contract of immediate exchange, by which the transferee and the payer immediately enter into a new relationship.
column7: The payer must be a debtor to the transferor at the time of the contract, so that the transferred debt is settled from the payer's debt to the transferor immediately.
column8: It is a contract of sale of debt, which must be concluded on a spot basis.
column9: It is a contract of courtesy that is not binding on the parties.
column11: Per the basis on form, Hawalah is an immediate transfer creating an immediate relationship; suspending it conflicts with its nature.

column5: Reciprocal possession stipulated in the contract of Sarf (transaction in gold, silver and currencies) is:
column6: Delivery by one party within the session, with the delivery by the other party deferred to an agreed date.
column7: Delivery and acceptance of delivery within three business days of the contract.
column8: Registration of the transfer in the books of the institution, even if it takes place after the session of the contract.
column9: Delivery and acceptance of delivery within the session of the contract on a spot basis (Yadan Bi Yadin).
column11: Per 3/7, reciprocal possession in Sarf is delivery and acceptance of delivery within the contract session on a spot basis (Yadan Bi Yadin).

column5: If the Waqf superintendent lends the Waqf assets:
column6: The borrower has to pay the normal rent for similar assets.
column7: The borrower owes nothing, since lending is a form of donation.
column8: The superintendent personally has to pay the normal rent for similar assets.
column9: The loan is void, and the borrower owes nothing for the period of use.
column11: Per 5/3/5, the superintendent shall not lend Waqf assets; if he does, the borrower has to pay the normal rent for similar assets.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for stating that profit is not realised unless the capital is recovered or maintained intact is:
column6: The consensus reported by Ibn Al-Mundhir on the permissibility of Mudarabah.
column7: The Hadith that Al-'Abbas Ibn Abdul-Muttalib stipulated to the Mudarib that he should not travel by sea, pass by valleys or trade in livestock.
column8: The Hadith that the instance of a Musali is that of a businessperson who will not secure profit unless the capital is secured.
column9: The Hadith that Umar Ibn Al-Khattab gave an orphan's funds to a man for Mudarabah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Musali Hadith shows that profit cannot be distributed before the capital is recovered or kept intact.

column5: The cards have five parties, which are:
column6: The card issuer, the cardholder, the card acceptor, the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, and the card network.
column7: The card issuer, the cardholder, the card acceptor (the merchant), the acquirer (bank of the merchant), and the card network.
column8: The card issuer, the cardholder, the card acceptor, the acquirer, and the correspondent bank of the cardholder.
column9: The card issuer, the cardholder, the card acceptor, the guarantor of the cardholder, and the card network.
column11: Per 2/1, the five parties are the issuer, cardholder, card acceptor (merchant), acquirer (merchant's bank) and card network.

column5: A Shari'ah Supervisory Board should be formed for the Islamic reinsurance company in order to:
column6: Supervise the establishment of the company, verify its contracts and documents, oversee its applications and report on its activities.
column7: Act as the agent of the reinsurance account in managing it.
column8: Approve only the reinsurance arrangements with traditional reinsurance companies, and not the contracts of the Islamic reinsurance company itself.
column9: Determine the reinsurance premiums and the compensations payable to the insurance companies, in the light of the actuarial studies of the company.
column11: Per 8/2, the SSB supervises establishment, verifies contracts and documents, overviews applications and issues Shari'ah reports.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: Among the conditions that must be fulfilled for revocation by exercise of a cooling-off option to be valid:
column6: Existence of the cause triggering the option to revoke at the time of conclusion of the contract, and its being known to the other party.
column7: Notification of the revocation by the owner of the option to the other party as required by custom.
column8: Consent of the other party to the revocation.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/1–6/4, the cause must exist at the time of revocation and notification is required; the other party's consent is not a condition.

column5: The Mudarib is not entitled to sell items for the Mudarabah operation at less than the common or market price, or to buy items at a price higher than common prices:
column6: Unless the difference in price does not exceed one-third of the common price at the time of the transaction.
column7: Unless it is intended to achieve an objective obviously in the interest of the Mudarabah.
column8: Unless the capital provider is informed of it afterwards and does not object to it within a reasonable time.
column9: Under any circumstances whatsoever, even if the capital provider has consented.
column11: Per 9/5, such sales or purchases are barred unless intended to achieve an objective obviously in the Mudarabah's interest.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of underwriting issues of shares without taking consideration is that:
column6: It is a form of agency with remuneration, the underwriter acting as agent of the company.
column7: It is a donation of the nominal value of the shares to the company, made by the underwriter to secure the success of the issue.
column8: It is an undertaking not involving an impermissible act, such as taking a commission for a guarantee.
column9: It is a sale of shares that the underwriter does not own, to be delivered at a later date.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, underwriting without consideration involves no impermissible act such as a commission for a guarantee.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: A customer bought a car on the stipulation that it be automatic. On delivery it turned out to be manual, and the customer, who could return it, chose to keep it. The customer:
column6: Is entitled to a partial refund equal to the difference in price between an automatic car and a manual car.
column7: Pays only the price of a manual car.
column8: Is entitled to compensation for inferiority (Arsh), as in the case of a defect.
column9: Accepts it for its full price without any entitlement to compensation.
column11: Per 4/3/1, he may return it or keep it for the full price without compensation; a partial refund applies only if return is impossible.

column5: If the lessee becomes insolvent during the Ijarah term and the court considers continuity of the Ijarah to be in the interest of the creditors, the lessor shall receive the rent amount in full.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/5/2, where the court considers continuity in the creditors' interest, the lessor receives the rent in full.

column5: Regarding expenses in Islamic insurance:
column6: All expenses are shared between the company and the fund in proportion to their respective capital.
column7: The company bears all the expenses of its operations, including those relating to its tasks for investing the insurance assets, while the fund bears all direct expenses of managing insurance operations.
column8: The company bears all direct expenses pertaining to management of insurance operations, while the fund bears the expenses of investing its assets as well as the company's general overheads, which are charged to the fund at the end of each year.
column9: The fund bears all the expenses, including those relating to the company's tasks for investing the insurance assets.
column11: Per 3/1 and 3/2, the company bears its own operating and investment-task expenses; the fund bears direct insurance management expenses.

column5: The most important meanings of Muwata`ah (Tawatu') in Fiqh terminology include:
column6: Explicit or implicit intention of the parties to the contract to use a certain trick for practicing Riba through a Shari'ah accepted contractual form.
column7: An unrevealed prior agreement between the two parties to perform a Shari'ah-permissible act or deal for the sake of finding a Shari'ah-accepted exit (acceptable trick).
column8: Coincidence of the intentions of parties to the contract at the stage of preparatory negotiations that precede the signing of the contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/1, Muwata`ah has several meanings, and all three listed are among the most important.

column5: When the relationship between the Institutions participating in a syndicated financing operation is arranged on the basis of Mudarabah:
column6: The syndication manager acts as a Mudarib and becomes the exclusive operation manager according to the Mudarabah contract.
column7: The syndication manager becomes entitled to remuneration whether profit is actually materialized or not.
column8: The lead manager undertakes to manage the operations for no reward, and the financing Institutions share the profit.
column9: The Institutions participate jointly in providing the funds, and may select a joint committee to undertake management.
column11: Per 6/1, under Mudarabah the syndication manager is the Mudarib and the exclusive operation manager.

column5: In Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, the method of transferring the title in the leased asset to the lessee must be evidenced in a document separate from the Ijarah contract, using one of the following methods:
column6: A promise to sell for a token or other consideration, or by accelerating the payment of the remaining rental, or by paying the market value of the leased property.
column7: A sale contract executed along with the Ijarah that becomes effective on a future date.
column8: A promise to give it as a gift contingent upon payment of the remaining instalments, inserted as a clause within the Ijarah contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/1 and 8/7, promises of sale or gift in a separate document are allowed; a future-effective sale or a promise inside the Ijarah contract is not.

column5: A customer paid an Institution US dollars and asked it to transfer the equivalent amount in euros to a beneficiary abroad. The euros reach the beneficiary after a short period, so spot delivery of the exchanged currencies is not realized. Under the Standard on Combination of Contracts, this is:
column6: Permissible, only if the Institution does not charge any fee for the transfer.
column7: Impermissible, because combining currency exchange with Ju'alah is an example of contradictory contracts, and the fee charged for the transfer would be a price for the currency, which must be settled on the spot.
column8: Forgivable, because violation of the rules of currency exchange, such as spot delivery, in a contract combining exchange with money transfer is forgiven in subsidiary and implicit contracts.
column9: Impermissible, because spot delivery can never be ignored in currency exchange.
column11: Per 5/2/3, ignoring spot delivery where currency exchange is combined with money transfer is forgivable as a subsidiary matter.

column5: An electronic message sent by the offering party through website or e-mail is considered to be an announcement or an invitation for contracting rather than an offer, when:
column6: It does not indicate all the rights and commitments relating to the contract in question.
column7: The sender stipulates a condition that he should have the right of withdrawal even if the message is accepted.
column8: It is addressed to the public in general rather than to a specific person.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/3, a message lacking all rights and commitments, or reserving withdrawal after acceptance, is an invitation to contract, not an offer.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a bilateral binding promise in Murabahah to the purchase orderer is that:
column6: It falls under the heading of sale of debt.
column7: It is in exchange for the right to contract, which is a mere intention and wish that is not a subject of exchange.
column8: It amounts to a contract prior to acquisition of the item to be sold.
column9: It leads to the buyer guaranteeing the share of the other party, which is Riba.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a promise binding both parties amounts to a contract concluded before the Institution acquires the item.

column5: Any extension of time by the lessor after the stipulated time for prompt payment of accelerated rentals is considered as a consent to deferral of payment throughout the extension period, and not a right of the lessee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 6/2.

column5: If an Institution manages transactions on the basis of Mudarabah, Musharakah or investment agency, its guaranteeing the fluctuations of currency exchange rates, so that the investors will recover their investment shares irrespective of the behaviour of the currency market, is:
column6: Prohibited, because it is tantamount to the Mudarib, partner or agent guaranteeing the capital of other partners or investors.
column7: Permissible, because it is a guarantee of currency risk and not of the capital, so that the investors bear no loss resulting from the behaviour of the currency market.
column8: Permissible, if the Institution charges no fee for the guarantee.
column9: Permissible, if the guarantee is limited to a specified percentage of the capital.
column11: Per 3/3/4, guaranteeing exchange rate fluctuations amounts to the manager guaranteeing the investors' capital.

column5: In Monetization, the client shall not delegate the Institution or its agent to sell, on his behalf, a commodity that he purchased from the same Institution. An exception to this rule is:
column6: When the regulations do not permit the client to sell the commodity except through the same Institution, in which case he may delegate the Institution to do so after he, actually or constructively, receives the commodity.
column7: When the regulations do not permit the client to sell the commodity except through the same Institution, in which case he may delegate the Institution to do so even before he receives the commodity, so as to safeguard the deal from being nullified by the law.
column8: When the Institution undertakes the agency free of charge, since agency without remuneration does not link the purchase and sale contracts.
column9: When the client is unable to find a buyer for the commodity within the period agreed upon in the Murabahah contract.
column11: Per 4/7, delegation to the Institution is allowed only where regulations require selling through it, and only after actual or constructive receipt.

column5: A solvent customer, unable to pay a Murabahah instalment on time, asked the IFI to extend the maturity of his outstanding debt by one year. The IFI agreed on condition that the customer pay an additional 5% of the outstanding debt for the extension. This arrangement is:
column6: Permissible, because the customer is solvent and agreed to the additional payment.
column7: Impermissible, because the date of payment of the debt may not be extended in exchange for an additional payment, whether the debtor is solvent or insolvent.
column8: Permissible, provided the additional 5% is spent on charitable causes approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board and not kept by the Institution, since the additional payment is then a donation and not an increase over the debt.
column9: Permissible, provided the extension is documented as a new Murabahah on the same commodity.
column11: Per 5/7, extension against additional payment is barred for solvent and insolvent debtors alike; refinancing the same commodity is also barred (2/2/8).

column5: An IFI issued a letter of guarantee for USD 1 million, valid for one year, in favour of a contractor's client, and charged the contractor 1% per annum of the guaranteed amount, described as a 'guarantee commission'. The contractor will use the guarantee for a permissible project. This charge is:
column6: Permissible, because the letter of guarantee is without cover and the IFI bears the risk, so that the commission is a fee for risk assumed rather than for administrative services, and its amount is known at the outset.
column7: Impermissible, because it is remuneration for the guarantee per se, computed on the amount and duration; the IFI may charge only administrative expenses not exceeding what others charge.
column8: Permissible, because the contractor uses the guarantee for a permissible project.
column9: Permissible, because it is a final letter of guarantee and not a preliminary one.
column11: Per 6/1/1-6/1/2, a fee based on amount and duration is consideration for the guarantee per se; only administrative expenses are allowed.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: Conduct that transfers ownership and creates rights for third parties, such as selling or gifting the sale item, is an impediment to revocation by exercise of a cooling-off option.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/3, conduct that transfers ownership to a third party, such as sale or gift of the item, prevents revocation.

column5: If the mortgagor, at the request of the mortgagee, arranges Islamic insurance for the mortgaged asset, and the compensation for its damage is received in the form of a cash amount:
column6: The amount is paid to the mortgagee in settlement of the debt before its maturity, and the mortgage ends upon his receipt of it.
column7: The amount is paid to the mortgagor free of the mortgage, and the mortgage ends, unless the mortgagee agrees to its continuation as a loan.
column8: The amount is mortgaged with its returns, by depositing it in a frozen investment account of the mortgagor.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8, cash insurance compensation replaces the asset and is mortgaged with its returns in a frozen investment account owned by the mortgagor.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The expenses of the investment departments and the bodies which endorse their decisions, as well as the expenses of the follow-up and accounting departments, may be charged to investment accounts as part of their share of shared expenses.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/2/2, these are expenses of tasks the Mudarib must perform and may not be charged to investment accounts.

column5: The fees of the covered card are not restricted to the actual direct cost; however, if the cover was provided through an interest-free loan from the card issuer, the fees of the card become subject to the rulings of the lending-based card.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2/2/2 and 6/2/2/3, fees follow 5/1/2, but a loan-funded cover brings in the lending-based card rulings.

column5: A customer owing an IFI 8,000 mortgaged to it gold jewellery worth 10,000 at the time of mortgaging. Due to the negligence of the IFI's staff, the jewellery was lost on a date when its value was 12,000. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The IFI owes no compensation, but the debt is reduced by the value of the jewellery.
column7: The IFI is liable to compensate the value of the jewellery on the date of mortgaging (10,000), and the debt is extinguished, since the value of the jewellery at that time exceeded the debt.
column8: The debt is extinguished, and the IFI owes nothing further, because the mortgaged asset is a trust in its hands and the loss occurred while it was in the possession of the mortgagee.
column9: The IFI is liable to compensate the value of the jewellery on the date of its perish (12,000); the debt of 8,000 remains valid, and the parties may perform clearance.
column11: Per 3/2/4, on loss through negligence the mortgagee compensates the value on the date of perish; the debt stays valid and set-off may be made.

column5: Fulfilling a bilateral promise to perform an act that is permitted but not binding under the Shari'ah is a religious obligation on both parties, but is not legally binding except:
column6: Where a real commercial transaction is impossible without a binding bilateral promise because of legal requirements or commercial custom, and the aim is not merely financing.
column7: Where the objective of the bilateral promise is to provide financing to the client, provided that it is documented in writing and the institution owns the asset at the time of the promise.
column8: Where both parties agree in writing that the bilateral promise shall be binding.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2, it binds only where the transaction is impossible otherwise by law or custom, and the aim is not merely financing.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for Ju'alah being non-binding for the worker is that:
column6: The work to be done is uncertain, thus it resembles Mudarabah, which is not binding.
column7: The accrual of the compensation is contingent upon a condition, thus it resembles bequest, which is not binding.
column8: The worker is a trustee over the offeror's property.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, for the worker it resembles Mudarabah (uncertain work); the bequest analogy applies to the offeror.

column5: Combining sale and lending in one contract is permissible, provided that each of the two contracts is permissible on its own.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1, combining sale and lending in one contract is explicitly banned by Shari'ah.

column5: The Hadith of Ibn Umar about selling camels at Al-Baqi' for a price quoted in dinar and taking dirham is evidence that:
column6: A debt may be settled in another currency at the rate agreed on the day the debt was incurred.
column7: A debt may be settled in another currency based on the price of the day, provided the parties do not leave each other with something remaining owed between them.
column8: A binding bilateral promise to exchange currencies is permissible when the price is quoted in one currency and paid in another.
column9: Currencies of the same kind may be exchanged with inequality, provided it is hand to hand.
column11: Per the basis, the Prophet allowed taking the other currency at the price of the day provided nothing remained owed between them.

column5: It is prohibited in Shari'ah:
column6: To use an index to determine the portion of the variable Ujrah (rent) that represents the return.
column7: To conclude option contracts on indices, or contracts on the Index Contracts' Multiplier.
column8: To link the amount of a donation to a charitable body, in case of delayed settlement, with a particular index.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/2 and 6/3, options on indices and contracts on the multiplier are prohibited; 5/4 and 5/8 permit the other two uses.

column5: The basis for permitting Mudarabah capital to be constituted by the value of tangible assets is that the objective of Mudarabah, making profit, can be realised whether the capital is contributed in tangible assets or in cash.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis (Maliki and Hanbali view), profit can be realised whether capital is in tangible assets or cash.

column5: Provision for indemnity, made for a confirmed commitment relating to an initial legal verdict (before appeal) stipulating payment of a specific amount as indemnity:
column6: Is never deductible from zakatable assets, even after a final verdict.
column7: Should be deducted from zakatable assets at half its amount until the appeal is decided.
column8: Should not be deducted from zakatable assets until it becomes due for payment by virtue of a final verdict.
column9: Should be deducted from zakatable assets in full once the initial verdict is issued.
column11: Per 7/3/7, the indemnity provision is not deducted until it becomes due for payment by a final verdict.

column5: Ju'alah may be used for the realisation of scientific discoveries, inventions and designs, such as symbols and trade marks, where entitlement to compensation is contingent upon the realisation of the discoveries, the registration of patents or the creation of designs conforming to the offeror's conditions.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/5, such Ju'alah is allowed, with the Ju'l contingent on realisation, patent registration or conforming designs.

column5: Natural things that are not subject to transformation by manufacture or construction by man, such as animals, fruits and vegetables, are not by definition covered by the term Istisna'a.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 3/1/1.

column5: An IFI and its customer stipulated arbitration in their Murabahah contract. When a dispute arose, they signed an arbitration document appointing an arbitrator and specifying a period of three months. The period expired without issuance of the verdict, and the two parties did not agree on extending it. One month later, the arbitrator issued his verdict. The correct ruling is:
column6: The verdict is valid, because the arbitrator may extend the arbitration period at his own discretion.
column7: The verdict is valid as long as it conforms to the rules of Shari'ah.
column8: The arbitrator became terminated on expiry of the arbitration period, so he no longer had the mandate to issue the verdict.
column9: The verdict is binding, because arbitration was stipulated as a condition in the contract.
column11: Per 9/6, when the arbitration period expires without a verdict, the arbitrator becomes terminated unless the two parties agree to extend it.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of stipulating compensation in a sale contract as a condition for waiver of the revocation right is:
column6: Analogy to Iqalah, which is a form of contract revocation and has to be performed without any increase or decrease in considerations.
column7: That Shari'ah prohibits waiver of some rights, such as pre-emption and demarcation rights, against compensation.
column8: That the party who waives his right owns a benefit that makes him entitled to remuneration.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the bar rests on analogy to Iqalah and on the prohibition of waiving rights such as pre-emption against compensation.

column5: The receipt of a cheque requiring prompt payment constitutes constructive possession of the amount written on it, making it usable in transactions that stipulate possession, if the cheque is:
column6: A banker's cheque.
column7: A certified cheque, or one legally deemed a certified cheque whereby a certain amount is mandatorily maintained in the drawer's account.
column8: An ordinary uncertified cheque drawn by the client on his account.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/1-7/2, banker's and certified (or deemed certified) cheques give constructive possession; ordinary cheques do not.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring substitution of the Waqf asset if the underlying subject of Waqf turned into a prohibited one includes:
column6: The analogy upon the sale of a pledged asset to discharge the debt, since the Waqf asset then becomes unfit to remain as a Waqf, and the overseer must sell it and distribute the price to the beneficiaries.
column7: The right of the Waqif to resile from the Waqf if its subject becomes prohibited.
column8: One of the conditions of the Waqf asset is that it should be permissible (mubāḥ), and the statement of the Prophet (PBUH): Allah is Good, and accepts only that which is good.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 10/1/3, the Waqf asset must be permissible, and the Ḥadīth: Allah is Good and accepts only what is good.

column5: Mortgaging an income which is still to be owned is:
column6: Impermissible, because the mortgaged object does not yet exist and its quantity is unknown at the time of the mortgage, which is excessive Gharar.
column7: Permissible only if the income is mortgaged along with the principal, and not independently of it.
column8: Permissible if the principal (income earning asset) is specified, whether the income is mortgaged along with the principal or independently.
column9: Permissible even if the principal is not specified, since the income is certain to be earned in the future.
column11: Per 7, future income may be mortgaged if its income-earning principal is specified, either with the principal or independently.

column5: The Institution has the right to charge the cost of the feasibility study of the project it prepares, provided that:
column6: The client requests such a study for his own interest.
column7: The cost of the study is agreed upon beforehand.
column8: The feasibility study leads to approval of the financing.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/3/1/5, the cost may be charged when the client requests the study for his own interest and the cost is agreed upon beforehand.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: The characteristic that distinguishes the credit card from the charge card is that the credit card:
column6: Involves a percentage commission received by the issuer from the party accepting the card.
column7: Provides a revolving credit facility within the credit limit and credit period determined by the issuer, the cardholder being allowed to defer payment and being charged interest for the duration of the credit.
column8: Is used to pay for goods and services and to obtain cash, within a credit limit determined by the issuer, the cardholder being obliged to pay by the end of a prescribed credit period following receipt of a statement.
column9: Involves a direct obligation on the issuer to pay the party accepting the card for the cardholder's purchases, within a specified transaction credit limit (or the agreed increase thereon).
column11: Per 2/3/1 and 2/3/3, revolving interest-bearing credit is its distinguishing feature; per 2/3/4 the other features are shared with the charge card.

column5: Following the declaration of insolvency, the debts owed to the creditors are attached to:
column6: The existing property of the debtor at the time of sequestration, as well as any property that accrues to him without his dealing, such as gifts.
column7: Only the existing property of the debtor at the time of sequestration, excluding any gifts he receives afterwards.
column8: All property the debtor acquires after sequestration, including property acquired through his new sale and purchase transactions.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/2, debts attach to existing property and property accruing without his dealing, e.g., gifts; new dealings attach to his liability (5/4).

column5: An investor sold shares of a listed company that he did not own, relying on a broker's promise to lend him the shares on the delivery date. The broker stipulated that the investor pay him the price of the shares so that the broker could deposit it and earn interest in return for the loan. This transaction is:
column6: Permitted, provided that the shares are delivered to the buyer on time and the sale price is paid to the broker.
column7: Not permitted, because the broker's promise to lend does not constitute ownership or possession, and the prohibition is stronger given the interest stipulation.
column8: Permitted, because the broker's promise to lend the shares constitutes constructive possession, and the investor will deliver them on the delivery date and the sale is therefore valid.
column9: Permitted, provided that the investor donates the interest earned to charity and the broker does not keep any part of it.
column11: Per 4/1/2/7, selling unowned shares is prohibited; a broker's promise to lend is not ownership, especially with interest.

column5: According to the resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy cited as the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, a bilateral promise can be made binding on the two parties:
column6: Where a sale cannot be concluded because the seller does not own the commodity, and public interest requires obligating both parties to contract in future, as in letters of credit for imports.
column7: Whenever the parties so agree in writing, as both parties are bound by their conditions, whatever the nature of the transaction.
column8: In all Murabahah transactions to the purchase orderer, since the institution purchases the commodity in reliance on the customer's promise, whether or not it takes ownership of the commodity beforehand.
column9: Where the objective of the parties is merely to provide financing, provided that the bilateral promise is documented.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (Fiqh Academy Res. 157), binding bilateral promises are allowed where needed, as with letters of credit.

column5: It is permitted to sell an entity that is in existence and has ongoing permissible activities, or a share of it, without considering the provisions of the sale of debt in respect of its debts:
column6: Provided that its debts do not exceed 50% of its assets, and the debts are generated from the turnover of its business.
column7: Whatever the ratio of debts, as long as they are generated from the turnover of its business, provided the entity is not entirely composed of debt.
column8: Provided that its debts do not exceed one third of its assets, and the entity is not entirely composed of debt, so that they remain ancillary.
column9: Provided that its tangible assets exceed 50% of its assets at all times, and the entity is not entirely composed of debt, whatever the source of its debts.
column11: Per 8/1, debts arising from turnover are ancillary to the activity, whatever their ratio, unless the entity is entirely debt.

column5: Delivery of al-Muslam Fihi before the due date:
column6: May take place if the goods conform to the agreed specifications and quantities; the buyer must accept them unless he has a valid reason for rejecting them.
column7: Is not permissible, because it changes the terms of the contract regarding the date of delivery and the buyer cannot be compelled to accept it, whatever its conformity to the agreed specifications.
column8: May always be refused by the buyer, since delivery must be on the due date and early delivery deprives the seller of the right to payment.
column9: Must be accepted by the buyer even if he has a valid reason for rejecting the goods, since the seller has performed earlier than required.
column11: Per 5/5, conforming early delivery must be accepted unless the buyer has a valid reason to reject it.

column5: If the Waqif, being a lessee who owns the usufructs, creates a Waqf over those usufructs, it is required that:
column6: The Waqif is not prevented by the lessor from subleasing.
column7: The term of the Waqf should not be longer than the lease period.
column8: The usufructs be utilized only by the Waqf beneficiaries personally and not leased out.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per 2/4/12, the lessee-Waqif must not be barred from subleasing and the Waqf term may not exceed the lease; usufruct Waqf may be leased.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If the bank did not decide on an immediate and comprehensive conversion and decided to adopt a gradual or partial conversion:
column6: It is not regarded as a converted bank and may not be granted a licence as an Islamic bank unless the conversion process is completed.
column7: This standard may not be used as a guideline for identifying its steps of conversion.
column8: It is regarded as a converted bank in respect of the part of its activities that has been converted.
column9: It may be granted a licence as an Islamic bank, provided it undertakes to complete the conversion within the announced period.
column11: Per 2/2, a gradual or partial conversion is not a converted bank and gets no Islamic licence until conversion is complete.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: An Islamic bank operates in a country whose courts apply a specific school of Fiqh, which is also the official school in that country. The bank asked its Board to issue all its Fatwas according to that school. The correct position is:
column6: The Board must comply, since it is the official school in the host country and the courts would apply only the opinions of that school; any Fatwa of another school would be void before the judiciary and the bank.
column7: The Board should disregard the school applied by the courts in all cases.
column8: The institution may choose, for each issue, the school whose opinion is easiest.
column9: The institution should not demand Fatwa according to a specific Madhab; however, attention should be given to situations where the judiciary observes a specific school and the issue may later reach the courts.
column11: Per 6/4, no specific Madhab should be demanded even if official, but regard is due where courts apply a school and litigation is possible.

column5: In a partnership in commendum:
column6: All the partners are jointly liable for the obligations of the company from their personal wealth, whether they manage the company or are sleeping partners.
column7: The managing partners are jointly liable for the company's obligations from their personal wealth, while the liability of each sleeping partner is limited to the number of lots he owns.
column8: The liability of all the partners is limited to the lots they own, so that no partner is liable from his personal wealth for the obligations of the company, whether or not he manages it.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/3/1/2, managing partners bear joint unlimited liability; each sleeping partner's liability is limited to his lots.

column5: Actual possession is realised in immovable property through:
column6: Relinquishment and enabling transactions in it.
column7: Registration of the property in the land register only.
column8: Physical occupation of the property by the buyer.
column9: Delivery of the title deeds only.
column11: Per 3/2, actual possession of immovable property is realised through relinquishment and enabling transactions in it.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: When the conversion is initiated by outsiders who acquired the conventional bank for the purpose of converting it, the Zakah for the past financial periods:
column6: Is not due at all, because the earnings of those periods were impermissible.
column7: Is divided between the new owners and the previous owners in proportion to their periods of ownership.
column8: Is the liability of the previous owners, and the Zakah liability of the new owners starts from the date of the decision to convert.
column9: Is the liability of the new owners, since they now own the bank's assets.
column11: Per 11, past-period Zakah is the previous owners' liability; the new owners' liability starts from the decision to convert.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If the percentage of pure gold in a gold alloy mixed with substances other than silver exceeds 50%, the necessary condition for selling it for pure gold is:
column6: Spot exchange, and that the pure gold weighs less than the gold in the alloy, so that the deficiency is the counter-value to the non-gold substance.
column7: Spot exchange, and that the pure gold weighs more than the gold in the alloy, so that the excess is the counter-value to the non-gold substance.
column8: Spot exchange only, since the alloy contains substances other than gold.
column9: Spot exchange, and equality of the weight of the pure gold with the total weight of the alloy, so that the non-gold substance is disregarded.
column11: Per 3/3/1/1 (second form, first type, a), the exchange must be spot and the pure gold must outweigh its kind in the alloy.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: If the object of commitment turns out to be partly owned by someone else other than the committed party:
column6: The commitment remains effective in its entirety, since the committed party owns the major part of the object.
column7: The committing party is bound to accept the remaining part, and is only entitled to compensation for the part owned by the other person, as the commitment is divisible.
column8: The commitment in that part becomes null and void, and the committing party has the option of accepting or declining the remaining part of the commitment object.
column9: The whole commitment becomes null and void, and the committing party has no option to accept the remaining part, even if the other owner consents.
column11: Per 5/3, the commitment is void in the part owned by another; the committing party may accept the remainder or terminate due to fragmentation of delivery.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting self-Waqf (Waqf on oneself) includes:
column6: The rule that the Waqif may resile from his Waqf at any time.
column7: The analogy upon the charity given to oneself, and the Ḥadīth: Start with yourself and spend it on yourself.
column8: The Waqif's ownership of the Waqf asset continues after the creation of the Waqf, so he may use it as before.
column9: The analogy upon the gift, in which the donor may revoke his gift, and the Waqif may thus keep it for himself.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/4/2, analogy with charity to oneself and the Ḥadīth: Start with yourself and spend it on yourself.

column5: ………… is a process of agreement among a group of persons to handle the injuries resulting from specific risks to which all of them are vulnerable. It involves payment of contributions as donations, and leads to the establishment of a fund that enjoys the status of a legal entity and has independent financial liability:
column6: Conventional insurance.
column7: Reinsurance.
column8: Islamic insurance.
column9: Social insurance arranged by the state.
column11: Per clause 2, this is the definition of Islamic insurance, based on donated contributions to a fund with independent liability.

column5: With respect to the charges imposed on credit cards for cash withdrawals from bank teller machines, it is not permissible for the institution:
column6: To link the charge to the amount withdrawn.
column7: To slice the withdrawals as a device for obtaining repeated charges.
column8: To take into account the period of repayment of the amount withdrawn.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/3/2, the charge must be a certain, reasonable amount; linking it to the amount, slicing withdrawals or the repayment period is barred.

column5: A service agent, in the Standard on Liability of the Investment Manager, is someone whose duties are confined to:
column6: Providing non-investment services, such as leasing the assets, procuring their insurance, maintaining them or collecting asset revenues, and the like.
column7: Implementing investment plans prepared by the investment manager, without making investment decisions, while also acting as an investment agent for a fee.
column8: Making investment decisions under the supervision of the Mudarib or the managing partner, while being a Mudarib or managing partner in respect of other funds.
column9: Providing financing to the investment manager for the purpose of the investment.
column11: Per 4/3/1, a service agent provides non-investment services only and neither implements investment plans nor makes investment decisions.

column5: A worker (irrigator) became unable to work for a reason within his control, and the owner revoked the Irrigation Partnership contract. The worker:
column6: Is entitled to his stipulated share of the crop, less the actual loss suffered by the owner as determined by experts, once the crop is harvested.
column7: Is entitled to a wage at the market rate for the period worked, with no liability towards the owner.
column8: Is entitled to a market-rate wage for the period worked, and is liable to indemnify the owner for the actual loss, as determined by experts.
column9: Is not entitled to anything for the period worked, and must indemnify the owner for the actual loss suffered.
column11: Per 13/2/1/2, he gets a market wage for time worked but indemnifies actual loss.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: The issuance of credit cards is prohibited in all cases, even where the card is free from Riba and from any other legal prohibition.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the basis (item 3), only interest-based revolving credit cards are prohibited; credit cards free from Riba are permissible.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Bay' al-Thunya, which refers to partial sale of a property while retaining the remaining part as an exception (e.g., selling a multistory building with the exception of one floor):
column6: Is permissible, because Gharar in it relates to a corollary of the subject matter.
column7: Is permissible only if the retained part of the property is specified.
column8: Is permissible if the price is reduced in proportion to the retained part, even if that part is not specified.
column9: Is absolutely impermissible, because it involves Gharar in the subject matter.
column11: Per item 7, Bay' al-Thunya with an unspecified retained part is void for Gharar in the subject matter; it is permissible only if that part is specified.

column5: In case all or part of al-Muslam Fihi is not available to the seller on the due date, the buyer shall have the option:
column6: To wait until al-Muslam Fihi is available.
column7: To cancel the contract and recover the paid capital.
column8: To claim a penalty for the delay in addition to the capital.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/8, the buyer may wait or cancel and recover the capital; the parties may also agree on replacement under 4/2. Penalties are barred (5/7).

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Among the conditions on the member of the Board as a Fatwa issuer:
column6: He shall have no personal interest in the matter for which the Institution seeks Fatwa.
column7: He shall be known for his discernment, cautiousness and knowledge about the circumstances and traditions of people.
column8: He must be competent in all areas of Fiqh.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1 and 5/3, (a) and (b) are conditions; per 5/2 competence in all areas of Fiqh is not required.

column5: If debts and tangible assets are combined in a sale contract, subjected to accounting separation, or separated in an account held with the Institution, even in the form of a portfolio not registered with the relevant authorities:
column6: The combination may be sold without restriction, since it includes tangible assets.
column7: The rules for a legally recognized entity in which commingling is materialized apply, if tangible assets exceed 50%.
column8: The provisions of the sale of debt to a third party apply.
column9: The rule for entities with ongoing activities applies, whatever the ratio of debts.
column11: Per 8/3, without a legal entity realizing commingling, the sale of debt provisions of item 5 apply.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: Among the Shari'ah bases for the option to revoke due to defect is the Hadith narrated by 'A'ishah about a man who returned a defective serf after setting him to work, in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) said:
column6: "Muslims are bound by their conditions."
column7: "Overcharging a trusting buyer is forbidden."
column8: "No yield without risk taking."
column9: "No harm and no reciprocal harm."
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for item 2, the Prophet said "No yield without risk taking" ("No gain without risk taking").

column5: With regard to the Institution's membership of the card network, it is permitted for the Institutions:
column6: To pay to the card network interest amounts stipulated by it, provided they are disclosed to the cardholders and approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Institution, as a cost of membership that is unavoidable.
column7: To join the membership of the card network, provided avoiding any Shari'ah violations stipulated by it, such as interest or penalty on lending, and to receive incentive amounts from it for issuing cards managed by it.
column8: To stipulate on the cardholder to pay the penalty on lending required by the card network, provided that the penalty does not exceed the amount charged to the Institution by the network.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/3/1-5/3/3, joining and receiving incentives are permitted, avoiding violations; fees paid may not include interest.

column5: Specific Waqf Assets, where the Waqif's intention aimed to appropriate specifically an asset as it is, include:
column6: Waqf of real estate.
column7: Waqf of usufructs.
column8: Waqf of moral rights.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/2/1, Specific Waqf Assets include Waqf of real estate, and also Waqf of usufructs and Waqf of moral rights.

column5: One of the cases in which arbitration is binding is:
column6: Only when the arbitration verdict meets the consent of the two parties of the dispute.
column7: When it is stipulated as a condition in the contract.
column8: When the arbitrator is not entitled to remuneration, in which case arbitration is binding for the arbitrator.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 5/1, arbitration is binding when stipulated in the contract or agreed with a pledge to observe it; an unpaid arbitrator is not bound (5/2).

column5: Protecting a partner in Musharakah or Mudarabah from the risks of dealing in currencies by way of a guarantee is permissible:
column6: If one of the partners volunteers to guarantee the other partner, provided this guarantee is not stated in the contract.
column7: If a third party volunteers to be a guarantor for that purpose, provided this guarantee is not stated in the contract.
column8: If a third party is the guarantor, provided this guarantee is stated in the contract.
column9: In none of the above cases.
column11: Per 2/9/3, a partner may not guarantee the other; a third party may volunteer as guarantor provided the guarantee is not stated in the contract.

column5: If the Waqif has not specified the remuneration of the overseer:
column6: The overseer shall not be entitled to any remuneration, since he is a volunteer who acts for the reward of the Hereafter and for the Waqf beneficiaries.
column7: It shall be specified by the Waqf beneficiaries, by majority vote, and the relevant authorities have no role in it.
column8: It shall be specified by the relevant authorities, if any; otherwise, the overseer is entitled to his remuneration at the prevailing market rate.
column9: The overseer shall be entitled to a fixed percentage of the Waqf asset, as stipulated by custom, irrespective of the revenue of the Waqf.
column11: Per 3/9/2, absent the Waqif's specification, the relevant authorities set it; otherwise the overseer receives the prevailing market rate.

column5: At the liquidation of a Sharikah whose capital was contributed in the form of tangible assets, each partner is entitled to take back the same assets he contributed.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, each partner is entitled to the equivalent value of the assets presented at the conclusion of the Sharikah.

column5: An Ijarah contract signed with several lessees entitled to the same specified usufruct of a particular asset and duration of rent, without specifying a particular period of time for a particular person, each lessee benefiting during the time assigned to him according to specified rules, is one form of:
column6: Muhaya'ah (time-sharing) in benefiting from the usufruct.
column7: Re-leasing of an asset already leased.
column8: Successive leases.
column9: Co-ownership of the usufruct by way of sub-lease.
column11: Per 4/2/3, several lessees sharing the same usufruct and term with turns set by rules is a form of Muhaya'ah (time-sharing).

column5: An IFI received in advance one year's fees for services to be provided to a client over the next twelve months. On the date when Zakah is due, services for eight months remain undelivered. The prepaid income relating to the undelivered services:
column6: Is subject to Zakah in full, as it is in the hands of the IFI and forms part of its cash assets.
column7: Is subject to Zakah, as it is treated like earnest money forwarded on conclusion of an exchange-based contract, which is owned by the IFI even before delivery.
column8: Should be deducted only if the client has a contractual right to its refund.
column9: Should be deducted from zakatable assets, because it is not finally owned and the Ijarah (hiring) contract could be terminated on occurrence of an excuse or a force majeure situation.
column11: Per 6/3/9, prepaid income for undelivered services is not finally owned and is deducted; earnest money, by contrast, is owned and zakatable.

column5: A shareholder who underwrites an issue of shares without consideration may ask for consideration for services provided other than the underwriting, such as conducting feasibility studies or marketing the shares.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1/2/4, consideration is allowed for services other than underwriting, such as feasibility studies or marketing.

column5: The lapse of a period of time between purchasing an asset from the lessee and selling it back to him under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek is required because the Hadith prohibits two sales in one sale.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the lapse prevents 'Inah, as changes in the asset or its value give it the character of a different asset.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The relationship between the holders of investment accounts and the institution is the typical relationship between the Mudarib (the work provider) and Rab al-Mal.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/1, the relationship between investment accountholders and the institution is that of Rab al-Mal and Mudarib.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, reinsurance coverage should be for the actual harms and not at all for making a wealth out of it, in line with the Hadith: "No harm and no reciprocal harm".
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, coverage rests on "No harm and no reciprocal harm" and is for actual harm, not for gaining wealth.

column5: If the mortgaged asset perishes in the hands of the mortgagee, the notary or the agent, for a reason other than transgression or negligence:
column6: The debt is extinguished to the extent of the value of the perished asset.
column7: No responsibility shall rest with him, and the debt shall still remain valid.
column8: He shall compensate the mortgagor at the value of the asset on the date of mortgaging.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 3/2/4, the mortgaged asset is a trust; if it perishes without transgression or negligence there is no liability and the debt remains.

column5: ………… entails indemnification for actual injury, and comprises insurance against fire, car accidents, airplane accidents, liability, breach of trust, etc.:
column6: Reinsurance.
column7: Takaful against disability and death.
column8: Property insurance.
column9: Person insurance.
column11: Per 6/1, property insurance indemnifies actual injury and covers fire, accidents, liability, breach of trust, etc.

column5: Muwata`ah to form up Riba tricks, in which the two parties agree to practice Bay' al-'Inah or its reverse, Bay' al-Wafa` (Bay' al-Raja`) or Riba al-Fadl, is:
column6: Prohibited by Shari'ah, and the contract so designed is invalid.
column7: Permissible if the Muwata`ah is not stipulated in the contract.
column8: Permissible if there is a need or lawful interest that justifies it.
column9: Prohibited, but the contract so designed remains valid.
column11: Per 6/3/1, Muwata`ah to form Riba tricks is prohibited and the contract so designed is invalid.

column5: The reinsurance fund formed under Islamic reinsurance assumes the task of covering:
column6: All the risks encountered by the insurance funds, without exception.
column7: The risks of traditional insurance companies only.
column8: The risks encountered by the shareholders of the insurance companies.
column9: Part of the risks encountered by the insurance funds.
column11: Per 2/1, the reinsurance fund covers part of the risks which the insurance funds may encounter.

column5: Participation or trading in shares of a corporation for purposes of conversion is permitted:
column6: For one who can effect conversion by adopting a resolution for conversion in accordance with the Shari'ah at the first general meeting, or by striving for conversion.
column7: For anyone, irrespective of his ability to effect or strive for conversion.
column8: For one who undertakes to sell the shares within one year if conversion is not achieved, and donates all dividends received in the interim to charity and informs the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of his intention.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/3, it is permitted for one able to effect conversion at the first general meeting, or who strives for conversion.

column5: In Istisna'a used as a credit facility, the institution which provides finance has no right to sign a Parallel Istisna'a contract with another party to manufacture the asset in question.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/5, the financing institution has the right to sign a Parallel Istisna'a contract with another party to manufacture the asset.

column5: A company's total prohibited income for the financial year amounted to USD 2,000,000, and the number of its shares is 10,000,000. An investment fund owned 50,000 of these shares at the end of the financial period. The amount that the fund must eliminate is:
column11: Per 3/4/6/4, prohibited income per share is 2,000,000/10,000,000 = 0.20, multiplied by 50,000 shares = USD 10,000.

column5: As per Shari'ah, dealing in a contract of purchasing invoices at a discount (factoring) is:
column6: Permitted if the factor has recourse to the institution.
column7: Not permitted unless the purchase is for a commodity, usufruct or service whose subject delivery is ascertained.
column8: Permitted if the discount does not exceed the factor's actual costs.
column9: Not permitted in any case, even if the invoices are purchased for a commodity with spot delivery or for a service whose subject delivery is ascertained.
column11: Per 9/6/2, factoring is permitted only where the invoices are bought for a commodity, usufruct or service with ascertained delivery.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Permissibility of distributing the profit on the basis of constructive liquidation, after ensuring the safety of the capital, is based on:
column6: The fact that the two parties are the sole owners of the profit.
column7: Acceptance of valuation in Shari'ah in several applications, including Zakah as well as theft incidents.
column8: The fact that the holders of the accounts have implicitly exchanged mutual relief from commitment.
column9: The fact that profit is deserved for contribution of funds, work or guarantee.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, constructive liquidation relies on Shari'ah's acceptance of valuation, e.g. in Zakah and theft, and the slave-valuation Hadith.

column5: The decision of granting credit facilities is usually issued in the form of a letter addressed from the Institution to the client, indicating that:
column6: The letter does not constitute any commitment from the part of the Institution unless transactions are actually commenced.
column7: The letter becomes binding on both parties once it is countersigned by the client.
column8: The client is bound to utilize the facility within the specified period of validity, otherwise he shall compensate the Institution.
column9: The letter constitutes a binding commitment on the Institution to finance the client up to the approved financial limit during the period of validity.
column11: Per 2/4, the approval letter states that it constitutes no commitment on the Institution unless transactions are actually commenced.

column5: The general principle is that a Mudarabah contract is not binding, i.e. each of the contracting parties may terminate it unilaterally, except:
column6: When the Mudarib has already commenced the business, in which case the contract becomes binding up to the date of actual or constructive liquidation.
column7: When the contracting parties agree to determine a duration for the contract, in which case it cannot be terminated prior to the end of that duration except by mutual agreement.
column8: When the capital provider has delivered the capital to the Mudarib, even if the business has not commenced.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/3, the two exceptions are commencement of business and an agreed duration; mere delivery of capital is not one of them.

column5: An IFI, as Rab al-Mal in a Mudarabah, stipulated that the Mudarib mortgage his house to the IFI to secure the return of the Mudarabah capital in all cases, including loss without transgression. This stipulation is:
column6: Impermissible, because mortgage may not be stipulated in trust-based contracts unless confined to indemnity in case of transgression, negligence or breach of the contract.
column7: Permissible, provided that the house is kept by a notary.
column8: Permissible, because mortgage can be stipulated for any commitment owed to the IFI, including a commitment to return the Mudarabah capital in all cases, since the mortgagor has agreed to it.
column9: Impermissible absolutely, even if the mortgage is confined to indemnity for transgression or negligence, because Mudarabah capital is a trust.
column11: Per 3/3/2, mortgage cannot be stipulated in trust contracts like Mudarabah except to cover transgression, negligence or breach.

column5: If the Waqf was for restricted and specific persons and there is a shortfall in the Waqf revenue, the shortfall applies to all the beneficiaries in proportion to their shares.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/10/3, a shortfall applies to all such beneficiaries in proportion to their shares.

column5: Regarding the methods of judgment, procedures and proving in arbitration, the following are true, except:
column6: When the arbitrator rejects an attestation, that attestation is to be denied in other arbitrations and in the judiciary.
column7: The arbitrator is not required to follow the procedural rules of the judiciary, nor is he obliged to observe laws, unless such laws are part of public order.
column8: The arbitrator is not supposed to stick to the legally stipulated rules of evidence, provided that the evidence he accepts does not contradict with the rules of Shari'ah.
column9: The arbitrator should not make judgment on the basis of his own opinion.
column11: Per 10/1, rejecting an attestation does not cause its denial elsewhere unless the judiciary also rejects it. The other statements follow 10/1, 10/3, 10/4.

column5: There is no enforceable Zakah law in the country of an Islamic bank, its articles of association do not stipulate payment of Zakah, and its general assembly has not issued a Zakah commitment resolution. The correct ruling is:
column6: The bank must still pay Zakah directly on behalf of its shareholders and investment account holders, deducting it from their dividends and profits, since Zakah is an obligation of the bank as a legal person and the shareholders are not required to do anything.
column7: Payment of Zakah is the responsibility of the shareholders and holders of investment accounts, and the bank has to indicate the amount of Zakah payable per share or per a given balance of an investment account.
column8: The bank's Shari'ah Board becomes responsible for calculating and paying Zakah on behalf of the shareholders from the bank's funds, as part of its supervisory duties.
column9: No Zakah is due on the shares of the bank or on its investment accounts.
column11: Per 2/2/5, absent the 2/2/1 conditions, Zakah is the shareholders' and account holders' duty; the bank states the Zakah per share or per account balance.

column5: In a Monetization transaction in which the customer is the beneficiary, it is impermissible:
column6: For the Institution to arrange proxy of a third party to sell, on behalf of the client, the commodity that the client purchased from the Institution.
column7: To link the contract for purchasing the commodity on deferred payment basis and the contract for selling it for a spot price in such a way that the client loses his right to receive the commodity.
column8: For the commodity to return back to the seller by virtue of prior agreement or collusion between the two parties, or according to tradition.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: All three are prohibited: third-party proxy arranged by the Institution (4/8), linking the two contracts (4/6), return to the seller by collusion or tradition (4/5).

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Khiyar al-Taghrir, Khiyar al-Tadlis and Khiyar al-Ghabn do not transfer to the heirs of their holder upon his death.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/5, 3/6 and 4/6, none of these options transfers to the heirs upon the death of its holder.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If the debtor defaults in settling his debt at maturity, the creditor holding gold as a pledge:
column6: Becomes the owner of the pledged gold at its market value at the time of the pledge.
column7: May sell the pledged gold at the value agreed at the time of the pledge contract.
column8: May demand the sale of the pledged gold to recover his dues from the proceeds and return the remainder to the debtor, at the market value prevailing when the debt is recovered.
column9: May take an amount of gold equal to the debt at its value on the maturity date, without sale, since gold is a Ribawi item which is exchanged only at spot, and the debtor bears any shortfall.
column11: Per 7/1/3, the creditor may demand sale, recover his dues and return the rest, at the market value when the debt is recovered.

column5: The lessee's leasing of the tangible asset back to its owner within the term of the first Ijarah is:
column6: Permitted only after the expiry of the term of the first Ijarah.
column7: Not permitted in any case, since the owner cannot be a lessee of his own asset.
column8: Permitted only if the rent in the second Ijarah equals that in the first.
column9: Permitted, provided that this does not constitute 'Inah.
column11: Per 5/3, the lessee may lease the asset to its owner within the first Ijarah term, provided this does not constitute 'Inah.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: An IFI appointed a customer as its agent to purchase and take possession of gold on its behalf. After the customer purchased and took possession of the gold, he wished to purchase it from the IFI. This is:
column6: Not permissible, because an agent may not purchase from his principal what he has purchased on the principal's behalf, unless a third party intervenes.
column7: Permissible, provided that the price is deferred and the IFI retains liability for the gold until the price is paid.
column8: Permissible through an exchange of offer (Ijab) and acceptance (Qabul), and liability for the gold then transfers to the customer as purchaser.
column9: Permissible, and the sale is concluded automatically upon the agent's taking possession.
column11: Per 5/1/3, after purchase and possession the agent may buy the gold from the principal by offer and acceptance, and liability passes to him.

column5: The creditors who apply for a declaration of insolvency are required to prove that they are the sole creditors of the debtor.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/4, creditors are not required to prove they are the sole creditors; a creditor appearing before distribution shares pro-rata.

column5: The partners in a Sharikah may agree to make profit-sharing not proportionate to their contributions to capital, provided that:
column6: The additional percentage does not exceed 10% of the total profit.
