column7: The additional percentage of profit is in favour of the partner who contributed the largest share of the capital.
column8: The losses are also shared in the same disproportionate ratio.
column9: The additional percentage of profit over the percentage of contribution to the capital is not in favour of a sleeping partner.
column11: Per 3/1/5/3, disproportionate profit sharing is allowed provided the excess is not in favour of a sleeping partner.

column5: Liquidity management means:
column6: Holding the maximum possible amount of cash in order to cover withdrawals at all times, regardless of the cost.
column7: The ability to redeem Sukuk and investment funds or sell them in the secondary market.
column8: Achieving a balance between obtaining liquidity as swiftly and cheaply as possible and investing and deploying it effectively.
column9: The ability to swiftly convert securities into cash in the money market.
column11: Per 2/2, it is balancing swift, cheap obtaining of liquidity with its effective deployment; C and D describe liquidity in given settings.

column5: It is permissible for the partners to agree at the conclusion of the Sharikah contract that one partner will be liable for a percentage of loss that does not match his share of ownership, provided all the partners consent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/5/4, losses must match capital shares; only a voluntary assumption at the time of loss, without prior condition, is valid.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, Salam was so named because the capital must be paid in advance; if payment is delayed, the transaction is not called Salam.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in the Shari'ah basis for 3/1/3.

column5: An investor provided funds to an IFI on a restricted Mudarabah basis and stipulated that the funds be invested only in trading a particular seasonal fruit, outside its season, when it is in very limited supply. This restriction is:
column6: Not acceptable, because restricting Mudarabah to certain commodities requires that they be commonly available, so that the restriction does not defeat the objectives of the Mudarabah.
column7: Acceptable, because the capital provider may restrict the Mudarabah to a single commodity without any condition, and the Mudarib is bound to observe the restriction whatever the availability of the commodity.
column8: Not acceptable, because a Mudarabah may never be restricted to a single commodity, whatever its availability.
column9: Acceptable, provided the IFI is paid a fixed fee in addition to its share of profit, since the commodity is in limited supply.
column11: Per 9/2, restriction to commodities is allowed only if they are commonly available, not scarce, out of season or in very limited supply.

column5: Selling al-Muslam Fihi by the buyer before taking possession of it is:
column6: Permitted, through the issue of tradable Salam Sukuk.
column7: Permitted, if it is sold back to the seller at the capital of Salam.
column8: Not permitted, as it is a form of sale of debts.
column9: Permitted, if it is sold to a third party at the same price as the capital of Salam.
column11: Per 4/1, the buyer may not sell al-Muslam Fihi before possession, as this is a sale of debts; tradable Salam Sukuk are barred (7).

column5: It is permitted for a third party to give a commitment to Rab Al Maal for reparation (jabr) of loss in the capital or shortfall in the profits, or purchasing the investment assets for a specified value, subject to the following conditions:
column6: The third party should be independent from the investment manager, and if there is a common shareholding between them, the ownership holding of one party should not exceed 50% of the other.
column7: The obligor shall have no recourse to the investment manager for what was undertaken by it.
column8: The undertaking shall be extended voluntarily.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/1–4/1/3, independence (holding not over 50%), no recourse to the manager and a voluntary undertaking are all required.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Conditions of validity of the cooling-off option include:
column6: The option must be stipulated in the contract, unless it is implied by a pre-existing custom or the parties agree to subsequently include it in the contract.
column7: The stipulated cooling-off period must coincide with the beginning of the contract period.
column8: If the contract relates to several items, it must specify those items to which the option relates.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/1, 2/2/3 and 2/2/4, all three are conditions of validity of the cooling-off option.

column5: It is permissible, immediately upon issue and up to the date of maturity, but after the passing of ownership of the assets to the holders of the Sukuk, to trade in Sukuk that represent ownership of existing leased assets or assets to be leased on promise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/4, such Sukuk may be traded from issue to maturity once ownership of the assets has passed to the Sukuk holders.

column5: An IFI received funds from a customer on a Mudarabah basis. The contract was silent on the ratio of profit distribution, and it was established that there is no customary practice regarding the distribution of profit in this kind of Mudarabah. The correct ruling is:
column6: Profit is distributed equally between the IFI and the customer, since there is no customary practice or agreement to the contrary, and neither party can claim a larger share than the other.
column7: The Mudarabah contract is void ab initio, and the IFI as Mudarib receives a common market price for the kind and amount of services it provided.
column8: All the profit belongs to the customer and the IFI receives nothing for its services, since no ratio was agreed in the contract.
column9: Profit is distributed in accordance with the highest ratio prevailing in the market for similar Mudarabah contracts.
column11: Per 8/4, with no stipulated ratio and no custom, the Mudarabah is void ab initio and the Mudarib gets the market price of his services.

column5: The duty of the owner of the trees in Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) is to:
column6: Carry out the pruning, pest control and seasonal work himself.
column7: Give the worker (irrigator) full access to the trees and remove any impediments to his work.
column8: Pay the wages of anyone the worker hires to perform the worker's customary work, in addition to the worker's share.
column9: Take care of the crop alone before harvesting, since the trees are his property.
column11: Per item 7, the owner must give the worker full access to the trees and remove impediments to his work.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of one party bearing the losses, or of each party bearing a portion of losses not proportionate to his share in the capital, is:
column6: The Hadith of Al-Sa'ib Ibn Abu Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi, the partner of the Prophet (peace be upon him), on the permissibility of partnership in trade and the sharing of its proceeds.
column7: The saying of Ali Ibn Abu Talib: 'Profit distribution is according to the partners' agreement and loss must be borne in proportion to the contribution in the capital.'
column8: The Hadith of Ibn Umar concerning selling camels at Al-Baqi' in one currency and taking payment in another, at the price of the day of payment.
column9: The legal maxim: 'The law is flexible in things that follow from another', which allows a partner to bear the loss of another.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the rule rests on the saying of Ali: profit per agreement, loss per capital contribution.

column5: Under the net assets method, the following are deducted from zakatable assets in calculating the Zakah base:
column6: Liabilities payable during the financial year as at the date of the balance sheet, and all installments of liabilities which will become due during the coming financial period.
column7: Rights of the holders of non-restricted investment accounts, and minority rights.
column8: Sovereign rights, Waqf rights, charitable rights, and rights of non-profit-earning organizations that have no specific owner.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the formula in 2/1/1, all these items are deducted from zakatable assets to reach the Zakah base.

column5: In a card based on lending, the following fees charged by the card issuer from the cardholder are not permitted to be more than the actual direct cost:
column6: The fee of cash withdrawal from the ATMs of the issuing institution.
column7: The fee of limit increase and the fees for converting the used amounts into instalments.
column8: The cost of currency exchange if the card was used in a currency other than the currency of the card.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/1, all three are fees linked to the loan and may not exceed the actual direct cost.

column5: The overseer has a fiduciary capacity while holding Waqf assets; therefore:
column6: He is not liable for other than misconduct, negligence, or breach of the Waqif's terms and conditions.
column7: He shall be held liable for misconduct only, but not for negligence.
column8: He shall guarantee a minimum return on the investment of the Waqf assets.
column9: He shall be held liable for any loss of the Waqf assets, whatever its cause, since he has taken possession of them.
column11: Per 3/7/5, as a fiduciary the overseer is liable only for misconduct, negligence or breach of the Waqif's terms.

column5: Asking an applicant for a letter of guarantee to bear the administrative expenses incurred in issuing a letter of guarantee of either type (preliminary or final) is permissible, provided:
column6: The remuneration for such expenses does not exceed the commission that others would charge for such services.
column7: The expenses are calculated on the basis of the amount guaranteed and the duration of the guarantee.
column8: The letter of guarantee is without cover.
column9: The letter of guarantee is a final one and not a preliminary one.
column11: Per 6/1/2, administrative expenses are allowed if they do not exceed what others charge for such services.

column5: Concluding a valid mortgage contract:
column6: Requires that the debt be due at the time of signing the mortgage, otherwise the mortgage is not binding on the mortgagor.
column7: Must be preceded by establishing the debt, otherwise the mortgage is invalid, since a mortgage cannot exist without an existing debt.
column8: Need not be preceded by establishing the debt; the mortgage contract can be signed before or at the same time as the debt contract.
column9: Must take place at the same time as signing the debt contract, and not before or after it, so that the mortgage is part of the debt contract.
column11: Per 3/3/1, the debt need not be established first; the mortgage may be signed before or at the same time as the debt contract.

column5: In the case of Waqf of Sukuk or units of investment funds, the initial presumption is that the Waqf asset will be:
column6: Their value, unless the Waqif has stipulated that the Waqf is for those particular Sukuk and units.
column7: Their nominal value at issuance, in all cases.
column8: Those particular Sukuk and units, unless the Waqif has stipulated that the Waqf is for their value.
column9: Their market value at the date of creation of the Waqf, to which the rulings of cash Waqf apply.
column11: Per 2/4/15/1(b), the presumption is that the particular Sukuk and units are the Waqf asset, unless the Waqif stipulates their value.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The use of the procedures and mechanisms of conversion becomes obligatory when the conversion cannot be realised without them, because conversion is obligatory and the means to an obligation becomes an obligation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, since conversion is obligatory, the tools without which it cannot be achieved become obligatory.

column5: When the employee refrains from delivery of the service as required, and fails to present the suitable alternative as agreed upon:
column6: The employer has the right to terminate the contract and demand indemnification for the actual harm caused to him by the act of the employee.
column7: The employer may demand double the pay as a penalty.
column8: The employer may terminate the contract, but may not demand any indemnification, since termination is his only remedy.
column9: The contract continues, and the employee must be granted a new period to deliver the service or present an alternative.
column11: Per 8/1/2, the employer may terminate and claim indemnity for the actual harm caused by the employee's act.

column5: When the Islamic insurance company is liquidated, all provisions and accumulated reserves pertaining to insurance should be:
column6: Distributed among the shareholders of the company.
column7: Transferred to the statutory reserve of the company.
column8: Spent on charitable purposes.
column9: Distributed among the current policyholders in proportion to their contributions.
column11: Per 5/6 and 10/5, on liquidation insurance provisions, reserves and the accumulated balance are spent on charitable purposes.

column5: As a rule, the entitlement of the worker to compensation in a Ju'alah:
column6: Is established upon conclusion of the contract, whether or not any work is done.
column7: Is not established until the work is completed and delivered.
column8: Is established upon commencement of the work, in proportion to the part done.
column9: Accrues in proportion to the work done during the period, even if the result is not realised.
column11: Per 5/3/2/3, the general rule is that the Ju'l is earned only once the work is completed and delivered.

column5: An IFI sold a customer, on Murabahah, a quantity of cement stored in the IFI's warehouse in City A. The customer stipulated in the contract that the cement be delivered at his site in City B at the expense of the IFI, and the IFI agreed. Later, the IFI asked the customer to bear the transportation costs. The correct ruling is:
column6: The IFI is bound to deliver the cement at the customer's site in City B and to bear the expenses of transporting it there.
column7: The transportation costs are shared equally, because the place of delivery differs from the place where the commodity is present.
column8: The stipulation is void, because delivery must take place where the commodity is present at the time of the contract.
column9: The customer bears the transportation costs, because the expenses of moving the commodity from its place are always the buyer's responsibility.
column11: Per 4/1/3, where delivery at another place at the seller's expense is stipulated, the seller must deliver there and bear the transport costs.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: It is the duty of the board to issue Fatwa to the Institution due to the relationship that binds the two by virtue of the decision of the management of the Institution.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the relationship arises from the decision of the general assembly (equity owners), not the management.

column5: If there is an excess amount of the income of the Waqf of a specific mosque which has not been spent on its own interests:
column6: It may be transferred to any charitable purpose determined by the Waqf superintendent, even if other mosques lack income for their maintenance.
column7: It must be distributed among the poor and needy, since the income of a mosque's Waqf may not be transferred to another mosque.
column8: It is permissible to transfer such amount to another mosque that does not have enough income to cover its expenses, or the cost of its maintenance and renovation.
column9: It must be retained for the same mosque in all cases.
column11: Per 5/4, the excess income of a specific mosque's Waqf may be transferred to another mosque lacking income for expenses, maintenance or renovation.

column5: According to the view that gives the seller the right to reclamation, the conditions of this right include:
column6: The insolvent should be alive at the time of recourse; in the case of an institution or company, it should remain existent.
column7: The whole asset should remain in the ownership of the insolvent.
column8: The right of another person should not relate to the asset, e.g., when the insolvent has pledged it as security, except when the mortgagee renounces his right.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for item 6, all three are among the conditions for the right to reclamation.

column5: If the worker (irrigator) dies and the Irrigation Partnership contract does not stipulate that the work is non-assignable:
column6: The contract terminates automatically upon the worker's death, and his successor is entitled to a wage for the period worked.
column7: The successor has the option to complete the work on the same terms, either himself or by hiring workers, in return for the deceased's share of the crop.
column8: The successor is obliged to complete the work himself on the same terms, in return for the deceased's share of the crop.
column9: The owner must complete the work, and the successor receives the deceased's full share of the crop.
column11: Per 12/3, absent a non-assignability stipulation, the successor may complete the work, personally or by hiring, for the deceased's share.

column5: It is not permissible for the Institution:
column6: To discount accepted bills of exchange, i.e. to purchase them before maturity at less than their nominal value.
column7: To negotiate, for less than their nominal value, documents payable on sight or payable bills of exchange.
column8: To act as an intermediary, by payment or notification, between the beneficiary and the issuing or confirming bank to facilitate trading in deferred payment documents.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/7/2-4, discounting, negotiating below nominal value and intermediating in such trading are all prohibited.

column5: If it is stipulated that all or part of the compensation in a Ju'alah be paid in advance, before completion of the entire work:
column6: The advance is considered 'subject to accounts'; the worker is not entitled to it without realisation of the result, and the offeror may reclaim it if the work is not realised.
column7: The stipulation is impermissible, since the compensation is earned only on completion of the work and an advance would create a debt on the worker, who may not be required to refund it.
column8: The worker keeps the advance once he has commenced the work, whether or not the result is realised, since it is a gift from the offeror and is not subject to any later accounts.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/3/2/4, advance payment is allowed but is subject to accounts and reclaimable if the result is not realised.

column5: In case of default of the mortgagor:
column6: The mortgagee has the right to stipulate a condition that he should own the mortgaged asset in case of default.
column7: There is no prohibition for the mortgagee to purchase the mortgaged asset from the mortgagor at market value, and take the portion of the value to which he is entitled.
column8: After repayment of the mortgagee's debt from the sale value of the mortgaged asset, the remaining value should be given to the mortgagor.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 3/4/1-2, the surplus goes to the mortgagor and the mortgagee may buy at market value, but may not stipulate ownership on default.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of endorsement of commercial papers is that it does not go beyond the meaning of:
column6: Either Kafalah (guarantee) or Rahn (mortgage), both of which require consideration.
column7: The sale of debt to a person other than the debtor, which is valid at its face value.
column8: Either Hawalah or Wakalah, both of which are permissible.
column9: Qard (loan) only, repayable on maturity.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, endorsement is in the meaning of Hawalah or Wakalah, both permissible.

column5: In addition to managing the insurance operations, the company (or the committee of policyholders) invests the assets of the insurance fund through:
column6: Mudarabah.
column7: Investment agency.
column8: A Musharakah between the company and the policyholders' fund.
column9: (a) or (b).
column11: Per clause 3 and 4/2, the fund's assets are invested through Mudarabah or investment agency.

column5: Selling or buying indices is prohibited because:
column6: The index is the property of its developer and may not be sold without his permission, so that any sale or purchase of it would infringe his intellectual property rights and entitle him to a share of the price.
column7: It involves Riba al-Nasi'ah, since the price is settled after the contract.
column8: It is a sale of a debt for a debt.
column9: It is nothing more than payment or receipt of money for the mere existence of a certain reading or figure, which constitutes a form of gambling and is the sale of an imaginary object that never exists.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis and the IIFA resolution, trading indices is pure gambling: money paid for a mere reading, an imaginary object.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the option to revoke due to non-payment lapsing upon the death of its owner is that:
column6: It is inconsistent with the stipulations of Qabd in Sarf and Salam, which require possession at the session.
column7: It constitutes a readiness and willingness to act, and is therefore not transferable to heirs.
column8: The testator has an established ownership in the objects of the option, which the heirs inherit.
column9: The heirs would need to identify their selection among the items.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/4, it is mere readiness to act and not transferable.

column5: A client purchased goods from a foreign supplier on his own account. Afterwards, the IFI signed a partnership contract with the client in these goods and then sold its share of the goods to the same client on a deferred payment basis. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because the partnership contract was concluded after the client's purchase and the sale was a separate transaction.
column7: Permissible, as long as the sale was not stipulated in the partnership contract and the price is not a fixed profit.
column8: Not permissible, because selling its share in goods purchased by the client back to him on deferred payment amounts to Bay' al-'Inah.
column9: Not permissible, because a partnership in goods purchased by the client is prohibited in all cases, whatever the terms of the sale or its timing.
column11: Per 3/6/2 and its basis, partnership in goods bought by the client is allowed, but deferred sale of the share to him is 'Inah.

column5: The subject-matter of the contract at the time of trading of shares is:
column6: The undivided share in the capital and assets of the corporation and the rights associated with it.
column7: The right to dividends only.
column8: The share certificate as a document of value in itself.
column9: The nominal value of the share as a debt owed by the corporation to the shareholder.
column11: Per 3/1, a share represents an undivided share in the capital and assets of the corporation, which is the subject-matter of trading.

column5: The Institution is not obliged to inquire as to how the guarantee produced by the customer has been obtained by him.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/5, the Institution need not inquire how the customer obtained the guarantee.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: If the amounts retained for liquidity purposes are never invested by the bank, because they are withheld in the accounts of the central bank or the bank's treasury to meet withdrawal requests, there is no return for which a ruling can be indicated.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/10/1, uninvested liquidity amounts held with the central bank or treasury generate no return on which to rule.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: In accepting non-paid agency, silence is also considered as sufficient acceptance, while a negative response is indicative of rejection of agency.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/2, silence is sufficient acceptance in non-paid agency, and a negative response indicates rejection.

column5: If the Mudarib appoints another party on an Ijarah (hiring) basis to carry out work that any similar asset or fund manager would, by custom, be liable to do:
column6: The wages of the worker must be paid from the personal funds of the Mudarib and not from the Mudarabah funds.
column7: The wages are shared between the Mudarib and the capital provider according to the profit-sharing ratio.
column8: The wages are deducted from the profit before its distribution.
column9: The wages of the worker are paid from the Mudarabah funds at the prevailing rate.
column11: Per 9/4, customary work is the Mudarib's own duty, so a hired worker for it is paid from his personal funds.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Agency becomes binding in the following cases, excluding:
column6: When it involves rights of others, as when the mortgagor appoints the mortgagee as an agent.
column7: When a time limit is specified for the agency.
column8: When the principal or the agent undertakes not to revoke the contract within a certain period.
column9: When agency is a paid agency.
column11: Per 4/3 the first three make agency binding; per 4/4/2 a time limit only restrains the agent from starting new operations afterwards.

column5: In case funds were paid to the Institution to be invested in its general pool, and the Institution did not invest them in that pool whereas the pool made a profit:
column6: The investor is entitled only to the return of his capital, since his funds did not participate in the pool.
column7: The Institution is liable for the capital and the expected profits, owing to its breach.
column8: The investor is entitled to a profit share according to the percentage agreed in the contract, and bears loss or damage in proportion to his contributed capital.
column9: The investor is entitled to the entire profit attributable to his capital, and the Institution forfeits its share, since the funds were not commingled in the pool, and he bears no loss or damage.
column11: Per 7/3, the investor gets the agreed profit share and bears loss or damage in proportion to his capital contributed.

column5: Tender security amounts may be invested for the benefit of the customer with his consent, unless he requests that they be credited to his current account.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/8/1, such amounts may be invested for the customer with his consent unless he asks to credit his current account.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar violates the transaction when it satisfies a number of conditions, excluding:
column6: It is not justified by a Shari'ah-recognizable need.
column7: It relates to a corollary (Tabi') of the primary subject matter of the contract.
column8: It is involved in an exchange-based contract or any contract of that nature.
column9: It is excessive in degree.
column11: Per item 4, the Gharar must relate to the primary subject matter; Gharar in a corollary has no effect on the contract (4/3).

column5: Since the concession license is a financial right, its owner may dispose of it:
column6: Through selling, leasing, mortgaging, partnership or securitization according to Shari'ah rulings, as well as the conditions imposed by the licensor.
column7: Through selling only, with the consent of the licensor, since the license is a personal right that cannot be leased, mortgaged or made the subject of a partnership.
column8: Through leasing only, since the license is a usufruct.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 9, the license may be sold, leased, mortgaged, used in partnership or securitized per Shari'ah and the licensor's conditions.

column5: ………… is a written undertaking by a bank given to the seller as per the buyer's instruction, or issued by the bank for its own use, undertaking to pay up to a specified amount within a certain period of time, on condition that the seller presents documents for the goods conforming to the instructions.
column6: Bill of exchange.
column7: Promissory note.
column8: Documentary credit.
column9: Letter of guarantee.
column11: Per 2/1, this is the definition of documentary credit: a bank's undertaking to pay subject to conformity of documents.

column5: In a sale, the wages of employing a cubic measure, weight, linear measure and counting to ascertain the sold commodity are, unless there is a stipulation or customary practice to the contrary:
column6: Borne by the party who requested the ascertainment.
column7: The responsibility of the buyer, being part of the expenses of taking delivery.
column8: Shared equally between the seller and the buyer.
column9: The responsibility of the seller, being part of the expenses of delivering the sold commodity.
column11: Per 4/1/1, expenses of presenting and ascertaining the sold commodity (measuring, weighing, counting) are the seller's responsibility.

column5: Among the general principles that govern almost all indices, the absolute value of the index:
column6: Loses its accuracy if the values of the index at different periods are multiplied or divided by a constant figure.
column7: Has no implication when presented as a single figure; it becomes meaningful only when compared to the past and future values of the index.
column8: Represents the average market price of the components of the index.
column9: Indicates by itself whether the market is a rising or a declining market.
column11: Per 3/3/1, a single index value has no implication; it is meaningful only when compared with past and future values.

column5: It is permissible to include penalty clauses in:
column6: Contracts for construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts.
column7: Murabahah contracts, in case of delay in paying the deferred price.
column8: Ijarah contracts, in case of delay in paying the rentals.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/3, penalty clauses are allowed in construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts; for debts they are Riba (2/1/2).

column5: Ownership of a sold debt and its risk are transferred to the buyer only when the buyer actually collects the debt from the debtor.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/1, they pass by any means that customarily allows the buyer to claim the debt.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: The basis for the lapse of the option to revoke due to the buyer's disposal of the sale item after discovering the deception is that such disposal is equivalent to an explicit consent to waive the option.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, disposal after discovering the deception is equivalent to explicit consent to waive the option.

column5: A person created a temporary Waqf for three years over 1,000 particular Sukuk (not over their value), whose remaining term is five years, with the periodic distributions going to a hospital. At the end of the three-year Waqf period:
column6: The Sukuk become a perpetual Waqf for the hospital, since they have not yet been cancelled.
column7: The Sukuk are sold, and their proceeds are reinvested for the benefit of the hospital.
column8: The Waqif shall recover the same number of Sukuk.
column9: The Waqif shall recover the market value of the Sukuk at the date of creation of the Waqf.
column11: Per 2/4/15/1(b)(2), if the Waqf period is shorter than the Sukuk term, the Waqif recovers the same number of Sukuk at the end of the period.

column5: The manufacturer may fulfil his obligation in an Istisna'a contract by using items produced by other parties that existed before the contract was concluded:
column6: Absolutely, since the items will be delivered according to the specification, even if the ultimate purchaser stipulated that the manufacturer should use his own resources.
column7: Only if the ultimate purchaser did not stipulate that the manufacturer should use his own resources, and this is not used as a device for deferring both the price and the commodity for items not intended to be produced.
column8: Only if those items are specifically identified in the contract and were produced by a manufacturer approved by the ultimate purchaser, who bears the risk of their non-conformity to the specification after delivery and cannot reject them.
column9: Under no circumstances, since Istisna'a requires the manufacturer to produce the items himself, and the purchaser may rescind the contract if items produced by others are delivered.
column11: Per 3/1/5, pre-existing items made by others may be delivered unless own production was stipulated, but not as a device to defer both counter-values.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: The basis for a cooling-off option not abating when the item is offered for sale is that this is meant to probe the fairness of the price; the option does abate upon an actual sale, which serves as a testimony to acceptance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 2/4/4, offering probes the price; an actual sale is disposal as owner, evidencing acceptance.

column5: In a sale with a unilateral promise to buy back, the first sale and the subsequent sale may be for deferred prices, provided that the promise is documented in a separate deed from the first contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/1/1, both contracts must be for a spot price; a separate deed (5/1/2) is an additional requirement.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Gold mixed with silver, where each metal in the alloy is intended per se, may be sold for pure gold or pure silver provided that:
column6: The exchange of the counter-values is spot, and the weight of the pure counter-value is more than that of its kind in the alloy.
column7: The exchange of the counter-values is spot, and the weight of the pure counter-value is equal to that of its kind in the alloy.
column8: The exchange of the counter-values is spot only.
column9: The exchange of the counter-values is spot, and the weight of the pure counter-value is less than that of its kind in the alloy.
column11: Per 3/3/1/1 (first form), the exchange must be spot and the pure counter-value must outweigh its kind in the alloy; equal or lighter is barred.

column5: If the investment agency is remunerated, the agent's fee:
column6: May be linked to a benchmark known to both parties without the need for maximum and minimum limits, provided that the fee of the first period is determined and the benchmark is notified to the agent before each period.
column7: May be a percentage of the profit realised, as in Mudarabah, provided that the percentage is agreed upon at the time of contract.
column8: Should be a fixed amount or a percentage of the amount invested; it may also be linked to a known benchmark referred to before each period after the first period's fee is set, provided it is capped and floored.
column9: Must be a fixed amount only, determined at the conclusion of the contract, and may not be a percentage of the amount invested.
column11: Per 5/1, the fee is a fixed amount or a percentage of the amount invested, or benchmark-linked with a cap and floor.

column5: Regarding the insurance portfolio in Islamic insurance:
column6: The insurance company pays Zakah on the fund in its capacity as agent.
column7: The insurance portfolio pays Zakah on the contributions at 2.5%, since it has an independent financial liability.
column8: The policyholders should pay Zakah annually on their contributions held in the fund, since any surplus may be returned to them.
column9: No Zakah is payable by the insurance portfolio, since the contributions constitute a fund with an independent financial liability and are given as a donation.
column11: Per 5/3/5, contributions are donations to a fund with independent liability that need not be returned, so no Zakah is payable by the portfolio.

column5: It is permissible to draw up an Istisna'a contract for real estate developments on designated land:
column6: Owned by either the ultimate purchaser or the contractor, or on land of which either owns the usufruct.
column7: Only if the land is owned by the ultimate purchaser, since the contract concerns a particular identified place.
column8: Only if the land is owned by the contractor, since the building is then delivered together with its land.
column9: It is not permissible, since the land is a particular identified place and the building cannot be specified apart from it.
column11: Per 3/1/8, the land may belong to either party or either may own its usufruct; the contract concerns specified buildings, not the land.

column5: Certificates of equal value issued for the purpose of providing future services through a described provider (such as educational benefits from a university without naming the educational institution) and obtaining the fee in the form of subscription income are called:
column6: Istisna'a certificates.
column7: Certificates of ownership of services of a specified party.
column8: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of described future assets.
column9: Certificates of ownership of described future services.
column11: Per 3/2/4, where the provider is described but not named, these are certificates of ownership of described future services.

column5: The expenses relating to reparation of the mortgaged asset and its preservation against decay should be borne by:
column6: The mortgagor and the mortgagee equally.
column7: The mortgagee.
column8: The notary, if the asset is kept by a notary.
column9: The mortgagor.
column11: Per 3/2/10, the mortgagor bears all actual expenses of reparation of the mortgaged asset and its preservation against decay.

column5: A joint-liability company is:
column6: A form of financing partnership in which the liability of the partners is limited to their shares, whatever the obligations of the company towards third parties.
column7: A form of personal partnership, and it is necessary that it be publicly declared as a registered company assigned a unique title (trademark).
column8: A partnership that has no juristic personality, because people other than the partners do not know about it, and it need not be registered.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 4/2/1/1-2, it is a personal partnership publicly registered under a unique title, with its own juristic personality.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: An IFI agreed with a supplier to obtain fuel regularly for the generators of its branches, with the price to be determined at the end of each month according to a published price index, even after the fuel has been consumed. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, being Bay' al-Istijrar, which involves forgivable Gharar in the price.
column7: Impermissible, because the price is left to be determined by a third party.
column8: Impermissible, because the goods are consumed before the price becomes known.
column9: Permissible only if the total quantity of fuel is fixed in advance.
column11: Per 5/2/2, in Bay' al-Istijrar goods are obtained regularly at a price set by normal prices or an index, even after consumption; the Gharar is forgivable.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: When the Fatwa offers the chance for choice between two permissible actions:
column6: Preference shall be given to the stricter, as a precaution, even if the easier one realizes a lawful interest for the Institution and its clients, and in all circumstances without exception.
column7: Preference shall be given to the easier; but if choosing one would realize a lawful interest while choosing the other would open the door for blight, the latter should be avoided.
column8: The choice shall be left to the management of the Institution, which is better aware of the interests of its shareholders and clients, without referring back to the Board.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/3, the easier option is preferred, unless it would open the door to blight while the other realizes a lawful interest.

column5: The revenues of a Waqf commercial building are insufficient to cover the necessary repairs of the building. The overseer allowed the current lessee to carry out the repairs under commonly accepted technical norms. The ruling is:
column6: Permissible, and the lessee becomes a co-owner of the building in proportion to the cost of the repairs, and may sell his share.
column7: Impermissible, because the lessee of a Waqf asset may not carry out its maintenance.
column8: Permissible, and the lessee will have the priority to remain a lessee of the Waqf asset till he recovers the Waqf's debt owed to him.
column9: Permissible, but the lessee has no right to recover the cost, as the repair is deemed a donation to the Waqf, even if the overseer undertook to repay it.
column11: Per 4/3, if funds are insufficient the lessee may repair, and he has priority to remain lessee until he recovers the Waqf's debt to him.

column5: In principle, the Shari'ah concessions that can be granted to implicit and subsidiary contracts at the time of combining contracts:
column6: Are granted automatically, without any need for clearance by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column7: Can be granted only to the main contract of the combined set.
column8: Cannot be granted to the same contracts when concluded independently.
column9: Can also be granted to the same contracts when concluded independently.
column11: Per 5/1, concessions given to implicit and subsidiary contracts in a combination cannot be given to the same contracts concluded independently.

column5: Stipulating set-off between the customer and the Institution in respect of debts to the Institution arising out of sales on deferred payment, commonly known as set-off and consolidation:
column6: Is not permissible, because it is an agreement on set-off of future debts, which is uncertain and involves Gharar, even if the conditions of contractual set-off are met.
column7: Is always a compulsory set-off, since it was pre-stipulated in the agreement, so that a fresh agreement is never required at the time of set-off even if one debt is superior.
column8: Is always a contractual set-off, which requires a fresh agreement at the time of set-off whenever the currencies differ or one debt is superior to the other, and can never take the form of a compulsory set-off.
column9: May take place either compulsorily or contractually depending on whether the conditions of each are met; pre-stipulating it may avoid a fresh agreement when the currencies differ or one debt is superior.
column11: Per 4/1, it may be compulsory or contractual per the conditions met; pre-stipulation avoids a fresh agreement.

column5: The licensor has the right to perform, directly or through deputation, monitoring and inspection to ascertain observation of the conditions and specifications stipulated in the contract, and to impose the penalties stipulated in the contract in case of breach by the licensee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/5, the licensor may monitor and inspect, and impose contractual penalties for breach.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: It is permissible to specify a ceiling for the expenses charged to investment accounts, above which all the expenses are to be borne by the Mudarib.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/2/2, a ceiling may be specified for expenses, above which all expenses are borne by the Mudarib.

column5: A guarantor guaranteed a debt of USD 10,000. He then reached an agreement with the creditor to settle the debt by delivering a quantity of wheat worth USD 9,000. The guarantor is entitled to recover from the debtor:
column6: The full amount of the guaranteed debt, USD 10,000.
column7: The exact amount of the commodity provided as consideration, or the exact amount of the debt, whichever is less.
column8: The value of the wheat plus a fee for his service.
column9: Nothing, since the debt was settled in a commodity of a different type, and the guarantor is deemed to have made a donation to the debtor.
column11: Per 3/3/2, when settling in a different commodity the guarantor recovers the commodity or the debt amount, whichever is less.

column5: In 2010, an IFI created a cash Waqf of USD 1,000,000 for scholarships, without stipulating anything regarding its revenues. By 2025, inflation had reduced the purchasing power of this amount by 30%. With respect to the Waqf asset:
column6: The Waqf asset remains USD 1,000,000, as there is no influence of change in the purchasing power on the value of cash Waqf assets.
column7: The Waqf asset is deemed reduced to USD 700,000, and the Waqf beneficiaries bear the difference.
column8: The overseer must withhold part of the revenues until the Waqf asset regains its original purchasing power.
column9: The Waqf asset is deemed to be USD 1,300,000, being the amount adjusted for inflation.
column11: Per 2/4/13/4, the money nominated at creation is the Waqf asset; purchasing power changes have no effect (the Waqif may stipulate adding revenue).

column5: If the supplier (owner) of the item has a blood relationship or marital relationship with the customer:
column6: Murabahah on the item is permissible only if the supplier is not the spouse of the customer.
column7: Murabahah on the item is absolutely impermissible, because the transaction is tantamount to 'Inah.
column8: Murabahah on the item is absolutely permissible without any verification, because each party has an independent legal liability.
column9: The Institution shall verify, before entering into Murabahah, that the sale is not fictitious and not a stratagem for the sale of 'Inah.
column11: Per 2/2/4, kinship or marriage does not bar Murabahah, but the Institution must first verify the sale is not fictitious or a stratagem for 'Inah.

column5: Zakah cannot be paid before its due time under any circumstances.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/6, Zakah can be paid before its due time, subject to specific conditions on which Shari'ah boards should be consulted.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for allowing normal expenses to be included in computing the Murabahah selling price of the commodity is that:
column6: Both parties equally benefit from these expenses.
column7: The customer has relinquished his right to object to them.
column8: These expenses are paid to a third party.
column9: These expenses follow the ownership of the goods.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, normal expenses may be included in the selling price because they are paid to a third party.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Unless the seller expressly absolves himself of any latent defects in the sold gold, the buyer has the right to exercise the Option to Revoke Due to Defect if and when defects appear.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/2, absent an express absolution, the buyer has the option to revoke for latent defects in the gold.

column5: Company X owes Bank A USD 50,000 and has a current account with Bank B with a credit balance of USD 80,000. X issues a cheque for USD 50,000 drawn on Bank B in favour of Bank A in settlement of its debt. This transaction is:
column6: A form of Hawalah in which Bank B is the transferor, X is the payer and Bank A is the transferee.
column7: A form of Hawalah in which X is the transferor, Bank B is the payer and Bank A is the transferee.
column8: Impermissible, since it is a sale of debt to a party other than the debtor.
column9: An agency contract for collection, since Bank A is not a creditor of X.
column11: Per 12/1, a cheque to a creditor is Hawalah: the issuer is transferor, the drawee bank payer and the beneficiary transferee.

column5: Instruments and processes used to protect capital and investments must fulfil the following conditions:
column6: The investment partners should bear the risks and losses according to their respective shares in the capital.
column7: The objective should not be to hold the investment manager liable in cases other than wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.
column8: The means adopted must not be a non-Shari'ah compliant contract and should not be a pretext to achieve an objective violating Shari'ah.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/1-4/1/3, all three are conditions for instruments and processes used to protect capital.

column5: In order to avoid interest between the institution and its correspondents, there is no restriction if the institution:
column6: Agrees with its correspondents that overdrafts will bear a profit rate equal to the market benchmark, provided that the rate is settled at the end of each month.
column7: Comes to an agreement with other correspondent banks to place a ceiling upon the overdrafts of one drawn upon the other without any claims for profits (interest).
column8: Maintains compensating balances with the correspondent on which it receives interest that offsets the overdraft interest, provided that the net result of the two is nil.
column9: Pays its correspondents interest on overdrafts and donates an equivalent amount to charity.
column11: Per 10/4, the institution may agree with correspondents on a ceiling for mutual overdrafts without any claim for interest.

column5: In deploying liquidity through Salam, the institution purchases commodities on a Salam basis (immediate payment for deferred delivery) and then:
column6: Sells them after taking physical or constructive delivery, personally or by appointing the seller, in a separate contract, as agent to sell to his customers.
column7: Sells them back to the same seller before taking delivery, at a higher price.
column8: Appoints the seller as its agent to sell them, by a condition stipulated in the Salam contract itself, even before taking physical or constructive delivery of them.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/3, it sells after physical or constructive delivery, personally or via the seller appointed as agent in a separate contract.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Saving accounts which carry no authorization for investing them to the benefit of their holders:
column6: Become subject to the rulings on current accounts.
column7: Become subject to the rulings on restricted investment accounts.
column8: Are held on trust basis, without any guarantee by the institution.
column9: Become subject to the rulings on unrestricted investment accounts.
column11: Per 2/2/3, saving accounts without investment authorization follow the rulings on current accounts; with it, those on investment accounts.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The following sale of gold is permissible without the requirement of immediate exchange of the counter-values:
column6: Sale of gold for silver, regardless of disparity in the weight of the counter-values, since the two are of different genus.
column7: Sale of gold for currencies at any mutually agreed price, provided that the currency is a recognized legal tender.
column8: Sale of gold for commodities other than gold, silver or currencies, or for a usufruct or a service, at any price.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/3–3/1/4, gold for silver or currencies requires spot exchange; gold for other commodities, usufruct or service does not.

column5: Bilateral promises in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek are not allowed because they resemble a contract, i.e. a contract effected before taking ownership of the subject matter of the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 8/2.

column5: The basis for the permissibility of discounting the Istisna'a price for unconditional earlier payment is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in the case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b and his debtor: "Write off a portion of your debt".
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 4/1/3, supported by an International Islamic Fiqh Academy resolution.

column5: An IFI entered into a diminishing Musharakah with a customer to acquire a commercial building. The customer issued a binding promise to purchase the IFI's units gradually over ten years at the original price paid by the IFI for each unit, regardless of the market value at the time. This arrangement is:
column6: Permitted, provided the customer also leases the IFI's share and pays the rental at the prevailing rate.
column7: Permitted, because a binding promise by one partner to buy the other's share is permissible, whatever the price at which it is to be fulfilled or the value of the building at that time.
column8: Not permitted, because acquiring the equity share at its original or face value constitutes a guarantee of the Institution's equity by the other partner.
column9: Not permitted, because the promise to buy in a diminishing Musharakah must not be binding on the partner who issues it.
column11: Per 5/7, a binding promise is allowed at market value or agreed price at acquisition, not at original/face value (capital guarantee).

column5: When there is a price change in the articles of trade during the period between the date of accrual and the date of payment of Zakah:
column6: The lower of the two prices should be adopted.
column7: The price at the date of Zakah accrual should be adopted.
column8: The price at the date of payment of Zakah should be adopted.
column9: The average of the two prices should be adopted.
column11: Per 5/2/2, the price at the date of Zakah accrual should be adopted.

column5: An IFI bought 20 generators by Istisna'a from a manufacturer, paying the price in cash at conclusion to provide it with liquidity, for delivery on 30 June. It then sold 20 generators of the same specification to a hospital by Parallel Istisna'a for delivery on 31 May. The two contracts are separate. This arrangement is:
column6: Impermissible, because the Institution may not sell items acquired by Istisna'a by way of Parallel Istisna'a.
column7: Permissible, because the IFI paid the price in cash to provide liquidity to the manufacturer.
column8: Impermissible, because the delivery date in the parallel (sale) contract must not precede that in the original purchase contract.
column9: Permissible, because the two contracts are separate from each other.
column11: Per 7/1, the parallel sale's delivery date (31 May) may not precede the original purchase's delivery date (30 June).

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith "The neighbour of the house has a greater right to the house" is reconciled with the Hadiths limiting Shuf'ah to undivided property by:
column6: Applying it to movable property only.
column7: Considering it abrogated by the Hadiths on undivided property.
column8: Ascribing it to a neighbour who is also a co-owner or shares easement rights.
column9: Applying it to every neighbour, whether or not he shares easement rights.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith is applied to a neighbour who is also a co-owner or shares easement rights.

column5: Perishable objects cannot be mortgaged, because they cannot be kept until the debt falls due.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/2, perishable objects can be mortgaged, as they can be sold and replaced by their value.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: Contingencies which constitute external reasons for termination of the contract lead to termination of commitments without intervention of any of the two parties, and bearing of the consequences is assigned to the competent party, as when an owner has to bear the consequences relating to what he owns.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5, such contingencies terminate commitments without either party's intervention, and the competent party (e.g., the owner) bears the consequences.

column5: The worker (irrigator) may employ others to assist him to carry out part or all of the contracted work.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2, the worker may employ others to assist him in part or all of the work (at his own cost, per 8/3).

column5: In the charge card (non-revolving credit card):
column6: The arrangement does not provide revolving credit facilities, as the cardholder is supposed to settle the price of the merchandise or the withdrawn cash within the specified period.
column7: The cardholder may pay the debited amount in instalments over periods specified by the card issuer against interest, provided that the interest is disclosed in the card agreement and does not exceed the market rate.
column8: The card can be used only for settling prices of goods and services, but not for withdrawing cash.
column9: The card is a settlement instrument only and not a credit instrument.
column11: Per 3/3/3, the charge card gives no revolving credit; the cardholder settles within the specified period. It is also a credit instrument (3/3/1).

column5: An IFI bought a machine for 100,000 at the request of a customer who had given a binding promise to buy it by Murabahah for 110,000 and had paid Hamish Jiddiyyah of 15,000. After the IFI took possession, the customer refused to buy. The IFI sold the machine to a third party for 96,000. The correct treatment of the Hamish Jiddiyyah is:
column6: The IFI refunds the whole 15,000 and may oblige the customer to take delivery of the machine at 110,000.
column7: The IFI retains the whole 15,000 as Hamish Jiddiyyah.
column8: The IFI deducts 4,000 and refunds 11,000 to the customer.
column9: The IFI deducts 14,000 and refunds 1,000 to the customer.
column11: Per 2/5/4, damage = cost 100,000 − resale 96,000 = 4,000; the lost mark-up of 10,000 is excluded, so 11,000 is refunded.

column5: The contract for provision of online access service by the institution to the beneficiary is characterized as:
column6: A shared-hiring contract (Ijarah Mushtarakah), subject to the rulings of hiring of persons in general and hiring of a shared employee in particular.
column7: An agency contract with remuneration, subject to the rulings of Wakalah and the rights of the principal.
column8: A Ju'alah contract between the institution and the beneficiary, under which the fee is payable on completing the access.
column9: A private-hiring contract with a private employee (Ajir Khass), who is committed to serve only the beneficiary and not any other client of the institution during the access period.
column11: Per 3/2, online access is a shared-hiring contract (Ijarah Mushtarakah), subject to the rulings on hiring persons and hiring a shared employee.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Khiyar al-Ghabn lapses in the following situations:
column6: Destruction or consumption of the sale item, or the attachment of a third-party right over it.
column7: Inaction of the buyer during the period enabling him to revoke, after discovering the price gouging.
column8: Any disposal of the sale item by the buyer after discovering the price gouging.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/5 (a)-(c), all three situations cause Khiyar al-Ghabn to lapse.

column5: Seasonal discounts offered by a seller for stock clearance of unsold goods or of old models are impermissible, because they constitute a sale of goods at below market price.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/6/2/1/2, such discounts are permissible, precisely because they constitute a sale at below market price.

column5: The expenses of preparing the documents of the Murabahah contract between the Institution and the customer:
column6: May be fixed as a percentage of the Murabahah selling price, as agreed between the two parties.
column7: Are to be borne evenly by the two parties, unless they agree that one party bears them wholly, provided they are proportional to the actual amount of work involved.
column8: Must be borne wholly by the Institution as seller, and any agreement to the contrary is void.
column9: Must be borne wholly by the customer as purchase orderer, because the documents are prepared for his benefit, and the Institution may not charge any other fee in respect of the transaction.
column11: Per 2/4/3, document costs are shared evenly unless agreed otherwise, and must match actual work so as not to hide a commitment or facility fee.

column5: Islamic reinsurance constitutes the Islamic alternative for the reinsurance provided by traditional reinsurance companies, which is based on:
column6: Cooperation among the participating insurance companies.
column7: Donation commitments, rather than exchange of premiums and compensation.
column8: Mudarabah between the reinsurer and the insurance companies.
column9: Exchange of the reinsurance premiums and compensation, rather than on donation commitments.
column11: Per 2/2, traditional reinsurance rests on exchange of premiums and compensation rather than on donation commitments.

column5: It is permitted to issue the covered card with the following condition(s):
column6: The cardholder should be required to deposit the cover of the card in a current account, so that it remains available for settlement.
column7: It should be stated that the card issuer will not be obligated to lower the instalments of the financing receivables, and if it lowers one instalment, it is not required to repeat that in future.
column8: The card issuer should undertake to lower the financing instalments according to the usage of the cover during each instalment period, so that the profit of the financing is reduced accordingly in each period.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/2/2/1, the cardholder chooses a current or investment account for the cover, and the issuer is not obliged to lower instalments.

column5: The contract between the Institution and the supplier may be completed through the exchange of notices of offer and acceptance, either in writing or by any form of modern communication customarily practiced according to known principles.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/2, besides a meeting of the parties, exchange of offer and acceptance by writing or modern communication is permitted.

column5: Ownership of the sold debt and its risk are transferred to the buyer:
column6: Only upon the buyer's collection of the debt from the debtor.
column7: By the effect of any means that customarily allows the buyer to claim the debt.
column8: Upon the maturity of the debt.
column9: Upon notification of the debtor and his consent to the sale.
column11: Per 7/1, ownership and risk pass by any means that customarily enables the buyer to claim the debt.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: The institution must disclose its method of profit calculation. This requires that:
column6: It allows its clients to inquire about such methods.
column7: It discloses such methods when mentioning profit in its advertising campaigns and product marketing brochures, in order to prevent any deception.
column8: In contracts, it discloses the total price or the cost price and the profit, either as a lump sum or as a percentage of the cost price.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per item 9, all three disclosure requirements apply to the institution.

column5: Institutions need liquidity to meet numerous requirements, such as:
column6: To distribute profits, which may rely on the liquidation of assets.
column7: To discharge liabilities, to face contingent liabilities, or to liquidate investment vehicles or the institution itself.
column8: To expand its activities, to achieve capital adequacy or to improve its credit rating.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1 and 3/2, all of these are listed as requirements for which institutions need liquidity.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the seller does not have the right to stipulate a condition that he shall retain the ownership of the sold commodity until he receives the price which is deferred for a certain period, because:
column6: He has willingly relinquished spot payment of the price, so he cannot cancel the other party's right to get the sold commodity.
column7: A sold commodity cannot be mortgaged against its own price, since the buyer does not yet own it at the time of the contract.
column8: The sold commodity may only be mortgaged with a notary, and the seller has no means of registering such a mortgage himself.
column9: Such a condition is one of the conditions that serve the interest of the contract, and a seller may stipulate every such condition without limit.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (Hanbali view), having willingly deferred the price, the seller cannot cancel the buyer's right to the commodity.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of a penalty clause in an Istisna'a contract is that:
column6: Such a clause is in the interest of the contract, and is laid down in respect of an obligation regarding items to be produced and delivered in the future, not a monetary debt.
column7: Al-Masnoo' is a debt, and payment in excess of the principal of a debt may be stipulated in Istisna'a, as it is in the sale of debts.
column8: The manufacturer has spent money to manufacture according to specification, and the penalty compensates him for the cost of the items he has produced, whether or not the purchaser takes delivery.
column9: It is an undertaking to make a donation approved by the Maliki scholars, and is therefore payable to charity and not to the ultimate purchaser.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the penalty serves the contract and relates to a future duty to produce and deliver, not a monetary debt.

column5: For the determination of the percentages relating to interest-based loans, interest-taking deposits and prohibited income, recourse is to be had to:
column6: The average of the last five years' financial statements.
column7: The last budget or verified financial position.
column8: Market estimates prevailing at the time of purchase.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/4/5, the last budget or verified financial position is used to determine these percentages.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If the converting bank is unable to terminate some of the interest-based loans it made before the decision to convert:
column6: The bank must waive the principal amounts of these loans.
column7: The bank may use the interest earned to cover the costs of conversion.
column8: The bank must dispose of the interest earned by channelling it to charity and general public utilities.
column9: The bank may keep the interest earned, since the loans were made before the decision to convert.
column11: Per 7/2 and 10/2, interest on loans that cannot be terminated must be channelled to charity, not used by the bank.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: In case of a change in laws leading to more financial commitments to be borne by one of the two parties, determination of the party who shall bear the additional burden is reached:
column6: By assigning the burden to the client in all cases, because the Institution may not bear any new obligation.
column7: By assigning the burden to the Institution in all cases, being the financier.
column8: By resort to law or as per the stipulations of the contract.
column9: By sharing the additional burden equally between the two parties in all cases.
column11: Per 4/4, the party bearing the additional burden from a change in laws is determined by resort to law or as per the contract's stipulations.

column5: The basis for permitting the owner of a current account to use a chequebook and ATM card without compensation is that the benefit is common to both parties; the benefit to the client is secondary, while the primary benefit accrues to the bank.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 10/1/3, the benefits are mutual and set off; the client's benefit is secondary.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting the Waqf to be suspended (taʿlīq) or made effective from a future date includes:
column6: Gharar, the cause for preventing suspension of contracts or making them effective from a future date, is non-effective in donation contracts such as Waqf.
column7: Waqf is an exchange-based contract in which the parties may agree on any condition, including the suspension of the contract on a future event.
column8: Suspension does not affect Waqf because the Waqf beneficiary's acceptance is a condition for its conclusion, and the acceptance may itself be suspended by the beneficiary.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/1/3, gharar, the reason for barring suspension, is non-effective in donation contracts such as Waqf.

column5: It is not permissible to stipulate the satisfaction (repayment) of Qard at a place other than that where the loan was made, since such a stipulation may benefit the lender.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2, stipulating repayment at another place is permissible; the basis notes this holds whether or not the lender benefits.

column5: An admission by a debtor who has been declared insolvent of a liability to another person relating to his sequestered assets:
column6: Has legal effect provided that it is documented and certified as required by official procedures, and the person in whose favour it is made then shares the sequestered assets.
column7: Has no legal effect, whether it relates to a debt incurred before or after the declaration of insolvency, unless the creditors accept that such debt was incurred before the declaration of insolvency.
column8: Has legal effect if it relates to a debt incurred before the declaration of insolvency, even if the creditors do not accept that the debt was incurred before the declaration.
column9: Has legal effect, and the person in whose favour it is made shares the sequestered assets pro-rata with the creditors.
column11: Per 5/1, such an admission has no legal effect unless the creditors accept that the debt was incurred before the declaration.

column5: It is not permitted:
column6: To purchase shares using interest-based loans, provided by either a broker or any other person, in consideration for mortgaging the shares as a security for payment.
column7: To sell shares that one does not own, relying on the promise of a broker to lend the shares to him at the date of delivery.
column8: For the relevant authorities to organise trading in shares so that trading will not take place except through specific licensed stockbrokers.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/1/2/6-7, (a) and (b) are prohibited; per 4/1/2/8, restricting trading to licensed brokers is permissible.

column5: Applying the rules of the expenses of possession to other financial commutative contracts, in the absence of a customary practice or stipulation to the contrary:
column6: The expenses of taking possession of the leased property are borne by the lessee, and the expenses of delivering the lease value are borne by the lessor.
column7: The expenses of delivering the Salam commodity are borne by the seller, and the expenses of delivering the capital (Ras al-Mal) are borne by the Rab al-Salam (the buyer).
column8: The expenses of conveyancing and registration are always borne by the seller, irrespective of any stipulation.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/4, in Salam the seller bears delivery of the commodity and the Rab al-Salam the delivery of the capital; in Ijarah it is lessor/lessee.

column5: Should the lessee in a lease of a described asset receive an asset that does not conform to the description, he is entitled to reject it and demand an asset that conforms to the description.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the rule in 3/5.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: The Shari'ah basis for not stipulating a maximum profit limit is:
column6: The Quranic Verse {"…except it be a trade amongst you, by mutual consent"}, as confirmed by the Fiqh Academy resolution that traders are bound by no fixed profit rate.
column7: AAOIFI Accounting Standard No. (20) on deferred sales, which does not cap profit.
column8: The Quranic Verse {"Allah has permitted sale"}, as referring to the deferred sale, to which interest is compared, and which the Fiqh Academy confirmed has a maximum profit rate.
column9: The Hadith: "Muslims are bound by their conditions", since the profit rate is agreed upon by the parties.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1, it is the verse on trade by mutual consent.

column5: Both parties to a Mudarabah contract should possess the legal capacity to appoint agents and accept agency. The Shari'ah basis for this rule is that:
column6: The Mudarib is a guarantor of the Mudarabah capital against loss of any kind.
column7: The Mudarabah contract is binding from the moment of its conclusion, whatever the stage of the work.
column8: Each party acts as an agent of the other party and appoints him to act on his behalf.
column9: The capital provider is entitled to work with the Mudarib in the business, as a partner in management.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, each party acts as agent for, and appoints, the other; capacity for agency entitles one to conclude Mudarabah.

column5: It is not permissible to use a bill of exchange or a promissory note as a counter-value in:
column6: A contract of Sarf (currency exchange).
column7: The purchase of ascertained goods by the beneficiary of a paper not yet due, with delivery of the goods.
column8: The lease of the usufruct of an ascertained asset by the beneficiary of a paper not yet due, with delivery of the asset.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2, they may not be used where possession is required, e.g. Sarf or Salam capital; 6/3 permits them as price for ascertained goods.

column5: A customer gave an IFI funds on a Mudarabah basis without specifying a duration. Two months later, after the IFI had purchased goods and commenced trading, the customer notified the IFI that he was terminating the contract with immediate effect and demanded the return of his capital. The correct ruling is:
column6: The contract terminates automatically, and the goods must be sold at cost to return the capital, with the Mudarib bearing any shortfall.
column7: The customer may terminate the contract at once, because Mudarabah is a non-binding contract and no duration was specified, and the Mudarib is entitled to nothing for his work, since he has not yet realised any profit.
column8: The customer may terminate the contract, provided he pays the Mudarib remuneration for similar services for the period during which he has worked.
column9: The customer may not terminate the contract unilaterally at this stage, because once the Mudarib has commenced the business the contract becomes binding until actual or constructive liquidation.
column11: Per 4/3/1, once the Mudarib commences business the Mudarabah binds until actual or constructive liquidation.

column5: Possession of a mortgaged debt takes place:
column6: Only when the mortgaged debt is collected from the debtor and handed over to the mortgagee.
column7: By possession of the debt's document or by attestation of the debt when it is mortgaged.
column8: Only if the debt is owed by the mortgagee himself, as he alone can possess it on behalf of the mortgagor.
column9: Only when the debt falls due.
column11: Per 3/2/12, a mortgaged debt is possessed by holding its document or by its attestation at the time of mortgaging.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the rule that the borrower does not come to own the wealth lent except through possession is that:
column6: The contract of Qard combines commutative and donation aspects, the donation aspect being predominant, so its rule is similar to that of gift (Hibah), where ownership is transferred with the taking of possession.
column7: Qard is a purely commutative contract, like sale, in which ownership is transferred by the mere conclusion of the contract, and possession is only a matter of performance, so the lender may recover the identical wealth.
column8: Qard is a trust (Amanah), like Wadi'ah.
column9: The lender retains ownership of the wealth lent until repayment.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, donation predominates in Qard, so like Hibah ownership passes with possession.

column5: Permissibility of hiring of persons for doing deferred services is based on:
column6: What Omar did in the presence of the Sahabah (companions of the Prophet), which was adopted by Ahmad.
column7: The Hadith narrated by Hakim Ibn Hizam: 'Don't sell what you do not have', and the analogy between hiring and sale.
column8: The Fatwa of the Unified Shari'ah Supervisory Board of Al Baraka Group, and the resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on enforceability of pledges.
column9: The practice of the Prophet (peace be upon him) when he and Abu Bakr hired a man from Bani Al-Dail to serve them as a guide after three days, and the fact that hiring is a time-based contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, deferred hiring rests on the hiring of a guide from Bani Al-Dail after three days, and on hiring being time-based. Omar's act backs 'Arboun.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Among the permissible applications of international commodity sales is:
column6: Sale by the agent of the purchased commodity before actually or legally taking delivery.
column7: The institution making the payment of the purchase price contingent upon the agent providing a guarantee for the payment of the sale price.
column8: Purchase by the institution of a commodity on a spot basis and its subsequent sale to another on a deferred payment basis, with the avoidance of buy-back being stipulated.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/4, spot purchase and deferred resale avoiding buy-back is permitted; (a) and (b) are prohibited by 4/2/4 and 4/2/11.

column5: All the rules of Salam explained in the standard are applicable to Parallel Salam as well.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 6/4.

column5: Waqf overseership is a right established for the interest of the Waqif.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/1, Waqf overseership is a right established for the interest of the Waqf.

column5: The basis for the permissibility of unilateral termination of participation in an allotment (Muhassah) partnership is that unilateral termination is allowed in principle, provided such action inflicts no damage to any of the partners.
