column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, citing the Hadith 'No harm to be inflicted and no reciprocal harm.'

column5: A bank engaged a collection agency on the basis of Ju'alah to collect a debt of 1,000,000 owed to it, for a compensation of 50,000 contingent upon collection. The agency managed to collect 600,000 only. The agency is entitled to:
column6: Nothing, because the whole debt was not collected.
column7: Reasonable wages, irrespective of the amount collected.
column11: Per 8/2, if part of the debt is collected, compensation proportionate to the amount collected is due: 60% of 50,000.

column5: The guarantee amount (seriousness margin) paid by the client who pledges to hire the institution's services can be:
column6: Invested by the institution for its own account, with the profit belonging to the institution.
column7: Kept as a deposit with the institution without being disposed of.
column8: Used by the institution as an interest-free loan for financing its own operations.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2, it can be kept as an undisposed deposit, invested on the client's behalf via Mudarabah or investment agency, or frozen in the client's current account.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Preventing the Institution from adopting the Fatwas of other boards, except when allowed by its own board, stems from:
column6: The need to bar the way to any tendency of fabrication or attempt to pursue Shari'ah exemptions without observing their controls, context and circumstances, which leads to adoption of irrelevant Fatwas.
column7: The need to protect the confidentiality of the Institution's operations and of the data of its clients, which would be disclosed to other boards if their Fatwas were adopted.
column8: The principle that the Fatwa of one board cannot be overridden by that of another, since every Fatwa issued by a Shari'ah board is final and binding on all other boards and institutions, whatever the reasons of the dispute.
column9: The need to reduce the fees paid to Shari'ah boards.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it bars fabrication and pursuit of exemptions out of context, which leads to adopting irrelevant Fatwas.

column5: The basis of the Shari'ah ruling that the company should not guarantee the insurance assets is that:
column6: The company owns the contributions, and one cannot guarantee his own property, so the company is liable only for the indemnities it has itself undertaken to pay out of its own capital.
column7: The company is an agent, and the Fuqaha unanimously agree that an agent should not guarantee the property except against misconduct, negligence or breach of the contract.
column8: A guarantee by the company would turn the contributions into Qard.
column9: The company is a partner of the policyholders and shares the losses with them.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the company is an agent, and agents by consensus guarantee only for misconduct, negligence or breach.

column5: A valid guarantee may be given for a debt that will arise in the future; however, the guarantor may withdraw it before the future debt is actually created, after notifying the person having interest in the guarantee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2, a future debt may be guaranteed, and the guarantee may be withdrawn by notice before the debt arises.

column5: It is permissible for either party to unilaterally amend the restrictions in the investment agency contract, provided that the other party is notified in advance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4, it is not permissible for any one of the parties to unilaterally amend the restrictions in the agency contract.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for revocation of the Musaqat contract by mutual consent of the two parties (Iqalah) is:
column6: The Hadith: "Anyone who consents to revoke the contract upon the request of a regretting counterparty, Allah shall forgive his regretful sins on the Day of Judgment".
column7: The practice of the companions in Khaybar until Umar evacuated them, without any objection from anyone, which proves that revocation by consent is permissible.
column8: The Verse {"O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations"}, which permits revocation by agreement.
column9: The Hadith: "There should be neither harm nor malice", since the worker would otherwise be excessively harmed and the owner would be deprived of his property without any remedy.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 13/1, Iqalah is based on the Hadith on accepting a regretting party's request to revoke.

column5: A customer's Murabaha debt of 100 has matured. The IFI accepted a commodity from the customer in substitution of the debt and then sold the same commodity back to the customer for 115 payable after one year. This transaction is:
column6: Permitted, as it is a new Murabaha independent of the first debt.
column7: Permitted, if the customer is solvent.
column8: Prohibited, since it increases the debt against an increase in tenure and takes the form of 'Inah.
column9: Permitted, provided that the IFI took possession of the commodity before reselling it to the customer.
column11: Per 4/1/3/3, substituting a debt with a commodity then reselling it to the debtor at a higher deferred price is a prohibited form of 'Inah.

column5: To obtain liquidity through Istisna'a, the institution concludes:
column6: An Istisna'a-based sale contract in which advance payment is obligatory, and a parallel Istisna'a-based purchase contract with immediate payment, the two contracts being interdependent.
column7: A single Istisna'a contract in which the institution is both the manufacturer and the purchaser, with deferred payment of the price.
column8: An Istisna'a-based purchase contract with immediate payment and a parallel Istisna'a-based sale contract for a deferred price.
column9: An Istisna'a sale contract stipulating advance payment, although it is not obligatory, and a parallel Istisna'a purchase contract with deferred or installment payment.
column11: Per 4/2/2, the institution sells by Istisna'a with advance payment (not obligatory) and buys by parallel Istisna'a on deferred terms.

column5: Prohibition of Muwata`ah as an excuse for Riba originates from the application of the principle of:
column6: Sadd al-Zara`i' (blocking the means).
column7: Al-Kharaj bil-Daman (entitlement to gain is linked to bearing liability).
column8: Al-Darurat Tubih al-Mahzurat (necessities permit prohibitions).
column9: Al-Ghunm bil-Ghurm (gain is linked to risk).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (6/3/2), it applies Sadd al-Zara`i', which bars permissible acts used as means to banned objectives.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The shareholders must accelerate the redemption of all impermissible mortgages attached to the assets of the bank. In the case of external conversion:
column6: The buyer may keep them until the maturity of the secured loans, provided the interest on the loans is disposed of.
column7: The buyer must redeem them out of the bank's interest income.
column8: The buyer must stipulate that the seller replaces impermissible mortgages with permissible ones.
column9: The buyer must replace them with personal guarantees for the same loans, and accelerate the redemption of the loans.
column11: Per 9/3, in external conversion the buyer must stipulate that the seller replace impermissible mortgages with permissible ones.

column5: With regard to taking care of the crop in Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat):
column6: Before and after harvesting, the owner alone is obligated to take care of the crop, since he owns the trees.
column7: After harvesting, the worker alone is obligated to take care of the crop, and before harvesting the owner alone is.
column8: Before harvesting, both parties take care of the crop in proportion to their shares; after harvesting, the worker alone is obligated to do so, unless custom or a term of the contract dictates otherwise.
column9: After harvesting, the worker and the owner must take care of the crop, each in proportion to his share; before harvesting, the worker must do so unless custom or a contract term dictates otherwise.
column11: Per 8/1, after harvest both care for the crop pro-rata; before harvest the worker does, unless custom or contract says otherwise.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar in a corollary (Tabi') of the primary subject matter has no effect on the contract. An example of this is:
column6: Selling unripe fruits apart from the trees and without a stipulation for awaiting harvesting.
column7: Selling the unripe fruits along with the trees.
column8: Selling fish in the water when it is not found in a confined place.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/3, selling unripe fruits with the trees is Gharar in a corollary; selling them alone voids the sale, as does selling fish in open water (5/4).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting the creation of Waqf for the benefit of those who are non-existent at the time of its creation includes:
column6: Narratives reported from the Companions (RA) wherein Waqf was for the benefit of a progeny which had not yet been born.
column7: The rule that acceptance is required only from existing beneficiaries.
column8: The analogy upon Mudarabah, in which the profit does not exist at the time of the contract, and the labour of the Mudarib.
column9: The analogy upon the sale of a non-existent object.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/4/4, Companions' Waqfs for unborn progeny, and Waqf being an ongoing charity (ṣadaqa jāriyah).

column5: Salam is not permitted for:
column6: Fungible goods that may be weighed, measured or counted, the articles of which do not differ in any significant manner.
column7: Anything specific, like "this car".
column8: Products of companies manufactured in approximate units identified by trademarks and standardised specifications, and regularly and commonly available.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2/3, Salam is barred for a specific item such as 'this car'; fungibles (3/2/1) and standardised branded products (3/2/2) are allowed.

column5: The income statement (profit and loss account):
column6: Forms the basis for Zakah calculation, since Zakah is due only on profits.
column7: Is not referred to at all for Zakah purposes.
column8: Does not form a basis for Zakah calculation, yet it is referred to for knowing the income or profit of the income-earning fixed assets.
column9: Is used as the basis for Zakah calculation only in the years in which the Institution makes profits, since Zakah is not due in years of losses.
column11: Per 2/3/2, the income statement is not the Zakah basis (the balance sheet is), but it is referred to for income of income-earning fixed assets.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: An uncommissioned agent (Fodooli) is a person who:
column6: Discharges, in the absence of need or urgency, the affairs of others without being an agent or having a right to do so by virtue of Shari'ah.
column7: Discharges the affairs of others in case of need or urgency, without being an agent, and is entitled to be indemnified for his expenses by the owner.
column8: Acts on behalf of another under a non-paid agency.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 8/1, the Fodooli acts for others without agency or Shari'ah right and in the absence of any need or urgency.

column5: An IFI bought a commodity from Supplier S at a spot price and sold it on credit to Customer C. All three parties had agreed beforehand that C would resell the commodity to S at spot for less than the deferred price. This arrangement is:
column6: Permitted as Tawarruq, since the commodity is sold at spot to someone other than the IFI.
column7: Permitted, because C resells the commodity to S and not to the IFI, so that the sale is a tripartite one outside the rule of 'Inah.
column8: Not permitted, since it is a stratagem for 'Inah, and engaging a third party does not change the essence of the transaction.
column9: Permitted, provided that the IFI and C each take possession of the commodity.
column11: Per 4/4 and its basis, collusion to return the commodity to the first seller at a lower spot price is a stratagem for 'Inah.

column5: Among the conditions for exempting subscription and dealing in shares of corporations that sometimes undertake transactions in Riba, even though their primary activity is permissible, is:
column6: That the corporation does not state in its memorandum of association that one of its objectives is to deal in interest, or in prohibited goods or materials like pork.
column7: That the amount of income generated from a prohibited component does not exceed 5% of the total income of the corporation.
column8: That the total amount of interest-taking deposits does not exceed 30% of the market capitalization of total equity.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/4/1, 3/4/3 and 3/4/4, all three are among the conditions of the exemption.

column5: Protecting capital by permissible means is:
column6: Impermissible in Mudarabah, since the capital provider must bear the risk of loss.
column7: Compulsory upon the capital provider in all investments.
column8: Disliked, as it conflicts with the principle that the capital provider bears the risk.
column9: Desirable in Shari'ah, as it serves the objectives of Shari'ah with regard to wealth.
column11: Per 3/1, protecting capital by permissible means is desirable as it serves the objectives of Shari'ah regarding wealth.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Hiring of Persons covers:
column6: Mudarabah and investment agency, in which the institution manages the funds of investors against a share in the profits of the investment.
column7: Musaqat, Muzara'ah and Istisna'a, in which work is performed on trees, land or manufactured goods against a share in the output or a price.
column8: Hiring of the service or work of persons between the institution and others, whether the institution is the employee or the employer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per item 1, the Standard covers hiring of persons with the institution as employee or employer, and excludes Mudarabah, investment agency, Musaqat, Istisna'a etc.

column5: If the cause for which a reserve was created out of the Waqf revenues ceases, the reserve shall be added to the Waqf asset.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/8, if the cause of the reserve ceases, the reserve is disbursed in the avenues of Waqf disposal.

column5: When an allocation is made for defective or slow-moving goods prepared for trade, the allocation should be deducted from zakatable assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/6/1, such goods are valued at market price, and an allocation made for them should not be deducted from zakatable assets.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar relating to sale of a non-owned commodity nullifies the sale contract. The exceptional cases here (subject to their respective conditions) are:
column6: Istisna'a and Ju'alah.
column7: Salam and Istisna'a.
column8: Salam and Bay' al-Istijrar.
column9: Murabahah and Ijarah.
column11: Per 5/5, Salam and Istisna'a are the exceptions to the nullity of selling what the seller does not have at contracting.

column5: Institutions can apply utilization concession contracts in the following forms, excluding:
column6: Musharakah, fixed or diminishing, where the Institution contributes a share in the required capital.
column7: Ijarah, where the State gives the land on lease to the licensee for a rent payable as a predetermined share of the output.
column8: Ju'alah or Parallel Ju'alah, where the licensee receives a specific share of the output as remuneration.
column9: Mudarabah, where the State provides the land to the licensee in return for a fixed lump sum guaranteed to the State as profit.
column11: Per 7/3, Mudarabah is based on a predetermined rate of profit sharing, not a guaranteed lump sum; the other forms are in 7/1, 7/2, 7/4.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for prohibiting the receipt of commitment commission is that:
column6: It is a commission for a guarantee, and a guarantee is a gratuitous contract.
column7: It amounts to the sale of a debt for a debt.
column8: Its amount is unknown at the time of contracting, which entails Gharar, since it depends on the extent to which the financing is actually utilised by the customer and on the date of utilisation.
column9: Such commission is paid for exercising the right of contracting, which is a matter of will and desire, rather than a subject matter of compensatory deals.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, commitment commission is paid for the right of contracting, a matter of will, not a subject of exchange.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: It is impermissible for Institutions to join the membership of international card regulatory organizations, since those organizations also deal with interest-bearing credit cards.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/1, membership is permissible provided the Institutions avoid any Shari'ah infringements prescribed by those organizations.

column5: If the Institution has stipulated in a contract dealing with indebtedness that it may recoup amounts due from a late-paying debtor out of his accounts with it, this may be done:
column6: Only with the fresh consent of the debtor at the time of recoupment.
column7: From current accounts only, since investment accounts are invested on the basis of Mudarabah and cannot be touched without the fresh consent of the investor, whatever the currency of the account.
column8: From accounts in any currency, at the rate of exchange prevailing on the date the debt was established.
column9: From current or investment accounts, without any further consent of the debtor, provided the balance is in the currency of the debt; otherwise at the then prevailing rate of exchange.
column11: Per 2/5/3, recoupment from current or investment accounts needs no further consent; other currencies use the then prevailing rate.

column5: An IFI purchased a quantity of cotton stored in a public warehouse and received a warehouse receipt issued in its name, through which the cotton was ascertained and by which the IFI was able to undertake transactions in it. Before physically moving the cotton, the IFI sold it on Murabahah to its customer. This transaction is:
column6: Impermissible, because the cotton must first be physically transported to the IFI's premises.
column7: Impermissible, because possession of documents is not deemed possession of goods that are estimated by weight.
column8: Permissible, because possession of the warehouse receipt in these conditions is deemed constructive possession of the cotton.
column9: Permissible only if the IFI first weighs the cotton in the presence of the customer.
column11: Per 3/5, a receipt in the IFI's name through which goods are ascertained and dealt in is constructive possession, so the IFI may resell.

column5: A Hawalah liability comes to an end by:
column6: Settlement of the debt, or the payer's refusal to pay.
column7: Settlement of the debt, or the death of the transferor.
column8: Settlement of the debt, or unilateral termination by either the transferor or the transferee, since Hawalah is a contract of courtesy.
column9: Settlement of the debt, mutual agreement to terminate it, or the debt being written off by the transferee.
column11: Per 11, it ends by settlement, mutual termination or write-off by the transferee; it is binding (4/2) and survives death (10).

column5: If a discount card is issued against a subscription fee by the same entity that offers the discounts, and the fee is exclusively for providing discounts and for no other services, the card is:
column6: Not permissible, as it involves Gharar and Jahalah.
column7: Permissible, because the issuer is deemed to be a broker.
column8: Permissible, as it constitutes a promise (Wa'ad) to voluntarily reduce the price on the basis of Tabarru'.
column9: Permissible, because the discount is incidental to the card.
column11: Per 3/6/2/2/2 Scenario (2), a fee exclusively for discounts, charged by the discounting entity, makes the card impermissible for Gharar and Jahalah.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to receive a fee for a feasibility study that it undertakes, in case such study is requested by the customer and for his benefit and the customer agrees to pay the fee; the customer is entitled to a copy of the study if he so requires.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the wording of 2/4/5.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Without being an agent, and in the absence of any need or urgency, Khalid sold a piece of land owned by Saeed to an IFI. At the time of signing the contract, Khalid did not declare that he had no authority. When Saeed learned of the sale, he refused to approve it. The ruling is:
column6: The act becomes binding on Khalid.
column7: The sale becomes binding on Saeed, since the IFI acted in good faith.
column8: The sale becomes binding on Saeed if the price was not less than the market price.
column9: The sale remains suspended until the IFI revokes it.
column11: Per 8/2, if the owner does not approve, the Fodooli's act binds the Fodooli himself, as he did not declare his lack of authority.

column5: It is permitted to create Waqf of:
column6: Bonds, provided that the interest earned on them is disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries.
column7: Usufructs owned by the Waqif as a lessee, for a term longer than the lease period.
column8: Movable assets, such as vehicles, machinery, equipment, production tools, websites, and digital applications.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4/7 movables may be Waqf; bonds must be substituted with permissible assets (2/4/10); a lessee's Waqf may not exceed the lease term (2/4/12).

column5: With regard to stipulating financial compensation as a penalty clause in respect of a delay by a debtor in settling his debt:
column6: It is permitted if the amount of compensation is not pre-determined in the contract but is assessed at the time of default.
column7: It is not permitted, in cash or other consideration, whether or not the amount is pre-determined, and whether for loss of income (opportunity loss) or for loss due to a change in the value of the currency.
column8: It is permitted if the compensation is for a loss due to a change in the value of the currency of the debt.
column9: It is permitted if the compensation is limited to the actual loss of income (opportunity loss) suffered by the creditor, provided it is assessed by the court after the default is established and is paid in cash.
column11: Per 2/1/2, any compensation for delay is prohibited, pre-determined or not, for opportunity loss or currency loss alike.

column5: The view that Waqf should not be for an impermissible purpose, while it can be for non-charitable purposes, is based on Waqf being a donation (Tabarru'). This viewpoint belongs to:
column6: The Hanafi School, whereas the Maliki School is of the opinion that the Waqf purpose should be charitable.
column7: The Maliki School, whereas the Hanafi School is of the opinion that the Waqf purpose should be charitable.
column8: The Shafi'i School, whereas the Maliki School is of the opinion that the Waqf purpose should be charitable.
column9: All the Schools of Fiqh unanimously.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, this is the Maliki view; the Hanafi School holds that the Waqf purpose should be charitable.

column5: If the Murabahah is carried out by means of syndicated financing, the Institution which acts as the arranger of the syndicate:
column6: Is entitled to an arrangement fee to be paid by the participants in the syndicate.
column7: Is entitled to a commitment fee from the customer for the period before execution of the Murabahah.
column8: Is not entitled to any fee, because any such fee is a commitment fee.
column9: Is entitled to a fee for providing the credit facility, to be paid by the customer.
column11: Per 2/4/4, the arranger of a syndicated Murabahah is entitled to an arrangement fee paid by the syndicate participants.

column5: Claimants in one debt may divide it among themselves in proportion to their respective shares, so that each claimant reserves his respective share in it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/1, co-claimants may divide one debt pro rata so each reserves his share.

column5: Regarding goods imported through documentary credits covered by the Institution, including the expenses of opening the credit and the amounts retained by intermediary banks:
column6: No Zakah is paid on the amounts retained for the credit until the goods are received, then Zakah is paid on their cost.
column7: Zakah should be paid on the expenses of opening the credit only.
column8: Zakah should be paid on the amounts retained for the credit, and not the expenses; when the goods are owned, Zakah is paid on them on the basis of their market value.
column9: Zakah should be paid on both the amounts retained for the credit and the expenses of opening it, since both are paid for the goods.
column11: Per 5/2/6/7, Zakah is paid on the amounts retained for the credit, not on expenses; once the goods are owned, on their market value.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: A buyer who is enticed by deceptive conduct and decides to retain the sale item is entitled to compensation for the difference in value.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4/1 and 3/4/3, he may return or retain the item, but is not entitled to compensation if he retains it.

column5: The amount of the Mudarabah capital may be left undetermined at the conclusion of the contract, provided that it is determined at the date of liquidation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/2, the capital must be clearly known and defined in quality and quantity, eliminating any uncertainty.

column5: When there is acceptance by the customer of an offer from the supplier that is either addressed to him personally, or that has no addressee:
column6: The Institution may carry out Murabahah on the same item, provided it pays the price directly to the supplier.
column7: The sale is concluded with the customer, and it is not permissible for the Institution to carry out Murabahah on the same item.
column8: The Institution may still carry out Murabahah on the same item, provided the customer has not yet paid the price to the supplier.
column9: The customer may assign the contract executed with the supplier to the Institution, which then sells the item to him by Murabahah.
column11: Per 2/2/1, the customer's acceptance concludes the sale with him, so the Institution may not carry out Murabahah on that item.

column5: A legally binding promise is enforceable against both the promisor and the promisee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/5, it is enforceable only against the promisor; the promisee may demand performance or waive it.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: Revocation by exercise of a cooling-off option cannot take place in the case of:
column6: Destruction of the sale item caused by a natural disaster before delivery.
column7: Destruction of the sale item caused by the buyer, whether before or after delivery.
column8: Destruction of the sale item caused by the seller before delivery.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/1–7/2, destruction by natural disaster is an impediment only after delivery, while destruction by the buyer is one before or after delivery.

column5: When the profit from investing the premiums retained by the Islamic insurance company on behalf of a traditional reinsurance company is distributed as per the ratios agreed upon:
column6: The share of the traditional reinsurance company is added to its account, whereas the share of the Islamic insurance company goes to its shareholders as the remuneration of the Mudarib, since the participants' fund has no independent personality in this respect.
column7: The whole profit is added to the account of the participants.
column8: The traditional reinsurer's share is added to its account with the Islamic insurance company, whereas the share earned by the insurance company for performing the investment as an independent personality goes to the participants' account.
column9: The whole profit is paid to the traditional reinsurance company, being Rab al-Mal.
column11: Per 6/2, the traditional reinsurer's share is credited to its account; the Islamic insurer's investment share goes to the participants' account.

column5: If the leased asset was purchased from the lessee before it was leased back to him on the basis of Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek:
column6: The asset may be sold back to the lessee at any time during the lease.
column7: The transaction is absolutely impermissible, because it is a form of 'Inah, and the lessor may in no case lease back an asset purchased from the same customer, even where a long period has elapsed between the two contracts.
column8: The asset may be sold back to the lessee only at the end of the lease term, regardless of its duration, and not before half of the lease term has elapsed.
column9: A reasonable period must have expired between the lease contract and the sale of the asset to the lessee, long enough for the property or its value to have changed, to avoid 'Inah.
column11: Per 8/5, a reasonable period long enough for the asset or its value to change must pass before selling it back, to avoid 'Inah.

column5: The sale of a monetary debt to a third party against cash is not permitted, because it contains (……….) if the counter-value differs in value from the monetary debt, and (……….) if the counter-value is equal in value to it.
column6: Ribā al-nasī'a … ribā al-faḍl and ribā al-nasī'a
column7: Ribā al-faḍl … ribā al-faḍl and ribā al-nasī'a
column8: Ribā al-nasī'a … ribā al-faḍl
column9: Ribā al-faḍl and ribā al-nasī'a … ribā al-nasī'a
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/1, unequal value involves both ribā al-faḍl and ribā al-nasī'a; equal value involves ribā al-nasī'a.

column5: If the Institution and its customer exchange bilateral promises that debts which may be created between them in the future will be settled by way of set-off, and the currencies of the two debts differ:
column6: The exchange rate should be fixed at the time of exchanging the promises, so as to avoid disputes at the time of actual set-off.
column7: The set-off will take place at the exchange rate prevailing when the debts are created, since the promise is binding on both parties from the outset.
column8: The promise should be concluded on the basis that set-off will take place at the current exchange rate at the time of actual set-off.
column9: The promise is not permissible, because a bilateral promise relating to currencies is prohibited.
column11: Per 3, the current rate at actual set-off must apply, to prevent Riba by roundabout methods or implied agreement.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: In Mudarabah financing, setting different profit ratios or rates:
column6: Is permissible as per the different tenors, and may also be triggered when the profit of either party reaches a specified hurdle rate, provided no party is totally deprived of profit.
column7: Is permissible as per the different tenors or upon reaching a hurdle rate, even if one of the parties is totally deprived of profit in some periods, provided that this is agreed in writing.
column8: Is impermissible, because the profit-sharing ratio must remain fixed for the whole term of the Mudarabah.
column9: Is permissible according to the different tenors of the Mudarabah only, and not upon the profit of either party reaching a hurdle rate.
column11: Per 7/1, different ratios by tenor or hurdle rate are permissible, but no party may be totally deprived of profit.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of leasing a property on the basis of specifications, even if the lessor does not own it, is that:
column6: Ijarah, unlike sale, is a contract that involves time.
column7: Leasing back an asset to the person from whom it was acquired does not involve 'Inah.
column8: The lessee has ownership of the usufruct by virtue of the Ijarah contract.
column9: This will not lead to dispute, in which case it is similar to a Salam contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a lease of a described asset does not lead to dispute and is similar to Salam.

column5: In the absence of sufficient amounts for maintenance and renovation of a leased Waqf asset:
column6: The Waqf asset must be exchanged (Istibdal) for another asset.
column7: The Waqf superintendent has the right to allow the tenant to make such maintenance and renovation, against having the priority to continue as a tenant of the Waqf asset until getting full repayment of his debt.
column8: The superintendent must stop paying the beneficiaries and borrow for the Waqf until the Waqf income covers the cost of maintenance.
column9: The superintendent may allow the tenant to make the maintenance and renovation, and the tenant becomes a co-owner of the Waqf asset in proportion to his expenditure.
column11: Per 8/1/3, the superintendent may let the tenant do it, with priority to remain tenant until his debt is fully repaid.

column5: With regard to the contract of guarantee:
column6: It is permissible in contracts of exchange, e.g. a contract of sale, or contracts of rights, e.g. right of intellectual property.
column7: It does not affect the permissibility of the original contract in which it is required.
column8: It is permissible to stipulate a guarantee into the body of an original contract, because guarantee is appropriate to, or relevant in, contracts.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1/1, all three statements are correct.

column5: In principle, Zakah on articles of trade is to be paid in cash, yet:
column6: It may always be paid in kind from the same articles of trade, at the option of the Zakah payer, even in the absence of trade recession.
column7: It may never be paid in kind.
column8: In case of trade recession it can be paid in kind (from the same articles of trade), provided that the interest of Zakah recipients is thus achieved.
column9: It may be paid in kind in case of trade recession, even if the interest of Zakah recipients is not achieved thereby, and the goods are valued at their cost price.
column11: Per 5/2/4, payment in kind from the same articles is allowed in trade recession, provided the interest of Zakah recipients is achieved.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: ………… are contracts in which both counter-values are deferred, with the legal effects of the contracts taking place at a determined future date, and delivery and possession take place at that time:
column6: Forward contracts.
column7: Spot contracts.
column8: Futures commodity contracts.
column9: Istisna'a contracts.
column11: Per 2/2/2, forward contracts defer both counter-values, with effects, delivery and possession at a determined future date.

column5: The following are included in the insolvency assets of an insolvent institution:
column6: Restricted deposits, funds and portfolios in which the institution's responsibility is limited to managing on a paid agency or Mudarabah basis.
column7: Current accounts held with the institution, because these are its liabilities which must be borne by it alone and should not be borne by the investment accountholders.
column8: Securities belonging to third parties and safety deposit boxes held by the institution as custodian.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 9/1/1, current accounts are included; independent investment vehicles (9/2) and custody assets (9/3) are not.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: The effects of Jawa`ih (calamities) are originally noticeable in selling of fruits and other agricultural products, where the occurrence of such an incident leads to:
column6: Discounting the price in proportion to the damage in the product.
column7: Termination of the whole sale contract without any discount.
column8: The buyer bearing the entire loss once the contract is signed.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 5/5, in selling fruits and agricultural products a calamity leads to discounting the price in proportion to the damage in the product.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: ………… means taking possession of a piece of land and marking it with certain recognised markers with the permission of the government:
column6: Tahjir.
column7: Private easement.
column8: Shuf'ah.
column9: Occupancy.
column11: Per 9/1, Tahjir is taking possession of land and marking it with recognised markers with government permission.

column5: ………… is a contract in which one of the parties offers a specified compensation to anyone who will achieve a determined result in a known or unknown period.
column6: Istisna'a.
column7: Ijarah of persons.
column8: Ju'alah.
column9: Agency with remuneration.
column11: Per 2, Ju'alah: the Ja'il offers a specified Ju'l to any 'Amil who achieves a determined result in a known or unknown period.

column5: Among the bases for permitting the lender to charge the actual direct cost is the verse (And neither scribe nor witness should be harmed), as evidence that the charges of writing the debt deed fall on the debtor for their actual amount.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 5/1/1, this verse shows that the costs of writing the debt fall on the debtor at their actual amount.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: A person who has carried out Tahjir on a piece of land:
column6: Becomes the owner of the land once he has marked it, but may not waive his entitlement for consideration, nor may he give it to another person, because ownership of the land is personal to him.
column7: Becomes the owner of the land, and may sell it.
column8: May neither waive his entitlement nor sell the land.
column9: Has exclusivity and priority over others and may waive his entitlement to another for consideration, but may not sell the land as he does not yet own it.
column11: Per 9/2-3, Tahjir gives exclusivity and priority, not ownership; the holder may waive it for consideration but may not sell the land.

column5: Insurance of the mortgaged asset is permissible because, if the asset is damaged, the compensation received can be used for replacing the mortgage, thus ensuring the continuation of the role of mortgage in preservation of rights and documentation of debts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, insurance compensation replaces the mortgage so its role in preserving rights continues.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Sale by the agent of the purchased commodity before actually or legally taking delivery is prohibited. Legal delivery includes:
column6: The transfer of liability to the buyer (agent) by ascertaining the commodity in a manner that distinguishes it from other things.
column7: The mere signing of the purchase contract by the agent, since the contract itself transfers the liability for the commodity to him even before it is ascertained.
column8: Payment of the price by the agent.
column9: The agent's notification to the principal of the purchase.
column11: Per 4/2/4, legal delivery includes transfer of liability to the agent by ascertaining the commodity so it is distinguished from others.

column5: Khiyar al-Naqd in the hiring of persons refers to:
column6: The employer's right to terminate the contract when the private employee fails to report to work.
column7: The employer's right to terminate the contract on the existence of a defect that makes the service useless, or when the employee fails to deliver the service as required.
column8: The right of the party who stipulated a conditional option to terminate the contract within its specified period.
column9: The employee's right to stipulate termination of the contract when the employer fails to make or delays payment of the pay, or does not pay one installment or more.
column11: Per 8/2/3, Khiyar al-Naqd is the employee's stipulated right to terminate for non-payment or delay of pay.

column5: A lessee of an asset may enter into a sub-lease contract with a party other than the owner:
column6: Only for a rental payable on a spot basis.
column7: For a rental that is the same, lower or higher, payable currently or on a deferred basis, unless the owner stipulates that the lessee should not sublet, or not without his approval.
column8: Only with the approval of the owner in all cases, even if the owner has made no stipulation.
column9: Only for a rental that is the same as or lower than the rental he pays, to avoid profiting from what he does not own, and only if both rentals are payable on a spot basis, whether or not the owner has stipulated anything.
column11: Per 3/3, subletting is allowed at any rental, spot or deferred, unless the owner has stipulated otherwise.

column5: The Hamish Jiddiyyah taken from the purchase orderer as security for his binding promise is considered 'Arboun, which the Institution may retain if the customer fails to honour his promise.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/8/2, it is held on trust, not 'Arboun, since no contract has been established; only actual damage may be deducted.

column5: If an asset is mortgaged to more than one mortgagee and the mortgages are ranked in such a way that a succeeding mortgagee should get his debt repaid only when his precedent mortgagee does:
column6: The consent of the precedent mortgagee alone has to be sought.
column7: The consent of all the mortgagees has to be sought.
column8: No consent is required from any of the mortgagees.
column9: The consent of the succeeding mortgagee alone has to be sought.
column11: Per 3/2/3, where the mortgages are ranked, only the consent of the succeeding mortgagee has to be sought.

column5: A party says to another: "I promise to sell you this item", and the other party says: "I promise to lease to you such and such property". These promises:
column6: Are permissible only if both promises relate to the same subject matter.
column7: Are both legally binding, since each promise serves as consideration for the other.
column8: Constitute an impermissible bilateral promise, because they relate to two different commutative contracts.
column9: Are permissible, and neither of them is legally binding except if a promisor causes a promisee to incur a liability.
column11: Per 3/7, such promises on different subject matters are permissible and not binding unless a promisee is caused to incur a liability.

column5: The debt for which the mortgage is signed may be:
column6: A usurious loan, if the mortgagor accepts it and the mortgagee agrees to waive the usurious increment in case of default.
column7: The usufruct of a specific asset that is already in the hands of the lessee, such as a rented house.
column8: A sale income, a guarantee against damage, a Salam commodity, an Istisna'a commodity or an owed usufruct.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/3/1, the debt must be permissible (e.g. sale income, Salam or Istisna'a commodity); not a usurious loan or a non-debt like a specific usufruct.

column5: Based on the Waqf asset, cash Waqf and Waqf companies are examples of:
column6: Investment Waqfs.
column7: Private Waqf.
column8: Joint Waqf.
column9: Specific Waqf Assets.
column11: Per 2/2/2/2, investment Waqfs aim at development by turnover and deployment on commercial considerations, e.g., cash Waqf and Waqf companies.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for requiring a specific term for the 'Arboun option is to avoid Gharar that may result from an unknown term.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, a specific term is required to avoid Gharar (Jahalah) arising from an unknown 'Arboun term.

column5: When the hiring contract relates to a specific service, it is impermissible for the institution (as the employee) to sign a contract with the client:
column6: Before receiving the full pay in advance from the client, by analogy to Salam.
column7: Before it possesses the service and becomes in a position to perform actual or constructive delivery.
column8: Before the client pays a seriousness margin to confirm his pledge to hire the service.
column9: Unless it performs the service through its own staff.
column11: Per 5/1/5, for a specific service the institution must own the service and be able to deliver it, actually or constructively, before contracting.

column5: The arbitrator does not have the right to retreat from his verdict:
column6: Unless one of the two parties of the dispute objects to it within the arbitration period, in which case he may amend it after hearing the objection.
column7: Unless he declares that he has committed a mistake in it, in which case he can cancel or amend his verdict in view of the Shari'ah rules and in a way that ensures justice.
column8: In any case, even if he discovers that he has committed a mistake in it, since the verdict becomes binding on the two parties once issued and cannot be reviewed by anyone.
column9: Unless the judiciary refuses to execute it.
column11: Per 13/3, the arbitrator cannot retreat from his verdict unless he declares a mistake; then he may cancel or amend it per Shari'ah to ensure justice.

column5: Among the permitted scenarios for buyback, even if the deferred price is more than the spot price:
column6: If the buyback is free of any collusion or customary practice.
column7: If the price change is due to the deferral period rather than to alterations in the asset's characteristics or value.
column8: If the buyer in the second contract is an entity majority-owned by the first seller.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/5/2, freedom from collusion is a permitted case; a price change due to deferral, or a majority-owned buyer, is not.

column5: If the card is cancelled by the card issuer for a reason not attributed to the cardholder:
column6: The card issuer retains all the fees, since the cancellation is its right under the agreement and the cardholder has no claim to any refund, whatever the reason for cancellation.
column7: The card issuer returns the fees of the services only, but not the issuance fees.
column8: The card issuer may return to the cardholder the issuance fees and other services fees on a proportionate basis for the remaining period of the card.
column9: The cancellation is subject to the ruling of cancellation at the request of the cardholder.
column11: Per 5/2/5, issuance and service fees are returned pro rata for the remaining period.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: Excluding the seller's liability for defect (Bay' al-Bara'ah - sale on the basis of 'as is where is'):
column6: Is permitted in Ijarah and Istisna'a contracts, but not in sales.
column7: Is prohibited in all sale contracts.
column8: Is prohibited in Ijarah and Istisna'a contracts.
column9: Does not affect the buyer's option to revoke due to defect.
column11: Per 2/2/4, an exclusion clause removes the option to revoke for defect, but excluding liability is prohibited in Ijarah and Istisna'a.

column5: If no period is stipulated in Qard, it is binding upon the borrower to return its substitute (Badal) on demand.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6, absent a stipulated period, the borrower must return the substitute on demand.

column5: A management concession contract may be rescinded by the licensee, on condition that the licensee takes the measures that ascertain the provision of the services to the public.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/3, the licensee may rescind provided he ensures continued provision of services to the public.

column5: A lender stipulated in a loan contract that the borrower should offer him accommodation in his house free of charge during the loan period. This arrangement:
column6: Is a Muwata`ah for obtaining Shari'ah exits, which is permissible.
column7: Is permissible if the accommodation is offered for a short period only.
column8: Is permissible, since accommodation is not a monetary benefit.
column9: Is a misuse of combination of contracts as an excuse for practicing Riba.
column11: Per 4/3, stipulating that the borrower house the lender or give him a present misuses combination as an excuse for Riba.

column5: The Hadith of Jabir Ibn Abdullah, in which Abu Qatadah Al-Ansari undertook to pay the two dinars owed by a deceased person, is cited as evidence for:
column6: The permissibility of the Suftajah.
column7: The permissibility of treating tangible security as Rahn, with the creditor entitled to sell it on the debtor's death without reference to the heirs.
column8: Considering acceptance by the drawee as an undertaking to pay the debt represented by the commercial paper on the date of maturity.
column9: The permissibility of Da' wa Ta'ajjal, whereby the creditor accepts part of the debt in return for early payment by a third party.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Abu Qatadah's accepted undertaking supports treating acceptance as a binding obligation to pay.

column5: If the liquidation of a Sharikah is based on the expiry date, all the existing assets shall be sold according to current market values and the proceeds will be used in the following order:
column6: Payment of liquidation expenses; then return of the capital to the partners; then payment of financial liabilities.
column7: Payment of liquidation expenses; then payment of financial liabilities from the net assets; then distribution of the remaining assets among the partners in accordance with their percentage of contribution to the capital.
column8: Return of the capital to the partners; then payment of liquidation expenses; then payment of financial liabilities.
column9: Payment of financial liabilities; then payment of liquidation expenses; then distribution of the remaining assets among the partners in accordance with their profit-sharing ratio.
column11: Per 3/1/6/3, proceeds go first to liquidation expenses, then liabilities, then to partners per capital contribution.

column5: An IFI issued listed Sukuk on an SPV whose assets were 60% leased tangible assets and 40% Murabaha receivables. A year later, owing to the destruction of some leased assets, acknowledged by the Shari'ah Board as a supervening event, tangible assets fell to 30% of the SPV's assets. The correct course is:
column6: The Sukuk-holders must be notified that the Sukuk are no longer negotiable except under the Shari'ah conditions for trading debts, and the Sukuk must be delisted.
column7: The Sukuk may continue to be traded until the end of the period specified by the Shari'ah Board for restoring the ratio, whatever the tangible ratio reached in the meantime.
column8: The Sukuk may continue to be traded normally, since the decline resulted from a supervening event acknowledged by the Shari'ah Board.
column9: The IFI must guarantee the Sukuk-holders' capital until the ratio is restored, since the decline arose from the destruction of its leased assets.
column11: Per 8/2/3, once tangible assets fall below 33%, holders are notified the Sukuk are non-negotiable except per debt rules, and listed Sukuk are delisted.

column5: When the mortgagor mortgages to the mortgagee an asset already held by the mortgagee as a guaranteed asset (such as current accounts and assets retained after nullification of contracts):
column6: The mortgagee continues to keep the asset on guarantee basis.
column7: The status of the mortgagee changes from keeping the asset on guarantee basis to keeping it on the basis of trust.
column8: The status of the mortgagee changes from keeping the asset on trust basis to keeping it on guarantee basis.
column9: The mortgage is invalid, because the asset is already in the hands of the mortgagee.
column11: Per 3/2/5, when a guaranteed asset held by the mortgagee is mortgaged to him, he then holds it on trust rather than guarantee basis.

column5: A guarantor is liable for anything for which the debtor whose debt is guaranteed is liable, because:
column6: The guarantor acts as the agent of the debtor in settling the debt.
column7: The guarantee transfers the debt from the debtor to the guarantor, and the debtor is discharged.
column8: The guarantor is the owner of the debt once he guarantees it.
column9: Standing as a surety adds one obligation to another with respect to the liability.
column11: Per the basis on the guarantor, suretyship adds one obligation to another, so the guarantor bears what the debtor bears.

column5: The investment fund manager may undertake to purchase investment units from investors upon their exit from the fund:
column6: Only if the units were sold to the investors on behalf of others, and at any agreed price fixed in advance at the time of subscription, regardless of the market value at exit.
column7: At the subscription price of the units, to protect the investors, provided that the units were sold to them directly by the manager.
column8: Whether the units were sold to them by the manager directly or on behalf of others, provided that the purchase is at the market value at the time of exit.
column9: At the net asset value of the unit at the time of subscription, provided that the investor exits within the first year.
column11: Per 5/5, the fund manager may undertake to buy units on exit, however sold, provided it is at their market value at the time of exit.

column5: The owners of investment Sukuk of different types should pay Zakah:
column6: On the basis of the underlying assets of these Sukuk.
column7: Not at all, since the Institution managing the Sukuk assets pays Zakah on them.
column8: On the profits distributed to them only.
column9: On the nominal value of the Sukuk, at the rate of 2.5%.
column11: Per 5/1/4/2, Sukuk holders pay Zakah based on the underlying assets; the managing Institution holds them in trust and pays only on its profit or commission.

column5: Borrowing for the Waqf, when it is not sanctioned by a condition stipulated by the Waqif, is justified in the following cases:
column6: Need for maintenance or necessary development of the Waqf and absence of sufficient Waqf income for that.
column7: Inability to pay the wages of the employees working in the Waqf or those who serve its purposes, and fear from endangering the benefits of the Waqf.
column8: Spending on the beneficiaries of the Waqf when the Waqf has no income.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/3/6/2, (a) and (b) justify borrowing; per 5/3/6/3, borrowing should not be for spending on the beneficiaries.

column5: In case the total revenue of the Waqf is less than the remuneration of the overseer:
column6: The outstanding remuneration shall be forfeited, unless the Waqf beneficiaries agree to pay it from their shares.
column7: Priority shall be given to the maintenance expenses and similar necessary expenditures, and the outstanding remuneration remains a liability against the Waqf.
column8: Priority shall be given to the remuneration of the overseer over the maintenance expenses, since it is a right of a person, unlike the expenses of the asset, which can be deferred.
column9: The outstanding remuneration shall be paid by selling part of the Waqf asset, as the overseer's right may not be forfeited.
column11: Per 3/9/5, maintenance and similar necessary expenses come first, and the unpaid remuneration remains a liability of the Waqf.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: If the seller stipulates that the buyer provide security, surety or any other form of guarantee and the buyer fails to provide it, the seller is entitled to revoke the contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 11/4, failure to provide a stipulated security, surety or other guarantee entitles the seller to revoke.

column5: The pay in the hiring contract:
column6: Should be well known to the extent that leaves no room for dispute, whether it is in cash, in-kind or in the form of a service.
column7: Must be fixed, since variable pay is impermissible in hiring of persons, as it leads to disputes between the parties.
column8: Cannot be determined as a percentage of the output, due to ignorance (Jahalah) of the pay, because the output is not known at the time of contracting.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/2/1 pay may be cash, kind or service, fixed or variable, but well known; per 5/2/6 it may be a percentage of output.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: When there is more than one Fiqh opinion on the same issue:
column6: The board shall declare the specific opinion that it subscribes to, and if the issue is controversial, it has to explain the specific bases of its choice.
column7: The board shall present all the opinions and leave the choice to the Institution.
column8: The board shall follow the opinion of the majority of the Fuqaha without any explanation, since the explanation of the bases is the duty of the Institution's management.
column9: The board shall refrain from issuing the Fatwa until the issue is settled by a Fiqh academy, and the Institution shall suspend the related operations in the meantime.
column11: Per 9/2, the board declares the opinion it adopts and, if the issue is controversial, explains the bases of its choice.

column5: It is permissible for a creditor to demand that a debt be settled by:
column6: The guarantor only, once the debtor is in default.
column7: The debtor or the guarantor, even if the guarantor stipulated that the settlement must first be sought from the debtor.
column8: The debtor only, and by the guarantor only after the debtor is proven insolvent.
column9: The debtor or the guarantor of the debtor, unless the guarantor stipulated that the settlement must first be sought from the debtor.
column11: Per 2/2(a), either may be asked to pay unless the guarantor stipulated that the debtor be asked first.

column5: Possession (Qabd) is:
column6: The transfer of ownership of a thing by virtue of the contract, whether or not it is delivered.
column7: The physical transportation of a thing from the place of the seller to the place of the buyer.
column8: The gathering of a thing or what takes its rule, according to the requirements of customary practice.
column9: The registration of a thing in the name of the person entitled to it in an official register.
column11: Per 2, possession is the gathering of a thing or what takes its rule, according to the requirements of customary practice.

column5: A State granted a company the right to manage a public port for ten years, against the State receiving 30% of the profit (net income after expenses and allocations). The contract between the State and the company is:
column6: Mudarabah, wherein the capital is the original facility or the project itself.
column7: Istisna'a, in which the price is the port's income.
column8: Ijarah, in which the rent is 30% of the profit, payable to the State at the end of each year.
column9: Ju'alah, in which the State is the Ja'il.
column11: Per 10/2/1, where the price is a percentage of profit (net income), the contract is Mudarabah and the capital is the facility itself.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Swaps, in the forms in which they are practised in commodity exchanges, are:
column6: Permitted for hedging purposes only.
column7: Permitted if the interest rates exchanged are fixed.
column8: Not permitted.
column9: Permitted if concluded through a binding promise.
column11: Per 5/3/2, swaps are not permitted in the forms in which they are practised in commodity exchanges.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In providing banking services after conversion, uncovered documentary credits should be treated through:
column6: An interest-free loan with a commission proportionate to the amount and period of the credit.
column7: Interest-based financing, with the interest donated to charity until an alternative is worked out.
column8: Murabahah, Musharakah or Mudarabah in accordance with the rules of Shari'ah.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5, an Islamic alternative such as Murabahah, Musharakah or Mudarabah must be worked out for uncovered credits.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The basis for the right of retention includes the Verse {And if you punish, then punish them with the like of that with which you were afflicted…}, which indicates the permissibility of reciprocal treatment, so that a person may retain property until he receives his own rights from others.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the Verse permits reciprocal treatment, so one may retain property until receiving one's own rights.

column5: The reality of current accounts is that they are:
column6: Loans (Qurud), so that the institution comes to own the amounts and a liability to repay the amount is established against it.
column7: Deposits (Wadi'ah) held as a trust, which the institution may not employ and must return in the identical form in which they were received.
column8: Investment accounts on the basis of Mudarabah.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 10/1/1, current accounts are loans, not deposits; the institution owns the amounts and is liable to repay them.

column5: It is permissible for an Institution:
column6: To open, issue and confirm all types of documentary credit, on the basis of the client's order or for the Institution itself.
column7: To participate, or play an intermediary role, in such dealings and to notify, amend or execute such credit for its own use or on behalf of another institution or bank.
column8: To act as advising bank for a credit pertaining to goods prohibited by Shari'ah, provided it does not issue the credit itself.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/2, (a) and (b) are permitted; per 3/1/3, no role at all is allowed in credits for goods prohibited by Shari'ah.

column5: The Standard on Banking Services in Islamic Banks covers:
column6: Loan and investment services rendered by the Institutions to their customers, including the financing of trade, the granting of Murabahah to the purchase orderer and the management of investment portfolios on behalf of customers.
column7: The most important banking services that do not involve lending and borrowing, which the Institutions render to their customers, directly or through other parties, to facilitate their internal and external operations.
column8: Trading in currencies, and debit and credit cards.
column9: Investment accounts and investment Sukuk.
column11: Per the scope (clause 1), it covers key non-lending services; loans, investments, currencies, cards, accounts and Sukuk are excluded.

column5: It is permissible to use a certified cheque as the capital (Ras al-Mal) of Salam, since its receipt constitutes constructive possession of the amount written on it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/1, a certified or banker's cheque is constructive possession and may be used as Salam capital.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Undertaking futures transactions in commodities is:
column6: Permitted if they end in actual delivery and possession, even though the price and the commodity are both deferred at the time of contracting.
column7: Not permitted according to the Shari'ah, either through their formation or by trading in them.
column8: Permitted in their formation, but not in trading them.
column9: Permitted if they are used for hedging only.
column11: Per 3/3 and 5/1/2, futures are not permitted either through their formation or by trading in them.

column5: Shari'ah compliant modes of hedging should be followed to protect the principal amount of the cash Waqf and to hedge against the risk of foreign currency fluctuations and change of its value.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/13/5, Shari'ah compliant hedging should be used to protect cash Waqf principal and against currency risk.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the investment manager not being liable for the loss of the capital, except in cases of his wilful misconduct and negligence, is:
column6: The Hadith: "Muslims are bound by their conditions", since the contract does not stipulate his liability.
column7: That Takaful is an undertaking to make donations between the participants, which covers any loss of capital, including that caused by the manager's negligence.
column8: The consensus of Muslim jurists, because he takes the capital with the owner's permission and deals with it for the owner's benefit.
column9: The Quranic Verse: {"O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations"}.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is the jurists' consensus: he holds the capital with the owner's permission as his representative.

column5: Under an Istisna'a contract price of 500,000, the manufacturer was appointed as agent to sell the subject-matter if the ultimate purchaser delayed taking delivery. The purchaser delayed; the manufacturer sold it for 460,000 and incurred selling expenses of 5,000. The manufacturer may recover from the ultimate purchaser:
column6: Nothing, since the sale was made on the purchaser's behalf.
column7: 5,000 only, being the selling expenses.
column8: 45,000, i.e. the shortfall of 40,000 plus the selling expenses of 5,000.
column9: 40,000 only, since the manufacturer bears the selling expenses.
column11: Per 6/5, the manufacturer has recourse for the shortfall below the contract price (40,000), and the purchaser bears selling expenses (5,000).

column5: An exploration license granted by the State for a certain area and a certain period:
column6: May entitle its holder to become the sole explorer in that area and to conduct the works required for exploration.
column7: Is granted against payment of a specific amount of fee or rent to the State.
column8: Entitles its holder to the utilization concession even if he does not discover the minerals by the end of the exploration period.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/2/2, (a) and (b) are true; per 5/2/4, without discovery by the end of the period there is no entitlement to utilization concession.

column5: Shari'ah-compliant alternatives to repurchase agreements for liquidity management include:
column6: Bilateral loans with a points system, in which preferential points are given to the party that provides liquidity first, and extra points accrue for delayed repayment of the counter-loan, as a penalty clause.
column7: Selling Shari'ah-compliant securities or investment units with a unilateral promise from the buyer to sell them back, or from the seller to buy them back, at a specified future date, per the buyback rules.
column8: Tawarruq with the pledge of securities, where the pledgee may stipulate the right to sell the pledged securities if the debtor defaults, and may sell the commodity back to its original seller at spot.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/6/3/1, sale with a unilateral buyback or resale promise is an alternative; preferential points and selling pledged securities are barred.

column5: The sale of a commodity debt before taking possession of it is not permitted because it contains gharar.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/3 and its Shari'ah basis, selling a commodity debt before possession involves gharar.

column5: Borrowing for the Waqf is permissible for the sake of spending on the beneficiaries of the Waqf when the Waqf has no income.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/3/6/3, borrowing should not be for the sake of spending on the beneficiaries of the Waqf.

column5: Creating reserves to protect the capital is permissible through deductions from:
column6: The investment manager's share of profits only, since the reserve protects the manager against liability for loss.
column7: The investors' share of profits, but not from the investment manager's share of profits due to him in his capacity as the Mudarib.
column8: The capital itself, if the profit is insufficient.
column9: Both the investors' and the investment manager's shares of profits, pro-rata to their respective entitlements.
column11: Per 4/2/6, reserves are deducted from the investors' share of profits, not the Mudarib's share.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Selling unripe fruits apart from the trees and without a stipulation for awaiting harvesting:
column6: Is valid, because the Gharar involved is medium and medium Gharar does not affect the contract.
column7: Is valid, because the Gharar is in a corollary (Tabi') of the primary subject matter.
column8: Is valid, provided that the buyer is granted the option of viewing the fruits.
column9: Is null and void, because the Gharar relates to the primary subject matter of the contract.
column11: Per 4/3, Gharar in the primary subject matter voids the contract, as when unripe fruits are sold apart from the trees without a harvest stipulation.

column5: In an Ijarah Mawsufah fi al-Dhimmah (contract for an unidentified asset undertaken by the lessor to be delivered according to agreed specifications), in case of total or partial destruction of the asset:
column6: The contract terminates, even if the owner offers an alternative asset with a similar specification, and the lessee is entitled to a refund of the rentals paid for the remaining period only, together with the rentals due up to the date of destruction.
column7: The lessee bears the loss, since he took possession of the asset.
column8: The owner must offer an alternative asset of similar specification, unless otherwise agreed, and the Ijarah continues for the remaining time; if no substitute can be provided, the contract is terminated.
column9: The lessee must continue to pay the rentals without being provided with a substitute asset, since the contract is binding on both parties and may not be terminated except by mutual consent.
column11: Per 7/1/6, in a described Ijarah the owner must substitute a similar asset and the Ijarah continues; if impossible, it terminates.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Gold ingots stored in a warehouse that are not distinguishable by serial numbers are considered allocated, and each owner bears the loss of his own ingots.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/5/4, such ingots are unallocated and subject to joint ownership, with losses borne pro rata.

column5: In Muzara'ah certificates (Muzara'ah Sukuk), the issuer of the certificates may be:
column6: The owner of the land (the principal owner or owner of the usufruct of the land), with the subscribers being the cultivators on the basis of a Muzara'ah contract, and the realised funds being the cultivation cost.
column7: The cultivator (the worker), with the subscribers being the owners of the land (investors whose subscription amounts are used to buy the land).
column8: The buyer of the crop on the basis of Salam, with the subscribers being the sellers of the crop and the realised funds being the Salam capital.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1/5/9 (a) and (b), the issuer may be the landowner (subscribers are cultivators) or the cultivator (subscribers are landowners).

column5: When the Institution itself is the beneficiary of Monetization:
column6: It may use Monetization as a means of mobilizing liquidity for its operations, as Monetization is one of the modes of investment and financing.
column7: It shall resort to Monetization only when it faces the danger of a liquidity shortage that could interrupt the flow of its operations and cause losses for its clients.
column8: It shall appoint a third party as its agent for selling the Monetization commodity, so as to avoid selling it through its own bodies.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1, Monetization is not a mode of investment or financing; the Institution uses it only facing a damaging liquidity shortage. 5/2 bars proxy in selling.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If a conventional bank is converted by its existing shareholders into an Islamic bank, the process of disposing of interest and impermissible earnings:
column6: Commences from the date of the decision to convert, and the bank itself must dispose of all impermissible earnings distributed before conversion, recovering them from the shareholders and depositors who received them, even if this requires legal action against them.
column7: Covers all impermissible earnings since the establishment of the bank, whether distributed or not.
column8: Commences at the beginning of the financial period following that in which the conversion takes effect.
column9: Commences at the beginning of the financial period in which the conversion takes effect; earnings distributed before conversion should, on ethical grounds, be disposed of personally by the shareholders and depositors who received them, the bank not being bound.
column11: Per 8/1/2, disposal starts from the beginning of the conversion period; recipients of earlier distributions dispose of them personally.

column5: A contract for hiring of persons can be concluded verbally, in writing or through modern means of communication.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1, hiring of persons may be concluded in any form that normally indicates it, including verbally, in writing or by modern means.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: An IFI paid the holders of its investment accounts monthly advance amounts on account of profit. At the end of the year, after constructive liquidation, the realized profit due to the holders turned out to be less than the amounts advanced to them. The IFI:
column6: Must deduct from the advanced amounts so that each holder receives his exact share of the profit.
column7: Must bear the difference as Mudarib, since it decided to pay the advances.
column8: Must treat the advanced amounts as final, since they were paid as profit.
column9: Must carry the difference forward as a loss to be covered from the profits of the next period, without recovering it from the holders.
column11: Per 5/3, advances are provisional; after liquidation the institution adds to or deducts from them so each holder gets his exact profit share.

column5: As for bad debts (non-repayable debts) and doubtful debts owed to the Institution:
column6: The Institution does not have to pay Zakah on them except for one year after collection of such debts.
column7: The Institution should pay Zakah on them annually, since they are part of its receivables.
column8: On collection, the Institution has to pay Zakah on them for the whole past period.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/3/1, Zakah on bad and doubtful debts is due for one year after collection. Paying for the whole past period applies to postponed good debts (5/3/2).

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, the buying and selling of the equity share of the Institution:
column6: Must be stipulated in the partnership contract to protect the Institution, so that the buyer cannot refuse to purchase the units at maturity.
column7: Must be concluded at the inception of the partnership for all the units, with deferred delivery, so that the price of each unit is known in advance and the Institution is protected against any fall in their market value.
column8: Should not be stipulated in the partnership contract; the buying partner may give only a promise to buy independent of the partnership contract, and the sale agreement must also be independent of it.
column9: May be entered into as a condition for concluding the partnership contract, provided the price of the units is fixed at the outset.
column11: Per 5/1, sale is not stipulated in the partnership contract; only an independent promise to buy, and separate sale contracts.

column5: If the hired service/work is specifically defined and has to be delivered in the future, the employer has the right to hire out to someone else an identical service/work. This is called:
column6: Parallel hiring.
column7: Spontaneous renewal of hiring.
column8: Deferred hiring.
column9: Shared hiring.
column11: Per 5/1/3, hiring out an identical well-defined future service to another is parallel hiring. Deferred hiring is hiring starting at a later agreed date (4/8).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of the compensation being a portion of the subject matter of Ju'alah, even though it is uncertain and does not exist, is that:
column6: It is an uncertainty that does not prevent delivery and involves no Gharar, as entitlement to compensation arises only when the task is accomplished.
column7: Uncertainty in compensation is overlooked in all commutative contracts, since the parties accept the risk of their transaction and no dispute can arise from it.
column8: The offeror is entitled to determine the compensation after completion, whatever the amount offered at the outset.
column9: The compensation is like wages in Ijarah, which may be unknown at the time of the contract and determined after the work is completed and delivered.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, this uncertainty does not prevent delivery and involves no Gharar, as the Ju'l is earned only on completion.

column5: In Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, if the leased asset is destroyed without the cause being attributable to the lessee, and the rental specified in the contract is higher than the prevailing rate of rental:
column6: No refund is due, since the rentals were due under a binding contract, and the lessor bears no liability for destruction not caused by him.
column7: All the rentals paid must be refunded to the lessee, as the lease is void from its inception once the asset is destroyed.
column8: The lessee must pay the remaining instalments, since he promised to acquire the asset and the promise is binding on him.
column9: The difference between the prevailing rental rate and the rental specified in the contract must be refunded to the lessee.
column11: Per 8/8, rent is adjusted to the market rate and the excess refunded, as the lessee paid more in return for the promise of title.

column5: If the worker in a Ju'alah is specified:
column6: The contract is converted into an Ijarah for persons, and the worker becomes an employee of the offeror.
column7: He must undertake the work himself, or with the offeror's express consent through someone under his supervision and control.
column8: His acceptance of the offer becomes a condition, failing which the contract is void, and the compensation is not due.
column9: He may assign the whole work to anyone else without the consent of the offeror, provided the result is delivered to him and the worker remains responsible for it.
column11: Per 5/1, a specified worker must do the work himself, or with the offeror's express consent through someone he supervises.

column5: In a partnership in creditworthiness (liability partnership), the percentage of liability sharing of each partner must be equal to his percentage of profit sharing.
