column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/1, the liability percentage may, by agreement, differ downwards or upwards from the profit percentage.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: In the sale of gold, it is impermissible:
column6: That the sale contract be contingent on an event or occurrence, or be a forward contract (deferred to the future).
column7: To stipulate Khiyar al-Shart (cooling-off option).
column8: To stipulate deferment of both the counter-values, as in the case of forward or futures contracts.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2/2–3/2/3, contingent and forward sales, Khiyar al-Shart and deferment of both counter-values are all impermissible in gold.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Regarding the Fatwas of other Shari'ah boards and schools of Fiqh, the institution:
column6: Should not follow the Fatwas of other Shari'ah Advisory Boards except with the permission of its own Board.
column7: May follow the Fatwas of other Shari'ah Advisory Boards freely, if they are more lenient.
column8: Should demand Fatwa according to the official school of Fiqh of its host country.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/3, other boards' Fatwas need its own Board's permission; per 6/4 it should not demand Fatwa per a specific Madhab.

column5: In the service of leasing safe deposit vaults:
column6: The institution guarantees the safety of the items kept in the vault in all cases, including loss that occurs without any misconduct or negligence on its part or on the part of the customer.
column7: The institution is not responsible for ensuring the safety of the vault itself, since the customer alone is responsible for the vault he leases.
column8: The institution is responsible for ensuring the safety of the vault, but does not guarantee the safety of its contents except in case of misconduct or negligence.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/7/2, the institution ensures the vault's safety but guarantees its contents only for misconduct or negligence.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, the unrestricted Hawalah is permitted by:
column6: The majority of jurists, by analogy with the deferred guarantee contract, provided the payer is a debtor to the transferor and the transferee consents to the transfer.
column7: All four schools unanimously, as with restricted Hawalah.
column8: The Hanafis only, based on the Prophet's order that a Hawalah must be accepted, without indicating whether the payer must be a debtor to the transferor.
column9: The Malikis only, based on public interest.
column11: Per the basis, restricted Hawalah is unanimously permitted, while unrestricted Hawalah is permitted by the Hanafis only.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If the property assets of the bank are locations designated for non-permissible activities, they should be changed to locations designated for permissible operations and services.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/1/6 and its basis, the prohibition concerns the use of the location, not the location itself.

column5: Contemporary transactions such as Murabahah on Order of Purchase comprise a number of contracts and pledges that the parties agree beforehand to execute in a specific manner and according to an agreed number of successive stages.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/1, such arrangements comprise contracts and pledges agreed beforehand to be executed in successive stages.

column5: A Waqif created a Waqf of a house for the residence of his three sons, who are at par in their entitlement, but the house cannot accommodate all of them at the same time. The enjoyment of the usufruct shall be:
column6: Via usufruct sharing (muhāyaʾa), and if it is not feasible, the beneficiaries may settle (ṣulḥ) whereby some enjoy the usufruct and the others are compensated by the usufructuary party.
column7: Assigned by the overseer to the eldest son, without any compensation to the others, since he is the first in entitlement by custom.
column8: By selling the house and dividing its price among the three sons equally, since the house cannot accommodate all of them at the same time.
column9: Via a settlement (ṣulḥ) first, and only if the settlement is not feasible, via usufruct sharing (muhāyaʾa), whereby the sons enjoy the house in turn, with the overseer ordering the turns by his discretion.
column11: Per 9/10/2, usufruct sharing (muhāyaʾa) applies first; if not feasible, a settlement with compensation by the usufructuary party.

column5: With respect to the parties whose signatures appear on the commercial paper, including the drawer, the endorser and the guarantor:
column6: Each of them is liable only for a proportionate share of the value of the paper, and the holder may have recourse to each of them only for that share, after the drawer's refusal to pay, and he may not claim the balance from the others.
column7: Only the drawer is liable to the holder; endorsers and guarantor bear no liability.
column8: They are jointly responsible to pay the holder the value of the paper, who may have recourse to them severally or jointly after the drawer (or the issuer of a promissory note) refuses to pay.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/2, all signatories are jointly responsible; the holder may claim severally or jointly after the drawer/issuer refuses.

column5: An increase in the market value of Waqf shares constitutes (……….), whereas bonus shares sourced from the earnings of the company represent (……….), unless the Waqif stipulated to add them to the Waqf asset.
column6: Revenue of the Waqf .... revenue of the Waqf.
column7: A capital gain on the Waqf asset .... revenue of the Waqf.
column8: Revenue of the Waqf .... a capital gain on the Waqf asset.
column9: A capital gain on the Waqf asset .... a capital gain on the Waqf asset.
column11: Per 2/4/14/2, a rise in value is capital gain on the Waqf asset, while bonus shares from earnings are revenue unless the Waqif stipulates otherwise.

column5: An undertaking by the customer, in the contract of Murabahah, to pay an amount of money or a percentage of the debt in the event of delay in paying instalments on their due date is:
column6: Permissible on the basis of an undertaking to donate it, and the Shari'ah Supervisory Board must know that it is spent on charitable causes and not for the benefit of the Institution.
column7: Permissible, provided the Institution keeps only the amount of its actual damage and donates the rest to charitable causes approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, since compensation for delay is permitted up to the actual damage.
column8: Permissible, and the amount becomes income of the Institution as compensation for the delay.
column9: Absolutely impermissible, because it is an increase over the debt and thus Riba.
column11: Per 5/6, a commitment to donate on late payment is allowed if the SSB knows it goes to charity, not to the Institution.

column5: The Standard on Sale of Debt does not deal with:
column6: The discharge of debt by the debtor, in whole or in part, where it does not take place through a commutative arrangement.
column7: Novation (ḥawāla).
column8: Set-off (muqāṣa).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per item 1, non-commutative discharge of debt, ḥawāla and muqāṣa are all outside the scope of the Standard.

column5: Ibn Al-Mundhir explained that traveling is referred to in the Verse as the predominant case where mortgage is needed, and that the Verse does not stipulate it as a condition for concluding mortgage contracts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, Ibn Al-Mundhir held that travel is mentioned as the usual case of need, not as a condition.

column5: The basis for the entitlement of the lessor to the rentals even though the lessee returns the leased asset or stops using it is that Ijarah is a binding contract that cannot be terminated unilaterally by the lessee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 7/1/7.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: In absolute agency:
column6: The agent may perform barter and deferred payment sales without the prior consent of the principal.
column7: The agent may sell at less than the market price, if this serves a speedy disposal of the asset.
column8: The agent is bound by customary practices and the interest of the principal.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/2, absolute agency is bound by custom and the principal's interest; selling below market or barter/deferred sales need consent.

column5: The impermissibility of selling the items to be produced under Istisna'a prior to taking possession of them is based on the fact that it is a form of sale of debt for debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, it is selling a non-existent item and selling what one does not own.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, charging the client for the credit study is justified by the fact that:
column6: The credit study is an integral part of the financing contract and cannot be separated from it.
column7: The benefit from the study is shared between the financier and the financed party, rather than confined to the former only.
column8: The benefit from the study is confined to the financier, who uses it to assess the credit worthiness of the client.
column9: The fee for the study must be equal to the actual cost of its preparation.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the study is a separate remunerable service whose benefit is shared by the financier and the financed party.

column5: Mortgaging shares that are lawful according to the Shari'ah is:
column6: Permissible only if the assets of the corporation are predominantly tangible assets, whereas shares of a corporation whose assets are mainly cash or debts may not be mortgaged, since the conditions for selling them at liquidation cannot be met.
column7: Permissible, whether the assets of the corporation are cash, tangible assets or debts or a combination of them, irrespective of one type being predominant, in conformity with the conditions for selling shares at liquidation.
column8: Impermissible, because the value of shares constantly fluctuates.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/10, lawful shares may be mortgaged whatever the composition of assets, subject to the conditions for selling them at liquidation.

column5: In Shari'ah characterisation, a promissory note is considered:
column6: A restricted Hawalah.
column7: An unrestricted Hawalah.
column8: A certificate of debt.
column9: An agency for collection.
column11: Per 2/2, a promissory note, whereby the debtor promises to pay the creditor, is characterised as a certificate of debt.

column5: A discount card issued against a subscription fee is permissible:
column6: If the card issuer is a third party that charges the fee against which other entities provide the discounts, because the issuer is deemed to be a broker.
column7: If the card issuer is the same entity that offers the discounts, and the discount is associated with other services or benefits that may be a consideration for the fee.
column8: If the card issuer is the same entity that offers the discounts and the fee is exclusively for providing discounts, provided that the discount rate is specified.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/6/2/2/2, a third-party (broker) issuer, or an issuer whose discount is incidental to other services, is permissible; a fee solely for discounts is not.

column5: Regarding guarantees for provision of the pay and the service:
column6: The employee has the right to obtain the permissible guarantees in their different forms so as to document his eligibility for receiving the pay.
column7: The employer has the right to obtain guarantees for receiving indemnity in case of any transgression or negligence or breach of the contract from the part of the employee.
column8: The employer has the right to obtain a guarantee from the private employee for any damage to what he works on, even without transgression or negligence.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/1, both may take permissible guarantees: the employee for his pay, the employer for indemnity on transgression, negligence or breach.

column5: When adopting the Fiqh viewpoint that gives the right of utilization of minerals to the owner of the land or its usufruct against a fee payable to the State, the following lands should not become subject to concession contracts:
column6: Privately-owned lands, whether vacant or built on.
column7: Wastelands that have been contracted for development according to the relevant Shari'ah stipulations and legal rulings.
column8: Lands allotted by the State to natural or legal persons, whether through change of ownership title or for temporary utilization.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/4/2/1-5/4/2/3, all three types of land are excluded from concession contracts under this viewpoint.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for prohibiting the joining together of the contract for purchasing the commodity and the contract for selling it in Monetization is:
column6: Joining them together would impose a commitment on the client to sell the commodity right away, and such immediate transfer of ownership may not enable the client to receive it.
column7: Joining them together turns the transaction into a loan from the Institution to the client that yields a benefit.
column8: Joining them together makes the price of the second sale unknown at the time of the first contract, which is a form of excessive Gharar that nullifies both contracts.
column9: Joining them together means the commodity necessarily returns to the original seller, which is 'Inah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, joining the contracts commits the client to sell right away, so he may not receive the commodity; the same reason bars agency commitments.

column5: A default of the third party to its undertaking for reparation of loss, or voidness of that undertaking, results in the vitiation (fasād) of the investment contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2, default or voidness of the third-party undertaking does not vitiate the investment contract.

column5: In case the rental in an Ijarah contract is subject to changes (floating rental):
column6: The rentals of all periods, including the first period, may be determined according to the benchmark, provided the benchmark is based on a clear formula not subject to dispute and is subject to a ceiling on both maximum and minimum levels.
column7: The rental of the first period must be specified in a lump sum, and subsequent rentals may be determined according to a benchmark based on a clear formula not subject to dispute, with a ceiling at both maximum and minimum levels.
column8: The rental of the first period may be determined at the end of that period according to the benchmark.
column9: The benchmark need not be subject to any ceiling, since fluctuation may favour either party.
column11: Per 5/2/3, the first-period rent is a fixed lump sum; later rents follow a clear benchmark with maximum and minimum ceilings.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The scoring method for distribution of profit among the participants of general investment accounts takes into account:
column6: The amount contributed by each investor only, regardless of the period of its stay in the investment.
column7: The amount contributed by each investor and the period of its stay (currency unit x time unit).
column8: The number of deposit and withdrawal transactions made by each investor.
column9: The period of stay of each account only, regardless of its amount.
column11: Per 5/1, scoring weighs each investor's amount by its period of stay (currency unit x time unit), even with repeated deposits and withdrawals.

column5: Diversifying the investment assets to achieve an appropriate return and minimize risks may include:
column6: Combining real assets, such as real estate and commodities, with financial assets (such as stocks and Sukuk), or combining assets denominated in two different currencies.
column7: Dividing the capital into two parts: the first used in Murabahah contracts with parties that have strong credit ratings so that the principal and Murabahah profit protect the initial capital, and the second invested in Musharakah contracts.
column8: Dividing the capital into two parts: the first used in Ijarah contracts with parties that have strong credit ratings so that the principal and rental protect the initial capital, and the second invested in Musharakah contracts.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/2/7 (a)-(c), all three are listed methods of diversifying investment assets.

column5: If the customer refuses to conclude the Murabahah transaction after the Institution has taken possession of the asset:
column6: The Institution may not force him to take delivery and pay the price; it is entitled only to compensation for its actual damage if he breached a binding promise.
column7: The Institution may force the customer to take delivery of the asset and pay the Murabahah selling price as promised.
column8: The Institution may claim from the customer the agreed mark-up, as the profit it would have earned from the transaction, in addition to its actual damage, if he breached a binding promise.
column9: The Murabahah contract is deemed automatically concluded by the Institution's taking possession of the asset.
column11: Per 4/1–4/2, possession does not conclude the Murabahah and the customer cannot be forced to buy; only actual damage is compensable.

column5: Several IFIs agreed to provide syndicated Istisna'a financing for the construction of certain parts of a power plant. The remaining parts of the same project are financed by conventional banks through interest-bearing loans. The participation of the IFIs is:
column6: Permissible only if the share of the IFIs in the project exceeds that of the conventional financing.
column7: Permissible, provided that the IFIs and the conventional banks appoint one lead manager for both types of financing.
column8: Not prohibited, on condition that the accounts and lead manager arrangements of the two types of financing are kept separate.
column9: Prohibited, because the project receives usurious financing for its remaining parts.
column11: Per 5/5, IFIs may finance parts of a project financed conventionally elsewhere if accounts and lead manager arrangements are kept separate.

column5: The Institution may accept a payment from a debtor who is in default that is in excess of the amount of the debt, provided:
column6: The excess is agreed between the two parties at the time of the default.
column7: The excess does not exceed the actual loss suffered by the Institution as a result of the delay, as assessed at the time of default.
column8: There is no contractual condition, written or verbal, or custom or mutual agreement relating to this additional amount.
column9: The excess is spent on charitable causes.
column11: Per 2/5/2, an excess payment may be accepted only if not stipulated, customary or mutually agreed.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When an agent conducts deals with his ascendant or descendant relatives, who are neither under his guardianship nor are the agent's spouse, the deal is permissible unless it encompasses injustice or favoritism.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/1/1, such deals are permissible unless they involve injustice or favoritism.

column5: Ibn Al-Qayyim said: It is permissible in principle to form up contracts and conditions, except for what has been prohibited by Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis quotes Ibn Al-Qayyim to this effect in support of the permissibility of combining contracts.

column5: An Ijarah contract may only be executed for an asset owned by the lessor; it cannot be executed for a usufruct owned by a sub-lessor.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/1, Ijarah is executed for an asset owned by the lessor or a usufruct owned by the sub-lessor.

column5: It is not permitted to lend funds of the Waqf, and the Waqf cannot be the guarantor of a third party's debts, unless:
column6: This act is stipulated by the Waqif among the purposes of the Waqf.
column7: It serves the interest of the Waqf with the permission of the relevant authority.
column8: The borrower is a relative of the overseer, without the need for any guarantees.
column9: a. or b.
column11: Per 7, lending or guaranteeing is allowed only if stipulated by the Waqif or in the Waqf's interest with authority permission, with guarantees.

column5: Among the key modern applications of possession, the following is deemed constructive possession:
column6: Payments for a credit card, with respect to such payments.
column7: Possession by the beneficiary of a bank draft or personal cheque, with respect to the amount payable by the drawee bank, even though there is delay in the payment of the actual amount.
column8: A deposit by a person of an amount in a bank account of another, upon the latter's demand or with his consent, whether by cash, by endorsement or by cheque.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1, 5/2 and 5/3, cheques/drafts, credit card payments and deposits into an account on demand or with consent are constructive possession.

column5: The Ijarah contract intended in this Standard is the lease of tangible assets, which is a contract giving a legal title to legitimate and identified usufruct for a defined period of time in exchange for a legitimate and determined consideration.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the definition given in the Shari'ah basis.

column5: The ruling that a Waqf property shall not be lent is based on the fear from favoritism which is part of human nature.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the bar on lending is because lending reduces the chances for investing the property; favoritism is the basis for 5/3/2.

column5: An IFI sold to a customer a quantity of metal for a deferred price on a Murabahah basis. In the same set of documents, the customer appointed the IFI as his agent to sell the metal to a third party for a spot price immediately upon signing, and the IFI accepted this appointment. The regulations in the customer's country permit him to sell the commodity himself. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because the commodity is sold to a third party for a spot price and does not return to the Institution, so the transaction is not a form of 'Inah.
column7: Impermissible, because the client shall not delegate the Institution to sell, on his behalf, a commodity that he purchased from it, and the Institution shall not accept such delegation.
column8: Impermissible only because metals may not be used in Monetization, which must be in local goods.
column9: Permissible, provided that the IFI does not charge the customer any fee for the agency.
column11: Per 4/7, the client may not delegate the selling Institution, nor may it accept, unless regulations require it and only after receipt; neither applies here.

column5: The Standard on Buyback covers:
column6: The buyback of a tangible asset that has moved out of the ownership of the contracting party through a gift or any other non-commutative contract, such as a bequest.
column7: Dissolution (Iqala) of the sale contract, whereby the item returns to its seller by rescission.
column8: Wafa Sale, being a sale in which the item returns to its seller upon repayment of the price.
column9: The buyback of a tangible asset or a usufruct that has moved out of the contracting party's ownership through sale or similar commutative contracts.
column11: Per item 1, the Standard covers buyback after sale or similar commutative contracts, not Wafa Sale, Iqala or transfers other than sale.

column5: It is not permissible to rent shares:
column6: For pledging them.
column7: For the purpose of selling the rented shares and returning shares similar to them, as is done in the stock markets.
column8: For acquiring their profits, or for showing a stronger financial position of the hirer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/15, renting shares is not permissible for pledging, short selling, acquiring profits, window-dressing or any other reason.

column5: The Shari'ah characterization of a conventional repurchase agreement is that it is:
column6: A valid sale accompanied by a binding bilateral promise to repurchase, in which the difference between the two prices is a lawful profit.
column7: A Tawarruq transaction, since the seller obtains cash for the financial assets, and the repurchase price is the deferred price of the commodity.
column8: A sale with a cooling-off option (Khiyar al-Shart) in favour of the seller, in which the difference between the two amounts is the price of the option and the assets remain with the seller.
column9: A ribā-based loan with interest secured by financial assets, since the sale confers no transfer of risk or entitlement to yield, the repo rate being the interest.
column11: Per 5/6/2, a conventional repo is an interest-bearing loan secured by the assets, which stay collateral; the repo rate is the interest.

column5: When the arbitration process leads to incurring expenses, and there is no prior agreement assigning their payment to a specific party or to the condemned party:
column6: All expenses are borne by the party that requested the arbitration.
column7: Expenses pertaining to the application of any of the disputing parties are borne by that party alone, whereas common expenses are shared by the parties, unless it is proved that one party has deliberately intended to cause harm to the other through such expenses.
column8: All expenses, including those pertaining to the application of each party, are shared equally by the dispute parties, even if one party has deliberately intended to cause harm to the other, because arbitration is a joint interest of both parties.
column9: All expenses, whether pertaining to the application of either party or common expenses, are borne by the condemned party, even without a prior agreement to that effect, and even if the condemned party has not caused any harm to the other party through such expenses.
column11: Per 14/2, each party bears expenses of its own application, common ones are shared, and a party intending harm through expenses bears them.

column5: The company managing Islamic insurance:
column6: Should guarantee the insurance assets, since it manages them against a fee.
column7: Should not guarantee the insurance assets except in case of misconduct, negligence or breach of contractual obligations.
column8: May guarantee the insurance assets if the policyholders agree to that in the policy, since the guarantee is then a stipulated condition of the contract.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 10/2, the company should not guarantee the insurance assets except for misconduct, negligence or breach.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Agency in selling a mortgaged asset is treated as an exceptional case where:
column6: The contract does not expire on the death of the agent, and the agency is pursued by his inheritors, in order to preserve the rights of the mortgagee.
column7: The contract expires on the death of the mortgagee only, and the agency is then pursued by his heirs, in order to protect the rights of the mortgagor.
column8: The agency becomes non-binding once the debt falls due.
column9: The mortgagor may revoke the agency at any time before the sale.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, such agency survives the agent's death (pursued by heirs) and is irrevocable, to preserve the mortgagee's rights.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to require the customer to provide cheques or promissory notes before the execution of the contract of Murabahah, as a guarantee of the indebtedness that will be created after the execution of the contract:
column6: On the written condition that the Institution may not use them except on their due dates; this is not permissible where they could be presented for payment before their due date.
column7: Provided that the Institution cashes them immediately and holds the proceeds as Hamish Jiddiyyah, to be returned to the customer on completion of the Murabahah and deducted from the price.
column8: Provided that they are drawn by a third-party guarantor and not by the customer himself.
column9: Absolutely, regardless of whether they can be presented for payment before their due dates.
column11: Per 5/3, cheques may be taken on written condition they are used only on due dates; not where they can be presented before then.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The owner of the ground floor of a residential building carried out alteration works in a negligent manner, causing his storey to collapse and exposing the upper storeys to harm. The correct ruling is:
column6: He is liable to reconstruct the lower storey so that the owners of the upper storeys are not harmed.
column7: The owners of the upper storeys must share the cost of reconstruction with him, since they co-own the land.
column8: He bears no liability, since he has the right of complete disposition over his own property.
column9: The courts have decisive authority to settle the matter, since each owner owns only his own floor.
column11: Per 6/2/1, if a lower storey collapses due to its owner's fault, he must rebuild it so the upper storey owners are not harmed.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Among the possible alternatives to the reserve amount required by law, instead of accepting the freezing of the cash account with the central bank, is:
column6: Depositing interest-bearing government bonds and donating the coupons to charity.
column7: Depositing receivables represented by commercial paper to be paid later by customers.
column8: Maintaining interest-bearing deposits with the central bank and using the interest to cover the costs of conversion.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1, commercial paper receivables payable later by customers may be deposited instead of freezing cash.

column5: Non-employee contractors (such as tradesmen) and lessors of transport vehicles:
column6: Share the insolvency assets pro-rata with the other creditors, and must surrender to the administrators any of the debtor's property in their possession before receiving their share.
column7: Are entitled to retain the insolvent debtor's property in their possession as their own in lieu of their fees, without it reverting to the insolvency assets.
column8: Are entitled to declare a lien over any of the insolvent debtor's property in their possession in order to recover their full fees from the insolvency assets, and such property reverts to the insolvency assets once the fees are paid.
column9: Are paid before the fees of the administrators who manage the process of sale and distribution.
column11: Per 8/3/3, they may declare a lien to recover their full fees, after which the property reverts to the insolvency assets.

column5: The investment manager who commits misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions:
column6: Is not automatically dismissed unless this was stipulated in the contract, and is dismissed upon dismissal by Rab Al Maal.
column7: Is automatically dismissed, since the authorization is based on trust that has been breached, and may be reinstated only by a new contract.
column8: Is automatically dismissed in investment agency, but not in Mudaraba.
column9: Cannot be dismissed by Rab Al Maal before the end of the contract term, but remains liable.
column11: Per 7/6, there is no automatic dismissal for misconduct unless stipulated, but Rab Al Maal may dismiss him.

column5: A condition that precedes the signing of the contract has the same validity and binding nature as the normal conditions of the contract, since it constitutes the bases of the contract mutually agreed upon by the two parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2/3, a condition precedent has the same validity and binding nature as the contract's normal conditions.

column5: In a sale with a unilateral promise to buy back:
column6: The promise may originate from a Mudarib to buy back the assets at their face value, provided that it is unilateral.
column7: The promisor may be obliged to fulfil the promise even in case of total loss of the asset promised for sale or purchase.
column8: The promisee must not be obligated to enter into the second contract by virtue of regulation, custom, collusion or the like.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1/4–5/1/6, the promisee must not be bound; no capital-guaranteeing promise by a Mudarib; no obligation on total loss of the asset.

column5: It is stipulated that the rule on trading in shares of corporations whose assets are debts shall not be adopted as a means for bargains in debts by merging parts of tangible assets and benefits with the debts as a legal device for transacting in debts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/20, merging some tangible assets with debts may not be used as a device for trading in debts.

column5: A customer signed a binding promise to purchase a car from an IFI by Murabahah and paid a Hamish Jiddiyyah of USD 2,000. The IFI bought the car for USD 20,000. The customer then refused to buy, and the IFI sold the car to a third party for USD 19,200. The IFI may:
column6: Retain the whole USD 2,000 as 'Arboun.
column7: Not deduct anything and return the whole USD 2,000, since no contract was concluded.
column8: Deduct USD 800 from the security deposit and return USD 1,200 to the customer.
column9: Deduct USD 800 in addition to the profit it expected to earn from the Murabahah.
column11: Per 6/8/2, actual damage is cost (20,000) minus resale price (19,200) = 800; the rest of the trust deposit is returned.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Setting an expected rate of return for investment accounts:
column6: Is permissible, and final distribution of profits should be based on such expected rate, without waiting for actual or constructive liquidation of the investments.
column7: Is binding on the institution if it is reached through a feasibility study.
column8: Is impermissible, because it resembles a fixed interest rate and amounts to a guarantee of the return on capital by the institution, even where a feasibility study supports the rate, and is therefore treated as a debt owed to the investors.
column9: Is not prohibited and is not binding if not achieved, even if reached through a feasibility study; final distribution is based on profit realized after actual or constructive liquidation.
column11: Per 5/2, an expected rate is allowed but not binding; final distribution rests on profit realized after actual or constructive liquidation.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the mortgagee does not have the right to make free of charge benefit from the mortgaged asset, because:
column6: The mortgaged asset is held by the mortgagee on guarantee basis.
column7: The mortgagor bears the expenses of the mortgaged asset.
column8: Otherwise he will be committing Riba.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, free benefit from the mortgaged asset by the mortgagee would amount to Riba.

column5: The countervalues of the same currency need not be of equal amount if one of them is in paper money and the other is in coin of the same country.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/1/2, same-currency countervalues must be equal even if one is paper money and the other coin of the same country.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: ………… are rights arising from the liability of another person, such as debts payable by a debtor:
column6: Secondary proprietary rights.
column7: Personal rights (rights in personam).
column8: Proprietary rights (rights in rem).
column9: Rights to intangible assets.
column11: Per 3/1, personal rights (in personam) arise from another person's liability, such as debts payable by a debtor.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the requirement of possession before a sale contract is to ensure that the Institution becomes liable for the risk of destruction of the commodity before it is entitled to sell it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis stated for 3/2.

column5: The total debts of an IFI amount to 10 million, and it is difficult to know the amount of debt that has arisen from acquiring zakatable assets. The IFI's zakatable assets constitute 40% of its total assets. The amount of debt to be deducted from the Zakah base is:
column6: 10 million.
column7: 4 million.
column8: Nothing, since the debt cannot be traced to zakatable assets.
column9: 6 million.
column11: Per 6/2/3, the ratio of zakatable assets to total assets is applied: 40% of total debts (4 million) is deducted.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of Salam in shares includes:
column6: The subject-matter of Salam is a debt and not an ascertained thing, while shares of corporations can only be ascertained, by mentioning the name of the corporation.
column7: Salam in shares implies the sale of ascertained things that are not owned.
column8: The constant availability of the specified shares in the market at the end of the period cannot be guaranteed.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/11, all three reasons are given for the impermissibility of Salam in shares.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The basic elements of agency include:
column6: The form, the subject matter of agency, and the two parties to the contract (the principal and the agent).
column7: The form, the remuneration of the agent, and the two parties to the contract (the principal and the agent).
column8: The principal, the agent, the agency period and the remuneration agreed upon.
column9: The offer, the acceptance, and the guarantee provided by the agent to the principal.
column11: Per 2/2/1, the basic elements are the form, the subject matter and the two parties (principal and agent).

column5: The management of a partnership in commendum may be delegated:
column6: To one of the joint-liability partners or to a third party.
column7: To one of the sleeping partners, who then becomes liable jointly with the others.
column8: Only to a third party who is not a partner in the company or its subsidiaries.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/3/1/4, management goes to a joint-liability partner or a third party; sleeping partners may not manage.

column5: An overseer appointed by the Waqif cannot dismiss himself unless the Waqif consents to it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/10/1, the overseer can dismiss himself even if the Waqif appointed him, informing the Waqif or authorities within a reasonable period.

column5: In Murabahah, it is not permitted:
column6: To issue negotiable Sukuk where the underlying asset consists of Murabahah receivables or other receivables only.
column7: To renew a Murabahah contract on the same commodity that was the subject matter of a previous Murabahah contract with the same customer, i.e. to refinance the transaction.
column8: For the Institution to purchase the item from the supplier on a "sale or return" basis with an option to return it within a specified period.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/2/7–2/2/8, Sukuk of receivables only and refinancing on the same commodity are barred; buying with an option to return is allowed (2/3/5).

column5: An IFI concluded a Salam contract with a manufacturer to buy 10,000 units of a trademarked product with standardised specifications, for delivery in six months. The contract stipulated that the IFI would pay the capital ten days after signing. This contract is:
column6: Not valid, because the capital of Salam must be paid immediately; delay is allowed for two or three days at most.
column7: Not valid, because trademarked manufactured products cannot be the subject of Salam, as their units are identified by trademark.
column8: Valid, because the delay is shorter than the delivery period of six months stipulated in the contract.
column9: Valid, because the delay was stipulated in advance by agreement of the parties and does not affect the contract.
column11: Per 3/1/3, only a delay of two or three days at most is tolerated; branded standardised goods may be sold by Salam (3/2/2).

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: With regard to the rights resulting from ownership:
column6: Ownership of usufruct entitles the owner to use it directly or through another person, subject to the terms stipulated by the owner of the asset.
column7: Ownership of a license to use gives the licensee the right to transfer it to a third party for consideration.
column8: The owner of usufruct bears no liability for the asset, even in case of misuse, negligence or breach of condition, because the asset belongs to another.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 4/2-3, the usufruct owner may use it directly or via others, bearing liability for misuse; a license to use is personal and non-transferable.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Gold is, in principle:
column6: A fungible item that ceases to be Ribawi once it is fashioned into jewelry.
column7: A non-fungible item, since gold articles differ in workmanship, and is subject to the rulings for the sale of commodities.
column8: A fungible item (measured by weight) and a Ribawi commodity, and is subject to the Shari'ah rulings for currency exchange (al-Sarf).
column9: A commodity that is subject to the rulings for currency exchange (al-Sarf) only when it is minted into coins.
column11: Per item 2, gold is in principle a fungible item measured by weight, a Ribawi commodity, and subject to the rulings of al-Sarf.

column5: A client obtained the approval of an IFI for a credit facility, but did not use it during its period of validity. The IFI then claimed from the client compensation for keeping the funds available for him. This claim is:
column6: Valid only to the extent of the actual harm caused to the IFI.
column7: Not valid, because the client is free to use the facility within the specified period or not, and is not committed to pay any compensation if he refrains.
column8: Valid, because the IFI would likewise be committed to compensate the client had it rejected his application to utilize the facility, and the funds were kept available for him.
column9: Valid, because the decision of granting the facility is a binding promise on the client, who must bear the cost of keeping the funds available.
column11: Per 5/2, neither party compensates the other: the client is free not to use the facility, and the IFI owes nothing on rejecting utilization.

column5: A valid Hawalah:
column6: Discharges the transferor only after the payer has paid the debt, the transferee until then retaining recourse against the transferor in all cases, even if the payer is solvent.
column7: Discharges the transferor from both the debt liability and any claims in respect of it, so the transferee has no recourse against him, unless acceptance was conditional on the payer being solvent and he is not.
column8: Does not discharge the transferor, who remains a guarantor of the payer's payment.
column9: Discharges the transferor, and the transferee has no right of recourse against him in any case, even if acceptance was conditional on the payer being solvent, or the payer is declared bankrupt in his lifetime or dies in a state of bankruptcy.
column11: Per 7/1, Hawalah discharges the transferor, save recourse where solvency of the payer was stipulated and he is insolvent.

column5: If the company invests the policyholders' funds through investment agency, the deal is subject to the Shari'ah rulings on Mudarabah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/7, investment through investment agency is subject to the Shari'ah rulings on remunerated agency.

column5: It is not permissible that the Institution's role in Istisna'a be that of a financial intermediary between a buyer and a third party, especially if the buyer has become unable to meet his obligations toward such a third party. This prohibition applies:
column6: Only if the buyer has actually defaulted on his obligations toward the third party.
column7: Only if such a role takes place after the commencement of the work.
column8: Whether such a role would take place before or after the commencement of the work.
column9: Only if such a role takes place before the commencement of the work.
column11: Per 2/1/3, the Institution may not be a mere financial intermediary, whether before or after work commences.

column5: The Zakah year for cash and commercial assets as well as livestock is a lunar year (354 days).
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/4, the Hawl for cash, commercial assets and livestock is a lunar year of 354 days.

column5: In Murabahah, it is not permissible for the Institution to receive:
column6: A commitment fee from the customer.
column7: A fee for providing a credit facility.
column8: A fee for a feasibility study that it undertakes at the customer's request and for his benefit, where the customer agrees to pay the fee.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/4/1–2/4/2, commitment and facility fees are barred; a feasibility study fee agreed by the customer is allowed (2/4/5).

column5: If the option period expires without the buyer paying the remaining price to the seller and without the seller having agreed an extension:
column6: The contract is considered binding, and the seller may claim the remaining price from the buyer.
column7: The contract is considered revoked and the buyer is not entitled to recover the 'Arboun (Earnest Money).
column8: The contract is considered revoked and the 'Arboun (Earnest Money) must be returned to the buyer.
column9: The contract is considered revoked, and the seller may retain only that part of the 'Arboun which covers his actual damage.
column11: Per 5/2, on expiry without payment or agreed extension the contract is revoked and the buyer cannot recover the 'Arboun.

column5: Regarding prizes for current accounts:
column6: It is impermissible to assign prizes exclusively to holders of current accounts, but it is permissible once they are joined with investment accounts, whatever the weightage of the investment accounts.
column7: It is permissible to assign prizes exclusively to holders of current accounts, provided that the winners are determined through a draw.
column8: It is impermissible to assign prizes exclusively to holders of current accounts, and the same ruling applies to current accounts joined with investment accounts that represent a minor percentage with lower weightage compared to overall accounts.
column9: It is permissible to assign prizes exclusively to holders of current accounts, provided that the prizes are paid out of the shareholders' funds.
column11: Per 3/5/1, prizes exclusive to current accounts are impermissible, as is joining them with a minor share of investment accounts, a possible stratagem.

column5: Zakah is obligatory on fixed assets which generate income and which are not acquired for trade, such as leased assets, at the rate of 2.5% of their market value.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/4 and 4/2, such assets are not zakatable; only the unexpended portion of their income is subject to Zakah at year end.

column5: Ju'alah, in principle, is not a binding contract. However:
column6: It becomes binding for the Ja'il (offeror) when the worker commences work.
column7: If the worker undertakes not to revoke the contract during a specified period, it is binding on him to abide by the undertaking.
column8: It becomes binding for both parties as soon as the offer reaches the worker.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/1, Ju'alah binds the Ja'il once work commences and binds the worker if he undertook not to revoke for a period.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: If the cooling-off option is owned by both parties or just the seller:
column6: Ownership is held jointly by the two parties until the option lapses or the contract is confirmed.
column7: Ownership of the sold item transfers to the buyer immediately, but the legal rights related to it remain with the seller until the option lapses or the contract is confirmed.
column8: Neither countervalue changes ownership, and legal rights related to the subject matter remain solely with the seller to the exclusion of the buyer.
column9: Ownership of the sold item transfers to the buyer, while the seller retains the right to the price and the legal rights.
column11: Per 2/5/1, no ownership transfers in either countervalue; if only the buyer holds the option, ownership passes to him (2/5/2).

column5: If the contract stipulates a certain percentage of profit and the agent invests in lower-yielding transactions, the agent is not liable for the stipulated percentage if it is higher than the prevalent market rate, as that would be tantamount to acquiring another's wealth by illegitimate means.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 10/2, he compensates up to the market average only; more would be taking wealth illegitimately.

column5: The permissibility of a third party undertaking to make up capital loss or profit shortage is based on its being an undertaking to donate, which does not turn into a guarantee by the investment manager.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1, it is an undertaking to donate and does not amount to a guarantee by the investment manager.

column5: In the case of card cancellation, the card issuer may similarly not return the amounts of the service fees to the cardholder, even if it approved the cancellation, provided it was stated in the agreement of card issuance, if:
column6: The card issuer cannot retrieve an amount against the services from the actual provider.
column7: It was not possible to make the services available to another cardholder.
column8: The cardholder has never used any of the services.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per 5/2/4, both conditions are needed: no recovery from the actual provider and no possibility of reassigning the services.

column5: If the leased asset is made available to the lessee only after a period longer than what customary practices deem proper, then no rental payment shall be obligatory.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 5/2/2.

column5: The Hadith of Ibn Abbas, in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to Banu Al-Nadir, who had claims not yet due, 'Reduce the amounts to hasten payments', is cited as evidence for:
column6: Paying an amount less than the value of the commercial paper to the first beneficiary prior to the date of maturity.
column7: Discounting commercial papers with banks, i.e. selling the paper to a third party for less than its face value before maturity.
column8: Dealing in cheques of bank transfers.
column9: Endorsement of commercial papers.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hadith supports Da' wa Ta'ajjal: paying the first beneficiary less than the paper's value before maturity.

column5: If the contractor is unable to continue to discharge his obligation, and the failure to perform has not been caused by either the contractor or the ultimate purchaser (the owner of the land):
column6: The ultimate purchaser acquires ownership of the incomplete structures without giving consideration to the contractor, since the land belongs to him and the structure is attached to it.
column7: The ultimate purchaser is liable only for the value of the structure already in place, and neither party has to compensate the other for loss or damage.
column8: The contractor is entitled to the value of the work he has completed plus compensation for any damage or loss he has suffered.
column9: The ultimate purchaser pays the value of the structure, and the contractor compensates him for actual damage caused by the failure to complete.
column11: Per 4/2/4, where neither party caused the failure, the owner pays only for the structure in place and no compensation is due.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The basis for prohibiting the stipulation of a guarantee by the agent is that the agent is a trustee and does not provide a guarantee except for cases of transgression, negligence or going against the constraints of agency.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 4/2/11 and 4/2/12.

column5: Prohibited scenarios of buyback in the presence of collusion or custom include the following, excluding:
column6: Selling an asset on deferred payment terms and then purchasing it at a higher price for an even more extended deferment period.
column7: Selling an asset for cash and then purchasing it at a higher deferred price.
column8: Selling an asset at a deferred price and then the first seller repurchasing it at a lower price for spot, or for a deferred payment that falls due before the maturity of the first price.
column9: Selling a commodity on deferred payment terms and then buying it back from an auction, even at a lower cash price.
column11: Per 3/5/1 the first three are prohibited 'Inah scenarios; per 4/3, buying back at an auction, even at a lower cash price, is permitted.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of presenting usufruct as the capital in a Salam contract is:
column6: The Hadith: "Whoever pays on a deferred delivery basis should do so on the basis of a specified scale, weight and date of delivery", which also requires that the capital be paid in goods.
column7: The principle that Salam is a low cost form of sale, which justifies the buyer paying less than the spot price for the usufruct.
column8: The view of the Maliki scholars, who regard it as immediate receipt of the capital on the maxim: "Taking possession of part of a thing is like taking possession of the whole".
column9: The consensus of scholars reported by Ibn al-Mundhir.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, usufruct as capital rests on the Maliki view; delivering the asset is immediate receipt, so it is not a sale of debt.

column5: If the compensation in a Ju'alah contract is unknown, unlawful or not deliverable:
column6: Payment of reasonable compensation becomes binding.
column7: The offeror may choose any compensation he deems fit.
column8: The contract is void and the worker is entitled to nothing.
column9: The worker is entitled to the value of the compensation as estimated at the conclusion of the contract.
column11: Per 5/3/2/1, an unknown, unlawful or undeliverable compensation is replaced by binding reasonable compensation.

column5: In bilateral loans with a points system used as an alternative to repurchase agreements:
column6: The points system must ensure fairness between the parties, so no preferential terms or increase in points may be stipulated for a party, whether at the time of borrowing or as a penalty for delayed repayment.
column7: It is not permitted to convert the transaction into a monetary consideration, such as converting points into cash upon non-settlement.
column8: Only the principal of the loan and its term are considered, and interest charges may not be calculated.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/6/3/2 (a)–(c), fairness of points, no conversion into cash and no interest are all rules of bilateral loans with points.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the rule that ownership in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek cannot be made contingent on a future date is that:
column6: A bilateral promise resembles a contract effected before ownership, and the lessor would then be selling what he does not yet own.
column7: A sale contract cannot be dependent on a future date, as 'sale' means that its effect (transfer of ownership) takes place immediately.
column8: This prevents the contract from becoming an 'Inah transaction, because the sale price would otherwise be paid before the lessor acquires ownership.
column9: Ijarah, unlike sale, is a contract that involves time.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a sale's effect, transfer of ownership, is immediate, so a sale cannot be made dependent on a future date.

column5: The stipulation of an excess for the lender in Qard:
column6: Is prohibited and amounts to Riba, whether the excess is in terms of quality or quantity, a tangible thing or a benefit, and whether stipulated in writing or by customary practice.
column7: Is prohibited only if the excess is in terms of quantity, but is permissible if it is in terms of quality.
column8: Is prohibited only if it is stipulated at the time of the contract, but is permissible if it is stipulated during the period of delay, since the prohibition of Riba applies to the contract alone.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1, any stipulated excess for the lender is Riba, whatever its form, timing, or whether written or customary.

column5: With regard to the Hadith that prohibited concluding partnership with Jews and Christians unless the selling and buying is in the hands of the Muslim, the cause of the prohibition is:
column6: The difference of religion between the partners in itself, which makes the partnership contract invalid whoever manages the funds of the venture and however the profit is shared.
column7: The prohibition of guaranteeing the capital of a non-Muslim partner, who cannot be trusted with the funds of the Muslim partner.
column8: The fear of being involved in interest-based transactions or impermissible contracts, which is absent when there are guarantees to observe Shari'ah rulings.
column9: The inability to enforce the partnership contract before courts, as the courts do not recognise partnerships with non-Muslims.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the cause is fear of Riba or impermissible contracts, absent where Shari'ah observance is guaranteed.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: The requirement that the other party be notified of revocation is based on:
column6: Analogy to Iqalah, which has to be performed without any increase or decrease in considerations.
column7: The prevailing viewpoint of the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools that revocation nullifies the contract immediately, even before the other party is notified, because the right of revocation is absolute and needs no knowledge by the other party.
column8: The opinion of Abu Hanifah and Muhammad Ibn Al-Hasan, contrary to the majority of jurists, because notification averts harm from the other party who, unaware of the revocation, may act to his detriment.
column9: The opinion of the majority of jurists, because revocation is a unilateral act that is not effective until it is known.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, notification follows Abu Hanifah and Muhammad Ibn Al-Hasan, against the majority, to avert harm to the other party.

column5: Among the bases for the validity of Waqf of movable assets is the saying of the Prophet (PBUH):
column6: As for Khālid, he kept his armour and weapons for Allah's Cause.
column7: Allah is Good, and He, therefore, accepts only that which is good.
column8: My heir will not distribute dīnār or dirham.
column9: O Banī Najjār! Suggest a price for your orchard.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/7, Khālid's armour and weapons; the Banī Najjār Ḥadīth supports Waqf of a common share (2/4/11).

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: When the Mudarib mixes the Mudarabah funds with his own funds:
column6: The Mudarib's own funds earn no profit, because he is not a Rab al-Mal.
column7: The Mudarib loses his share of profit as a Mudarib, and gets only the profit of his own funds, since mixing is a transgression that forfeits his entitlement.
column8: The Mudarabah contract becomes null and void, and the Mudarib is entitled only to the wage of similar work, the whole profit going to the Rab al-Mal, since mixing the funds is a breach of the contract in all cases.
column9: He becomes a partner by subscribing his funds and a Mudarib for the other party's funds; the profit is divided between the two capitals, and he gets the profit of his work as well as of his funds.
column11: Per 4/7, by mixing his funds the Mudarib becomes partner and Mudarib, earning profit for both his work and his funds.

column5: Tangible security stipulated by the holder of commercial paper to ensure the securing of his right:
column6: Is not permissible, since commercial paper is itself a security.
column7: Is deemed a personal guarantee (Kafalah).
column8: Is deemed a Mortgage (Rahn) and is governed by the rules of Rahn.
column9: Is deemed a Hawalah of the right.
column11: Per 8/3, tangible security taken by the holder is a Rahn, governed by the rules of Rahn.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: It is permissible to increase the profit in credit sales as compared to cash sales, provided that it is incorporated into the price and that the amount of debt is not increased due to any late payment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per item 5, a higher profit in credit sales is permissible if built into the price and not increased for late payment.

column5: The procrastinating debtor is liable for:
column6: Compensation for the opportunity loss suffered by the creditor as a result of the delay.
column7: Legal and other expenses incurred by the creditor in order to recover his debt.
column8: Compensation for the decline in the value of the currency of the debt during the period of delay.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1/4 he bears recovery expenses, as he caused them; per 2/1/2 no compensation for opportunity or currency loss is allowed.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the mortgaged asset should be a Shari'ah-permissible property, because:
column6: The mortgaged asset must generate permissible income for the mortgagee throughout the period of the mortgage contract.
column7: The mortgaged asset must be insured with an Islamic insurance company, which is why impermissible property is excluded.
column8: The objective is to sell the asset to settle the debt on default, and impermissible property cannot be sold.
column9: The mortgagee is entitled to benefit from the mortgaged asset.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, mortgage aims at selling the asset to settle the debt, and an impermissible property cannot be sold for that.

column5: The basis for permissibility of trading in investment Sukuk when such Sukuk represent shares in tangible assets or usufruct is that the trading is, in fact, on the assets and usufructs; since these assets may be traded, so too may the certificates that represent them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis stated for trading Sukuk representing tangible assets or usufructs.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Examples of minor Gharar, which does not affect the contract, include:
column6: Sale of a house to a buyer who has not seen its foundation.
column7: Leasing the house for one month while months differ in length.
column8: Sale of underground commodities or commodities that cannot be known unless broken.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2/2, (a) and (b) are minor Gharar; sale of underground commodities is cited as medium Gharar under 4/2/3.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for allowing an Ijarah contract to take effect based on future events is that:
column6: Ijarah is one of the contracts for transferring ownership that depends on an exchange of counter-values.
column7: A conditional gift is valid, as in the gift sent by the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Negus.
column8: Ijarah, unlike a sale contract, is a contract that involves time, so it is relevant that it be contingent on future events.
column9: Without a designated term there would be an uncertainty that might lead to dispute.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Ijarah, unlike sale, involves time, so it may be made to take effect on future events.

column5: The condition that all instalments become due if the debtor is late in paying one instalment is valid because:
column6: The debtor's delay is a breach that cancels the original contract of sale, so that the creditor may claim the price immediately and compensation for delay.
column7: There is no Shari'ah text to the contrary and it serves a lawful interest of the creditor, provided the debtor consented to it when the contract was agreed.
column8: It is a form of compensation for delay that does not increase the amount of the debt, and it is therefore permitted even if the debtor did not consent to it.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis (IIFA Resolution 51), the condition is valid with the debtor's consent at contracting; no text forbids it and it serves a lawful interest.

column5: The following provisions are not deductible from zakatable assets:
column6: Provision for leaves.
column7: Provision for maintenance.
column8: Provision for insurance of fixed assets.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/3/5, 7/3/8 and 7/3/9, provisions for leaves, maintenance and insurance of fixed assets are all not deductible from zakatable assets.

column5: With regard to the form of creation (ṣīgha) of Waqf:
column6: Waqf is not concluded unless it is documented in writing and authenticated through the procedures of legal authentication, even if the Waqif has expressed it verbally.
column7: An offer from the Waqif creates Waqf verbally or in writing, but it requires the acceptance of the Waqf beneficiary if he is specific, and of the overseer if the beneficiaries are not specific.
column8: An offer from the Waqif creates Waqf through any means indicating the same, verbally, in writing or otherwise, and does not require acceptance of the Waqf beneficiary, whether specific or not.
column9: Waqf is created by the offer of the Waqif and the acceptance of the overseer, who acts on behalf of the Waqf beneficiaries, and it takes effect only upon the overseer's possession of the asset.
column11: Per 2/4/1/1, the Waqif's offer by any indicative means creates Waqf, with no acceptance needed from the beneficiary, specific or not.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, it is not permitted for the owner of a right of Tahjir to sell it, because:
column6: The right of Tahjir cannot be inherited by his heirs.
column7: The land remains public property in which people share like water, pasturage and fire.
column8: The right of Tahjir cannot be transferred to anyone else in any manner.
column9: His entitlement is confined to his personal use, like the right of Shuf'ah (preemption).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Tahjir holder's entitlement is confined to his personal use, like Shuf'ah, though it passes to heirs and transferees.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: A buyer who knew at the time of contract that the deal would become fragmented retains the option to revoke owing to deal fragmentation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2, the option is subject to the buyer not knowing that the deal would become fragmented.

column5: The basis for not permitting a card based on Tawarruq consequential to lending is that rolling over the debt via Tawarruq from the lender with the borrower, conditioned for settling the loan, is an artifice to delay the settlement of the loan with an increase in it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 6/3/2, such qalb al-dayn is an artifice to defer the loan while increasing it.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the prohibition of Murabahah tradable securities or the refinancing of a Murabahah transaction is that:
column6: These fall under the heading of sale of debt, which is prohibited by Shari'ah.
column7: These are a pre-Islamic form of Riba of extension of time.
column8: These lead to the buyer guaranteeing the capital of the other party.
column9: These amount to a contract prior to acquisition of the item to be sold.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Murabahah receivable securities and refinancing fall under the prohibited sale of debt.

column5: Ahmad owes a supplier USD 10,000 and issues him a cheque for this amount drawn on his current account, which has a zero balance. The bank accepts the overdraft and honours the cheque. This transaction is characterised as:
column6: An unrestricted transfer of debt.
column7: An agency contract for collection.
column8: A restricted transfer of debt.
column9: Not a transfer of debt, and the supplier may have recourse to Ahmad.
column11: Per 12/2, where the payee is a creditor and the bank accepts the overdraft, it is an unrestricted transfer of debt.

column5: Bank B and Bank C entered into a Sharikah. Company G, which owns 60% of the capital of Bank B, undertook, without any consideration and independently of the Sharikah contract, to make up any loss of Bank B's capital in the Sharikah. This guarantee is:
column6: Permissible, because Company G is not a party to the Sharikah contract, and its capacity as guarantor is independent of the Sharikah.
column7: Not permissible, because a guarantee of the capital of a partner is prohibited even from an independent third party, whether or not it is given for consideration.
column8: Not permissible, because the guarantor owns more than half of the capital of the guaranteed entity, which makes it in substance a guarantee by a partner.
column9: Permissible, because the guarantee is provided without consideration and independently of the Sharikah contract, whatever the guarantor's shareholding.
column11: Per 3/1/4/3 and its basis, the guarantor may not own over half of the guaranteed entity; otherwise it is a partner guarantee.

column5: The Institution should arrange its relationships with other institutions and correspondent banks on the basis of non-payment of interest and avoidance of prohibited transactions in covering operations resulting from documentary credit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/7/6, inter-bank covering operations must avoid interest and prohibited transactions.

column5: If the holder of a travellers' cheque, the value of which he has paid to the issuing Institution, endorses the cheque in favour of his creditor, this is:
column6: A sale of debt to a party other than the debtor.
column7: A restricted transfer of debt, the amount of the debt being the value of the cheque for which the Institution received payment.
column8: An unrestricted transfer of debt, since the issuing Institution pays from its own funds and not from an amount owed to the holder, the value being only a deposit.
column9: An agency contract for collection of the value of the cheque.
column11: Per 12/3, the issuer is the holder's debtor, so endorsing to a creditor is a restricted Hawalah for the paid value.

column5: If the assets of a corporation are composed of tangible assets, benefits, cash and debts, and its purpose and activity pertain to trading in tangible assets, benefits and rights, trading in its shares is permissible without taking into account the rules of Sarf or transactions in debts, provided that:
column6: The total market value of assets, benefits and rights is not less than 30% of the total assets value of the corporation.
column7: The debts do not exceed 30% of the market capitalization.
column8: The tangible assets are not less than 70% of the total assets, and the cash and debts do not exceed 30% of the market capitalization.
column9: The cash and debts do not exceed 50% of the total assets.
column11: Per 3/19, tangible assets, benefits and rights must be at least 30% of total assets value; cash and debts are then secondary.

column5: An IFI issued Sukuk of ownership of leased assets. Before maturity, one of the certificate holders asked the IFI, as issuer, to redeem his certificates. The IFI may redeem them:
column6: It may not redeem them prior to maturity.
column7: At the market price or at a rate agreed upon, at the date of redemption, between the certificate holder and the issuer.
column8: At the nominal value plus the rentals accrued up to the date of redemption, as fixed in the prospectus.
column9: Only at their nominal value as stated in the prospectus.
column11: Per 5/2/5, the issuer may redeem certificates of leased assets before maturity at market price or a rate agreed at the date of redemption.

column5: If the investment results in profit or capital gain in case of a breach that is advantageous to the principal, such profit or capital increase belongs to the principal, and the agent loses its right to the performance incentive.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/2, the gain belongs to the principal without affecting the agent's right to its performance incentive.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: An agent who breaches the contract by selling or buying at a price other than the price agreed upon has to indemnify the principal for the difference between the price agreed upon and the price he accepted or offered.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the basis and 6/3/2, he indemnifies the difference between the price he accepted/offered and the market price.

column5: According to the Hadith reported from Anas Ibn Malik, when a lender is offered a gift or a free ride on an animal by the borrower, he is not to accept it, unless such a practice was prevalent among them prior to the Qard.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This Hadith is cited in the Shari'ah basis for 5/1 on non-stipulated benefits prior to repayment.

column5: The Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) contract is valid:
column6: Only for an indefinite period.
column7: Until the time of harvest or for a defined period in which the crop is normally enough for harvest.
column8: For any period agreed by the parties, even if it is shorter than the time needed for the crop to materialize.
column9: For a maximum period of one year.
column11: Per 5/3, it is valid until harvest or for a defined period normally enough for the crop to be harvested.

column5: It is not permissible to take remuneration for issuing a letter of guarantee:
column6: Whether it is with cover or without cover, if it is consideration for the guarantee per se, since the amount guaranteed and the duration of the guarantee are usually taken into account in computing remuneration.
column7: Only if it is with full cover, since the Institution bears no risk.
column8: Only if it is without cover, since the Institution then bears the risk.
column9: If the remuneration is for administrative expenses that do not exceed the commission others would charge for such services, in the case of a letter of guarantee issued with full or partial cover, since the cover reflects the guarantee itself.
column11: Per 6/1/1, no remuneration for the guarantee per se is allowed, with or without cover.

column5: In collection and payment services, the institution:
column6: May collect commercial papers by way of discounting them, provided that the customer consents and the discount is calculated according to the period remaining until maturity.
column7: Should refrain from collection when it realizes that it involves an impermissible practice, or leads to discounting of a commercial paper.
column8: May not receive fees for collection, since collection of debts is a form of Qard and any benefit derived from it would be Riba.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/5/4, the institution must refrain from collection involving impermissible practice or discounting; per 2/5/1 fees are allowed.

column5: Concessions granted to implicit and subsidiary contracts comprise relief from:
column6: Gharar, which affects financial contracts.
column7: Jahalah, with regard to the object of a subsidiary contract.
column8: Sale-based Riba and violation of currency exchange rules, as when spot delivery is ignored in a contract that combines currency exchange with money transfer.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/2/1 to 5/2/3, Gharar, Jahalah in the object, sale-based Riba and exchange rules may all be overlooked in subsidiary contracts.

column5: Hiring comes to an end at the end of the contract period, yet:
column6: It remains when it is needed for a reasonable excuse or for avoidance of harm, for a pay to be agreed upon, otherwise the normal pay for similar services is applied.
column7: It remains when it is needed for a reasonable excuse or for avoidance of harm, and in that case it is always at the same pay as the original contract.
column8: It may be extended only by order of the judiciary.
column9: It is renewed spontaneously for the same period and the same pay in all cases, even without a condition in the contract.
column11: Per 8/2 (third 8/2/3), hiring continues where needed for a reasonable excuse or to avoid harm, at an agreed pay, else the normal pay for similar services.

column5: A customer asked an IFI to finance the production of 50 buses by Istisna'a. The IFI concluded an Istisna'a with the customer and a Parallel Istisna'a with a bus factory selected through competitive bidding. It later emerged that 40% of the factory is owned by the customer. This transaction is:
column6: Impermissible, because one third or more of the facility in which the subject-matter will be produced belongs to the customer, even though the deal was won through competitive bidding.
column7: Permissible, because the factory was selected through competitive bidding, which removes any suspicion of a sale and buy back transaction (Bay' al-'Inah).
column8: Impermissible only if the customer's ownership of the factory exceeds 50%, since only majority ownership makes the subject-matter return to the customer.
column9: Permissible, because the customer does not own a majority (more than 50%) of the factory, and the Istisna'a and the Parallel Istisna'a are independent contracts with different parties, so no interest-based financing arises.
column11: Per 2/2/4, a customer stake of one third or more in the producing facility makes it an interest-based device, even if won by bidding.

column5: A person announced a Ju'alah offering a reward for retrieving his lost property. A worker commenced the search, but the offeror then prevented him from continuing the work. The offeror is:
column6: Bound to pay half of the reward announced.
column7: Bound to pay the worker reasonable wages.
column8: Not bound to pay anything, since Ju'alah is not binding.
column9: Bound to pay the full reward announced.
column11: Per 6/2, if the offeror prevents the worker after the work has commenced, he must pay reasonable wages.

column5: With respect to the distribution of profit in a Sharikah:
column6: It is not permitted that the final allocation of profit take place based on expected profit.
