column7: It is permissible to allocate some funds to any of the partners on account before actual or constructive valuation, on condition that the final settlement takes place later and any excess received is reimbursed.
column8: It is not permitted to distribute any amount to the partners before the liquidation of the Sharikah.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/5/10-11, final allocation must be on actual profit, while distributions on account subject to settlement are allowed.

column5: Default in payment by a debtor who is capable of paying the debt is Haram (prohibited).
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/1/1, default by a debtor able to pay is prohibited; the Hadith says default by a solvent debtor is unjust.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of guaranteeing unknown debts includes:
column6: The general meaning of the Hadith "The guarantor is liable", which makes no distinction between guaranteeing the known and the unknown, since the unknown will become known after the debt is incurred.
column7: The Quranic verse "... for him who produces it, is (the reward of) a camel load and I will be bound by it", where the guarantor guaranteed a camel load although it was not yet a debt.
column8: The consensus of the Fuqaha that Gharar is tolerable in all contracts of guarantee for consideration.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per the basis, both the Hadith and the verse of Yusuf are cited; no consensus on Gharar in guarantees for consideration is cited.

column5: An undertaking by the investment manager to assume the liability of losses arising from exchange rate fluctuations is among the prohibited forms of assuming liability.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/5/2, such an undertaking is a prohibited form of liability, subject to 3/2 and 3/4.

column5: The institution issuing travellers' cheques may not take any commission for their issuance, since this would be a commission on a loan.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/3(e), the issuer may take a commission for intermediation at issuance or payment, provided it includes no Riba.

column5: Upon the request of a solvent debtor customer, it is permitted to execute a new Murabaha that results in a new debt greater than the first debt, even if the customer settles the first debt with the sale price of the commodity, subject to rules including:
column6: The new Murabaha does not require a credit approval, since the customer is already a debtor of the Institution.
column7: The customer is obliged to sell the commodity purchased under the new Murabaha and to settle the first debt from its proceeds, as stipulated in the financing documentation of the new Murabaha, so that the first debt is settled on the same day.
column8: The new Murabaha is a financing transaction independent of the transaction that established the first debt, and settling the first debt from the sale price is not required in the contract or financing documentation.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/3/4 (a)–(b), the new Murabaha must be independent and credit-approved, and the customer has no obligation to sell the commodity.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of issuing preference shares with financial priority is that:
column6: They are a form of Salam in shares.
column7: They are bearer instruments.
column8: They are sold before they are owned by the corporation, since the preference attaches to shares not yet issued or allotted.
column9: This leads to the severance of participation in profit and the imposition of injustice on the other shareholders.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 2/6, financial priority severs participation in profit and wrongs the other shareholders.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the transfer of the debt and its risk to the buyer once he is enabled to claim it is:
column6: The analogy of ḥawāla (novation), by which the risk of the debt transfers to the assignee upon the assignment.
column7: The saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Muslims act up to their conditions", so that the parties may agree on the time at which the debt and its risk transfer to the buyer, whatever the custom.
column8: That the risk of the subject of sale transfers to the buyer by possession or by tamkīn (enabling him to take possession), and the buyer of a debt is deemed the possessor if enabled to claim it.
column9: The concept of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 7/1, risk passes by possession or tamkīn, and a buyer enabled to claim the debt is its possessor.

column5: A Hawalah transaction shall not be annulled due to the death of the transferee, and the heirs shall replace the transferee; in case of liquidation of a transferee Institution, the liquidator takes its place for settlement.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/3, the heirs or the liquidator replace the transferee and the Hawalah continues.

column5: In hiring of persons, it is permissible to stipulate a penalty code indicating a specific amount which:
column6: Either party pays to the other as a fixed percentage of the pay for any delay, irrespective of normal practice or justice.
column7: The employer should pay to the employee in case of delay in paying the pay, determined with due consideration to normal practice as well as justice.
column8: The employee should pay to the employer in case of delay in performing the work/service within the specified period, determined with due consideration to normal practice as well as justice.
column9: The employer pays to the employee for every month by which payment of past pay is rescheduled.
column11: Per 7/1/3, a penalty on the employee for delay in the work is allowed, set by normal practice and justice; any increment on the employer's overdue pay is barred (5/2/8).

column5: If the sold commodity in an online contract is computer software or the like, possession in the strict Shari'ah sense takes place:
column6: When the purchaser, after signing the contract, downloads the software or the data from the website to his personal computer.
column7: When the seller sends the purchaser the invoice and the licence key by e-mail, even if the purchaser has not downloaded the software.
column8: Upon payment of the price by the purchaser through the website.
column9: Upon signing the contract, even before the software is downloaded.
column11: Per 7/2, possession of software occurs when the purchaser, after signing, downloads it from the website to his personal computer.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The ruling that Gharar does not affect Rahn (Mortgage) contracts is based on the fact that:
column6: Rahn is primarily based on donation, and Gharar is forgiven in all donation-based contracts.
column7: Rahn is always justified by a Shari'ah-recognizable need, whether public or private, which enjoys the status of necessity.
column8: The Rahn contract is not meant in itself, being a corollary contract signed for documentation.
column9: Rahn is a corollary contract based on delegation of the right of disposal to the mortgagee.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Rahn is a corollary contract for documentation, not meant in itself. 'Delegation of the right of disposal' is the basis for suretyship.

column5: Where the Institution separates debts and tangible assets in a legally recognized entity in which commingling is materialized and whose assets are not turned over on an ongoing basis, it may sell or securitize the entity, subject to the following rule:
column6: The ratio of tangible assets and the like may be as low as 33% of the value of the entity's assets at issuance, provided that the Shari'ah Board approves it and the remaining assets are debts generated from business turnover.
column7: The sale results in its Shari'ah effects, including transfer of ownership and risk to the buyer, and the seller may not be stipulated to bear such risks at any stage.
column8: The seller may bear the risks of the tangible assets until the maturity of the Sukuk, provided that this is disclosed in the prospectus.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/2/1–8/2/2, ownership and risk must pass to the buyer with no seller risk-bearing, and tangible assets must exceed 50% of value.

column5: When the customer defaults on instalments of the Murabahah selling price, the Institution may impose an additional payment on him for its own benefit, provided it does not exceed the actual damage it has suffered.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/8, the amount due is only the unpaid price; no additional payment for the Institution's benefit, subject to 5/6.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Regarding the documents and financial statements of the institution and disputes with accountholders:
column6: The cost of proving the accusation shall be borne by the institution when the accountholder files the claim against it.
column7: It is permissible to stipulate the authoritative status of the documents and financial statements of the institution, unless they are proved to be wrong by the accountholder.
column8: The documents and financial statements of the institution are final, and a dispute about them may not be referred to experts, arbitration or law.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 2/2/9-10, the institution's statements may be made authoritative unless proved wrong; disputes go to experts, arbitration or law; the claimant bears proof cost.

column5: It is permitted to sell a commodity on deferred payment terms and then:
column6: Buy it back from an auction, even at a lower cash price.
column7: Buy it back from the buyer only at a price equal to the deferred price, paid at spot.
column8: Buy it back directly from the buyer at a lower spot price by prior collusion.
column9: Buy it back from a third party at a lower spot price, where all parties have colluded on that resale.
column11: Per 4/3, buyback from an auction is permitted even at a lower cash price; collusive buybacks are barred (3/5, 4/4).

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The Shari'ah basis for impermissibility of charging the whole loss to one of the two parties is the statement of Ali Ibn Abu Talib: "Profit is to be distributed as per the agreement of the two parties, whereas loss should be borne according to the ratios of contribution to the capital".
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis cites this statement of Ali Ibn Abu Talib; shifting one party's loss to the other is oppressive and invalid.

column5: It is permitted to purchase a tangible asset and then lease it to the one who sold it under an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, subject to the relevant provisions of the Standard on Ijarah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2, an asset may be bought and leased to its seller under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, subject to Standard No. 9.

column5: The Institution, acting as ultimate purchaser, may appoint the manufacturer, after taking possession of the subject-matter, as an agent to sell it to the manufacturer's customers on behalf of the Institution:
column6: Only free of charge, since the manufacturer is already remunerated by the price of the Istisna'a contract.
column7: Only for a fixed fee, and not for a percentage of the sale price, since a percentage would make the consideration unknown.
column8: Whether free of charge, for a fixed fee or for a percentage of the sale price, on condition that the agency and Istisna'a contracts were not entered into in connection with each other.
column9: Even before taking possession of the subject-matter, provided the agency is free of charge and the manufacturer bears the risk of its sale, which makes the agency independent of the Istisna'a.
column11: Per 6/8, after possession the manufacturer may sell as agent, free or for a fixed fee or percentage, if the agency is not linked to the Istisna'a.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: International commodity sales end in one of the following ways:
column6: Actual delivery for both counter-values or for one of them.
column7: Liquidation between the two parties.
column8: Cash settlement by agreement, or counter-contracts.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/3, these sales end by actual delivery, liquidation between the parties, cash settlement by agreement, or counter-contracts.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: With regard to gold in non-commutative contracts (Uqud al-Tabarru'at), it is permissible:
column6: To lend (I'arah) non-fungible gold, and fungible gold if identifiable.
column7: To lend (Qard) gold if it is fungible.
column8: To endow gold as Waqf, such as endowment for lease where the rent constitutes the yield, or for lending (I'arah), or to extend it as a loan (Qard).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/1–6/3, I'arah of gold, Qard of fungible gold and Waqf of gold (for lease, I'arah or Qard) are all permissible.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Any amount of profit distributed before ensuring the protection of the capital is considered:
column6: An advance payment, rather than realized profit.
column7: Realized profit that cannot be recovered from the holders of the accounts.
column8: A donation by the Mudarib to the holders of the accounts.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/1/1 (see 5/3), profit distributed before the capital is protected is an advance payment, not realized profit.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the realisation of actual possession with respect to gold, silver and currencies through actual physical possession is:
column6: The consensus (Ijma') of the jurists on acknowledging custom as the basis of possession.
column7: The tradition: 'He who buys food is not to sell it until he takes possession of it', which requires actual physical possession of gold, silver and currencies.
column8: The tradition reported from Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit: "Gold for gold, silver for silver ... like for like, equal for equal, from hand to hand ..."
column9: A resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on banking practice.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, physical possession in gold, silver and currencies rests on the hadith of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit (from hand to hand).

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The distinction between proprietary rights and personal rights is that:
column6: The owner of a proprietary right can directly enforce it against specific property by permissible means, whereas the owner of a personal right cannot claim any specific property.
column7: Personal rights are independent rights that do not rely on the existence of any other right, whereas proprietary rights always rely on another right, which is why only personal rights can be transferred.
column8: The owners of both rights are able to enforce their rights by claiming specific property.
column9: The owner of a personal right is able to directly enforce his right to specific property, whereas the owner of a proprietary right cannot, because the latter depends on another person's liability.
column11: Per 3/2/3, a proprietary right can be enforced directly against specific property; a personal right cannot be enforced by claiming specific property.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: Current accounts are:
column6: Amounts deposited with the institution on trust basis, and hence the institution is not committed to guarantee their repayment, except in case of transgression, negligence or breach of the contract.
column7: Amounts which the institution receives from clients who are not seeking investment, which represent loans that the institution has to guarantee their repayment on demand without any increment.
column8: Amounts on which the institution may pay a variable increment linked to its profits, as long as it is not stipulated in advance.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 2/2/1-2, current accounts are guaranteed loans repayable on demand without increment; trust-based holding describes investment accounts.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for allocating to the investment agent any profit amount in excess of the expected profit is that:
column6: It is compensation for any loan advanced by the agent to the principal.
column7: It is a type of conditional gift and is an incentive.
column8: It is part of the fee for similar services.
column9: It is the agent's share of profit in his capacity as a partner.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/4, the excess profit allocated to the agent is a type of conditional gift and an incentive.

column5: The basis for not obligating the holder of the covered card to deposit the cover in a current account includes:
column6: Current accounts do not generate returns, so the cardholder would be deprived of profit, which contradicts the principle of fairness in dealing with customers and the requirement of equal treatment of all account holders.
column7: The current account is a trust (amānah), and a trust may not be used to secure a debt.
column8: The current account is adapted as a loan, so obligating its deposit would stipulate a loan in a financing arrangement, falling under the proscription of combining a loan and a sale.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 6/2, a current account is a loan; requiring it would stipulate a loan in a financing deal (loan combined with sale).

column5: The worker (irrigator) is entitled to revoke the Irrigation Partnership contract if the owner refuses to allow him to work.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 13/3, the worker may revoke the contract if the owner refuses to allow him to work.

column5: Unlike other partnerships, ………… combines rules of agency and guarantee simultaneously.
column6: Sharikat al-Wujuh.
column7: Sharikat al-'Inan.
column8: Sharikat al-Muhassah.
column9: Sharikat al-Mufawadah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Sharikat al-Mufawadah combines rules of agency and guarantee simultaneously.

column5: The division of a single debt or several debts among partners is characterized as a sale of debt and is therefore subject to the rules of the sale of debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis for 6/1–6/2, such a division is a separation and not a sale.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Examples of verbal deception (Taghrir) include:
column6: Painting an old car to hide its age and give the impression that it is new.
column7: Deliberate misinformation about the original cost price or expense in a Murabahah, Tawliyah or Hatitah sale.
column8: Adding lubricants or other substances so that the product appears in a better condition, without disclosing it.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2(a), misstating cost in Murabahah is verbal deception; painting and lubricants are deceptive conduct (Tadlis, 3/3).

column5: When the managing bank commits misconduct or negligence, or resorts to fraud and trickery in the studies it prepares, it should indemnify the partners for the injury it has deliberately caused to them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis on guarantees by the lead bank, it indemnifies partners for misconduct, negligence or fraud in its studies.

column5: When any of the two parties refrains from appointing an arbitrator from his own side as per the contract:
column6: The arbitration condition lapses, and the dispute must be referred to the judiciary for judgment.
column7: The other party has the right itself to appoint an arbitrator to represent the refraining party, provided that the arbitration condition in the contract does not specify another way for such appointment.
column8: The other party has the right to resort to the judiciary for appointing an arbitrator to represent the refraining party, provided that the arbitration condition in the contract does not specify another way for appointing such arbitrator.
column9: The arbitrator appointed by the other party becomes the sole arbitrator in the dispute, unless the arbitration condition in the contract specifies another way for appointing the arbitrators.
column11: Per 8/5, the other party may ask the judiciary to appoint an arbitrator for the refraining party, unless the clause sets another way of appointment.

column5: Accrued income, which represents income of the current period that has not yet been received, shall be subject to Zakah on debts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/3/4/7, accrued income is subject to Zakah on debts as indicated in 5/3/1.

column5: Appreciation in the value of the mortgaged asset as well as its income:
column6: Belong to the mortgagor free of the mortgage, unless the two parties agree otherwise.
column7: Are considered to be mortgaged along with the principal, unless the two parties agree otherwise.
column8: Are mortgaged only if the mortgaged asset is an investment account.
column9: Belong to the mortgagee, in return for keeping the mortgaged asset.
column11: Per 3/2/8, appreciation and income of the mortgaged asset are mortgaged with the principal unless the parties agree otherwise.

column5: A participant's insured property suffered a loss of 30,000, while the insurance amount stated in the policy is 50,000. As per regulations, the participant shall receive:
column6: 30,000, in addition to any compensation he receives from the party who caused the injury.
column7: 40,000, being the average of the loss and the insurance amount.
column8: 50,000, being the insurance amount stated in the policy.
column9: 30,000, being the lesser of the loss incurred and the insurance amount.
column11: Per 11/1 the participant gets the loss or the insurance amount, whichever is less; per 11/2 he may not also keep other compensation.

column5: The ruling that the offering party does not have the right to retreat from his offer within the period specified for its validity is based on:
column6: The viewpoint of some Maliki scholars that an offer announced to be valid for a specific period should remain valid throughout it, as emphasized by Al-Hattab quoting Abu Bakar Al-Arabi.
column7: The resolution of the Al Baraka Seminar that an online contract between parties who cannot hear each other is a contract between two absent parties, whose offer may be withdrawn at any time before acceptance.
column8: The fact that Shari'ah scholars define contract as "the concordance of two wills".
column9: The general texts of Shari'ah which instruct people to avoid harm and achieve justice.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the binding term-offer rests on the view of some Maliki scholars (Al-Hattab quoting Abu Bakar Al-Arabi) and an IIFA resolution.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the right of certificate holders to management is that:
column6: The prospectus appoints them as agents of the issuer.
column7: They are creditors of the issuer and are entitled to protect their debts.
column8: They own the property that their certificates represent, and management is part of ownership.
column9: The issuer guarantees their capital and must therefore consult them.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, holders own the property represented by their certificates, and management is part of ownership.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: With respect to cash withdrawal using a card, it is permissible for the Institution issuing the card to charge:
column6: A fee calculated as a percentage of the amount withdrawn, provided it is agreed in advance.
column7: A fee that varies with the amount withdrawn, where the withdrawal exceeds the cardholder's available funds.
column8: A flat service fee for cash withdrawal, proportionate to the service offered, but not a fee that varies with the amount withdrawn.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/5/2, only a flat fee proportionate to the service is allowed, not a fee that varies with the amount withdrawn.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not permitting the discounting of commercial paper is that:
column6: The holder is not the first beneficiary of the paper, and cannot therefore discount it without his consent.
column7: Discounting involves a sale of goods by description as a liability, with delayed delivery of both counter-values, which the Shari'ah does not permit.
column8: The commercial paper is not in the possession of the holder, who has only a right against the drawer and the endorsers, and cannot therefore transfer it to anyone.
column9: In reality, discounting amounts to a loan with interest, as shown by the fact that the charge varies with the value of the paper and its date of maturity.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, discounting is in reality an interest-bearing loan, the charge varying with the paper's value and maturity.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to enter into a partnership contract with non-Muslims or conventional banks to carry out operations acceptable by Shari'ah:
column6: Provided that the non-Muslim partner or the conventional bank is given the exclusive right to manage the partnership, since it has the larger expertise, and that the profit is distributed according to the conventional partner's accounting rules.
column7: Unless it has become evident that the funds or items presented by these entities for the partnership are from non-permissible sources, and with arrangements to obtain the necessary assurances and guarantees that Shari'ah rules are observed during operations.
column8: Even if the funds presented by these entities are from non-permissible sources, since the Institution is not responsible for the sources of its partners' funds, provided the Institution's own share is kept separate from theirs and the operation itself is permissible.
column9: Only where the Institution's contribution exceeds half of the partnership capital.
column11: Per 3/1/1/2, it is permissible unless their funds are evidently from non-permissible sources, with guarantees that Shari'ah rules are observed.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: If the object of commitment is damaged before being delivered to the committing party, the loss should be borne by the committing party.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2, damage before delivery to the committing party is borne by the committed party, unless caused by the committing party's act.

column5: The court has the sole authority to declare a person insolvent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/5, the court has the sole authority to declare a person insolvent.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for preventing the lending of Waqf funds includes:
column6: Lending is a form of Riba, since the lender benefits from protecting his funds and the borrower returns an equivalent amount.
column7: Waqf funds are owned by the Waqf beneficiaries, who alone may lend them.
column8: The analogy upon preventing the lending of minors' funds, since lending may result in the loss of Waqf funds.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 7, the analogy with barring the lending of minors' funds, as it may cause loss of Waqf funds.

column5: In case of a third party's undertaking to guarantee the loss of capital of a partner in a Sharikah, if the guarantor fails to meet his voluntary promise to cover the loss:
column6: The beneficiary partner is not entitled to claim that the Sharikah contract becomes null and void, nor to refuse to meet his obligations under the contract.
column7: The beneficiary partner may claim that the Sharikah contract is void, since he entered into it relying on the guarantee.
column8: The beneficiary partner may refuse to meet his obligations under the Sharikah contract until the loss is covered.
column9: The other partners must make up the loss of the beneficiary partner's capital.
column11: Per 3/1/4/3, the beneficiary may neither claim nullity of the Sharikah nor refuse his obligations if the guarantor defaults.

column5: The rules on commissions and expenses in documentary credit apply only to transactions between the Institution and its client, and not where the Institution deals with other institutions and banks.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/3/2, the rules apply equally to dealings with clients and with other institutions and banks, incl. as intermediary.

column5: In principle, the selection of arbitrators should be subject to:
column6: The conditions agreed upon by the two parties only, since arbitration is an agreement between them, without any Shari'ah conditions such as those for judges, including non-partiality.
column7: The same Shari'ah conditions for selection of judges, including non-partiality; in case of necessity some of these conditions could be dropped, such as the condition that the arbitrator be a Muslim.
column8: The same Shari'ah conditions for selection of judges, including non-partiality, none of which may be dropped in any case, even in case of necessity, such as the condition that the arbitrator be a Muslim.
column9: The conditions for the acceptance of witnesses' attestation.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, arbitrators are selected under judges' conditions incl. non-partiality; in necessity some, e.g. being Muslim, may be dropped.

column5: It is not permitted to sell the debt to the debtor in exchange for a new debt established as an obligation upon him that is more than the existing debt, because:
column6: This is a sale of a commodity debt before taking its possession.
column7: The consent of the debtor to the sale is not obtained.
column8: This is a form of extinction of debt in debt (faskh al-dayn), which is prohibited.
column9: This constitutes Tawarruq, which requires a third party.
column11: Per 4/1/3/1, exchanging a debt for a larger new debt on the debtor is extinction of debt in debt (faskh al-dayn), which is prohibited.

column5: When the remuneration for construction of the project is determined in terms of the right to utilize the project for a specific period, the contract is considered as Istisna'a against a price determinable in terms of utilizing the constructed facility for a specific period before handing it over to al-Mustasni'.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/3/1, the price in this Istisna'a is the utilization of the facility for a specific period.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of set-off on demand is:
column6: The person entitled to the superior debt has agreed to forgo the advantage attached to his debt, which the Shari'ah does not object to.
column7: The Hadith: "Muslims are bound by the conditions and agreements they have made ...", on which both parties have agreed to extinguish their debts.
column8: The consent of both parties to extinguish their obligations towards each other, and the exchange of bilateral promises between them.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis, set-off on demand rests on the superior creditor forgoing his advantage; the Hadith grounds contractual set-off.

column5: It is permitted to sell a tangible asset or a usufruct and then buy it back from the buyer or from another party, subject to rules including:
column6: The sale should be real, effectuating the transfer of ownership and its consequences, such as the buyer's entitlement to the yield and his assumption of the risks of price change and of loss by taking possession.
column7: There must not be a bilateral promise (muwaꜤada) binding upon both parties to enter into the second contract.
column8: There must not be a collusion (muwāṭa') or custom of buyback whereby the deferred price in the first or the second contract is higher.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1, 3/4 and 3/5, a real sale, no binding bilateral promise and no collusion or custom on a higher deferred price are all required.

column5: The ultimate purchaser is regarded as the owner of the materials in the manufacturer's possession for producing the subject-matter from the moment the Istisna'a contract is concluded.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/3, he is not the owner unless the manufacturer undertook, as a guarantee of completion, to use them only for his order.

column5: The permissibility of repurchasing a commodity at an auction, even at a price lower than the deferred price, is based on the absence of collusion, since the asset may be bought by someone other than the original seller and the price is set by the auction mechanism.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/3, no collusion exists and the auction sets a market, not predetermined, price.

column5: Where some of the debts of an entity under the commingling rule are settled and the entity purchases new debts:
column6: The entity may purchase the new debts at a discount, since it is an ongoing business, provided that the Shari'ah Board approves the discount.
column7: It must abide by the rules for the sale of debt to a third party; substitution of part of the assets or a new Murabaha to the same debtor is not deemed turnover, so the ongoing-activity rule does not apply.
column8: A new Murabaha extended to the same debtor is deemed turnover, so the rules for the sale of debt do not apply, and the entity may trade freely at any price.
column9: The rule for entities with ongoing activities applies, since the purchase of new debts to replace the settled debts is a turnover of the business, provided that the debts are purchased at their face value and not at a discount.
column11: Per 8/2/4, new debts follow item 5; asset substitution or a new Murabaha to the same debtor is not turnover, so 8/1 does not apply.

column5: Partnership between a Muslim and a Non-Muslim, such as the participation of a conventional bank with Islamic financial Institutions in syndicated financing:
column6: Is not prohibited or cannot be judged right away as invalid, except in case of Shari'ah-banned dealings, since what really matters is the conformity of the deal to the rulings of Shari'ah.
column7: Falls under the Hadith prohibiting partnership with a Jew or a Christian unless purchase and sale take place by the hands of the Muslim, and is therefore prohibited.
column8: Is subject to Karahah (disinclination) according to the four Schools, and this Karahah applies to a syndication led by a conventional bank.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, such partnership is valid unless dealings are banned; the Hadith and the Schools' Karahah do not cover this case.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Where there is a cooling-off option and one party voluntarily makes payment or delivery, the other party is obliged to deliver his countervalue in return.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/3, the other party may hold back, and the first party may then demand return of what it paid or delivered.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the rulings relating to Jawa`ih (calamities) is:
column6: The fact that Muslims should strive for appropriate disposition without rushing to termination of the commitment.
column7: The fact that implementation of a useless commitment is an act of futility, while there is no room for futility in Shari'ah legislation, which therefore obliges termination of every commitment that has become useless.
column8: The Hadith: "An extorter is indebted with what he takes until he returns it back".
column9: The Hadith which states that the Prophet (peace be upon him) forbade Bay' al-Sinin (sale of agricultural produce for many years to come), and permitted value discounts on calamities.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the rulings on Jawa`ih rest on the Hadith forbidding Bay' al-Sinin and permitting value discounts on calamities.

column5: Obtaining cheques or promissory notes from the debtor as a means to force him to make timely payment of instalments in cash:
column6: Has no Shari'ah objection (unless not allowed by law); they are returned if he pays on time and may be produced for recovery on default, and he may obtain an undertaking that they will be used only for timely recovery without any addition.
column7: Is permissible, and the Institution may present them for collection before the due dates of the instalments, and the debtor has no right to obtain any undertaking as to their use, whether or not the law allows such cheques as security, even before any default has occurred.
column8: Is permissible, provided the amounts of the cheques include compensation for late payment.
column9: Is not permissible, since it constitutes a security in excess of the amount of the debt, and the cheques may not be returned to the debtor even if he pays the instalments on time, nor be produced for recovery on default in cash, even if no default has occurred.
column11: Per 6/3, such cheques or notes are allowed, returned on timely payment and used only to recover due debts without addition.

column5: In the Debit Card, it is not permitted:
column6: That dealing with it results in lending against interest, like overdrawing the card against a consideration.
column7: To exclusively exempt or lower the fee of the current account card, if the cards for the saving or investment accounts are issued for a fee or without lowering it.
column8: To make offering the card contingent on the current account balance reaching a specified amount, if the card is issued for no fee or a fee less than the actual direct cost of its issuance.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/1-4/1/3, all three are prohibited: overdraft against consideration, exclusive fee waiver for current accounts, and the balance condition.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Khiyar al-Ghabn is a buyer's right to revoke a contract or accept it if it is discovered that:
column6: The seller has portrayed the item as being in a better condition than its actual condition.
column7: The price paid exceeds the seller's cost price by more than the profit customarily charged in the market.
column8: The price paid is higher than the average market price, by any amount, even if it is within the experts' estimates, provided the buyer was unaware.
column9: The price paid exceeds the highest estimate of the market experts, to an extent deemed excessive by certified valuators in commercial custom.
column11: Per 4/1, Ghabn arises where the price exceeds experts' highest estimate, to a degree certified valuators deem excessive by custom.

column5: The investment manager is not liable for opportunity cost in cases of misconduct because it is non-existing and unrealized money (Mal); realized profit, however, is deemed and treated as capital.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 7/1, opportunity cost is unrealized Mal, whereas realized profit is treated as capital.

column5: The Institution can postpone Zakah on its outstanding (collectible) debts until full or partial collection. On collection:
column6: No Zakah is due for the past period.
column7: The Institution pays Zakah for the current year only, at the rate applicable at collection.
column8: The Institution has to pay Zakah for the whole past period.
column9: The Institution has to pay Zakah for one year only.
column11: Per 5/3/2, Zakah on outstanding debts may be postponed until collection, and on collection is paid for the whole past period.

column5: Borrowing for the Waqf is not allowed for spending on the beneficiaries, because:
column6: Borrowing for the beneficiaries would be a loan that yields a benefit to the lender, since it is repaid from the Waqf income, and every loan that yields a benefit is Riba and is prohibited.
column7: The debt would fall on the Waqf superintendent personally.
column8: Borrowing is meant to safeguard the Waqf against the harm of being useless, whereas refraining from payment to beneficiaries when there is no income does not involve such harm.
column9: The beneficiaries do not own the Waqf asset, and therefore the Waqf cannot be indebted for amounts spent on them, as the Waqf is not capable of owing any debt.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, borrowing protects the Waqf from becoming useless; withholding payments to beneficiaries when there is no income involves no such harm.

column5: If the participant refrains from or delays payment of his contribution:
column6: The company may impose a late payment penalty and credit it to the income of the insurance fund.
column7: The contract terminates automatically, without notice.
column8: The company has the right to terminate the contract or pursue legal enforcement of payment.
column9: The company must continue the coverage, since contributions are donations.
column11: Per 8/2, the company may terminate the contract or pursue legal enforcement of payment.

column5: Salam is permitted for land, buildings and trees, provided their specifications are drawn up accurately.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/3, Salam is not permitted for things the seller cannot be held responsible for, such as land, buildings or trees.

column5: In Murabahah, it is impermissible for the Institution to purchase the item from:
column6: A party in which the customer holds a minority shareholding of less than 50%.
column7: The customer himself, and then sell it back to him through a Murabahah transaction.
column8: A supplier who is the customer's brother, absolutely and without exception.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/2/3, the seller must be a third party other than the customer or his agent; buying from him and reselling to him is tantamount to 'Inah.

column5: For the Institutions in which investment accounts are invested:
column6: Such accounts are a liability of the Institution, which must therefore pay Zakah on their balances and profits on behalf of the account holders, as part of its cash assets.
column7: An account of this type represents a trust (Amanah) rather than a liability, and these Institutions should pay Zakah only on their share of the profits or their commissions, as part of their cash assets.
column8: The Institution pays Zakah on the full balances of these accounts, then recovers it from the account holders at the end of the year.
column9: The Institution pays no Zakah at all on any amount related to these accounts.
column11: Per 5/1/3/2(a), investment accounts are a trust for the investing Institution, which pays Zakah only on its profit share or commissions.

column5: The institution may ask the client who pledges to hire its services to pay a specific amount as a guarantee for his seriousness. In case of withdrawal from the part of the client:
column6: The deduction from this guarantee amount should not exceed the actual harm caused to the institution.
column7: The guarantee amount must be returned to the client in full.
column8: The institution may deduct from the guarantee amount the profit it expected to earn from the hiring.
column9: The whole guarantee amount is forfeited to the institution.
column11: Per 3/2, on the client's withdrawal the deduction from the guarantee amount should not exceed the actual harm caused to the institution.

column5: It is not a condition in Ju'alah that the worker be specified; therefore, Ju'alah is concluded by the issuance of an offer directed at the general public, and acceptance of the offer is not stipulated as a condition.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1 and 5/2, the offer may be to the public and acceptance is not a condition.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: ………… is the right of a buyer to revoke a contract due to deception by the seller or a colluding party, inaccurately describing the sale item so that the buyer purchases it at a price higher than the market price:
column6: Khiyar al-Shart (stipulated option).
column7: Khiyar al-Taghrir (option to revoke on grounds of verbal deception).
column8: Khiyar al-Ghabn (option to revoke on grounds of price gouging).
column9: Khiyar al-Tadlis (option to revoke on grounds of deceptive conduct).
column11: Per 2/1, this is Khiyar al-Taghrir; Tadlis concerns deceptive conduct and Ghabn concerns excessive price.

column5: The obligatory Zakah on 40 cows (freely grazing most of the year) is:
column6: 2 Tabee'a or 2 Tabee'ah.
column7: Nothing, until the number reaches 60.
column8: Tabee'a or Tabee'ah (at 2nd year of age).
column9: Musinnah (at 3rd year of age).
column11: Per the table in 11/2, 40 to 59 cows require one Musinnah (at 3rd year of age).

column5: If the syndicated company's cash money, debts and financial rights are predominant, an Institution may dispose of its share before liquidation at the value agreed upon, without reference to the Shari'ah rulings on currency exchange and debt-related transactions.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/2, where cash, debts and financial rights predominate, the rulings on currency exchange and debts must be applied.

column5: An Istisna'a contract is permissible only for:
column6: Natural things such as animals, fruits and vegetables, provided they are subject to specification.
column7: Existing and identified capital assets, such as a particular designated factory.
column8: Raw materials that can be transformed from their natural state by a manufacturing or construction process involving labour.
column9: Items that are not subject to specification but are commonly available.
column11: Per 3/1/1, Istisna'a applies only to materials transformed by manufacture or construction involving labour.

column5: An IFI approved a credit facility limit for a trading company, valid for one year, and charged a fee of 0.5% of the limit against allocating and specifying it, payable whether or not the company uses the facility. The IFI also charged a fee for a credit study it had prepared on the company's creditworthiness, and handed the study to the company. The ruling is:
column6: Both fees are impermissible, because the facility has not yet been used.
column7: Both fees are permissible, because they were agreed upon by the two parties.
column8: The 0.5% fee is permissible because it compensates for funds kept available, whereas the fee for the credit study is impermissible because the IFI is its main beneficiary.
column9: The fee for the credit study is permissible, whereas the 0.5% fee against allocating the facility limit is impermissible.
column11: Per 5/3/1/1-2, a credit study fee is permissible as the client benefits, but commission for offering (allocating) credit facilities is impermissible.

column5: Liquidity should only be deployed using Shari'ah-compliant modes, which include:
column6: Placing liquidity in interest-bearing deposits with conventional banks, provided that the interest is purified.
column7: Subscription to purchase Shari'ah-compliant stocks, investment Sukuk or shares in investment funds.
column8: Providing overdraft facilities to customers against a commission.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/7, subscription to Shari'ah-compliant stocks, Sukuk or fund shares is a permitted mode; interest and overdrafts are prohibited (4/1).

column5: Zakah on operational fixed assets:
column6: Is not obligatory, such as on the premises and equipment of the institution, intangible assets like patents and software, and moveable assets acquired for operation such as spare parts, even if kept in warehouses.
column7: Is not obligatory on premises and equipment, but is obligatory on intangible operational assets such as patent rights, trademarks and software, at 2.5% of their book value, since they are tradable.
column8: Is obligatory at 2.5% of their book value.
column9: Is not obligatory on premises and equipment, but is obligatory on spare parts and tools kept in the warehouses, since they are moveable current assets that are not used in operation, and therefore the Zakah is due on them at 2.5% of their cost.
column11: Per 4/1, no Zakah is due on operational fixed assets, operational intangibles, or operational moveables like spare parts, even if warehoused.

column5: If the sold debt is secured by an established pledge or an established guarantee, the pledge and the guarantee transfer to the buyer along with the debt:
column6: Automatically in all cases, being accessories of the debt, whether or not the pledgor or guarantor stipulated non-assignability or the buyer asked for them.
column7: If the buyer stipulated it upon the seller, or custom admitted it, and the pledgor or guarantor has not stipulated non-assignability.
column8: In no case, since a pledge and a guarantee are personal to the original creditor and cannot be assigned even by custom.
column9: Only with the fresh consent of the pledgor or guarantor at the time of sale, even if the buyer stipulated it upon the seller.
column11: Per 7/2, the security passes by stipulation or custom, unless the pledgor or guarantor stipulated non-assignability.

column5: Excluded from the sale of the insolvent debtor's sequestered assets are:
column6: His home in all cases, even if it exceeds his requirements.
column7: Real estate assets in all cases, since a reasonable period must be allowed before selling them, even if the debts exceed their value.
column8: His tools of trade, what he needs to continue his business, and a suitable home and basic expenses for him and his dependents.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/2, tools of trade, business needs, a suitable home and basic expenses are excluded; a home exceeding his needs is sold and replaced.

column5: Special conditions in the Islamic insurance policy:
column6: May relate to periods of insurance, denial of indemnity in specific cases (as when the participant fails to notify the company about occurrence of risk on time), or charging the participant with a specific portion of the indemnity.
column7: Remain binding as long as they do not contradict the rules of Shari'ah or the prerequisites of the contract.
column8: Are not permissible, because the contract is based on donation.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 9/1, there is no Shari'ah restriction on such special conditions, and they bind unless they contradict Shari'ah or the contract.

column5: A contract of Istisna'a is binding on the contracting parties provided that certain conditions are fulfilled, which include:
column6: Specification of the type, kind, quality and quantity of the subject-matter to be produced.
column7: That the price of the subject-matter be known.
column8: That the delivery date be determined, if necessary.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/1, binding Istisna'a requires specification of type, kind, quality and quantity, a known price and, if needed, a delivery date.

column5: It is permissible to grant certain shares, in addition to being entitled to the rights attached to common shares:
column6: Procedural and administrative privileges, such as a right of vote.
column7: A priority at the date of liquidation of the company over other shareholders.
column8: A priority at the date of distribution of profit over other shareholders.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 4/1/2/14, only procedural/administrative privileges (e.g. voting) are allowed; financial priority makes them preference shares.

column5: When the price for offering a management concession is determined as a lump sum amount of money or a percentage of total income, the contract between the State and the licensee is:
column6: Ijarah.
column7: Ju'alah.
column8: Istisna'a.
column9: Mudarabah.
column11: Per 10/2/1, a lump sum or a percentage of total income makes the management concession an Ijarah.

column5: Regarding the work customarily undertaken by workers (irrigators) in similar Irrigation Partnerships:
column6: The worker is solely responsible for performing it, and it does not entitle him to any increase in his share of the crop.
column7: If the worker hires others to perform it, their wage is his sole responsibility and should not be taken from the overall crop.
column8: The worker may hire others to perform it on the account of the Irrigation Partnership.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 8/3, (a) and (b) are correct; only work customarily beyond his duties may be hired on the partnership's account.

column5: The ruling that a hiring contract which relates to a future service does not become null and void on the death of the employee is based on the fact that:
column6: In this case the service, as a debt, is considered as existent.
column7: Hiring is a binding contract that survives the death of either party in all cases.
column8: Normal practice requires the employer to tolerate such events.
column9: The heirs of the employee become entitled to the pay.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a future service is a debt and so considered existent; contracts relating to the employee in person end on his death.

column5: Regarding penalty clauses in an Istisna'a contract, it is permissible to stipulate:
column6: A penalty clause against the ultimate purchaser for default on payment, if it is fair and its amount does not exceed the actual damage suffered by the manufacturer and is agreed in the contract.
column7: A penalty clause against the manufacturer for late delivery, even if the delay is caused by force majeure, provided the amount agreed is fair to the manufacturer.
column8: A fair penalty clause stipulating an agreed amount to compensate the ultimate purchaser if the manufacturer is late in delivery, provided the delay is not caused by force majeure.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/6, a fair penalty for late delivery not due to force majeure is allowed; a penalty on the purchaser for late payment is not.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for allowing termination of a Mudarabah contract due to the death of the Mudarib is that:
column6: The heirs of the Mudarib are liable for the capital, and the contract therefore ends on the death of the Mudarib, and they must restore it from their own estate.
column7: A Mudarabah contract is similar to a contract of agency or at least includes agency, and an agency contract is terminable by the death of the agent.
column8: The capital has been lost, so the Mudarib can no longer put it to work, and the contract has lost its subject matter and the heirs cannot continue it.
column9: A Mudarabah is a binding contract that ends only by the death of either party, since the work is personal.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Mudarabah includes agency, and agency terminates on the death of the agent.

column5: The Institution should not perform Monetization for the benefit of conventional banks in any case, whether or not it discovers that such banks are going to use the liquidity for interest-based lending.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2, the prohibition applies when the Institution discovers that the conventional bank will use the liquidity for interest-based lending.

column5: When the insurance assets along with indemnities received from reinsurance companies fall short of covering indemnity commitments, the company may cover the deficit from:
column6: An interest-bearing loan debited to the account of the insurance fund.
column7: The policyholders, even if they have not undertaken to settle the deficit in the insurance policy.
column8: Project financing or Qard Hasan debited to the account of the insurance fund.
column9: The surpluses of the previous years that have already been distributed to policyholders, by recovering them without their consent.
column11: Per 10/8, a deficit may be covered by project financing or Qard Hasan to the fund, or from policyholders only if they undertook it.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Medium Gharar, such as sale of underground commodities, sets the contract null and void unless it is justified by a Shari'ah-recognizable need.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2/3, medium Gharar (between excessive and minor) does not affect the contract.

column5: On the consent of the two parties, the hiring contract can be terminated before its effectiveness.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/2 (second 8/2/3), the hiring contract can be terminated before its effectiveness on the consent of both parties.

column5: If the two rentals are of the same amount, it is permissible for the lessee to lease the asset back to its owner in the first lease period even if the first rental is deferred for one month and the second rental for two months.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4, this example is impermissible because varying the deferral leads to 'Inah.

column5: Among the causes of termination of the Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat) contract:
column6: The death of the owner of the trees.
column7: The death of the worker (irrigator), in all cases, even where his heirs are able to continue the work.
column8: Harvest and division of the crop, if the partnership was linked to the produce of a specific season.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 12/1, harvest and division end a season-linked Musaqat; the worker's death ends it only if work is non-assignable (12/3).

column5: In Shari'ah characterisation, a cheque is considered:
column6: A certificate of debt in all cases, whether or not the drawer has funds with the drawee, and the drawee is always bound to pay it.
column7: A restricted Hawalah if the drawer is a debtor to the drawee; otherwise, an unrestricted Hawalah with respect to the drawer.
column8: An agency for collection of the amount written on it, which the drawee may refuse to pay if the drawer is not his debtor.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 2/3, a cheque is a restricted Hawalah if the drawer is a debtor to the drawee, otherwise an unrestricted Hawalah.

column5: Regarding subsidies and concessions related to agriculture:
column6: Neither cash subsidies nor free-of-charge land and equipment shall be included in the Zakah base.
column7: Free-of-charge land and equipment shall be included in the Zakah base, whereas cash subsidies should not.
column8: Cash subsidies shall be included in the Zakah base as part of liquid assets, whereas free-of-charge land and equipment should not.
column9: Both cash subsidies and free-of-charge land and equipment shall be included in the Zakah base.
column11: Per 5/4/10, cash subsidies are included as liquid assets, while free-of-charge land and equipment are not.

column5: The compensation due in case of trespassing of commercial websites should comprise:
column6: A lump sum fixed in advance by the website owner in the terms and conditions of the website, whatever the actual loss.
column7: Direct financial loss and the expected loss of earnings as assessed by the offended website owner himself, without need of any proof or expert assessment.
column8: Direct financial loss as well as actual loss of earnings, and expert advice can be sought for assessment of compensation when need arises.
column9: Direct financial loss only, excluding any loss of earnings.
column11: Per 8/1/5, compensation covers direct financial loss and actual loss of earnings; expert advice may be sought for its assessment.

column5: The lessor may stipulate that the Ijarah contract be terminated if the lessee does not pay the rent or fails to pay it on time.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/2/2; its basis is that contractual stipulations are primarily valid and enforceable.

column5: In diminishing Musharakah transactions, the promise given by the institution that it will lease its share of the asset to the other co-owner and the promise given by the client to buy units of the institution's share at stipulated intervals are legally binding.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per item 5, both promises in diminishing Musharakah are legally binding.

column5: With regard to the commission for credit study:
column6: The study becomes the property of the Institution, and the client has no right to take it.
column7: The Institution is permitted to take commission for the credit study it prepares internally or through an external party.
column8: The Institution is entitled to the commission only if the study leads to acceptance of the client's request.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 5/3/1/1, the study may be internal or external; the fee is due regardless of acceptance or rejection, and the study becomes the client's property.

column5: If the worker (irrigator) is unable to work for a reason outside his control, such as an illness, he is entitled to receive a wage at the market rate for similar work for the period of time worked.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 13/2/1/1, for a reason outside his control he gets a market-rate wage for the period worked.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The requirement that the gold be sold at the market price where the exporter has utilized the amount deposited with it by the importer aims:
column6: To ensure fairness, since the conversion takes place in the absence of the depositor.
column7: To fulfil the requirement of taking possession at the inception of the contract.
column8: To avoid Gharar resulting from an unknown price.
column9: To prevent rendering the deposit into a loan that is associated with benefits.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 10/5, the market-price rule prevents the deposit becoming a loan that brings a benefit.

column5: For development of the Waqf land, the following is permissible:
column6: Selling the Waqf land to the financier with a promise to buy it back after construction of the building, provided that the repurchase price equals the sale price.
column7: Application of diminishing Musharakah, where the Waqf contributes the Waqf land as its share, and the financing partner gradually owns the land by purchasing units from the Waqf in instalments.
column8: Application of diminishing Musharakah, where the Waqf and the financing partner construct the building through joint financing (excluding the land), and the Waqf gradually owns the building.
column9: Mortgaging the Waqf land to obtain a loan for construction of the building, since the debt is for the benefit of the Waqf and its beneficiaries.
column11: Per 7/2/2, diminishing Musharakah is joint financing of the building (excluding the land), with the Waqf gradually owning the building.

column5: ………… is a person who takes up the duty of Waqf's supervision and management, developing its resources, protecting its assets and disbursing its revenues in the avenues of Waqf disposal as per the stipulation of the Waqif:
column6: The Waqf beneficiary.
column7: The investment agent.
column8: The overseer (Nāẓir).
column9: The Waqif.
column11: Per 3/1, this is the definition of the overseer (Nāẓir), also called mutawalī.

column5: If the benefit from the leased asset is impaired wholly or partially as a result of the lessee's misconduct, while the property remains under lease:
column6: The lessee is obliged to restore or repair the usufruct, and the rent for the time during which the benefit is lost is not waived.
column7: The lessor must repair the asset at his own cost, and the rent for the period of lost benefit is waived.
column8: The lessee must repair the asset, but the rent for the period of lost benefit is waived.
column9: The Ijarah contract is terminated, and the lessee is liable for the remaining rentals.
column11: Per 5/1/6, where the lessee's misconduct impairs the benefit, he must restore it and the rent for the lost period is not waived.

column5: In applying Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a to construction concession contracts:
column6: The State is al-Mustasni', the Institution is al-Sani', the licensee is a parallel Mustasni', and the price is the income from the fees or rent collected from the public for provision of the services.
column7: The Institution is al-Mustasni' and the State is al-Sani'.
column8: The licensee is al-Sani' and the price is a lump sum paid by the public in advance, while the State acts as a guarantor of the licensee's obligations to the Institution and bears the cost of any delay in delivery.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8/2, the State is al-Mustasni', the Institution al-Sani', the licensee a parallel Mustasni'; the price is the fees/rent from the public.

column5: With regard to the end of Waqf:
column6: Restricted Waqf ends only by the expiry of a specified term, and the occurrence of the restriction has no effect on its continuity, whatever its nature.
column7: Temporary Waqf ends on the expiry of its term, restricted Waqf on the occurrence of the restriction, and any Waqf, whether temporary, restricted or perpetual, ends with the total loss of the Waqf asset.
column8: Perpetual Waqf never ends, even with the total loss of the Waqf asset, since its avenue of disposal continues, and the insurance proceeds or the substitute of the asset take its place in all cases without exception.
column9: Temporary Waqf ends with the death of the Waqif, even before the expiry of its term, and the asset then reverts to his heirs.
column11: Per 11, temporary Waqf ends at expiry, restricted Waqf on the restriction, and any Waqf on total loss of the Waqf asset.

column5: The manufacturer in an Istisna'a contract is discharged from liability if:
column6: The subject-matter is delivered to the ultimate purchaser.
column7: The subject-matter is delivered to a person appointed by the ultimate purchaser.
column8: The ultimate purchaser is enabled to exercise full control over the subject-matter.
column9: In all the above-mentioned cases.
column11: Per 6/1, delivery to the purchaser or his appointee, or enabling his full control, discharges the manufacturer.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: Where the profit rate is time-bound, it is permissible to re-schedule debt obligations by increasing the profit and the total amount through extending the duration, provided that the client agrees.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per item 9, where the profit rate is time-bound, rescheduling by increasing profit or total amount through extension is impermissible.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: In temporary agency, unless the contract stipulates otherwise:
column6: The agency becomes invalid at the end of the agreed period only upon a request from either party to revoke the contract.
column7: The agent may commence new operations during the contract period even if the effects of such operations will succeed the period of the contract.
column8: The principal may not terminate the agent before the end of the agreed period.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/4/3, new operations may start within the period even if their effects run beyond it; per 4/4/1 expiry needs no request.

column5: The Zakah payer (Institution) cannot discharge its Zakah commitment by:
column6: Paying Zakah in terms of the equivalent value of the subject commodity.
column7: Relieving its debtors from their debt obligations.
column8: Paying Zakah to debtors who are Zakah recipients, who then repay their debts from it, provided there is no collusion or pre-stated condition.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 10/1, relieving debtors does not discharge Zakah; recipients may repay debts from Zakah absent collusion or condition. Payment by value is allowed (10/7).

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Suretyship (Kafalah) can involve a degree of Gharar that is not permitted in sale. Accordingly, suretyship can be:
column6: Conditional, provided that the condition does not contradict with the stipulations of the contract.
column7: For an unknown period.
column8: Related to a future obligation.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/2, suretyship may be conditional (if the condition is consistent with the contract), for an unknown period, or relate to a future obligation.

column5: A participant in Takaful against death named his son as the beneficiary. The participant was later murdered, and it was established that the son was involved in the murder. The ruling is:
column6: The son is not entitled to any compensation, as should be stipulated in the insurance policy.
column7: The son is entitled to half of the compensation, and the rest goes to the other inheritors.
column8: The son is entitled to the compensation, since he is the named beneficiary.
column9: The compensation becomes the property of the managing company.
column11: Per 6/2/1/5, the policy should stipulate that a beneficiary or inheritor involved in the murder gets no compensation.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Examples of price gouging include:
column6: Sale to a Mustarsil, i.e., a purchaser who does not negotiate the price because he trusts the seller not to overcharge him.
column7: Collusion between brokers and sellers that leads to price spikes or increases of prices above fair market levels.
column8: False branding of products using counterfeit labels to promote sales.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/3/1-4/3/2, (a) and (b) are price gouging; false branding is an example of deceptive conduct (3/3/1).

column5: The basis for the permissibility of a deferred Hawalah contract is that:
column6: It is analogous to the permissibility of a deferred guarantee contract, a right due by virtue of Hawalah being similar to a right due by virtue of a guarantee.
column7: Hawalah is not a binding contract, so it may be deferred.
column8: The transferee may waive his right to immediate payment.
column9: Hawalah is a contract of sale of debt, and deferred sales are permissible, provided the price is fixed at the time of the contract and the transferred debt is not of the same kind as the price.
column11: Per the basis, deferred Hawalah is permitted by analogy with deferred guarantee, the rights being similar.

column5: A Sharikah between two partners reached its expiry date. Partner A had contributed 600,000 and Partner B 400,000. All the assets were sold for 900,000; the liquidation expenses were 20,000 and the financial liabilities of the partnership were 80,000. The remaining assets are distributed as follows:
column6: 400,000 to each partner.
column7: 480,000 to Partner A and 320,000 to Partner B.
column8: 540,000 to Partner A and 360,000 to Partner B.
column9: 600,000 to Partner A and 200,000 to Partner B.
column11: Per 3/1/6/3, 900,000 - 20,000 - 80,000 = 800,000, shared pro rata to capital (60:40) since partners cannot recover all capital.

column5: ………… resembles letters of guarantee, with a clause that payment is conditional upon the beneficiary's (in this case the contractor's) failure to perform.
column6: Syndicated credit (partnership credit).
column7: Back-to-back credit.
column8: Confirmed credit.
column9: Standby credit (guarantee credit).
column11: Per 2/3/3, standby (guarantee) credit resembles a letter of guarantee, paid upon the contractor's failure to perform.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: All impermissible earnings acquired by the bank before conversion that need to be disposed of as per the rules of this standard:
column6: May be paid to charity gradually over a period determined by the board of directors at its discretion and approved by the general assembly of shareholders, even where prompt disposal would not lead to the collapse of the bank or its bankruptcy.
column7: Must be paid to charity immediately, even if this leads to the collapse of the bank.
column8: May be retained as a reserve to cover the losses arising from conversion.
column9: Must without delay be paid to charity, unless it is difficult, e.g. where prompt complete disposal would lead to the bank's collapse or bankruptcy, in which case implementation can reasonably be gradual.
column11: Per 10/1, disposal must be immediate unless it would cause collapse or bankruptcy, in which case it may be gradual.

column5: Arrangement, implementation and follow up of syndicated financing operations should take place under the supervision of:
column6: The Shari'ah supervisory boards of the participating Institutions, provided that no joint committee may make decisions binding to all parties, and each Institution applies its own board's decisions to its own share only.
column7: The Shari'ah supervisory board of the Institution that has the largest contribution in the syndication.
column8: The Shari'ah supervisory board of the lead manager only, whose decisions are binding to all parties.
column9: The Shari'ah supervisory boards of the participating Institutions; preferably, a joint committee of these boards could be formed and delegated to make decisions that become binding to all parties.
column11: Per 5/4, all participants' Shari'ah boards supervise; preferably a joint committee is formed whose decisions bind all parties.

column5: Examples of what may be sold and traded without considering the provisions of the sale of debt, on the basis of ongoing permissible activity, include:
column6: Shares of joint-stock companies, including Islamic banks.
column7: An entity entirely composed of debts.
column8: A portfolio of receivables separated in an account held with the Institution.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/1, shares of operating companies qualify; an all-debt entity does not, and an account-based portfolio falls under 8/3.

column5: It is permissible for an institution to accept funds based on Wakalah from conventional banks and invest them in its activities approved by its Shari'ah Supervisory Board, provided that:
column6: The institution guarantees the capital to the conventional bank.
column7: The conventional bank is a subsidiary of an Islamic financial institution.
column8: The conventional bank has among its activities Shari'ah-compliant modes of financing with proper Shari'ah supervision and Shari'ah audit.
column9: The contract is free from conditions and restrictions that are prohibited by the Shari'ah.
column11: Per 12/3/2, the condition is that the contract be free of prohibited conditions.

column5: It is impermissible to make Waqf:
column6: For the benefit of the rich.
column7: For the benefit of non-Muslims, even if the cause to be served does not involve a sin.
column8: For an impermissible purpose.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/1, Waqf may not be for an impermissible purpose; per 3/3/2, Waqf for the rich and for non-Muslims (no sin involved) is permissible.

column5: A Utilization Concession contract is an agreement between the State and a natural or legal person (Institution) according to which the latter:
column6: Becomes the owner of the land containing the minerals.
column7: Becomes the sole owner of the right of extracting and producing the minerals, water or any other object in question against a specific remuneration.
column8: Constructs a specifically defined public utility project and hands it over to the State.
column9: Is given the right of managing public utilities and providing services to the public against a specific price, and becomes the owner of the facilities constructed by him.
column11: Per 5/1, the licensee becomes the sole owner of the right of extracting and producing the resource against a specific remuneration.

column5: ………… is the spontaneous discharge of two debts that is not contingent on the request or consent of both or either party:
column6: Set-off on demand.
column7: Contractual set-off.
column8: Compulsory set-off.
column9: Waiving of obligation.
column11: Per 2/1/1, compulsory set-off is the spontaneous discharge of two debts, not contingent on either party's request or consent.

column5: The basis for permitting compensation for agency-related services in documentary credit is that the fee is in lieu of the guarantee provided by the Institution to the beneficiary.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, the fee is in lieu of services rendered as the client's agent; guarantee may not be compensated.

column5: An Institution that performs the preparatory tasks of a syndicated financing operation against commission must be the lead manager of the syndication.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/1, the Institution performing preparatory tasks against commission may or may not be a lead manager.

column5: Ahmad borrowed USD 50,000 from his colleague Khalid as a Qard for one year. Two months later, Ahmad offered Khalid the free use of his holiday villa for a week in appreciation of the loan. There was no prior practice of such hospitality between them. The ruling is:
column6: It is not permissible, because the benefit is extended during the period of the Qard for its sake, and there was no prior continuing practice between them.
column7: It is permissible, because an excess over Qard is permissible whenever it is not stipulated.
column8: It is permissible, provided that the value of the benefit does not exceed 5% of the loan amount and that the lender accepts it only after half of the period of the Qard has elapsed.
column9: It is permissible, because the benefit was not stipulated in the contract.
column11: Per 5/1, a benefit from borrower to lender during the Qard, for its sake, is prohibited absent a prior continuing practice.

column5: If more than one bank participate in the execution of a documentary credit, the accounts are settled in accordance with the terms of coverage agreed upon between the banks.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/5, coverage between participating banks follows the terms agreed among them.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The sale of non-gold articles decorated or gilded with a proportionately insignificant amount of gold, not intended per se, is subject to the Shari'ah rulings for the sale of gold.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/3/1/3, such articles are not subject to the Shari'ah rulings for the sale of gold.

column5: In a contract of sale on a deferred payment basis, the seller is entitled to stipulate that, if the buyer fails to pay the price within a certain period of time:
column6: The price shall increase in proportion to the period of delay.
column7: The seller may repossess the sold asset only by recourse to the courts, and after the buyer has been declared insolvent.
column8: The seller is entitled to revoke the contract and repossess the sold asset without recourse to the courts.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/2, the seller may stipulate revocation and repossession without recourse to the courts.

column5: Bank A owes Bank B GBP 1 million and Bank B owes Bank A USD 1.2 million; both debts are due. The two banks agree to set off the two debts at the current exchange rate, the remaining balance being paid to the party owed the larger debt. This set-off is:
column6: A permissible contractual set-off, since it does not require the two debts to be similar in kind, provided it does not result in Riba.
column7: Permissible only if it is conducted through a clearing-house, and the remaining balance is settled at the exchange rate prevailing on the day the debts arose.
column8: A compulsory set-off, since both banks are creditors and debtors simultaneously.
