column9: An impermissible set-off, since the two debts differ in kind and a contractual set-off requires debts that are similar in kind, type and maturity.
column11: Per 2/2/2-2/2/3, mutual consent permits set-off of debts differing in kind, at the current rate, with the balance payable.

column5: Where the buyer in the first Salam contract concludes a separate Parallel Salam with a third party to sell a commodity of corresponding description, he becomes the buyer in the second Salam contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/2, the buyer in the first Salam becomes the seller in the second Salam.

column5: The basis for the view that the expenses of delivering the sold commodity are borne by the seller is that delivery is obligatory on the seller by virtue of the contract, and a thing without which an obligation cannot be fulfilled is also obligatory.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 4/1/1 placing delivery expenses of the sold commodity on the seller.

column5: A contractual set-off is permissible even without the need for the two debts to be similar in kind, type, description or maturity, because:
column6: The set-off is spontaneous and not contingent on the consent of either party, whatever the nature of the debts.
column7: By agreeing to the set-off, each party relinquishes any extra privilege associated with his debt.
column8: The set-off is requested by the creditor for the superior debt, who consents to forgo the excess of the amount he is owed.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/2/3, agreeing to contractual set-off means each party relinquishes any extra privilege attached to his debt.

column5: Spending on maintenance, reparation and renovation of the Waqf assets:
column6: Should follow distribution of the Waqf income among beneficiaries, and requires a prior condition to be stipulated by the Waqif.
column7: Should be financed by borrowing, so that the beneficiaries' entitlements are not reduced.
column8: Should precede distribution of the Waqf income among beneficiaries, and does not require a prior condition to be stipulated by the Waqif.
column9: Is permissible only when the Waqif has stipulated it as a condition.
column11: Per 8/1/1, maintenance and renovation precede distribution to beneficiaries and need no prior condition by the Waqif.

column5: Among the underlying causes stated by jurists for the ruling that the buyer bears the burden of returning goods with a defect is that:
column6: The card issuer took possession of the goods on behalf of the buyer.
column7: The buyer's possession of the sold goods is a trust-based possession, and the trustee bears the costs of returning.
column8: The buyer's possession of the sold goods is a liability-based possession, not a trust-based one, and any liability-based possession bears the burden of returning.
column9: The seller is deemed a violator of religious injunctions (fāsiq) whenever the goods are defective, so the return costs are to fall on the buyer as a penalty on the seller.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/7, the buyer's possession is liability-based, so he bears the costs of returning, unlike a trust-based possession.

column5: A private or shared hiring contract which relates to the employee in person, as per normal practice, shall be terminated:
column6: On the death of the employee, or when the employee loses his entire legal competence.
column7: When, due to injury or sickness, the employee becomes unable to work anymore or for a period which is normally considered to be too long for the employer to tolerate.
column8: When the employee-institution encounters liquidation, bankruptcy, or freezing of activities.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/1/1, all three events terminate a hiring contract that relates to the employee in person.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the depositor bearing the costs of deposit and recovery in a contract of deposit (Ida') is:
column6: That the depositee is liable for the deposit in all cases.
column7: That the deposit is in reality a loan to the depositee.
column8: The principle that gains are based on the bearing of costs, since the benefit of the deposit and its return belongs to the depositor alone.
column9: Customary banking practice confirmed by a resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on the expenses of safekeeping, which are borne by the depositee.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/3, the burden falls on the one who benefits: gains are based on bearing costs, and the depositor alone benefits.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to take 'Arboun (Earnest Money) in Murabahah:
column6: Only if the Institution has not taken Hamish Jiddiyyah, in which case it may be taken at the promise stage.
column7: Upon conclusion of the Murabahah sale with the customer.
column8: During the contractual stage at which the customer has given his promise to purchase.
column9: Either at the promise stage or upon conclusion of the Murabahah sale, at the Institution's option.
column11: Per 2/5/6, 'Arboun may be taken upon conclusion of the Murabahah sale, not during the promise stage.

column5: Applying two rates of pay linked to two different periods for performing the work is impermissible, because such an arrangement leads to Gharar and Jahalah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/9 and its basis, two rates of pay are permissible as they do not lead to Gharar or Jahalah and have been approved by Fiqh scholars.

column5: The risk that constitutes the subject matter of Islamic insurance should be:
column6: One that could probably occur, that does not relate to the absolute will of the participant, and that does not encounter any Shari'ah prohibition.
column7: One that relates to the will of the participant, provided that it does not encounter any Shari'ah prohibition and that the participant has declared it in the policy.
column8: Any risk agreed upon between the participant and the company.
column9: One that is certain to occur, so that the contribution can be determined accurately.
column11: Per 7/3, the risk must be probable, not within the participant's absolute will, and free from Shari'ah prohibition.

column5: If the promisor says to the promisee: "If you buy this item from me, I will give you a gift of another specified item", fulfilling such a promise is a religious obligation and is legally binding.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/6, this benevolent promise is conditional on the promisee's purchase, which makes it legally binding.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, the Institution can even stipulate a condition that the credit study should be prepared by a third party.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the credit study is a remunerable service and the institution may stipulate that a third party prepare it.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The basis for the invalidity of a condition stipulating that the seller retains ownership in a sale contract is that:
column6: Transfer of ownership is a legal effect of the sale contract, and therefore it is not permissible for a sale to take place without it.
column7: Such a condition involves Riba.
column8: Such a condition leads to Gharar and Jahalah about the price.
column9: The seller is not permitted to retain even possession of the sold item as security against deferred instalments.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, ownership transfer is a legal effect of sale; the seller may retain possession, not ownership, as security (IIFA 51 (6/2)).

column5: Permissible security may be taken in Ijarah:
column6: To secure the rental payments.
column7: As a security against misuse or negligence on the part of the lessee.
column8: In the form of an assignment of rights over assets of the lessee held by third parties, even if such rights are a permissible life or property insurance indemnity in favour of the lessee.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/1, security of all permissible kinds may secure rent or cover misuse, including assignment of the lessee's insurance indemnity.

column5: The control that prohibits using combination of contracts as a trick for practicing Riba al-Fadl is based on the Hadith in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) instructed one of his employees to:
column6: Buy the high-quality dates on deferred payment and pay for them with low-quality dates.
column7: Exchange the low-quality dates for the high-quality dates in equal quantities, hand to hand.
column8: Exchange more low-quality dates for less high-quality dates, provided the exchange is hand to hand.
column9: Sell his low-quality dates first, and then buy the high-quality dates he wanted.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (4/2), he was told to sell the low-quality dates first and then buy the good ones in a separate deal.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Rights to trade names, trading addresses, trademarks, copyrights, inventions and patents possess recognised monetary value in contemporary business and commercial custom, and since they are recognised and protected by the Shari'ah, it is not permissible to violate them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/3/3/1, these rights have recognised monetary value and are protected by Shari'ah, so violating them is impermissible.

column5: It is permissible to secure international transactions using documentary credit, provided that the secured transactions do not violate the rules of the Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/2, documentary credit may secure international transactions that do not violate Shari'ah.

column5: Investment in shares for the sake of trading should be valued at market price, and in the absence of any market for such shares, valuation can be made by experts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/3/4/13, trading shares bear the articles-of-trade rate at market price, or expert valuation where there is no market.

column5: The expenses of conveyancing, witnessing, preparation of instruments that record a sale and the formalities of registration are borne by the buyer, and any stipulation of the parties to the contrary is not valid.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/2, these expenses are borne as stipulated by the parties; absent a stipulation, customary practice is relied upon.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Interest and other non-permissible earnings may be used by the converted bank for training its own staff, provided this is approved by its Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/2, the bank may not use such money directly or indirectly for its own benefit; training is for non-staff.

column5: To promote a prize draw, a company charges no entry fee, but participants can enter only by calling a number charged at a rate above the normal tariff. The ruling on this draw is:
column6: It is permissible, since no fee is charged directly for entering into the draw.
column7: It is impermissible, because charging a fee for entry, directly or indirectly, such as by raising phone call rates above the normal tariff, is impermissible.
column8: It is permissible, provided that the prizes offered are Shari'ah compliant.
column9: It is permissible, provided that the excess over the normal tariff is donated to charity, since no benefit then accrues to the company and the participants intend charity.
column11: Per 3/3/3/5, a fee for entering a draw is impermissible whether direct or indirect, such as call rates above the normal tariff.

column5: When the Institution has purchased an asset for a deferred price, with the intention that it will be sold on a Murabahah basis:
column6: The Institution may not sell the asset by Murabahah until it has paid the supplier in full.
column7: The Institution is obliged to disclose to the customer that the asset was purchased by it on a deferred payment basis.
column8: The Institution may sell the asset by Murabahah only on deferred payment terms matching its own deferred purchase.
column9: The Institution is not obliged to disclose the deferred purchase, since the cost of the asset is the same.
column11: Per 4/3, a deferred-price purchase must be disclosed, since Murabahah is a trust contract and a deferred price is higher.

column5: Unless failure to pay was caused by force majeure, it is permissible to stipulate that all outstanding instalments become due once the procrastinating debtor fails to pay an instalment, and:
column6: It is obligatory that this clause is implemented only after obtaining a court order and after the lapse of a reasonable period of time from the date of default.
column7: The clause is valid only if the debtor consents to it again at the time of default.
column8: It is preferable that this clause is implemented only after notifying the debtor and after the lapse of a reasonable period of time.
column9: The creditor may also increase the amount of the debt in proportion to the accelerated period.
column11: Per 2/1/6, notice and a reasonable period before applying acceleration are preferable, not obligatory.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: The owner of a cooling-off option may test the sold item:
column6: And does not thereby lose his right to revoke, except if he does so repeatedly without need or acts as owner contrary to the contract and/or custom.
column7: Only with the consent of the other party; otherwise he loses his right to revoke.
column8: But he loses his right to revoke as soon as he uses the item, since use indicates acceptance.
column9: Only if the right to test the item is expressly stipulated in the contract; otherwise testing ends his option, even if the testing is done once and for a customary period.
column11: Per 2/4/2, testing does not forfeit the option unless repeated without need or he acts as owner contrary to contract or custom.

column5: The Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Islamic insurance company:
column6: Shall be formulated for issuance of Fatawa that are binding to the company, along with establishment of an internal unit for Shari'ah monitoring and auditing.
column7: Replaces the need for an internal unit for Shari'ah monitoring and auditing, since its members attend to the day-to-day operations of the company and review every contract before it is signed.
column8: Issues non-binding recommendations to the company.
column9: Is appointed by the policyholders to manage the insurance fund.
column11: Per 5/9, an SSB issues Fatawa binding on the company, and an internal Shari'ah monitoring and audit unit is established.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Combining agency and personal guarantee in one contract at the same time (i.e. the same party acting in the capacity of an agent and as a guarantor) is:
column6: Permissible, provided that the guarantee covers the capital of the investment only and not its proceeds, and that the agent receives a separate fee for the guarantee from the principal.
column7: Not permissible, unless the agent is a related party of the principal.
column8: Permissible in paid agency, because paid agency falls under the rulings on Ijarah.
column9: Not permissible, because such a combination conflicts with the nature of the two contracts, and a guarantee by an investment agent turns the transaction into an interest-based loan.
column11: Per 5/2 (quoting SS 5, 2/2/2), the combination conflicts with the nature of both contracts and turns investment into a Riba loan.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for considering the issue prospectus as an offer and the fact of subscription as an acceptance is that:
column6: The offer must always come from the party that owns the assets to be securitized.
column7: The prospectus is approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, which makes it binding on the issuer, and an offer binding in this way must be accepted by every subscriber in the same form and at the same time.
column8: Valid contracts take place on the basis of anything that indicates consent without a particular form of expression, and it is not objectionable that an offer comes from one person and acceptance from many.
column9: Subscription is a binding promise to purchase, which is enforceable by the courts.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, contracts are valid by anything indicating consent, and an offer from one person may be accepted by many.

column5: A term in a debt contract to the effect that, if the debtor defaults on the payment of one or more instalments, some or all of the future instalments shall fall due immediately:
column6: Is permissible and becomes effective immediately upon default, without the need for any notice or lapse of a reasonable period of time, whether or not the default was caused by force majeure or unforeseeable events, since deferment is a right of the creditor.
column7: Is permissible, provided the default was not caused by unforeseeable intervening events or force majeure, but it takes effect only after the debtor has been served with a reminder notice and a reasonable period has elapsed.
column8: Is not permissible, because deferment of payment is the right of the debtor.
column9: Is permissible, even if the default was caused by force majeure, provided the debtor is notified and a reasonable period of time has elapsed, and the creditor obtains a court order.
column11: Per 5/1, acceleration is permitted absent force majeure, effective only after a reminder notice and a reasonable period.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a contract of Istisna'a to be drawn up on the basis of a Murabahah sale, e.g. by determining the price on a cost-plus basis, includes that:
column6: The Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a contracts are independent in obligations and effects, so the price of one cannot be derived from the cost under the other.
column7: The subject-matter of Murabahah must already exist and be owned, with known cost, before the sale, whereas Istisna'a is concluded before ownership and the actual cost is known only after completion of the work.
column8: Istisna'a is analogous to an Ijarah contract, in which the wage may be fixed on the basis of the cost incurred by the worker, as it is in Murabahah, and the price may therefore be revised after completion of the work.
column9: Murabahah is a trust-based contract that requires disclosure of the cost price, and a cost-plus price cannot be reconciled with the deferred payment of the price in Istisna'a.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Murabahah needs an existing, owned item of known cost; Istisna'a precedes ownership and its cost is known only later.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of trading in Salam certificates is that:
column6: The certificate represents a share in the Salam debt, in which case the certificate is subject to the rules of debt trading.
column7: The Salam capital is a deferred debt owed by the certificate holders to the issuer, and the issuer is entitled to trade it.
column8: The issuer of Salam certificates is the buyer of the Salam goods.
column9: Salam certificates represent tangible assets that cannot be divided into equal shares, and the subscribers therefore own the Salam goods before delivery.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a Salam certificate represents a share in the Salam debt, so it is subject to the rules of debt trading.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of overdrafts between institutions and their correspondents is:
column6: That the correspondents are conventional banks, to which the prohibition of Riba does not apply, so that overdraft interest charged by them may be paid by the Islamic institution in the course of mutual dealing.
column7: That it is a case of "You give me a loan and I will give you a loan", which is permissible.
column8: General need, and the benefit being mutual and not specific to the lender alone; it does not fall under the category of Qard but is a step for transacting with one who deals with you.
column9: That the overdrafts bear market interest, which is permitted by necessity.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 10/4, it rests on general need and mutual benefit, and does not resemble "lend me and I lend you".

column5: The original ruling on trading in currencies is that it is permissible, as long as there is no reason for considering the dealing prohibited or objectionable; whenever one of the Shari'ah precepts is not met, the dealing is not permissible.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, currency trading is originally permissible, and becomes impermissible when any precept is not met.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of a profit share that is disproportionate to the contribution of each party in the capital is that an individual deserves a share in profit on the basis of:
column6: The funds contributed.
column7: The work done.
column8: The risk borne.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (Hanafi and Hanbali view), profit is deserved through funds, work or risk.

column5: If the card fees were charged as an aggregate amount without differentiating between the issuance and other services, the card issuer may, upon accepting the cancellation, retain an amount of the fees on a proportionate basis for the period which elapsed from issuing the card till its cancellation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/3, undifferentiated fees may be retained pro rata for the period from issuance to cancellation.

column5: In the exchange of two dissimilar kinds of currencies, only bilateral taking of possession is required, and the amounts exchanged may be different.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, equality plus possession is required for the same kind; for different kinds only bilateral possession is required.

column5: For a Mudarabah contract to be valid, it is sufficient that the capital be partially put at the disposal of the Mudarib, or that the Mudarib have free access to the capital.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/4, the capital must be wholly or partially at the Mudarib's disposal, or he must have free access to it.

column5: A bilaterally binding promise to sell the debt to the debtor is prohibited because it is a means to achieve ribā artificially.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/2, such a bilaterally binding promise is a means to achieve ribā artificially.

column5: An Islamic bank declared one of its buildings as Waqf for financing students' scholarships, by a resolution of its board of directors. The ruling on this Waqf decision is:
column6: It is valid, since the board of directors manages the assets of the bank and acts on behalf of its shareholders.
column7: It is invalid, because a legal person cannot be a Waqif.
column8: It is valid, provided that the bank's Shari'ah Supervisory Board approves it and the bank's auditors certify the value of the building.
column9: The Waqf decision of a legal person should be made by the general assembly and not the board of directors.
column11: Per 3/2/1, the Waqif may be a legal person, but its Waqf decision should be made by the general assembly, not the board of directors.

column5: It is permissible for the seller to stipulate in the sale contract that payment be made through documentary credit; such a condition is valid and its performance is binding upon the buyer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2/1, the condition is valid and binding, being like a stipulation to provide a specific guarantor for payment.

column5: As a result of intervening contingencies (force majeure), the contract price of an Istisna'a contract:
column6: May be amended upwards only, to protect the manufacturer, whether by agreement or by judicial procedure.
column7: May be amended unilaterally by the manufacturer, provided he notifies the ultimate purchaser within a reasonable period.
column8: May be amended upwards or downwards, by agreement of the parties or by arbitration or judicial procedure.
column9: Cannot be amended, since the contract is binding and force majeure does not affect the obligations of the parties.
column11: Per 4/2/1, force majeure allows the price to be amended up or down by agreement, arbitration or judicial procedure.

column5: An agreement may be reached between the Islamic insurance company and the traditional reinsurance company to retain a portion of the premiums payable to the traditional reinsurance company. In this case, the Islamic insurance company can invest the retained funds through:
column6: Interest-bearing deposits, kept as cash reserves for ongoing risks.
column7: Qard Hasan extended to the traditional reinsurance company.
column8: Mudarabah, where the traditional reinsurance company assumes the role of the Mudarib and the Islamic insurance company the role of Rab al-Mal.
column9: Mudarabah or investment agency, where the Islamic insurance company assumes the role of the Mudarib and the traditional reinsurance company assumes the role of Rab al-Mal.
column11: Per 6/2, retained premiums may be invested by Mudarabah or investment agency, the Islamic insurer as Mudarib and the traditional reinsurer as Rab al-Mal.

column5: An IFI acting as investment agent, with the principal's consent, set aside a portion of the profit to create a profit equalisation reserve. Upon liquidation, a balance remained in the reserve. This balance:
column6: Is returned to the principal, without affecting the agent's entitlement to the fixed fee or performance incentive for the period of the reserve.
column7: Is returned to the principal, and the agent's performance incentive for that period is recalculated accordingly, with the excess refunded by the agent.
column8: Belongs to the agent as an additional performance incentive, since the reserve was set aside from the profit.
column9: Is shared equally between the principal and the agent, as both contributed to generating the profit.
column11: Per 6/6-6/7, the reserve is for the principal's benefit and its balance returns to him, without affecting the agent's fee or incentive.

column5: It is permissible for the beneficiary to treat commercial paper that is not yet due as the price for:
column6: Goods sold by description as a liability, provided they are delivered on the maturity date of the paper.
column7: Ascertained goods or usufruct, provided the goods or asset are delivered actually or legally.
column8: Currencies to be delivered on the maturity date of the paper, as agreed by the parties.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/3, it may be the price of ascertained goods or usufruct with actual or legal delivery, not goods sold by description.

column5: Assets prepared for trade are to be assessed for Zakah in terms of:
column6: Their cost or market price, whichever is less.
column7: Their book value as shown in the balance sheet at the beginning of the year.
column8: Their expected cash value (selling market value) at the time when Zakah is due.
column9: Their historical cost as recorded in the books.
column11: Per 2/1/2 and 5/2/2, trade assets are valued at expected cash (selling market) value when Zakah is due, not at the lower of cost or market.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: ………… is the right given to a neighbour or co-owner of real estate property to acquire a sold property from its buyer, with or without their consent, for the price at which it was sold:
column6: Right of lien.
column7: Shuf'ah (preemption).
column8: Right of occupancy.
column9: Tahjir.
column11: Per 7/1, Shuf'ah is the neighbour's or co-owner's right to take a sold real property from its buyer at the sale price.

column5: Even where the investment agency is binding for a specified period, it is permissible for the contract to stipulate the right of one of the parties to terminate it unilaterally in specific circumstances.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2, the contract may give one party a unilateral right to terminate in specific circumstances.

column5: It is permissible for the institution to undertake to underwrite the unsubscribed issue of Sukuk, in which case:
column6: The obligation of the underwriter is based on a non-binding promise, and the underwriter is entitled to a commission in lieu of the underwriting.
column7: The obligation of the underwriter is based on a binding promise, and the underwriter is entitled to a commission calculated as a percentage of the unsubscribed amount.
column8: The obligation of the underwriter is based on a binding promise, and the underwriter should not receive any commission in lieu of such underwriting.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/1/9, underwriting the unsubscribed issue is a binding promise, and no commission may be received in lieu of the underwriting.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Cooling-off options apply to:
column6: Non-binding contracts, such as unpaid agency and gratuitous loans, which either party may terminate at will.
column7: Binding financial contracts, such as sale, lease, debt transfer, guarantee, division of wealth and Waqf.
column8: Salam and currency exchange contracts, provided that the option period does not exceed three days from the contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/3, they apply to binding contracts, not to non-binding ones or those needing advance or spot payment (Salam, exchange).

column5: Acceptance of the Waqf is not a condition for its validity when the beneficiary is not specified, because acceptance cannot be expected in this case.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, acceptance cannot be expected from an unspecified beneficiary; a specific one may accept even implicitly by silence.

column5: An electronic message which does not indicate all the rights and commitments relating to the contract, or in which the sender reserves the right of withdrawal even after acceptance, is not considered as an offer, because:
column6: From a Shari'ah point of view, an offer should be categorically obvious and bear no other meaning.
column7: It has not been confirmed by an electronic signature of the sender, which is a condition of every offer.
column8: It has not been sent to a specific person.
column9: It constitutes an adhesion contract that must first be subject to state control, before it can be accepted by any party.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, an offer must be categorically obvious and incapable of bearing another meaning; such a message is not.

column5: In the second stage of insolvency, if the debtor refuses to pay, the creditors can petition the competent authorities to prevent the debtor from:
column6: Making donations and providing loans.
column7: Pre-paying debts that are not yet due.
column8: Travel that causes harm to the creditors without appointing a surety to ensure his attendance if required.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/2/1, 4/2/2, 4/2/5 and 4/2/7, all these measures may be sought from the competent authorities in the second stage.

column5: The ruling that a shared employee has to guarantee what he works on is based on:
column6: What has been reported about some of the Sahabah, because the shared employee does what he has been paid to do in the absence of the owner, and works for many employers rather than a particular employer.
column7: The general principle in trust-based contracts, since the shared employee holds what he works on as a trust.
column8: The fact that the contract comprises an interest for the employee since he receives the pay, and the Hadith 'No harm, and no reciprocal harm', which apply to all employees.
column9: The analogy between hiring and Salam, since the shared employee's work is a debt owed to the employer.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the shared employee's liability rests on reports from Sahabah; he works in the owner's absence and for many employers.

column5: The two parties of the arbitration have the right to impose any permissible limitation on the arbitration. Permissible limitations may include:
column6: Issuance of the verdict within a specific time limit.
column7: Issuance of the verdict in view of a certain School of Fiqh or a certain law that does not contradict the Shari'ah.
column8: Consultation with experts specified in name or by description, whose viewpoints the arbitrator is then bound to accept.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 9/5, (a) and (b) are permissible limitations; consulting named experts is also allowed, but the arbitrator is not bound by their views.

column5: Goods that have been earmarked for the buyer after concluding the sale contract, but which he has not yet possessed:
column6: Remain part of the seller's zakatable assets until delivery.
column7: Are subject to Zakah, even though the buyer has not yet possessed them.
column8: Are subject to Zakah only if the price has been paid in full.
column9: Are not subject to Zakah until the buyer possesses them.
column11: Per 5/2/5, Zakah has to be paid on goods earmarked for the buyer after concluding the contract, even if he has not yet possessed them.

column5: A contract of Istisna'a may be drawn up on the basis of a Murabahah sale by determining the price on a cost-plus basis, provided the costs are disclosed to the ultimate purchaser.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/5, an Istisna'a contract cannot be drawn up on a Murabahah (cost-plus) basis.

column5: Waqf can be declared as effective starting from a future date, as when the donor declares his property to become Waqf starting from next year.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/3, Waqf can be declared effective from a future date.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, a worker who works on usurped trees while aware of the usurpation is entitled to the prevailing wage, because he worked on a commutative basis.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 11/2 and its basis, an aware worker is a transgressor and gets nothing: "Ill-gotten sapling shall have no right therein".

column5: It is permitted to issue a card based on Qard Hasan with fees:
column6: Provided that the fees are waived in all cases.
column7: Absolutely, as its fees are against operational and banking services, such as issuance, renewal and cash withdrawal, and are therefore not linked to the loan, whatever their amount or the way they are calculated.
column8: Provided that all its fees abide by the rulings on card fees, so that fees linked to the loan, such as issuance, renewal and cash withdrawal fees, do not exceed the actual direct cost.
column9: Provided that the fees are a percentage of the amount used by the cardholder.
column11: Per 6/1/2, it is permitted provided all fees follow 5/1, i.e., loan-linked fees capped at actual direct cost.

column5: Regarding supervision of the execution of an Istisna'a contract:
column6: The additional costs of supervision must always be borne by the manufacturer, as the party responsible for conformity with the specification.
column7: The parties may appoint a technically experienced consulting firm to determine whether the subject-matter conforms to the specification and to advise on payment, delivery or acceptance.
column8: The Institution as manufacturer may appoint the ultimate purchaser as its supervising agent only through a clause within the Istisna'a contract itself, and not by an independent and separate contract of agency.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1–5/3, a consulting firm may be appointed; agency of the purchaser is by a separate contract; parties agree who bears supervision costs.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: The profit in a Murabahah contract may be stipulated as:
column6: A fixed amount added to the cost price.
column7: A percentage of the cost price.
column8: A percentage of the actual profit the customer will realise from the commodity.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/1, Murabahah profit may be a fixed amount added to cost or a percentage of the cost price.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Concession Contracts does not cover:
column6: Legal or consensual concession rights, which are subsidiary rights.
column7: Franchises.
column8: Concession contracts for the management of projects.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 1, legal or consensual concession rights and franchises are excluded; management concessions are covered (10).

column5: An IFI and a supplier entered into a binding bilateral promise under a supply agreement for the IFI to buy goods at 200. The IFI defaulted and the contract could not be concluded. To mitigate his loss, the supplier sold the goods to a third party for 170. The supplier's cost was 180. The IFI is liable to indemnify the supplier for:
column9: Nothing.
column11: Per 4/3, indemnity covers actual loss (cost 180 less 170 obtained); lost profit is opportunity cost and is excluded.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution and the applicant for documentary credit to agree on investing the cash cover of the credit:
column6: In an interest-bearing deposit, with the interest given to charity.
column7: As a loan to the Institution with a fixed return to the applicant.
column8: In accordance with Mudarabah partnership.
column9: Only in the purchase of the goods subject of the credit.
column11: Per 3/4/3, the cash cover may be invested on the basis of Mudarabah.

column5: Payment of 'Arboun (Earnest Money) is permissible in:
column6: Salam contracts, provided that the 'Arboun is credited towards the capital of Salam and the option period does not exceed three days.
column7: Currency exchange contracts, provided that the option period is specified.
column8: Istisna'a, leases of identified assets and leases of assets described for future delivery (Ijarah Mawsufah Fi al-Dhimmah).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1–3/2, 'Arboun is permissible in sales, Istisna'a and leases (identified or described), but not in Salam and currency exchange contracts.

column5: The following are requirements of the mortgaged asset, excluding:
column6: It should be a tangible asset, and may not be a debt or a cash amount.
column7: It can possibly be delivered.
column8: It should be a Shari'ah-permissible property.
column9: It should be well specified (through pointing, naming or description).
column11: Per 3/2/1-2, the asset must be permissible, specified and deliverable; tangible is the principle, but debts and cash may also be mortgaged.

column5: Institutions may charge fees for providing banking services because:
column6: The fees compensate the Institutions for the use of the customers' funds, since the Institutions invest those funds and bear the risk of loss on behalf of the customers.
column7: The fees represent a share in the profits that the customers earn from the services, as a Mudarabah partner entitled to a share of the profits on the customers' transactions.
column8: The fees constitute a remuneration which the Institutions deserve for the tasks they perform, since it is permissible in Shari'ah to get reward for tasks that result in permissible benefits to others.
column9: The fees are a remuneration for the credit that the Institutions extend to their customers, since the customers benefit from the funds of the Institutions during the period of the service, which is a permissible return for the credit.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, fees are remuneration for tasks yielding permissible benefits to others, which is permissible.

column5: An Islamic insurance company, permitted by necessity, reinsured part of its risks with a traditional reinsurance company. The traditional reinsurer offered it: (1) a reinsurance commission; (2) a share in the redistribution of its insurance surplus; and (3) a discount on the premiums. The Islamic insurance company may accept:
column6: The reinsurance commission and the premium discount only.
column7: The share in the insurance surplus and the premium discount only.
column8: All three.
column9: Only the premium discount.
column11: Per 7/2-3, commission and surplus redistributions from a traditional reinsurer are not allowed, but premium discounts may be sought.

column5: An Institution may dispose of its share in the syndicated investment to an external or internal party before liquidation, as per the contract conditions and at the value agreed upon:
column6: Only at the nominal value of its share.
column7: Only to an internal party, since disposal to an external party before liquidation is not permissible.
column8: If the physical assets and usufructs of the company exceed its cash money, debts and financial rights.
column9: If the cash money, debts and financial rights of the company exceed its physical assets and usufructs.
column11: Per 10/2, disposal at the agreed value is allowed when physical assets and usufructs exceed cash, debts and financial rights.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The fee (commission) which the institution may charge for the services of opening investment accounts has to be:
column6: A percentage of the amount deposited, charged annually, so that the fee rises with the size of the account and the period of its stay.
column7: A lump sum, preferably not exceeding the average actual cost, charged once at the time of opening the account.
column8: A lump sum amount equal to the expected profit of the first period.
column9: A lump sum amount charged monthly for maintaining the account, provided that it does not exceed the average actual cost.
column11: Per 2/2/4, the opening fee is a lump sum, preferably not above average actual cost, charged once when the account is opened.

column5: Where the Institution, by the order of the customer, debits his account and credits another account in a different currency, a delay in making the transfer:
column6: Is not allowed, because possession must be taken of the whole amount at the closing of the transaction.
column7: Is allowed, and the payee may dispose of the currency during the transfer period, since constructive possession has already taken place by the crediting of the account to the payee, even before the transfer has taken effect.
column8: Is allowed to the Institution, consistent with prevailing business practices in currency markets; however, the payee may not dispose of the currency until the transfer has taken effect.
column9: Is allowed only if the Institution guarantees to the payee the exchange rate prevailing on the day the transfer takes effect.
column11: Per 2/6/5(a), delay per market practice is allowed, but the payee may not dispose of the currency until the transfer takes effect.

column5: An IFI with surplus cash bought commodities for cash and sold them on deferred terms to Bank B, which sold them at spot to a third party. B's Murabaha debt was secured by a pledge of shares owned by B and held with the IFI, and the parties agreed that the cash dividends on the shares would be used to reduce B's debt. This arrangement is:
column6: Not permitted, since the dividends of pledged shares belong to the pledgee.
column7: Permitted only if the shares are registered in the name of the IFI.
column8: Not permitted, since the dividends must be pledged together with the principal and may not reduce the debt.
column9: Permitted, since the parties may agree that the dividends of the pledged securities be used to pay off or reduce the debtor's debt.
column11: Per 5/6/3/4 (d), the parties may agree that dividends of the pledged securities be used to pay off or reduce the debt.

column5: Subscribing to an Islamic insurance coverage as security for doubtful or bad debts is permissible, although it falls within the meaning of a guarantee, because:
column6: It is a form of mortgage of the policyholder's contributions.
column7: The instalments paid are remuneration for the guarantee, which is permitted in insurance, since the insurer bears the risk of the debtor's default and may take a fee for assuming it.
column8: The insurance company acts as a non-recourse guarantor in return for a fee, which is permitted because the fee is paid by the policyholders as a donation to the common fund.
column9: Islamic insurance is based on donation, in which Gharar is tolerable, and the guarantee is not provided in return for conditional consideration as such.
column11: Per the basis, Islamic insurance rests on donation where Gharar is tolerated, and no conditional consideration is given for the guarantee.

column5: The purpose of stating that the issuer of the covered card is not obligated to lower the financing instalments is to avoid riba al-fadl in the exchange of the cover.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Basis of 6/2/2/1, an obligation would make the instalments (the consideration) unknown; no custom of discount should arise.

column5: The capital of Salam may be in the form of:
column6: A debt owed by the seller to the buyer as a result of previous transactions.
column7: Fungible goods, such as wheat and other cereals, provided the parties make sure that they do not fall into Riba.
column8: The general usufruct of a particular asset, which is not, however, regarded as immediate receipt of the Salam capital.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/1, fungibles (avoiding Riba) may be capital; usufruct delivered is immediate receipt; a debt may not be capital (3/1/4).

column5: A seller who offers a buyer a gift by increasing the quantity of the sold goods engages in a permissible practice, as it is considered a reduction in price.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/6/1/3, a gift by increasing the quantity sold is permissible as it is considered a reduction in price.

column5: The decision to offer a credit facility and the facility agreement are considered in Shari'ah as:
column6: A complete financing contract whose Shari'ah status is that of a loan.
column7: Means of mutual understanding and exchange of non-binding promises for entering into transactions.
column8: A binding bilateral promise (Muwa'adah) on both parties.
column9: A binding promise on the Institution only, which it must honor once the client requests utilization.
column11: Per 4, the offer decision and facility agreement are non-binding promises; the status of utilization depends on the contract used.

column5: Islamic reinsurance companies should observe the Shari'ah controls on the activities of Islamic insurance companies indicated in Shari'ah Standard No. (26), with due consideration to the fact that the participants in this case are:
column6: The insurance companies.
column7: The shareholders of the Islamic reinsurance company.
column8: The traditional reinsurance companies.
column9: The individual policyholders of the insurance companies.
column11: Per 8/1, Islamic reinsurers follow the controls of Standard No. (26), bearing in mind that their participants are the insurance companies.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: To avoid the sale of the same commodity at the same time to more than one institution, it is necessary to be precise about the numbers of the title documents of the commodity, along with fixing liability on the person causing a discrepancy.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/8, precision in title document numbers and fixing liability for discrepancies is required.

column5: The superintendent of a Waqf building found that its income was insufficient to pay the wages of the employees serving the Waqf, which endangered the benefits of the Waqf. The Waqif had not stipulated any condition regarding borrowing. The superintendent:
column6: May borrow for the Waqf on permission of the legal authorities and in case of necessity, with due consideration to the ability of the Waqf to bear the debt and the sufficiency of its income for repayment.
column7: May borrow for the Waqf on permission of the legal authorities, and the debt obligation then falls on him personally rather than on the Waqf, which is then not liable for it.
column8: May mortgage the Waqf building to obtain the required loan, provided that the legal authorities permit it.
column9: May not borrow for the Waqf under any circumstances, since borrowing is permissible only in fulfillment of a condition stipulated by the Waqif and no other case justifies establishing a debt on the Waqf, even if its benefits are endangered.
column11: Per 5/3/6, borrowing is allowed with authorities' permission, in necessity, and within the Waqf's capacity; unpaid wages is a listed case. Mortgaging is barred.

column5: An IFI bought 100 tons of wheat by Salam. On the delivery date, the market value of the wheat is 30,000. The seller offered to deliver rice instead, and the IFI is willing; no substitution was stipulated in the contract. The IFI may accept the rice:
column6: Only if rice were of the same kind as wheat, because delivery of a different commodity is permitted only within the same genus.
column7: It may not accept it, since the substitution was not stipulated in the contract and the parties may not agree to it afterwards.
column8: Whatever the market value of the rice, since the parties agree and the substitution was not stipulated in the contract.
column9: Provided the market value of the rice does not exceed 30,000 and rice is suitable as al-Muslam Fihi for the Salam capital.
column11: Per 4/2, after the due date a different-kind substitute is allowed if not pre-stipulated, suitable as Salam goods and worth no more than the wheat.

column5: Under a new Murabaha executed with an indebted customer, the customer may use the sale price of the commodity he purchased to settle the first debt, as per his choice:
column6: After one working day following receipt or deposit of the sale price.
column7: After three working days following his receipt of the sale price or its deposit in his account.
column8: On the same day, by automatic debit of his account upon the deposit of the sale price.
column9: Only after the maturity of the new Murabaha.
column11: Per 4/1/3/4 (c), he may choose to settle the first debt after one working day following receipt or deposit of the sale price.

column5: The Zakah year for cash and commercial assets is a lunar year (354 days). In case of adopting the solar year for cash and commercial assets, the Zakah rate becomes:
column11: Per 3/2/4, with the solar year the rate becomes 2.577% (2.5775% in a leap year, per the footnote).

column5: An IFI is considering investing in the shares of a listed telecommunications company. Its last verified financial statements show: market capitalization USD 500 million; interest-based loans USD 180 million; interest-taking deposits USD 40 million; income from interest 2% of total income. Investing in these shares is:
column6: Permissible, because the interest-taking deposits do not exceed 30% of the market capitalization.
column7: Permissible, because the prohibited income does not exceed 5% of total income.
column8: Impermissible, because the interest-based loans exceed 30% of the market capitalization.
column9: Impermissible, because the interest-taking deposits exceed 5% of the market capitalization.
column11: Per 3/4/2, loans of 180/500 = 36% exceed the 30% limit, so the exemption does not apply even though other ratios are met.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of paying the rent (Ujrah) in gold, even if the leased item is also gold, is:
column6: That the lessee can utilize the usufruct of gold while its corpus remains intact.
column7: That the gold paid as rent is in lieu of the usufruct rather than the corpus.
column8: That there is a different Illah (ratio legis) in each of the counter-values.
column9: The consensus of jurists on the permissibility of Salam when gold is one of the countervalues.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/3/3, gold paid as rent is for the usufruct, not the corpus.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: With regard to current accounts and investment accounts:
column6: The institution should guarantee full repayment of the amounts of the current accounts to their holders.
column7: The institution is not committed to guarantee investment accounts; it is only committed to distribute their profit or loss among their holders as per the ratios agreed upon.
column8: The institution may assume the commitment to pay a fixed increment on the principal amounts of current accounts, provided this is stated in the application for opening the account.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/2/2, current accounts are guaranteed with no increment (which would be usurious), while investment accounts are not guaranteed.

column5: Three parties formed a Sharikat al-'Inan. Partner A contributed 50% of the capital and stipulated in the contract that he would be a sleeping partner who does not take part in the work, and the contract allocated 60% of the profit to him. This allocation is:
column6: Permissible, because profit is distributed according to the agreement of the partners, who may stipulate any ratio they wish.
column7: Permissible, provided that Partner A bears 60% of any loss, so that profit and loss follow the same ratio.
column8: Impermissible, because profit must always be proportionate to the contribution to the capital, whatever the work done by the partner in the business.
column9: Impermissible, because the additional percentage of profit over the percentage of contribution may not be in favour of a sleeping partner.
column11: Per 3/1/5/3, a partner who stipulated being sleeping cannot get profit above his capital share; disproportion is otherwise allowed.

column5: An IFI sold an identified piece of equipment to a customer, who paid 'Arboun (Earnest Money) with a 30-day option to revoke. During the option period, the IFI sold the same equipment to another party at a higher price. The ruling on the IFI's second sale is:
column6: It is subject to the rules of uncommissioned (Fodooli) disposals: if the first buyer ratifies it, he loses his option, owes the IFI the remainder of the price and receives the sale price; if not, the second sale is void.
column7: It is subject to the rules of uncommissioned (Fodooli) disposals: if the first buyer ratifies it, he retains his option and is entitled to recover his 'Arboun from the IFI, while the sale price is paid to the IFI; if he does not ratify it, the second sale remains valid.
column8: It is void in all cases, and the first buyer is entitled to recover his 'Arboun with compensation.
column9: It is valid and binding, and the first contract is thereby revoked, provided the 'Arboun is returned to the first buyer.
column11: Per 9/1, the seller may not dispose of an identified item; his disposal is Fodooli, and ratification by the buyer ends the buyer's option.

column5: With regard to the compensations and commissions presented to Islamic insurance companies by traditional reinsurance companies, the Islamic insurance company:
column6: May receive reinsurance commission from the traditional reinsurance company.
column7: May accept redistributions of insurance surplus forwarded by the traditional reinsurance company.
column8: May receive the amounts of the insurance coverage from the traditional reinsurance company.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 7/1-3, coverage amounts may be received, but reinsurance commission and surplus redistributions from traditional reinsurers may not.

column5: In a Sharikah contract, with respect to a partner who contributes in managing the Sharikah funds or provides some form of other services, such as accounting:
column6: It is not permitted to specify a fixed remuneration for him in the Sharikah contract, but he may be given a greater share of profit than his share in the capital alone would entitle him to.
column7: It is permitted to specify for him in the Sharikah contract both a fixed remuneration and a share of profit, provided the total does not exceed one-third of the profit.
column8: It is not permitted to give him a share of profit greater than his share in the partnership capital, since profit must follow capital contribution.
column9: It is permitted to specify for him a fixed remuneration in the Sharikah contract, to be included in the expenses of the Sharikah, provided it is reasonable and customary in the same trade and approved by all partners.
column11: Per 3/1/3/4, no fixed remuneration may be specified for a managing partner, but he may be given a larger profit share.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The standard on Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank does not cover:
column6: The treatment of the prohibited assets in the possession of the bank before conversion and the ways of disposing of them.
column7: Activities of the converting bank that are naturally permissible or the profit made by permissible means, and activities of Islamic windows or departments in conventional banks.
column8: The treatment of the receivables and liabilities realized by the bank prior to the conversion, whether or not they are received or paid, and the treatment of impermissible profits realised during the period of conversion.
column9: The effect of conversion on the methods used to solicit and receive deposits and to invest them.
column11: Per the scope (1), naturally permissible activities and profits, and Islamic windows of conventional banks, are excluded.

column5: Trading in and redemption of investment Sukuk that represent common ownership of tangible assets, usufructs or services is permissible:
column6: After closing subscription only, even before the allotment of the Sukuk.
column7: After closing subscription, allotment of Sukuk and commencement of activity.
column8: Only on the date of maturity.
column9: Immediately upon publication of the prospectus.
column11: Per 5/2/1, such Sukuk may be traded and redeemed after closing subscription, allotment and commencement of activity.

column5: Murabahah is analogous to the form of sale called Tawliyyah, which means selling at the purchasing price plus a defined profit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, Tawliyyah is selling at the purchasing price without making profit.

column5: When the lessor's promise to sell the leased asset in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek is fulfilled:
column6: Ownership is automatically transferred upon payment of the last rental instalment, without any contract.
column7: Ownership is automatically transferred by virtue of the original promise document.
column8: The sale contract signed together with the Ijarah contract becomes effective.
column9: A new contract must be drawn up, since ownership is not automatically transferred by virtue of the original promise document.
column11: Per 8/3, transfer by sale or gift requires a new contract when the promise is fulfilled; the promise itself does not transfer ownership.

column5: The ultimate purchaser may oblige the manufacturer to introduce modifications and changes to the subject-matter of an Istisna'a contract without the manufacturer's consent, provided the price is adjusted accordingly.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/2, the ultimate purchaser cannot oblige the manufacturer to make changes without his consent.

column5: The basis for the permissibility of a share being in a person's name, to his order or for bearer is that the Lawgiver wishes to establish rights through writing and other forms, but He has not determined a particular form for this.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 2/8.

column5: ………… refers to the act of an authorized party granting another party the right of utilizing, constructing or managing a project for agreed upon consideration:
column6: Concession.
column7: Ju'alah.
column8: Istisna'a.
column9: Franchise.
column11: Per 2, concession is an authorized party's grant to another of the right to utilize, construct or manage a project for consideration.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of mortgaging the shares of corporations is:
column6: The established principle that a thing can be mortgaged if its sale is permissible.
column7: The Hadith of Ibn Umar on the sale of a slave who has wealth.
column8: The principle that the secondary is subservient.
column9: General need and removal of hardship, which permit the mortgaging of any asset whose sale is otherwise prohibited.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/10, what may be sold may be mortgaged; since shares may be sold, they may be mortgaged.

column5: Constructive possession of movables by relinquishment takes place:
column6: Only in things that are acquired by hand in practice.
column7: Only in things in which delivery is stipulated through one of the customary units of measure (cubic measure, weight or linear measure), but not in commodities sold by estimate or acquired by hand in practice.
column8: Irrespective of the thing being one acquired by hand in practice, one delivered through a customary unit of measure, or a commodity to which these measures are not applied, as in sale by estimate.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/3, relinquishment constitutes constructive possession whatever the kind of movable, including sale by estimate.

column5: The basis for permitting trading in shares of corporations that include cash and debts, without regard for the rules of Sarf and dealing in debts, is that such assets are deemed secondary, and in secondary things matters that are not normally overlooked are overlooked.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 3/19 (the secondary is subservient).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of stipulating that a defaulting debtor is obliged to donate a sum of money, to be spent by the Institution on charitable causes, is that:
column6: The Institution is entitled to compensation for the damage inflicted on it by the debtor.
column7: It is a form of settlement between the creditor and the debtor endorsed in the case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b.
column8: It is an instance of the commitment to make a donation, which is well established in the Maliki school of law.
column9: It is a form of 'Arboun to secure performance.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is a commitment to make a donation, well established in the Maliki school (Ibn Nafi', Ibn Dinar).

column5: A customer bought gold jewellery from a jeweller and paid with an ordinary personal cheque payable on sight, which is neither a banker's cheque nor a certified cheque, and the gold was delivered to him. This transaction is:
column6: Permitted, because the cheque is payable on sight, and the jeweller can obtain its amount from the bank at any time on presentation, which is equivalent to possession of the gold's price.
column7: Not permitted, because receipt of such a cheque is not constructive possession of its amount, and possession is stipulated in the purchase of gold.
column8: Permitted, because a cheque is a Hawalah, and Hawalah is equivalent to possession of the amount transferred to the payee at once.
column9: Permitted, provided the jeweller deposits the cheque in his account on the same day and the bank credits it without delay to him.
column11: Per 7/2, an uncertified cheque is not constructive possession and may not be used where possession is required, e.g. buying gold.

column5: Assigning the role of the Musharakah lead manager of a syndication to a conventional bank is:
column6: Permissible absolutely, since conventional banks may participate in syndicated financing.
column7: Permissible only if the conventional bank initiates the mechanisms and conditions of operation management jointly with Islamic financial Institutions.
column8: Acceptable only if the contracts, projects financed and the modes of financing are all Shari'ah-compliant.
column9: Not permissible, because the syndication should be led by an Islamic financial Institution.
column11: Per 5/3, a conventional bank may lead, alone or with IFIs, only if contracts, projects and modes of financing are all Shari'ah-compliant.

column5: In case of stealing money or confidential data from a protected website, the owner of the site is by no means chargeable for such act, provided that:
column6: The person who committed the theft directly has been identified and charged, even if the owner did not take measures to protect his site.
column7: He has taken all possible measures to protect his site, and has not pledged to shoulder such responsibility under all circumstances.
column8: The clients whose money or data was stolen had agreed in advance to bear such risk, in the terms of the website.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 8/1/7, the site owner is not liable if he took all possible protective measures and did not pledge to bear such responsibility in all cases.

column5: It is permissible for an institution to have the status of a worker in Ju'alah and to contract out the work through another Ju'alah in the nature of a parallel Ju'alah:
column6: Provided that the two Ju'alahs are linked so that the second depends on the outcome of the first, and the institution bears no risk.
column7: Only if the offeror in the first Ju'alah is another institution and not an individual or a company.
column8: Even if it is stipulated that the institution will carry out the work itself, since the two Ju'alahs are independent of each other.
column9: Unless it is stipulated that the institution will carry out the work itself, and provided the two Ju'alahs are not linked.
column11: Per 9/1, a parallel Ju'alah is allowed unless personal performance is stipulated, and the two Ju'alahs must not be linked.

column5: It is permissible to deal in the forward currency market if the purpose is hedging to avoid a loss of profit on a particular transaction effected in a currency whose value is expected to decline.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/3, dealing in the forward currency market is prohibited even if the purpose is hedging.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a partner to promise to buy the share of the other partner in a Musharakah on a Murabahah basis is that:
column6: This falls under the heading of sale of debt, which is prohibited by Shari'ah.
column7: This amounts to a sale and buy-back ('Inah) between the two partners.
column8: This involves a commitment fee in exchange for the right to contract.
column9: This will lead to the buyer guaranteeing the share of the other partner, which is Riba.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, such a promise makes the buyer guarantee the other partner's share, which is Riba.

column5: Permissibility of freezing the balances of current accounts and the like as mortgages is based on the fact that this is similar to mortgaging assets which are previously held under the guarantee of the mortgagee, which is permissible.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, freezing current account balances resembles mortgaging assets already held under the mortgagee's guarantee.

column5: When the Waqf superintendent or the Waqf partner asks for the division of an indivisible common Waqf property:
column6: The request should be rejected, since Waqf property cannot be sold.
column7: The refraining party should be forced to accept selling, and the sale proceeds should be distributed among the beneficiaries.
column8: The refraining party should be forced to accept selling, and the income obtained from selling should be used for purchasing a Waqf property of the same kind.
column9: The refraining party should be forced to accept division.
column11: Per 3/4/4/2, for an indivisible Waqf the refraining party is forced to sell and the proceeds buy a like Waqf property; forced division applies if divisible.

column5: It is not permissible for the employer to agree with the employee that the latter's pay be determined as a percentage of the output (e.g., 10% of the output), due to ignorance (Jahalah) of the pay.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/6, the pay can be a percentage of the output or a part of the thing made; the basis says such a share is known and leads to no dispute.

column5: The permissibility of syndicated financing is derived from:
column6: Qard, since the participating Institutions lend jointly to the customer.
column7: Kafalah, since the participating Institutions guarantee each other.
column8: Wakalah only, since the lead manager is always an agent of the other Institutions.
column9: Musharakah, which encounters no Shari'ah restriction.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the permissibility of syndicated financing is derived from Musharakah.

column5: The original principle is that all documents and contracts concerned with the execution of the sale of the item must be in the name of the customer, since he is the purchase orderer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/6, they must be in the Institution's name, unless the customer acts as its agent in acquiring the item.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, the stipulation of the penalty clause is permissible only for:
column6: Obligations arising from sale contracts on deferred payment.
column7: The obligations of the guarantor.
column8: Non-financial obligations.
column9: Financial obligations.
column11: Per the basis, penalty clauses are permissible only for non-financial obligations; any increase on a debt is Riba.

column5: The overseer is barred from:
column6: Lending the Waqf asset for no consideration to a party other than the Waqf beneficiary, in which case he shall be liable for the fair rent.
column7: Leasing the Waqf asset to an unrelated third party at the fair rent, even for a term suited to the nature of the asset.
column8: Collecting the Waqf revenues and settling the liabilities of the Waqf, including the remuneration of the overseer and the maintenance expenses.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/8/4, lending the Waqf to a non-beneficiary is barred and the overseer owes the fair rent; leasing and collecting revenue are permitted duties.

column5: The transfer by the owner of the ownership of leased assets to an investor, so that the investor takes his place in the ownership and in the entitlement to the rent, is prohibited in the same way as re-leasing an asset already leased out.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, such a transfer of ownership is expressly distinguished from the prohibited re-leasing.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The option to revoke due to defect requires that both the buyer and the seller be unaware of the hidden defect at the time of contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2/3, the buyer must be unaware of the defect, irrespective of the seller's awareness of it at the time of contract.

column5: Regarding the specification of al-Muslam Fihi:
column6: It is sufficient if the specification is explained in a manner that removes uncertainty, except for minor discrepancies customarily ignored and not regarded as grounds for dispute.
column7: The reference for determining the descriptions that identify al-Muslam Fihi is the seller's own discretion, since he alone bears responsibility for the conformity of the goods to the specification.
column8: The specification must be so precise that no discrepancy whatsoever is tolerated, even where customarily ignored, so that no dispute can ever arise between the parties.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2/5–3/2/6, specification must remove uncertainty, minor customary discrepancies aside; descriptions follow custom and experts.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Selling a good for one thousand pounds in cash or two thousand on deferred payment, without concluding any of the two deals, is:
column6: Permissible, since the price is known in each of the two alternatives.
column7: Bay' al-Thunya, which is permissible only if the retained part is specified.
column8: Combining two sales in one sale (Bay'atayn fi Bay'ah), which nullifies the contract.
column9: Bay' al-Istijrar, which involves forgivable Gharar in the price.
column11: Per 5/1/1, this is combining two sales in one sale, a form of Gharar in the form of the contract that nullifies it.

column5: It is permissible to issue Sukuk on a short-term, medium-term or long-term basis in accordance with the principles of the Shari'ah; however, Sukuk may not be issued without specifying a period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/1/10, Sukuk may also be issued without specifying a period, depending on the nature of the underlying contract.

column5: Combining two contracts for the same contract value, even if the two contracts differ with regard to Shari'ah status and rulings, is permissible according to:
column6: The Maliki Fuqaha only.
column7: Ibn Taymiyyah only, who restricted combination to contracts having a single value.
column8: No School, since contracts differing in status may not share one value.
column9: The Hanbali and Shafi'i Fuqaha, as widely reported.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hanbali and Shafi'i Fuqaha permit it; Ibn Taymiyyah permitted combining contracts with two separate values.

column5: If there is no agreement between the parties on the Mudarib's living expenses from the Mudarabah funds:
column6: The Mudarib is entitled to a fixed percentage of the capital as living expenses.
column7: The Mudarib should take living expenses in accordance with custom and reason.
column8: The Mudarib is not entitled to any living expenses.
column9: The Mudarib may take whatever living expenses he deems appropriate.
column11: Per 9/7, absent agreement, living expenses are taken according to custom and reason, since custom acts as a condition.

column5: What remains out of the Waqf revenue, after meeting the necessary needs of the Waqf and its avenues of disposal as specified by the Waqif, shall be:
column6: Paid to the overseer as an incentive for good performance, in addition to his remuneration, since the Waqf beneficiaries have no right to it and the Waqif specified no further avenue for it.
column7: Either invested for the interest of the Waqf, or disbursed in available charitable causes similar to those stipulated by the Waqif; otherwise, in general charitable causes.
column8: Transferred to the public treasury, to be disbursed on public interests by the ruling authority, and not to charitable causes at all.
column9: Returned to the Waqif or his heirs, since the Waqf revenue beyond the avenues he specified remains his property.
column11: Per 9/4, the surplus is invested for the Waqf or given to similar charitable causes; otherwise to general charitable causes.

column5: In principle, Ijarah may be effected directly on the asset without any requirement of a preceding master agreement.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2, a master agreement is permissible but not required.

column5: If the investor has required the investment manager to adopt certain Shari'ah-compliant ways to protect the capital and the manager does not do so, he is liable for any resulting loss of capital.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/11, the manager must adopt the protective methods required by the investor, or be liable for resulting loss.

column5: If a borrowed or rented mortgage is used for repayment of the defaulted debt, the owner of the asset:
column6: Has no right of recourse, because he permitted the mortgaging of his asset, and the mortgagee sold it on his behalf.
column7: Has the right of recourse on the mortgagor for compensation, in kind if the asset is fungible, or in value if otherwise.
column8: Has the right of recourse on the mortgagor for compensation in value in all cases, whether the asset is fungible or not.
column9: Has the right of recourse on the mortgagee, who has sold his asset, for the difference between its price and its value.
column11: Per 3/2/6, the owner recovers from the mortgagor: in kind for a fungible asset, otherwise in value.

column5: If cash Waqf is invested in buying assets:
column6: These assets are owned by the overseer, and the Waqf is entitled only to their revenue.
column7: These assets become the Waqf asset instead of the cash, and they may not be sold, even if the sale is more beneficial for the Waqf, since the Waqf asset is not to be replaced.
column8: These assets become the Waqf asset, and they may be sold only after fulfilling the conditions of substitution and obtaining the approval of the relevant authorities and of the Waqf beneficiaries.
column9: These assets are deemed something other than the Waqf asset, they may be sold for a more beneficial investment for the Waqf, and the Waqf asset remains the cash amount.
column11: Per 2/4/13/3, assets bought with cash Waqf are not the Waqf asset; they may be sold for better investment, and the cash remains the Waqf asset.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: ………… is the option of a buyer to revoke or continue with the contract arising from a hidden defect that the buyer did not notice at the time of contract:
column6: The option to revoke owing to deal fragmentation.
column7: The option to revoke due to defect.
column8: The option to revoke on grounds of deceptive conduct (Khiyar al-Tadlis).
column9: The option to revoke due to breach of description.
column11: Per 2/1, this defines the option to revoke due to defect.

column5: The expenses related to the investment, such as transportation, storage, taxes, maintenance and insurance:
column6: Are paid by the agent, and their reimbursement by the principal may be deferred and made subject to the yield of the investment, provided that this is stipulated in the contract.
column7: Are borne by the principal and the agent equally, unless the contract provides otherwise.
column8: Are borne by the agent out of his fee, since they are incurred in the course of performing the agency.
column9: Are the principal's responsibility; the agent may not be required to pay them from his own funds, nor may his reimbursement be deferred or made subject to the investment yield.
column11: Per 6/2, investment expenses are the principal's; the agent bears only its own employee and equipment expenses.

column5: In property insurance, indemnity:
column6: May be received by the participant in addition to compensation from other parties for the same injury, so that he recovers more than the actual loss he has suffered, as the indemnity is a donation from the fund.
column7: Should be the insurance amount stated in the policy, whatever the actual loss.
column8: Should be confined to what has been provided for in the regulations, and may comprise subsidiary losses that can be appropriately estimated according to the actual injury.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 11/3, indemnity is confined to the regulations and may include estimable subsidiary losses; 11/1-11/2 bar the other options.
