column5: A customer instructed his broker to sell 1,000 shares of a company with a permissible activity, which he does not own, expecting prices to fall. The broker promised to lend him the shares at the time of delivery. This sale is:
column6: Not permissible, because it is a sale of shares that the seller does not own (short sale), and the broker's promise to lend them is of no consequence.
column7: Permissible, provided the customer buys the shares before the settlement date.
column8: Not permissible only if the activity of the company is impermissible.
column9: Permissible, because the broker has promised to lend the shares at the time of delivery, so the seller is able to deliver them on the settlement date.
column11: Per 3/6, a short sale of shares not owned is prohibited, and the broker's promise to lend at delivery is of no consequence.

column5: The prohibition on presenting perquisites to the owners of current accounts also applies to perquisites and incentives that are not specific to current accounts.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 10/2, perquisites and incentives that are not specific to current accounts are not governed by this rule.

column5: The Shari'ah concessions granted to implicit and subsidiary contracts are subject to clearance by the regulatory authority rather than by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Institution.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/1, the concessions are subjected to clearance by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the Institution.

column5: The standard on the Procrastinating Debtor covers:
column6: Debtors who are insolvent or bankrupt, as well as solvent debtors who delay payment, together with guarantors of such debtors, whether or not a penalty clause has been stipulated in the contract or in any other agreement.
column7: Debtors who delay payment for an established Shari'ah reason.
column8: Cases of default on the part of a solvent debtor or a solvent guarantor, and the case of a contractor or concessionaire who is late in completing work and so becomes a debtor under a penalty clause.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the scope (1), insolvent or bankrupt debtors and those delaying for a Shari'ah reason are excluded.

column5: A company leased equipment from its owner for 100 dinars payable on a spot basis. During the first lease period, the company sub-leased the same equipment back to the owner for 110 dinars payable after six months. This transaction is:
column6: Impermissible, because it leads to a contract of 'Inah by varying the rent and the duration.
column7: Permissible, because the lessee may sub-let for a rental that is the same, lower or higher, payable currently or deferred.
column8: Permissible, because a lessee may lease the asset back to its owner for a higher rental.
column9: Impermissible, because a lessee may never lease the asset back to its owner.
column11: Per 3/4, this exact pattern (100 spot, 110 deferred) is given as 'Inah; leasing back is allowed only if both rentals are spot.

column5: In a Salam contract for wheat:
column6: It is not permissible to stipulate that the wheat must be from a specific piece of land; on the delivery date the seller may present any conforming wheat, whether from his own fields or elsewhere.
column7: The seller must deliver wheat produced from his own fields; if he delivers conforming wheat purchased elsewhere, the buyer may cancel the contract and recover the capital.
column8: The buyer may reject conforming wheat if it is not produced on the seller's own fields, and the seller must then deliver wheat from his own fields on the delivery date.
column9: It is permissible to stipulate that the wheat must be from the seller's specific farm, so as to ensure its quality, provided the farm is identified in the contract and its area and expected yield are stated.
column11: Per 3/2/3, the goods may not be tied to a specific piece of land; conforming goods may come from anywhere.

column5: The lack of legal effect of the insolvent debtor's acts of sale, gift or endowment:
column6: Applies only to acts in favour of blood relatives and group entities.
column7: Also applies during the period of uncertainty that precedes the declaration of insolvency, as assessed by the competent authority.
column8: Applies only to gifts and endowments, while sales at the market price remain effective even after the declaration.
column9: Applies only from the date on which the declaration of insolvency is announced according to official procedures.
column11: Per 5/3, the lack of legal effect extends to the period of uncertainty preceding the declaration, as assessed by the competent authority.

column5: Among the essential differences between Islamic (solidarity) reinsurance and commercial reinsurance mentioned in the Shari'ah basis:
column6: In Islamic reinsurance the company is an agent of the reinsurance account, whereas in commercial reinsurance the company is a principal party who signs the contract in his own name.
column7: In Islamic reinsurance the company does not own the contributions, which are owned by the reinsurance account.
column8: In Islamic reinsurance companies the participant and the reinsurance client are in fact the same person, even if legally considered as separate personalities.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (differences b, c and h), all three statements distinguish Islamic from commercial reinsurance.

column5: The Shari'ah substitute for bonds is:
column6: Zero-coupon bonds.
column7: Preference shares.
column8: Investment Sukuk.
column9: Tamattu' shares.
column11: Per 6, investment Sukuk are the Shari'ah substitute for bonds.

column5: Bilateral contracting between two parties at different remote places using modern communication means has the same juristic consequences as execution of the contract in one and the same place.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/8/1, remote contracting by modern means has the same juristic consequences as contracting in one place.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: It is permissible for Institutions to pay membership fees, service charges and other fees to international card regulatory organizations:
column6: Absolutely, because these fees are charges for services rendered by those organizations, whether or not they include an element of interest on granted credit.
column7: So long as these do not include interest payments, even indirectly, such as increasing the service charge to cater for the granted credit.
column8: Provided these fees are a flat amount and not a percentage of transactions.
column9: Provided these organizations do not deal in credit cards that provide interest-bearing revolving credit, even if the fees are not linked to such credit.
column11: Per 4/1/2, the fees are permissible so long as they include no interest, even indirectly by raising the service charge for the credit granted.

column5: The institution which provides online access services should take all necessary precautions and measures to prevent impermissible use of the internet by the beneficiaries to whom it provides the service.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/3, the access provider must take all necessary measures to prevent beneficiaries' impermissible use of the internet.

column5: It is a condition in Hawalah that the payer be a debtor to the transferor.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/3, this is not a condition; if the payer is not the transferor's debtor, it is an unrestricted Hawalah.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Non-paid agency is permissible because it is considered a form of donation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, non-paid agency is permissible as it is considered a form of donation.

column5: Issuing tradable Sukuk based on the debt from a Salam contract is:
column6: Permitted, provided the Sukuk are traded at their nominal value.
column7: Permitted, because Salam is a form of financing of working capital.
column8: Permitted after the delivery date of al-Muslam Fihi falls due, even before possession.
column9: Not permitted, because trading in such Sukuk is a form of sale of debt.
column11: Per 7 and its basis, tradable Salam Sukuk are barred, as trading them is a sale of debt.

column5: In case of stealing money or confidential data from a protected website, the responsibility should rest with:
column6: The person who committed the theft directly; and if it is not possible, for a permissible reason, to charge him, the one who facilitated the act.
column7: The owner of the site in all cases, because the website is his private property and he controls all the transactions through it.
column8: The one who facilitated the act, in the first place, and then the person who committed the theft directly, if it is possible to charge him at all.
column9: The person who committed the theft and the one who facilitated the act, equally, whether or not it is possible to charge the former.
column11: Per 8/1/7, liability rests first with the direct thief, then, if he cannot be charged for a permissible reason, with whoever facilitated the act.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the overseer's entitlement to remuneration includes:
column6: The analogy upon the guarantor, who is entitled to a fee for his guarantee, since the overseer guarantees the Waqf assets.
column7: The analogy upon the Mudarib, who is entitled to a share of the profit, so the overseer is entitled to a share of the Waqf revenue, whatever the Waqif stipulated and whether the revenue is realized or not.
column8: What was stated in ʿUmar's (RA) Waqf deed: its administrator could eat in a reasonable and just manner and feed his friends without intending to be wealthy by it.
column9: The overseer's ownership of a share in the Waqf asset.
column11: Per the Basis of 3/9/1, ʿUmar's Waqf deed and the Ḥadīth on provision for the Prophet's wives and servants.

column5: If the Waqf that is subject to Istibdal is a real estate:
column6: It can be sold for cash in all cases, and the money kept with the Waqf superintendent until a new real estate or another asset of equal value is purchased.
column7: It should be exchanged for a real estate; when there is no risk of misuse, it can be sold for cash, and the money kept with the judiciary until a new real estate is purchased.
column8: It may be exchanged for any asset that maximizes the interest of the Waqf.
column9: It may be exchanged only with the permission of the Waqif or his heirs.
column11: Per 9/3/5, real estate Waqf is exchanged for real estate; if no risk of misuse, it may be sold for cash held by the judiciary until a new one is bought.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to hedge against the future devaluation of the currency by recourse to:
column6: Executing back to back interest free loans using different currencies without receiving or giving any extra benefit, provided these two loans are not contractually connected to each other.
column7: Where the exposure is in respect of an account payable, selling goods on credit or by Murabahah in the currency of the exposure.
column8: Dealing in the forward currency market, since the purpose is hedging and not speculation.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/4/1 and 2/4/2, (a) and (b) are permitted hedging methods; per 2/3 the forward market is prohibited even for hedging.

column5: It is not permitted to start the allocation of profit between the partners in a Sharikah unless:
column6: The operating costs, expenses and taxes are deducted in calculating the profit and the capital of the Sharikah is maintained intact.
column7: All the assets of the Sharikah have been actually sold, since constructive valuation is not acceptable.
column8: A profit equalisation reserve has been set aside.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/5/6, costs, expenses and taxes must be deducted and capital kept intact; constructive valuation is allowed (3/1/5/9).

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The condition that Gharar violates the contract only if it is in the primary subject matter rather than in a corollary is based on the Fiqh principle:
column6: What can be forgiven in corollaries is not so elsewhere.
column7: Any property that neither exists at present nor does its existence in the future is ensured should not be sold.
column8: Need, whether public or private, enjoys the same status of necessity.
column9: If you purchase food, do not sell it until you hold it.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the third condition rests on the Qa'idah 'What can be forgiven in corollaries is not so elsewhere' (Majallah item 45).

column5: Upon the declaration of insolvency, the debtor's undue debts:
column6: Become due, and their creditors are entitled to share the sequestered assets with the creditors of due debts.
column7: Become due, and their creditors thereby acquire a present right to demand a declaration of his insolvency.
column8: Remain deferred, and their creditors may claim only on the original due dates.
column9: Become due, but their creditors are paid only after the creditors of due debts have been paid in full.
column11: Per 5/5/1, undue debts become due and share the sequestered assets, though their creditors had no present right to demand insolvency.

column5: ………… is a lease contract signed with the aim of keeping the Waqf land in the hands of the tenant as long as he pays the normal rent for similar property as it changes according to circumstances:
column6: Haqq al-Qarar (Kardar).
column7: Istibdal.
column8: Hikr.
column9: Irsad.
column11: Per 6/3/1, this is Hikr. Haqq al-Qarar involves a lump sum (Kardar) plus below-normal rent (6/3/2).

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Options to revoke due to non-payment transfer to the heirs of the owner of the option upon his death.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4, they lapse upon the death of the owner of the option, whether seller or buyer.

column5: A mining company holding a utilization concession ceased extraction for a year without a reasonable excuse, although the contract commits it to continue utilization. The State wishes to cancel the license immediately. The correct ruling is:
column6: The license is cancelled automatically once utilization ceases, without any grace period.
column7: The State may cancel the license only after three years of non-utilization.
column8: The licensee may be given a reasonable grace period to restart and preserve utilization; otherwise, the State has the right to cancel the license.
column9: The State may not cancel the license during its period under any circumstances, even if the licensee has ceased utilization without a reasonable excuse.
column11: Per 5/6, a licensee who stops without reasonable excuse may be given a reasonable grace period; otherwise the State may cancel.

column5: In the credit card (revolving credit card), the cardholder is given a grace period to settle what he owes without interest, including the amounts of cash withdrawal.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4/3, the interest-free grace period applies in cases other than cash withdrawal.

column5: It is permissible in Shari'ah to launch commercial websites, provided that:
column6: The owner of the website obtains the approval of the state for the terms of its contracts before launching it, and registers the site with the Shari'ah Supervisory Board of the institution and the central bank.
column7: Such sites do not involve any impermissible act, such as promotion of impermissible goods and services, or use of impermissible means to promote permissible ones.
column8: Access to the site is restricted to the existing clients of the institution, who have signed a framework agreement.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 2/1, the only proviso is that the site involves no impermissible act, such as promoting impermissible goods or using impermissible promotion means.

column5: Muwata`ah for obtaining Shari'ah exits, which refers to tricks that do not violate Shari'ah rules, or contradict with Shari'ah objectives, or result in any harm to others, is:
column6: Permissible.
column7: Prohibited, based on the principle of Sadd al-Zara`i'.
column8: Permissible only if it is not stipulated in the contract.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 6/3/3, Muwata`ah for Shari'ah exits that breach no rule, objective or third-party interest is permissible.

column5: A customer pledged his land to the IFI as security for a Murabahah debt. Thereafter, the customer created a Waqf over the land for an orphanage. Six months later, the IFI waived its rights in the pledge. The ruling is:
column6: The Waqf is valid, but it is not enforceable until the Murabahah debt is fully settled, despite the waiver.
column7: The Waqf is valid, and it is enforceable from the time of its creation.
column8: The Waqf is valid, and it is enforceable from the time of the waiver by the IFI.
column9: The Waqf is null and void, because a pledged asset cannot be made the subject of Waqf.
column11: Per 2/4/5/4, Waqf of a pledge is valid; once enforced (e.g., by the pledgee's waiver) its enforceability runs from the time of its creation.

column5: Unpaid interest on a debt that has arisen from interest-based borrowing should be deducted from zakatable assets, since it is a commitment of the Institution.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/2/4, unpaid interest is not deducted, because impermissible commitments cannot lead to a Shari'ah-recognizable debt.

column5: An asset may be acquired by the Institution from a party and then leased to that same party. In this case:
column6: The transaction is permissible only if the rental is paid in full in advance.
column7: The transaction is impermissible, because leasing back an asset to its seller is always a form of 'Inah.
column8: The Ijarah transaction must be stipulated as a condition of the purchase contract in order to protect the Institution.
column9: The Ijarah transaction should not be stipulated as a condition of the purchase contract by which the Institution acquires the asset.
column11: Per 3/2, sale-and-leaseback is allowed, but the Ijarah may not be made a condition of the purchase contract.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: It is permissible to buy the shares of a company that operates in the extraction of gold, provided that the relevant Shari'ah parameters are complied with.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/4, shares of gold-extraction companies may be bought subject to the relevant Shari'ah parameters.

column5: The Institution is entitled to include as a condition of the contract that, in case of the customer's refusal, after the execution of the Murabahah contract, to take delivery of the asset at the prescribed time:
column6: The Institution could sell the asset to a third party for its own account and retain any surplus over the amount due from the customer, bearing any shortfall itself, since the asset is deemed to have remained in the ownership of the Institution until delivery.
column7: The customer forfeits any part of the price he has already paid, and the asset reverts to the Institution.
column8: The Institution could revoke the contract or sell the asset to a third party on behalf of the customer and for his account, recovering the amount due and having recourse to him for any balance.
column9: The Institution could charge the customer a daily penalty for its own benefit until he takes delivery.
column11: Per 4/11, the Institution may stipulate revocation or resale for the customer's account, recovering its due and claiming any shortfall.

column5: The Waqf superintendent may mortgage the Waqf assets for a debt to be obtained for the Waqf or the beneficiaries.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/3/4, mortgaging Waqf assets for a debt for the Waqf or the beneficiaries is among what the superintendent shall not do.

column5: Among the conditions of validity of Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat):
column6: The contract may stipulate for the worker (irrigator) a lump-sum amount in lieu of a share of the produce.
column7: The contract should stipulate for each party a predetermined, defined, indivisible share of the produce.
column8: The contract may stipulate for the owner a specified quantity of the produce, with the remainder going to the worker.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/1, each party must have a predetermined, defined, indivisible (common) share of the produce.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The use of gold as capital in Musharakah, Mudharabah and Investment Wakalah is:
column6: Not permissible in any case, because gold is a Ribawi item.
column7: Permissible without valuation, since gold is a fungible item whose quantity is known by weight, and the shares of the partners are then determined by weight.
column8: Permissible, and the gold is valuated at the time of liquidation to determine the shares of the partners, provided that the valuation is agreed in writing.
column9: Permissible, provided that the gold is valuated and its monetary value in the currency of capital is determined at the contract date by mutual agreement.
column11: Per 4/1, gold may be capital if valued in the capital currency at the contract date by agreement; without valuation it is not permissible.

column5: When an institution obtains liquidity by selling commodities on a Salam basis, receiving payment up-front, and then purchasing the relevant commodities for delivery on the maturity date:
column6: It is permitted to secure a promise to sell from a third party commodity broker, to mitigate the risk of price fluctuation between sale and purchase.
column7: It is impermissible to secure any promise from a third party in connection with the commodities, since this would amount to a sale of what the institution does not own.
column8: The institution must purchase the commodities before it receives the Salam price.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/1, a promise to sell from a third-party commodity broker may be secured to mitigate price-fluctuation risk.

column5: The joint stock company performs the tasks of managing the insurance operations, including preparation of policies, collection of contributions and payment of indemnities:
column6: Necessarily free of charge, since the operation is cooperative.
column7: Against a fee determined by the company at the end of each financial year, according to the actual expenses incurred in managing the insurance operations.
column8: Against a specific fee, which should be stated in the agreement in order to obtain the participant's approval thereon by signing the contract.
column9: Against a share of the insurance surplus.
column11: Per 10/1, the company manages against a specific fee stated in the agreement so that the participant approves it by signing.

column5: Provisions relating to current assets:
column6: Are not considered as part of liabilities to be deducted from zakatable assets, since Zakah is calculable on the basis of market value.
column7: Are deducted from zakatable assets if they relate to doubtful debts or slow-moving goods, since they represent probable shortage of assets.
column8: Are deducted from zakatable assets in all cases.
column9: Are added to zakatable assets as reserves.
column11: Per 7/2/2, current asset provisions are not deducted since valuation is at market value, unless assets were valued at a book value above market value.

column5: If the client who paid Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit) at the stage of offering his binding pledge in Murabahah retreats from concluding the contract:
column6: The entire Hamish Jiddiyyah must be returned to the client without any deduction.
column7: The amount of actual harm caused to the institution shall be deducted from the Hamish Jiddiyyah.
column8: The institution may deduct from the Hamish Jiddiyyah the profit it expected to earn from the Murabahah.
column9: The institution becomes the owner of the entire Hamish Jiddiyyah, as in 'Arboun.
column11: Per 5/3/1/6, if the client retreats, only the actual harm caused to the institution is deducted from the Hamish Jiddiyyah.

column5: The Waqf property should fulfill the following condition:
column6: It shall be real estate or subordinate to real estate.
column7: It shall be known.
column8: Other persons may have a right of disposition in it at the time of establishing the Waqf, provided that the Waqif is one of its owners.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/4/1, it must be Shari'ah-accepted, known, and solely owned by the Waqif. Movables, money, shares and Sukuk may also be Waqf (3/4/3).

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: With respect to remuneration for agency, it is not permissible:
column6: To leave remuneration for agency undetermined and allow the agent to take an unspecified share from the entitlements of the principal.
column7: To define remuneration in terms of an amount of income to be known in the future, as when it is linked to an indicator quoted at the beginnings of different intervals of time.
column8: To add a certain share of the output to the specific remuneration of the agent, as a motivation.
column9: To define remuneration as a share of a specific amount of income.
column11: Per 4/2/3, leaving the fee undetermined so the agent takes an unspecified share is impermissible; the others are allowed (4/2/3, 4/2/6).

column5: It is compulsory for an investment manager, whether he is a Mudarib, an investment agent or a managing partner, in his fiduciary capacity, to exercise due diligence to protect the funds from loss, decrease or destruction; if he fails to do so using usual means of protection, he is liable.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/2, the manager must exercise due diligence and is liable if he fails to use the usual means of protection.

column5: It is permissible to buy and sell shares of corporations, on a spot or deferred basis in which delay is permissible, if the activity of the corporation is permissible:
column6: Irrespective of its being for investment (acquiring the share to profit from it) or for dealing (to benefit from the difference in prices).
column7: Only for investment, and not with the intention of benefiting from the difference in prices, since the latter amounts to speculation in shares.
column8: Only on a spot basis.
column9: Only if the shares are held for at least one financial period.
column11: Per 3/2, buying and selling permissible shares is allowed for investment or for benefiting from price differences, spot or deferred.

column5: Regarding investments in shares with the aim of retaining them (Nama'):
column6: If the company has no zakatable assets, no Zakah is due on such shares at all, even on the remaining part of the net income at the end of the year.
column7: An allocation for deterioration in the value of such share investments should be deducted from zakatable assets, in the same way as for articles of trade, at the full amount of the deterioration.
column8: If it is possible to know through the company the exact amount of zakatable assets (cash, articles of trade and repayable debts) per share, Zakah is levied on that amount.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/2/4, Zakah is on zakatable assets per share; if none, on the remaining net income. No allocation for value deterioration is deducted.

column5: If the losses of a Mudarabah are greater than its profits at the time of liquidation:
column6: The Mudarib bears the net loss in proportion to his agreed share of profit, up to the amount of the profit he has received.
column7: The Mudarib must compensate the capital provider from his own funds, since he managed the operations and the loss occurred while the funds were in his hands.
column8: The net loss is shared equally between the capital provider and the Mudarib, as partners in the Mudarabah operations.
column9: The net loss must be deducted from the capital, and the Mudarib, as a trustee, is not liable for it unless there is negligence or misconduct on his part.
column11: Per 8/7, net loss at liquidation is deducted from capital; the trustee Mudarib bears it only for negligence or misconduct.

column5: The company could manage the insurance account against a fee or free of charge because:
column6: The relationship is a Ju'alah, in which the reward is optional.
column7: The relationship is viewed as agency, which the Fuqaha unanimously approve, with or without remuneration.
column8: The management is a donation by the shareholders to the policyholders.
column9: The relationship is a Mudarabah, in which the Mudarib may waive his share of profit.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, management is agency, which the Fuqaha unanimously approve with or without remuneration.

column5: Constructive possession, in ascertained movables as well as in those established as a liability by description, takes place, after their ascertainment by one of the methods known for their ascertainment:
column6: Only by physical corporeal delivery of the thing to the person entitled to it, or by its transportation to his premises, since mere enabling him to take it is not sufficient.
column7: By relinquishing the thing for the person entitled to it, enabling him to deliver it without any obstacle, even when no transportation or transmission has taken place.
column8: Only by registration of the thing in an official register valid under the law.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/3, constructive possession of movables is by relinquishment enabling delivery without obstacle, even without transportation.

column5: ………… is a transaction where the payer is restricted to settling the amount of the transferred debt from the amount of a financial or tangible asset that belongs to the transferor and is in the possession of the payer:
column6: Transfer of right.
column7: Restricted Hawalah.
column8: Deferred Hawalah.
column9: Unrestricted Hawalah.
column11: Per 5/1/1, settlement restricted to the transferor's asset held by the payer is restricted Hawalah.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The Shari'ah basis for not applying the rulings for currency exchange (al-Sarf) where gold is not the primary asset of a commercial entity that is sold along with that gold is:
column6: The consensus of jurists (Ijma' al-Fuqaha) on the permissibility of Salam when gold is one of the countervalues, so that the sale of the entity along with gold is treated as Salam.
column7: The maxim that, in terms of ruling (Hukm), majority is tantamount to the whole.
column8: The resolution of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on the exemption of spot exchange of countervalues in gold trading by way of Istisna'a.
column9: The maxims: "A thing which is not permissible in itself, may be permissible as an accessory" and "a thing may be permissible implicitly if it is made impermissible intentionally".
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/1/2, the rule rests on the maxims on accessories and on implicit permissibility.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not entitling the ultimate purchaser (the owner of the land) to acquire ownership of incomplete building structures without giving consideration to the builder is that:
column6: The construction was initiated by the builder at the request of the ultimate purchaser, which is stronger than a mere permission to build on his land.
column7: The builder retains ownership of the land on which he built, and the purchaser holds only a right of usufruct over the structure.
column8: The Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a contracts are independent, so the failure in one does not affect the other contract at all.
column9: The penalty clause is in respect of an obligation to deliver items in the future, and the structure is therefore subject to the penalty in respect of its late delivery.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the builder built at the owner's request, which is stronger than mere permission to build on his land.

column5: Regarding the renewal of an Ijarah contract:
column6: Renewal may only be made by a new contract signed after the expiry of the original term; automatic renewal is not permissible.
column7: After the expiry of the term, the lease remains operative for any reason at the original contractual rental.
column8: Renewal may be made before the expiry of the original term, or automatically by a renewal provision, unless either party serves notice of its desire not to renew.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/2/6, renewal may be agreed before expiry or occur automatically under a renewal clause unless either party gives notice.

column5: In Islamic insurance, the insurance fund is managed by:
column6: A joint stock company that owns the contributions against its commitment to pay the insurance amount, and receives the underwriting surplus as its profit, while the policyholders retain only the right to the insurance amount.
column7: The Shari'ah Supervisory Board, which also invests the assets of the fund.
column8: The regulatory authority, on behalf of the participants.
column9: Either a selected group of policyholders, or a joint stock company that manages the insurance operations and invests the assets of the fund, against a specific fee.
column11: Per clause 2, the fund is managed by a selected group of policyholders or by a joint stock company against a specific fee.

column5: In case of foreclosure of the security provided by the lessee, the lessor may deduct from such amounts:
column6: What is due in respect of rental for previous periods.
column7: All rental instalments, including instalments not yet due and those for periods in which the lessee has not had the benefit of the leased asset.
column8: All legitimate compensations necessitated by the lessee's breach of contract.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 6/5, the lessor may deduct past-due rentals and legitimate compensation for breach, but not rentals for periods not yet enjoyed.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting gold as capital of Salam where the subject matter is not gold, silver or currency, and gold as the subject matter of Salam where the capital is not gold, silver or currency, is:
column6: That the gold paid is in lieu of the usufruct rather than the corpus.
column7: That such practices serve valid purposes and needs of the contracting parties.
column8: That gold is a valuable item of wealth (Mal Mutaqawwim) whose sale is permissible.
column9: That there is no Riba involved, owing to a different Illah (ratio legis) in each of the counter-values.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/2, no Riba arises because each counter-value has a different Illah.

column5: An IFI concluded a Murabahah sale with a customer payable over three years, stating in the contract that the profit for each year would be the LIBOR rate prevailing at the beginning of that year plus 2%. This Murabahah is:
column6: Permissible, because the profit is a percentage of the cost price plus expenses.
column7: Permissible, because LIBOR is a known indicator that may be used to determine the rate of profit, and the margin of 2% is fixed in the contract and known to both parties on signature.
column8: Impermissible, because the profit must be fixed and known on signing, and may not depend on variations determinable in the future such as a future LIBOR rate.
column9: Permissible, provided a maximum cap on the annual profit is agreed in the contract.
column11: Per 4/6, profit may not depend on a future LIBOR rate; known indicators may serve only as a comfort reference at the promise stage.

column5: Using Shari'ah-compliant instruments and processes to protect an investment from the risks of inflation or the fluctuation of exchange rates is:
column6: Permissible, as is protection from the risks of loss of capital and depreciation in value.
column7: Impermissible, because only the loss of capital may be protected against.
column8: Permissible only through Takaful obtained by the investors themselves.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/3, Shari'ah-compliant instruments may protect against loss of capital, depreciation, inflation, exchange-rate fluctuation, etc.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting a partner in an ownership partnership (Sharikat al-Mulk) to undertake to buy his partner's share at a predetermined price is:
column6: That the partner is a third party with respect to his partner's share, neither disposes of the other's share without permission, and the undertaking leads to no Shari'ah violation.
column7: That the benefit is shared by both parties, by analogy to Suftajah, so that a predetermined price is permitted as a mutual benefit.
column8: That the rent is paid in return for the usufruct and is renewable over the term, so the price of the share may be fixed in advance.
column9: That the market value reflects the profit or loss of the partnership at the time of execution, and a binding promise at that value does not shift the risk of loss from one partner to the other.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/4/3, the co-owner is an outsider to his partner's share, so a fixed-price undertaking involves no violation.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of dealing in crossed and account payee cheques, and the obligation of the payee bank to abide by the conditions stipulated for them, is:
column6: The verse on writing down debts contracted for a fixed period, since the bank's undertaking must be documented in writing.
column7: The Hadith of Ibn Abbas on the expulsion of Banu Al-Nadir.
column8: The generality of the Hadith 'Muslims abide by the conditions they stipulate', as such a condition promotes the inherent interest of the contract.
column9: The Hadith of Jabir Ibn Abdullah about Abu Qatadah undertaking to pay the debt of a deceased, since the bank thereby becomes a guarantor of the payee's right.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, these conditions are upheld by 'Muslims abide by the conditions they stipulate'.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: The option to revoke on grounds of deceptive conduct (Khiyar al-Tadlis) lapses if:
column6: The item is destroyed or consumed by the buyer before the deception is discovered, or an impediment arises preventing return.
column7: The buyer keeps the item but claims compensation for the deception from the seller within the period customarily acceptable for return.
column8: The item is destroyed or consumed by the buyer after the deception is discovered, or the buyer fails to return it despite being able to do so.
column9: The seller informs the buyer of the deception after the conclusion of the contract.
column11: Per 3/5, Tadlis lapses on destruction or consumption after discovery, or failure to return when able.

column5: When the customer has fulfilled his promise and executed the contract of Murabahah:
column6: The Institution may retain the Hamish Jiddiyyah, because it is considered as 'Arboun.
column7: The Institution must refund the Hamish Jiddiyyah to the customer, or agree that it be deducted from the price payable under the Murabahah.
column8: The Institution may deduct from the Hamish Jiddiyyah its opportunity loss for the period before execution, and refund the balance to the customer, since the Hamish Jiddiyyah secures the Institution's rights until the price is paid in full.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/5/5, Hamish Jiddiyyah must be refunded, or by agreement set off against the price; it is not 'Arboun (2/5/3).

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: If it is not possible to return an item that breaches the stipulated description, the buyer is entitled to a partial refund equal to the difference in price between an item that fulfils the description and one that does not.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/3/2, where return is impossible, the buyer gets a partial refund equal to that price difference.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: Spot contracts in international commodity sales require immediate delivery and acceptance of delivery; however, delivery and possession may take place:
column6: At any future date determined in the contract, as agreed upon by the parties and the regulations of the market.
column7: Within a week, as agreed by the parties.
column8: Only within the session of the contract, without any delay.
column9: Within the limit of a day or two days in accordance with the regulations of the market.
column11: Per 2/2/1, delivery and possession in spot contracts may take place within a day or two according to market regulations.

column5: Muwata`ah, when provided for in the contract and used for combination of contracts in contemporary applications:
column6: Is not binding, because it precedes the signing of the contract.
column7: Is binding on the customer only, since he initiates the transaction and the Institution may withdraw without any liability at any time before signing the contract.
column8: Should be observed by, and remain binding to, the parties to the contract, subject to permissible commercial and banking conventions.
column9: Is binding on the Institution only, and not on the customer.
column11: Per 7/2, Muwata`ah provided for in the contract binds the parties, subject to permissible commercial and banking conventions.

column5: On the basis of his interests, the capital provider may stipulate each of the following, excluding:
column6: That the Mudarabah operations be restricted to certain sectors, such as services or trade.
column7: That the capital provider has a right to work with the Mudarib and to be involved in selling and buying activities.
column8: That the Mudarib may only invest in a specified country or in a market of a particular country.
column9: That the Mudarib may only invest the Mudarabah funds during a particular time period.
column11: Per 9/2, time, place and sector restrictions are allowed; per 9/3, he may not stipulate a right to work with the Mudarib.

column5: Non-compliance with the principles, bases and parameters of good governance, accounting, and management in line with the prevailing practices is an example of negligence by the overseer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/7/5, such non-compliance is given as an example of the overseer's negligence.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to charge a fee for providing the required services in documentary credit:
column6: Only in the form of a lump sum, and never as a percentage of the credit amount, whatever the services provided to the client or the amount of the credit or the risk it entails.
column7: Only to the extent of the actual expenses incurred in issuing the credit, and never as a fee for services.
column8: As a percentage of the credit amount that increases with the duration of the credit, to reflect the Institution's exposure.
column9: Whether in the form of a lump sum or a certain percentage of the credit amount, provided that the duration of the credit is not considered in determining it.
column11: Per 3/3/1, the service fee may be a lump sum or a percentage of the credit, but the credit's duration may not be a factor.

column5: Muwata`ah for combining contracts is an agreement between two parties to conclude contracts and fulfill pledges in the future.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/2/1, Muwata`ah is an agreement between two parties to conclude contracts and fulfill pledges in the future.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to undertake that it will underwrite the remaining shares offered for subscription after the expiry of the offer period:
column6: Provided it receives a commission for underwriting proportionate to the number of shares underwritten.
column7: Provided the shares are underwritten at the offer value without any consideration for the underwriting per se.
column8: Provided the shares are underwritten at a discount from the offer value.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/7/1, underwriting is allowed at the offer value with no consideration for the underwriting per se.

column5: It is not permitted to make a judicial demand on a debtor in default to pay:
column6: The debt out of the proceeds of the sale of the asset mortgaged as collateral for the debt.
column7: Financial compensation, in the form either of cash or of other consideration, for a delay in settling his debt.
column8: The outstanding instalments that have become due by virtue of a stipulation accelerating the instalments.
column9: The legal and other expenses incurred by the creditor in order to recover his debt.
column11: Per 2/1/3, a judicial claim for compensation for delay is not permitted; expenses, acceleration and sale of collateral are allowed.

column5: It is permitted to create Waqf over cash:
column6: Even if it is an outstanding debt, e.g., the current account balances.
column7: Provided that it is only extended as Shari'ah compliant loans and is not invested.
column8: Provided that the cash is adjusted periodically for changes in its purchasing power.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4/13/1, cash Waqf is permitted even as a debt (e.g., current accounts), used by lending or investing; per 2/4/13/4 purchasing power has no effect.

column5: Trading in Murabahah certificates is permissible after the purchase of the Murabahah commodity has taken place and before it is sold, because the certificates then represent assets that can be traded.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2/15 and its Shari'ah basis, before sale the certificates represent tradable assets.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting participation in a corporation by one who has the ability to convert it, or who makes an effort to convert it, is that:
column6: It is a form of Mudarabah with the other shareholders.
column7: Shareholders are not responsible for the decisions of the corporation.
column8: The prohibited income of such corporations is less than 5% of their total income, which is considered negligible in the Shari'ah, and the shareholder is therefore not bound to eliminate it.
column9: It is a means to alter the rejected and belongs to the category of enjoining good and forbidding evil (al-Amr Bil-Ma'ruf Wa al-Nahy 'An al-Munkar).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/3, such participation is a means to change what is rejected, i.e. enjoining good and forbidding evil.

column5: One party selling his house to another for one thousand dinars and renting his car to the same party for one hundred dinars per month is an example of combined contracts concluded for separate values.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/2/2, this is the Standard's example of combined contracts concluded for separate values.

column5: Any growth in (increase to, and/or yield of) the sale item that is physically separate from it and occurs during the 'Arboun option period:
column6: Belongs to the seller if it occurs before delivery to the buyer, and to the buyer if it occurs after delivery, and no stipulation to the contrary is permissible in either case, since growth follows ownership.
column7: Always belongs to the buyer, since ownership passes to him upon the conclusion of the contract.
column8: Belongs to the party who is liable for the sale item, and it is not permissible to stipulate otherwise.
column9: Is in principle part of the sale item, before or after delivery, and the party liable for the sale item may stipulate that it belongs to him, even if ultimate ownership is not vested in him.
column11: Per 8/2, separate growth is in principle part of the sale item before or after delivery; the party liable for the item may stipulate it for himself.

column5: ………… is the earnest money which constitutes part of the price paid in advance in sale and lease contracts, and which is owned by the seller or the landlord when the buyer or the tenant uses his right of terminating the contract:
column6: Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit).
column7: Commitment fee.
column8: 'Arboun.
column9: Arrangement fee.
column11: Per 5/3/2/2, 'Arboun is part of the price paid in advance and is owned by the seller or landlord if the buyer or tenant terminates.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the validity of cash Waqf includes:
column6: The consensus of all the early jurists from the time of the Companions on the validity of cash Waqf, including the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools.
column7: The Shari'ah objective of Waqf is achieved in it, and money cannot be specific by identification; rather, its substitute will be in its place.
column8: Cash is the only asset that does not depreciate, so the perpetuity of the Waqf is guaranteed.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 2/4/13/1, the objective of Waqf is achieved and money's substitute takes its place; only one group of early jurists held it valid.

column5: An Ijarah contract may be executed for an asset undertaken by the lessor to be delivered to the lessee according to accurate specifications, even if the described asset is not owned by the lessor. In this case:
column6: It is not a requirement that the rental be paid in advance, as long as the lease is not executed according to the contract of Salam (or Salaf).
column7: The rental must be paid in full in advance, as in Salam.
column8: The lessee must accept the asset delivered even if it does not conform to the description, with a reduction of the rental.
column9: The lessor must own the described asset at the time of the contract.
column11: Per 3/5, advance rental is not required unless executed as Salam; a non-conforming asset may be rejected and a conforming one demanded.

column5: If the Institution replaces a contractor and enters into an Istisna'a contract with a customer to complete a project started by the customer's previous contractor:
column6: The Institution is bound to deal with the previous contractor to complete the project, and may not stipulate that the work be carried out by any other means.
column7: The project should be assessed on its existing status at the customer's cost, outstanding debts of the incomplete contract are the customer's personal responsibility, and a new Istisna'a may be concluded for the remaining work.
column8: The Institution assumes the outstanding debts arising from the incomplete Istisna'a contract, and may recover them from the customer only upon completion of the remaining work, after the previous contractor has been paid in full.
column9: The cost of assessing the project is borne by the Institution as the new contractor, which then deducts it from the price of the new Istisna'a contract.
column11: Per 4/2/2, the customer pays for the assessment and owes the old contract's debts; the Institution need not use the previous contractor.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: There is no harm in providing more information than what has been requested by the seeker of the Fatwa, in order to leave no room for confusion, or to serve a future need of the Fatwa seeker.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/5, extra information may be given to avoid confusion, distinguish the opinion or serve a future need.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: With respect to a guarantee of the sale price by the seller (agent) in international commodity sales:
column6: It is permissible to stipulate that he guarantees the sale price under all circumstances, since he chose the buyers and bears the risk of their default, and the principal bears no liability in this regard.
column7: It is prohibited to stipulate that he guarantees the sale price under all circumstances; he is obliged to provide a guarantee only in case of tort, negligence or breach of the provisions of agency.
column8: He is not obliged to provide a guarantee even in case of tort or negligence.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2/12, a guarantee of the sale price in all circumstances is prohibited; he is liable only for tort, negligence or breach of agency terms.

column5: In construction concession contracts, the licensee is entitled to collect fees or rent for provision of services to the public only in the form where the project and its usufructs become the property of the licensee for a specific period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/1/3, in all three forms of construction concession the licensee may collect fees or rent from the public.

column5: If a service partnership requires capital goods (e.g. equipment or tools), each of the following is permissible, excluding:
column6: The partners contribute funds to acquire the goods on the basis of a partnership in ownership.
column7: A party provides the capital goods in consideration for fees that will be charged against the Sharikah operation as expenses.
column8: A party provides the capital goods in consideration for a lump sum to be paid to him out of the profit of the partnership.
column9: Each party provides the goods that his services require, in which case each partner owns the goods he has provided.
column11: Per 3/3/4 the first three are allowed; per 3/3/3 the contract may not specify a lump sum from profit to a partner.

column5: The lessor may stipulate an increase in the rental due in case of delay in payment by the lessee, provided the increase does not exceed the lessor's actual damage.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/3, no increase in the rental due may be stipulated for delay in payment; this is a form of Riba.

column5: According to the majority of the Jurists from among the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, possession in things that are estimated by cubic measure, weight, linear measure and counting is attained by:
column6: Registration of the things in the name of the buyer.
column7: Relinquishment alone, without using these measures.
column8: Taking delivery through these measures accompanied by relinquishment.
column9: Physical transportation of the things to the buyer's premises.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the majority hold that such things are possessed by taking delivery through these measures accompanied by relinquishment.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Issuing Fatwa to institutions:
column6: Does not require competence in all areas of Fiqh; it can be issued by a scholar competent only in the area of financial transactions performed by institutions.
column7: Requires that the scholar adhere to the official school of Fiqh of the host country, so that the Fatwa is acceptable to the local courts and regulators.
column8: Requires competence in all areas of Fiqh.
column9: Requires that the scholar be a member of a Fiqh academy recognized by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, regardless of his specialization in financial transactions.
column11: Per 5/2, competence in all of Fiqh is not required; competence in institutions' financial transactions suffices.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for permitting debts to be incurred as a liability upon the Waqf to grow investment Waqfs is:
column6: Customs, the intention of the Waqif and the nature of function of such Waqfs.
column7: The analogy upon lending the funds of orphans.
column8: The analogy upon the pledge of tangible Waqf assets.
column9: Necessity, since the suspension of these interests would result in the suspension of the Waqf.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/2, customs, the Waqif's intention and the nature of such Waqfs; the necessity rationale is the basis of 5/1.

column5: It is not permissible for the Institution that manages the syndication as a Mudarib, partner or an agent:
column6: To guarantee the debtors of its partners.
column7: To guarantee the contributions of its partners against exchange rate fluctuations.
column8: To receive commission for preparatory tasks that exceeds the actual cost it incurs.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 8/2, the manager may not guarantee partners' debtors or their contributions against FX moves; per 7/1 the fee may exceed cost.

column5: It is permissible for the Islamic reinsurance company to provide reinsurance services to traditional insurance companies, subject to the following conditions:
column6: The contract to be used should be the Islamic reinsurance contract.
column7: There should be no linkage.
column8: Reinsurance should not involve a Shari'ah prohibited object.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 8/3, all three conditions apply: the Islamic reinsurance contract is used, there is no linkage, and no Shari'ah-prohibited object is involved.

column5: Treating a management concession as Mudarabah, with the State's entitlement being a share of the net profit after allocations, is supported by:
column6: The narration from Umar Ibn Al-Khattab on wasteland left undeveloped for three years, which shows that the capital of the managed asset reverts to the State on expiry of the contract.
column7: The Hadith: "Whom who develops a piece of wasteland shall become its owner."
column8: The view of the Hanbalis permitting Mudarabah on income-generating assets like animals, and the need to preserve the project's capital, which is the managed asset.
column9: The Maliki view that minerals are the property of Bayt al-Mal.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 10/2/1, the Hanbalis allow Mudarabah on income-generating assets; sharing net profit preserves the capital.

column5: The investment agent is permitted to appoint a sub-agent for the prescribed investment activities:
column6: For activities outside its area of expertise.
column7: For what is normally outside the capacity of the agent or its employees.
column8: Where the principal grants the agent permission to subcontract.
column9: In all the above-mentioned cases.
column11: Per 9/1, a sub-agent may be appointed in each of these three cases.

column5: Ju'alah is distinguished from Ijarah on the following grounds, excluding:
column6: Ju'alah does not require acceptance.
column7: As a rule, Ju'alah is binding, while Ijarah is terminable.
column8: Ju'alah is valid despite uncertainty of the work, deeming the determination of the required result by the offeror as sufficient.
column9: Ju'alah is valid even if the other party is not known.
column11: Per 7/5, it is the reverse: as a rule Ju'alah is terminable while Ijarah is binding; the other grounds are in 7/1, 7/2, 7/4.

column5: With respect to a partner giving out loans from the funds of a Sharikah:
column6: A partner is not entitled to give out grants or loans that damage the partnership unless all the partners have consented to such an action.
column7: A partner may give out short-term minor loans that will not, according to customary practice, affect the operation of the partnership.
column8: A partner may give out any loan he deems fit, since each partner is an agent for the remaining partners.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/3/1, grants and loans need all partners' consent, except short-term minor loans that customarily do not affect operations.

column5: It is permissible for the second buyer of the usufruct of existing and specified assets to resell them; however, he is not entitled to issue certificates in this respect.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/12, the second buyer of such usufruct may resell it and is also entitled to issue certificates in this respect.

column5: A Mudarabah contract can be liquidated:
column6: On the date of maturity, if the two parties had earlier agreed to set a time limit for it.
column7: On the death of the Mudarib or the liquidation of the institution that acts as Mudarib.
column8: When the funds of the Mudarabah contract have been exhausted or have suffered losses.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/1, all three are among the ways a Mudarabah is liquidated, along with unilateral termination and mutual agreement.

column5: In dealing with the syndication funds, the lead manager (being a Mudarib, partner or an agent):
column6: Is a guarantor of the funds if he is an agent, but a trustee if he is a Mudarib or a partner, because an agent's fee is consideration for the risk that he assumes in respect of the funds.
column7: May guarantee the funds if he receives a separate fee for the guarantee.
column8: Is considered a trustee, and therefore should not guarantee these funds except in case of misconduct, negligence or breach of the conditions of the syndication arrangement.
column9: Is a guarantor of the funds, since he exclusively manages the operation.
column11: Per 8/1, the lead manager in any capacity is a trustee and guarantees only for misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.

column5: As in commercial insurance, the insurer and the participant in Islamic insurance are totally different persons.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, in Islamic insurance the insurer and participant are in fact the same person, though differing in recognition.

column5: There is no Zakah on fixed assets which generate income, like Mustaghallat (leased assets), if such assets are not acquired for trade. Nevertheless:
column6: No Zakah is obligatory on the income of such assets.
column7: Zakah is obligatory on the gross income generated by such assets at the time of its receipt, at the rate of 10%.
column8: Zakah is obligatory, at the end of the year, on the unexpended portion of the income generated by such assets, by adding it to the other zakatable assets and applying the Zakah rate.
column9: Zakah is obligatory on the market value of such assets at the end of the year, by adding it to the other zakatable assets and applying the Zakah rate.
column11: Per 4/2, the unexpended income of such assets is added to other zakatable assets at year end and Zakah applied.

column5: In order to secure the future payment of debts on a single payment or instalment basis, it is permissible for the Institution to stipulate that it is entitled to:
column6: Freeze the customer's investment account.
column7: Revoke the customer's right to withdraw money from his investment account entirely.
column8: Block an amount in the customer's investment account equivalent to the debt, which is the preferred option.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/5/1, all three are permissible, blocking an amount equal to the debt being the preferred option.

column5: The duties of the worker (irrigator) include:
column6: Watering, pollinating, fertilising, weeding, maintaining irrigation channels, pruning, controlling pests, harvesting and the seasonal work usually required for each tree type.
column7: Carrying out, at his own expense, work that is customarily beyond the scope of his duties, as well as any other work the owner may require of him during the term of the contract.
column8: Subcontracting his work to a third party without the permission of the owner whenever he is unable to work.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/1/1, (a) lists his duties; he may not subcontract without permission (6/1/2), and extra work may be on the partnership's account (8/3).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the termination of the lease contract due to total destruction of the leased asset is that the rent is in consideration of the benefit of the leased asset, and if the latter is destroyed there is no justification for payment of the rental.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 7/1/3.

column5: An IFI sold a car to a customer by Murabahah payable in 24 monthly instalments. The contract stipulates that if the customer fails, without force majeure, to pay any instalment, all outstanding instalments become due, and that he undertakes to donate 2% of the overdue amount to charitable causes through the IFI. The customer also mortgaged a plot of land, with a mandate to the IFI to sell it without recourse to the courts. The permissible stipulations in this contract are:
column6: The acceleration of the outstanding instalments.
column7: The undertaking to donate 2% of the overdue amount to charitable causes through the IFI.
column8: The mandate to sell the mortgaged land without recourse to the courts.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1/6, 2/1/8 and 2/1/5, acceleration (absent force majeure), the charity undertaking and the sale mandate are all permissible.

column5: The revolving of endorsements of a bill of exchange, from the first beneficiary to another party and from the second beneficiary to a third party and so on, is a form of successive Hawalah which is not objectionable in Shari'ah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 12/5/3, successive endorsements are successive Hawalah and are acceptable (subject to 12/5/1).

column5: The distribution of profit in a Mudarabah must be on the basis of:
column6: A lump sum.
column7: A percentage of the capital.
column8: An agreed percentage of the profit.
column9: (a) or (b).
column11: Per 8/1, profit must be distributed by an agreed percentage of the profit, not a lump sum or a percentage of capital.

column5: With respect to the service partnership (professional or vocational partnership):
column6: It has no monetary capital, because the subject matter of the partnership is rendering services.
column7: Profit must be distributed in proportion to the services actually rendered by each partner.
column8: The contract may specify that a lump sum be paid from the profit to the partner who renders most of the services.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/2-3, it has no monetary capital; profit follows the agreed ratio and no lump sum from profit may be specified.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the obligatory ruling of insolvency and interdiction against the one who has more debts than he can pay is:
column6: The act of the Prophet (peace be upon him), who interdicted Mu'adh Ibn Jabal, sold his property for his debts and distributed it among his creditors.
column7: The Hadith: "Allah will pay (the debts of) a person who takes the wealth of others with the intention of repaying it", which encourages leniency towards debtors.
column8: The Hadith: "No harm and no reciprocal harm", since the debtor's dispositions would harm the creditors.
column9: The opinion of Abu Hanifah, which is the formal legal opinion of the Hanafis on interdiction.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is the Prophet's interdiction of Mu'adh; this is the majority view, against Abu Hanifah.

column5: The worker (irrigator) acts in a fiduciary capacity. If a loss arises from his wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of the terms of the contract:
column6: He is not liable, since he acts in a fiduciary capacity.
column7: He is liable to indemnify the owner against any actual loss caused, but remains entitled to his share of the crop.
column8: He is liable to indemnify the owner and also forfeits his share of the crop for that season.
column9: He forfeits his share of the crop, but is not liable to indemnify the owner for the loss caused.
column11: Per 6/3, he indemnifies actual loss caused by misconduct, negligence or breach, but keeps his share of the crop.

column5: In certificates of investment agency (Wakalah Sukuk):
column6: The issuer is the Mudarib, the subscribers are the owners of capital and the realised funds are the Mudarabah capital.
column7: The issuer is the investment agent, the subscribers are the principals and the realised funds are the entrusted capital of the investment.
column8: The issuer is the principal, the subscribers are the investment agents and the realised funds are the agency fee.
column9: The certificate holders do not own the assets represented by the certificates, but they are entitled to a fixed return on the entrusted capital.
column11: Per 5/1/5/8, the issuer is the investment agent, subscribers are principals; holders own the assets with benefits and risks and are entitled to profits, if any.

column5: The general basis of Sharikah is:
column6: Hire (Ijarah), because each partner is paid for his work, and the Sharikah is a lessee of the partners' services for the duration of the contract.
column7: Agency (Wakalah), because each partner acts as a principal and as an agent for the remaining partners in the interest of the partnership.
column8: Mudarabah, because one partner provides capital and the other provides work, and profit is shared between them.
column9: Guarantee (Kafalah), because each partner guarantees the obligations of the others and is liable for them in full, in proportion to his share in the capital of the Sharikah.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Sharikah rests on Wakalah: each partner is a principal and an agent for the others.

column5: The institution or the company is committed to pay Zakah directly in the following cases:
column6: Enactment of an enforceable Zakah law.
column7: Stipulation of commitment to pay Zakah in the articles of association.
column8: Issuance of a Zakah commitment resolution by the board of directors.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/2/1, the cases are a Zakah law, the articles of association, or a resolution of the general assembly, not the board of directors.

column5: Among the classifications of documentary credit:
column6: Back-to-back credit means that the credit issued is guaranteed by another credit.
column7: Revolving credit means that the beneficiary can repeatedly submit new documents for new operations within the limits of the credit amount and during its validity.
column8: Syndicated credit describes participation by more than one bank due to the huge amount of credit, each bank providing a letter of guarantee to the leading bank to the extent of its participation.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/3/3, all three descriptions of back-to-back, revolving and syndicated credit are correct.

column5: It is permissible to enter into back-to-back bilateral promises in order to replicate derivatives, provided that each of the promises is legally binding on one party only.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per item 6, back-to-back bilateral promises to circumvent prohibitions, such as back-to-back derivatives, are impermissible.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The Shari'ah does not prohibit the owner and the tenant agreeing that the tenant will pay a lump sum of money over and above the periodic rental amount, on condition that:
column6: It is non-refundable and becomes the property of the owner even if the lease is terminated early, irrespective of the period elapsed.
column7: It is paid to the previous tenant in exchange for vacating the premises.
column8: It is part of the agreed rent for the whole lease period, so that on early termination the rules applicable to rent apply to it.
column9: It is held as a security deposit, to be returned in full at the end of the lease.
column11: Per 8/1, such a lump sum is part of the rent for the whole lease period; on early termination the rules on rental payments apply to it.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When the agent breaches the contract in a way that does not serve the interest of the principal:
column6: The contract is void and cannot be approved by the principal.
column7: The contract becomes binding on the principal, and the agent compensates him for the price difference only.
column8: The principal is free to maintain the contract or declare it invalid.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/3/1, for a breach not in his interest the principal may either maintain the contract or declare it invalid.

column5: The basis for permitting the worker to seek assistance from others, when there is no stipulation for his personal services, is that Ju'alah is similar to agency, in which seeking help from others is valid.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, Ju'alah resembles agency, in which seeking help from others is valid.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing the subject-matter of Istisna'a to be a specific identified item is that:
column6: Exclusion of liability for defects is valid only in the sale of identified goods, whereas the manufacturer in Istisna'a may stipulate it for specified goods too, provided the purchaser inspects and accepts the goods at delivery.
column7: Istisna'a is a sale for future delivery based on specification, so selling specific identified items would be selling what the seller does not own, which is prohibited by the Hadith "Do not sell what you own not".
column8: Natural things are not covered by the term Istisna'a, which is confined to items transformed by labour from raw materials and delivered in stages of completion.
column9: It is normal for people to deal in items that have equivalents in the market, and specific items have none that could replace them if destroyed.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, an identified item not owned by the seller would breach 'Do not sell what you own not'; items to be made do not yet exist.

column5: ………… refers to the participation of a group of institutions in a joint financing operation through one of the Shari'ah-compliant modes of financing, the accounts of which are kept independent from the accounts of the participating Institutions:
column6: Diminishing Musharakah.
column7: Investment Sukuk.
column8: Syndicated financing.
column9: Restricted Mudarabah.
column11: Per clause 2, syndicated financing is joint financing by a group of institutions via a Shari'ah-compliant mode, with independent accounts.

column5: An IFI offered one of its customers an interest-free loan of USD 500,000, on condition that all of the customer's currency dealing be effected with the IFI and with no other institution. The customer will then trade only in amounts he owns. This transaction is:
column6: Impermissible, because it combines a loan and a contract of exchange, which results in a benefit to the lender.
column7: Impermissible, because it is not permissible for the Institution to lend a customer money that is used in currency trading in any case.
column8: Permissible, provided the currency exchange is carried out at the spot rate on the day of each transaction.
column9: Permissible, because the loan is interest free and the customer deals only in amounts that he owns.
column11: Per 2/12/2 and its basis, the condition to trade with the lender combines loan and exchange, a benefit to the lender; without it there is no prohibition.

column5: The service agent may implement investment plans and make investment decisions, provided that its duties also include leasing, insuring and maintaining the assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/3/1, a service agent neither implements investment plans nor makes investment decisions.

column5: Discounting a negotiable instrument, by settling it to its first beneficiary before maturity for an amount less than its value, is permitted if the discount reflects the remaining period to maturity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/1/2, such discounting is not permitted.

column5: According to the majority of the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali Fuqaha, the set of combined contracts:
column6: Must be judged as a single new contract having its own independent rulings.
column7: Is permissible only if the combined contracts are concluded for separate values.
column8: Is prohibited if it combines two contracts that differ in Shari'ah status and rulings, such as a binding contract with a non-binding one, or a commutative contract with a donation.
column9: Can always be judged in the light of its individual components; if each contract individually satisfies the requirements of permissibility, the combined set is also permissible.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the majority judge the set by its components: if each contract is permissible, the set is permissible.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The sale of gold for gold is permissible provided that:
column6: The counter-values are equal in weight, regardless of being new or old, and both counter-values are exchanged as required by Shari'ah.
column7: Any difference in weight is compensated by a separate fee for the workmanship.
column8: The counter-values are equal in value, even if they differ in weight owing to the workmanship of one of them, provided that both are exchanged at spot.
column9: The counter-values are equal in weight, though deferment of one of them is permissible if the gold is used.
column11: Per 3/1/1, gold for gold requires equal weight, new or old, with exchange of both counter-values as required by Shari'ah.

column5: The treatment of the insurance surplus in Islamic insurance is based on:
column6: The Islamic rules of inheritance.
column7: The rules of profit distribution in Mudarabah.
column8: The cooperative nature of the contract and the practice of the Sahabah with regard to Nihd.
column9: The principle that the managing company owns the premiums as soon as it signs the contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, surplus treatment rests on the contract's cooperative nature and the Sahabah's practice of Nihd.

column5: In the constructive valuation of the assets of a Mudarabah, the receivables shall be measured:
column6: Taking into consideration the time value (interest rate), as for any deferred amount owed to the Mudarabah.
column7: At the cash equivalent, or net realisable value, i.e. after deducting a provision for doubtful debts.
column8: After a discount on current value for extension of the period of payment, as consideration for earlier collection.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 8/8, receivables are measured at net realisable value; time value and discount for extension are not considered.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Rights are extinguished by the passage of time once the limitation period after which a claim cannot be made in court has elapsed.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 12/2(a), rights are not extinguished by passage of time, though a limitation period may bar a claim in court.

column5: The principles of Islamic insurance, which shall be explicitly mentioned in the articles of association or the rules or documents of the corporation, include:
column6: The managing company is entitled to a share of the insurance surplus as an incentive for good management.
column7: The participant donates his contribution and the returns thereon to the insurance account for payment of indemnity, and may undertake to bear any deficit that may occur, as per regulations.
column8: When the company is liquidated, the provisions and accumulated reserves pertaining to insurance are distributed among the shareholders in proportion to their shares, after payment of the indemnities due.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/1, the donation commitment is a principle; per 5/5 the company gets no surplus, and per 5/6 reserves go to charity.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for using options (khiyar) when the Institution buys on Murabahah is:
column6: The case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b and his debtor, where the Prophet (peace be upon him) suggested writing off a portion of the debt.
