column7: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab in the presence of some companions of the Prophet (peace be upon him).
column8: The purchase by the Prophet (peace be upon him) of a she-camel from Abu Bakr at the acquisition price.
column9: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh, to whom the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave a three-day period for any goods bought.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the use of options rests on the Hadith of Hibban Ibn Munqidh granting a three-day option.

column5: It is permissible to issue both nominative shares ('to the order of') and bearer shares, the common ownership of bearer shares being vested in the holder of the certificate at any time.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1/2/12-13, both nominative and bearer shares may be issued; bearer shares belong to the certificate holder.

column5: With regard to an asset mortgaged as collateral for the debt, the creditor is entitled to:
column6: Apply for the sale of the mortgaged asset for the liquidation of the debt.
column7: Stipulate that the debtor must give a mandate to the creditor to sell the mortgaged asset without recourse to the courts.
column8: Take ownership of the mortgaged asset automatically in satisfaction of the debt upon the debtor's default.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/1/5, the creditor may apply for sale of the collateral or stipulate a mandate to sell it without court recourse.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, it is impossible to imagine a debt arising from commodities purchased through Salam, because:
column6: The capital (price) has to be paid in advance.
column7: Salam commodities are purchased for trading purposes only.
column8: Salam commodities are always fungible goods.
column9: The Salam buyer owns the commodity on signing the contract.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, in Salam the capital (price) is paid in advance, so no debt arises on the purchaser for the price of Salam goods.

column5: An agent or a Mudarib:
column6: Has the right of accepting arbitration absolutely, since he manages the funds on behalf of others and arbitration is part of the management of these funds, so no consent is needed.
column7: Does not have the right of accepting arbitration, except with the consent of the principal for the agent and the owners of the capital for the Mudarib, or on the basis of a clause in the Mudarabah conditions.
column8: May not accept arbitration even with the consent of the principal or the owners of the capital, since he was appointed to manage the funds and not to resolve disputes concerning them, and any such acceptance makes him liable for the resulting loss.
column9: May accept arbitration without the consent of the principal if he is an agent, but a Mudarib may accept it only with the consent of the owners of the capital.
column11: Per 8/7, an agent or Mudarib may accept arbitration only with the principal's or capital owners' consent, or under a Mudarabah clause.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: It is permissible for the institution to make the payment of the purchase price of the commodity contingent upon the agent providing a guarantee for the payment of the sale price, by the agent himself or by another person.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2/11, this is among the international commodity sales prohibited by the Shari'ah.

column5: With regard to increasing the fees of the card in return for features:
column6: It is permitted to increase the fees of any card in return for the feature of returning a percentage of the price of merchandise (cash back).
column7: In a lending-based card, it is permitted to increase its fees beyond the actual cost of the features, provided the features are Shari'ah compliant.
column8: It is not permitted to increase the fees of the card in return for a feature contingent on the usage of the card, or a feature which has no known limit.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/6/2, fees may not be raised for cash back, usage-contingent or unlimited features, nor beyond actual cost in lending-based cards.

column5: An investor paid an IFI 100,000 at spot for deferred delivery of a commodity, the parties having agreed beforehand that, upon the delivery date, the commodity would be substituted with 110,000 in cash. This arrangement is:
column6: Prohibited, since it is a legal artifice (ḥīla) for ribā.
column7: Permitted as a Salam contract, with substitution of the subject of Salam after maturity.
column8: Permitted, since the substitution takes place after the maturity date.
column9: Permitted, provided that the market value of the commodity at delivery equals 110,000.
column11: Per 4/1/2, colluding on spot cash for deferred goods to be swapped on delivery for more cash is a ḥīla for ribā.

column5: The debit card may only be issued free of charge, since it is a settlement instrument and not a credit instrument.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/3, the debit card is issued for a fee or free.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Stipulating Khiyar al-Shart (cooling-off option) in the sale of gold is permissible, provided that the option period does not extend beyond the contracting session.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/2/2, Khiyar al-Shart in the sale of gold is impermissible, as it contravenes the spot-exchange requirement.

column5: The basis for the condition that all instalments become due upon delay in payment is that payment on a deferred basis is the right of the buyer, who may relinquish the deferral entirely or make payment of all instalments contingent on default in one instalment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 5/1, along with the Hadith 'Muslims are bound by the conditions they made'.

column5: If the sale item is destroyed before delivery to the buyer during the 'Arboun option period, the buyer's option is canceled and he is required to pay the balance of the price to the seller.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per item 6, destruction before delivery voids the contract and the earnest money must be returned; the stated effect applies after delivery.

column5: Making cash loans or financing receivables owed to the Institution by a customer the capital of a Salam contract with that customer is:
column6: Not permitted, since making a debt the Salam capital is a form of extinction of debt in debt.
column7: Permitted, provided that the Salam price equals the amount of the debt.
column8: Permitted, provided that the commodity is delivered at maturity and the loan is repaid in full by then.
column9: Permitted, if the customer is solvent.
column11: Per 4/1/3/2 and its basis, a debt may not be made Salam capital, being a form of extinction of debt in debt.

column5: If the purchaser of a leased asset knows about the Ijarah contract and consents to it:
column6: He may terminate the Ijarah contract and take possession of the asset, since the lessee's consent is not necessary for the sale.
column7: He takes the place of the previous owner in his entitlement to the rental for the remaining period.
column8: The sale requires the consent of the lessee.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/1/2, a purchaser who knows of and accepts the lease steps into the lessor's place for the remaining rent; the lessee's consent is not needed.

column5: It is not permitted for the Institution to issue a letter of guarantee in favour of an applicant who will use it to acquire an interest-based loan or to conclude a prohibited transaction. The basis of this prohibition is:
column6: It is analogous to the prohibition of giving assistance in committing a sin, and the guarantor has a stronger role in establishing and recovering a debt than the writer and witnesses cursed in the Hadith.
column7: The guarantee would be for an unknown debt, and a valid guarantee may be given only for a debt whose exact amount is known when the guarantee is issued, as well as for a debt that has already arisen and is due at the time of the guarantee.
column8: The Institution would be taking a fee for the guarantee per se, which is prohibited even where the applicant uses the letter of guarantee for a permissible purpose and the debt is of a known amount.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/1/3 and its basis, it is assisting in sin; the guarantor's role exceeds that of the Riba writer and witnesses in the Hadith.

column5: In order to enable policyholders to exercise their control rights and protect their interest:
column6: Each investment of the fund's assets must be approved by the general assembly of policyholders, whose decisions bind the Board of Directors, and the company may not act without such approval.
column7: Policyholders should appoint the members of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column8: Preference should be given to policyholders to participate in management of the insurance operations through appropriate legal arrangements, such as representation on the Board of Directors.
column9: Policyholders must own the majority of the shares of the managing company.
column11: Per 5/7, policyholders should be given preference to take part in management, e.g. through representation on the Board.

column5: After the customer has given a promise but before the execution of the Murabahah, the Institution and the customer:
column6: May have the terms of the promise revised unilaterally by the Institution in line with market conditions, provided the customer is notified in advance.
column7: May not revise the terms of the promise, because this amounts to rescheduling of debt.
column8: May agree to revise the terms of the promise, whether as to the deferment of payment, the mark-up or other terms, but only by mutual consent.
column9: May revise only the period of deferment, but not the mark-up agreed in the promise.
column11: Per 2/3/4, the terms of the promise may be revised before execution, but only by mutual consent; a promise is not a contract.

column5: The following are given in the standard as examples of Istisna'a transactions that would be a legal device for mere interest-based financing, except:
column6: The Institution buys items from the contractor on a cash payment basis and sells them back to the manufacturer on a deferred payment basis at a higher price.
column7: The manufacturer fulfils his obligation using items produced by other parties before the contract, the ultimate purchaser not having stipulated otherwise.
column8: One third or more of the facility in which the subject-matter will be produced belongs to the customer.
column9: The party ordering the subject-matter to be produced is the manufacturer himself.
column11: Per 2/2/4, the first three are interest-based devices ('Inah); per 3/1/5, using others' pre-existing items is allowed absent a contrary stipulation.

column5: ………… is a settlement instrument and not a credit instrument, for which the cardholder deposits with the card issuer a balance specifically for the card, which may be in a particular currency or in currencies different than the local currency:
column6: Debit Card.
column7: Credit Card.
column8: Prepaid Card.
column9: Charge Card.
column11: Per 3/2/1 and 3/2/2, the prepaid card is a settlement instrument with a balance deposited specifically for the card.

column5: The basis for not considering the receipt of an uncertified cheque as possession of its amount is the probability that there is no balance to cover it or that the balance is insufficient.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, an uncertified cheque may lack sufficient balance; possession is based on custom.

column5: The two parties to a hiring contract agreed that if the work is done within a certain period the pay will be this much, and if it is done in a shorter period the pay will increase to that much. This arrangement is:
column6: Permissible, as it is permissible to agree upon more than one rate of pay.
column7: Impermissible, because it involves Gharar and Jahalah in the pay.
column8: Impermissible, because two rates of pay may only be linked to different places of work, not to different periods.
column9: Permissible only if the higher rate is linked to the longer period.
column11: Per 5/2/9, more than one rate of pay may be agreed, linked to periods, places, types or specializations; the basis says it involves no Gharar or Jahalah.

column5: All financial gains which Islamic insurance companies receive from Islamic reinsurance companies:
column6: Are considered doubtful income which has to be purified.
column7: Should be credited to the account of the shareholders of the Islamic insurance company, as a return on their capital and management.
column8: Should be spent on charitable purposes.
column9: Are lawful gains and should be credited to the account of policyholders (the participant companies of the scheme), as revenues.
column11: Per 9, gains from Islamic reinsurers are lawful and are credited to the policyholders' account as part of revenues.

column5: It is not permitted for a partner in a joint enterprise to extend to his partner a binding promise to buy back the share sold to that partner if the promise is:
column6: At a price agreed by the contracting parties at the time of performance of the promise, where that price differs from the market value of the share.
column7: For a specified price determined at the time of undertaking the promise, regardless of the market value of the share at performance.
column8: To buy back the share gradually over the term of the diminishing Musharaka.
column9: At the market value of the share at the time of performance of the promise.
column11: Per 5/4/2, a fixed-price buyback promise contradicts risk and reward sharing; market value or a price agreed on performance is permitted.

column5: It is permitted for the investment manager to undertake to purchase the underlying assets from the certificateholders of Sukuk based on Mudaraba, Musharaka and Wakala:
column6: At the net asset value (NAV), the market value, the fair value, or a price agreed on at the time of purchase.
column7: At a price specified at the time of making the contract, provided that the undertaking is given voluntarily after the contract.
column8: At a price specified at the time of making the contract, such as the nominal value of the Sukuk.
column9: At the nominal value of the Sukuk plus the expected profit, provided that this is disclosed in the prospectus.
column11: Per 3/5/1, a purchase undertaking at a price fixed at contracting is prohibited; at NAV, market, fair or agreed price on purchase it is permitted.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Ownership of a license to use gives the licensee the right to personal use only, which cannot be transferred to a third party.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/3, a license to use confers only a personal right of use that cannot be transferred to a third party.

column5: A manufacturing company's last verified financial statements show interest-based debt of 20% and interest-taking deposits of 10% of its market capitalization. Its total income was USD 10 million, of which USD 700,000 came from interest and other prohibited sources. Subscription in its shares:
column6: Is permissible, provided the investor eliminates the prohibited income.
column7: Is not permissible, because the interest-based debt exceeds 10% of market capitalization.
column8: Is permissible, because its debt and deposits are within the 30% limits.
column9: Is not permissible, because the income from prohibited components exceeds 5% of total income.
column11: Per 3/4/4, prohibited income of 7% exceeds the 5% limit, so the exemption fails; elimination does not cure it.

column5: Regarding defects of the leased asset, the lessor:
column6: Is responsible only for impairment caused by his own doing, and not for events outside his control.
column7: Must accept responsibility for any defects which impair the intended use of the asset, and may not exclude his liability for impairment, whether by his own doing or from events outside his control.
column8: May exclude his liability for defects, provided the rental is reduced accordingly.
column9: May stipulate that he is free from responsibility for all or some of the defects of the leased asset, as in Bay' al-Bara'ah (sale on 'as is' basis), provided the defects are disclosed to the lessee and the rental is not reduced.
column11: Per 5/1/5, the lessor bears defects impairing use and cannot exclude liability, whether caused by him or by events beyond his control.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: General agency includes all methods of disposing of assets, including making donations, provided that the interest of the principal and the customary practices are well observed.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/1/1, disposal under general agency does not include donations unless the principal authorizes the agent to do so.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of stipulating that the Murabahah contract would be terminated for default in payment is that:
column6: The customer has caused the Institution to enter into a deal that it would not otherwise have concluded, and must therefore bear the Institution's lost profit.
column7: The safety of the goods is the responsibility of the owner.
column8: Discount for early payment is a form of settlement between the creditor and the debtor, which Shari'ah endorses in the case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b, as acknowledged by the debtor and the creditor.
column9: The original principle in respect of stipulations is validity and permissibility, and a condition neither renders permissible an impermissible act nor prohibits a permissible one.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, stipulations are valid in principle; Muslims are bound by their conditions unless they permit the forbidden or forbid the permitted.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: One of the conditions for the permissibility of concluding spot contracts in the commodity markets is:
column6: That the commodity be delivered within the session of the contract.
column7: That a portion of the price be deposited with the intermediary as security.
column8: That the price be paid on a spot basis.
column9: That the buyer accept a set-off for value instead of taking delivery of the commodity.
column11: Per 3/1/4, the price must be paid on a spot basis; an unstipulated delay in delivery does not affect validity, and set-off clauses are barred (3/1/3).

column5: In Shari'ah terminology, ………… refers to making a property invulnerable to any disposition that leads to transfer of ownership, and donating the usufruct of that property to beneficiaries:
column6: Hikr.
column7: Waqf.
column8: Istibdal.
column9: Irsad.
column11: Per 2/1, this is the Shari'ah definition of Waqf (Habs). Irsad is outside the Standard's scope; Hikr and Istibdal are Waqf leasing and exchange.

column5: ………… are shares that entitle the holder to a participation in the net profit, but not to vote, and which are gradually redeemed before the termination of the company through distribution of profits; their issuance is not permitted.
column6: Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares.
column7: Bearer shares.
column8: Nominative shares ('to the order of').
column9: Preference shares.
column11: Per 4/1/2/15, these are Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares, which may not be issued.

column5: Ignoring sale-based Riba and non-fulfillment of the requirements of currency exchange in subsidiary contracts is based on the Hadith:
column6: When somebody purchases a palm tree that has not yet been pollinated, the fruits should belong to the seller unless the buyer stipulates otherwise.
column7: In which the Prophet (peace be upon him) prohibited combining sale with lending.
column8: In which the Prophet (peace be upon him) instructed an employee to sell his low-quality dates first and then buy the high-quality dates.
column9: When somebody buys a slave who has money, the slave's money should go to the seller, unless the buyer stipulates in the contract that he should get the money.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis (5/2/3), the Hadith of the slave sold with his money permits ignoring exchange rules in a subsidiary matter.

column5: After the declaration of insolvency, the debtor's subsequent acts of sale, purchase, admission (of liability) or guarantee:
column6: Are attached to his future liability and not to the sequestered assets, and those whose rights attach to his liability are not entitled to share the sequestered assets with the creditors.
column7: Are void and of no effect whatsoever, and he cannot be required to discharge such liabilities even after revocation of the sequestration.
column8: Are attached to the sequestered assets, and those dealing with him after the declaration share these assets pro-rata with the existing creditors.
column9: Are attached to the sequestered assets, but are paid only after the creditors of due debts have been paid in full.
column11: Per 5/4, they attach to his future liability, payable after revocation; such parties do not share the sequestered assets.

column5: The Mudarib may do the following, either by permission or appointment of the capital provider:
column6: Combine a Mudarabah contract and a partnership (Sharikah) contract, whether at the outset or after commencement of operations, and whether the partnership contribution is from himself or from a third party.
column7: Accept funds from a third party on a Mudarabah basis, if this new contract will not affect his investment and management responsibility in respect of the first Mudarabah.
column8: Charge the Mudarabah a fee for work which, by custom, is his own responsibility.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 9/1/6, (a) and (b) are allowed with permission; per 9/4, customary work is his duty and earns no fee.

column5: Conventional insurance is banned by Shari'ah because:
column6: It is a Mu'awadah (mutual compensation) contract that seeks profit out of the insurance operation itself, and hence is subject to the Shari'ah rulings on financial dealings that involve Gharar.
column7: It covers the risks of disability and death.
column8: It involves payment of contributions as donations to a fund that has an independent legal entity, and the fund is managed on a non-profit basis by the participants themselves, who share its surplus among them.
column9: It is managed by a joint stock company against a specific fee.
column11: Per clause 2, conventional insurance is a profit-seeking Mu'awadah contract subject to the rules on Gharar, hence banned.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of issuing Tamattu' shares is that:
column6: They are issued at a premium over the nominal value.
column7: Their owners claim their rights to profit and their redemption is only in form, as they remain owners of the shares and are entitled to rights at liquidation.
column8: They are issued for the bearer.
column9: They represent a debt owed by the company to the shareholders, repayable out of profits before any distribution to the other shareholders and redeemable at nominal value at the time of liquidation.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 2/7, redemption of Tamattu' shares is only in form since holders keep rights to profit and liquidation.

column5: If, after the issuance of Sukuk, the required ratio of tangible assets is no longer maintained due to a supervening event acknowledged by a competent Shari'ah Board:
column6: The Sukuk remain tradable at any ratio, since the event is supervening, and the Shari'ah Board need not specify any period for restoring it.
column7: The Institution must undertake to buy back the Sukuk at their nominal value, and the Sukuk remain tradable until the buyback is completed.
column8: The Sukuk are automatically redeemed at their face value upon the occurrence of the event, and the Institution must pay the redemption price out of its own funds if the assets are insufficient, because it guarantees the capital of the Sukuk-holders.
column9: The Institution must restore the ratio within a period specified by the Shari'ah Board, and if tangible assets fall below 33%, the Sukuk-holders are notified that the Sukuk are no longer negotiable except under the rules for trading debts.
column11: Per 8/2/3, the ratio must be restored within the Board's period; below 33% the Sukuk become non-negotiable except under debt-trading rules.

column5: When acting in the capacity of an ultimate purchaser in Istisna'a, the Institution may give the manufacturer guarantees in the form of:
column6: A stipulation that the manufacturer is not liable for defects in the subject-matter, if the ultimate purchaser agrees to it, as a guarantee for the manufacturer's performance.
column7: An undertaking to pay an increased price if payment of the price is delayed beyond the agreed period of time.
column8: A mortgage, personal guarantee, assignment of rights, current account, investment account or consent to blocking withdrawal from an account.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/2, the Institution as purchaser may give mortgages, personal guarantees, assignments, accounts or blocking consent.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The option to revoke due to breach of description:
column6: Can transfer to all types of successors and assignees.
column7: Transfers to general heirs, but not to special successors or assignees.
column8: Lapses upon the death of the buyer.
column9: Transfers to heirs only if this is stipulated in the contract.
column11: Per 4/5, the option for breach of description can transfer to all types of successors and assignees.

column5: If a period is stipulated in Qard:
column6: The borrower must return it prior to the end of the period if the lender needs it.
column7: The borrower is under no obligation to return it prior to the termination of the period, nor can the lender demand it back prior to the end of the period.
column8: The stipulation is void, and the borrower must return the loan on demand.
column9: The lender may demand the loan back at any time, but the borrower is not obliged to return it before the end of the period.
column11: Per 6, a stipulated period binds both: no early return is required and the lender cannot demand repayment before it ends.

column5: A promise from one party only to purchase or sell currencies is impermissible if the promise is binding.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/9/1, only a binding bilateral promise is forbidden; a promise from one party is permissible even if binding.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar pertaining to failure in delivery nullifies the contract. An example of such Gharar is:
column6: Sale of a house to a buyer who has not seen its foundation, which is hidden underground and whose inspection is not customary.
column7: Leasing a house for one month while months differ in length, because the number of days in the month is not specified in the contract.
column8: Selling fish in the water, unless found in a confined place and does not require fishing.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/4, selling fish in the water (unless confined) is Gharar in delivery; (a) and (b) are minor Gharar that does not affect the contract (4/2/2).

column5: With regard to the Waqf beneficiary:
column6: It is required that the Waqf beneficiary exists at the time of creation of the Waqf, otherwise the Waqf is null and void from the start.
column7: It is valid to stipulate that the Waqf beneficiary is the Waqif himself, e.g., to say: I made this Waqf for myself and then for charitable causes.
column8: The Waqif may not single out some of his children as Waqf beneficiaries or increase their shares, even if there is a valid reason such as poverty or special needs.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4/4/2 self-Waqf is valid; per 2/4/4/4 the beneficiary need not exist at creation; per 2/4/4/5 children may be singled out for a valid reason.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In internal conversion, if the liabilities are in the form of obligations to provide non-permissible services:
column6: The bank should fulfil them, since they were undertaken before the decision to convert, and donate any consideration it receives to charity, provided the services are completed within the financial period of conversion.
column7: The bank may fulfil them and donate the consideration received to charity.
column8: The bank is obliged to make every effort to terminate such liabilities by refunding the consideration, even if it has to pay compensation for non-fulfilment.
column9: The bank should terminate them without refunding the consideration received.
column11: Per 9/1/2, the bank must terminate them by refunding the consideration, even at the cost of compensation.

column5: ………… is the Waqf in which the income/usufruct is reserved for specifically described persons, usually family members and relatives, and goes to a charitable purpose when none of these persons is existent:
column6: Self-dedicated Waqf (al-Waqf 'Ala al-Nafs).
column7: Charitable Waqf (al-Waqf al-Khayri).
column8: Family Waqf (al-Waqf al-Ahli).
column9: Joint Waqf (al-Waqf al-Mushtarak).
column11: Per 2/3/2, this is family Waqf. Joint Waqf serves family and charitable purposes together (2/3/3).

column5: The buyer of the debt may stipulate upon the seller of the debt:
column6: To secure the debt by a Shari'ah-compliant guarantee from a third party, such as Islamic insurance (Takaful) on the debt before its sale.
column7: To guarantee the debt owed by the debtor, so that the buyer has recourse to the seller for the portion of the debt not recovered.
column8: To buy back the debt from him at a higher price on a future date.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/3–7/4, the buyer may stipulate a third-party guarantee (e.g., Takaful) or the seller's own guarantee with recourse.

column5: A customer and an IFI jointly bought a warehouse, the customer owning 30% and the IFI 70%. The customer then leased the IFI's share from it. The prevailing rental for the whole warehouse is 100,000 a year. The rental receivable by the IFI should be determined:
column6: In proportion to the customer's 30% share, as he is the user of the asset.
column7: On the whole warehouse, less the customer's share of the profit of the IFI, since the customer is a co-owner of the warehouse and bears a part of its risk.
column8: In proportion to the IFI's 70% share in the ownership of the warehouse, since the lessee pays rent only on the share he does not own.
column9: On the whole warehouse (100,000), since the customer uses the whole warehouse and the IFI cannot use any part of it.
column11: Per 3/6, a co-owner lessee pays rent only on the share he does not own, so the IFI's rental is in proportion to its 70% share.

column5: When an institution issues investment Sukuk to obtain liquidity, if it is only the lessee and not the manager of the Sukuk assets, it may promise to purchase them at face value.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2/5, a manager may promise to buy at market or agreed price; a mere lessee (not manager) may promise to buy at face value.

column5: Regarding the rulings relating to Zakah disbursement:
column6: Zakah should not necessarily cover all the eight heads of its disbursement; it can permissibly be confined to some of them.
column7: Zakah funds can be transferred from the place of payment to another place due to an obvious interest to be judged by the Shari'ah boards of the institutions.
column8: Zakah can be paid before its due time, subject to specific conditions on which Shari'ah boards should be consulted.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/8, 10/9 and 10/6, Zakah may be confined to some heads, transferred for an obvious interest, and paid early under conditions set with the Shari'ah board.

column5: An IFI purchased natural gas under a Salam contract for a cash capital. On the maturity date, the seller offered to deliver oil instead, without any prior stipulation. The market value of the gas at the delivery time is 1,000,000, and that of the oil offered is 1,100,000. This substitution is:
column6: Permitted, since oil is fit to be the subject of Salam for a cash capital.
column7: Permitted, since the oil is of a different kind from the gas and substitution of a different kind is allowed without any condition.
column8: Not permitted, since the substitute's market value exceeds that of the subject of Salam at the delivery time.
column9: Permitted, provided that the IFI pays the seller the difference of 100,000.
column11: Per 4/1/1/3, the substitute's market value may not exceed the market value of the Salam subject at the delivery time.

column5: A seller offers an unspecified gift along with a good or service. The Shari'ah ruling on this promotional gift is:
column6: It is impermissible, owing to the ambiguity (Jahalah) of the gift.
column7: It is permissible and is subject to the same Shari'ah ruling as the increase in the object of sale.
column8: It is permissible absolutely, since it is a donation (Tabarru').
column9: It is permissible, provided that the price is not increased against the gift.
column11: Per 3/6/1/2, an unspecified gift with a good or service is permissible provided the price is not increased against it.

column5: In the application of Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek for a specifically described property to be delivered in the future, for development of Waqf land:
column6: The financier leases the building to the Waqf after constructing it on the Waqf land, and becomes the owner of the land at the end of the lease period against the rentals.
column7: The Waqf land is leased to the financier who constructs a building on it, and at the end of the lease period the financier becomes the owner of the land and the building.
column8: The Waqf land is leased to the financier who constructs a building on it and delivers it to the Waqf to execute the lease contract, and at the end of the contracting period the Waqf becomes the owner of the building.
column9: The Waqf sells the land to the financier and leases it back, then repurchases it at the end of the lease period.
column11: Per 7/2/3, the land is leased to the financier, who builds and delivers the building to the Waqf under the lease; the Waqf owns the building at the end.

column5: An IFI in need of liquidity sold one of its office buildings to an investor for immediate cash, and then leased the building back on rent payable in arrears. This arrangement is:
column6: Permissible only if the rent is paid in advance rather than in arrears, so that the sale price is not a disguised loan.
column7: Impermissible, because liquidity may only be obtained through Mudarabah and investment agency.
column8: A permissible mode of obtaining liquidity, taking into consideration what is stated in Shari'ah Standard No. (9), item 5/8, on Ijarah.
column9: Impermissible, because an institution may not lease back an asset it has sold, whether the rent is paid in advance or in arrears.
column11: Per 4/2/3, selling assets for immediate cash and leasing them back on rent payable in arrears is a permissible mode, subject to SS 9, 5/8.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In external conversion, the buyer of the bank must redeem the impermissible mortgages attached to the bank's assets himself after the acquisition; he may not stipulate that the seller replace them.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/3, in external conversion the buyer must stipulate that the seller replace impermissible mortgages with permissible ones.

column5: In a Hawalah on a deferred payment basis in which the transferred debt is already due but the payer required that it be transferred for future payment at an agreed date:
column6: The Hawalah is invalid, because a debt that has fallen due cannot be deferred.
column7: The payer cannot be asked for payment before the agreed date.
column8: The transferee may demand payment immediately, since the debt has already fallen due.
column9: The transferor remains liable for the debt until the agreed date.
column11: Per 5/1/4, where the payer stipulated future payment of a due debt, he cannot be asked to pay before the agreed date.

column5: It is permissible that the subject-matter of an Istisna'a contract be:
column6: Only items intended for consumption, and not items intended for use with their substance kept intact, since the latter are identified by designation and cannot be specified.
column7: An item with unique descriptions required by the ultimate purchaser, even if it has no substitutes in the market, provided it is subject to specification.
column8: Only items that have no perfect substitutes in the market, because items with substitutes can be obtained by Salam instead.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/2, unique items (if specifiable) and items with perfect substitutes are allowed, whether for consumption or for use.

column5: Constructive possession, in the forms mentioned in the standard, is on an equal footing with actual possession because:
column6: The Shari'ah never prescribed a particular method for taking possession, so reference must be made to the prevailing custom in the business community.
column7: Constructive possession transfers ownership of the currency even if its risk remains with the transferor, since ownership passes upon the mere agreement.
column8: It is permitted by way of necessity (Darurah) for modern banking only, and it is not permitted where actual possession is feasible.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per the basis, Shari'ah set no particular method of possession; custom governs, giving ability to dispose and transfer of risk.

column5: Zakah on Murabahah debtors (the amounts owed by purchasers) is payable on:
column6: The total price, including profits.
column7: The cost of the goods only, excluding profits.
column8: The profits only.
column9: Nothing, until the installments are collected.
column11: Per 5/3/4/9, Zakah on Murabahah debtors is payable on the total price including profits, as per 5/3/1.

column5: Trading in financial securities whose underlying assets comprise debts owed by a third party is subject to the rules of the Standard on Sale of Debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/4/1, such trading is subject to the rules of this Standard.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Deposits of gold (Wadi'ah):
column6: Are held by the depository on a liability basis, so that it is liable for any loss even without misconduct.
column7: Are held in trust with the depository, who may not use, dispose of or commingle them with other gold without allocation; if the depositor permits commingling, joint ownership rulings apply.
column8: May be used by the depository, provided that it guarantees the return of an equivalent quantity of gold.
column9: May be commingled by the depository with other gold without the depositor's permission, since gold is fungible and an equivalent quantity can always be returned, provided that the depository bears any loss.
column11: Per 5/4/1, gold deposits are a trust; no use, disposal or unallocated commingling, and permitted commingling follows joint ownership (3/5).

column5: If the credit transaction includes a provision that it is subject to the prevalent principles and practices that unify documentary credit:
column6: The provision is accepted absolutely, since these practices are international custom and the Institution has no authority to amend them or to qualify them in any manner whatsoever, and the credit remains valid even if it provides for interest.
column7: The provision is valid only if the correspondent bank is an Islamic bank, and the credit is fully covered by the client.
column8: The credit becomes impermissible and the Institution must refrain from dealing in it, even if the interest provision is expressly excluded.
column9: It is necessary to qualify such a statement with the stipulation that it will not violate Shari'ah rules and principles, and to state explicitly that a provision for interest will not be acted upon.
column11: Per 3/7/1, such reference must be qualified by non-violation of Shari'ah and an explicit statement that interest will not be acted upon.

column5: The Mudarib is entitled to travelling expenses from the Mudarabah funds in accordance with custom and reason.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 9/7, the Mudarib is entitled to travelling expenses in accordance with custom and reason.

column5: Money can be donated as a Waqf because this is the original form of Waqf, and shares and Sukuk come under this type of Waqf.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, money is an original form of Waqf (per Al-Ansari, supported by Ibn Taymiyyah), and shares and Sukuk come under it.

column5: The Shari'ah controls on combination of contracts include that:
column6: It should not include the cases that are explicitly banned by Shari'ah, like combining sale and lending in one contract.
column7: It should not be used as a trick for committing Riba, such as agreement between two parties to practice Bay' al-'Inah or Riba al-Fadl.
column8: Combined contracts should not reveal disparity or contradiction with regard to their underlying rulings and ultimate goals.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1, 4/2 and 4/4, all three are Shari'ah controls on combining contracts.

column5: A worker (irrigator) stopped working after the crop materialized but before it was ready for harvest. A third party was hired to complete the work for a wage of 3,000. After the crop was harvested and sold, the worker's share amounted to 2,000. In this case:
column6: The third party's wage is deducted from the overall crop before division.
column7: The worker is not entitled to any share, and the owner bears the third party's wage.
column8: The wage is deducted from the worker's share, and the worker must make up the difference of 1,000.
column9: The worker receives his full share of 2,000, and the owner pays the third party's wage.
column11: Per 8/4, the third party's wage is deducted from the worker's share and he must make up any shortfall.

column5: Where there is a common shareholding between a third party giving a commitment for reparation of loss and the investment manager, the ownership holding of one party in the other must not exceed:
column11: Per 4/1/1, with a common shareholding, the holding of one party must not exceed 50% of the other.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In arriving at distributable profit, investment accounts may be charged with:
column6: The expenses of the investment departments and the bodies which endorse their decisions, as well as the salaries of the Board of Directors.
column7: The expenses relating to the institution's own activities.
column8: The expenses of the follow-up and accounting departments.
column9: The direct expenses incurred in executing each operation in which the investment account balances are utilized.
column11: Per 3/1/2/2, accounts bear direct operation expenses and their share of shared expenses, but not the Mudarib's own tasks or the institution's activities.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Gharar due to ignorance of the amount of the sold commodity, such as Bay' al-Juzaf (sale of an unknown quantity):
column6: Nullifies the contract, except when there exist conditions that make Gharar forgivable, such as viewing the sold commodity at the time of sale.
column7: Does not affect the contract at all, since it is minor Gharar.
column8: Nullifies the contract absolutely, as ignorance of the amount always leads to dispute.
column9: Nullifies the contract, unless the buyer is given the option of viewing the commodity after the sale is concluded.
column11: Per 5/2/1/5, it nullifies the contract except where Gharar is made forgivable: viewing at sale, possible estimation, or the quantity as a whole matters.

column5: To attract larger current account balances, an IFI announced that every customer who maintains a current account balance exceeding USD 100,000 will receive a free safe deposit box and an exemption from money transfer charges. This offer is:
column6: Not permissible for the safe deposit box only, since transfer charges relate to withdrawals.
column7: Not permissible, because these are benefits not related to deposits and withdrawals, presented to the owners of current accounts in lieu of such accounts.
column8: Permissible, because the benefits are not stipulated in the current account contract, and a benefit that is not stipulated in a Qard may be given to the lender at any time during the period of the Qard.
column9: Permissible, because the institution may distinguish between owners of current accounts.
column11: Per 10/2, exemptions such as free deposit boxes and transfer charges given in lieu of current accounts are prohibited perquisites.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: A commercial lease expired and was not renewed, either expressly or by operation of a provision for automatic renewal. The tenant refused to vacate unless the owner paid him an amount for vacating the premises. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: Payment for vacating is not permitted, and the owner may take back his property after expiry of the term.
column7: The tenant is entitled to the payment if such payment is customary in the market.
column8: The tenant is entitled to the payment as compensation for waiving his right to the usufruct after expiry of the lease.
column9: The tenant is entitled to the payment if he has improved the premises during the lease.
column11: Per 8/2, payment for vacating is allowed only during the lease; after expiry without renewal none is permitted and the owner retakes the property.

column5: With respect to the ratio of profit distribution in a Mudarabah:
column6: Once agreed at the conclusion of the contract, it may not be changed, even if both the capital provider and the Mudarib agree to change it.
column7: It may be left to be determined at the date of liquidation according to the results, if the capital provider and the Mudarib agree to this in the contract.
column8: It may be changed only at the date of liquidation, and not before any profit has been realised.
column9: The parties shall agree on it when the contract is concluded, and may change it at any time and define the duration for which the agreement remains valid.
column11: Per 8/3, the ratio is agreed at conclusion and may be changed at any time, with the parties defining the period of validity.

column5: In the Shari'ah classification of utilization concession contracts as a form of Ju'alah:
column6: The State is the Ja'il (Ju'alah initiator), the licensee Institution is the 'Amil (hired party), and the specific amount received by the latter is the Ju'l.
column7: The State is the lessor of the mineral resources, the licensee is the lessee, and the Ju'l is the rent, which the licensee pays to the State in advance of extraction.
column8: The State is the Rabb al-Mal and the licensee is the Mudarib.
column9: The licensee Institution is the Ja'il and the State is the 'Amil.
column11: Per 5/3, the State is the Ja'il, the licensee is the 'Amil and its remuneration is the Ju'l.

column5: Musharakah certificates (Musharakah Sukuk) may be managed:
column6: On the basis of participation (Musharakah), by appointing one of the partners or another person to manage the operation.
column7: On the basis of Mudarabah, by appointing one of the partners or another person as the Mudarib for the management of the operation.
column8: On the basis of an investment agency, by appointing an agent to manage the operation on behalf of the certificate holders.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/6, Musharakah certificates are managed on the basis of participation, Mudarabah or an investment agency (3/6/1, 3/6/2).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of Musaqat from the Sunnah is:
column6: The Hadith narrated by Rafi' Ibn Khadij that there is no objection to paying the rental of land in gold and silver.
column7: The Hadith: "The Pen has been lifted from writing the deeds of three…", which establishes the competence of the parties and the permissibility of the contract.
column8: The Hadith: "Ill-gotten sapling shall have no right therein", narrated in the chapter on wasteland.
column9: The Hadith narrated by Ibn Umar that the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave the land of Khaybar to its inhabitants to cultivate for half of its yield.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it is the Khaybar Hadith of Ibn Umar; the other Hadiths support other rules.

column5: ………… is a partnership in profit whereby one party provides capital and the other party provides labour.
column6: Partnership in creditworthiness.
column7: Sharikat al-A'mal (service partnership).
column8: Mudarabah.
column9: Sharikat al-'Inan.
column11: Per 2, Mudarabah is a partnership in profit: Rab al-Mal provides capital and the Mudarib provides labour.

column5: In addition to its own share in the product, the State has the preemptory right of purchasing the quantities it needs from the output of a utilization concession:
column6: At the cost of production.
column7: Free of charge, as the owner of the minerals.
column8: According to the prevailing prices and contractual terms.
column9: At a price lower than the prevailing prices, in pursuance of public interest.
column11: Per 5/7/2, the State may buy the quantities it needs from the output according to the prevailing prices and contractual terms.

column5: The relationship between the policyholders and the insurance fund takes the form of:
column6: Mudarabah, in which the policyholders are Rabb al-Mal and the fund is the Mudarib, sharing the profit of investing the contributions in agreed proportions and bearing no liability for losses.
column7: A Mu'awadah contract in which contributions are paid against the insurance amount.
column8: Donation commitment at the stage of making contributions, and indemnification commitment at the stage of providing compensation for injury, as per regulations and underlying documents.
column9: Qard, in which the contributions are loans to be repaid out of the insurance surplus.
column11: Per 4/3, it is a donation commitment when contributing and an indemnification commitment when compensating injury.

column5: The partners in a Sharikah appointed, from the outset, an outside manager who is not a partner in return for 20% of the profit earned. At the end of the year, the manager claimed, in addition to his share of profit, a monthly salary for his management services. The correct ruling is:
column6: The manager is entitled only to remuneration for similar services, and the whole profit belongs to the partners, since he bears no loss of capital.
column7: The manager is classified as a Mudarib; he is entitled only to his share in the profit, if any, and deserves no further remuneration for management.
column8: The appointment is void, because a person who is not a partner may not manage a Sharikah, and the profit share is therefore unlawful.
column9: The manager is entitled to both the agreed share of profit and a salary for similar services, since management is a separate service from investing the capital.
column11: Per 3/1/3/3, a manager engaged from the outset for a profit percentage is a Mudarib, entitled only to his profit share.

column5: An IFI appointed an agent to sell its stock of a commodity, and instructed him to dispose of the commodity at the market price once a specific commodity index reaches a certain reading. This is:
column6: Permissible.
column7: Permissible, provided that the agent guarantees the selling price.
column8: Not permissible, because it links a sale contract to a specific index.
column9: Not permissible, because it constitutes trading in an index.
column11: Per 5/6, deals of the agent or Mudarib may be linked to an index so he sells at market price when the index hits a certain reading.

column5: It is permissible to stipulate that all outstanding instalments become due once the procrastinating debtor fails to pay an instalment, even if the failure to pay was caused by force majeure.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/1/6, acceleration may be stipulated unless the failure to pay was caused by force majeure.

column5: A cardholder asked a merchant to enter USD 1,050 on the payment terminal (POS), in the currency of the card, and to hand him USD 1,000 in cash. This is:
column6: Permitted, as the USD 50 is a service fee for the merchant.
column7: Not permitted.
column8: Permitted if the card is a debit card, since he takes cash out of his own balance.
column9: Permitted, provided the USD 50 does not exceed the actual direct cost of the service.
column11: Per 5/8/2, getting cash at a card acceptor that is less than the amount entered on the POS is not permitted (riba of excess per its basis).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a simultaneous combination of Ijarah and sale is:
column6: That Ijarah, unlike sale, is a contract that involves time.
column7: Making purchase contracts contingent upon leasing contracts is impermissible, being prohibited by the Hadith prohibiting two sales in one sale.
column8: The Hadith that prohibits one from selling what he does not own, since the lessor does not own the usufruct at the time of contracting, and a lease cannot be concluded before the asset is acquired by the lessor.
column9: That the lessee's ownership of the usufruct is limited.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, making purchase contingent on leasing is barred by the Hadith prohibiting two sales in one sale.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of giving an excess, in quantity or quality, at the time of repayment by way of generosity and goodwill, when it is neither stipulated nor customary, is:
column6: Resolution No. 13 (1/3) of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy on the recovery of actual costs.
column7: The Hadith of Abu Rafi' that the Prophet (peace be upon him) repaid a young camel with a full grown four year old camel, saying: 'The best people are those who do better in repayment.'
column8: The saying: "A Salaf (loan) and sale (in one contract) are not permitted."
column9: The Hadith of Anas Ibn Malik: 'When one of you grants a Qard and a gift is made to him by the borrower ... he is not to accept this from him, unless such a practice was prevalent among them prior to the Qard.'
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/2, the Hadith of Abu Rafi' (repaying with a better camel) permits an unstipulated excess at repayment.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: Need that justifies Gharar in a contract refers to:
column6: The situation when refraining from commitment of impermissible Gharar would lead to mortality, and only a public need, not a private need, is recognized for this purpose, even if there is no other permissible way.
column7: Any situation in which the contract involving Gharar brings the parties a greater profit than its permissible alternatives.
column8: The situation when refraining from commitment of impermissible Gharar leads to severe hardship, though may not amount to mortality, even if there is a permissible way of accomplishing the task through another contract.
column9: The situation when refraining from commitment of impermissible Gharar leads to severe hardship, though may not amount to mortality, provided there is no permissible way of accomplishing the task except through the contract that involves excessive Gharar.
column11: Per 4/4, need (public or private) is severe hardship short of mortality, and it must be inevitable: no permissible alternative way exists.

column5: The investment agent acts in a fiduciary capacity and is therefore not liable for any loss except in cases of wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract, unless:
column6: The breach happens to benefit the principal, such as selling an asset for more than the price he required.
column7: The loss occurs after the expiry of the agency term and before the funds are returned.
column8: The agency is unremunerated, in which case the agent is not liable even for negligence.
column9: The loss exceeds the amount of the fee to which the agent is entitled for the relevant investment period, in which case he bears the excess.
column11: Per 7/1, a breach advantageous to the principal (e.g., selling above the required price) does not make the agent liable.

column5: The state voluntarily pledged to indemnify the investors in an investment project against loss of capital, without any right of recourse to the investment manager. A state-owned holding company owns 70% of the investment manager. This undertaking is:
column6: Not valid, because a third party may never indemnify against loss of capital without recourse to the investment manager.
column7: Valid, provided that the state receives no fee for the undertaking.
column8: Not valid, because there is a direct or indirect ownership relationship of more than a half between the investment manager and the third party.
column9: Valid, because the state is a third party acting in the public interest.
column11: Per 4/2/4, the third party must be administratively independent with no ownership link of more than half with the manager.

column5: It is not permitted to impose on a customer who is the purchase orderer a guarantee regarding:
column6: The good performance by a supplier suggested by the customer of his contractual obligations towards the Institution.
column7: Hazards that may affect the item, such as damage and destruction during a period of shipment or storage.
column8: Compensation of actual damage to the Institution arising from his breach of a binding promise.
column9: Payment of the Murabahah debt by way of cheques or promissory notes provided before execution of the contract.
column11: Per 2/5/2, the purchase orderer may not be made to guarantee damage or destruction of the item during shipment or storage, as he is not its owner.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, specifying a lump-sum compensation for the worker in Musaqat:
column6: Will divert the contract away from the features of Musaqat; a known common share is required to avert impermissible obscurity (Jahalah).
column7: Is permissible if it is combined with a share of the produce.
column8: Is permissible, as it removes the uncertainty of the produce and thereby avoids Jahalah.
column9: Is permissible if the lump sum does not exceed the market wage for similar work, since the worker is then a hired worker.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/1, a lump sum diverts the contract from Musaqat; a known common share averts Jahalah.

column5: A master agreement (general framework) between an institution and a client wishing to enter into Murabahah transactions:
column6: Binds the institution, but not the client, to enter into the future transactions on the terms and conditions agreed in the framework.
column7: Is a concluded transaction which obliges the client, upon signing the framework, to enter into the Murabahah contracts described in it, whether or not the institution has yet acquired the assets, failing which the client owes damages.
column8: Is a bilateral promise that binds neither party to enter into those transactions; once a Murabahah contract is concluded by offer and acceptance, it becomes subject to the master agreement's terms.
column9: Is a prohibited bilateral promise, since it relates to future sales and binds both parties to their terms.
column11: Per 4/4, a master agreement is a non-binding bilateral promise; each party has an option, and concluded contracts adopt its terms.

column5: Prohibiting all matters that may increase the debt in volume or value against an increase in the time of settlement is based on its being a form of ribā al-jāhiliyah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1/3/3, an increase of debt against deferment is ribā al-jāhiliyah.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: A gold trading platform sells customers gold ingots for currency. Each customer receives a statement showing the weight of gold he owns from the platform's general stock, without any serial numbers or distinct marks, and customers cannot request physical delivery. This sale is:
column6: Permissible, provided that the gold stock is insured by the platform.
column7: Permissible, because the statement realizes constructive possession of the ingots, being issued by a recognized agency.
column8: Permissible, provided that the statement is issued on the trade date (T+0) by a recognized agency, even if the ingot is unallocated.
column9: Not permissible, because it is not permissible to sell an unspecified (unallocated) ingot without physical possession.
column11: Per 3/4, an unallocated ingot may not be sold without physical possession; constructive possession needs a specified, deliverable ingot.

column5: The guarantee given by the customer of the good performance of a supplier he suggested lapses if the Murabahah contract is not executed, because the customer gives it in his capacity as purchase orderer.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/5/1, the customer gives it in his personal capacity, so it remains valid even if the Murabahah is not executed.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: A Fatwa issuer may issue different Fatwas on the same subject and the same issue, according to the source of the Fatwa request.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 12/2, the Fatwa issuer should avoid issuing different Fatwas on the same issue according to the source of the request.

column5: If the Institution has not been enabled to invest a legal deposit retained by a bank on request of the concerned authorities for licensing, it shall pay Zakah on it for only one year at the time of refund.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/3/4/8, an uninvestable legal deposit attracts Zakah for one year only, at the time of refund.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: With regard to fees charged by the depository for safekeeping gold:
column6: They may be a lump sum or a percentage of the value of the deposited gold; but if the gold is collateral against the depositor's loan, they shall not exceed the actual cost of safekeeping.
column7: They may be a percentage of the value of the gold in all cases, including where the gold is collateral against a loan, provided that the percentage is agreed at the outset and does not exceed the market rate.
column8: No fee may be charged where the gold is deposited as collateral against a loan.
column9: They must be a lump sum and may not be a percentage of the value of the deposited gold.
column11: Per 5/4/2, fees may be lump sum or a percentage, but for gold held as collateral for the depositor's loan they are capped at actual cost.

column5: In the prepaid card, the card issuer may allow the cardholder to use more than the card balance (overdrawing the balance) against a consideration, provided that the consideration is agreed upon in advance.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2/1, the prepaid card must not lead to lending on interest, e.g., overdrawing the balance against a consideration.

column5: In valuing the receivables of a Sharikah at constructive valuation, it is permissible to discount the amount of the debt on the basis of current value as consideration for earlier payment.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/5/9, time value of money and discounting on the basis of current value are not permitted in valuing receivables.

column5: If the remuneration for the construction of a project under a construction concession is determined in terms of a certain amount of money:
column6: The licensee must hand over the project to the State immediately upon completion, and the price becomes a debt owed by the State, payable in instalments out of the revenues of the project during the concession period, with no right of utilization for the licensee.
column7: The licensee retains the ownership of the project to ascertain his right to the price through its utilization, and may arrange a clearance deal with the licensor to receive the full price and hand over the project before the end of the period.
column8: The licensee may utilize the project for the specified period only, even if he has not received the full amount agreed upon.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/3/2, the licensee keeps the project to recover the price by utilization, unless a clearance deal pays him in full earlier.

column5: In the charge card, the card issuer usually:
column6: Receives no commission on the goods and services paid for by the card.
column7: Levies a charge on the cardholder as a percentage of the prices of goods and services paid for by the card, in addition to the commission it receives from the acquirer and the card network.
column8: Receives a commission directly from the card acceptor, without the involvement of the acquirer.
column9: Does not levy a charge on the cardholder for the goods and services paid for by the card, but receives from the acquirer a commission as a percentage of their prices.
column11: Per 3/3/5, the issuer usually charges the cardholder nothing on purchases but receives a percentage commission from the acquirer.

column5: The Institution, when acting as manufacturer, may appoint the ultimate purchaser as its agent to supervise the manufacturing process because agency is permissible and there is nothing against it in Istisna'a, provided it is done with the agreement of the parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 5/2.

column5: ………… binds the payee bank to fulfil its conditions by crediting the amount of the cheque to the beneficiary's account.
column6: Banker's cheque.
column7: Travellers' cheque.
column8: Account payee cheque.
column9: Overdraft cheque.
column11: Per 3/3(d), an account payee cheque binds the payee bank to credit the amount to the beneficiary's account.

column5: In principle, the mortgaged object should be a tangible asset; yet it can be:
column6: A share of common property, even if it cannot be identified or sold separately.
column7: A debt, a cash amount, a fungible asset or a consumable commodity.
column8: An asset that is not yet specified, provided that it can possibly be delivered.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 3/2/2, it may be a debt, cash, fungible or consumable; a common share must be identifiable and separately saleable; per 3/2/1 it must be specified.

column5: Protection of capital and investments differs from a guarantee of invested capital in that:
column6: Protection is narrower than a guarantee, as it covers only the loss of capital and not its decrease or destruction, while a guarantee covers all three.
column7: There is no difference, since both mean that the investment manager bears the loss of capital.
column8: Protection means using available methods to prevent loss, decrease or destruction, and is wider than a guarantee, which is an undertaking by a particular party to bear any loss, decrease or destruction of the capital.
column9: Protection is an undertaking by a particular party to bear any loss, decrease or destruction of the capital, while a guarantee refers to the safeguarding of capital by available methods.
column11: Per item 2, protection (safeguarding by available methods) is wider than a guarantee (a party's undertaking to bear the loss).

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The necessary measures for conversion include:
column6: Forming a Shari'ah supervisory board and an internal Shari'ah compliance department in accordance with the Governance Standards issued by AAOIFI.
column7: Amending the bank's by-laws so that they include objectives and operational measures appropriate to Islamic banking, and cleansing them from anything that contradicts the nature of Islamic banking.
column8: Reformatting or designing standard contracts or specimens of documents that comply with Shari'ah rules and principles.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2, 3/4 and 3/5, all three are necessary measures for conversion.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for stipulating that wealth given as Qard be known is:
column6: To enable the borrower to return a similar substitute of the wealth of Qard.
column7: To enable the institution to determine the service charges as a percentage of the loan.
column8: That Qard is a purely commutative contract like sale.
column9: To enable the lender to calculate the return on the loan.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Qard wealth must be known so that the borrower can return a similar substitute.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: Regarding the upper limit for profits in transactions:
column6: Profit must not exceed the prevailing market interest rate for the same tenor, in order to avoid exploitation.
column7: There is no upper limit for profits, provided the transaction is based on mutual consent, with due regard to kindness, contentment and clemency.
column8: Profit must not exceed one third of the cost price, even if the transaction is based on mutual consent.
column9: The upper limit for profits is set by each institution's Shari'ah Supervisory Board, according to the type of transaction and the cost of funds.
column11: Per 4/1, there is no upper limit on profit where there is mutual consent, with regard for kindness, contentment and clemency.

column5: It is permissible, with the approval of the creditors, to agree to reduce an undue debt that was accelerated by the declaration of insolvency. In this case, the guarantors:
column6: Are released completely from the guarantee.
column7: Are liable only for the difference between the amount originally guaranteed and the reduced amount.
column8: Are liable to pay the reduced amount, rather than the amount originally guaranteed.
column9: Remain liable for the amount originally guaranteed.
column11: Per 5/6, guarantors are liable to pay the reduced amount, rather than the amount originally guaranteed.

column5: The hiring contract can be terminated on the basis of a conditional option (Khiyar al-Shart), by the party who has stipulated such option, and within its specified period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/2/2, a conditional option allows the stipulating party to terminate within the option period.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the requirement that the capital must be paid at the conclusion of a Salam contract includes:
column6: That Salam was so named because the capital must be paid in advance, and delaying payment of the capital until the parties disperse renders the transaction a sale of debt for debt.
column7: That the seller must be able to deliver at the date of delivery, and the buyer must therefore verify the seller's solvency before concluding the contract and may require security for the capital paid in advance.
column8: That a penalty may not be stipulated in excess of the principal amount of debts, which would otherwise turn the delayed capital into a loan with benefit.
column9: That the consideration in exchange contracts must be known so as to remove any uncertainty, and the capital must therefore be stated in a single currency and in a definite amount.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Salam means payment in advance; delaying the capital after the parties disperse makes it a prohibited sale of debt for debt.

column5: If the Institution, under an authority received from the customer, sells the asset as a result of the customer's failure to pay the selling price on its due date:
column6: It may retain the whole proceeds of sale as compensation for the default.
column7: It must confine itself to recovering the amount due to it and must return the balance to the customer.
column8: It may retain from the proceeds the amount due plus an additional late-payment charge for its own benefit.
column9: It must pay the balance, after recovering the amount due, to charitable causes.
column11: Per 5/4, on selling the asset for non-payment the Institution recovers only its due and returns the balance to the customer.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the permissibility of Musaqat may also be deduced by analogy with Mudarabah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, Musaqat's permissibility may also be deduced by analogy with Mudarabah.

column5: Constructive possession includes:
column6: The registration of a mortgage of immovables through registration that is valid under the law.
column7: The registration of hypothecation of mobile movables like cars, trains, steamers and airplanes through registration that is valid under the law.
column8: The possession of documents, like bills of lading and warehouse receipts, issued in the name of the possessor or acknowledging his interest therein, if the goods are ascertained through them and the possessor is able to undertake transactions in them.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/4 and 3/5, registered mortgages/hypothecations and qualifying documents of title are all forms of constructive possession.

column5: An endorsement of a bill of exchange on behalf of a client who requires the Institution to transfer, after collection, the amount of the instrument into his account is:
column6: Not a Hawalah, but a contract of agency that is permissible with or without consideration.
column7: A restricted Hawalah, since the Institution holds the client's account.
column8: A contract of agency that is permissible only without consideration.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 12/5/2, this is not Hawalah but agency, permissible with or without consideration.

column5: According to the view that recognises the right to reclamation, reclamation is the cancellation of the sale, and it requires the decision of a judge.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, reclamation takes place immediately and does not need a judge's decision or the authority's knowledge.

column5: In all cases of substitution of Waqf assets, the following conditions are required:
column6: The substituting asset shall not be less in value or lower in revenue generation than the substituted asset, based on the evaluation of fair experts.
column7: Suspicion and favouritism in the substitution are dismissed.
column8: The purchase of the substituting asset may be deferred until the end of the financial year to obtain a better price, whatever the need.
column9: a. and b.
column11: Per 10/1/5, (a) and (b) are required; the substituting asset must be bought immediately unless needed to find a suitable one.

column5: The basis of prohibiting the card issuer from charging an increase over the actual direct cost for the fees linked to the loan in the card includes:
column6: Such fees are against services offered by the card network, which do not include lending, and are therefore capped at the amounts that the network charges the issuer, no matter what other costs the issuer bears.
column7: It would be an artifice to charge an increase over the loan, so it would be a loan carrying benefit, falling under the Ḥadīth: It is not permitted to sell with a loan.
column8: It would involve gharar, since the actual cost is unknown at the time of contracting.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/1/1, an excess is an artifice for a loan with benefit; option A is the basis for unrestricted fees (5/1/2).

column5: It is permissible for the creation of Waqf:
column6: To be contingent upon a condition, e.g., the Institution creates a Waqf over some of its assets subject to the approval of the supervisory authority.
column7: To be concluded with an undertaking to create Waqf, provided that the Waqif fixes a date for its execution.
column8: To be contingent upon the Waqif's death, in which case it is a binding Waqf from the time of creation and is not limited to any portion of his estate.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4/1/3 Waqf may be contingent on a condition; an undertaking does not create Waqf (2/4/1/2); Waqf upon death is a bequest within one-third (2/4/1/4).

column5: ………… is the method in which the insurance company presents the individual risk which constitutes the subject matter of reinsurance to the reinsurer, along with a summary of all the information related to it, so that the reinsurer can decide whether to accept the risk or not:
column6: Comprehensive reinsurance (reinsurance agreement).
column7: Risk sharing reinsurance.
column8: Selective reinsurance.
column9: Loss reinsurance.
column11: Per 4/1, in selective reinsurance each individual risk is presented to the reinsurer, which is bound only by what it accepts.

column5: A customer instructed a merchant to purchase a specific item and resolutely promised to buy it from him. The merchant purchased the item for 100 solely in reliance on the promise, but the customer refused to buy it. The merchant sold the item to a third party for 90, whereas he would have earned a profit of 10 had the customer bought it. The customer must indemnify the merchant for:
column6: 100, against the merchant delivering the item to him.
column7: 10, being the difference between the cost of the item and the price obtained by the merchant.
column8: Nothing, since a promise is only a religious obligation.
column9: 20, being the difference between the cost and the price obtained, plus the lost profit.
column11: Per 3/4, the promisor indemnifies actual loss (cost minus price obtained); actual loss does not include opportunity cost.

column5: If the debt owed to the Institution is a cash amount, the Institution should pay Zakah on it only when the debt becomes due.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/3/1, Zakah is paid annually on cash debts owed to the Institution whether due or not, since it will certainly receive them.

column5: A worker (irrigator) died after working for six months under an Irrigation Partnership contract with no non-assignability stipulation. His heir chose not to complete the work, and the owner completed it by hiring others. Upon materialization of the crop, the heir is entitled to:
column6: A wage at the market rate for similar work for the period worked by the deceased, without any cap, payable by the owner.
column7: The deceased's full stipulated share of the crop, as the work was completed on his behalf.
column8: Nothing, since the heir chose not to complete the work under the contract.
column9: A market-rate wage for the period worked by the deceased, capped at his stipulated share of the crop.
column11: Per 12/3, the successor gets a market wage for the deceased's period of work, capped at the stipulated share.

column5: The Institution buys items by Istisna'a on the basis of a clear specification and pays the price in cash at conclusion, to provide liquidity to the manufacturer. It then sells similar items to another party by Parallel Istisna'a. This is permissible on condition that:
