column6: The delivery date in the parallel (sale) contract precedes that in the original purchase contract, so that the Institution can deliver in time.
column7: The two contracts are linked, so that delivery under the sale contract depends on delivery under the purchase contract, and the Institution bears no risk of non-performance by the manufacturer.
column8: The delivery date stipulated in the parallel (sale) contract does not precede that in the original purchase contract, and the two contracts remain separate.
column9: The price in the parallel contract does not exceed the price in the original contract, so that the Institution makes no profit from the two.
column11: Per 7/1, the parallel sale's delivery date may not precede the original purchase's, and the two contracts must remain separate.

column5: Among the Shari'ah bases for the prohibition of stipulating a contract of sale within the contract of Qard is:
column6: The Hadith of Abu Rafi' on repaying a young camel with a better one, which shows that any stipulated excess over the loan is permitted.
column7: The Hadith of Anas Ibn Malik on not accepting a gift or free ride from the borrower.
column8: The saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "A Salaf (loan) and sale (in one contract) are not permitted ..."
column9: The reports from the Companions on repayment in another land.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 7, the Hadith "A Salaf and sale are not permitted" prohibits combining Qard and sale in one contract.

column5: The insurance contract expires at the end of its stipulated period just like Ijarah, because it is a time-specific contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, the insurance contract is time-specific and expires at the end of its period like Ijarah.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The Shari'ah rulings for gold set out in the Standard also apply to:
column6: Platinum, palladium and nickel, which are called white gold in some countries.
column7: White gold.
column8: Precious metals other than gold and silver.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/6 the rulings apply to white gold (and per 10/1 to silver), but not to platinum, palladium or nickel, nor other precious metals.

column5: ………… is a form of partnership in which one of the partners promises to buy the equity share of the other partner gradually until the title to the equity is completely transferred to him.
column6: Allotment (Muhassah) partnership.
column7: Partnership in commendum.
column8: Partnership in creditworthiness.
column9: Diminishing Musharakah.
column11: Per 5/1, this is the definition of diminishing Musharakah.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of stipulating a defect exclusion clause in respect of the leased asset is that:
column6: Such a condition defeats the purpose of the contract, the exchange of usufruct for rentals; if the usufruct is impaired, receipt of rentals becomes unjust enrichment.
column7: Contractual stipulations are primarily valid and enforceable.
column8: The owner of the asset is responsible for insuring it, and the lessor is the owner, so that any defect must be covered by insurance that the lessor takes out at his own expense, which cannot be excluded.
column9: A buyer may relinquish his right to require guarantee of hidden defects.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, excluding defects defeats the exchange of usufruct for rent, making rentals for impaired usufruct unjust enrichment.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: An IFI purchased a quantity of copper on a spot basis from Broker X and sold it to its customer on a deferred payment basis. The customer then sold the copper on a spot basis to Broker X, from whom the IFI had initially bought it, at a price lower than the deferred price. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because the customer sold to Broker X and not to the IFI itself, and buy-back is prohibited only between the parties to the deferred sale, whatever the price at which the commodity is resold.
column7: Prohibited only if the price paid by Broker X is less than 90% of the deferred price.
column8: Prohibited, because the avoidance of buy-back is stipulated in this application, and the customer sold the commodity to the one from whom it was initially bought on a spot basis at a lesser price.
column9: Permissible, because each sale was concluded with a separate offer and acceptance.
column11: Per 4/1/4, avoiding buy-back is required: the buyer may not resell to the original spot seller at less than the deferred price.

column5: With respect to commercial papers that are not yet due, it is permitted:
column6: To pay an amount that is less than the value of the paper to the first beneficiary before maturity.
column7: To have the paper discounted by a bank for a fee proportional to the period remaining.
column8: To sell the paper to a third party for an amount less than its value, whether in cash or on deferred payment.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 6/1, discounting is not permitted, but paying the first beneficiary less than the value before maturity is.

column5: According to the Standard, a promise to perform a permissible action or financial transaction:
column6: Is neither a religious nor a legal obligation, unless the promise is documented in a separate written undertaking.
column7: Is legally binding only if it is documented in writing, even if the promisee incurs no liability as a result of it, and the promisor has no excuse for non-performance.
column8: Is a religious obligation to fulfil, but legally binding only where there is real need, such as when the promisor causes the promisee to incur a liability.
column9: Is legally binding in all cases, since breaking a promise without an excuse is a sin.
column11: Per 3/4, fulfilling it is a religious duty; it is legally binding only where there is a real need, e.g., the promisee incurs a liability.

column5: The payer is entitled to all rights associated with the securities that were available to the transferor, since these securities are associated with the debt that is the subject matter of the Hawalah.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis on 9/2, securities attached to the transferred debt pass with it, so the payer is entitled to them.

column5: The standard on Guarantees does not cover:
column6: The distinction between liabilities and the assets held on trust.
column7: Guarantees against torts.
column8: Securities in the form of written documents and attestations.
column9: Securities in the form of mortgages, cheques and promissory notes.
column11: Per the scope (1), guarantees against torts are excluded; the other items are expressly covered.

column5: Where the parties draw up a memorandum of understanding (general framework) for concluding successive Salam contracts, the memorandum determines:
column6: The framework of the contract and the intention of the parties to buy and sell.
column7: The quantity and specifications of the goods, the manner of their delivery, the basis for determining the price, and the manner of payment.
column8: The types of guarantees and other prospective arrangements.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1/1, the memorandum sets the framework, intention, quantity, specifications, delivery, price basis, payment and guarantees.

column5: The contract of a Muhassah (allotment) partnership is binding, and a partner may not terminate his participation before the liquidation of the company's assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/5/2/3-4, it is not binding unless agreed for a period; a partner may withdraw with notice if no damage results.

column5: An Istisna'a contract may include a clause that extra expenses resulting from additional conditions later imposed by directives of the relevant authorities, which the manufacturer is not obliged to bear under the contract or by law, will be borne by the ultimate purchaser.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is permitted by 4/2/5, as it is agreed by the parties and does not affect the purpose of the contract.

column5: In principle, the division of the produce in Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat):
column6: Covers only the produce of the first season, unless the parties agree otherwise.
column7: Covers the fruits and the trees themselves, in proportion to the stipulated shares.
column8: Covers all recurring produce of the trees, such as fruits and palm leaves, unless the parties agree to restrict it to the fruits.
column9: Is restricted to the fruits, unless the parties agree in writing to include other recurring produce such as palm leaves and prunings.
column11: Per 9/1, all recurring produce is shared in principle, unless the parties restrict sharing to the fruits.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of constructive valuation in distributing profit includes:
column6: The Hadith of Al-Sa'ib Ibn Abu Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi, the partner of the Prophet (peace be upon him).
column7: The Hadith: 'If a co-owner of a slave frees his part, the slave will be set free against his property if he has property; otherwise, it will be valued by fair value and freed.'
column8: The Hadith of Ibn Umar concerning selling camels in one currency and collecting payment in another, which allows payment at the price of the day of payment and so permits valuation.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, constructive valuation is supported by the Hadith on the co-owned slave, and its use in Zakah and theft.

column5: When a current account is mortgaged for the benefit of the same institution with which it is opened:
column6: The mortgage is invalid, because the account is a debt owed by the mortgagee himself, and a debt cannot be mortgaged to its debtor under any condition.
column7: The institution should not use the account unless the two parties agree to transfer it to an investment account, and thus make it subject to the rulings on Mudarabah instead of the rulings on loan.
column8: The institution may use the account, provided it pays the account holder a fixed return, which is agreed upon in the mortgage contract.
column9: The institution may use the account freely, since a current account is a loan guaranteed by the institution, and any benefit from it is the institution's right, so the account holder cannot object to its use.
column11: Per 5, the institution must not use a mortgaged current account unless it is converted into an investment account governed by Mudarabah.

column5: The borrower comes to own the subject-matter of Qard (the wealth loaned):
column6: By the mere conclusion of the contract, even before possession, and he is then liable for the repayment of a similar subject-matter.
column7: Through possession, and he becomes liable for the repayment of a similar subject-matter.
column8: Only upon the expiry of the period of the loan.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/4/1, the borrower owns the loaned wealth through possession and becomes liable for a similar subject-matter.

column5: The permissibility of the lessee leasing the asset back to its owner is based on the lessee owning the usufruct, so that he may dispose of it by leasing it to the owner or to others.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/3, the lessee owns the usufruct and may lease it to the owner or others.

column5: Holding the documents which represent the ownership of the goods as a mortgage is permissible, because:
column6: The documents are financial papers that can be traded independently of the goods.
column7: It is a form of darak guarantee.
column8: Possession of the documents is considered as possession of the goods themselves.
column9: The documents represent a debt owed by the carrier.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, possessing the documents counts as possessing the goods, and the holder can dispose of the goods like an owner.

column5: With regard to Islamic insurance (Takaful) as a benefit for the cardholder:
column6: The Institution, with the consent of the cardholder, may obtain an additional Islamic insurance for his benefit and deduct the subscription from him, whether or not with a commission for the Institution.
column7: The Institution may provide conventional life insurance if no Takaful company is available.
column8: The Institution may obtain an additional Islamic insurance for the cardholder and deduct the subscription from him without his consent, provided that the subscription is disclosed in the card agreement and is not excessive.
column9: The Institution may obtain an additional Islamic insurance for the cardholder, but it may not take any commission for that.
column11: Per 5/6/3, with the cardholder's consent the Institution may obtain extra Takaful and deduct the subscription, with or without commission.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: All interest-based investment instruments must cease to be used and must be replaced by permissible investment instruments, such as:
column6: Mudarabah, all Shari'ah-nominate partnerships, diminishing Musharakah and sharecropping partnerships.
column7: Financing by way of deferred sales, Murabahah, Salam, Istisna'a, operating Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek.
column8: Interest-based loans whose interest is channelled to charity.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/1, (a) and (b) are listed alternatives; interest-based lending must cease entirely.

column5: The opening of credit by the buyer (orderer):
column6: Is not a final payment of the price; the buyer remains liable until the bank pays the value of the documents, but the seller may not request payment from the buyer while the credit subsists and is valid.
column7: Is considered a final payment of the price that discharges the buyer from any further liability, even if the bank fails to pay the value of the documents to the seller, who may then claim only from the bank.
column8: Entitles the seller to request payment directly from the buyer at any time, even while the credit is valid, since the buyer remains liable for the price until it is paid in full by the bank or by himself.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 2/4/2, opening the credit is not final payment; the buyer stays liable, but the seller cannot claim from him while the credit is valid.

column5: Where the assets of a corporation are cash exclusively, whether during the period of subscription, prior to the commencement of its business or at the time of liquidation, trading in its shares is not permissible except:
column6: At their nominal value and with the condition of delivery of possession.
column7: At market value, with deferred settlement, provided that the price is paid within three days.
column8: At a premium not exceeding 5% of the nominal value.
column9: After observing the rules for dealing in debts.
column11: Per 3/17, shares of an all-cash corporation may be traded only at nominal value with delivery of possession.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: The Board of an Institution issued a Fatwa declaring a new product structure permissible. The management, for practical reasons, decided not to offer the product. The correct position is:
column6: The Institution may refrain from following the Fatwa, but its rejection of the Board's Fatwa should be reported to the General Assembly of the Institution.
column7: The Institution must seek a Fatwa from another board before refraining.
column8: The Institution may refrain from following the Fatwa without reporting to anyone, since a Fatwa of permissibility creates no obligation.
column9: The Institution is obliged to offer the product, since it must follow the Fatwa regardless of the satisfaction of the management.
column11: Per 6/1, a Fatwa of permissibility may be declined for practical needs, but the rejection must be reported to the General Assembly.

column5: ………… is a bilateral agreement between two or more parties to conclude a partnership to buy assets on credit on the basis of their reputation for the purpose of making profit, whereby they undertake to fulfil their obligations according to the percentages determined by the parties.
column6: Sharikat al-'Inan, in which each partner contributes capital.
column7: Service partnership (Sharikat al-A'mal), in which the partners render professional services.
column8: Partnership in creditworthiness (liability partnership).
column9: Allotment (Muhassah) partnership, which has no juristic personality.
column11: Per 3/2/1, this is the definition of the partnership in creditworthiness (Sharikat al-Wujuh, liability partnership).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for acknowledging custom ('Urf) as the basis for the realisation of possession is:
column6: Analogy (Qiyas) with the contract of Sarf.
column7: A resolution of the Islamic Fiqh Academy only.
column8: The view of the Hanafi school alone.
column9: The consensus (Ijma') of the Jurists (Fuqaha).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, recourse to custom for possession rests on the consensus (Ijma') of the jurists.

column5: It is not permissible to combine agency and personal guarantees in one contract at the same time (the same party acting as agent and as guarantor), because:
column6: Such a combination conflicts with the nature of these contracts.
column7: A guarantee given by a party acting as an agent in respect of an investment turns the transaction into an interest-based loan, since the capital is guaranteed in addition to the proceeds of the investment.
column8: The agent would be entitled to two remunerations for one service.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 2/2/2, both (a) and (b) are the stated reasons; the double-remuneration reason is not mentioned.

column5: ………… are shares that grant the participant compensation in lieu of his shares, whose value is redeemed during the existence of the company, while granting him the rights of shares based on capital, except that they are entitled to lesser profit and share in the assets at winding up only after the owners of capital shares are paid:
column6: Tamattu' shares.
column7: Preference shares.
column8: Ordinary shares.
column9: Bearer shares.
column11: Per 2/7, these are Tamattu' shares, whose issuance is not permissible.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The right of an individual to a public easement may be transferred to others for consideration, since public easements are financial rights.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/1, an individual's right to a public easement is restricted to personal use only.

column5: Hikr is subject to the following conditions, except:
column6: There is no person who is willing to have fixed-term rent and make advance payment so as to be spent on developing the Waqf.
column7: The Waqf has no income to be used for its development.
column8: Istibdal (exchange) of the Waqf is not possible.
column9: The tenant pays, at the time of signing the lease contract, a lump sum amount for development of the Waqf.
column11: Per 6/3/1, the three conditions of Hikr are those it lists. The lump sum (Kardar) belongs to Haqq al-Qarar under 6/3/2.

column5: The basis of giving the card issuer the right to retain the service fees on a pro-rata basis upon cancellation is:
column6: The fees are compensation for the damage suffered by the issuer due to the cancellation.
column7: The card network has already charged the issuer for the whole validity period.
column8: The fees are against a specific job which was completed upon issuance of the card, so the issuer is entitled to all of them, whatever the period elapsed and whether or not the services remained available.
column9: The service provider is entitled to the fee by enabling possession of the usufruct, which can be estimated by the period elapsed from the time of making it available.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/2/2, the fee is earned by enabling possession of the usufruct, measured by the elapsed period.

column5: It is permitted to sell a monetary debt to a third party:
column6: For a commodity with deferred delivery, such as making a debt owed by a third party the Salam capital.
column7: For cash at a discount reflecting the remaining term, since the buyer then bears the risk of the debtor's insolvency or procrastination.
column8: For a usufruct or service with unascertained subject delivery, provided that the debtor acknowledges the debt.
column9: For a commodity with spot delivery, or for a usufruct or service whose delivery can be ascertained at the time of sale.
column11: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may be sold for a spot commodity or an ascertained usufruct or service, not for deferred or unascertained ones.

column5: Prior possession of a tangible thing stands in place of subsequent lawful possession due to a cause acknowledged by the Shari'ah:
column6: Only if the prior possession was on the basis of the liability to bear loss (Daman).
column7: Only if the prior possession and the subsequent possession are of the same nature (both of liability or both of trust), since a possession of trust cannot replace one of liability, nor can one of liability replace one of trust.
column8: Irrespective of the prior possession being on the basis of liability (Daman) or of trust (Amanah), and of the subsequent possession entailing liability for loss or a burden of trust.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/6, prior possession replaces subsequent possession irrespective of either being of liability (Daman) or trust (Amanah).

column5: Debt, for the purposes of the Standard on Sale of Debt, does not include liabilities arising out of misconduct or negligence.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per item 2, debt includes debts arising out of a loan, a commutative contract, or misconduct or negligence.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: It is permissible to lease gold:
column6: Only as an identified asset, with the rent payable in advance, since a lease described in the lessor's liability involves Gharar.
column7: In the form of jewelry only, since ingots are a medium of exchange that cannot be leased, and the rent for such jewelry may be payable in arrears only, never in advance or in gold.
column8: Whether as jewelry or ingots, provided the corpus is not consumed; the rent may be payable in advance or in arrears, for an identified asset or Ijarah Mawsufah Fi Zhimmah.
column9: Provided that the rent is not payable in gold.
column11: Per 5/3/1, jewelry or ingots may be leased if the corpus is not consumed; rent may be advance or arrears, identified or described.

column5: Among the bases for the impermissibility of futures contracts for shares is that they imply the stipulation of delay in the delivery of an ascertained sold thing (shares), and that delay in both the price and the priced thing is the sale of a debt for a debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. These are among the grounds given in the Shari'ah basis for 3/12.

column5: If a prize is meant for one or a limited number of persons and a larger number becomes entitled to it, a draw may be resorted to in order to determine the winner(s).
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/4, where more persons become entitled to a limited prize, a draw may determine the winner(s).

column5: It is not permitted to sell the debt to a third party if the sale has excessive gharar, such as:
column6: The debt is not established either by acknowledgement or by evidence.
column7: Lack of knowledge (jahāla) of the amount of debt.
column8: The debtor has not consented to the sale.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/5, an unestablished debt or an unknown amount entails excessive gharar; the debtor's consent is not required (5/6).

column5: ………… is the transfer of ownership in fungible wealth to a person on whom it is binding to return wealth similar to it:
column6: Wadi'ah (deposit).
column7: Qard (loan).
column8: Credit sale.
column9: Hibah (gift).
column11: Per 2, Qard is the transfer of ownership in fungible wealth to a person bound to return wealth similar to it.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, Murabahah is one of the trust-based contracts that depends on transparency as to the actual purchasing price or cost price in addition to common expenses.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis defines Murabahah as a trust-based contract depending on transparency of cost and common expenses.

column5: It is permissible for a partner in a Sharikah to issue a binding promise to buy, either within the period of operation or at the time of liquidation, all the assets of the Sharikah:
column6: On the basis of their face value, as agreed at the time of the promise.
column7: On the basis of the original cost of the assets, as agreed in the promise.
column8: At their market value or as agreed at the date of buying.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/6/2, the promise may be at market value or a price agreed at the date of buying; face value is not allowed.

column5: In Tawarruq with the pledge of securities, the commodity may be sold to the seller from whom it was purchased, provided that the sale is at spot.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/6/3/4 (c), the commodity may not be sold to the seller from whom it was purchased.

column5: It is permissible for the buyer in Salam to exchange al-Muslam Fihi for other goods:
column6: Except currency, after the delivery date falls due, if not stipulated in the contract, whether or not similar in kind, provided the substitute is suitable as al-Muslam Fihi for the capital and its market value is not greater than that of al-Muslam Fihi at delivery.
column7: Including currency, at any time before or after the delivery date, provided the market value of the substitute is not greater than that of al-Muslam Fihi at delivery.
column8: Only if the substitution was stipulated in the Salam contract, and the substitute is of the same kind and of a market value not exceeding that of the capital paid by the buyer at the time of contracting.
column9: Only if the substitute is of the same kind as al-Muslam Fihi and its market value equals the market value of al-Muslam Fihi when the contract was concluded, and provided the substitution was agreed after the delivery date had fallen due, and the seller consents to it.
column11: Per 4/2, substitution (not currency) is allowed after the due date if not pre-stipulated, and its value may not exceed al-Muslam Fihi's.

column5: In principle, Zakah should be spent on its eight heads, yet if need arises Zakah funds can be utilized in investment projects, provided that:
column6: The profits of the projects are distributed to the Zakah recipients, while the projects themselves remain owned by the Institution, even before the urgent needs of the recipients are met.
column7: The projects are, at the end, owned by the Zakah recipients or put under the supervision of the competent Shari'ah body for Zakah, and investment is after fulfilling the urgent needs of recipients with sufficient safeguards against losses.
column8: The projects are approved by the general assembly of the Institution, whatever the needs of the recipients.
column9: The investment yields a guaranteed minimum return for the Zakah recipients, and the projects are approved by the general assembly of the Institution.
column11: Per 10/4, Zakah-funded projects must end up owned by recipients or under the competent Shari'ah Zakah body, after urgent needs, with loss safeguards.

column5: An IFI entered into an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek for 60 monthly instalments, combined, through a separate document, with a gift of the asset contingent upon payment of the remaining rental instalments. The lessee paid 59 instalments and then failed to pay the last one. The ruling is:
column6: Ownership is not transferred to the lessee, since the condition of the gift has not been fulfilled.
column7: Ownership is transferred, since the lessee has paid the substantial majority of the instalments.
column8: Ownership is transferred in proportion to the instalments paid (59/60).
column9: Ownership is transferred, but the last instalment remains a debt on the lessee.
column11: Per 8/4, if payment falls short of even one instalment, the contingent gift's condition is unmet and ownership does not pass.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Mudarabah covers:
column6: Mudarabah contracts between the Institution and other entities or individuals, and joint and special purpose investment accounts if administered on the basis of Mudarabah.
column7: Sukuk of Mudarabah (Mudarabah Certificates), which are issued to the public to finance a project and are tradable in the secondary market after the subscription period, and also in the primary market.
column8: Other types of partnership contracts, such as Sharikat al-'Inan, in addition to Mudarabah contracts of every kind.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per the Scope, it covers Mudarabah contracts and Mudarabah-based investment accounts; Mudarabah Sukuk and other partnerships have separate standards.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If the deposited gold is damaged or defected due to misconduct, negligence or violation of the contractual terms by the depository, the depository shall indemnify the depositor with:
column6: Either equivalent gold or its value at the time of the claim, at the depositor's option, whether or not equivalent gold of the same kind is available to the depository.
column7: An equivalent gold amount of the same kind, if possible; otherwise, the value of the damaged gold at the time the damage or defect occurred.
column8: The value of the gold at the time it was deposited.
column9: The value of the damaged gold at the time of the court judgment.
column11: Per 5/4/3, indemnity is equivalent gold of the same kind if possible, otherwise its value at the time the damage or defect occurred.

column5: A jewellery trader asked an IFI to buy gold bullion and sell it to him by Murabahah, payable in six monthly instalments. The IFI would take actual possession of the gold before selling it. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, provided the profit is fixed as a lump sum and not as a percentage, and the IFI has taken actual possession of the gold.
column7: Impermissible, because Murabahah on deferred payment terms is not permitted where the asset is gold, silver or currencies.
column8: Permissible, because the IFI takes actual possession before the sale.
column9: Permissible for gold and silver, but not for currencies.
column11: Per 2/2/6, Murabahah on deferred terms is barred for gold, silver and currencies, which must be exchanged hand to hand.

column5: If the sale under an 'Arboun (Earnest Money) arrangement relates to an identified item, the seller:
column6: Cannot deliver a different item even with the same specifications, except with the consent of the buyer, in which case what the buyer has paid remains 'Arboun.
column7: May deliver a different item having the same specifications without the buyer's consent.
column8: Cannot deliver a different item in any case, even with the consent of the buyer.
column9: May deliver a different item with the buyer's consent, in which case what the buyer has paid ceases to be 'Arboun and the buyer's option lapses.
column11: Per 9/2, a different item may be delivered only with the buyer's consent, and what he paid remains 'Arboun.

column5: The stock company has a juristic personality through its incorporation by law, which separates the liability of the company from the liability of its shareholders and establishes for it a separate legal capacity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1/1/2, incorporation gives it a juristic personality with liability and legal capacity separate from shareholders.

column5: If the investment manager does not exert efforts suitable for the nature of the relevant investment, or does not take professional measures that normally provide suitable protection for the funds:
column6: He loses his share of profit but is not liable for loss of capital.
column7: He will be deemed negligent.
column8: He is liable only if this was expressly stipulated in the contract.
column9: The investment contract becomes void.
column11: Per 3/5, failing to exert suitable efforts or take normal professional protective measures makes him negligent.

column5: If an entity is composed entirely of debts, the principle of appurtenance is disapplied and the original rulings of the sale of debt are observed.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/1 and its Shari'ah basis, appurtenance does not apply to an entity made up purely of debts.

column5: If a partner did not stipulate a condition that he be a sleeping partner, then he is entitled to stipulate an additional profit share over his percentage of contribution to the capital even if he did not work.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/5/3, only a partner who stipulated being a sleeping partner is barred from an extra profit share.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column5: Revocation by exercise of a cooling-off option:
column6: Nullifies the contract retroactively from the time of contract, and any growth in the sale item belongs to the seller.
column7: Nullifies the contract at the moment of revocation, and any growth physically attached to the sale item belongs to the party in possession of it.
column8: Nullifies the contract at the moment of revocation; separate growth occurring before the buyer takes delivery belongs to the seller, and that occurring after delivery belongs to the buyer.
column9: Nullifies the contract at the moment of revocation, and any separate growth belongs to the buyer, whether it occurs before or after delivery.
column11: Per item 8, revocation nullifies the contract at that moment; separate growth before delivery goes to the seller, after delivery to the buyer.

column5: If a natural disaster destroys part of the crop in an Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat):
column6: The parties divide what remains according to their stipulated shares.
column7: The owner takes the remaining crop and pays the worker a wage at the market rate.
column8: The worker bears the loss alone, since he is responsible for the crop before harvest.
column9: The worker is not entitled to anything.
column11: Per 10/1, the remainder is divided per the stipulated shares; total loss leaves the worker with nothing.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The impermissibility for the agent to represent both parties to the contract is based on:
column6: The Maliki School, to avoid Gharar in determining the price.
column7: The Hanbali School, to prevent the agent from earning two remunerations for the same work, since a remuneration for the same service from both parties entails unjust enrichment and Gharar.
column8: The Hanafi School and the predominant view in the Shafi'i School, to avoid assigning both offer and acceptance to the same party and hence any probable self bias.
column9: The consensus of all Schools, because such representation always leads to Riba.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Hanafi and predominant Shafi'i view is adopted to avoid one party giving offer and acceptance and self bias.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: It is permissible for the capital provider to stipulate that the Mudarib does not employ the funds in investment activities where the expected profit rate falls below a specific percentage, provided that the Mudarib guarantees that minimum rate.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 7/2, such a restriction is permissible, but guaranteeing the capital, the profit or both is not permissible.

column5: The mortgage contract ceases to be valid:
column6: When the mortgaged asset perishes, unless a compensation for it is obtained (through solidarity insurance, for instance).
column7: On settlement of the debt or relief from it.
column8: On termination of the contract by the mortgagee, or relinquishment of the mortgage right.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/6, mortgage ends on perishing of the asset (absent compensation), settlement or relief of debt, termination by mortgagee or relinquishment.

column5: The fundamental rule is that each loan bears its own specific charges. Where this becomes difficult, as in the case of a group or common loan:
column6: No charges at all may be recovered from the borrowers.
column7: There is no restriction in bearing direct collective charges for all the loans on the basis of the entire sum, as laid down by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, each loan bearing its proportionate share.
column8: The institution may charge a lump sum including indirect expenses, distributed equally among the loans, irrespective of the amount of each loan, the actual charges it entails or the approval of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 9/1, for group loans direct collective charges may be borne on the entire sum, by an SSB-set method, each loan bearing its share.

column5: A customer mortgaged his current account held with an IFI to the same IFI as security for his Murabahah debt. The two parties then agreed to transfer the account to an investment account. As a result:
column6: The account holder is not entitled to any profit, because the account is frozen as a mortgage, and the IFI is not allowed to invest the funds of a mortgaged account.
column7: The IFI takes the whole profit, in its capacity as mortgagee.
column8: The account holder becomes entitled to a fixed return agreed upon with the IFI.
column9: The account holder becomes entitled to his profit share as Rab al-Mal, while the IFI becomes entitled to its profit share as Mudarib.
column11: Per 5, on conversion to an investment account the holder takes profit as Rab al-Mal and the institution as Mudarib.

column5: Investment Sukuk represent undivided shares in the ownership of tangible assets, usufructs, services or the assets of particular projects; however, this is true after:
column6: Issuance of the prospectus, even before the subscription is closed, provided that the issuer has announced the purpose for which the funds will be employed and the prospectus has been approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column7: Receipt of the value of the Sukuk, closing of subscription and employment of the funds for the purpose for which the Sukuk were issued.
column8: Maturity of the Sukuk and redemption of their nominal value.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2, the undivided ownership exists after receipt of the Sukuk value, closing of subscription and employment of the funds for the purpose of issue.

column5: Since no contractual link is permissible between the obligations under the Istisna'a contract and the Parallel Istisna'a contract, it is not permissible for a party to the ordinary Istisna'a contract:
column6: To withdraw his contractual obligations or delay delivering the subject-matter because the obligation under the Parallel Istisna'a did not take place.
column7: To increase the price of the goods to be delivered because of an increase in the cost of goods in the Parallel Istisna'a.
column8: To stipulate conditions and requirements when concluding the Parallel Istisna'a as a purchaser.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/4, neither withdrawal/delay nor a price increase may be tied to the parallel contract; setting conditions as purchaser is unrestricted.

column5: If the Waqif has not stipulated that the benefit is to be availed only personally by the Waqf beneficiary:
column6: The Waqf beneficiary may benefit from the Waqf only personally.
column7: The Waqf beneficiary may lease the Waqf only with the approval of the relevant authorities and the overseer, and for a term not exceeding one year.
column8: The Waqf beneficiary may benefit from the Waqf personally or through a third party, even by leasing it to that party.
column9: The Waqf beneficiary may benefit through a third party, but not by leasing it to him.
column11: Per 2/6/5, absent a stipulation of personal benefit, the beneficiary may benefit personally or via a third party, including by leasing.

column5: The Institution is entitled to include the name of a debtor in default in a list of undesirable customers (black list) and to send a warning admonition to other companies about him:
column6: Only after obtaining a court judgement establishing the default, and after the debtor has been given a reasonable period to settle.
column7: Only when there is an inquiry from other companies about the debtor, and never when such black lists are exchanged directly between companies, unless the debtor consents.
column8: Either when there is an inquiry from other companies about the debtor or when such black lists are exchanged between companies directly.
column9: None of the above is true, as this is prohibited slander.
column11: Per 2/4, blacklisting and warning other companies is allowed on inquiry or through direct exchange of black lists.

column5: If Sukuk are issued and part of their proceeds is used in Murabaha transactions and the other part in tangible assets, such as the assets of Mudaraba, Ijarah or service agency:
column6: Trading of such Sukuk is subject to the rules for an entity in which commingling is materialized, provided that the issuance does not guarantee what is not permitted.
column7: Trading of such Sukuk is permitted without restriction, since the other part of the proceeds is used in tangible assets.
column8: Trading of such Sukuk is subject only to the rules of the sale of debt, since part of the proceeds is used in Murabaha transactions, which create debts, and the tangible assets are then treated as ancillary to them.
column9: Such Sukuk are not tradable at all, since the proceeds are commingled between debts and tangible assets.
column11: Per 8/4, trading such mixed Sukuk follows 8/2, provided the issuance guarantees nothing impermissible.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: A contract by means of which a right is bestowed -but not an obligation- for the purchase or sale of an identified item (like shares, commodities, currencies, indexes or debts) at a determined price and for a determined period is called:
column6: A swap.
column7: A futures contract.
column8: 'Arboun (earnest money).
column9: An option.
column11: Per 5/2/1, this is an option; it binds only the seller of the right, and is not permitted in formation or trading (5/2/2).

column5: Once the mortgage contract is concluded:
column6: It is binding for the mortgagor, who cannot revoke it from his own side, whereas the mortgagee has the right to do so.
column7: It is binding on both parties, and neither the mortgagor nor the mortgagee has the right to revoke it from his own side, until the debt is repaid.
column8: It is not binding on either party until the mortgaged asset is actually possessed by the mortgagee.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/1/1, the mortgage is binding on the mortgagor once concluded; only the mortgagee may revoke it.

column5: With regard to the priority right of recovery and the right to follow up:
column6: The Institution is entitled to recover first its tangible items that were sold to or manufactured for a customer and have not been paid for and can be identified among the assets of the customer.
column7: The Institution is entitled to protect the integrity of the subject of a guarantee, such as a mortgaged asset, and pursue a legal action against misusing it where the holder uses it in a manner that may lead to losses to be borne by the Institution.
column8: The rights of the parties holding mortgages of security shall be given priority over the rights of the parties who are unsecured.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 6/9/1, 6/9/2 and 6/9/3, all three statements are correct.

column5: An example of a condition that shall be deemed void, while the Waqf remains valid, is to stipulate:
column6: That the disbursement always begins with the Waqf beneficiaries, even if the Waqf requires maintenance and repair.
column7: That the revenue of the charitable Waqf be disbursed first to the poor from the Waqif's progeny, and then the remainder to charitable causes.
column8: That the Waqf beneficiary shall benefit from the Waqf only personally.
column9: The right to amend the terms and conditions of the Waqf without prejudicing the essence of Waqf.
column11: Per 2/6/4, a condition obstructing the Waqf's interest, e.g., always paying beneficiaries first even if repair is needed, is void.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Revenues not yet received that are of doubtful permissibility:
column6: Must be waived and not collected from the customers.
column7: Are not subject to compulsory disposal, whether earned before or during the financial period in which the bank decides to convert.
column8: Must be disposed of if they were earned during the financial period in which the bank decides to convert, but not if earned before it.
column9: Must be collected and donated to charity.
column11: Per 8/1/3, unreceived revenues of doubtful permissibility are not subject to compulsory disposal, whenever earned.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: In international commodity sales, there is no restriction in delaying:
column6: The price, while observing the standard on Deferred Sale.
column7: The commodity sold, while observing the Shari'ah Standard on Salam and Parallel Salam.
column8: Both counter-values, provided that the commodity is ascertained.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/2/4, one counter-value may be delayed (price or commodity); delaying both, even for an ascertained commodity, is barred (3/2/2/2).

column5: The Shari'ah basis for making the term of Musaqat equal to the period ending with the time the produce materializes is:
column6: The Verse {"O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations"}, which makes the contract binding upon commencement and fixes its term at one season.
column7: That the worker acts in a fiduciary capacity as the owner's agent in caring for the trees.
column8: The rules of justice, so that the owner does not exclusively benefit from the produce while the worker receives nothing.
column9: Avoidance of Gharar in the identification of the trees and their being arable in usual circumstances.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/3, justice requires that the worker not be deprived of the produce by shortening the term.

column5: With regard to securitization in the issuance of investment Sukuk:
column6: It is permissible to securitize tangible assets only; usufructs and services may not be securitized.
column7: It is permissible to securitize tangible assets, usufructs and services by dividing them into equal shares and issuing certificates for their value, but not to securitize debts owed as a liability for the purpose of trading.
column8: It is permissible to securitize tangible assets, usufructs, services and debts owed as a liability, for the purpose of trading, provided that the certificates are issued in equal shares and their value is received in cash from the subscribers.
column9: It is permissible to securitize debts owed as a liability for the purpose of trading, provided that the certificates are traded at their nominal value.
column11: Per 5/1/2, tangible assets, usufructs and services may be securitized; debts owed as a liability may not be securitized for the purpose of trading.

column5: Regarding debtors of Salam goods purchased by the Institution for trading purposes and not yet received:
column6: No Zakah is due until the goods are received.
column7: The Institution should pay Zakah on the Salam capital.
column8: The Institution should pay Zakah on the market value of the goods at the date of delivery.
column9: The Institution should deduct the Salam capital from its zakatable assets.
column11: Per 5/3/4/10, the Institution pays Zakah on the Salam capital of goods bought for trade; for operating or income purposes, 4/1 and 4/2 apply.

column5: If the Waqf beneficiary is discontinued:
column6: The Waqf remains valid, and its revenue is transferred to the public treasury.
column7: The Waqf remains valid, and it will be used for similar charitable causes.
column8: The Waqf becomes null and void from the start, because perpetuity is a condition in Waqf.
column9: The Waqf ends, and the Waqf asset returns to the Waqif or his heirs.
column11: Per 2/4/4/3, the Waqf remains valid if the beneficiary is discontinued and is used for similar charitable causes.

column5: The capital account and the issuance premium are deductible from zakatable assets, since capital is usually referred to under liabilities.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/2/2, capital and issuance premium are not debt obligations of the company and are not deductible from zakatable assets.

column5: Since a contract of Istisna'a is binding:
column6: The contracting parties need not renew an exchange of offer and acceptance after the subject-matter is completed.
column7: The ultimate purchaser may nonetheless withdraw unilaterally at any time before completion of the subject-matter.
column8: The parties must sign a sale contract through a new offer and acceptance once the subject-matter is completed, as in the promise in Murabahah.
column9: The manufacturer may nonetheless withdraw unilaterally before commencing the work.
column11: Per 2/2/2, Istisna'a binds both parties; unlike the promise in Murabahah, no new offer and acceptance is needed on completion.

column5: Set-off is in line with the objectives of the Shari'ah, as it encourages discharging individuals from liability of debt without involving futile processes of debt recovery.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, set-off serves the Shari'ah objective of discharging debt liabilities without futile recovery processes.

column5: If the investment agent co-mingles his own funds with the principal's funds, he may not purchase for his own account any assets owned by the co-mingled funds:
column6: Under any circumstances, even with prior notice to the principal or the approval of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, since the agent may not buy from funds he manages.
column7: Without the approval of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board on each occasion, in addition to notice to the principal, and the requirement cannot be waived in any case.
column8: Without giving notice on each occasion, to establish transfer of ownership and liability to his account; this may be waived for investment accounts as impracticable.
column9: Unless the purchase is at market price, in which case no notice is required, as the principal suffers no harm.
column11: Per item 11, notice is required on each occasion to establish transfer of ownership and liability; it may be waived for investment accounts.

column5: It is not permissible:
column6: To purchase shares by raising interest-bearing loans through a broker or another (margin sales), or to mortgage the shares for such a loan.
column7: To sell shares that the seller does not own (short sale), and the promise of a broker to lend these at the time of delivery is of no consequence.
column8: For the buyer of a share to sell it to another after the completion of the formalities of the sale and the transfer of liability to him, before the final settlement in his favour.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/5 and 3/6, margin purchases and short sales are prohibited; reselling after formalities and transfer of liability is allowed (3/7).

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: Where deal fragmentation occurs, the buyer:
column6: May accept what remains for its portion of the price and also claim compensation, even if what remains is free from defects, because the fragmentation is a defect.
column7: May accept what remains for the full price and claim compensation for the missing part of the deal.
column8: Must accept what remains of the deal for the full price, since the price was agreed for the package as a whole.
column9: May either revoke the contract or accept what remains for the corresponding portion of the price, without compensation unless what remains is defective.
column11: Per 3/4, the buyer revokes or keeps the remainder at its share of the price; no compensation unless the remainder is defective.

column5: Regarding the participation of conventional banks in syndicated financing:
column6: Originally, syndicated financing shall take place among Islamic financial Institutions.
column7: There is no Shari'ah restriction against participation of conventional banks and Islamic financial Institutions in syndicated financing, as long as subscription and utilization of funds are arranged according to Shari'ah-compliant forms.
column8: Conventional banks may participate, provided that their total share does not exceed half of the syndicated financing.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1 and 5/2, syndication is originally among IFIs, yet conventional banks may join if funds are raised and used in compliant forms.

column5: With respect to underwriting an issue of shares (an undertaking to subscribe all the remaining shares that are not subscribed at their nominal value):
column6: It is permissible for a shareholder to underwrite an issue of shares without any consideration.
column7: It is permissible for the underwriter to take a commission for the underwriting itself.
column8: It is permissible for the underwriter to subscribe the remaining shares at a discount to their nominal value in consideration for the underwriting.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/2/4, underwriting is permissible only without consideration; fees are allowed only for other services.

column5: It may be agreed that the rental consist of two specified parts: one paid to the lessor, and the other held by the lessee to cover expenses approved by the lessor, such as major maintenance and insurance. In this case:
column6: Any excess of the second part is treated as an advance to the lessor on account, while the lessor bears any shortage.
column7: Any excess of the second part belongs to the lessee, while the lessee bears any shortage, since he holds the amount on his own account.
column8: Any excess of the second part belongs to the lessor, while the lessee bears any shortage, since the lessee holds the amount.
column9: Any excess of the second part belongs to the lessee, while the lessor bears any shortage, since the lessor approved the expenses.
column11: Per 5/2/4, the excess of the second part is an advance to the lessor on account, and the lessor bears any shortage.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of the investment manager volunteering, at his own will, to guarantee realized losses wholly or partially is:
column6: That it is an unimpeded public interest (Maslahah Mursalah) enforced by the ruling authorities.
column7: That he has waived his right with consent, which raises no contravention to Shari'ah.
column8: That he does so out of benevolence in this specific case, and there is no cause for blame upon the doers of good.
column9: That it constitutes an undertaking to donate by a third party.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, voluntary guarantee of realized losses is benevolence, and there is no blame on doers of good.

column5: With regard to the credit card (revolving credit card):
column6: It is permitted for the Institutions to issue it, provided that interest is charged only after the grace period expires.
column7: It is permitted for the Institutions to issue it for purchases only, and not for cash withdrawals.
column8: It is not permitted for the Institutions to issue revolving credit cards by extending a loan which will be settled by the cardholder in deferred instalments against interest.
column9: It is permitted for the Institutions to issue it, provided that the interest rate is lower than the prevailing market rate and does not exceed a ceiling fixed by the Shari'ah Board.
column11: Per 4/4, Institutions may not issue revolving credit cards based on a loan repaid in instalments against interest.

column5: Possession by the beneficiary of a bank draft or personal cheque is deemed constructive possession of the amount payable by the drawee bank, even though there is delay in the payment of the actual amount.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1, such possession is deemed constructive possession of the payable amount despite delay in actual payment.

column5: The following contract is permissible with respect to shares:
column6: Mortgage (pledge) of shares that are lawful according to the Shari'ah.
column7: Options on shares.
column8: Renting shares for the purpose of pledging them, as the pledgee is entitled to the benefit of the pledged shares.
column9: Salam in shares.
column11: Per 3/10, lawful shares may be mortgaged; Salam (3/11), options (3/13) and renting shares (3/15) are not permissible.

column5: In a set-off on demand, the creditor for the superior debt should consent to relinquish his additional right or privilege. Superiority in terms of quality exists, for example:
column6: When one debt is now due and the other is not yet due, so that the debt which is now due is the superior debt in terms of quality.
column7: When the duration of one of the debts is shorter than that of the other.
column8: When the debt is secured by a mortgage, or when a third party has given a guarantee to pay the debt.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1/4(b), a mortgage or third-party guarantee is superiority in quality; a shorter or matured debt is superiority in duration.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: Set-off between two back-to-back debts, where one of the debts is gold and the other is silver or denominated in a currency, is:
column6: Permissible, provided that the rulings for currency exchange (al-Sarf) are complied with.
column7: Permissible on the lesser amount, without regard to the rulings for currency exchange.
column8: Not permissible in any case, because the two debts are of different kinds.
column9: Permissible only if the two debts are equal in weight.
column11: Per 7/5/2, set-off between a gold debt and a silver or currency debt is permissible if the rulings of al-Sarf are observed.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The following sale is void because of Gharar in the form of the contract (random selection of the sold object):
column6: Bay' al-Istijrar, in which the buyer obtains goods regularly from the seller for a price subject to an index.
column7: Sale of a non-specified car from a number of cars in a car showroom.
column8: Sale conducted by using a programmed machine to determine the sold good irrespective of the choices of the seller and the buyer.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1/2, machine-based random selection voids the sale. The showroom car is Gharar in the object (5/2/1/3); Istijrar is permitted (5/2/2).

column5: The ruling which exempts charitable Waqf from Zakah is also applicable to:
column6: Investment funds established by the founders of charitable institutions.
column7: Irsad (allocation) of public funds and properties for educational, charitable and social institutions that have no specific owner, provided that such institutions make no profits.
column8: Trust funds, as well as Irsad of public funds and properties for (non-profiteering) educational, charitable and social institutions which have no specific owner, even if such institutions make profits.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/1/7, the exemption extends to trust funds and Irsad for non-profiteering institutions with no specific owner, even if they make profits.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The agent is considered as a trustee in holding the asset in question. He shall be held responsible for indemnity:
column6: Whenever he sells at a higher price or buys at a lower price than that specified by the principal.
column7: Only when the damage results from his own misconduct, negligence or breach of terms or stipulations of the contract.
column8: In all cases of damage, because the asset is in his possession.
column9: Only when the agency is a paid agency.
column11: Per 5/2, the agent is a trustee liable only for misconduct, negligence or breach; acts in the principal's interest are not a breach.

column5: The leased asset in the possession of the lessee:
column6: Is held by him in a fiduciary capacity, and in case of misconduct he is liable only for the amount of damage by valuation, never for replacement, even where the asset is replaceable and the lessor demands a replacement, since the lessee holds the asset only as a trustee.
column7: Is held by him in a fiduciary capacity on behalf of the lessor; he is not liable for its damage or destruction unless caused by his misconduct or negligence, in which case he must replace it if replaceable, otherwise pay the damage by valuation.
column8: Is held by him as a guarantor, so he is liable for any damage or destruction whatever its cause, and the lessor is not required to prove any misconduct or negligence on his part.
column9: Is at his risk once the lessor has delivered it, unless the lessor has insured it.
column11: Per 7/1/4, the lessee holds on trust; liable only for misconduct or negligence, by replacement if replaceable, otherwise by valuation.

column5: If a Waqf company is liquidated, the Waqf ends and the liquidation proceeds return to the Waqif or his heirs.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/14/3, rulings of substitution apply per the Waqif's stipulation and the interest of the Waqf and its beneficiaries.

column5: An IFI leased equipment to a company under a five-year Ijarah. In the third year, the lessee was declared insolvent, and the court did not consider continuity of the Ijarah to be in the interest of the creditors. With respect to the rent, the IFI is entitled to:
column6: The rent for the period of enjoyed usufruct, pro-rata with other creditors; and for the remaining period, the option either to terminate the Ijarah or to continue it and claim the remaining rent on the insolvency assets.
column7: Only the rent for the period during which the usufruct was enjoyed, pro-rata with other creditors, since the Ijarah terminates automatically upon the declaration of the lessee's insolvency and the lessor may not continue it.
column8: The rent for the whole Ijarah term in full, in priority to the other creditors, since the lessor remains the owner of the leased equipment throughout the term and the court's decision cannot affect his right to it.
column9: The rent for the period during which the usufruct was enjoyed in full and in priority to other creditors, and the rent of the remaining period pro-rata with the other creditors.
column11: Per 5/5/2, past rent is shared pro-rata; for the remaining period the lessor may terminate or continue with claims on the insolvency assets.

column5: The basis that profit distribution depends on the availability of liquidity is that there cannot be any profit except after the protection of the capital, and this protection is realized by liquidating the assets.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/1, no profit exists before capital is protected, which is realized by liquidating assets.

column5: 'Arboun (Earnest Money) can be paid:
column6: In cash or in kind, but not with a usufruct.
column7: In cash only.
column8: In cash, provided that it does not exceed a specified percentage of the price.
column9: In cash, in kind and with a usufruct.
column11: Per 2/3, 'Arboun can be paid in cash, in kind and with a usufruct.

column5: An excess over Qard in terms of quantity or quality, or the offering of tangible property or extending of a benefit, at the time of satisfaction (repayment):
column6: Is permissible when it is neither stipulated nor customary, irrespective of the subject-matter of Qard being cash or kind.
column7: Is permissible even if stipulated, provided it is in terms of quality only.
column8: Is prohibited in all cases, because it amounts to Riba.
column9: Is permissible only if the subject-matter of Qard is in kind and not cash, since an excess over a cash Qard always entails Riba, even if it is not stipulated.
column11: Per 5/2, an unstipulated, non-customary excess at repayment is permissible, whether the Qard is cash or kind.

column5: If the collective amount raised by a corporation as loans on interest does not exceed 30% of its market capitalization, raising such loans becomes permissible for the corporation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/4/2, the 30% limit only governs dealing in its shares; raising loans on interest is prohibited whatever the amount.

column5: The memorandum of understanding on the basis of which Mudarabah financing contracts are concluded should indicate:
column6: The intention of the parties to use either unrestricted or restricted Mudarabah financing, either through revolving transactions or separate transactions.
column7: The profit ratio.
column8: The type of guarantees to be presented by the Mudarib to cover situations of negligence, misconduct or breach of contract.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2, the MoU defines the framework (restricted/unrestricted, revolving/separate), the profit ratio and the Mudarib's guarantees.

column5: In brokerage activities based on Ju'alah, the broker is entitled to his compensation once he introduces the parties to each other, even if the contract for which intermediation is undertaken is not concluded.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/4, the broker's entitlement is contingent upon conclusion of the contract for which intermediation is undertaken.

column5: When the contract is concluded through website, with regard to clicking on the acceptance icon:
column6: If the system in the website requires confirmation of acceptance, clicking on the acceptance icon constitutes acceptance even without making such confirmation.
column7: Clicking on the acceptance icon is never considered as acceptance in the strict Shari'ah sense, and acceptance must be sent separately by e-mail.
column8: Clicking on the acceptance icon is considered as acceptance in the strict Shari'ah sense if the system in the website does not require confirmation of acceptance.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/4, clicking the icon is acceptance if the site requires no confirmation; if it requires confirmation, acceptance needs that confirmation.

column5: Incidental credit, in which indebtedness is only probable at the end of the transaction, includes:
column6: Bank suretyship and letters of guarantee.
column7: Bills of acceptance.
column8: Letters of documentary credit.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/1, incidental credit includes bank suretyship, letters of guarantee, bills of acceptance and letters of documentary credit.

column5: If the subject-matter of Istisna'a does not conform to the specification agreed upon, the customer is obliged to accept it, subject to a reduction of the price.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/2/1, the customer has the option to accept or to refuse non-conforming subject-matter.

column5: The buyer who has paid 'Arboun (Earnest Money) loses his right to revoke the contract:
column6: If he informs the seller that he has confirmed the contract.
column7: If he disposes of the sold item in a manner that indicates confirmation.
column8: As soon as he takes delivery of the sale item during the option period.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1 the option lapses by informing the seller or by disposal indicating confirmation; per item 7, delivery alone does not indicate confirmation.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for making a Mudarabah contract binding once the work has commenced is that:
column6: A Mudarabah contract is, in essence, an agency contract, and agency is a binding contract, so neither party may terminate it once concluded.
column7: A unilateral termination at this stage might frustrate the objective of the parties to make profit and might damage the Mudarib, who might receive no compensation for his work.
column8: The Mudarib becomes a guarantor of the capital once the work commences, so that the capital provider can no longer terminate.
column9: The capital provider loses his ownership of the capital once the work commences, and the Mudarib becomes the owner of the assets purchased with it, which the capital provider then buys back at the end of the term.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, termination after commencement may frustrate the profit objective and harm the uncompensated Mudarib.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Fatwa becomes the personal duty of an individual if he happens to be the only one in the community who is eligible to issue it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1, Fatwa is a collective duty that becomes personal if the individual is the only eligible one in the community.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Examples of charitable channels for interest and other non-permissible earnings include:
column6: Training people other than the staff of the bank.
column7: Funding research and providing relief equipment.
column8: Training the bank's own staff on Islamic banking practices.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 10/2, training non-staff and funding research or relief are charitable channels; the bank may not benefit, even indirectly.

column5: Among the Shari'ah bases cited is that lending Waqf funds would be permitted if lending were more secure for the funds, as Abdullah bin ʿUmar (RA) used to lend orphans' funds to protect them from loss.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 7, lending is permitted if it is more secure for the funds, as with Ibn ʿUmar lending orphans' funds.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, the viewpoint that a gift is binding only when it is possessed is reported from:
column6: Imam Malik.
column7: Ali and Ibn Mas'ud.
column8: Abu Bakar and Omar.
column9: The Hanbali scholars, in all things including those measured by volume and weight.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, Abu Bakar and Omar considered a gift binding only on possession; Ali and Ibn Mas'ud held it valid without possession.

column5: It is not permitted to sell a monetary debt to a third party other than the debtor:
column6: Against cash.
column7: For a monetary debt.
column8: For a commodity with spot delivery.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/1–5/2, a monetary debt may not be sold to a third party for cash or a monetary debt, but may be sold for a commodity with spot delivery.

column5: It is permissible to trade in Mudarabah, Musharakah and investment agency certificates:
column6: After closing of subscription, allotment of the certificates and commencement of activity with respect to the assets and usufructs.
column7: Only after the maturity of the Sukuk.
column8: Only after the assets of the activity have been fully converted into cash.
column9: Immediately after closing of subscription, even before the allotment of the certificates, provided that the issuer has received the value of the Sukuk.
column11: Per 5/2/16, these certificates may be traded after closing of subscription, allotment and commencement of activity.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis, mortgage is permissible even when the contracting parties are not on travel, because:
column6: The Prophet (peace be upon him) mortgaged his armor plate to a Jew in Al-Madinah and took some barley from him to his family.
column7: Mortgage is obligatory in all deferred debts.
column8: Mujahid interpreted the Verse as permitting mortgage only on travel.
column9: The Verse {And if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, then let there be a pledge taken} stipulates travel as a condition.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Prophet mortgaged his armor to a Jew in Al-Madinah, so travel is not a condition for mortgage.

column5: Permissibility of signing a hiring contract for a service to be delivered in the future is judged by analogy to:
column6: Ju'alah.
column7: Murabahah.
column8: Salam.
column9: Istisna'a.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, hiring for a future service is judged by analogy to Salam, and because it does not lead to dispute.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Withdrawal of a certain Fatwa, or refraining from its dissemination, for fear of its being misused is based on the principle of:
column6: Maslahah Mursalah.
column7: Istihsan.
column8: Talfiq.
column9: Sadd al-Zara`i'.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, it rests on Sadd al-Zara`i', which prohibits a permissible act that would certainly or probably lead to blight.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: When one of the two parties in Mudarabah-based investment accounts stipulates a lump sum amount for himself:
column6: The contract remains valid, but the stipulation is null and void.
column7: The stipulation is permissible if the party stipulating it is the institution as Mudarib, because its work justifies a fixed remuneration in addition to its share of profit.
column8: The Mudarabah becomes null and void; however, this does not include an agreement that, if the profit exceeds a certain limit or index, the excess is taken by one of them.
column9: The stipulation is permissible, provided that the lump sum is less than the expected profit and is determined at the time of contracting, and the remainder is divided in agreed ratios.
column11: Per 4/4, a lump sum stipulation voids the Mudarabah, but agreeing that profit above a limit or index goes to one party is allowed.

column5: The traditional Fiqh-nominate partnerships classified under Sharikat al-'Aqd in the standard include:
column6: Sharikat al-'Inan (contractual partnership).
column7: Sharikat al-Wujuh or Al-Dhimam, i.e. partnership of creditworthiness or reputation (liability partnership).
column8: Sharikat al-A'mal (vocational partnerships and partnerships for undertaking difficult work or accepting jobs).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/2/1, the traditional Fiqh-nominate partnerships are 'Inan, Wujuh (Dhimam) and A'mal.

column5: The capital provider is permitted to obtain guarantees from the Mudarib that are adequate and enforceable, provided that:
column6: The guarantees are provided by a third party, not by the Mudarib himself, and the third party receives a fee proportional to the capital guaranteed.
column7: The guarantees cover the return of the capital in all cases, including loss not caused by the Mudarib's misconduct or negligence.
column8: The capital provider will not enforce these guarantees except in cases of misconduct, negligence or breach of contract by the Mudarib.
column9: The guarantees cover a minimum level of profit, which the Mudarib must pay even if the Mudarabah realises no profit at all.
column11: Per 6, guarantees may be taken from the Mudarib but enforced only for misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column5: An agreement among partners in a joint property containing tangible assets, debts and cash that some of them will take debts and cash and others will take tangible assets is classified in Shari'ah as:
column6: A sale of debt.
column7: Ṣulḥ (settlement) among the partners.
column8: A separation (division) that is not a sale, as in the division of a single debt.
column9: Ḥawāla (novation).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 6/3, this division is a form of ṣulḥ; dividing one or several debts (6/1–6/2) is separation, not sale.

column5: When a contract is concluded for the sale of an amount of currency, it is sufficient that possession be taken of the major part of the amount at the closing of the transaction, provided the remainder is delivered within the customary settlement period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/6/1, possession must be taken of the whole amount that is the subject matter of the contract at the closing of the transaction.

column5: If the Waqif stipulates that his Waqf be limited to a period, then upon maturity of the term of the Waqf:
column6: The stipulation is void, since Waqf must be perpetual, and the Waqf continues.
column7: The Waqf asset shall return to the original owner or his heirs.
column8: The Waqf asset is transferred to the Waqf beneficiaries as owners.
column9: The Waqf turns into a Charitable Waqf, and its revenue is disbursed to general charitable causes.
column11: Per 2/4/1/5, Waqf is presumed perpetual but may be time-limited by stipulation; at maturity the asset returns to the owner or his heirs.

column5: A third party's voluntary undertaking to compensate investment losses may be made a condition for the enforcement of the Mudarabah contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/6 and IIFA Resolution 30, the undertaking must be independent and not a condition for enforcing the contract.

column5: If the worker (irrigator) enters into an Irrigation Partnership with a party who, unbeknown to the worker, has usurped the trees:
column6: The produce, if any, belongs to the owner of the trees, and the worker is entitled to a wage at fair market rate.
column7: The produce is divided between the worker and the usurper according to the stipulated shares.
column8: The worker is entitled to his stipulated share of the produce from the owner of the trees.
column9: The worker is not entitled to any remuneration.
column11: Per 11/2, the produce goes to the owner and the unaware worker gets a fair market wage; an aware worker gets nothing.

column5: If a guarantee is not stipulated in the agency contract and the agent voluntarily provides a guarantee to his clients independently of the agency contract:
column6: The agent becomes a guarantor in a different capacity from that of agent, and remains liable as guarantor even if discharged as agent.
column7: The agent becomes a guarantor, but his liability as guarantor ends once he is discharged from acting as agent, unless the clients have stipulated otherwise.
column8: The guarantee is void, since the same party cannot be both agent and guarantor.
column9: The agent may take remuneration for the guarantee, since it is independent of the agency contract.
column11: Per 2/2/2, he becomes guarantor in a separate capacity and stays liable even after discharge from the agency.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: A seller added substances to a product so that it appeared to be in a better condition, and sold it. Before the contract was revoked, the product's condition improved to a condition not less than the original specification. The buyer:
column6: May revoke the contract, because the deception existed at the time of the contract.
column7: Has no right of revocation, because the deception is no longer continuing.
column8: May retain the product and claim compensation for the deception.
column9: May revoke the contract only if the seller colluded with a third party.
