column11: Per 3/2/3, the deception must be continuing; if the item improves to at least the original specification before revocation, no right to revoke.

column5: Regarding the duration of an Ijarah contract:
column6: It may be left unspecified, provided the rental per month is specified.
column7: It must be specified in the contract, and should commence on the date of execution unless the parties agree on a specified future commencement date, resulting in a future Ijarah.
column8: It commences on the date of payment of the first rental instalment.
column9: It must always commence on the date of execution of the contract; a future Ijarah is not permissible, since the lessor must own the asset at the time of the contract and the rentals cannot be deferred.
column11: Per 4/1/2, the duration must be specified and starts on execution unless a future start date is agreed (future Ijarah).

column5: Commercial insurance is prohibited because it involves Gharar, based on the Hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (peace be upon him) prohibited sales which involve Gharar.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. The Shari'ah basis cites Abu Hurayrah's Hadith prohibiting Gharar sales as the ground for prohibiting commercial insurance.

column5: If the lessee stops using the leased asset or returns it to the owner without the owner's consent:
column6: The lessor may lease the property to another lessee and still claim the full rental from the current lessee, since the lessee has stopped using the asset by his own choice and without the lessor's consent, and the lessee may not relinquish the remaining period to him even by agreement.
column7: The lease is automatically terminated from the date of return.
column8: The rental continues to be due for the remaining period, and the lessor may not lease the property to another lessee but must keep it at the lessee's disposal, unless the lessee relinquishes the remaining period, in which case the lease expires.
column9: The rental ceases to be due from the date of return, but the lessee must compensate the lessor for actual damage, and the lessor may lease the asset to another lessee for the remaining period.
column11: Per 7/1/7, rent remains due and the asset is kept for the lessee, unless he relinquishes the remaining period and the lease expires.

column5: The basis for the permissibility of stipulating a right to freeze a customer's investment account is the permissibility of pledging funds; it is a form of mortgage to secure a possible future debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, freezing an investment account rests on the permissibility of pledging funds, securing a possible future debt.

column5: Discounting bills of exchange by transferring the ownership of their value, before their due date, to an Institution or others for a discounted immediate payment is:
column6: Permissible as a form of successive Hawalah.
column7: Not permissible, because the transaction in this manner is a form of Riba.
column8: Permissible, provided the discount reflects only the actual collection costs.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 12/5/4, discounting bills of exchange for immediate payment before maturity is a form of Riba.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility of irrevocable documentary credit is:
column6: A combination of sale and Ijarah, in which the bank sells the goods to the buyer and leases the documents to the seller.
column7: A combination of Mudarabah and agency, to which Rahn is added when the credit is uncovered and the bank advances funds to the beneficiary, and in which the bank shares in the profit of the underlying sale.
column8: Hawalah of debt from the buyer to the bank, to which Kafalah is added when the credit is confirmed by another bank.
column9: A combination of guarantee and agency, to which Qard is added when the institution pays for a credit that is totally or partially uncovered; it also derives permissibility from Rahn.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, irrevocable credit combines guarantee and agency, plus Qard for uncovered credit, and derives from Rahn.

column5: ………… is a written, signed and unconditional order from a person to another person to pay a certain sum of money at sight or at a particular or determinable date to a third person, or to the order of that third person, or to the bearer of that order.
column6: Cheque.
column7: Promissory note.
column8: Suftajah (demand note).
column9: Bill of exchange.
column11: Per 2/1, this is the definition of a bill of exchange.

column5: The prohibition against seeking a guarantee in trust contracts is more stringent in Musharakah and Mudarabah contracts, since:
column6: It is not permitted to require any guarantee from the manager or the partners, even to cover misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions, whether the guarantee is required by the Institution or offered voluntarily by a third party.
column7: It is not permitted to require the manager, agent or a partner to guarantee the capital or promise a guaranteed profit, nor to market or operate these contracts as a guaranteed investment.
column8: It is not permitted for any third party to volunteer to compensate the investment losses.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/2/1, no capital or profit guarantee may be required from the manager or partners, nor may these be marketed as guaranteed investments.

column5: Stipulating the purchase of certain goods or services to qualify for entering into a prize draw is permissible subject to conditions, including:
column6: The price is not increased vis-à-vis the same goods or services that do not confer the right to enter the draw.
column7: The purchase of the goods or services is intended for the purpose of winning the prize, as a condition of eligibility.
column8: Customers who purchase larger quantities are given greater chances of winning.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/3, the price must not be increased, the purchase must be intended irrespective of the prize, and the draw must give equal chances.

column5: It is a requirement that al-Muslam Fihi be:
column6: Commonly available under normal circumstances at the place where it should be on the delivery date.
column7: Owned by the seller at the time the Salam contract is concluded, so that he can deliver it from his own stock.
column8: Produced by the seller himself, so that he is able to deliver it on the delivery date.
column9: In existence at the time the Salam contract is concluded, and identified by the buyer at that time.
column11: Per 3/2/8, al-Muslam Fihi must be commonly available where required on the delivery date, so the seller can deliver it.

column5: In hiring for performing a future service that is well described and specified, the pay:
column6: Should not necessarily be made in advance, unless the contract is a Salam or Salaf contract.
column7: Must be paid in installments linked to stages of the service.
column8: Must be paid in full in advance at the time of contracting, by analogy to Salam.
column9: Must be deferred until delivery of the whole service.
column11: Per 5/1/6, advance payment is not necessary unless the contract is Salam or Salaf; the basis cites the Shafi'i and Hanbali view.

column5: The investment agent must adhere to a restriction requiring it to consult the principal before any investment, and if any breach by the agent results in loss, the agent shall bear it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/1, such a restriction must be observed, and the agent bears any loss resulting from its breach.

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, the stipulation that one partner should bear all the cost of insurance or maintenance on the ground that he will eventually own the subject matter of the partnership is:
column6: Permitted for maintenance, but not for insurance.
column7: Not permitted, because insurance in all its forms is impermissible.
column8: Not permitted, because this condition is in conflict with the nature of the partnership contract.
column9: Permitted, because he will eventually become the sole owner of the subject matter.
column11: Per 5/3 and its basis, such a condition is prohibited as it conflicts with the nature of the partnership contract.

column5: An arbitrator who is not entitled to remuneration:
column6: Is not bound by arbitration, and can terminate himself after accepting the task.
column7: Can terminate himself after accepting the task, provided that he appoints an alternate arbitrator.
column8: Is bound by arbitration once he accepts the task, and should bear any actual harm resulting from his withdrawal.
column9: Can terminate himself only before accepting the task.
column11: Per 5/2, arbitration is not binding for an unpaid arbitrator, who can terminate himself after accepting; a paid one is bound and bears actual harm.

column5: Unless otherwise stipulated, the applicable rule in Qard is the return of:
column6: An amount similar to the loan amount at the place chosen by the lender at the time of repayment.
column7: The value of the loan amount at the date of repayment, at the place of the lender's residence.
column8: An amount similar to the loan amount at the place where it was delivered.
column9: The very same wealth that was lent, at the place where it was delivered.
column11: Per 3/4/2, the rule is the return of an amount similar to the loan amount at the place where it was delivered.

column5: A contractor building a warehouse under Istisna'a on land owned by the ultimate purchaser abandoned the work half-way due to his own misconduct. The ultimate purchaser suffered actual losses from the delay. The correct ruling is:
column6: The ultimate purchaser takes the structure without paying anything, since the contractor is at fault and abandoned the work half-way.
column7: The ultimate purchaser pays the value of the structure, and neither party compensates the other, since the contract was left incomplete.
column8: The contractor is entitled to the value of the work completed plus compensation, since the structure benefits the land owner and the delay was not caused by the owner.
column9: The ultimate purchaser is liable only for the value of the structure in place, and the contractor must compensate him for the actual damage or loss he suffered.
column11: Per 4/2/4, if the contractor is at fault the owner pays only the structure's value and the contractor compensates actual damage.

column5: If a Waqf is created over shares of Shari'ah compliant shareholding companies:
column6: The companies may not turn over their assets, since these assets have become the subject of Waqf.
column7: The Waqf asset shall be the market value of the shares, and the overseer may sell them freely whenever he deems it beneficial, without conditions of substitution, provided that the proceeds are reinvested in other shares of Shari'ah-compliant companies.
column8: The Waqf is invalid, since shares fluctuate in value and are not specific assets.
column9: The Waqf asset shall be those specific shares, and no disposition of them is permitted except by following the conditions of substitution, while the companies' asset turnover is allowed under the regulations and norms.
column11: Per 2/4/14/1, the shares are the Waqf asset, disposed of only per substitution conditions; the companies may turn over their assets.

column5: A seller and a buyer agreed that the price would be paid through documentary credit, and the credit was opened. The credit expired before the seller presented the documents. In this case:
column6: The seller loses his right to the price, because expiry of the credit revokes the sale contract, and he may only claim damages from the buyer for the delay.
column7: The seller has the right to claim payment directly from the buyer, because the expiry of the credit does not in itself revoke the sale contract.
column8: The seller may not claim payment from the buyer unless a new credit is opened or the old credit is extended by the bank.
column9: The seller can only claim payment from the issuing bank, which remains bound by the credit even after its expiry date.
column11: Per 2/4/2, if the credit expires before documents are presented, the seller may claim directly from the buyer; the sale stands.

column5: Regarding payment of the price in an Istisna'a contract:
column6: The price must be paid in full at the conclusion of the contract, as in Salam.
column7: The price may be deferred or paid in instalments within a certain period of time.
column8: Payment may be connected with the stage of completion of the work, even where such stages are not, by custom, subject to specification.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/2/2, the price may be deferred or paid in instalments, or tied to stages that are customarily specifiable and will not cause dispute.

column5: The expenses relating to safekeeping, documentation and selling of the mortgaged asset should be borne by:
column6: The mortgagor in all cases, being the owner of the mortgaged asset.
column7: The mortgagor and the mortgagee equally.
column8: The mortgagee, except when the two parties agree that the mortgagor should bear such expenses.
column9: The mortgagor, except when the two parties agree that the mortgagee should bear such expenses.
column11: Per 3/2/10, safekeeping, documentation and selling expenses fall on the mortgagee unless the parties agree that the mortgagor bears them.

column5: A discount card issued without any subscription fee is impermissible, owing to the ambiguity as to the amount of the discount the holder will obtain.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/6/2/2/1, it is permissible as a promise to reduce the price on a Tabarru' basis; ambiguity in Tabarru' is forgiven.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: It is permissible for the agent, after the purchase of the commodity on account of the principal, to buy it for himself from the principal, provided that:
column6: The agent pays the price on a spot basis.
column7: The liability of the agent is distinguished from that of the principal for the commodity by ensuring two independent offers and acceptances between the principal and the agent.
column8: The sale takes place before the principal takes possession of the commodity, and the agent's liability for the commodity as agent is carried over to the sale without any new offer and acceptance.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/1/3, two independent offers and acceptances (e.g. two advices) must separate the agent's liability from the principal's.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: It is permissible to execute an Istisna'a contract in gold, provided that:
column6: The price of Istisna'a is paid in full at the contracting session.
column7: The price of Istisna'a is gold equal in weight to the manufactured item.
column8: The price of Istisna'a is not gold, silver or currencies.
column9: The gold is provided by the customer (Mustasni').
column11: Per 5/2/3, Istisna'a in gold is permissible if the price is not gold, silver or currencies.

column5: Where partners have entered into a binding promise for the continuity of the partnership for a period of time, it is still permissible for them to agree to terminate the partnership before such a fixed period, and obligations and actions that took place before termination remain unaffected.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/6/1, they may agree to terminate early, and prior obligations and actions continue to exist.

column5: An IFI leased equipment to a customer. The contract is silent on expenses of possession and there is no customary practice in this respect. The expenses of taking possession of the leased equipment, and the expenses of delivering the lease value (rentals), are borne respectively by:
column6: The lessor ... the lessor.
column7: The lessor ... the lessee.
column8: The lessee ... the lessee.
column9: The lessee ... the lessor.
column11: Per 4/1/4, the lessor bears the expenses of possession of the leased property and the lessee those of delivering the lease value.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The documents that establish the existence of the commodity, its ownership and distinguish it from others are sufficient proof that the commodity sold in a spot contract is in existence, owned by the seller and ascertained.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/2, such documents are sufficient proof of the conditions in 3/1/1 and 3/1/2.

column5: In the contract of Qard, it is stipulated:
column6: For the lender, that he has the legal capacity for making a donation.
column7: For the borrower, that he has the legal capacity to undertake transactions.
column8: For the subject-matter, that it be known fungible (Mithli) marketable wealth.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2, 3/3 and 3/4, these are the conditions for the lender, the borrower and the subject-matter of Qard.

column5: All things that may lead to an increase in the amount or value of the debt against an increase in its tenure, or that could be a means to it, are prohibited:
column6: Only if the debtor is insolvent.
column7: Irrespective of whether the debtor is solvent or insolvent.
column8: Unless the increase is effected through the sale of a commodity.
column9: Only if the increase is stipulated in the original contract.
column11: Per 4/1/3/3, any increase of debt against more time is barred whether the debtor is solvent or insolvent, including via a commodity.

column5: As long as no services or obligations are required, the rule that the Institution may not charge an amount in addition to the actual expenses incurred applies to:
column6: Endorsing (confirming) a credit facility issued by another bank.
column7: Participation in the issuance and endorsement of credit.
column8: Issuance of standby credit (guarantee credit).
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/1(a), endorsement is an addition over guarantee; the rule extends to participation and standby credit.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: The ruling that a wrong Fatwa should be rectified is supported by:
column6: The incident when Caliph Umar denied some brothers the right of inheritance by a Fatwa and later granted it, saying the former case was subject to his previous Fatwa and the new one to the new Fatwa.
column7: The Hadith: Make things easier not harder.
column8: The verse: {Allah intends for you ease, and He does not want to make things difficult for you}.
column9: The statement of the Prophet (peace be upon him), when asked about seawater for Wudu': Seawater is pure and sea carcasses are permissible, which shows that a Fatwa issued in error need not be revoked once it is acted upon.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, rectification is supported by Umar's two Fatwas on the brothers' inheritance.

column5: Using cheques of bank transfers where the currency to be transferred differs from that in which payment is to be made, by first converting between the two currencies, deeming constructive possession sufficient, and then making the transfer, is a form combining:
column6: Hawalah and Wakalah.
column7: Currency exchange (Sarf) and Qard.
column8: Currency exchange (Sarf) and Hawalah.
column9: Suftajah and Rahn.
column11: Per 7/3, conversion first (with constructive possession) then transfer is a combination of Sarf and Hawalah.

column5: According to the fiqh principles cited in the Shari'ah basis, prohibition for the sake of blocking the way to excuses is more forceful than prohibition per se.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per the Shari'ah basis, prohibition for blocking the way to excuses is less forceful than prohibition per se.

column5: It is invalid for a debtor to create a Waqf if it should be detrimental to his creditors.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/4/1/8, a debtor's Waqf is invalid if it is detrimental to his creditors.

column5: As regards the commodity sold in a Monetization transaction:
column6: It may be any type of currency other than the currency in which the deferred price is fixed.
column7: It may be gold or silver, provided that it is received on the spot by the buyer.
column8: It shall not be gold or silver or any type of currency.
column9: It shall be a local commodity, as the use of international commodities in Monetization is impermissible.
column11: Per 4/1, the commodity shall not be gold, silver or any currency. Local commodities are only 'more preferable' (4/3), not obligatory.

column5: A Waqif may donate as Waqf the usufruct of an asset which he acquires through rent. In this case:
column6: The Waqf is to be made temporary according to the period of the original rent, and this is possible when the owner of the property does not deprive the lessee of the right of subleasing.
column7: The Waqif may lease the asset again only with the consent of the beneficiaries, even if the owner of the property has not deprived him of the right of subleasing.
column8: The Waqf is eternal, and the Waqif must renew the lease at the end of its period so that the beneficiaries continue to benefit from the usufruct.
column9: The Waqf is impermissible, since a usufruct is temporary and cannot be donated as Waqf.
column11: Per 3/4/6, Waqf of a leased usufruct is temporary for the original rent period, allowed when the owner does not bar subleasing; proceeds go to beneficiaries.

column5: The ruling that an online contract is valid since the time the other party accepts the offer, whether the offering party knows of it or not, is based on the fact that Shari'ah scholars define contract as "the concordance of two wills".
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, contract is the concordance of two wills, which occurs once the accepting party declares his consent.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: If the bank invests the amounts retained for liquidity purposes in short-term investments and incurs a loss without any transgression or negligence, the loss should be borne by the bank, because it invested them without obtaining the consent of the accountholders.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/10/2, such a loss without transgression or negligence is borne by the accountholders as Arbab al-Mal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Regarding knowledge of the subject matter of agency by the agent, Jahalah (unknowability):
column6: Minor Jahalah that does not lead to dispute, or temporary uncertainty, may be dispensed with.
column7: It can be overlooked when, in absolute agency, the principal authorizes the agent to channel the funds in any form of investment.
column8: Any degree of Jahalah invalidates the agency contract, because the subject matter of agency should be known to the agent.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/3/1, minor Jahalah or temporary uncertainty is dispensed with, and so is Jahalah in absolute investment agency; (c) is wrong.

column5: The overseer of a Waqf leased a Waqf shop to a merchant for a rent that is flagrantly below the fair rent, without any preferred interest for the Waqf in doing so. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The overseer is liable to pay the difference, and he should demand the termination of the contract unless the lessee accepts the increase.
column7: The lessee is liable to pay the difference, and the lease continues without any right to demand termination.
column8: The lease is valid and binding, and the Waqf beneficiaries bear the shortfall in revenue.
column9: The lease is null and void from the start, and the overseer is automatically dismissed.
column11: Per 8/5, the overseer pays the difference and should seek termination unless the lessee accepts the increase.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: A creditor has the right to retain the debtor's property already in his possession until he receives payment of the due debt (right of lien). Forms of this right include:
column6: The right of the seller to retain the sold item until he receives the due price.
column7: The right of a manufacturer or worker to retain the product of their work until they receive the payment due.
column8: The right of the lessor to retain the lessee's property inside the leased asset until he receives the rent due.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 12/2(b), the forms of lien include the seller's, the manufacturer's or worker's, and the lessor's rights of retention.

column5: The exchange in which the cardholder chooses to pay in the currency of the card is not required to abide by the actual cost because it is carried out by an entity separate from the card issuer, so there is no objection of combining a loan with the exchange service.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 5/5/2, the exchange is by a separate entity, so no loan is combined with the exchange service.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: The agency contract does not expire:
column6: When the agent resigns.
column7: When the principal performs the task in question.
column8: When the principal dies, if the agency is interminable.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 7/2, interminable agency survives the principal's death; resignation and performance by the principal end agency (7/1/2, 7/1/3).

column5: The basis for the permissibility of a third party's promise to guarantee the capital of a partner is that it is a mere charitable act and an undertaking that is independent of the partnership contract.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, it is a charitable, independent undertaking that does not breach the ban on guaranteeing capital.

column5: An IFI holds a current account with a conventional bank, which credited interest to the account. At the date on which Zakah is due, the IFI should:
column6: Pay Zakah from the interest only, and retain the principal as it is not subject to Zakah.
column7: Pay Zakah from the principal amount and donate the whole amount of the interest for charitable purposes.
column8: Pay Zakah on both the principal and the interest, since the interest is part of the zakatable cash assets of the IFI.
column9: Pay Zakah on the principal, and retain the interest after paying Zakah on it, since the interest is the property of the IFI.
column11: Per 5/1/3/1, Zakah is paid from the principal of the current account, while the whole interest (though prohibited) is donated to charity.

column5: An IFI was asked by an exporter to confirm a documentary credit issued by a foreign bank. No services other than the confirmation are required. The IFI proposed to charge 0.5% of the credit amount for each quarter of the validity of the credit. This fee is:
column6: Not permissible, because confirmation is an addition over guarantee for which only actual expenses may be charged, without regard to the duration of the credit.
column7: Permissible, provided the issuing bank is a conventional bank and the fee is paid by the issuing bank.
column8: Permissible, if it is charged as a lump sum rather than a percentage and is independent of the credit's duration.
column9: Permissible, because it is a fee for the agency services involved in the credit, and the confirming bank bears the risk of the issuing bank for the whole period of the credit.
column11: Per 3/3/1(a), confirmation alone is a guarantee; only actual expenses may be charged, never a time-based percentage.

column5: Competitions are permissible if they do not include (nor lead to) anything prohibited by Shari'ah, such as the following, excluding:
column6: Inflicting damage on individuals, the society, animals, or the environment.
column7: Awarding a reward offered by one of the competing participants.
column8: Violating Shari'ah dress code and impermissible intermingling of men and women.
column9: Failure to perform a Shari'ah obligation such as prayer and fasting.
column11: Per 2/3/1/2 the first three are prohibited matters; per 2/3/2/2 a reward offered by one competitor is permissible.

column5: A customer mortgaged Shari'ah-compliant shares to an IFI. When the Zakah year ended, he argued that no Zakah was due on them because he could not dispose of them while they were mortgaged. The correct ruling is:
column6: The customer, as owner, should pay Zakah if payable; his inability to dispose of the mortgaged asset does not relieve him.
column7: No Zakah is due on the shares until the mortgage is released, because the mortgagor has no power of disposal over them during that period.
column8: The IFI, as mortgagee in possession, should pay the Zakah on the shares.
column9: Zakah is shared between the customer and the IFI in proportion to the debt secured by the mortgage and the value of the shares.
column11: Per 9/1, the owner pays Zakah on the mortgaged asset if payable; being unable to dispose of it does not relieve him.

column5: The Institution may receive, as security in the contract of Murabahah:
column6: A third party guarantee.
column7: A mortgage of the investment account of the customer, or of any item of real or moveable property.
column8: A mortgage of the subject matter of the Murabahah as a fiduciary mortgage (registered charge), either without taking possession, or by taking possession and releasing it progressively according to payments received.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/2, the Institution may take a third-party guarantee, a mortgage of the investment account or other property, or a charge over the asset.

column5: Shares of companies which originally pursue permissible activities, yet Riba-based and other prohibited dealings constitute a predominant part of their activities:
column6: May be mortgaged, because their original activities are permissible.
column7: May not be mortgaged.
column8: May be mortgaged only for the benefit of traditional financial institutions.
column9: May be mortgaged, provided that the mortgagee purifies the prohibited income.
column11: Per 4/3, such shares are among the financial papers that may not be mortgaged.

column5: With respect to the determination of the profit percentage of each partner in a Sharikah:
column6: It may be deferred until the realisation of profit if all partners consent, since the profit is not known at the time of the contract.
column7: Once determined at the conclusion of the contract, it may not be amended under any circumstances, not even by agreement of all the partners on the date of distribution or before the profit comes forth.
column8: A partner may not relinquish, on the date of distribution, any part of the profit due to him in favour of another party, as profit is determined at the contract.
column9: It must be determined at the conclusion of the contract and may not be deferred until the realisation of profit; the parties may, however, bilaterally agree to amend it on the date of distribution.
column11: Per 3/1/5/2, ratios must be set at conclusion, but may be amended or relinquished on the distribution date.

column5: After the revocation of his declaration of insolvency, a trader entered into credit transactions and acquired property through these new transactions. He also received a house as a gift from his father. He was later declared insolvent a second time. The creditors of the first insolvency:
column6: Are entitled to share in all the assets of the second insolvency, including property acquired through the new transactions, pro-rata with the new creditors.
column7: Are not entitled to a share of any of the assets of the second insolvency, including the gifted house, since their rights ended with the first distribution.
column8: Are not entitled to a share of the property acquired through the new transactions, but are entitled to a share of the gifted house based on morality/religious credence.
column9: Have priority over the creditors of the second insolvency in respect of all its assets.
column11: Per 10/3, first-insolvency creditors have no share in property from new transactions, but share gifted property on religious credence.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not requiring the debtor's permission to sell the debt to a third party is:
column6: The principle of appurtenance (tabaꜤīya).
column7: The saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Muslims act up to their conditions", which allows the debtor to stipulate his consent.
column8: That the debtor is deemed the possessor of what he owes, so that the creditor cannot sell it without his consent.
column9: The analogy of ḥawāla (novation), and that the creditor may demand his right himself or through a party acting on his behalf.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/6, the rule rests on analogy to ḥawāla; the Hadith on conditions supports requiring consent if agreed.

column5: In the charge card:
column6: The card network is obliged to settle the prices to the merchant from its own funds if the card issuer defaults.
column7: The cardholder is obliged to settle to the card issuer only the prices of goods and services, while cash withdrawals are settled by the card network.
column8: The card issuer is obliged to settle to the merchant, through the card network, the prices of the goods and services.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/7 the issuer settles the merchant via the network; per 3/3/8 the cardholder owes the issuer both purchase prices and cash withdrawals.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Mentioning the proof in the Fatwa:
column6: Is not, in principle, an underlying condition for issuing the Fatwa, and the Institution cannot impose it as a condition for accepting it; however, the board has to refer to the bases of its Fatwa.
column7: Is a condition for the validity of the Fatwa, so a Fatwa without its proof is void and need not be followed by the Institution.
column8: Is not required, nor is the board required to refer to the bases of its Fatwa, because the Fatwa is a binding decision of the board and needs no justification to the Institution.
column9: May be imposed by the Institution as a condition for accepting the Fatwa, since the Institution bears the responsibility for acting upon it before the regulator, the auditors and the General Assembly.
column11: Per 9/3, stating the proof is not a condition and cannot be imposed by the Institution, but the board must refer to its bases.

column5: If a predetermined amount of profit or a specific percentage of capital is assigned to one of the partners in a Sharikah contract, and this assignment is not amended before profit comes forth:
column6: Profit shall be divided equally between the partners, whatever their shares in the capital.
column7: The whole Sharikah contract becomes void, and the partners must restart the venture.
column8: The assignment is void, and profit is divided according to each partner's share in capital.
column9: The assignment is valid if all partners have consented to it, since profit is distributed by agreement.
column11: Per 3/1/5/7, such an assignment is void; unless amended before profit arises, profit is divided per capital shares.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: With respect to a partially capable person, such as a discriminating minor, acting as a principal:
column6: He may appoint an agent for matters that result in absolute benefit to him, such as accepting donations from others.
column7: He may appoint an agent in acts that may be harmful or useful, such as buying and selling, but the acts of that agent remain pending the approval of the principal's guardian or whosoever enjoys the similar right on behalf of the principal.
column8: He cannot appoint an agent in harmful matters like making donations.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1/2, all three statements are true: agency for absolute benefit is allowed, harmful acts barred, mixed acts await the guardian.

column5: In case of the partial destruction of the leased asset in a manner that impairs the benefits expected from it:
column6: The lessee may terminate the Ijarah contract.
column7: The lessor is entitled to rent for the period during which the lessee was not able to benefit from the asset, without having to make it up.
column8: The Ijarah contract is automatically terminated.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 7/1/5, the lessee may terminate; no rent is due for the lost-benefit period unless the lessor makes it up by agreement.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: All financial rights are in principle disposable, and the owner of a financial right has the absolute right to exercise and transfer his right in accordance with the rules and principles of the Shari'ah, and in particular:
column6: Rights may only be exercised or transferred with the permission of the state.
column7: Rights should not be exercised abusively to others, and the public interest has priority over a conflicting private property right.
column8: The owner may exercise his right in any manner, even if it harms others, since his right is absolute and the public interest cannot restrict it.
column9: The private property right is given priority when it conflicts with the public interest.
column11: Per 11/1, rights must not be exercised abusively, and public interest prevails over a conflicting private property right.

column5: Islamic reinsurance aims to achieve cooperation among the participating companies rather than profit, whereas commercial reinsurance aims to achieve profit from the reinsurance process itself.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis (f), Islamic reinsurance seeks cooperation among participants, commercial reinsurance profit from reinsurance itself.

column5: A company entered into contracts under which it receives money from the counterparty if a share index rises above a certain reading, and pays money if the index falls below it, without buying or selling any of the assets which the index represents. The company argues that it does so to hedge its share portfolio. The ruling on this dealing is:
column6: It is prohibited, even if it is practiced for the sake of hedging against potential risk.
column7: It is permissible if the amounts are settled on spot basis.
column8: It is permissible, since it is practiced for the sake of hedging.
column9: It is permissible if the index is an Islamic index supervised by a Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
column11: Per 6/1, paying or receiving money on index readings without dealing in real assets is prohibited, even for hedging.

column5: In developing Waqf land through Diminishing Musharaka ending with the transfer of ownership to the Waqf, the land of the Waqf is the subject of the Musharaka until the Waqf takes ownership of all the buildings.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 8/6/2, the Waqf land is not the subject of the Musharaka; the buildings' rental revenues are shared until the Waqf owns them.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The option to revoke due to defect ceases (abates):
column6: If the seller was unaware of the defect at the time of contract, since he cannot then be blamed for it.
column7: If the buyer delays returning the defective item beyond the customary period without excuse.
column8: If the defect is discovered only after delivery.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 2/8/4, unexcused delay beyond custom implies acceptance and abates the option; seller's knowledge is irrelevant (2/2/3).

column5: If the arbitrator is paid for his job, arbitration becomes binding for him; and if he terminates himself after accepting the task, he should bear any actual harm that may result from his act.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/2, a paid arbitrator is bound and bears any actual harm resulting from terminating himself after accepting.

column5: Implicit and subsidiary contracts, for the purpose of the Shari'ah concessions for combination of contracts, refer to:
column6: Contracts concluded subject to a prior agreement (Muwata`ah).
column7: Contracts concluded independently between the same parties at a later date, whether or not they are related to the original transaction, and for a separate counter value.
column8: Contracts that are stipulated as conditions in the main contract.
column9: Contractual commitments that are not explicitly embodied in the deal agreement, or those which succeed the original commitments of the transaction.
column11: Per 5/1, these are commitments not explicitly embodied in the agreement, or those succeeding the original commitments.

column5: The Hawl (Zakah year) is not considered for:
column6: Livestock, because what matters is the grazing season.
column7: Agricultural products, because what matters is harvesting.
column8: Cash and commercial assets, when the solar year is adopted.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 3/2/4, Hawl is not considered for agricultural products (harvest) or minerals and Rikaz (extraction); livestock follows the lunar year.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: In the following cases Gharar in the price is permitted and the contract does not become null and void, except:
column6: The price is left to be determined by one of the two parties of the contract.
column7: Commodities are purchased through Bay' al-Istijrar at a price to be determined subject to an index, even after consumption of the goods.
column8: The sale contract is concluded at the market price on the day of purchase.
column9: A lease contract is concluded for a variable rent to be indicated by a specialized index.
column11: Per 5/2/2, leaving the price to one party or a third party nullifies the sale; the other cases involve forgivable Gharar.

column5: The basis for permitting the card issuer not to return any part of the issuance fees when the cardholder cancels the card after its issuance is:
column6: The service provider is entitled to the fee by enabling possession of the usufruct, estimated by the period which elapsed, so the fee is refundable for the unexpired period.
column7: The issuance fees are a penalty for cancellation agreed in the card agreement.
column8: Such fees are against a specific job done by the issuer through issuing the card, and the service provider is entitled to them upon completion of the job.
column9: The cardholder is deemed to have waived his right by cancelling the card.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/2/1, issuance fees are for a specific completed job.

column5: The worker in a Ju'alah is liable for any loss of the offeror's property in his possession, even without negligence, since he is entitled to the compensation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/2, the worker holds the property as a trustee, liable only for negligence, misconduct or violating conditions.

column5: Among the evidences cited for the principle that debts and cash are secondary when a corporation's objective and activity is dealing in things and benefits is:
column6: The curse upon those who charge Riba, pay it, write it down and witness it.
column7: The Hadith of Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) forbade the sale of fruit before it has begun to ripen.
column8: The Hadith of Ibn Umar: "When a person buys a slave, who has wealth, then the wealth is for the seller, unless the buyer stipulates this too."
column9: The principle that a thing can be mortgaged if its sale is permissible.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 3/19, the Hadith of the slave's wealth shows that secondary cash or debts are disregarded.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the permissibility to protect the capital with Takaful against any type of investment risk is that:
column6: Takaful is an exchange contract in which the contribution is consideration for the guarantee.
column7: The extent of the losses covered is known at the inception of the contract, so there is no Gharar.
column8: Takaful is a guarantee provided by the investment manager in his fiduciary capacity.
column9: Takaful is an undertaking to make donations between the participants and not a contract to exchange counter-values (Mu'awadah).
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/2/1, Takaful is a donation-based undertaking, not Mu'awadah, so commercial insurance prohibitions do not apply.

column5: An IFI issues debit cards for current, savings and investment accounts. It charges a fee of USD 20 for the cards of savings and investment accounts, but it decided to exempt the holders of current accounts exclusively from this fee. This exemption is:
column6: Permitted, because it is a gift from the IFI to its customers, and ignorance does not affect gifts.
column7: Permitted, provided that the balance of the current account does not fall below a specified amount, since the IFI then benefits from the account funds.
column8: Permitted, because the debit card may be issued for a fee or free.
column9: Not permitted, because current accounts are adapted as loans, and singling them out by a waiver would turn them into a loan against interest.
column11: Per 4/1/2 and its basis, current accounts are loans; an exclusive waiver for them would make them a loan against interest.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In external conversion through acquisition, if the purchaser is capable of negotiating a deal that excludes all non-permissible receivables from the acquisition in a way that makes the seller solely liable for non-permissible liabilities:
column6: It is preferable but not required, since the purchaser may dispose of them after acquisition.
column7: The Shari'ah requires that the purchaser do so.
column8: The purchaser may choose either to exclude them or to keep them until maturity.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 9/2, if the purchaser can exclude them, the Shari'ah requires him to do so.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column5: The ruling that commitment shall become ineffective when the object of the contract turns out to be owned by someone else other than the committed party is based on the fact that unlawful seizure is unrecognizable as a basis of ownership.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, unlawful seizure is not a basis of ownership: "An extorter is indebted with what he takes until he returns it back".

column5: If the payer dies in a state of bankruptcy, the transferee is entitled to have recourse to the transferor.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/2 and 7/2, death of the payer in bankruptcy gives the transferee recourse to the transferor.

column5: The form of the Waqf:
column6: Comprises 'offer' only, as it does not necessitate 'acceptance'.
column7: Must be in writing in order for the Waqf to be valid.
column8: Comprises offer and acceptance only when the beneficiary is not specified.
column9: Comprises offer and acceptance, and the Waqf is void without the acceptance of the beneficiary.
column11: Per 3/1/1 the form is offer only; per 3/1/2 Waqf may be formed verbally, in writing or by any customary indicating disposition.

column5: If the offeror or the worker revokes the Ju'alah contract prior to the commencement of the work, the worker is not entitled to compensation.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/1, revocation by either party before work commences gives the worker no compensation.

column5: Among the permissible methods that the issuer or the certificate holders may adopt for managing risk and mitigating fluctuation of distributable profits (profit equalisation reserve) is:
column6: Establishing an Islamic insurance fund with contributions of certificate holders.
column7: The issuer's guarantee of a fixed percentage of profit to the certificate holders.
column8: The issuer's undertaking to purchase the Sukuk from their holders at their nominal value.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/1/11, an Islamic insurance fund from holders' contributions is permitted; issuer profit guarantees and buy-back at nominal value are not (5/1/8/7, 5/2/2).

column5: ………… refers to the agreement among insurance companies, on behalf of the insurance funds under their management, to devise a mechanism for the avoidance of part of the risks which the insurance funds may encounter:
column6: Islamic reinsurance.
column7: Commercial reinsurance.
column8: Islamic insurance.
column9: Loss reinsurance.
column11: Per 2/1, Islamic reinsurance is an agreement among insurance companies, for the funds they manage, to avoid part of the risks those funds face.

column5: It is permissible to state in an Istisna'a contract that the manufacturer will act as the agent of the ultimate purchaser to sell the subject-matter if the purchaser delays taking delivery within a particular period. In this case:
column6: The manufacturer has no recourse to the purchaser if the price obtained is less than the contract price, because he sold the subject-matter as agent.
column7: The manufacturer sells for his own account and keeps any surplus over the contract price, but has recourse to the purchaser for any shortfall and for the expenses of the sale if the surplus does not cover them.
column8: The manufacturer sells on behalf of the purchaser, deducts the agreed price and returns any balance; if the price is less, he has recourse to the purchaser, who also bears the selling expenses.
column9: The manufacturer bears the expenses incurred in selling the subject-matter, and deducts them from the balance of the price returned to the purchaser.
column11: Per 6/5, the manufacturer sells as agent, keeps the contract price, returns any surplus, recovers any shortfall, and the purchaser bears costs.

column5: Receipt of a cheque constitutes constructive possession, provided:
column6: The payee endorses the cheque in favour of the Institution before the parties disperse.
column7: The cheque is drawn on the same Institution that executes the currency exchange.
column8: The cheque is presented for collection within the period customary in currency markets, whatever the currency of the issuer's balance.
column9: The balance payable is available in the account of the issuer in the currency of the cheque and the Institution has blocked such a balance for payment.
column11: Per 2/6/5(b), a cheque is constructive possession if the balance is available in the cheque's currency and blocked for payment.

column5: Conversion of the balance of the prepaid card, or part of it, to a currency (or group of currencies) other than the local currency is subject to:
column6: The rulings of Hawalah (novation).
column7: The rulings of Qard (loan).
column8: The rulings of ṣarf (currency exchange).
column9: No specific rulings, as it is an internal transfer within the card.
column11: Per 4/2/2, the rulings of ṣarf apply to converting the prepaid card balance into other currencies.

column5: When Shari'ah-accepted shares and Sukuk are made Waqf:
column6: The income earned by them is to be spent on the Waqf beneficiaries, and in case of liquidation the Shari'ah rulings on Istibdal (exchange of Waqf property) should be applied.
column7: The Waqf is invalid, since the Waqf property must be real estate or subordinate to it.
column8: The shares and Sukuk must be sold, and the proceeds distributed among the beneficiaries, since only the income of real estate may be retained in Waqf.
column9: The income earned by them is spent on the beneficiaries, and in case of liquidation the proceeds are distributed among the beneficiaries of the Waqf.
column11: Per 3/4/3/4, Waqf of Shari'ah-accepted shares and Sukuk is permissible; income goes to beneficiaries and Istibdal rules apply on liquidation.

column5: Among the forms of construction concession is where the licensee constructs the project according to certain specifications on a piece of land owned by the State, and the State becomes the owner of the project, while the licensee:
column6: Shares the ownership of the land with the State.
column7: Is entitled to the usufruct of the project permanently.
column8: Is entitled to the usufruct of the project for a specific period, after which the ownership of the usufruct is transferred to the State.
column9: Becomes the owner of the land on which the project is constructed, while the State retains the ownership of the project constructed on it and its usufruct.
column11: Per 6/1/2/1, the State owns the project and the licensee has its usufruct for a specific period, after which it passes to the State.

column5: When the relationship between the syndication parties is Musharakah, the Institutions may delegate one of them to manage the company:
column6: Provided that it guarantees the contributions of the other partners.
column7: Against an increase in its profit share or a lump sum payment, and a separate management contract should be signed with the selected Institution.
column8: Only for no reward, since management is part of its obligations as a partner.
column9: Against an increase in its profit share only, without any need for a separate management contract, since management is part of the obligations of a partner and the increase is consideration for his additional capital.
column11: Per 6/2, a partner may manage for a higher profit share or a lump sum under a separate management contract.

column5: The right to follow up the subject of a mortgage is based on the fact that the aim of the mortgage is to facilitate recovery of the amount of the debt.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the basis, follow-up protects the mortgage's aim of facilitating recovery of the debt.

column5: In a partnership in creditworthiness (liability partnership), the loss is borne by each partner:
column6: According to his monetary contribution to the capital of the partnership, since each partner shares in the loss as in the capital.
column7: According to his percentage of profit sharing, since loss follows profit in every partnership.
column8: Equally between the partners, whatever their respective liability ratios.
column9: According to the ratio each partner undertook to bear in proportion to the overall assets purchased on credit.
column11: Per 3/2/3, loss follows the liability ratio each partner undertook for assets bought on credit; there is no monetary capital.

column5: The fee charged by the Institutions for a banking service may be a percentage of the value of the service because:
column6: Gharar in fees is tolerated in banking services.
column7: The customer may refuse to pay the fee after the service is rendered.
column8: When the percentage remuneration is calculated, it becomes like the lump sum amount.
column9: A percentage fee is a form of Mudarabah profit share.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a percentage fee is allowed because once calculated it becomes like a lump sum amount.

column5: The basic elements of Waqf include:
column6: The form of donation, the Waqif (the donor) and the donated property.
column7: Offer, acceptance and the Waqf superintendent.
column8: The Waqif, the beneficiary and the permission of the judiciary.
column9: The form of donation, the Waqif, the beneficiary's acceptance and the Waqf superintendent.
column11: Per item 3, the basic elements are the form, the Waqif and the donated property; the form is offer only, without acceptance (3/1/1).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: If the subject matter of Salam is gold, the seller (Muslam Elaihi) may assign the buyer to the assignee (the seller's debtor) provided that:
column6: The debt, or the assigned portion of the debt, are equal.
column7: The assignee's debt to the seller is denominated in currency.
column8: The assignee delivers the gold at the contracting session.
column9: The buyer pays a fee to the assignee for the assignment.
column11: Per 7/4/2, the seller in a gold Salam may assign the buyer to his debtor provided the debt or assigned portion is equal.

column5: Articles of trade should be valued for Zakah at:
column6: Cost or market price, whichever is less, according to the method of their sale at the end of the year.
column7: Their original purchase price.
column8: Selling market price at the location of the Institution's head office, regardless of where the goods exist, and according to the wholesale price in all cases.
column9: Selling market price in the place where they exist, and according to the method of their sale (retail or wholesale, or whichever is predominant if both).
column11: Per 5/2/2, valuation is at selling market price where the goods exist and per their method of sale; cost is used only if other methods are extremely difficult.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: It is permissible for an institution to purchase gold from a supplier at spot and to sell it:
column6: By way of Musawamah for a deferred price, if the gold is in the form of jewelry.
column7: By way of Murabahah for a deferred price payable in instalments.
column8: By way of Murabahah for a deferred price, provided that the customer gives a pledge.
column9: At spot by way of Murabahah or Musawamah, in compliance with the relevant Shari'ah requirements.
column11: Per 5/1/1, the institution may sell gold by Murabahah or Musawamah only at spot, meeting the spot-exchange requirement.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of options is that:
column6: They involve the sale of a commodity before its ascertainment.
column7: The subject-matter of the contract in them is not wealth that can be deemed compensation according to the Shari'ah.
column8: No actual exchange of counter-values takes place thereby, since the premium is paid only for the right to buy or sell in future.
column9: Both counter-values are delayed, creating two liabilities.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 5/2/2, the subject-matter of options is not wealth that can be compensated for in Shari'ah.

column5: If a contractor refuses to pay the amount due under a penalty clause in a construction contract:
column6: The Institution may deduct the amount from the contractor's dues only after obtaining a court order, since the amount is a debt in dispute.
column7: The penalty clause becomes null and void, since the amount has become a debt.
column8: The rulings relating to default by a debtor apply, and the amount may be deducted from outstanding amounts due to the contractor.
column9: The Institution may impose a further penalty for the delay in paying the penalty amount.
column11: Per 2/3, debtor-default rulings apply to the unpaid penalty and it may be deducted from amounts due to the contractor.

column5: When a legally competent beneficiary rejects a Waqf that has been earmarked for him:
column6: His rejection has to be concurred to, and the Waqf remains valid, but his share goes to the remaining beneficiaries of the Waqf rather than to charity.
column7: His rejection makes the Waqf null and void, and the property returns to the ownership of the Waqif, since the form of the Waqf requires acceptance.
column8: His rejection has to be concurred to, yet the Waqf shall still remain valid, and the Waqf (or the share of the rejecting beneficiary if beneficiaries are many) should go to charitable purposes.
column9: His rejection is disregarded, and the income of the Waqf is retained for him.
column11: Per 3/1/1, the rejection is accepted but the Waqf stays valid; the Waqf or the rejecting beneficiary's share goes to charitable purposes.

column5: It is not permitted to incur debt against tangible Waqf assets for other than essential purposes, even if it may serve an interest for the Waqf, unless it is stipulated by the Waqif or with the permission of the relevant authorities.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1, non-essential debt is barred even if beneficial, unless the Waqif stipulates it or the relevant authorities permit it.

column5: Buyback, under the conditions set out in the Standard, is considered among the permissible forms of contract combinations.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/1, buyback meeting the stated conditions is a permissible form of contract combination.

column5: If liability (ḍamān) is established upon the investment manager, the liability shall include:
column6: The capital amount and the profit amount realized before the occurrence of the loss due to negligence, misconduct or breach of conditions.
column7: The capital gain realized upon establishing the liability.
column8: The lost profit (opportunity cost) and the expected profits that were not realized.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/1, liability covers capital, profit realized before the loss and capital gain on establishing liability, but not lost or expected profits.

column5: After distribution, the creditors have no legal right to demand any unpaid debt from the debtor; however, the debtor has a moral obligation in Shari'ah to pay all the debts in full.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/8, no legal right to demand remains after distribution, but the debtor is morally obliged to pay in full.

column5: In person insurance, in case of death:
column6: The Takaful entitlements are distributed among the deserving persons, parties or purposes as indicated in the documents and the regulatory rules issued by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, while any investment balances of the deceased go to his inheritors according to the Islamic rules of inheritance.
column7: Both the Takaful entitlements and the investment balances of the deceased are distributed according to the documents.
column8: Both the Takaful entitlements and the investment balances of the deceased are distributed among the inheritors according to the Islamic rules of inheritance, since the Takaful entitlements form part of the estate of the deceased and are subject to the claims of his creditors and to the bequests made by him.
column9: The Takaful entitlements revert to the insurance fund, while the investment balances go to the inheritors.
column11: Per 6/2/1/4, Takaful entitlements go as the documents and SSB rules indicate; investment balances follow the rules of inheritance.

column5: Where the seller retains the legal registration of the sold asset, it is permitted:
column6: For the seller to be entitled to the yield of the asset until the deferred price is paid.
column7: For the seller to stipulate a condition to pledge the asset to its deferred price or its preservation with a custodian.
column8: For the seller's possession of the asset to be a liability possession (yad ḍamān), as security for the price.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/2, the seller may stipulate a pledge or custodian; the yield belongs to the buyer and the seller's possession is a trust.

column5: If a Waqf is created for a Shari'ah non-compliant purpose, the Waqf is void and the Waqf asset returns to the Waqif.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 2/4/1/7, such a Waqf is prohibited, but if it is created, its purpose must be changed to a Shari'ah compliant one.

column5: Subject to the conditions of a third-party commitment, the service agent may undertake reparation of loss of the capital or shortfall in the profit, provided that:
column6: The undertaking is included as a clause in the service agency contract, so that the two cannot be separated.
column7: The undertaking is effected via a contract independent from the service agency contract, so that voidness of one does not result in voidness of the other.
column8: If the agency is for a fee, the fee includes a premium over the prevailing market rate as a consideration for the undertaking, provided that the premium is disclosed to Rab Al Maal.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/3/2/2–4/3/2/3, the undertaking needs a separate contract and the fee must not exceed the market rate, to avoid a price for the undertaking.

column5: When reinsuring with traditional reinsurance companies, Islamic insurance companies:
column6: May keep cash reserves for ongoing risks that belong to the traditional reinsurance company and on which interest has to be paid, provided the interest is given to charity.
column7: Should stick to the minimum size of reinsurance with traditional reinsurance companies, and their Shari'ah Boards should undertake follow-up in this connection.
column8: Should sign long-term reinsurance agreements in order to obtain better premium rates.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 6/5, reinsurance with traditional companies is kept to a minimum under Shari'ah Board follow-up; 6/2-3 bar interest-bearing reserves and excess periods.

column5: Sharikat al-Muhassah (allotment partnership):
column6: Has a juristic personality and an independent financial liability unrelated to the liability of the partners, being registered as a company in the public register.
column7: Has no juristic personality, because people other than the partners do not know about it, and has no separate financial liability as an entity.
column8: Limits the liability of the partners to their contributions to the capital, as it is known to the public as a registered entity.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/5/1/2 and 4/5/2/2, it has no juristic personality or separate liability; partners are liable from their personal assets.

column5: The option period arising from the payment of 'Arboun (Earnest Money) must be specified:
column6: By express stipulation of the parties only, and custom is not taken into consideration.
column7: It need not be specified, since the buyer may revoke the contract at any time until he pays the remaining price.
column8: By the seller alone, at the time of delivery of the sale item to the buyer.
column9: Either by express stipulation of the parties, or by custom if there is an existing custom that specifies the option period.
column11: Per item 4, the option period is specified by express stipulation of the parties or by an existing custom that specifies it.

column5: Where the purchase orderer (customer) fails to honour his binding promise, with respect to the Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit):
column6: The Institution may not retain the security deposit as such; its rights are limited to deducting the amount of any damage actually incurred, i.e. the difference between its cost of the item and its selling price to a third party.
column7: The Institution must refund the security deposit in full without any deduction.
column8: The Institution may deduct the difference between the cost of the item and the agreed Murabahah selling price, including its expected profit, and retain the remainder of the deposit as 'Arboun in compensation for the breach of the promise.
column9: The Institution may retain the whole security deposit as 'Arboun.
column11: Per 6/8/2, only actual damage (cost minus resale price to a third party) may be deducted; the deposit is a trust, not 'Arboun.

column5: The conditions of Hawalah include:
column6: That all Hawalah parties be legally competent to act independently.
column7: That both the transferred debt and the debt to be used for settlement be known and transferable.
column8: That the payer be a debtor to the transferor.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/4 and 6/5, (a) and (b) are conditions; per 6/3 the payer need not be the transferor's debtor (unrestricted Hawalah).

column5: The lessor's entitlement to the rental runs from:
column6: The date of signing the Ijarah contract in all cases, even if the asset is made available to the lessee only after a long period.
column7: The date of payment of the first rental instalment.
column8: The time when the lessee starts to benefit from the asset, or once the lessor makes the usufruct available to the lessee.
column9: The date on which the lessor acquires ownership of the asset, even if the asset has not been made available to the lessee.
column11: Per 5/2/2, rent is earned from when the lessee benefits or the usufruct is made available, not necessarily from signing.

column5: Zakah is a right which becomes due in certain types of wealth and is disbursable to specific categories of recipients; it is an in rem duty when its conditions are satisfied.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah definition of Zakah in 3/1/1.

column5: The basis that change in purchasing power does not affect the value of cash Waqf assets is the analogy upon such assets not being affected in cash loans.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Basis of 2/4/13/4, the ruling is by analogy with cash loans, which are not affected by purchasing power changes.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for realising possession of ascertained movable property through relinquishment, rather than requiring actual physical possession by hand, is that:
column6: Actual possession by hand is prohibited in exchange contracts.
column7: Actual physical possession is a voluntary act of the one taking possession and is not within the ability of the person obliged to deliver; what is in his ability is to relinquish the thing and remove obstacles.
column8: Relinquishment is required by law in all countries.
column9: The buyer bears the expenses of possession, so he must collect the thing himself, and the seller is not obliged to enable him to take it by relinquishment but only by placing it in his hands, and the seller is discharged only upon such physical transfer.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the one obliged to deliver can only relinquish and remove obstacles; taking by hand is the receiver's voluntary act.

column5: The Institution which provides its services on website should include in the system a step for acceptance confirmation as a precautionary measure against dealers' mistakes.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/4/1, the Institution should include an acceptance confirmation step as a precaution against dealers' mistakes.

column5: It is permissible to mortgage usufruct-based Sukuk which represent common shares in the usufructs of specific assets, or assets in the form of a specific indebtedness.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/2, such usufruct-based Sukuk may be mortgaged, subject to Shari'ah Standard No. (17), item 5/1/5/2.

column5: According to the Shari'ah basis of the Standard, the entities most responsible for overseeing that the institutions' liquidity is compliant with Shari'ah are:
column6: The supervisory bodies, because they licensed the institutions to operate by Shari'ah-compliant procedures and prohibited what violates the Shari'ah.
column7: The investment accountholders, because their funds constitute the bulk of the institutions' liquidity.
column8: The external auditors of the institutions, because they audit the institutions' liquidity positions and financial statements and certify their compliance with Shari'ah.
column9: The Shari'ah Supervisory Boards of the institutions, because they approve each liquidity product and review its execution.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis for 4/1, supervisory bodies are most responsible, since they licensed institutions to operate per Shari'ah.

column5: Investment of Waqf income should be through permissible methods such as Mudarabah, Musharakah, Murabahah, Ijarah and Salam, and in low risk investments.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 7/1, Waqf income is invested through such permissible methods and in low risk investments.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: When the agent commences tasks that cannot be discontinued or phased out without causing injury to him or to the principal, agency remains binding until it is possible to suspend the work, or phase it out without causing injury to any of the two parties.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 4/3/3, agency stays binding until the work can be suspended or phased out without injury to either party.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: In Mudarabah-based investment accounts:
column6: It is permissible to allocate the profit of a certain financial period to one party, and the profit of another financial period to the other.
column7: It is impermissible for the institution to specify different profit ratios for different categories of holders of investment accounts.
column8: It is impermissible to earmark the profit of a specific type or portion of the capital, or of the assets into which capital is converted, for one of the two parties.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/5 and 4/3, earmarking profit of a portion of capital or of a period for one party is prohibited; different ratios by category are allowed.

column5: Failure of any of the parties to combined contracts to honor its contractual commitments:
column6: Does not entitle the other party to any indemnity, since each combined contract is judged independently.
column7: Gives the other party the right to claim indemnity only if a penalty clause is stipulated in the contract.
column8: Gives the other party the right of claiming indemnity for the actual injury encountered.
column9: Renders all the combined contracts void retroactively.
column11: Per 7/6, the defaulting party's failure entitles the other to indemnity for the actual injury encountered.

column5: It is permitted for the creditor to recover his monetary debt, in whole or in part, in a currency other than the currency of the debt, subject to the following conditions:
column6: Possession of the substitute of the debt is transferred in the contract session, so that no part of the debt amount converted into another currency remains outstanding.
column7: Discharge of the debt in another currency before the stipulated discharge time is not stipulated as a condition, noticeable by anticipation, or a customary practice.
column8: Discharge is at the exchange rate prevailing on the day of settlement, if the debt resulted from a loan contract or the debtor delayed settlement when the debt matured.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 4/1/1/2 (a)–(c), all three are conditions for recovering a monetary debt in another currency.

column5: If the commodity is not made available at the time of signing the Monetization contract:
column6: The client shall be given a full description or a sample that indicates the quantity of the commodity and the place of its storage, so that his act of purchasing the commodity becomes real rather than fictitious.
column7: It is sufficient to inform the client of the type of the commodity and its price, since receipt in Monetization may be constructive and the commodity need not be described in quantity or place of storage.
column8: The contract is void, since the commodity must be present at the contracting session.
column9: The Institution shall stipulate that the client sells the commodity through the Institution, so that the commodity need not be described to him.
column11: Per 4/3, the client gets a full description or a sample showing quantity and storage place, so that his purchase is real rather than fictitious.

column5: In investment agency, the profit in its entirety:
column6: Is shared between the principal and the agent according to an agreed ratio, as in Mudarabah, in addition to the agent's fixed fee, unless the contract provides that the principal alone bears losses.
column7: Belongs to the agent after paying the principal the expected profit.
column8: Is the right of the principal, unless it is stipulated that the agent gets all or part of any excess above the expected profit as a performance incentive in addition to its fee.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 6/5, all profit belongs to the principal, save any stipulated incentive from the excess above expected profit.

column5: An IFI accepted funds as Mudarib and stipulated in the Mudarabah contract that, in addition to 30% of the profit, it would charge the Mudarabah a monthly management fee for the routine buying and selling of goods, which by custom is part of the Mudarabah operations. This stipulation is:
column6: Permissible, provided that the fee is deducted only if profit is realised.
column7: Not permissible, because the Mudarib may not earn a fee in addition to a share of profit for work that by custom is his responsibility in the Mudarabah.
column8: Permissible, provided the fee is stipulated in a separate agreement, even though the work is by custom part of the Mudarabah operations.
column9: Permissible, because the fee covers management services and the profit share covers the capital risk.
column11: Per 8/2 and 9/4, no fee besides profit share; a separate fee is allowed only for work not customarily part of Mudarabah operations.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Monitoring all the activities stipulated in the agency contract, including donations, is the responsibility of the agent.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 6/2, the agent monitors the stipulated activities except donations, which should be assigned to the principal.

column5: The overseer of a Waqf:
column6: Must be a single natural person or a company, and the duty may not be assigned to a committee or a ministry, even if the Waqif so stipulated.
column7: May discharge the duty by himself or by appointing someone else, and may also be referred to as mutawalī or al-amīn (trustee).
column8: Must discharge the duty personally and may not delegate any of his powers.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/1, the overseer may be an individual, group, committee or ministry and may act himself or appoint another; per 3/7/4 he may delegate.

column5: It is permissible for Institutions to include conventional banks as partners in a syndicated financing which operates on the basis of Shari'ah, provided that:
column6: The share of the conventional banks does not exceed one-third of the syndication, and the Institution holds at least half of the capital.
column7: The Institution secures the right to manage the partnership's operations and the operations are subject to Shari'ah supervision.
column8: The conventional banks guarantee the capital of the Institution in the syndication, in return for a share of the management fees.
column9: The conventional banks receive their share of profit in the form of a fixed return, and the Institution receives the balance of the profit.
column11: Per 3/1/1/3, the Institution must secure the right to manage the operations, which must be subject to Shari'ah supervision.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: An IFI intends to issue a card enabling its holders to pay for purchases and withdraw cash within a limit, with a free credit period of 50 days, after which the cardholder may pay off the balance in instalments against an interest charge on the outstanding amount. The ruling on issuing this card is:
column6: It is permissible, provided the interest received is spent on charitable purposes.
column7: It is permissible, because the cardholder is not obliged to use the deferment facility and may pay within the free credit period, so that no interest need be incurred and the facility is only optional.
column8: It is not permissible, because the card enables the holder to withdraw cash beyond his available funds.
