column9: It is not permissible, because it provides an interest-bearing revolving credit facility, the cardholder paying interest for being allowed to pay off the debt in instalments.
column11: Per 3/3, issuing cards with an interest-bearing revolving credit facility is impermissible; cash beyond funds without interest is allowed (4/5/1).

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to give up part of the Murabahah selling price if the customer pays early:
column6: It is not permissible, because it is a form of Riba.
column7: Provided this was stipulated in the contract of Murabahah.
column8: Only if the customer is insolvent.
column9: Provided this was not part of the contractual agreement.
column11: Per 5/9, a rebate for early payment is allowed provided it was not part of the contractual agreement.

column5: The income and growth earned by mortgaged investment units or investment accounts:
column6: Belong to the Institution as mortgagee.
column7: Are mortgaged along with the principal only if the relationship is Mudarabah, but not investment agency, in which case the income and growth are paid to the client as realized, and the Institution has no claim on them even if the debt is not repaid.
column8: Are never mortgaged, and must be paid to the client as they are realized, whatever the agreement between the parties.
column9: Are considered to be mortgaged along with the principal, whether the relationship between the client and the Institution or the fund is Mudarabah or investment agency, unless the two parties agree on other arrangement.
column11: Per 6/2, income and growth are mortgaged with the principal, whether under Mudarabah or investment agency, unless agreed otherwise.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: Options to revoke due to non-payment are permissible in:
column6: Contracts that do not require spot payment at the time of contract.
column7: Salam contracts, where the price must be paid in full at the time of contract.
column8: Currency exchange contracts, where both currencies must be exchanged at the session.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2, they are permissible where spot payment is not required, and not permissible in Salam and currency exchange.

column5: When the State requests a specialized body to conduct survey or exploration on its behalf, the contractual relationship becomes subject to the rulings of:
column6: Mudarabah and Musharakah.
column7: Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a.
column8: Ijarah and Ju'alah.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/2/6, survey or exploration on the State's behalf is governed by the rulings of Ijarah and Ju'alah.

column5: If the supplier in an Istisna'a contract is declared bankrupt or insolvent while the items are still being produced and before any of them has been delivered:
column6: The ultimate purchaser has a prior right over other creditors to the items being produced, as they are his property.
column7: The ultimate purchaser owns the materials in the manufacturer's possession in all cases.
column8: The ultimate purchaser has no prior right over a third party to the items that are the subject-matter of the contract.
column9: The Istisna'a contract becomes a Salam contract for the remaining items.
column11: Per 3/1/3, before full or partial delivery, the ultimate purchaser has no priority over third parties to items still in production.

column5: It is permissible for the issuer to redeem Sukuk of ownership of the usufruct of tangible assets from the holder, after allotment and payment of the subscription price, at the market price or at an agreed price, even if the redemption price is deferred.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 5/2/7, such redemption is allowed on condition that the subscription amount or redemption price is not deferred.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: Financial rights can be acquired or established by:
column6: Long-standing continuous use without objection, or first use, without any need to fulfill the Shari'ah conditions required for the acquisition of such rights.
column7: Contract, stipulated conditions, inheritance or court order.
column8: Contract or inheritance only, and never by court order.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 3/4, rights arise by contract, conditions, inheritance or court order; long use or first use counts only if Shari'ah conditions are met.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column5: The option to revoke due to defect ceases if the buyer transfers ownership of the item after discovering the defect.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 2/8/4, transferring ownership after discovering the defect implicitly indicates acceptance and abates the option.

column5: Regarding Zakah on minerals extracted from the earth or the sea:
column6: If the extracted minerals are owned by the state no Zakah shall be paid on them; otherwise they are the property of their extractor, who pays Zakah on them at 2.5%.
column7: The state should pay Zakah on the minerals it owns at the rate of 2.5%, while minerals extracted by others are not subject to Zakah because they are not trade articles.
column8: The extractor should pay Zakah on the minerals at the rate of 10%, by analogy to the produce of non-irrigated lands, whether or not the minerals are owned by the state.
column9: Minerals are not subject to Zakah unless they are owned for trade.
column11: Per 5/5/2, the Zakah rate on minerals is 2.5%; state-owned minerals are exempt, otherwise the extractor owns them and pays Zakah.

column5: A contractor agreed with an IFI to construct a building, with a penalty clause of USD 1,000 for each day of delay in delivery. The contractor delayed delivery by 20 days, without unusual circumstances, and refused to pay the penalty. The IFI still owes the contractor USD 50,000 of the price. The IFI may:
column6: Deduct the penalty amount only if the penalty clause was agreed after the delay occurred.
column7: Not deduct anything, because penalty clauses are not permissible in construction contracts.
column8: Claim the penalty amount plus compensation for the contractor's delay in paying it.
column9: Deduct the penalty amount of USD 20,000 from the outstanding amounts due to the contractor.
column11: Per 2/3, penalty clauses are valid in construction contracts and the amount may be deducted from sums due to the contractor.

column5: When the contract is concluded through online bidding:
column6: The highest bidder should not retreat from his bid until the bidding process is over.
column7: The highest bidder may retreat from his offer after finalization of the bidding process, even if the seller had made a condition that the offer should remain binding for a certain period.
column8: The highest bidder may retreat from his bid at any time before the seller accepts it, even during the bidding process.
column9: (b) and (c).
column11: Per 4/3, the highest bidder may not retreat before the bidding ends, nor after it if the seller stipulated, or practice requires, a binding period.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: In external conversion, if the acquisition cannot be concluded unless all the assets of the bank, including non-permissible assets and receivables, are acquired:
column6: The acquisition is not permissible.
column7: The purchaser may keep the non-permissible liabilities until their maturity.
column8: The purchaser is required to act as quickly as possible to dispose of non-permissible liabilities, even if he has to suggest to the creditors an earlier repayment for a discount.
column9: The purchaser may pay the interest and deduct it from the price paid to the seller, since the seller is solely liable for non-permissible liabilities and the creditors cannot be asked for any discount.
column11: Per 9/2, the purchaser must dispose of them as quickly as possible, even by offering early repayment for a discount.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column5: If the Institution stipulates that the cardholder must deposit a sum of money prior to receiving approval to use the card, it is not permitted for the Institution to prevent the cardholder from investing the amount deposited, because this would be:
column6: Tantamount to a loan that draws extra benefit.
column7: A form of excessive Gharar in the card contract.
column8: A sale of debt for debt.
column9: A combination of a sale and a loan in one contract.
column11: Per the basis (item 9), blocking the deposit without investing it for the holder is a loan drawing benefit; hence profit-sharing investment.

column5: In principle Waqf should be temporary; an eternal Waqf is permissible only when the donor expressly stipulates it.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/4, in principle Waqf should be eternal; temporary Waqf is also permissible when the donor wants his property back after a period.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of a partner in a joint-liability company bringing in a substitute for himself without the consent of the other partners is that:
column6: The partners have agreed not to interfere in the management of the company, and a substitute would therefore be entitled to manage it.
column7: The contract of a joint-liability company is binding for its whole duration, so that no partner may withdraw or be replaced before its expiry, even if all the other partners consent in writing and the substitute is solvent.
column8: The personality of the partner is significant for the partners, because the company's liability includes his personal assets and the substitute may not be in the same financial position.
column9: The substitution amounts to a sale of a debt to a third party, which the other partners cannot approve.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the partner's personality matters as the company's liability extends to his personal assets.

column5: A shipment bought by an IFI for 100,000 for sale to a customer by Murabahah was destroyed by fire while owned and possessed by the IFI, before the sale. The insurer paid the IFI 120,000. The customer, who had given a promise to buy, claimed the excess of 20,000. The correct ruling is:
column6: The insurance amount is shared between the IFI and the customer in proportion to the cost and the agreed mark-up.
column7: The excess of 20,000 belongs to the customer, being the purchase orderer.
column8: The whole insurance amount belongs exclusively to the IFI, and the customer has no claim to it even if it exceeds the purchase price.
column9: The IFI keeps 100,000 and must spend the excess on charitable causes.
column11: Per 3/2/6, before sale to the customer the item and its insurance belong to the Institution, including any excess over the purchase price.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: The basis for allowing delay in the disposal of non-permissible earnings, if prompt disposal would lead to a total breakdown of the activities of the bank or its bankruptcy, is:
column6: That the prohibition relates to the use of the earnings and not to the earnings themselves.
column7: That the Shari'ah validates actions based on an interpretation believed to be valid.
column8: The principle of Da' wa Ta'ajjal.
column9: The view of the Fuqaha that a repentant may use impermissible earnings to cover his unavoidable needs.
column11: Per the basis, a repentant may use impermissible earnings for unavoidable needs, but the Institution may not benefit from them.

column5: There is no Shari'ah restriction on reconciling between the company and the party who causes the injury, if such reconciliation is in the interest of the participants and conforms to the relevant Shari'ah rulings.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/10, reconciliation with the wrongdoer is allowed if it serves the participants and conforms to Shari'ah.

column5: Before signing agreements with traditional reinsurance companies, Islamic insurance companies should seek the approval of their Shari'ah Supervisory Boards.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 6/4, prior Shari'ah Supervisory Board approval is required before agreements with traditional reinsurers.

column5: Stipulating a period during which the manufacturer remains liable for manufacturing or construction defects serves the purpose of the contract, because the ultimate purchaser wants to use the subject-matter, which is not possible unless it is free from defects.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis for 3/1/7.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column5: The need that justifies Gharar in a contract must be a public need; a private need is not recognized for this purpose.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 4/4, the need could be public or private; the basis cites 'Need, whether public or private, enjoys the same status of necessity'.

column5: When the client in an investment agency for working capital no longer requires financing, the relationship may be terminated on the basis of Takharuj, either by distributing the joint account pro-rata or by one party purchasing the share of the other at a price agreed upon at that time.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 12/2, termination may be by Takharuj: pro-rata distribution or purchase of the other's share at a then-agreed price.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: An IFI appointed a property management company as its paid agent to collect the rentals of a building for one year against a fixed fee. After four months, the IFI, without any reasonable excuse, forced the company to discontinue the work. The company is entitled to:
column6: Remuneration for the four months of work it has already performed.
column7: No remuneration, because agency is basically a non-binding contract.
column8: The full remuneration agreed upon.
column9: The prevailing market rate for similar effort for the four months.
column11: Per 4/2/7, if the principal stops the agent early without a reasonable excuse, the agent is entitled to the full agreed fee.

column5: Changing the avenue of Waqf disposal:
column6: Is permitted at the discretion of the overseer whenever he sees an interest in it, without approval from any authority.
column7: Is not permitted under any circumstances.
column8: Is not permitted unless there is a necessity to do so, and it is done after approval from the relevant authorities.
column9: Is permitted with the consent of the Waqf beneficiaries.
column11: Per 9/3, the avenue of disposal may be changed only out of necessity and after approval of the relevant authorities.

column5: The Institution is not entitled to include in the base cost of the item, for the purpose of calculating the Murabahah price:
column6: Transportation expenses paid to a third party.
column7: Payments made to its own staff for their work on the transaction.
column8: Insurance premiums paid to the insurer of the item.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/4, only direct expenses paid to third parties enter the cost; payments to the Institution's own staff may not be added.

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, the partners may arrange for the acquisition of the equity share of the Institution in a manner that serves the interests of both parties, including:
column6: A promise by the Institution's client to set aside a portion of the profit or return he may earn from the partnership for the acquisition of a percentage of the Institution's equity.
column7: Dividing the subject matter of the partnership into shares, which the client purchases in particular numbers at certain intervals until he becomes the sole owner.
column8: A stipulation that the client purchase the Institution's shares at their face value.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 5/8, both (a) and (b) are permitted methods; acquisition at face value is prohibited (5/7).

column5: Discounting a negotiable instrument, by settling it to its first beneficiary (the creditor) before its maturity for an amount less than its value, is:
column6: Not permitted.
column7: Permitted, if the discounting bank is the debtor.
column8: Permitted, provided that the instrument is a commercial paper arising from a genuine sale.
column9: Permitted, if the discount reflects the remaining period to maturity.
column11: Per 9/1/2, discounting a negotiable instrument to its first beneficiary before maturity for less than its value is not permitted.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: If the converted bank has, among its tangible assets, impermissible commodities:
column6: It is obliged to destroy them; if some were sold and the price is yet to be received, the price must be received and donated to charity.
column7: It must return them to the suppliers and recover their price.
column8: It may sell them and donate the sale proceeds to charity.
column9: It may sell them to parties who consider them permissible and keep the proceeds, since the prohibition applies only to the bank's own use of them.
column11: Per 8/1/5, impermissible commodities held must be destroyed; prices of those already sold are collected and donated.

column5: Permissibility of reinsurance with traditional reinsurance companies is based on the practical necessity arising from lack of Islamic reinsurance coverage and the dire public need which ranks up as necessity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis, it rests on practical necessity from the lack of Islamic coverage and dire public need ranking as necessity.

column5: The lease rental in an Ijarah contract:
column6: Must be a fixed amount for the whole duration; a variable rental is not permissible.
column7: Must be paid in full in advance as a lump sum covering the duration of the contract.
column8: May be in cash, in kind (goods) or a benefit (service), and must be specified.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/2/1, rent may be cash, goods or a service; it may be a lump sum or instalments, fixed or variable by an agreed method.

column5: It is permissible for the Institution to stipulate to the customer that instalments may become due before their originally agreed due dates:
column6: It is not permissible at all, because it amounts to rescheduling of debt.
column7: In case of the customer's refusal or delay in paying an instalment without valid reason, after the lapse of the time specified in a notice sent by the Institution within a reasonable period of the due date.
column8: Immediately upon any delay in paying an instalment, without the need for any notice or lapse of time, and even if the customer has a valid reason for the delay, since the debt is deemed due upon default.
column9: In case of any delay in paying an instalment, even if the customer has a valid reason, provided the Institution has sent a notice and allowed a reasonable period to elapse, and the amount of the instalment is increased.
column11: Per 5/1, acceleration may be stipulated for unjustified refusal or delay, after the period in a notice sent within a reasonable time of the due date.

column5: In Mudarabah certificates, the issuer is the Mudarib, the subscribers are the owners of capital, and the realised funds are the Mudarabah capital; the agreed upon share of the profits belongs to the owners of capital and they bear the loss, if any.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/1/5/7, this describes the relationship of the parties in Mudarabah Sukuk.

column5: It is permissible to terminate the Ijarah contract:
column6: By mutual consent of the two parties.
column7: By one party in case of force majeure, or where there is a defect in the leased asset that materially impairs its use.
column8: By a party who has secured an option to terminate the contract, during the specified period.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/2/1, termination is by mutual consent, or unilaterally for force majeure or a material defect, or by a holder of an option.

column5: It is not permitted for the card-issuing Institution to provide the cardholder with:
column6: Discounts on prices while making bookings at hotels, airlines or restaurants.
column7: Benefits prohibited as per Shari'ah, such as conventional life insurance, free access to prohibited places or offering prohibited gifts.
column8: Islamic insurance (Takaful) protection from theft or loss of the card or theft of the amounts withdrawn using it.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/6/1 prohibited benefits are barred; discounts (5/6/2) and Takaful cover (5/6/3) are permitted benefits.

column5: When a borrowed or rented mortgage asset perishes in the hands of the mortgagor:
column6: The mortgagor has to compensate the owner of the borrowed asset, whereas for the rented asset compensation is deserved only if the perish is due to his transgression or negligence.
column7: The mortgagor need not compensate the owner of the borrowed asset unless the perish is due to his transgression or negligence, since the borrower holds it as a trust, and the same applies to the rented asset.
column8: Compensation is deserved for the rented asset in all cases, whether or not the mortgagor has transgressed, since the mortgagor used it for his own benefit.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/2/6, a perished borrowed asset is always compensated by the mortgagor; a rented one only on his transgression or negligence.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column5: Damage of the subject matter of agency:
column6: Relieves the principal from paying any remuneration to the agent, since the agency expires with the loss of its subject matter, and the agent must return what he has received for the part of work already performed, whatever the cause of the damage.
column7: Entitles the agent to the full remuneration agreed upon for the whole agency period.
column8: Obliges the agent to indemnify the principal in all cases, because the asset was in his possession.
column9: Does not relieve the principal from paying remuneration to the agent for the part of work already performed; when the damage occurs because of misconduct or negligence of the agent, he is bound to indemnify the principal for it.
column11: Per 4/2/8, the fee for work done remains due; the agent indemnifies only if the damage results from his misconduct or negligence.

column5: When arbitration ends up with partial resolution of the points of dispute:
column6: Arbitration is incomplete, and the disputing parties have the right to demand a further decision from the arbitrator so as to resolve the remaining points of dispute.
column7: The resolved points are binding, and the remaining points can only be referred to the judiciary.
column8: The arbitrator may address issues outside the subject matter of dispute in order to compensate the parties.
column9: Arbitration is null and void as a whole, since it has not enabled the disputing parties to avoid resorting to legal suing, and the parties must restart the arbitration.
column11: Per 11/2, partial resolution makes arbitration incomplete; the parties may demand a further decision. 11/3 bars going beyond the subject matter.

column5: Examples of contradictory contracts that may not be combined include:
column6: Combining Mudarabah with lending the Mudarabah capital to the Mudarib.
column7: Selling a house to a party for one thousand dinars and renting a car to the same party for one hundred dinars per month.
column8: Concluding Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek through a number of successive stages.
column9: Selling a piece of land and renting a car to the same party for one month against one lump sum.
column11: Per 4/4, combining Mudarabah with lending its capital to the Mudarib is a contradictory combination; the others are permissible forms.

column5: Misconduct (taꜤddī) is:
column6: Exceeding the limit that is authorized by Shari'ah and agreed by the parties out of the conditions attainable as per practice or established by the acknowledged custom, at the time of disposal of the subject of the contract, whether the exceeding was intentional or not.
column7: Any loss incurred by the investment manager that exceeds the losses of peer investments.
column8: Exceeding only the limits expressly stipulated in the contract, irrespective of custom.
column9: Exceeding the limit that is authorized by Shari'ah and agreed by the parties out of the conditions attainable as per practice or established by the acknowledged custom, at the time of disposal of the subject of the contract, provided that the exceeding was intentional and caused a loss.
column11: Per 5/2, misconduct is exceeding limits set by Shari'ah, agreement or recognized custom when disposing of the subject, intentionally or not.

column5: The right of the State to fix the price of the product of a utilization concession is justified by the need to prevent social injury that could result from charging unduly high prices by the licensee.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the Shari'ah basis given for the State's right to fix the price (5/7).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column5: The pledgor bears the expenses of safekeeping the pledged gold because this serves his own interest, whereas the expenses of 'Arboun are borne by the seller, as it is for his own benefit.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per the Shari'ah basis for 7/1/6 and 7/3, each party bears the expenses that serve his own interest.

column5: The acts of a debtor subsequent to the declaration of insolvency that retain legal effect include:
column6: Sales of his assets at the market price.
column7: Acts relating to previous transactions, such as terminating a defective contract or exercising an option to revoke.
column8: Endowments (Waqf) of part of his property for charitable purposes, provided that the endowment is registered with the competent authority.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 5/3, sale, gift or endowment after the declaration has no legal effect, except acts relating to previous transactions.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for not allowing a debt owed by the Mudarib to the capital provider to be contributed as Mudarabah capital is that:
column6: A debt cannot be valued in terms of quality and quantity, so the share of each party in profit and loss could not be determined.
column7: Mudarabah capital must be an asset available for use in the operations at the conclusion of the contract, and treating a debt as capital involves potential Riba, since the creditor may be suspected of extending the debt for a consideration under the name of Mudarabah.
column8: The Mudarib cannot be both a debtor and a trustee in respect of the same funds, as this would amount to a guarantee of profit and would make the capital provider liable for the loss of the debt itself, which the Shari'ah does not allow in Mudarabah contracts of any kind.
column9: A debt is not a property that can be owned, and what is not owned cannot be put at the disposal of a Mudarib, nor can its profit be shared.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, a debt is not available for use at conclusion and involves potential Riba through extension of the debt.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: Concluding Salam or Istisna'a contracts as a permissible operation for acquiring funds for the converting bank requires that:
column6: The bank act as manufacturer in Istisna'a, the price being deferred, since advance payment of the price is not allowed in Istisna'a, and as purchaser in Salam with the Salam capital paid on delivery.
column7: The bank act as purchaser in Salam and pay the Salam capital in advance.
column8: The bank act as Mustasni' in Istisna'a and pay the price in advance.
column9: The bank act as supplier in Salam, or as manufacturer or builder in Istisna'a with the Istisna'a price paid to the bank in advance, although deferment of the price is allowed by Shari'ah.
column11: Per 6/2/3, the bank raises funds as Salam supplier or as Istisna'a manufacturer with the price paid in advance.

column5: A customer bought US dollars against euros through the website of an IFI. The euro amount was debited from his account at the time of contracting, while the US dollars were credited to his account three days later. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because online contracts concluded through access to site are contracts between two absent parties, for which delay of one counter-value is tolerated.
column7: Permissible, provided that the customer clicked on the acceptance confirmation step and received a confirmation message.
column8: Impermissible, because when the sold commodity is a currency, instant exchange of the two counter-values must be ascertained during the contract's signing session.
column9: Permissible, because the exchange rate was fixed at the time of contracting.
column11: Per 7/3, in online sale of currency, gold, silver and the like, instant exchange of both counter-values must occur during the contract session.

column5: It is permissible in Shari'ah to use indices:
column6: To discern the magnitude of change in a certain market, or to judge the performance of specialized managers by comparing the returns they achieve to the indices.
column7: To form up an idea about a portfolio or to estimate its systematic risks instead of monitoring the performance and risks of each financial paper independently.
column8: For forecasting the future situation of the market and discovering the pattern of changes that the market may undergo.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 5/1, all three uses are permissible, as using indices for guidance in real transactions is permissible.

column5: In a sale contract, the seller has the right to stipulate a condition that the buyer should mortgage the sold good to him against the deferred price:
column6: Only if the deferred price is payable in instalments.
column7: After actual or constructive possession of the good by the buyer.
column8: Before the buyer takes possession of the good, so that it remains with the seller.
column9: Only if the mortgage is kept by a notary.
column11: Per 3/2/7, the seller may stipulate that the buyer, after actual or constructive possession, mortgage the good to him against the deferred price.

column5: With regard to the determination of the price and the profit in Murabahah:
column6: Both the price of the item and the Institution's profit must be fixed and known to both parties on the signature of the contract of sale.
column7: There is no objection to referring to known indicators during the promise stage as a comfort indicator to determine the rate of profit, provided the profit at conclusion is a certain percentage of the cost not tied to LIBOR or a time factor.
column8: It is permissible to conclude the sale and make the profit dependent on the rate of LIBOR that will prevail in the future.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 4/6, price and profit must be fixed at signing; indicators may be referred to only at the promise stage, never future LIBOR.

column5: A trading company bought goods from an IFI and paid 'Arboun (Earnest Money) with a 15-day option, stipulating, with the IFI's acceptance, that it would offer the goods to its own clients during the option period. On the fifth day it displayed the goods to several clients, and on the tenth day it concluded a sale with one of them. The company's right to revoke the contract:
column6: Was never valid, because stipulating that the sale item be offered to the buyer's clients during the option period is impermissible.
column7: Lapsed on the fifth day, when it offered the goods to its clients.
column8: Remained valid after it offered the goods to its clients, and lapsed when it concluded the sale with one of them, as that sale is deemed confirmation of the contract.
column9: Remains valid until the end of the 15-day option period, even after the sale to its client.
column11: Per 9/3, offering the item to clients as stipulated keeps the option alive; concluding a sale to a client is deemed confirmation.

column5: The Shari'ah basis for the impermissibility of trading in Istisna'a certificates where the realised funds are used as a price in a parallel Istisna'a, or where the manufactured asset is delivered to the ultimate purchaser, is that:
column6: The Istisna'a contract is not binding on either party.
column7: The certificate represents a share in tangible assets that are not yet specified, so that trading in them would amount to the sale of a thing not yet owned and not in the seller's possession.
column8: The certificate represents the price in the liability of the purchaser, a monetary debt, so that trading at this stage is subject to the rules of debt trading.
column9: The manufactured asset is not yet in existence.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, the certificate then represents the price owed by the purchaser, a monetary debt, so debt-trading rules apply.

column5: If the payer dies, not being in a state of bankruptcy, or the Institution acting as payer is liquidated:
column6: The transferee may claim from the transferor or the payer's estate at his option, since the death of the payer or the liquidation of the Institution does not discharge the transferor from his debt.
column7: The Hawalah is annulled, and the transferee has recourse to the transferor.
column8: The Hawalah is not annulled, and the transferee has recourse against the estate of the payer, a personal guarantor, if any, or the pre-distribution assets of liquidation.
column9: The transferee loses his right to the debt.
column11: Per 10/2, the Hawalah survives; recourse is to the payer's estate, guarantor or liquidation assets (transferor only if death in bankruptcy).

column5: ………… is a contest between two parties or more for the purpose of determining the best amongst them:
column6: Ju'alah.
column7: A competition.
column8: A promotional prize.
column9: A prize.
column11: Per 2/1, a competition is a contest between two or more parties to determine the best amongst them.

column5: If the contract of a credit transaction stipulates that the debtor shall provide a guarantor and the debtor fails to provide one, the Institution is entitled to:
column6: Initiate legal action to force him to provide a guarantor or to terminate the contract.
column7: Increase the price of the credit transaction in return for the absence of a guarantor.
column8: Freeze his current account without his consent.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/3/5, the Institution may sue to compel provision of a guarantor or terminate the contract.

column5: A survey license granted by the State to a natural or legal person against payment of a specific fee or rent:
column6: Grants its holder the right to conduct works relating to extraction through mining and construction of the required facilities.
column7: Does not grant its holder the right of the sole surveyor in that area, nor the right to conduct works relating to extraction.
column8: Grants its holder the exclusive right of obtaining the utilization concession.
column9: Grants its holder the right of the sole surveyor in that area.
column11: Per 5/2/1, a survey license gives neither exclusivity as surveyor nor the right to conduct extraction works.

column5: In Parallel Salam, if the seller under the first Salam contract fails to deliver al-Muslam Fihi to the Institution:
column6: The Institution may terminate the Parallel Salam contract with the third party, since the first Salam contract has been breached by the original seller.
column7: The Institution may delay performing its obligations under the Parallel Salam contract until the seller under the first contract delivers.
column8: The Institution has no right to relate its loss to the Parallel Salam counterparty, and must perform that contract independently.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 6/3, the two Salam contracts stand alone; a breach in one gives no right to terminate or delay the other.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds) does not cover:
column6: Issuance of and trading in interest-bearing bonds.
column7: The rule for concluding futures, options and swap contracts on the basis of shares.
column8: Investment Sukuk.
column9: Renting, loaning, pledging and Salam in shares.
column11: Per 1, investment Sukuk have their own specific standard; the other matters are within this standard's scope.

column5: The Shari'ah Standard on Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations covers:
column6: Sharecropping partnerships, such as irrigation and agricultural partnerships.
column7: Sharikat al-Mufawadah, being the most common partnership in practice.
column8: Ownership partnership where the parties jointly own an asset.
column9: All modern forms of partnerships, including diminishing Musharakah.
column11: Per the Scope, the standard applies to all modern forms of partnerships incl. diminishing Musharakah; ownership, Mufawadah and sharecropping partnerships are excluded.

column5: The contract for hiring of persons:
column6: Is a non-binding contract which either party may terminate or amend by notice to the other, except when the employer has paid the pay in advance, in which case only the employee may terminate it.
column7: Is a binding contract, which neither party can terminate or amend without the consent of the other, except in case of contract breaching, an emergent excuse, or inevitable circumstances.
column8: Is binding on the employer, who cannot terminate it without the consent of the employee, but the employee may terminate it at any time.
column9: Is binding on the employee, who cannot leave the work without the consent of the employer, but the employer may terminate it at any time without an excuse, by paying one month's pay.
column11: Per 4/7, hiring of persons is binding on both; neither may terminate or amend it unilaterally except for breach, emergent excuse or inevitable circumstances.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column5: The right of Shuf'ah (preemption):
column6: Exists also where ownership is transferred by gift without consideration.
column7: Is enjoyed by a neighbour even if the two properties do not share any common easement rights.
column8: Exists only in relation to immovable property or movable property attached to it.
column9: (a) and (b).
column11: Per 7/1/1-2 and 7/2/6, Shuf'ah covers only real property (and movables attached), needs shared easements for neighbours, and no sale means no Shuf'ah.

column5: When the concerned authorities order the sale of the sequestered assets:
column6: Assets should be sold in this order: currencies different to the currency in which the insolvency is administered, fungibles, stocks, commodities, then real estate, and a reasonable period should be allowed before selling real estate.
column7: If the price offered at auction is less than the value of the asset, the auction should be repeated to obtain its value; otherwise, it is sold at whatever price is achieved on the third auction.
column8: If possible, it is recommended to make the sale subject, for a reasonable period of time, to an option to reverse the sale.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 7/1, all three statements describe the prescribed manner of selling the sequestered assets.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column5: Among the prerequisites of Khiyar al-Tadlis (option to revoke on grounds of deceptive conduct):
column6: The deception must result from the seller's conduct or instructions; if caused by something beyond his control or by unforeseen circumstances, the option is invalid.
column7: The option is valid whether the deception results from the seller's conduct or from unforeseen circumstances, since the buyer is harmed in either case and the cause is immaterial.
column8: The buyer may have been aware of the deception, provided that he objected at the time of the contract.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/2/1-3/2/2, the deception must stem from the seller's conduct or instructions and the buyer must be unaware of it.

column5: After the conclusion of a restricted Hawalah, the transferor:
column6: May reclaim the amount from the payer as long as the transferee has not yet collected it, since the debt of the payer to him subsists until payment is made to the transferee.
column7: Is no longer entitled to reclaim from the payer the amount transferred in respect of the debt, because the right to receive it has passed to the transferee.
column8: May reclaim the amount from the payer with the consent of the payer only.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 8, the transferor may not reclaim the amount from the payer, as the right to it has passed to the transferee.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column5: In principle, it is impermissible for a regulator to cap profits. However, it is permissible to fix the profit rate, provided it is not prejudicial:
column6: In monopoly situations, extraordinary circumstances and cases of clear public interest.
column7: Whenever the regulator considers the profit rates charged by institutions to be excessive.
column8: In Murabahah transactions only.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 4/2, fixing the profit rate is permissible, if not prejudicial, in monopoly, extraordinary circumstances and clear public interest.

column5: If the pledgor makes a Waqf over the pledged asset, the Waqf is valid, and its enforceability is dependent on:
column6: The waiver by the pledgee of his rights in the pledge.
column7: The settlement of the debt.
column8: Part of the pledge remaining after recovering the debt out of the pledge, in which case the Waqf will be enforced over what remains.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 2/4/5/4, enforceability depends on the pledgee's waiver, settlement of the debt, or a remainder after recovering the debt.

column5: It is not permitted to stipulate upon the investment manager:
column6: What is usually not carried by him, where the purpose of such stipulation is to impose the liability on him.
column7: That he be dismissed on grounds of misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.
column8: That he bear the evidentiary burden of the occurrence of the loss and the absence of misconduct or negligence on absolute terms.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 3/6 the first is barred; dismissal for misconduct may be stipulated (7/6) and so may an absolute evidentiary burden (6/1).

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: A conventional bank was converted by its own shareholders. It had not paid Zakah for the two previous financial years, during which a large part of its earnings was interest. The Shari'ah Supervisory Board should advise that:
column6: Zakah for the two previous years is not due, because the earnings were impermissible and must be disposed of entirely, and Zakah is payable only on permissible earnings and only for periods following the decision to convert.
column7: The shareholders must pay Zakah for the two previous years, even on impermissible earnings, as payment of Zakah is part of their obligation to dispose of impermissible earnings and interest.
column8: Zakah is due only from the date of the decision to convert.
column9: Zakah for previous periods is the liability of the bank's former management.
column11: Per 11, shareholders who convert must pay unpaid past Zakah, even on impermissible revenues, as part of disposing of them.

column5: The Standard on Islamic Reinsurance also covers Islamic insurance, in addition to Islamic reinsurance and participation with traditional insurance or reinsurance companies.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 1, the Standard does not cover Islamic insurance, which is covered in a separate standard.

column5: A customer owes an IFI USD 10,000 under a matured loan. At settlement, the customer offered to pay in euros, and the IFI agreed that he would pay the euro equivalent of USD 5,000 now and the euro equivalent of the other USD 5,000 next month, both at today's exchange rate. You explained the correct ruling as follows:
column6: The part paid now may be converted, but converting the remainder into euros payable next month is not permissible, since no part of the converted debt may remain outstanding.
column7: The arrangement is not permissible, since a debt arising from a loan may only be discharged in the currency of the loan, and the day-of-settlement rate applies only to a delayed debt.
column8: The whole arrangement is permissible, since today's exchange rate is applied to both parts and the euro portion payable next month is a separate debt.
column9: The whole arrangement is permissible, provided that the IFI charges no fee for the conversion and that the second payment is secured by a guarantee.
column11: Per 4/1/1/2 (a), the substitute must be received in the session so no converted part of the debt remains outstanding.

column5: In syndicated financing, it is permissible:
column6: To agree beforehand on the transfer of shares at their nominal value.
column7: For the investment agent to provide a commitment to safeguard any other party against exchange rate fluctuations.
column8: To agree on a closed syndicated financing operation that does not allow premature exit.
column9: All of the above are true.
column11: Per 10/1, a closed syndication without premature exit is allowed; transfer at nominal value (10/2) and FX safeguards (9/3) are not.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column5: During the cooling-off option period, increases that are separate from the sold item but grow out of it, such as dividends on shares and rent from leased assets:
column6: Belong to the buyer if he confirms the contract.
column7: Belong to the seller.
column8: Are divided equally between the parties.
column9: Belong to the owner of the option.
column11: Per 2/6/3, separate increases growing out of the original, such as dividends and rent, belong to the seller.

column5: Where the capital of Salam is the general usufruct of a particular asset, granting the seller access to the usufruct through delivery of the asset is regarded as immediate receipt (possession) of the Salam capital.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is stated in 3/1/1.

column5: Zakah can permissibly be paid in terms of the equivalent value of the subject commodity.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 10/7, Zakah can be paid in terms of the equivalent value of the subject commodity.

column5: It is permitted to trade in Shari'ah non-compliant bonds by way of assignment, though not by way of sale or purchase.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 9/2/1, trading in non-compliant bonds is not permitted by sale, purchase, assignment or otherwise.

column5: If the total Mudarabah expenses are equal to the total Mudarabah revenues, the capital provider will receive his capital back without either profit or loss, and there will be no profit in which the Mudarib is entitled to a share.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 8/7, break-even means return of capital only, with no profit for the Mudarib to share.

column5: ………… is a contract between the owner of an orchard or its usufruct and a worker (irrigator) agreeing to share the produce according to specific ratios stipulated at the time of contract:
column6: Muzara'ah (Agricultural Partnership).
column7: Ju'alah.
column8: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat).
column9: Mugharasah (Planting Partnership).
column11: Per item 2, this is the definition of Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat).

column5: A company issued a promissory note to its supplier (the first beneficiary) for 100,000 due in six months. Two months later, the company offered to pay the supplier 95,000 immediately in full settlement of the note, and the supplier agreed. This transaction is:
column6: Impermissible, because it is a form of discounting of commercial paper, with a charge that varies with the date of maturity.
column7: Permissible, being payment of less than the value of the paper to the first beneficiary before maturity (Da' wa Ta'ajjal).
column8: Impermissible, because it involves Riba al-Fadl, the supplier receiving less than he gave.
column9: Permissible only if a bank intermediates in the payment and charges a commission for it.
column11: Per 6/1 and its basis, reducing the debt for early payment between issuer and first beneficiary is permitted (Da' wa Ta'ajjal).

column5: In principle, the ruling on Waqf is that:
column6: It is an obligatory act (wājib) upon whoever owns surplus wealth, and it is binding upon the Waqif from the instance of its creation.
column7: It is a recommended act (mandūb), and the Waqif may resile from it during his lifetime as long as no revenue has been disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries.
column8: It is a recommended act (mandūb), and it is binding upon the Waqif from the instance of the creation of Waqf, and he cannot resile from it.
column9: It is a recommended act (mandūb), but it does not become binding upon the Waqif until the Waqf asset is delivered to the overseer or the Waqf beneficiaries.
column11: Per 2/3, Waqf is in principle mandūb and binding on the Waqif from its creation; he cannot resile from it.

column5: Where a legally binding promise has been made to enter into a contract in the future, and at the relevant time the offer is made by the promisor:
column6: The promisee is bound religiously and legally to accept it.
column7: The promisee must accept it or indemnify the promisor for his actual loss.
column8: The contract is concluded automatically, without the need for acceptance.
column9: The promisee has the option to accept or reject it.
column11: Per 3/8, the contract needs offer and acceptance; if the promisor offers, the promisee may accept or reject.

column5: The following is considered as constructive possession by the Institution of goods purchased on the international market:
column6: The mere signing of the purchase contract with the supplier, before the supplier gives the Institution control over the goods.
column7: Payment by the Institution of the price of the goods to the supplier.
column8: The receipt of a bill of lading by the Institution or its agent.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/2/4, receipt of a bill of lading by the Institution or its agent is constructive possession; signing or paying alone gives no control.

column5: If it transpires that the trees subject to the Irrigation Partnership belong to a third party:
column6: The crop is divided between the worker and the third party who owns the trees, according to the stipulated shares.
column7: The crop belongs to the third party, and the worker is entitled to a market-rate wage from the other party, capped at what his share of the crop would have been.
column8: The crop belongs to the third party, and the worker is entitled to a wage at the market rate for similar work, without any cap, from the other party who contracted with him, even if it exceeds the value of the entire crop.
column9: The worker is entitled to nothing in all cases, since the contract is void.
column11: Per 11/1, the crop goes to the third party; the worker gets a market wage capped at what his share would have been.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column5: After the decision to convert, the bank may not deal with conventional banks in any way.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/6 and 4/2, dealings with conventional banks continue on a Riba-free basis, limited to the magnitude of need.

column5: Waqf assets should not be leased at less than the rent of similar property. If there happens to be a new tenant who can pay the rent of similar property:
column6: The Waqf superintendent has the right to terminate the previous contract, unless the old tenant accepts the rent increment.
column7: The old tenant is obliged to accept the rent increment in all cases.
column8: The superintendent must terminate the previous contract, even if the old tenant accepts the rent increment.
column9: The previous contract remains binding on the Waqf until its expiry.
column11: Per 6/2, the superintendent may terminate the previous contract unless the old tenant accepts the rent increment.

column5: Three IFIs entered into a syndicated Musharakah denominated in US dollars. One of them paid its contribution in euros at the prevailing exchange rate on the day of payment, and stipulated to receive its profits in euros at the prevailing rate on the day of receipt. The lead manager also undertook to protect that IFI against any loss arising from dollar/euro fluctuations. The correct ruling is:
column6: All these arrangements are impermissible, as both contributions and profits must be in the syndication currency.
column7: All these arrangements are permissible, since they have been agreed upon by mutual consent.
column8: Paying the contribution and receiving the profits in euros at the prevailing rates is permissible, but the lead manager's undertaking against exchange rate fluctuations is impermissible.
column9: Paying the contribution in euros is impermissible, as contributions must be paid in the syndication currency, but the undertaking against exchange rate fluctuations is permissible.
column11: Per 9/1-9/2, other currencies are allowed at the day's prevailing rate; per 9/3 a commitment against FX fluctuations is impermissible.

column3: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
column5: Regarding the Fatwa manuscript (document):
column6: For Institutions, Fatwa may be issued orally, by signaling or by acting, without any need to be written, provided that the inquirer is informed of it in the presence of two witnesses.
column7: The content of a Fatwa issued by the concerned board need not be stated in the formal proceedings of the board meeting, as long as the Fatwa is communicated to the management by telephone.
column8: Fatwa shall be clearly handwritten or typed, each page shall be initialed, and it should carry the date of issuance and the official stamp of its source, if available.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 10/3, the Fatwa is written, initialed on each page, dated and stamped; 10/1 and 10/5 bar the other two.

column5: It is not permissible for the lessor to stipulate in the lease contract that the lessee provide a guarantee or mortgage of security so that he may use it to recover the amount of the lease rental if the leased property is damaged, unless:
column6: Such a stipulation is restricted to misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.
column7: The lease is an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, ending in the transfer of ownership of the property to the lessee.
column8: The lessee consents to the stipulation in writing.
column9: The lessee bears the insurance expenses and the cost of major maintenance of the leased property.
column11: Per 2/3, the lessee holds the asset on trust, so a guarantee may be stipulated only for misconduct, negligence or breach.

column5: The commission for letters of guarantee that accompany documentary credits, such as letters of guarantee for the advance payment of a portion of the amount or the shipping guarantee issued for releasing the goods before the arrival of documents, is determined:
column6: By the correspondent bank in accordance with international practice, the rules of the issuing bank and its own rates.
column7: As part of the agency fee of the documentary credit, without any restriction on its amount.
column8: Freely, as a percentage of the guaranteed amount and its duration, as in any banking service.
column9: By applying the ruling on commission for letters of guarantee stated in the Shari'ah Standard on Guarantees.
column11: Per 3/3/3, the Guarantees standard's ruling on letter-of-guarantee commissions applies to guarantees accompanying credits.

column5: An IFI concluded a Salam contract with a farmer to purchase a quantity of wheat for delivery after six months, and paid the Salam capital by endorsing to the farmer a promissory note due in three months. This transaction is:
column6: Permissible, because the promissory note is a certificate of debt that may be endorsed, and the Salam capital is thereby paid on the date of the endorsement.
column7: Permissible, because endorsement is binding with respect to its legal effects, including the transfer of possession of the debt to the farmer.
column8: Permissible, provided the promissory note matures before the delivery date of the wheat and is endorsed to the farmer.
column9: Not permissible, because a promissory note may not be used in transactions that require possession, such as the capital of Salam.
column11: Per 3/2, a bill of exchange or promissory note cannot be the capital (Ras al-Mal) of Salam, which requires possession.

column5: Differentiation between Monetization and 'Inah with regard to permissibility and prohibition stems from the fact that:
column6: 'Inah is concluded on a Musawamah (Bargaining) basis, whereas Monetization must be concluded on a Murabahah basis.
column7: 'Inah is a trick for practicing Riba, taking place between two parties who are in fact a borrower and a lender, whereas Monetization is not.
column8: The commodity in 'Inah is usually gold, silver or currency, whereas in Monetization it is a real commodity.
column9: In Monetization a third party guarantees payment of the deferred price, whereas in 'Inah there is no such guarantee.
column11: Per the Shari'ah basis, 'Inah is a trick for Riba between a de facto lender and borrower; the lender sells on deferred terms and buys back for less on spot.

column5: The investment manager acts in a fiduciary capacity with regard to the funds. He is not liable for loss of capital except in case of:
column6: His wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contractual terms and conditions.
column7: Any loss exceeding the profit realised on the investment during the period.
column8: A loss resulting from the fluctuation of exchange rates.
column9: A loss that occurs before actual or constructive liquidation.
column11: Per 3/4, the fiduciary manager is liable only for wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contractual terms and conditions.

column5: It is permissible to use as a cover for documentary credit:
column6: Cash and freezing of permissible accounts.
column7: Interest-based bonds.
column8: Shares of companies that deal in prohibited activities.
column9: None of the above is true.
column11: Per 3/4/1, cash and frozen permissible accounts are valid cover; per 3/4/2, interest-based bonds and prohibited shares are not.

column5: Stipulating in work rules and regulations pertaining to money-based employment contracts a provision on wage indexation (periodical adjustment of wages according to changes in the price level) is:
column6: Not permissible, because it links a monetary obligation to the price index.
column7: Permissible, and accumulated unpaid wages that become a debt may also be increased according to the index.
column8: Permissible only if the wages are paid in kind.
column9: Permissible; however, in case of accumulation of unpaid wage that takes the form of debt, Shari'ah rulings on debts should be observed.
column11: Per 5/5, wage indexation is permissible, but unpaid wages accumulated as a debt are subject to the Shari'ah rulings on debts.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column5: The profit authorized for investment at the end of the investment period is considered as part of the capital in the next period.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 3/1/1, profit authorized for reinvestment at the end of a period forms part of the capital of the next period.

column5: Among the conditions that the Institution must abide by with respect to fees and commissions in documentary credit:
column6: The aspect of guarantee must be taken into account in proportion to the risk of the applicant.
column7: The issuance of a credit facility should not involve Riba-bearing profits or become a means for such profits.
column8: A combination of contracts may be used in documentary credit to justify taking a commission for providing a guarantee, provided each contract is valid on its own.
column9: (a) and (c).
column11: Per 3/3/1(a)-(c), guarantee per se is not priced, no Riba is involved, and combined contracts may not be a cover for prohibitions.

column5: The mortgagee must release a part of the mortgaged asset in proportion to each part of the debt repaid, even if he does not accept partial releasing of the mortgage.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: False. Per 3/1/7, the mortgagee may keep the whole mortgaged asset for any part of the debt unless he accepts partial releasing.

column5: An Ijarah contract may be executed for a house or a chattel even with a non-Muslim, if the use to be made of it is permissible, unless the lessor knows in advance, or has reason to presume, that the asset will be used for an impermissible purpose.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. This is the rule in 5/1/3.

column5: The basis of non-permissibility of increasing card fees for the benefit of cash-back, any benefit dependent on card usage, or any benefit which has no known limit is that:
column6: Cash-back is a form of prohibited gift.
column7: It contradicts the requirements of transparency and disclosure.
column8: It would be a loan carrying benefit in all types of cards, including debit and prepaid cards, which do not involve lending.
column9: It would be gharar (uncertainty) and a form of gambling, with the probability of riba al-fadl.
column11: Per the Basis of 5/6/2, it is gharar resembling gambling, with probable riba al-fadl.

column5: In a diminishing Musharakah, the loss, if any, shall be borne periodically by the parties in accordance with the participation ratio of each partner as the equity stake of one partner decreases and the stake of the other partner increases.
column6: True
column7: False
column11: True. Per 5/4, losses are borne periodically according to each partner's changing participation ratio.

column5: It is not permissible to sell the subject-matter of Istisna'a prior to taking either actual or constructive possession of it. However, it is permissible:
column6: To assign the Istisna'a purchase contract to a third party for a profit before taking possession of the subject-matter, if the manufacturer consents and the purchaser's name is registered with the manufacturer.
column7: To conclude an Istisna'a contract to sell an item on the basis of a description similar to that of an item to be acquired from a manufacturer, called Parallel Istisna'a (Istisna'a Muwazi).
column8: To issue tradable certificates representing the subject-matter before its completion, provided the certificates are issued at their face value.
column9: To sell the subject-matter to a third party once half of the work has been completed and the price has been paid in full to the manufacturer.
column11: Per 6/7, the item may not be sold before possession, but a similar described item may be sold by Parallel Istisna'a.
